Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Saddanītippakaraṇaṃ

The Saddanīti Treatise

Dhātumālā

The Garland of Roots

15. Saravaggapañcakantika suddhassaradhātu

15. The Pure Vowel Roots of the Saravaggapañcaka

Ito [M 0.0001] paraṃ tu sarato, kakārantādibhedato;

Dhātuyo dhātunipphanna-rūpāni vividhāni ca.

From here on, however, starting from the vowels and based on distinctions such as those beginning with 'ka', are the roots and the various forms derived from roots;

Sāṭṭhakathe piṭakamhi, jinapāṭhe yathābalaṃ;

Nayaṃ upaparikkhitvā, samāsena kathessa’haṃ.

these I shall explain concisely, according to my ability, after having thoroughly examined the method in the Piṭaka with its commentaries and in the Conqueror's texts.

I gatiyaṃ. Yesaṃ dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho. Pavattipāpuṇānipi. Tatra gamanaṃ duvidhaṃ kāyagamanaṃ ñāṇagamanañca. Tesu kāyagamanaṃ nāma iriyāpathagamanaṃ, ñāṇagamanaṃ nāma ñāṇuppatti, tasmā payogānurūpena “gacchatī”ti padassa “jānātī”tipi attho bhavati, “pavattatī”tipi attho bhavati, “pāpuṇātī”tipi attho bhavati, iriyāpathagamanena gacchatītipi attho bhavati, ñāṇagamanena gacchatītipi attho bhavati. Tathā hi “sīghaṃ gacchatī”tiādīsu iriyāpathagamanaṃ “gamana”nti vuccati. Sundaraṃ nibbānaṃ gato. “Gatimā”tiādīsu [M 0.0002] pana ñāṇagamanaṃ. Evaṃ sabbesampi gatyatthānaṃ dhātūnaṃ yathāpayogaṃ attho gahetabbo.

The root 'i' is in the sense of 'to go.' For those roots whose meaning is 'going,' understanding is also their meaning. They also convey 'occurrence' and 'attainment.' Here, 'going' is twofold: bodily going and knowledge-going. Among these, bodily going is movement of posture, while knowledge-going is the arising of knowledge. Therefore, according to usage, the word 'gacchati' ('goes') can also mean 'knows,' 'occurs,' or 'attains.' It can mean 'goes' through postural movement or 'goes' through the arising of knowledge. For thus, in such phrases as 'sīghaṃ gacchati' ('goes quickly'), postural movement is called 'going.' But in examples such as 'sundaraṃ nibbānaṃ gato' ('one who has gone to beautiful Nibbāna') or 'gatimā' ('one who has understanding'), it refers to knowledge-going. Thus, for all roots with the meaning of 'going,' the meaning should be understood according to the usage.

Tassimāni rūpāni bhavanti – iti, eti, udeti. Kārite “udāyatī”ti rūpaṃ bhavati. Uṭṭhāpetīti hi attho, dukāro āgamo. Upeti, samupeti, veti, apeti, aveti, anveti, sameti, abhisameti, samayo, abhisamayo, īdi, udi, ekodi, paṇḍito, ito, udito, upeto, samupeto, anvito, apeto, sameto, etabbo, paccetabbo, paṭiyamāno, paṭicco, ento, adhippeto, adhippāyo, paccayo, aññānipi yojetabbāni. “Itā, ita”ntiādinā yathārahaṃ itthinapuṃsakavasenapi. Paccetuṃ, upetuṃ, samupetuṃ, anvetuṃ, sametuṃ, abhisametuṃ, icca, paṭicca, samecca, abhisamecca, apecca, upecca, paṭimukhaṃ itvā, itvāna, upetvā, upetvāna, upetuna, aññānipi buddhavacanānurūpato yojetabbāni.

From this root, these forms arise: iti, eti, udeti. In the causative, the form 'udāyati' arises, for its meaning is 'causes to rise,' with 'du' as an augment. Upeti, samupeti, veti, apeti, aveti, anveti, sameti, abhisameti, samayo, abhisamayo, īdi, udi, ekodi, paṇḍito, ito, udito, upeto, samupeto, anvito, apeto, sameto, etabbo, paccetabbo, paṭiyamāno, paṭicco, ento, adhippeto, adhippāyo, paccayo; other forms should also be supplied. According to suitability, by way of the feminine and neuter genders, forms such as 'itā' and 'ita' are made. Paccetuṃ, upetuṃ, samupetuṃ, anvetuṃ, sametuṃ, abhisametuṃ, icca, paṭicca, samecca, abhisamecca, apecca, upecca, paṭimukhaṃ itvā, itvāna, upetvā, upetvāna, upetuna; other forms should also be supplied in accordance with the word of the Buddha.

Itiiti kriyāsaddo, suttantesu na dissati;

Idamettha na vattabbaṃ, dassanāyeva me ruto.

The verbal form 'iti' is not seen in the Suttantas; this should not be said here, for my utterance is from observation alone.

“Itāyaṃ kodharūpena”, iti pāḷi hi dissati;

Aṅguttaranikāyamhi, munināhacca bhāsitā;

For the Pāli text, 'Itāyaṃ kodharūpena,' is indeed seen, spoken directly by the Sage in the Aṅguttara Nikāya;

Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā aṅguttaranikāye kodhaṃ nindantena –

For this was said by the Blessed One in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, when censuring anger:

“Itāyaṃ kodharūpena, maccuveso guhāsayo;

Taṃ damena samucchinde, paññāvīriyena diṭṭhiyā”ti.

'This one, in the form of anger, disguised as death, dwelling in the cave; one should cut it off completely with restraint, wisdom, energy, and view.'

Tatra itāyanti iti ayanti chedo. Itiiti ca gacchati pavattatīti attho. Ayaṃ panettha suttapadattho – yo [M 0.0003] doso loke “kodho”ti lokiyamahājanena vuccati, nāyaṃ atthato kodhoti vattabbo. Kinti pana vattabbo, eso hi sarīrasaṅkhātaguhāsayo maccurājā eva kodhavasena pamaddanto sattasantāne gacchatīti vattabbo. Taṃ evarūpaṃ “maccurājā”ti vattabbaṃ bahuno janassa anatthakaraṃ kodhaṃ hitakāmo damena paññāya vīriyena diṭṭhiyā ca chindeyyāti.

Here, 'itāyaṃ' is analyzed as 'iti ayaṃ'. And 'iti' means 'it goes, it proceeds.' The meaning of the Sutta passage here is this: that defilement in the world which is called 'anger' by ordinary people should not, in reality, be called anger. How then should it be called? It should be said that this is indeed the King of Death himself, dwelling in the cave that is the body, who proceeds in the mental continuum of beings, crushing them by means of anger. One who desires what is beneficial should, with restraint, wisdom, energy, and view, cut off that anger of such a kind, which causes harm to many people and should be called 'the King of Death'.

Etīti imassa pana āgacchatīti attho. “Etī”ti ettha hi āupasaggo sandhikiccena paṭicchannattā na pākaṭo valāhakāvattharito puṇṇacando viya. Tathā hi ettha ā iti etīti sandhiviggaho bhavati, ākārassa ca ikārena parena saddhiṃyeva ekārādeso. Tasmā “ayaṃ so sārathī eti. Etu vessantaro rājā”tiādīsu “āgacchati, āgacchatū”tiādinā attho kathetabbo. Byākaraṇasatthepi hi ā iti etīti sandhiviggaho dissati, tasmā ayampi nīti sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā. Atha vā itīti rassavasena vuttaṃ padaṃ gamanaṃ bodheti, etīti vuddhivasena vuttaṃ pana yathāpayogaṃ āgamanādīni. Mattāvasenapi hi padāni savisesatthāni bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? Sāsane pabbajito, raṭṭhā pabbājitoti. Saññogāsaññogavasenapi, taṃ yathā? Gāmā niggacchati. Yasaṃ poso nigacchati, tasmā ayampi nīti sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Of 'eti', however, the meaning is 'he comes.' For here in the word 'eti', the prefix 'ā', being concealed by the process of sandhi, is not apparent—like the full moon covered by a mass of clouds. Indeed, here the sandhi analysis of 'eti' is 'ā + iti', and the 'ā' together with the following 'i' is replaced by the single vowel 'e'. Therefore, in phrases such as 'ayaṃ so sārathī eti' ('this charioteer comes') or 'etu vessantaro rājā' ('let King Vessantara come'), the meaning should be explained as 'he comes' or 'let him come.' Indeed, even in grammatical treatises, the sandhi analysis of 'eti' as 'ā + iti' is found, so this principle should be carefully borne in mind. Alternatively, the word 'iti', spoken with a short vowel, indicates going, while 'eti', spoken with a strengthened vowel, indicates coming and other meanings according to usage. For words can have specific meanings even based on vowel length, for example: 'sāsane pabbajito' (one who has gone forth in the Dispensation) versus 'raṭṭhā pabbājito' (one who has been banished from the country). Similarly, meanings can differ based on connection or disconnection with a prefix. For example: 'gāmā niggacchati' (he goes out from the village) versus 'yasaṃ poso nigacchati' (the man attains fame). Therefore, this principle should also be carefully borne in mind. Herein, it is said:

I gatiyanti kathitā, dhātu vuddhiṃ gatā yadā;

Tadā āgamanatthassa, vācikā pāyato vasā.

The root 'i' is said to be in the sense of going; when that root has undergone strengthening, then it is generally, by convention, expressive of the meaning of coming.

Iriyāpathatthato he-sā niccāgamavācikā;

“Ayaṃ so sārathī eti”, iccādettha nidassanaṃ.

For, in the sense of physical movement, this root is always expressive of coming. 'This charioteer comes,' and so on, is the illustration here.

Aniriyāpathatthena[M 0.0004], vattane gamanepi ca;

Āgamane ca hotīti, dhīmā lakkheyya taṃ yathā.

In the non-physical sense, it occurs in the meanings of proceeding, going, and also coming; a wise person should discern this accordingly.

“Paṭicca phalametī”ti, evamādīsu vattane;

Vuddhippattā ikāravhā, esā dhātu pavattati.

In such expressions as 'Dependent on this, a fruit comes to be,' this root named 'i', having attained strengthening, operates in the sense of 'to occur'.

“Atthamentamhi sūriye, vāḷā” iccādīsu pana;

Gate, “etīti itī”ti-ādisvāgamane siyā.

But in such phrases as 'When the sun is setting...', it is in the sense of 'going'. In such words as 'eti' and 'īti', it would be in the sense of 'coming'.

Tathā hi ītīti anatthāya eti āgacchatīti īti, upaddavo, iti āgamanattho gahetabbo. Āha ca suttanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “etīti īti, āgantukānaṃ akusalabhāgīnaṃ byasanahetūnaṃ etaṃ adhivacana”nti.

For thus, 'īti' (affliction, calamity) is so called because it comes ('eti') for what is not beneficial ('anatthāya'); therefore, the meaning of 'coming' should be understood. And it is said in the commentary to the Suttanipāta: 'It comes ('eti'), thus it is an affliction ('īti'); this is a term for unwelcome arrivals, for those who partake of the unwholesome, for the causes of disaster.'

Idāni yathārahaṃ nipātākhyātanāmikapariyāpannānaṃ itiito saddānamatthuddhāro vuccate – tattha itisaddo hetuparisamāpanādipadattha vipariyāya pakārāvadhāraṇa nidassanādianekatthappabhedo. Tathā hesa “ruppatīti kho bhikkhave tasmā rūpanti vuccatī”tiādīsu hetuatthe dissati. “Tasmātiha me bhikkhave dhammadāyādā bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā. Atthi me tumhesu anukampā, kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ, no āmisadāyādā”tiādīsu parisamāpane. “Iti vā iti evarūpā visūkadassanā paṭivirato”tiādīsu ādiattho. “Māgaṇḍiyoti tassa brāhmaṇassa saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ nirutti byañjanamabhilāpo”tiādīsu padatthavipariyāye. “Iti kho bhikkhave sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito. Saupaddavo bālo, anupaddavo [M 0.0005] paṇḍito. Saupasaggo bālo, anupasaggo paṇḍito”tiādīsu pakāro. “Atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti puṭṭhena satā ādanda atthītissa vacanīyaṃ. Kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇanti iti ce vadeyya, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti iccassa vacanīya”ntiādīsu avadhāraṇe. “Atthīti kho kaccāna ayameko anto, natthīti kho kaccāna ayaṃ dutiyo anto”tiādīsu nidassane. Nipātavaseneva te payogā gahetabbā. “Itāyaṃ kodharūpenā”ti ettha pana ākhyātavasena gamane itisaddo dissati. Ayamevattho idhādhippeto, nipātattho pana na icchitabbo, viññūnaṃ atthaggahaṇe kosallupādanatthaṃ kevalaṃ atthuddhāravasena āgatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Itaro pana –

Now, the extraction of meanings for the words 'iti' and 'ito', which fall under particles, verbs, and nouns as appropriate, is stated. Among these, the word 'iti' has many distinctions of meaning such as cause, completion, 'etc.', reversal of word meaning, manner, determination, and illustration. Thus, it is seen in the sense of cause in passages like, 'It is afflicted, bhikkhus, therefore it is called form (rūpa).' In the sense of completion in passages like, 'Therefore, bhikkhus, be heirs of the Dhamma, not heirs of material things. I have compassion for you, thinking: "How might my disciples be heirs of the Dhamma, not heirs of material things?"' In the sense of 'etc.' (ādi) in passages like, 'He abstains from such spectacles as these, etc.' In the sense of reversal of word meaning in passages like, '“Māgaṇḍiya”—this is the designation, appellation, concept, usage, name, naming, nomenclature, etymology, expression, and utterance of that brahmin.' In the sense of manner in passages like, 'Thus, bhikkhus, the fool is fearful, the wise person is fearless. The fool is afflicted, the wise person is unafflicted. The fool is beset, the wise person is unbeset.' In the sense of determination in passages like, 'When asked, "Is there aging-and-death dependent on this condition?" one should say, "Yes, there is." If one should say, "Dependent on what is aging-and-death?" one should say, "Aging-and-death is dependent on birth."' In the sense of illustration in passages like, '“It exists,” Kaccāna, is one extreme; “it does not exist,” Kaccāna, is the second extreme.' Those usages should be understood as being by way of a particle. However, in the phrase 'itāyaṃ kodharūpenā' ('this one goes with an angry form'), the word 'iti' is seen in the sense of motion, by way of a verb. This very meaning is intended here; the meaning as a particle, however, is not desired. It should be understood as having come merely by way of meaning extraction for the purpose of imparting skill in grasping meanings to the wise. The other, however—

Gatyatthe cimasaddatthe, itosaddo pavattati;

Anvito”ti hi gatyatthe, paccattavacanaṃ bhave.

The word 'ito' occurs in the sense of going and in the sense of 'this'. For indeed, in the sense of going, a word like 'anvito' would be a personal expression.

Imasaddassa atthamhi, nissakkavacanaṃ bhave;

“Ito sā dakkhiṇā disā”, itiādīsu pāḷisu.

In the sense of 'this', it would be an ablative expression, as in Pāli passages like, 'From here is that southern direction,' and so on.

Gatyattho icchito ettha, itarattho na icchito;

Atthuddhāravasā vutto, kosallatthāya viññunaṃ.

Here, the meaning of going is intended, not the other meaning; it is stated by way of meaning extraction for the purpose of imparting skill to the wise.

Idha pana samayasaddassa atthuddhāraṃ sanibbacanaṃ vattabbampi avatvā upari ayadhātuvisayeyeva vakkhāma i e ayadhātuvasena tidhātumayattā samayasaddassa. Tatra itīti ikārānantaratyantapadassa ca “eti, udetī”tiādīnañca ekārānantaratyantapadānaṃ aññesañca evarūpānaṃ padamālā yathārahaṃ yebhuyyena attanopadāni vajjetvā yojetabbā. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu dukkarā kriyāpadamālā. Yasmā pana imasmiṃ pakaraṇe sukarā ca dukkarā ca tyantapadamālā jānitabbā[M 0.0006], tasmā bhūvādigaṇādīsu aṭṭhasu gaṇesu vihitehi channavutiyā vacanehi sabbasādhāraṇaṃ asabbasādhāraṇañca padamālānayaṃ brūma –

Here, however, without stating the extraction of meaning along with the etymology of the word 'samaya', which ought to be stated, we will speak later only concerning the sphere of the root 'aya', because the word 'samaya' is composed of three roots: 'i', 'e', and 'aya'. In this regard, the paradigms of forms for 'iti' (a word ending in 'ti' immediately after the vowel 'i'), and for words ending in 'ti' immediately after the vowel 'e' like 'eti', 'udeti', etc., and for other such words, should be formed as appropriate, generally avoiding the middle voice forms (attanopada). For in such cases, the verbal paradigms are difficult. However, since in this treatise the paradigms of words ending in 'ti', both easy and difficult, must be known, therefore, we declare the method of paradigms, both common and uncommon, with the ninety-six endings prescribed in the eight groups beginning with the bhū-group.

Akārānantaratyanta-padānaṃ pantiyo budho;

Bhavati rundhatādīnaṃ, yoje sabbattha sabbathā.

A wise person should apply the series of forms for words ending in 'ti' after the vowel 'a', such as 'bhavati', 'rundhati', and so on, everywhere and in every way.

Iti etī”ti cetesaṃ, padānaṃ pana pantiyo;

Suddhassarapubbakānaṃ, yoje viññū yathārahaṃ.

But for the series of forms for these words, 'iti' and 'eti', which are preceded by pure vowels, a discerning person should apply them as appropriate.

Ākārānantaratyanta-padānañcāpi pantiyo;

“Yāti suṇāti asnā-ti” iccādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ.

And also the series of forms for words ending in 'ti' after the vowel 'ā', such as 'yāti', 'suṇāti', and 'asnāti', should be applied as appropriate.

Ivaṇṇānantaratyanta-padānamapi pāḷiyo;

Yoje “rundhiti rundhīti”-iccādīnaṃ yathārahaṃ.

And also the series of forms for words ending in 'ti' after the vowel 'i' (short or long), such as 'rundhiti' and 'rundhīti', should be applied as appropriate.

Ukārānantaratyanta-sutiiti padassa ca;

Peraṇatthe pavattassa, yoje mālaṃ yathārahaṃ.

And for words ending in 'ti' after the vowel 'u', and for the word 'sutiiti', which occurs in the causative sense, one should apply the series as appropriate.

Ekārānantaratyanta-padānampi yathārahaṃ;

“Jeti rundheti kāreti, kārāpetī”tiādīnaṃ.

And also for words ending in 'ti' after the vowel 'e', such as 'jeti', 'rundheti', 'kāreti', and 'kārāpeti', one should apply the series as appropriate.

Okārānantaratyanta-padānampi padakkame;

“Karoti bhoti hotī”ti-ādīnaṃ yuttitovade;

And also for words ending in 'ti' after the vowel 'o', in the sequence of words, one should speak with reason concerning 'karoti', 'bhoti', 'hoti', and so on.

Iccevaṃ sattadhā vutto, padamālānayo mayā;

Ito mutto nayo nāma, natthi koci kriyāpade.

Thus, the method of paradigms has been explained by me in seven ways; beyond this, there is no other method whatsoever with regard to verbs.

“Ādatte kurute pete”, iccādi nayadassanā;

Yathārahaṃ yuttitoti, vacanaṃ ettha bhāsitaṃ.

Because of seeing the method for forms such as 'ādatte', 'kurute', 'pete', and so on, the statement 'as appropriate and with reason' was spoken here.

Idāni ikārānantaratyantapadassa kamo vuccate – iti, inti. Isi, itha. Imi, ima. Aparipuṇṇo vattamānānayo. Itu, intu. Ihi, itha. Imi, ima. Aparipuṇṇo pañcamīnayo. Ettha ca imesaṃ dvinnaṃ sāsanānurūpabhāvassa imāni sādhakapadāni [M 0.0007] “veti, apeti, anvetī”ti. Tattha vi iti veti. Vigacchatīti attho, itisaddo hettha gamanaṃ bodheti. Tathā apa iti apeti. Apagacchatīti attho. Anu iti anveti. Anugacchatīti attho. Garū pana anu eti anvetīti vadanti. Taṃ –

Now the sequence for a word ending in 'ti' after the vowel 'i' is stated: iti, inti; isi, itha; imi, ima. This is an incomplete present tense method. Itu, intu; ihi, itha; imi, ima. This is an incomplete imperative mood method. And here, as proof of the conformity of these two to the scriptural tradition, are these words: 'veti', 'apeti', 'anveti'. Therein, 'vi' + 'iti' is 'veti', meaning 'goes away'; here the word 'iti' signifies going. Similarly, 'apa' + 'iti' is 'apeti', meaning 'goes away'. 'Anu' + 'iti' is 'anveti', meaning 'follows'. But some teachers say that 'anveti' is from 'anu' + 'eti'. That is—

“Yathā āraññakaṃ nāgaṃ, dantiṃ anveti hatthinī;

Jessantaṃ giriduggesu, samesu visamesu ca;

Evaṃ taṃ anugacchāmi, putte ādāya pacchato”ti.

Just as a female elephant follows a wild tusker, a bull elephant, conquering in mountain defiles, in even and uneven places; even so do I follow you, taking my children behind.

Imāya pāḷiyā na sameti “jessantaṃ anvetī”ti vacanato “anugacchāmī”ti vacanato ca. Tathā hi etisaddo yattha ce iriyāpathavācako, tattha āgamanaṃyeva joteti, na gamanaṃ, tasmā āgamanatthassa ayuttito gamanatthassa ca yuttito vi itiādinā chedo ñeyyo. Etesañca itisaddavasena katachedānaṃ atthibhāvaṃ yuttibhāvañca “itāyaṃ kodharūpenā”ti pāḷiyeva sādheti, tasmāyeva “anu iti, anu inti, anu isī”tiādinā “anvetī”tiādīnaṃ chede labbhamānanayena vuttappakāro vattamānāpañcamīnayo parassapadavasena dassito. Sattamīrūpādīni sabbathā appasiddhāni.

This does not agree with this Pāli passage, because of the phrase 'anveti jessantaṃ' and the phrase 'anugacchāmi'. For wherever the word 'eti' is a term for movement, it signifies only coming, not going. Therefore, because the meaning of coming is inappropriate and the meaning of going is appropriate, the analysis as 'vi iti', etc., should be understood. The very Pāli passage 'itāyaṃ kodharūpenā' proves the existence and appropriateness of these analyses made by means of the word 'iti'. Therefore, by the method obtainable in the analysis of 'anveti', etc., as 'anu iti', 'anu inti', 'anu isi', etc., the aforementioned method for the present and imperative moods has been shown by way of the active voice. The optative mood forms and others are entirely unestablished.

Imāni pana bhavissantiyā rūpāni, sittā te lahumessati. Issati, issanti. Issasi, issatha. Issāmi, issāma. Issate, issante. Issase, issavhe. Issaṃ, issāmhe. Asabbadhātukattepi suddhassarattā dhātussa ikārāgamo na labbhati. Paripuṇṇo bhavissantīnayo.

These, however, are the future forms: 'sittā te lahumessati' (they will quickly go, having been sprinkled). Issati, issanti; issasi, issatha; issāmi, issāma. Issate, issante; issase, issavhe; issaṃ, issāmhe. Even though it is a non-sabbadhātuka tense, because the root is a pure vowel, the augment 'i' is not obtained for the root. The future tense method is complete.

Atha kālātipattiyā rūpāni bhavanti, issā, issaṃsu. Isse, issatha. Issaṃ, issamhā. Issatha, issisu. Issase, issavhe. Issaṃ, issāmhase. Kālātipattibhāve [M 0.0008] ca asabbadhātukatte ca santepi suddhassarattā dhātussa akārikārāgamo na labbhati anekantikattā vā anupapannattā ca akārāgamo na hoti. Dvinnañhettha suddhassarānaṃ anantarikānaṃ ekatosannipāto anupapatti. Paripuṇṇo kālātipattinayo.

Then the forms of the conditional arise: issā, issaṃsu; isse, issatha; issaṃ, issamhā. Issatha, issisu; issase, issavhe; issaṃ, issāmhase. And even though it is the conditional mood and is a non-sabbadhātuka tense, because of its pure vowel, the augment 'a' or 'i' is not obtained for the root; or because it is not invariable or because it is inappropriate, the augment 'a' does not occur. For here, the combination of two immediately consecutive pure vowels is an impossibility. The conditional method is complete.

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane sotūnaṃ payogatthesu paramakosallajananatthaṃ “nanu te sutaṃ brāhmaṇa bhaññamāne, devā na issanti purisaparakkamassā”ti pāḷito nayaṃ gahetvā vuttappakārehi bhavissantiyā rūpehi sabbaso samānāni asamānatthāni vattamānikarūpāni ca īsakaṃ aññamaññaṃ samānāni bhavissantīkālātipattīnaṃ rūpāni ca pakāsayissāma – vattamānāvasena tāva “issati, issanti. Issasi, issathā”ti sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Attho pana “issaṃ karotī”tiādinā vattabbo. Tasmiṃyeva atthe bhavissantīvasena “ississati, ississanti. Ississasi, ississathā”ti paripuṇṇaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Attho pana “issaṃ karissatī”tiādinā vattabbo. Kālātipattivasena pana “ississā, ississaṃsu. Ississe, ississathā”ti paripuṇṇaṃ yojetabbaṃ, attho pana “issaṃ akarissā”tiādinā vattabbo. Dhātvantaravasena saṃsandanānayoyaṃ.

In this context, to generate supreme skill in the meanings of usage for listeners of the Buddha’s word in the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries, taking the method from the Pāḷi text, “Have you not heard, brahmin, while it is being said, that the gods do not envy human effort?”, we will explain the present tense forms which are entirely similar to the aforementioned future tense forms but dissimilar in meaning, and also the future and conditional forms which are slightly similar to each other. First, in the present tense: 'issati', 'issanti'; 'issasi', 'issatha'—all should be conjugated. The meaning, however, should be expressed as 'he envies' and so on. In that same meaning, for the future tense: 'ississati', 'ississanti'; 'ississasi', 'ississatha'—should be fully conjugated. The meaning, however, should be expressed as 'he will envy' and so on. For the conditional: 'ississā', 'ississaṃsu'; 'ississe', 'ississatha'—should be fully conjugated. The meaning, however, should be expressed as 'he would have envied' and so on. This is a method of comparison by means of other roots.

Idāni ekārānantaratyantapadassa kamo vuccate –

Now the sequence of verbal forms with a stem ending in 'e' is stated—

Eti, enti. Esi, etha. Emi, ema.

He comes, they come. You come, you all come. I come, we come.

Etu, entu. Ehi, etha. Emi, ema.

Let him come, let them come. Come, you all come. Let me come, let us come.

Na ca appatvā dukkhantaṃ, vissāsaṃ eyya paṇḍito;

Nivesanāni māpetvā, vedehassa yasassino;

Yadā te pahiṇissāmi, tadā eyyāsi khattiya.

A wise person should not come to trust without having reached the end of suffering; having had dwellings built for the glorious Videha; when I send for you, then you should come, O warrior.

Eyya[M 0.0009], eyyuṃ. Eyyāsi, eyyātha. Eyyāmi, eyyāma. Etha, eraṃ. Etho, eyyāvho. Eyyaṃ, eyyāmhe.

He should come, they should come. You should come, you all should come. I should come, we should come. He might come, they might come. You might come, you all might come. I might come, we might come.

So puriso eyya, te eyyuṃ. Tvaṃ eyyāsi, tumhe eyyātha. Ahaṃ eyyāmi, mayaṃ eyyāma. So puriso etha, te eraṃ. Tvaṃ etho, tumhe eyyāvho. Ahaṃ eyyaṃ, mayaṃ eyyāmhe.

That man should come, they should come. You should come, you all should come. I should come, we should come. That man might come, they might come. You might come, you all might come. I might come, we might come.

Parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanīrūpāni sabbaso appasiddhāni.

The perfect, imperfect, and aorist forms are entirely unestablished.

Essati, essanti. Essasi, essatha. Essāmi, essāma. Essate, essante. Essase, essavhe. Essaṃ, essāmhe.

He will come, they will come. You will come, you all will come. I will come, we will come. He will come, they will come. You will come, you all will come. I will come, we will come.

Sammodamānā gacchanti, jālamādāya pakkhino;

Yadā te vivadissanti, tadā ehinti me vasaṃ.

The birds go forth rejoicing, taking the net with them; when they quarrel, then they will come into my power.

“Abhidosagato idāni ehī”ti vacanadassanato aparānipi bhavissantīrūpāni gahetabbāni.

From seeing statements such as, “Now that evening has come, come!”, other future forms should also be taken.

Ehiti, ehinti. Ehisi, ehitha. Ehimi, ehima. Ehite, ehinte. Ehise, ehivhe. Ehissaṃ, ehissāmhe.

He will come, they will come. You will come, you all will come. I will come, we will come. He will come, they will come. You will come, you all will come. I will come, we will come.

Essā, essaṃsu. Esse, essatha. Essaṃ essāmhā. Essatha, essisu. Essase, essavhe. Essiṃ, essāmhase.

He would have come, they would have come. You would have come, you all would have come. I would have come, we would have come. He would have come, they would have come. You would have come, you all would have come. I would have come, we would have come.

Athāparopi ekārānantaratyantapadakkamo bhavati;

Udeti, udenti; Udesi, udetha; Udemi, udema.

Then there is another sequence of verbal forms with a stem ending in 'e': Udeti, udenti; Udesi, udetha; Udemi, udema.

Udetu, udentu. Udehi, udetha. Udemi, udema, udāmase.

Let him rise, let them rise. Rise, you all rise. Let me rise, let us rise, let us rise.

Udeyya, udeyyuṃ. Sesaṃ neyyaṃ. Udissati, udissanti. Sesaṃ neyyaṃ. Udissā, udissaṃsu. Sesaṃ neyyaṃ.

He should rise, they should rise. The rest should be inferred. He will rise, they will rise. The rest should be inferred. He would have risen, they would have risen. The rest should be inferred.

Imāni suddhassaradhāturūpāni.

These are the forms of pure vowel roots.

Kakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ka'

Ku [M 0.0010] sadde ke ca. Koti, kavati, kāyati, evaṃ kattupadāni bhavanti. Kuyyati, kiyyati, evaṃ kammapadāni. Kānanaṃ, kabbaṃ, jātakaṃ, evaṃ nāmikapadāni. Kutvā, kutvāna, kavitvā, kavitvāna, kāvitvā, kāvitvāna, kāyituṃ, evaṃ abyayapadāni.

The root 'ku' and others in the sense of 'sound'. 'Koti,' 'kavati,' 'kāyati'—thus are the active forms. 'Kuyyati,' 'kiyyati'—thus are the passive forms. 'Kānanaṃ,' 'kabbaṃ,' 'jātakaṃ'—thus are the nominal forms. 'Kutvā,' 'kutvāna,' 'kavitvā,' 'kavitvāna,' 'kāvitvā,' 'kāvitvāna,' 'kāyituṃ'—thus are the indeclinable forms.

Tatra kānananti ṭhitamajjhanhikasamaye kavati saddaṃ karotīti kānanaṃ, vanaṃ. Tathā hi –

Therein, 'kānanaṃ' is so called because at the time of midday, it 'kavati,' that is, it makes a sound; it is a forest. For thus it is said:

“Ṭhite majjhanhike kāle, sannisīvesu pakkhisu;

Saṇateva brahāraññaṃ, sā rati paṭibhāti ma”nti

“At the fixed midday time, when the birds are settled, this great forest resounds—that delight appears to me.”

Vuttaṃ. Atha vā kokilamayūrādayo kavanti saddāyanti kūjanti etthāti kānanaṃ. Manoharatāya avassaṃ kuyyati paṇḍitehīti kabbaṃ. Kāviyaṃ. Kāveyyaṃ. Aññatra pana kavīnaṃ idanti kabbanti taddhitavasena attho gahetabbo. Keci tu kābyanti saddarūpaṃ icchanti, na taṃ pāvacane pamāṇaṃ sakkaṭabhāsābhāvato. Sakkaṭabhāsātopi hi ācariyā nayaṃ gaṇhanti. Jātaṃ bhūtaṃ atītaṃ bhagavato cariyaṃ, taṃ kīyati kathīyati etenāti jātakaṃ. Jātakapāḷi hi idha “jātaka”nti vuttā. Aññatra pana jātaṃ eva jātakanti gahetabbaṃ. Tathā hi jātakasaddo desanāyampi vattati “itivuttakaṃ jātakaṃ abbhutadhamma”ntiādīsu. Jātiyampi vattati “jātakaṃ samodhānesī”tiādīsu.

It has been said. Or else, 'kānanaṃ' is where cuckoos, peacocks, and others 'kavanti,' that is, make sounds, resonate, and chirp; therefore, it is 'kānanaṃ'. 'Kabbaṃ' is what is necessarily 'kuyyati' (composed) by the wise due to its beauty. 'Kāviyaṃ.' 'Kāveyyaṃ.' Otherwise, the meaning should be taken in a derivative sense as 'belonging to poets' ('kavīnaṃ idaṃ'). Some, however, prefer the word form 'kābyaṃ,' but that is not authoritative in the teachings, because it is a Sanskrit word. For teachers also derive principles even from the Sanskrit language. 'Jātakaṃ' is so called because the past conduct of the Blessed One, what was born and what has been, is narrated and told by this. Here, the Jātaka Pāḷi is called 'jātakaṃ.' Elsewhere, however, 'jātakaṃ' should be taken as simply 'what is born.' For the word 'jātaka' also occurs in reference to a discourse, as in “Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma,” etc., and in the sense of birth, as in “he related the birth,” etc.

Pakka nīcagatiyaṃ. Nīcagamanaṃ nāma hīnagamanaṃ hīnappavatti vā. Nīcasaddo hi hīnavācako “nīce kule paccājāto”ti ettha viya. Pakkati kriyāpadamettha dissati, na nāmikapadaṃ. Yattha yattha nāmikapadaṃ na dissati, tattha tattha nāmikapadaṃ upaparikkhitvā [M 0.0011] gahetabbaṃ. Kriyāpadameva hi duddasaṃ, kriyāpade vijjamāne nāmikapadaṃ natthīti na vattabbaṃ, tasmā antamaso “pakkanaṃ, takanaṃ” iccevamādīni bhāvavācakāni nāmikapadāni sabbāsu dhātūsu yathārahaṃ labbhantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The root 'pakka' is in the sense of 'low movement'. 'Low movement' means inferior movement or inferior occurrence. For the word 'nīca' denotes 'inferior', as in “born in a low family.” Here, 'pakkati' is seen as a verbal form, not a nominal form. Wherever a nominal form is not seen, a nominal form should be investigated and taken. For the verbal form itself is difficult to find; when a verbal form exists, it should not be said that no nominal form exists. Therefore, it should be understood that at least nominal forms expressing a state, such as 'pakkanaṃ,' 'takanaṃ,' etc., are found for all roots as appropriate.

Taka hasane. Hasanaṃ hāso. Takati.

The root 'taka' is in the sense of 'laughing'. 'Hasanaṃ' is laughter; 'hāso' is laughter. 'Takati' (he laughs).

Taki kicchajīvane. Kicchajīvanaṃ kasirajīvanaṃ. Taṅkati. Ātaṅkati. Ātaṅko. Ātaṅkoti kicchajīvitakaro rogo, tathā hi aṭṭhakathācariyā “appābādhaṃ appātaṅka”nti imasmiṃ pāḷippadese iti atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇesuṃ “ābādhoti visabhāgavedanā vuccati, yā ekadese uppajjitvā sakalasarīraṃ ayapaṭṭena bandhitvā viya gaṇhāti. Ātaṅkoti kicchajīvitakaro rogo. Atha vā yāpetabbarogo ātaṅko, itaro ābādho. Khuddako vā rogo ātaṅko, balavā ābādho. Keci pana ‘ajjhattasamuṭṭhāno ābādho, bahiddhāsamuṭṭhāno ātaṅko’ti vadantī”ti.

The root 'taki' is in the sense of 'difficult living'. 'Kicchajīvanaṃ' means laborious living. 'Taṅkati' (he lives with difficulty). 'Ātaṅkati' (he is distressed). 'Ātaṅko' (distress). 'Ātaṅka' is a disease that makes life difficult, for thus the commentary teachers explained the meaning in the Pāḷi passage “of little sickness, of little distress” as follows: “'Ābādha' is said to be a discordant feeling, which, having arisen in one part, seizes the entire body as if binding it with an iron band. 'Ātaṅka' is a disease that makes life difficult. Or alternatively, 'ātaṅka' is a manageable disease, while the other is 'ābādha.' Or, 'ātaṅka' is a minor disease, while 'ābādha' is a severe one. Some, however, say, 'An illness arising internally is 'ābādha,' an illness arising externally is 'ātaṅka.'”

Ātaṅko āmayo rogo,

Byādhā’bādho gado rujā;

Akallañceva gelaññaṃ,

Nāmaṃ rogābhidhānakaṃ.

Ātaṅka, āmaya, roga, byādha, ābādha, gada, rujā, akalla, and gelañña are names denoting disease.

Suka gatiyaṃ. Sokati, suko, sukī. Tatra sukoti suvo. Sokati manāpena gamanena gacchatīti suko. Tassa bhariyā sukī.

The root 'suka' is in the sense of 'movement'. 'Sokati' (he moves), 'suko' (a parrot), 'sukī' (a female parrot). Therein, 'suko' means a parrot. Because he goes with a pleasant movement, he is a 'suko.' His female is 'sukī.'

Bukka bhassane. Idha bhassanaṃ nāma sunakhabhassanaṃ adhippetaṃ “sunakho bhassitvā”ti ettha viya, na “āvāso gocaraṃ [M 0.0012] bhassa”ntiādīsu viya. Vacanasaṅkhātaṃ bhassanaṃ, bukkati sā.

The root 'bukka' is in the sense of 'barking'. Here, 'bhassanaṃ' is intended to mean the barking of a dog, as in “the dog having barked,” and not as in “dwelling, pasture, speech,” etc. 'Bhassanaṃ' is defined as vocalization; 'bukkati sā' (she barks).

Dhaka paṭighāte gatiyañca. Paṭighāto paṭihananaṃ. Dhakati.

The root 'dhaka' is in the sense of 'striking' and 'movement'. 'Paṭighāta' means striking. 'Dhakati' (it strikes).

Caka tittipaṭighātesu. Titti tappanaṃ, paṭighātaṃ paṭihananaṃva. Cakati.

The root 'caka' is in the senses of 'satisfaction' and 'resistance'. 'Titti' means satisfaction, that is, satiation. 'Paṭighāta' means resistance or repelling. 'Cakati' (he is satisfied/resists).

Aka kuṭilagatiyaṃ. Akati. Etā kuādikā akapariyantā dhātuyo parassa bhāsāti saddasatthavidū vadanti. Tesaṃ mate etā “ti anti, tu antu” iccādīnaṃyeva visayo. Pāḷiyaṃ pana niyamo natthi, tasmā na taṃ idha pamāṇaṃ.

The root 'aka' is in the sense of crooked movement. 'Akati' (it moves crookedly). Experts in language say that these roots, beginning with 'ku' and ending with 'aka,' belong to another language. In their view, these are exclusively the domain of endings such as 'ti,' 'anti,' 'tu,' 'antu,' etc. However, in Pāli, there is no such rule; therefore, that view is not an authority here.

I ajjhayane. Ajjhayanaṃ uccāraṇaṃ sikkhanaṃ vā, ayati, adhīyati, ajjhayati, adhīte, ajjhenaṃ, ajjhāyako. Dibbaṃ adhīyase māyaṃ. Adhīyanti mahārāja, dibbamāyidha paṇḍitā. Ajjhenamariyā pathaviṃ janindā. Tattha ajjhāyakoti ajjhayatīti ajjhāyako, mante parivattetīti attho.

The root 'i' is in the sense of study. 'Ajjhayana' means utterance or learning. Forms include: 'ayati,' 'adhīyati,' 'ajjhayati,' 'adhīte,' 'ajjhenaṃ,' 'ajjhāyako.' 'You study divine illusion.' 'They study, O great king, the wise study divine illusion here.' 'The noble ones studied upon the earth, O lord of men.' Therein, 'ajjhāyako' means 'one who studies'; the meaning is, 'one who repeats the sacred verses.'

U sadde. Avati, avanti. Avasi. Ettha “yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāvā”ti pāḷi papubbassa udhātussa payogoti daṭṭhabbo. Papubbassa vadadhātussa dakāralopappayogotipi vattuṃ yujjati.

The root 'u' is in the sense of sound. Forms include 'avati,' 'avanti,' 'avasi.' Here, the Pāli phrase 'yo ātumānaṃ sayaṃ eva pāvā' should be understood as a usage of the root 'u' with the prefix 'pa-.' It may also be said to be a usage involving the elision of the letter 'd' in the root 'vad' with the prefix 'pa-.'

Vaṅka koṭille. Vaṅkati. Vaṅkaṃ. Vaṅkasaddo hi vakkasaddena samānattho, vakkasaddo ca vaṅkasaddena. Tathā hi –

The root 'vaṅka' is in the sense of crookedness. 'Vaṅkati' (it is crooked). 'Vaṅkaṃ' (crookedness). The word 'vaṅka' indeed has the same meaning as the word 'vakka,' and the word 'vakka' has the same meaning as the word 'vaṅka.' For thus it is said:

“Yaṃ nissitā jagatiruhaṃ, svāyaṃ aggiṃ pamuñcati;

Disā bhajatha vakkaṅgā, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

That very world-tree, which we relied upon, emits fire; flee to the directions, O crooked-limbed ones, for fear has arisen from our refuge.

Pāḷi [M 0.0013] dissati. Ayaṃ pana vakkasaddo sakkaṭabhāsaṃ patvā kakārarakārasaññogakkhariko bhavati, dhātubhāvo panassa porāṇehi na vutto, tasmā kriyāpadaṃ na diṭṭhaṃ. Imassa pana vaṅkasaddassa “vaṅka koṭille”ti dhātubhāvo vutto, “vaṅkatī”ti kriyāpadañca, pāḷiyaṃ tu “vaṅkatī”ti kriyāpadaṃ na diṭṭhaṃ, tathā bhāvavācako vaṅkasaddopi. Vāccaliṅgo pana anekesu ṭhānesu diṭṭho. Tatta vaṅkatīti kriyāpadaṃ pāḷiyaṃ avijjamānampi gahetabbameva nāthatīti kriyāpadamiva. Bhāvavācakassa pana vaṅkasaddassa atthitā natthitā ca pāḷiādīsu punappunaṃ upaparikkhitabbā. Kecettha vadeyyuṃ “yadi bhāvavācako vaṅkasaddo natthi, kathaṃ ‘aṭṭhavaṅkaṃ maṇiratanaṃ uḷāra’nti ettha samāso”ti. Ettha pana aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vaṅkaṃ aṭṭhavaṅkaṃ, na aṭṭhavaṅkāni yassāti. Dabbavācako hi vaṅkasaddo, na bhāvavācakoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The Pāli is seen. However, when this word 'vakka' enters the Sanskrit language, it becomes a word with a conjunct consonant of 'k' and 'r', but its nature as a root is not stated by the ancients; therefore, a verbal form is not seen. For this word 'vaṅka,' however, its nature as a root, 'vaṅka in the sense of crookedness,' is stated, and also the verbal form 'vaṅkatī.' But in Pāli, the verbal form 'vaṅkatī' is not seen, nor is the word 'vaṅka' as an abstract noun. As an adjective, however, it is seen in many places. Therefore, the verbal form 'vaṅkatī,' though not found in Pāli, should still be accepted, just like the verbal form 'nāthatī.' As for the existence or non-existence of the word 'vaṅka' as an abstract noun, this must be repeatedly examined in the Pāli texts and other sources. Some might argue here: 'If the word 'vaṅka' as an abstract noun does not exist, how is the compound formed in 'aṭṭhavaṅkaṃ maṇiratanaṃ uḷāraṃ' (a magnificent jewel bent in eight places)?' Here, however, 'aṭṭhavaṅkaṃ' means 'crooked in eight places,' not 'that which has eight bends.' For the word 'vaṅka' here denotes a quality of a substance, not an abstract state—this should be understood.

Vaṅkaṃ vakkañca kuṭilaṃ, jimhañca rimhamanuju;

Vaṅkasaddādayo ete, vāccaliṅgā tiliṅgikā.

'Vaṅka,' 'vakka,' 'kuṭila,' 'jimha,' and 'anuju' (not straight); these words, beginning with 'vaṅka,' are adjectives, declinable in the three genders.

Atha vā vaṅkasaddoyaṃ, “vaṅkaghastā”tiādisu;

Baḷise giribhede ca, vattate sa pumā tadā.

Or alternatively, this word 'vaṅka,' in usages such as 'vaṅkaghastā,' is employed in the sense of a fishhook and a mountain fissure; in such cases, it is masculine.

Ayañhi “te’me janā vaṅkaghastā sayanti. Yathāpi maccho baḷisaṃ, vaṅkaṃ maṃsena chāditaṃ. Vaṅkaghastova ambujo”tiādīsu baḷise vattati.

For indeed, this word is used in the sense of a fishhook in passages such as: 'These creatures lie caught by hooks'; 'Just as a fish takes a fishhook, a hook covered with flesh'; 'Like a fish caught by a hook,' and so on.

Ettha siyā “nanu ca bho ‘yathāpi maccho baḷisaṃ, vaṅkaṃ maṃsena chādita’nti ettha vaṅkasaddo guṇavācako visesanasado, yena baḷiso visesito, tena vaṅkaṃ kuṭilaṃ baḷisanti attho viññāyatī”ti? Tanna, vaṅkasadde avuttepi baḷisasabhāvassa vaṅkattā kuṭilattho pākaṭoti natthi visesanasaddena [M 0.0014] payojanaṃ. Idaṃ pana “baḷisaṃ vaṅka”nti vacanaṃ “hatthi nāgo. Saroruhaṃ padumaṃ. Hatthī ca kuñjaro nāgo”tiādivacanamiva pariyāyavacanaṃ, tasmā “vaṅka”nti padassa “kuṭila”nti attho na gahetabbo. Atha vā yathā “yathā āraññakaṃ nāgaṃ, dantiṃ anveti hatthinī”ti ettha nāgasaddassa dantīsaddassa ca aññamaññapariyā yavacanattepi dantinti manoramadantayuttanti attho saṃvaṇṇito, tathā “baḷisaṃ vaṅka”nti imesampi aññamaññaṃ pariyāyavacanattepi vaṅkanti kuṭilanti attho vattabbo. Evañhi sati attho sālarājā viya suphullito hoti, desanā ca vilāsappattā, na pana “vaṅkaṃ baḷisa”nti saddānaṃ guṇaguṇīvasena samānādhikaraṇabhāvo icchitabbo “buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharatī”tiādīsu “buddho bhagavā”ti imesaṃ viya samānādhikaraṇabhāvassa anicchitabbattā. Na hi īdisesu ṭhānesu samānādhikaraṇabhāvo porāṇehi anumato.

Here it might be said: 'But, sir, in the phrase 'yathāpi maccho baḷisaṃ, vaṅkaṃ maṃsena chāditaṃ' (just as a fish takes a fishhook, a hook covered with flesh), is not the word 'vaṅka' a qualitative term, a specifying word, by which the fishhook is specified? Thus, the meaning is understood as a 'crooked' (kuṭila) fishhook.' That is not so. Even if the word 'vaṅka' were not stated, the meaning 'crooked' is evident from the inherent nature of a fishhook; thus, there is no need for a specifying word. This phrase 'baḷisaṃ vaṅkaṃ' is a synonymous expression, like 'hatthi nāgo' (an elephant, a nāga), 'saroruhaṃ padumaṃ' (a lotus, a paduma), and 'hatthī ca kuñjaro nāgo' (an elephant, a kuñjara, a nāga). Therefore, the meaning 'crooked' should not be taken for the word 'vaṅka.' Alternatively, just as in the phrase 'yathā āraññakaṃ nāgaṃ, dantiṃ anveti hatthinī' (as a female elephant follows a forest elephant, a tusker), even though the words 'nāga' and 'dantī' are synonyms, the meaning of 'dantī' is explained as 'possessing beautiful tusks'; similarly, in 'baḷisaṃ vaṅkaṃ,' even though these are synonyms, the meaning 'crooked' may be stated for 'vaṅka.' In this way, the meaning blossoms like a sāl-king in full flower, and the exposition attains elegance. However, one should not desire an appositional relationship between the words 'vaṅkaṃ' and 'baḷisaṃ' based on a quality-qualified relationship, just as in 'buddho bhagavā verañjāyaṃ viharati' (the Buddha, the Blessed One, dwells at Verañjā), an appositional relationship between 'buddho' and 'bhagavā' is not intended. Indeed, in such cases, an appositional relationship is not approved by the ancients.

“Yattha etādiso satthā, loke appaṭipuggalo;

Tathāgato balappatto, sambuddho parinibbuto”ti,

Where there is such a Teacher, in the world without an equal; the Tathāgata, who has attained the powers, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the one who is completely extinguished.

“Buddhaṃ buddhaṃ nikhilavisayaṃ suddhiyā yāva suddhi”nti ca ādīsu pana anumato. Ettha hi “etādiso”ti ca “appaṭipuggalo”ti ca “tathāgato”ti ca “balappatto”ti ca “sambuddho”ti ca “parinibbuto”ti ca imāni “satthā”ti anena padena samānādhikaraṇāni. Tathā “buddhaṃ buddha”nti dvinnaṃ padānaṃ pacchimaṃ purimena samānādhikaraṇaṃ bhavati.

However, in passages such as, 'Buddha, Buddha, whose scope is all-encompassing, up to the utmost purity,' it is approved. For here, 'of such a kind,' 'unequalled,' 'the Tathāgata,' 'attained to power,' 'the Perfectly Enlightened One,' and 'the one who is completely extinguished'—these are all in apposition with the word 'Teacher.' Similarly, in 'Buddha, Buddha,' the latter word is in apposition with the former.

Iti “yathāpi maccho baḷisaṃ, vaṅkaṃ maṃsena chādita”nti ettha vaṅkasaddo baḷisassābhidhānantaraṃ, na guṇavācako. Evaṃ vaṅkasaddo baḷise vattati. “Kaṅkaṃ gacchāma pabbataṃ. Dūre vaṅkatapabbato”tiādīsu [M 0.0015] pana girivisese vattati. Ettha ca “vaṅkapabbato”ti vattabbe sukhuccāraṇatthaṃ niruttinayena majjhe animittaṃ takārāgamaṃ katvā “vaṅkatapabbato”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā vaṅkoyeva vaṅkatā, yathā devo eva devatā. Yathā ca disā eva disatāti, evaṃ tāpaccayavasena vaṅkatā ca sā pabbato cāti “vaṅkatapabbato”ti vuttaṃ, majjhe rassavasena cetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā vaṅkamassa saṇṭhānamatthīti vaṅkatoti mantuatthe tapaccayo, yathā pabbamassa atthīti pabbatoti. Evaṃ vaṅkato ca so pabbato cāti vaṅkatapabbato. “Vaṅkapabbato” icceva vā paṇṇatti, pādakkharapāripūriyā pana “dūre vaṅkatapabbato”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Thus, in the phrase 'just as a fish takes a fishhook, a hook covered with flesh,' the word 'vaṅka' is another name for the fishhook, not a qualitative term. In this way, the word 'vaṅka' is used in the sense of a fishhook. However, in passages such as, 'We go to Mount Kaṅka. Far away is Mount Vaṅkata,' it is used for a specific mountain. Here, though one could say 'Vaṅkapabbato,' for ease of pronunciation and by grammatical rule, an uncaused 't' is inserted in the middle, and it is said as 'Vaṅkatapabbato.' Alternatively, 'vaṅka' itself becomes 'vaṅkatā,' just as 'deva' becomes 'devatā,' and 'disā' becomes 'disatā.' Thus, by means of the '-tā' suffix, it is 'vaṅkatā,' and that which is a mountain is called 'Vaṅkatapabbato'; this should be understood as involving a shortening in the middle. Or alternatively, 'vaṅkato' means 'it has a crooked shape,' where the '-ta' suffix is in the sense of 'possessing,' just as 'pabbato' means 'it has joints.' Thus, that which is 'vaṅkato' and is a mountain is 'Vaṅkatapabbato.' Or, the designation is simply 'Vaṅkapabbato,' but for the sake of completing the meter of the verse, it is said, 'Far away is Mount Vaṅkata.' This should be understood.

Loka dassane. Lokati. Loko. Ālokoti aññānipi rūpāni gahetabbāni. Curādigaṇaṃ pana patvā imissā “loketi, lokayati, oloketi, olokayatī”tiādinā rūpāni bhavanti. Lokoti tayo lokā saṅkhāraloko sattaloko okāsalokoti. Tattha “eko loko, sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti āgato saṅkhāro eva loko saṅkhāraloko. Sattā eva loko sattaloko. Cakkavāḷasaṅkhāto okāso eva loko okāsaloko, yo “bhājanaloko”tipi vuccati. Tesu saṅkhāro lujjatīti lokoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “lujjati palujjatīti kho bhikkhu tasmā lokoti vuccatī”ti. Lokiyati ettha puññapāpaṃ tabbipāko cāti satto loko. Lokiyati vicittākārato dissatīti cakkavāḷasaṅkhāto okāso loko. Yasmā pana lokasaddo samūhepi dissati, tasmā lokiyati samudāyavasena [M 0.0016] paññāpiyatīti loko, samūhoti ayampi attho gahetabbo. Atha vā lokoti tayo lokā kilesaloko bhavaloko indriyalokoti. Tesaṃ sarūpaṃ curādigaṇe kathessāma bahuvidhatañca. Bahiddhā pana kavīhi “loko tu bhuvane jane”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ.

The root loka is in the sense of 'seeing'. It sees. The world. Other forms such as āloka (light) should also be included. However, when it belongs to the curādi group, its forms are 'loketi, lokayati, oloketi, olokayati,' and so on. The world is threefold: the world of formations, the world of beings, and the world of space. Therein, regarding 'One world: all beings subsist on food,' the formation itself is the world, hence the world of formations. Beings themselves are the world, hence the world of beings. The spatial expanse known as the universe is the world, hence the world of space, which is also called the 'receptacle world.' Among these, because a formation disintegrates (lujjati), it is called the world (loka). For this was said by the Blessed One: 'It disintegrates, it breaks apart, O monk; therefore, it is called the world.' Because merit, demerit, and their results are perceived (lokiyati) herein, a being is the world. Because it is perceived (lokiyati) and appears in diverse forms, the spatial expanse known as the universe is the world. Moreover, since the word 'world' is also found in the sense of a collection, 'that which is designated collectively' is the world; this meaning, 'a collection,' should also be grasped. Alternatively, the world is threefold: the world of defilements, the world of existence, and the world of the sense faculties. We will discuss their nature and variety under the curādi group. Externally, however, poets have said only this much: 'The world is in the realm and among people.'

Siloka saṅghāte. Saṅghāto piṇḍanaṃ. Silokati, siloko, silokamanukassāmi. Akkharapadaniyamito vacanasaṅghāto siloko. So pajjanti vuccati, tathā hi “siloko yasassi pajje”ti kavayo vadanti.

The root siloka is in the sense of 'compiling'. Compiling means gathering. He composes a verse. A verse. 'I will recite a verse.' A verse (siloka) is a collection of words regulated by letters and feet. It is called pajja (verse), for indeed poets say, 'A verse is glorious in poetry.'

Deka dheka saddussāhesu. Saddo ravo, ussāho vāyāmo. Dekati. Dhekati.

The roots deka and dheka are in the sense of 'sound' and 'effort'. Sound is noise; effort is striving. He makes a sound. He exerts effort.

Reka saki saṅkāyaṃ. Rekati. Saṅkati, tasmiṃ me saṅkate mano. Saṅkā.

The roots reka and saki are in the sense of 'doubt'. He doubts. He doubts; 'my mind is in doubt concerning that.' Doubt.

Aki lakkhaṇe. Aṅkati, aṅko, sasaṅko.

The root aki is in the sense of 'marking'. He marks. A mark. The moon (lit. 'having a mark').

Maki maṇḍane. Maṇḍanaṃ bhūsanaṃ, maṅkati.

The root maki is in the sense of 'adornment'. Adornment is ornamentation. He adorns.

Kata loliye. Lolabhāvo loliyaṃ yathā dakkhiyaṃ. Kakati, kāko, kākī. Ettha “kāko, dhaṅko, vāyaso, bali, bhoji, ariṭṭho”ti imāni kākābhidhānāni.

The root kaka is in the sense of 'restlessness'. The state of agitation is restlessness, as is dexterity. He caws. A crow. A female crow. Herein, 'kāka, dhaṅka, vāyasa, balibhojin, ariṭṭha'—these are names for a crow.

Kuka vaka ādāne. Kukati, vakati, koko, vako. Ettha kokoti araññasunakho. Vakoti khuddakavanadīpiko, byagghotipi vadanti.

The roots kuka and vaka are in the sense of 'taking'. He takes. He takes. A wolf. A wolf. Herein, koka means a wild dog. Vaka means a small forest leopard; they also say it is a tiger.

Vaka dittiyaṃ paṭighāte ca. Ditti sobhā, vakati.

The root vaka is in the sense of 'shining' and 'striking against'. Shining is splendor. It shines.

Kaki [M 0.0017] vaki sakka tika ṭika seka gatyatthā. Kaṅkati, vaṅkati, sakkati, nisakkati, parisakkati, osakkati, vadhāya parisakkanaṃ. Biḷāranisakkamattampi. Tekati, ṭekati, ṭīkā sekati. Ettha ṭīkāti ṭikiyati jāniyati saṃvaṇṇanāya attho etāyāti ṭīkā. Etā idhātuādikā sekapariyantā dhātuyo “attanobhāsā”ti saddasatthavidū vadanti. Tesaṃ mate etā “te ante, taṃ antaṃ”iccādīnaṃyeva visayo, pāvacane pana niyamo natthi.

The roots kaki, vaki, sakka, tika, ṭika, and seka are used in the sense of 'going'. He limps (kaṅkati). He goes crookedly (vaṅkati). He moves (sakkati). He moves back (nisakkati). He moves around (parisakkati). He moves away (osakkati). 'Moving around in order to strike.' 'As much as a cat's moving back.' He goes (tekati). He goes (ṭekati). A commentary (ṭīkā). He goes (sekati). Herein, a ṭīkā is so called because a meaning is gone to (ṭikiyati), that is, known (jāniyati), by means of it for the purpose of elucidation. Experts in the science of words say these roots, from the beginning up to seka, are 'middle voice' (attanobhāsā). In their opinion, they are the domain of endings such as -te and -ante, but in the scriptures, there is no such restriction.

Hikka abyattasadde. Abyattasaddo avibhāvitatthasaddo niratthakasaddo ca. Hikkati, hikkate. Imaṃ “ubhayatobhāsā”ti vadanti. Idaṃ tu pāvacanena saṃsandati. Parassattanobhāsānañhi dhātūnaṃ “bhavati, bhavate, bādhate, bādhatī”tiādinā yebhuyyena dvidhā dvidhā rūpāni sāsane dissanti.

The root hikka is in the sense of 'indistinct sound'. An indistinct sound is an unclear sound, a sound with unclear meaning, and a meaningless sound. He hiccups (hikkati). He hiccups (hikkate). They call this 'used in both voices' (ubhayatobhāsā). This indeed accords with the scriptures. For roots that are used in both the active (parassabhāsā) and middle (attanobhāsā) voices, forms are generally seen in two ways in the Dispensation, such as 'bhavati, bhavate' and 'bādhate, bādhatī'.

Imāni kakārantadhāturūpāni.

These are the forms of the roots ending in the letter 'ka'.

Khakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'kha'.

Khā pakathane khyā ca. Pakathanaṃ ācikkhanaṃ desanaṃ vā. Khāti, saṅkhāti. Āpubbatte visadisabhāvena khātyakkharassa dvittaṃ, ākārassa ca saññogapubbattā rassattaṃ, akkhāti. Akkhāsi purisuttamo. Akkheyyaṃ te ahaṃ ayye. Dhammo saṅkhāyati. Akkhāyati. Atra pana kakāralopo. Svākhāto bhagavatā dhammo. Saṅkhāto. Akkhāto. Akkhātāro tathāgatā. Saṅkhātā sabbadhammānaṃ vidhuro. Saṅkhā, paṭisaṅkhā. Kriyaṃ ākyāti kathetīti ākhyātaṃ. Keci [M 0.0018] pana “svākhāto”ti ca “svākkhyāto”ti ca “svākhyāto”ti ca padamicchanti. Tattha pacchimāni sakkaṭabhāsāto nayaṃ gahetvā vuttāni, itaraṃ yathāṭhitarūpanipphattivasena, ato yathādassitapadāniyeva pasatthatarāni. Tattha saṅkhāsaddassa atthuddhāro nīyate – saṅkhāsaddo ñāṇakoṭṭhāsapaññattigaṇanāsu dissati. “Saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevatī”tiādīsu hi ñāṇe dissati. “Papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantī”tiādīsu koṭṭhāse. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhā samaññā”tiādīsu paññattiyaṃ. “Na sukaraṃ saṅkhātu”ntiādīsu gaṇanāyaṃ. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

The root khā, and also khyā, is in the sense of 'declaring'. Declaring means explaining or teaching. He declares. He designates. When preceded by ā, the letter kh is doubled, and the long ā is shortened because it precedes a conjunct consonant, thus: akkhāti. 'The supreme man declared.' 'I would declare to you, noble lady.' 'The Dhamma is designated.' 'It is declared.' Here, however, the letter k is elided. 'Well-declared is the Dhamma by the Blessed One.' Designated. Declared. 'The Tathāgatas are declarers.' 'The wise one who has comprehended all phenomena.' Designation; thorough designation. A verb (ākhyāta) is so called because it speaks of (ākhyāti) or tells (katheti) an action (kriya). Some, however, desire the forms 'svākhāto' and 'svākkhyāto.' Among these, the latter form is stated having adopted the method from the Sanskrit language, while the former is by way of the derivation of the form as it stands. Therefore, the words as shown are more commendable. Here, the extraction of the meaning of the word saṅkhā is undertaken: the word saṅkhā is seen in the senses of knowledge, division, designation, and counting. For in 'he pursues one thing with discernment (saṅkhāya)', it is seen in the sense of knowledge. In 'proliferations, perceptions, and designations (saṅkhā) arise', it is in the sense of a division. In 'the designation (saṅkhā), the convention for these various things', it is in the sense of designation. In 'it is not easy to count (saṅkhātuṃ)', it is in the sense of counting. Herein, this is said:

“Ñāṇapaññattikoṭṭhāsa-gaṇanāsu padissati;

Saṅkhāsaddoti dīpeyya, dhammadīpassa sāsane”ti.

The word saṅkhā is seen in the senses of knowledge, designation, division, and counting; thus should one explain it in the Dispensation of the Lamp of the Dhamma.

Khi khaye. Khiyanadhammaṃ khīyati. Sāsanānurūpena sare ikārassa iyyādeso, khiyyati. “Khayo, khaṃ” iccapi rūpāni ñeyyāni. Tattha khayoti khiyanaṃ khayo. Atha vā khiyanti kilesā etthāti khayo, magganibbānāni. Khayasaṅkhātena maggena pāpuṇiyattā phalampi khayo. Khanti tucchaṃ suññaṃ vivittaṃ rittaṃ, khanti vā ākāso.

The root khi is in the sense of 'destruction'. That which is of a nature to be destroyed, is destroyed. According to grammatical rule, the vowel i is replaced by iyya, thus: khiyyati. Forms such as 'khayo' and 'khaṃ' are to be known. Therein, khayo is destruction. Or, that wherein defilements are destroyed is khayo, namely, the path and Nibbāna. Because the fruit is attained by means of the path designated as 'destruction', the fruit is also khayo. Khaṃ means empty, void, secluded, barren; or, khaṃ means space.

Khi nivāse. Khīyati, khiyyati vā. Sāsanānurūpena ikārassa īya iyyādeso daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ divādigaṇepi pakkhipitabbo. Khaṃ khayaṃ. Abhiramaṇīyaṃ rājakkhayaṃ. Tattha khīyatīti nivasati. Khanti cakkhādiindriyaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ nivāsaṭṭhena. Khayanti nivesanaṃ. Rājakkhayanti rañño nivesanaṃ. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi –

The root khi is in the sense of 'dwelling'. It dwells, or it dwells. According to grammatical rule, the substitution of i with īya or iyya should be seen. This root should also be placed in the divādi group. Khaṃ, khayaṃ. 'A delightful royal abode.' Therein, khīyati means 'it dwells'. Khaṃ refers to a sense faculty such as the eye, because it is the dwelling place for eye-consciousness and so on. Khayaṃ means a dwelling. Rājakkhayaṃ means the king's residence. On this, there is this Pāli text:

“Sace [M 0.0019] ca ajja dhāresi, kumāraṃ cārudassanaṃ;

Kusena jātakhattiyaṃ, savaṇṇamaṇimekhalaṃ;

Pūjitā ñātisaṅghehi, na gacchasi yamakkhaya”nti.

'If today you accept the handsome prince, the Khattiya born of Kusa, wearing a golden, jeweled girdle, then you, being honored by the assembly of your relatives, will not go to Yama's abode.'

Tattha yamakkhayanti yamanivesanaṃ.

Therein, yamakkhayaṃ means Yama's dwelling.

Khu sadde. Khoti khavati.

The root khu is in the sense of 'sound'. It sounds. It sounds.

Khe khādanasattāsu. Khāyati. Undūrā khāyanti. Vikkhāyitakaṃ. Gokhāyitakaṃ. Assirī viya khāyati. Disāpi me na pakkhāyanti. Etthādimhi kāyatīti khādati. Atha vā upaṭṭhāti paññāyati.

The root khe is in the sense of 'eating' and 'appearing'. It eats/appears. 'Mice eat.' 'Gnawed.' 'Gnawed by a cow.' 'It appears like misfortune.' 'Even the directions do not appear to me.' Here, in the first sense, khāyati means 'it eats'. Alternatively, it means 'it appears' or 'it is manifest'.

Sukha dukkha takriyāyaṃ. Takriyāti sukhadukkhānaṃ vedanānaṃ kriyā, sukhanaṃ dukkhananti vuttaṃ hoti. Akammakā ime dhātavo. Sukhati, dukkhati. Sukhaṃ, dukkhaṃ. Sukhito, dukkhito. Sukhaṃ sātaṃ pīṇanaṃ, dukkhaṃ vighātaṃ aghaṃ kileso. Tattha sukhanti sukhayatīti sukhaṃ. Yassuppajjati, taṃ sukhitaṃ karotīti attho. Dukkhanti dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ. Yassuppajjati, taṃ dukkhitaṃ karotīti attho. Imāni nibbacanāni kāritavasena vuttānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ sukhadukkhasaddatthaṃ vadantehi garūhi sukhayati dukkhayatisaddānaṃ kammatthamādāya vivaraṇassa katattā. Tathā hi “sukheti sukhayati, sukhāpeti sukhāpayati, dukkheti dukkhayati, dukkhāpeti dukkhāpayatī”ti imāni tesaṃ kāritapadarūpāni, attānaṃ sukheti pīṇetīti ca, sukhayati sukhaṃ, dukkhayatīti dukkhanti ca,

The roots Sukha and Dukkha are used in the sense of 'activity'. That activity means the activity of the feelings of happiness and suffering; that is, it is said to be 'being happy' and 'suffering'. These roots are intransitive. He is happy, he suffers. Happiness, suffering. Happy, suffering. Happiness is pleasant, gratifying; suffering is destructive, misery, defilement. Here, 'sukhaṃ' (happiness) means 'it makes happy' (sukhayati). The meaning is that which arises makes one happy. 'Dukkhaṃ' (suffering) means 'it makes suffer' (dukkhayati). The meaning is that which arises makes one suffer. These explanations should be understood as stated in the causative sense, because in the commentary, when explaining the meaning of the words 'sukha' and 'dukkha', the teachers have made the explanation by taking the words 'sukhayati' and 'dukkhayati' in the sense of having an object. Thus, 'sukheti' (makes happy), 'sukhayati' (makes happy), 'sukhāpeti' (causes to be happy), 'sukhāpayati' (causes to be happy), 'dukkheti' (makes suffer), 'dukkhayati' (makes suffer), 'dukkhāpeti' (causes to suffer), 'dukkhāpayati' (causes to suffer) – these are their causative verbal forms. And also, 'it makes oneself happy, it gratifies,' and 'it causes happiness,' 'it causes suffering.'

“Sace [M 0.0020] ca kimhici kāle,

Maraṇaṃ me pure siyā;

Putte ca me paputte ca,

Sukhāpeyya mahosadho”ti ca

And if at any time, death should come to me before, may the Great Sage make my sons and grandsons happy.

Pāḷiādidassanato. Saddasatthe pana dhātupāṭhasaṅkhepe ca ime dhātavo curādigaṇeyeva vuttā. “Sukhayati dukkhayatī”ti ca akāritāni suddhakattupadāni icchitāni. Mayaṃ tu tesaṃ tabbacanaṃ suddhakattari ca tāni padarūpāni na icchāma pāḷiādīhi viruddhattā, tasmāyeva te imasmiṃ bhūvādigaṇe vuttā. Ayañhi suddhakattuvisaye asmākaṃ ruci “sukhatīti sukhito, dukkhatīti dukkhito”ti.

This is seen from the Pāli and other sources. However, in the Saddasattha and the Dhātupāṭhasaṅkhepa, these roots are stated as belonging to the Curādi group. And 'sukhayati' and 'dukkhayati' are desired as non-causative, pure agent forms. But we do not accept their statement, nor those verbal forms, because they contradict the Pāli and other sources. Therefore, they are stated here in this Bhūvādi group. Indeed, our preference in the pure agent sense is: 'sukhati' (he is happy), hence 'sukhito' (happy); 'dukkhAti' (he suffers), hence 'dukkhito' (suffering).

Nanu ca bho “sukhati dukkhatī”ti kriyāpadāni buddhavacane na dissantīti? Saccaṃ, evaṃ santepi aṭṭhakathānayavasena gahetabbattā dissantiyeva nāma. Na hi sabbathā sabbesaṃ dhātūnaṃ rūpāni sāsane loke vā labbhanti, ekaccāni pana labbhanti, ekaccāni na labbhanti. Evaṃ santepi nayavasena labbhantiyeva. “Kappayavho patissatā”ti hi diṭṭhe “caravho bhuñjavho”tiādīnipi nayavasena diṭṭhāniyeva nāma.

But, sir, do not the verb forms 'sukhati' and 'dukkhAti' appear in the Buddha's words? True, even so, since they are to be taken according to the commentarial method, they do indeed appear. For not all forms of all roots are found everywhere in the Teaching or in the world; some, however, are found, and some are not found. Even so, they are found by method. Just as 'Kappayavho patissatā' (Prepare yourselves, mindful ones) is seen, so too 'caravho' (you should wander), 'bhuñjavho' (you should eat), and so on, are indeed seen by method.

Tatra panāyaṃ nayo. Visuddhimaggādīsu hi “ekadviyojanamattampi addhānaṃ gatassa vāyo kuppati, gattāni dukkhantī”ti evaṃ bhūvādigaṇikaṃ akammakaṃ suddhakattuvācakaṃ “dukkhantī”ti kriyāpadaṃ dissati. Tasmiṃ diṭṭhiyeva “sukhati, sukhanti. Sukhasi, sukhatha. Sukhāmi, sukhāmā”tiādīni ca “dukkhati, dukkhanti. Dukkhasi, dukkhathā”tiādīnica diṭṭhāni nāma honti diṭṭhena adiṭṭhassa tādisassa anavajjassa nayassa gahetabbattā, tasmā “sukhatīti sukhito, dukkhatīti dukkhito”ti bhūvādinayo eva gahetabbo, na pana curādinayo. Aparampettha nibbacanaṃ, sukhaṃ sañjātaṃ [M 0.0021] etassāti sukhito, sañjātasukhoti attho. Esa nayo dukkhitoti etthāpi. Atha vā sukhena ito pavattoti sukhito. Esa nayo “dukkhito”ti etthāpi. Dullabhāyaṃ nīti sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā.

Here, however, is the method. For in texts like the Visuddhimagga, the verb 'dukkhanti' (they suffer) is seen as belonging to the Bhūvādi group, intransitive, and expressing the pure agent, as in: 'even for one who has gone a distance of one or two yojanas, the wind becomes disturbed, and the limbs suffer'. When that is seen, forms like 'sukhati', 'sukhanti', 'sukhasi', 'sukhatha', 'sukhāmi', 'sukhāmā', and so on, and similarly 'dukkhAti', 'dukkhanti', 'dukkhasi', 'dukkhathā', and so on, are indeed considered seen. Because a similar, faultless principle for what is unseen should be adopted based on what is seen, therefore, the principle of the Bhūvādi group ('sukhati' means 'sukhito', 'dukkhAti' means 'dukkhito') should be followed, and not the Curādi principle. Here is another explanation: 'sukhito' means 'one to whom happiness has arisen'; the meaning is 'one who possesses arisen happiness'. This principle also applies to 'dukkhito'. Alternatively, 'sukhito' means 'one who proceeds from here with happiness'. This principle also applies to 'dukkhito'. This is a subtle principle and should be carefully borne in mind.

Mokkha muccane. Akammakoyaṃ dhātu. Mokkhati. Mokkho. Pātimokkho. Kārite “mokkheti, mokkhayati, mokkhāpeti, mokkhāpayatī”ti rūpāni. Keci panimaṃ “mokkha mocane”ti paṭhitvā curādigaṇe pakkhipanti. Tesaṃ mate “mokkheti, mokkhayatī”ti suddhakattupadāni bhavanti. Etāni pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāya ca virujjhanti. Tathā hi “mokkhanti mārabandhanā. Na me samaṇe mokkhasi. Mahāyaññaṃ yajissāma, evaṃ mokkhāma pāpakā”ti pāḷiyā virujjhanti. “Yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehīti pātimokkho”ti aṭṭhakathāya ca virujjhanti, tasmā pāḷiyaṃ “mokkhesi mokkhemā”ti ca avatvā “mokkhasi, mokkhāmā”ti suddhakattuvācakaṃ vuttaṃ, tañca kho apādānavisayaṃ katvā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “mokkheti, mocetī”ti hetukattuvācakaṃ vuttaṃ, tampi apādānavisayaṃyeva katvā. Evaṃ imassa dhātuno suddhakattuvisaye akammakabhāvo vidito, hetukattuvisaye ekakammakabhāvo vidito muca paca chidādayo viya. Mokkhadhātu dvigaṇikoti ce? Na, anekesu sāṭṭhakathesu pāḷippadesesu “mokkheti, mokkhayatī”ti suddhakatturūpānaṃ adassanatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The root Mokkha is used in the sense of 'being liberated'. This root is intransitive. He is liberated. Liberation. The Pātimokkha. In the causative, the forms are 'mokkheti', 'mokkhayati', 'mokkhāpeti', 'mokkhāpayati'. Some, however, reading this as 'mokkha in liberating', include it in the Curādi group. According to their view, 'mokkheti' and 'mokkhayati' are pure agent forms. These contradict both the Pāli texts and the commentaries. For instance, they contradict passages in the Pāli like: 'They are liberated from the bonds of Māra.' 'You will not be liberated from me, ascetic.' 'We will perform a great sacrifice; thus we will be liberated from evil.' They also contradict the commentary: 'He who protects and guards him, liberates him from the sufferings of the lower worlds, etc. – this is the Pātimokkha.' Therefore, in the Pāli, instead of saying 'mokkhesi' or 'mokkhemā', the pure agent forms 'mokkhasi' and 'mokkhāmā' are used, and that too by taking the object in the ablative case. In the commentary, however, the causative agent forms 'mokkheti' and 'moceti' are used, also by taking the object in the ablative case. Thus, for this root, its intransitive nature is known in the pure agent sense, and its single-object nature is known in the causative agent sense, like the roots muc, pac, chid, and so on. If it is asked, 'Is the root Mokkha of two conjugational groups?' No, because in many Pāli passages with commentaries, the forms 'mokkheti' and 'mokkhayati' are not seen as pure agent forms. This should be understood.

Kakkha hasane. Kakkhati.

The root Kakkha is used in the sense of 'laughing'. He laughs.

Okha rākha lākha dākha dhākha sosanālamatthesu. Okhati. Rākhati. Lākhati. Dākhati. Dhākhati.

The roots Okha, Rākha, Lākha, Dākha, and Dhākha are used in the senses of 'drying' and 'sufficiency'. Okhati. Rākhati. Lākhati. Dākhati. Dhākhati.

Sākha [M 0.0022] byāpane. Sākhati. Sākhā.

The root Sākha is used in the sense of 'spreading'. It spreads. A branch.

Ukha nakha makha rakha lakha rakhi lakhi ikhi rikhi gatyatthā. Ukhati. Nakhati. Makhati. Rakhati. Lakhati. Raṅkhati. Laṅkhati. Iṅkhati. Riṅkhati.

The roots Ukha, Nakha, Makha, Rakha, Lakha, Rakhi, Lakhi, Ikhi, and Rikhi are used in the sense of 'going'. Ukhati. Nakhati. Makhati. Rakhati. Lakhati. Raṅkhati. Laṅkhati. Iṅkhati. Riṅkhati.

Rakkha pālane. Rakkhati. Rakkhā, rakkhaṇaṃ, sīlaṃ rakkhito devadatto, sīlaṃ rakkhitaṃ devadattena, sīlaṃ rakkhako devadatto.

The root Rakkha is used in the sense of 'protecting'. He protects. Protection, guarding. Devadatta has protected morality. Morality is protected by Devadatta. Devadatta is a protector of morality.

Akkha byattisaṅkhātesu. Akkhati, akkhi, akkhaṃ.

The root Akkha is used in the senses of 'manifestation' and 'enumeration'. Akkhati (it manifests/enumerates), akkhi (eye), akkhaṃ (axle/die).

Nikkha cumbane. Nikkhati, nikkhaṃ.

The root Nikkha is used in the sense of 'kissing'. Nikkhati (he/she kisses), nikkhaṃ (a gold coin).

Nakkha gatiyaṃ. Nakkhati. Nakkhattaṃ. Ettha nakkhattanti etto ito cāti visamagatiyā agantvā attano vīthiyāva gamanena nakkhanaṃ gamanaṃ tāyati rakkhatīti nakkhattaṃ. Porāṇā pana “nakkharanti na nassantīti nakkhattānī”ti kathayiṃsu. “Nakkhattaṃ, joti, nirikkhaṃ, bhaṃ” iccete pariyāyā.

The root Nakkha is used in the sense of 'movement'. Nakkhati. Nakkhattaṃ (constellation). Here, 'nakkhattaṃ' means that which protects its movement by going along its own path, not moving irregularly from here to there. The ancients, however, said, 'They do not perish (na kharanti), hence they are called 'nakkhattāni'.' 'Nakkhattaṃ, joti, nirikkhaṃ, bhaṃ'—these are synonyms.

Vekkha vekkhane. Vekkhati.

The root Vekkha is used in the sense of 'observing'. Vekkhati.

Makkha saṅkhate. Makkhati.

The root Makkha is used in the sense of 'disparagement'. Makkhati.

Takkha tapane. Tapanaṃ saṃvaraṇaṃ. Takkhati.

The root Takkha is used in the sense of 'heating'. Heating is covering. Takkhati.

Sukkha anādare. Sukkhati.

The root Sukkha is used in the sense of 'disregard'. Sukkhati.

Kakhi vakhi makhi kaṅkhāyaṃ. Satthari kaṅkhati. Vaṅkhati, maṅkhati. “Kaṅkhā kaṅkhāyanā kaṅkhāyitattaṃ vimati vicikicchā dveḷhakaṃ dvedhāpatho saṃsayo anekaṃsagāho āsappanā parisappanā apariyogāhanā thambhitattaṃ cittassa manovilekho” iccete kaṅkhāpariyāyā. Etesu pana –

The roots Kakhi, Vakhi, and Makhi are used in the sense of 'doubt'. One doubts the Teacher. Vaṅkhati, maṅkhati. 'Kaṅkhā, kaṅkhāyanā, kaṅkhāyitattaṃ, vimati, vicikicchā, dveḷhakaṃ, dvedhāpatho, saṃsayo, anekaṃsagāho, āsappanā, parisappanā, apariyogāhanā, thambhitattaṃ cittassa, manovilekho'—these are synonyms for doubt. Among these—

Vattanti [M 0.0023] lokavohāre, “kaṅkhā vimati saṃsayo;

Vicikicchā”ti etāni, nāmāniyeva pāyato.

In worldly usage, 'kaṅkhā, vimati, saṃsayo, and vicikicchā' are the names mostly used.

Kakhi iccāyaṃ. Dhanaṃ kaṅkhati, abhikaṅkhati, nābhikaṅkhāmi maraṇaṃ. Abhikaṅkhitaṃ dhanaṃ.

The root Kakhi is also used in the sense of 'desire'. One desires wealth, longs for it. 'I do not long for death.' Wealth is longed for.

Dakhi dhakhi ghoravāsite kaṅkhāyañca. Daṅkhati. Dhaṅkhati.

The roots Dakhi and Dhakhi are used in the sense of 'harsh speech' and also of 'doubt'. Daṅkhati. Dhaṅkhati.

Ukkha secane. Ukkhati.

The root Ukkha is used in the sense of 'sprinkling'. Ukkhati.

Kakha hasane. Kakhati.

The root Kakha is used in the sense of 'laughter'. Kakhati.

Jakkha bhakkhaṇe ca. Hasanānukaḍḍhanatthaṃ cakāro. Jakkhati.

The root Jakkha is used in the sense of 'eating' and also 'laughter'. The particle 'ca' is for the purpose of including the meaning of laughter. Jakkhati.

Likha lekhane. Likhati, sallekhati. Atisallekhatevāyaṃ samaṇo. Lekhā, lekhanaṃ, lekhako, likhitaṃ, sallekhapaṭipatti, etā dakhiādikā likhapariyantā “parassabhāsā”ti saddasatthavidū vadanti.

The root likha is in the sense of writing. Likhati, sallekhati. This ascetic excessively effaces himself. Lekhā, lekhanaṃ, lekhako, likhitaṃ, sallekhapaṭipatti—these roots, beginning with dakhi and ending with likha, are called 'parassabhāsā' (active voice) by the grammarians.

Dhukkha dhikkha sandīpanakilesanajīvanesu. Dhukkhati. Dhikkhati. Saddasatthavidū pana “dhukkhate dhikkhate”ti attanobhāsaṃ vadanti. Tathā ito parāni rūpānipi.

The roots dhukkha and dhikkha are in the senses of inflaming, defiling, and living. Dhukkhati. Dhikkhati. The grammarians, however, say that dhukkhate and dhikkhate are in the middle voice. Likewise for the forms that follow from here.

Rukkha vakkha varaṇe. Varaṇaṃ saṃvaraṇaṃ. Rukkhati. Vakkhati. Rukkho, vakkho. Ettha ca vakkhoti rukkhoyeva. Tathā hi “sādūni ramaṇīyāni, santi vakkhā araññajā”ti jātakapāṭho dissati. Imāni pana rukkhassa nāmāni –

The roots rukkha and vakkha are in the sense of covering. Varaṇa is covering. Rukkhati. Vakkhati. Rukkho, vakkho. And here, vakkho means a tree. For so it is seen in the Jātaka text: 'Sweet and delightful are the trees born in the forest.' Now, these are the names for a tree—

“Rukkho mahīruho vakkho, pādapo jagatīruho;

Ago nago kujo sākhī, sālo ca viṭapī taru;

Dumo phalī tu phalavā, gaccho tu khuddapādapo”ti.

'A tree is a rukkho, mahīruho, vakkho, pādapo, jagatīruho; ago, nago, kujo, sākhī, sālo, viṭapī, and taru; dumo. A fruit-bearing tree is a phalī or phalavā, and a gaccho is a small tree.'

Kecettha vadeyyuṃ “nanu ca sālasaddena sālarukkhoyeva vutto, nāñño ‘sālā phandanamāluvā’ti payogadassanato, atha kimatthaṃ sālasaddena yo koci rukkho [M 0.0024] vutto”ti? Na sālarukkhoyeva sālasaddena vutto, atha kho sālarukkhepi vanappatijeṭṭharukkhepi yasmiṃ kasmiñci rukkhepi “sālo”ti vohārassa dassanato aññepi rukkhā vuttā. Tathā hi sālarukkhopi “sālo”ti vuccati. Yathāha “seyyathāpi bhikkhave gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre mahantaṃ sālavanaṃ, tañcassa elaṇḍehi sañchannaṃ. Antarena yamakasālāna”nti. Vanappatijeṭṭharukkhopi. Yathāha –

Herein, some might say: 'Surely, by the word sāla, only the sāla tree is meant, and no other, as is seen from the usage, “sālā phandanamāluvā”? Why then is any tree whatsoever meant by the word sāla?' It is not that only the sāla tree is meant by the word sāla; rather, because the term sāla is found in usage for the sāla tree, for a chief forest tree, and for any tree whatsoever, other trees are also meant. For so the sāla tree itself is called sāla. As it is said: 'Just as, bhikkhus, not far from a village or a town, there might be a great sāla grove, and it might be covered with castor-oil plants... between the twin sāla trees...' And also a chief forest tree. As it is said:

“Taveva deva vijite, tavevuyyānabhūmiyā;

Ujuvaṃsā mahāsālā, nīlobhāsā manoramā”ti.

'Yours alone, O deva, is the conquered territory; yours alone the garden-lands; with straight trunks, the great sāla trees, of dark-blue lustre, are delightful.'

Yo koci rukkhopi. Yathāha “atha kho taṃ bhikkhave māluvabījaṃ aññatarasmiṃ sālamūle nipateyyā”ti. Atridaṃ vuccati –

And any tree whatsoever. As it is said: 'Then, bhikkhus, that māluvā seed might fall at the root of some tree.' Herein, this is said:

“Sālarukkhe jeṭṭharukkhe,

Yasmiṃ kasmiñci pādape;

Sālo iti ravo sālā,

Sandhāgāre thiyaṃ siyā”ti.

'For a sāla tree, a chief tree, or for any tree whatsoever, the term is sālo. Sālā in the feminine may be an assembly hall.'

Sikkha vijjopādāne. Sikkhati. Sikkhā, sikkhanaṃ, sikkhitaṃ sippaṃ, sikkhako, sikkhito, sekkho, asekkho. Kakāralope “sekho asekho”ti rūpāni bhavanti. Tattha sikkhitoti sañjātasikkho, asikkhīti vā sikkhito, tathā hi kattuppayogo dissati “ahaṃ kho pana susikkhito anavayo sake ācariyake kumbhakārakamme”ti.

The root sikkha is in the sense of acquiring knowledge. Sikkhati. Sikkhā, sikkhanaṃ, sikkhitaṃ sippaṃ, sikkhako, sikkhito, sekkho, asekkho. With the elision of the letter ka, the forms sekho and asekho occur. Therein, sikkhito means one who has acquired training. Or, sikkhito is used for the aorist sikkhī. For so the agentive usage is seen: 'I, indeed, am well-trained and flawless in my own teacher's craft of pottery.'

Bhikkha yācane. Bhikkhati. Bhikkhu, bhikkhā, bhikkhanaṃ, bhikkhako, bhikkhitaṃ bhojanaṃ. Ettha pana “bhikkhu yati samaṇo muni pabbajito [M 0.0025] anagāro tapassī tapodhano” iccetāni pariyāyavacanāni. Etesu sāsane “bhikkhū”ti upasampanno vuccati. Kadāci pana “bhikkhusataṃ bhojesi, bhikkhusahassaṃ bhojesī”tiādīsu sāmaṇerepiupādāya “bhikkhū”ti vohāro pavattati, tāpasāpi ca samaṇasaddādīhi vuccanti, “ahū atītamaddhāne, samaṇo khantidīpano”tiādi ettha nidassanaṃ.

The root bhikkha is in the sense of asking. Bhikkhati. Bhikkhu, bhikkhā, bhikkhanaṃ, bhikkhako, bhikkhitaṃ bhojanaṃ. Here, however, bhikkhu, yati, samaṇa, muni, pabbajita, anagāra, tapassī, and tapodhana—these are synonymous terms. Among these, in the Dispensation, a bhikkhu is said to be one who is fully ordained. Sometimes, however, as in 'he fed a hundred bhikkhus' or 'he fed a thousand bhikkhus', the term bhikkhu is used to include even novices. And ascetics are also referred to by terms such as samaṇa; 'There was in a past time, the ascetic Khantidīpana' is an example here.

Dakkha vuddhiyaṃ sīghatte ca. Dakkhati, dakkhiṇā, dakkho. Dakkhanti vaddhanti sattā etāya yathādhippetāhi sampattīhi iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti dakkhiṇā, dātabbavatthu. Dakkhati kusalakamme aññasmiñca kiccākicce adandhatāya sīghaṃ gacchatīti dakkho, cheko, yo “kusalo”tipi vuccati.

The root dakkha is in the sense of growth and swiftness. Dakkhati, dakkhiṇā, dakkho. That by which beings grow and increase, becoming powerful, prosperous, and eminent through desired attainments, is dakkhiṇā, a thing to be given. One who proceeds swiftly, without sluggishness, in wholesome deeds and other duties, is dakkho, an expert, who is also called kusalo.

Dikkha muṇḍiopanayananiyamabbatādesesu. Dikkhadhātu muṇḍiye, upanayane, niyame, vate, ādese ca pavattati. Dikkhati. Dikkhito muṇḍo. Ettha siyā – nanu ca bho sarabhaṅgajātake “gandho isīnaṃ ciradikkhitānaṃ, kāyā cuto gacchati mālutenā”ti etasmiṃ padese aṭṭhakathācariyehi “ciradikkhitānanti cirapabbajitāna”nti vuttaṃ. Na hi tattha “ciramuṇḍāna”nti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sante kasmā idha “dikkhadhātu muṇḍiye vuttā”ti? Saccaṃ, tattha pana dikkhitasaddassa pabbajite vattanato “cirapabbajitāna”nti vuttaṃ, na dhātuatthassa vibhāvanatthaṃ. Ida pana dhātuatthavibhāvanatthaṃ muṇḍiye vuttā. Tāpasā hi muṇḍiyatthavācakena dikkhitasaddena vattuṃ yuttā. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathācariyehi cakkavattisuttatthavaṇṇanāyaṃ “kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā”ti imissā pāḷiyā atthavivaraṇe “tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajantāpi hi paṭhamaṃ kesamassuṃ ohārenti, tato paṭṭhāya parūḷhakese [M 0.0026] bandhitvā vivaranti, tena vuttaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā”ti evaṃ attho saṃvaṇṇito.

The root dikkha is in the senses of shaving the head, initiation, observance, vows, and declaration. The root dikkha applies to shaving the head, initiation, observance, vows, and declaration. Dikkhati. Dikkhito means shaven. Here, it might be said: 'Indeed, sir, in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, in the passage, “The fragrance of the long-initiated seers, released from their bodies, travels on the wind,” the commentators have said that ciradikkhitānaṃ means “of those long gone forth.” It is not said there “of those long shaven.” This being so, why is it said here that the root dikkha is in the sense of shaving the head?' True, but there the word dikkhita was explained as “long gone forth” because it applies to one who has gone forth, not for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the root. Here, however, it is stated in the sense of shaving the head for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the root. For it is fitting to speak of ascetics with the word dikkhita, which expresses the meaning of being shaven. For so the commentators, in the explanation of the meaning of the Cakkavatti Sutta, have explained the meaning of the Pāli text, 'having shaved off hair and beard, having donned ochre robes,' thus: 'For those going forth into the ascetic life also first shave off their hair and beard; from then on, they bind up their grown hair and let it down. Therefore it was said, “having shaved off hair and beard.”'

Ikkha dassanaṅkesu. Ikkhati, upekkhati, apekkhati. Upekkhā, apekkhā, paccavekkhaṇā. Kakāralope “upekhā, apekhā, upasampadāpekho”ti rūpāni bhavanti.

The root ikkha is in the senses of seeing and marking. Ikkhati, upekkhati, apekkhati. Upekkhā, apekhā, paccavekkhaṇā. With the elision of the letter ka, the forms upekhā, apekhā, and upasampadāpekho occur.

Dukkha hiṃsāgatīsu. Dakkhati. Dakkhako.

The root dukkha is in the senses of harming and going. Dakkhati. Dakkhako.

Cikkha cakkha viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Cikkhati, ācikkhati, abbhācikkhati. Ācikkhako. Cakkhati, cakkhu. Ettha cakkhūti cakkhatīti cakkhu, samavisamaṃ abhibyattaṃ vadantaṃ viya hotīti attho. Atha vā “sūpaṃ cakkhati, madhuṃ cakkhatī”tiādīsu viya yasmā assādatthopi cakkhusaddo bhavati, tasmā “cakkhati viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ rūpaṃ assādentaṃ viya hotī”ti assādatthopi gahetabbo. “Cakkhuṃ kho māgaṇḍiyaṃ rūpārāmaṃ rūparataṃ rūpasammudita”nti hi vuttaṃ. Satipi sotādīnaṃ saddārāmatādibhāve nirūḷhattā nayane eva cakkhusaddo pavattati paṅkajādisaddā viya padumādīsu.

The roots cikkha and cakkha are in the sense of clear speech. Cikkhati, ācikkhati, abbhācikkhati. Ācikkhako. Cakkhati, cakkhu. Herein, it makes things clear, therefore it is a cakkhu; the meaning is that it is as if it speaks, making manifest what is even and uneven. Or, since the word cakkhu also has the meaning of tasting, as in 'he tastes the soup' or 'he tastes the honey', it should also be taken in the sense of tasting, as in 'it is as if it tastes the form established by consciousness'. For it is said: 'The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, is devoted to forms, rejoices in forms.' Although the ear and other senses have delight in sounds and so on, by established usage the word cakkhu applies only to the eye, just as words like paṅkaja apply to the lotus and so on.

Cakkha’kkhi nayanaṃ, locanaṃ diṭṭhi dassanaṃ;

Pekkhanaṃ acchi pamhaṃ tu, “pakhuma”nti pavuccati.

'The eye is cakkha, akkhi, nayanaṃ, locanaṃ, diṭṭhi, dassanaṃ, pekkhanaṃ, and acchi. But pamhaṃ is called pakhuma.'

Etā rukkhādikā cakkhapariyantā “attanobhāsā”ti saddasatthavidū vadanti.
