These roots, beginning with rukkha and ending with cakkhu, are called 'attanobhāsā' (middle voice) by the grammarians.

Khakārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of roots ending in the letter kha.

Gakārantadhātu

Roots ending in the letter ga.

Gu karīsussagge. Karīsussaggo vaccakaraṇaṃ. Gavati. Ge sadde. Gāyati. Gītaṃ.

The root gu is in the sense of discharging excrement. Discharging excrement is defecating. Gavati. The root ge is in the sense of sound. Gāyati. Gītaṃ.

Vagga [M 0.0027] gatiyaṃ. Vaggati. Vaggo, vaggitaṃ. Ettha samudāyavasena vagganaṃ pavattanaṃ vaggo. Vaggitanti gamanaṃ. Tathā hi nāgapetavatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yo so majjhe assatarīrathena catubbhi yuttena suvaggitena. Amhākaṃ putto ahu majjhimo so, amaccharī dānapatī virocatī”ti imissā pāḷiyā atthaṃ vadantehi “suvaggitenāti sundaragamanenā”ti. Kiñci bhiyyo kriyāpadampi ca diṭṭhaṃ “dhunanti vagganti pavattanti cambare”ti.

The root vagga is in the sense of movement. Vaggati. Vaggo, vaggitaṃ. Herein, a vaggo is the proceeding of a group by way of a collection. Vaggitaṃ means going. For so, in the commentary on the Nāgapetavatthu, when stating the meaning of this Pāli text: 'He who is in the middle, with a mule-chariot yoked with four, beautifully moving; he was our middle son, unselfish, a master of giving, he shines,' they say: 'suvaggitena means with beautiful movement.' Moreover, a verb form is also seen: 'They shake, they move, they proceed in the sky.'

Ragi lagi agi vagi magi igi rigi ligi tagi sagi gamane ca. Cakāro gatipekkhako. Raṅgati. Raṅgo. Laṅgati. Laṅgo, laṅgī. Aṅgati, aṅgeti. Aṅgo, samaṅgī, samaṅgitā, aṅgaṃ, aṅgaṇaṃ. Vaṅgati. Vaṅgo. Maṅgati. Maṅgo, upaṅgo, maṅgalaṃ. Iṅgati. Iṅgitaṃ. Riṅgati. Riṅganaṃ. Liṅgati. Liṅganaṃ. Ulliṅgati, ulliṅganaṃ. Taṅgati. Taṅganaṃ. Saṅgati. Saṅganaṃ. Tattha aṅganti yesaṃ kesañci vatthūnaṃ avayavo, sarīrampi kāraṇampi ca vuccati. Aṅgaṇanti katthaci kilesā vuccanti “rāgo aṅgaṇa”ntiādīsu. Rāgādayo hi aṅganti etehi taṃsamaṅgipuggalā nihīnabhāvaṃ gacchantīti “aṅgaṇānī”ti vuccanti. Katthaci malaṃ vā paṅko vā “tasseva rajassa vā aṅgaṇassa vā pahānāya vāyamatī”tiādīsu. Añjati makkhetīti hi aṅgaṇaṃ, malādi. Katthaci tathārūpo vivaṭappadeso “cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ, bodhiyaṅgaṇa”ntiādīsu. Añjati tattha ṭhitaṃ atisundaratāya abhibyañjetīti hi aṅgaṇaṃ, vivaṭo bhūmippadeso. Iccevaṃ –

The roots `ragi`, `lagi`, `agi`, `vagi`, `magi`, `igi`, `rigi`, `ligi`, `tagi`, and `sagi` are in the sense of 'going'. The particle `ca` refers to 'movement'. `Raṅgati`. `Raṅgo`. `Laṅgati`. `Laṅgo`, `laṅgī`. `Aṅgati`, `aṅgeti`. `Aṅgo`, `samaṅgī`, `samaṅgitā`, `aṅgaṃ`, `aṅgaṇaṃ`. `Vaṅgati`. `Vaṅgo`. `Maṅgati`. `Maṅgo`, `upaṅgo`, `maṅgalaṃ`. `Iṅgati`. `Iṅgitaṃ`. `Riṅgati`. `Riṅganaṃ`. `Liṅgati`. `Liṅganaṃ`. `Ulliṅgati`, `ulliṅganaṃ`. `Taṅgati`. `Taṅganaṃ`. `Saṅgati`. `Saṅganaṃ`. There, `aṅga` refers to the limb or part of any object, and it is also called the body or a cause. In some places, `aṅgaṇa` refers to defilements, as in `rāgo aṅgaṇa` (lust is a defilement), and so on. For lust and other defilements are called `aṅgaṇāni` because by them, individuals endowed with them go to a low state. In some places, it refers to dirt or mud, as in, "he strives for the abandonment of that very dust or `aṅgaṇa`," and so on. For `aṅgaṇa` is that which smears or anoints, such as dirt. In some places, it refers to an open space of such a kind, as in `cetiyaṅgaṇa` (the courtyard of a shrine), `bodhiyaṅgaṇa` (the courtyard of a Bodhi tree), and so on. For `aṅgaṇa` is that which, being situated there, makes manifest with extreme beauty—an open expanse of ground. Thus—

Rāgādīsu kilesesu, paṅke kāyamalamhi ca;

Vivaṭe bhūmibhāge ca, “aṅgaṇa”nti ravo gato.

In the defilements such as lust, in mud and bodily impurity, and in an open expanse of ground, the word `aṅgaṇa` is used.

Yugi [M 0.0028] jugi vajjane. Yuṅgati. Juṅgati.

The roots `yugi` and `jugi` are in the sense of 'avoiding'. `Yuṅgati`. `Juṅgati`.

Ragi saṅkāyaṃ. Raṅgati.

The root `ragi` is in the sense of 'doubt'. `Raṅgati`.

Laga saṅgeca. Ca kāro anantaravuttāpekkhako. Lagati. Ca jato na hoti laganaṃ. Baḷise laggo.

The root `laga` is also in the sense of 'attachment'. The particle `ca` refers to what was just said. `Lagati`. And clinging does not arise. `Laggo baḷise` (stuck on a hook).

Thagaṃ saṃvaraṇe. Thagati.

The root `thaga` is in the sense of 'covering'. `Thagati`.

Agga kuṭilagatiyaṃ. Aggatīti aggi, kuṭilaṃ gacchatīti attho.

The root `agga` is in the sense of 'crooked movement'. `Aggati` means `aggi` (fire); the meaning is 'it moves crookedly'.

Aggi dhūmasikho joti, jātavedo sikhī gini;

Aggini bhāṇumā tejo, pāvako tivako’nalo.

Smoke-crested, light, knower of beings, the flame-crested one, fire; fire, the luminous one, radiance, the purifier, the fierce one, and fire.

Hutāsano dhūmaketu, vessānaro ca accimā;

Ghatāsano vāyusakho, dahano kaṇhavattani.

Oblation-eater, smoke-bannered, belonging to all men, and the flame-filled one; ghee-eater, friend of the wind, the burner, and the one with a black path.

Etā guādikā aggapariyantā “parassabhāsā”ti saddasatthavidū vadanti.

These roots, beginning with `gu` and ending with `agga`, are called `parassabhāsā` (active voice), say those skilled in the science of words.

Gā gatiyaṃ. Gāti.

The root `gā` is in the sense of 'going'. `Gāti`.

Gu sadde. Gavati.

The root `gu` is in the sense of 'sound'. `Gavati`.

Gu uggame. Uggamo uggamanaṃ pākaṭatā. Gavati. Saddasatthavidū panimāsaṃ “gāte gavate”ti attanobhāsattaṃ vadanti.

The root `gu` is in the sense of 'rising'. `Uggamo` means 'rising' or 'manifestation'. `Gavati`. But those skilled in the science of words say that these roots, in the forms `gāte` and `gavate`, are `attanobhāsā` (middle voice).

Gakārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of roots ending in the letter `ga`.

Ghakārantadhātu

Roots ending in the letter `gha`.

Ghā gandhopādāne. Ghāti. Ghānaṃ. Gandhaṃ ghatvā. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “gandhaṃ ghatvā sati muṭṭhā”ti. Etissā pana divādigaṇaṃ pattāya “ghāyati ghāyitvā”ti rūpāni bhavanti.

The root `ghā` is in the sense of 'taking up scent'. `Ghāti`. `Ghānaṃ` (the nose). `Gandhaṃ ghatvā` (having smelled a scent). Here, this is the Pāli text: "Having smelled a scent, mindfulness is lost." But for this root, when it belongs to the `divādi` group, the forms `ghāyati` and `ghāyitvā` occur.

Ghu [M 0.0029] abhigamane. Abhigamanaṃ adhigamanaṃ. Ghoti.

The root `ghu` is in the sense of 'approaching'. `Abhigamanaṃ` means 'approaching' or 'arriving'. `Ghoti`.

Jaggha hasane. Jagghati, sañjagghati. Sañjagghittho mayā saha. Jagghitumpi na sobhati. Jagghitvā.

The root `jaggha` is in the sense of 'laughing'. `Jagghati`, `sañjagghati`. `Sañjagghittho mayā saha` (You laughed together with me). `Jagghitumpi na sobhati` (Even to laugh is not seemly). `Jagghitvā`.

Taggha pālane. Tagghati.

The root `taggha` is in the sense of 'protecting'. `Tagghati`.

Sighi āghāne. Āghānaṃ ghānena gandhānubhavanaṃ. Siṅghati, upasiṅghati. Upasiṅghitvā. Ārā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ. Etā “parassabhāsā”ti saddasatthavidū vadanti.

The root `sighi` is in the sense of 'smelling'. `Āghānaṃ` is the experiencing of scents through the nose. `Siṅghati`, `upasiṅghati`. `Upasiṅghitvā`. `Ārā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ` (From afar, I sniff the water-born). These are called `parassabhāsā` (active voice), say those skilled in the science of words.

Ghu sadde. Ghoti, ghavati.

The root `ghu` is in the sense of 'sound'. `Ghoti`, `ghavati`.

Raghi laghi gatyakkhepe. Gatyakkhepo gatiyā akkhepo. Raṅghati, laṅghati, ullaṅghati. Laṅghitā, ullaṅghikāpīti, laṅghitvā.

The roots `raghi` and `laghi` are in the sense of 'leaping movement'. `Gatyakkhepo` is the impetus of going. `Raṅghati`, `laṅghati`, `ullaṅghati`. `Laṅghitā`, `ullaṅghikāpīti`, `laṅghitvā`.

Maghi ketave ca. Cakāro pubbatthāpekkho. Maṅghati.

The root `maghi` is also in the sense of 'deceit'. The particle `ca` refers to the preceding meaning. `Maṅghati`.

Rāgha lāgha sāmatthiye. Rāghati. Lāghati.

The roots `rāgha` and `lāgha` are in the sense of 'ability'. `Rāghati`. `Lāghati`.

Dāgha āyāse ca. Āyāso kilamanaṃ. Cakāro sāmatthiyāpekkhako. Dāghati. Nidāgho.

The root `dāgha` is also in the sense of 'exertion'. `Āyāso` means 'weariness'. The particle `ca` refers to 'ability'. `Dāghati`. `Nidāgho`.

Silāgha katthane. Katthanaṃ pasaṃsanaṃ. Silāghati. Silāghā. Buddhassa silāghate. Silāghitvā. “Attanobhāsā”ti saddasatthavidū vadanti.

The root `silāgha` is in the sense of 'boasting'. `Katthanaṃ` means 'praising'. `Silāghati`. `Silāghā`. `Buddhassa silāghate` (He boasts of the Buddha). `Silāghitvā`. This root is `attanobhāsā` (middle voice), say those skilled in the science of words.

Gha kārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of roots ending in the letter `gha`.

Iti bhūvādāgaṇe kavaggantadhāturūpāni

Thus, the forms of roots ending in the `ka`-class in the `bhūvādi` group.

Samattāni.

Completed.

Cakārantadhātu

Roots Ending in the Letter `c`

Idāni [M 0.0030] cavaggantadhāturūpāni vuccante –

Now, the forms of roots ending in the ca-group are explained.

Suca soke. Socati. Soko, socanā, socaṃ, socanto, socantī, socantaṃ kulaṃ, socitvā.

The root 'suc' is in the sense of grief. He grieves. Grief, grieving, grieving; grieving (masculine), grieving (feminine), a grieving family; having grieved.

Kuca sadde tāre. Tārasaddo accuccasaddo. Kocati. Uccasaddaṃ karotīti attho.

The root 'kuc' is in the sense of a loud sound. The word 'tāra' means a very high sound. It sounds loudly. The meaning is: it makes a high sound.

Kuñca koṭilla’ppībhāvesu. Kuñcati. Kuñcikā, kuñcitakeso. Kuñcitvā.

The root 'kuñc' is in the senses of crookedness or diminishing. It bends. A key, one with curly hair. Having bent.

Luñca apanayane. Luñcati. Luñcako, luñcituṃ, luñcitvā.

The root 'luñc' is in the sense of removing. He plucks. A plucker, to pluck, having plucked.

Añcu gatipūjanāsu. Maggaṃ añcati. Buddhaṃ añcati. Uddhaṃ anuggantvā tiriyaṃ añcitoti tiracchāno. Kaṭukañcukatā.

The root 'añc' is in the senses of going or honoring. He goes along the path. He honors the Buddha. Having not gone upwards, it goes sideways—thus, an animal. The state of being pungent and crooked.

Vañcu cañcu tañcu gatiyaṃ. Vañcati. Cañcati. Tañcati. Mañcati. Santi pādā avañcanā. Avañcanāti vañcituṃ gantuṃ asamatthā.

The roots 'vañc', 'cañc', and 'tañc' are in the sense of going. He deceives. He wavers. He falters. He thinks. 'There are feet that are unswerving (avañcanā).' 'Avañcanā' means unable to go deceitfully.

Gucu gaṇecu theyyakaraṇe. Thenanaṃ theyyaṃ, corikā. Tassa kriyā theyyakaraṇaṃ. Gocati. Gaṇecati.

The roots 'guc' and 'gaṇec' are in the sense of committing theft. Stealing is theft, larceny. The action of that is committing theft. He steals. He steals.

Acca pūjāyaṃ accati. Brahmāsurasuraccito.

The root 'acc' is in the sense of honoring. He honors. Honored by Brahmās, asuras, and gods.

Tacca hiṃsāyaṃ. Taccati.

The root 'tacc' is in the sense of harming. He harms.

Cacca jacca paribhāsanavajjanesu. Caccati. Jaccati.

The roots 'cacc' and 'jacc' are in the senses of reviling and rejecting. He reviles. He rejects.

Kuca saṃpaccanakoṭillapaṭikkamavilekhanesu. Kucati, saṅkucati. Saṅkoco.

The root 'kuc' is in the senses of contracting, being crooked, recoiling, and scratching. He contracts, he shrinks. Contraction.

Taca saṃvaraṇe. Saṃvaraṇaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ. Tacati. Taco.

The root 'tac' is in the sense of covering. Covering is protection. It covers. Skin.

Dica [M 0.0031] thutiyaṃ. Dicati.

The root 'dic' is in the sense of praise. He praises.

Kuca saṅkocane. Kocati, saṅkocati. Saṅkoco.

The root 'kuc' is in the sense of contracting. He contracts, he shrinks. Contraction.

Byāca byājikaraṇe. Byājikaraṇaṃ byājikriyā. Byācati.

The root 'byāc' is in the sense of practicing deceit. Practicing deceit is a deceitful action. He deceives.

Vaca viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Viyattassa esā viyatti, tissaṃ viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, viyattāyaṃ vācāyanti adhippāyo. Viyattassa hi vadato puggalassa vasena vācā viyattā nāma vuccati. Yathā pana kucchisaddatiracchānagatādisaddo “abyattasaddo”ti vuccati, na evaṃ vacanasaṅkhāto saddo “abyattasaddo”ti vuccati viññātatthattā. “Vatti, vacati, vacanti. Vacasi” iccādīni suddhakattupadāni. “Vāceti, vācenti” iccādīni hetukattupadāni. “Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccati. Vuccanti. Santo sappurisā loke, devadhammāti vuccare” iccādīni kammapadāni. Garū pana vakārassa ukārādesavasena “uttaṃ uccate uccante”tiādīni icchanti, tāni sāsane appasiddhāni, sakkaṭabhāsānulomāni. Sāsanasmiñhi rakārāgamavisaye nipubbasseva vacassa vassa ukārādeso siddho “nirutti, niruttaṃ, nerutta”nti. Vacanaṃ, vācā, vaco, vacī, vuttaṃ, pavuttaṃ, vuccamānaṃ, adhivacanaṃ, vattabbaṃ, vacanīyaṃ, imāni nāmikapadāni. Vattuṃ, vattave, vatvā, vatvāna, imāni tumantādīni “parassabhāsā”ti saddasatthavidū vadanti.

The root 'vac' is in the sense of articulate speech. This articulation belongs to the articulate one; in that articulate speech, by that articulate speech, is the intention. Indeed, the speech of an articulate, speaking person is called 'articulate'. Just as the sound of the belly, of animals, and so on, is called 'inarticulate sound', so a sound designated as speech is not called 'inarticulate sound' because its meaning is understood. 'Vatti, vacati, vacanti. Vacasi' (He speaks, he speaks, they speak. You speak)—these and others are pure active forms. 'Vāceti, vācenti' (He causes to speak, they cause to speak)—these and others are causative active forms. 'Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccati' (Through understanding the meaning, the wise one is called learned). 'Vuccanti' (They are called). 'Santo sappurisā loke, devadhammāti vuccare' (The good and virtuous in the world are called godly)—these and others are passive forms. Some teachers, however, prefer forms like 'uttaṃ, uccate, uccante' by way of substituting 'u' for the letter 'v', but these are not established in the Teaching, being in conformity with the Sanskrit language. Indeed, in the Teaching, in the case of the augment 'r', the substitution of 'u' for the 'v' of 'vac' when preceded by 'ni' is established, as in 'nirutti, niruttaṃ, nerutta'. 'Vacanaṃ, vācā, vaco, vacī, vuttaṃ, pavuttaṃ, vuccamānaṃ, adhivacanaṃ, vattabbaṃ, vacanīyaṃ' (speaking, speech, word, utterance, what is said, declaration, being spoken, designation, what should be said, what is to be spoken)—these are nominal forms. 'Vattuṃ, vattave, vatvā, vatvāna' (to speak, to speak, having spoken, having spoken)—these and other forms beginning with the infinitive are what grammarians call 'parassabhāsā' (words for another, i.e., active voice).

Tattha vattīti vadati. Ākhyātapadañhetaṃ. Atthasaṃvaṇṇakehipi “vatti etāyāti vācā”ti nibbacanamudāhaṭaṃ. Saddasatthe ca tādisaṃ ākhyātapadaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. Ettha paneke vadanti “vacati, vacantītiādīni kriyāpadarūpāni buddhavacane aṭṭhakathāṭīkāsu satthesu ca anāgatattā chaḍḍetabbānī”ti. Tanna, yasmā sāsane “avaca, avaciṃsū”ti suddhakattupadāni ca “vāceti, vācentī”tiādīni hetukattupadāni ca dissanti, tasmā [M 0.0032] buddhavacanādīsu anāgatānipi “vacati, vacantī”tiādīni rūpāni gahetabbāni. Vaceyya, vuccatu, vucceyya. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ sabbattha vitthārato gahetabbaṃ.

Therein, 'vatti' means 'he speaks'. This is a verb form. Even by commentators on the meaning, the phrase 'speech is that by which one speaks' is cited as an example. And such a verb form is seen in grammatical treatises. But here some say, 'Forms such as "vacati, vacantī" (he speaks, they speak) are verb forms not found in the Buddha's words, commentaries, sub-commentaries, and treatises, and therefore should be discarded.' That is not so. Because in the Teaching, pure active forms such as 'avaca, avaciṃsū' (he spoke, they spoke) and causative active forms such as 'vāceti, vācentī' (he causes to speak, they cause to speak) are seen, therefore, even forms such as 'vacati, vacantī', though not found in the Buddha's words and so on, should be accepted. 'Vaceyya' (he might speak), 'vuccatu' (let it be said), 'vucceyya' (it might be said). The rest should all be understood in detail everywhere.

Parokkhārūpāni vadāma – vaca, vacu. Vace, vacittha. Vacaṃ, vacimha. Vacittha, vacire. Vacittho, vacivho. Vaciṃ, vacimhe.

We speak of the perfect tense forms: (Active) he spoke, they spoke; you spoke, you all spoke; I spoke, we spoke. (Middle) he spoke, they spoke; you spoke, you all spoke; I spoke, we spoke.

Hiyyattanīrūpāni vadāma – avacā, avacū. Avaco, avacuttha. Avocaṃ, avacumha. Avacuttha, avacutthuṃ. Avacase, avacuvhaṃ. Avaciṃ, avacamhase.

We speak of the aorist forms: (Active) he spoke, they spoke; you spoke, you all spoke; I spoke, we spoke. (Middle) he spoke, they spoke; you spoke, you all spoke; I spoke, we spoke.

Ajjatanīrūpāni vadāma – avaci, avocuṃ, avaciṃsu. Avoco, avocuttha. Avociṃ, avocumha. Avocā, avocu. Avacase, avocivaṃ. Avocaṃ, avocimhe.

We speak of the aorist forms: (Active) he spoke, they spoke, they spoke; you spoke, you all spoke; I spoke, we spoke. (Middle) he spoke, they spoke; you spoke, you all spoke; I spoke, we spoke.

Bhavissantīrūpāni vadāma – vakkhati, vakkhanti. Vakkhasi, vakkhatha. Vakkhāmi, vakkhāma. Vakkhate, vakkhante. Vakkhase, vakkhavhe. Vakkhassaṃ vakkhamhe.

We speak of the future tense forms: (Active) he will speak, they will speak; you will speak, you all will speak; I will speak, we will speak. (Middle) he will speak, they will speak; you will speak, you all will speak; I will speak, we will speak.

Imesaṃ pana padānaṃ “kathessati, kathessantī”tiādinā attho vattabbo. Vakkha roseti dhātussa ca “vakkhati, vakkhanti. Vakkhasī”tiādīni vatvā avasāne uttamapurisekavacanaṭṭhāne “vakkhemī”ti vattabbaṃ. Attho panimesaṃ “rosati, rosantī”tiādinā vattabbo. Ayaṃ vacavakkhadhātūnaṃ bhavissantīvattamānāvasena rūpasaṃsandanānayo. Aparānipi vacadhātussa bhavissantī sahitāni rūpāni bhavanti – vakkhissati, vakkhissanti. Vakkhissasi, vakkhissatha. Vakkhissāmi, vakkhissāma. Vakkhissate, vakkhissante. Vakkhissase, vakkhissavhe. Vakkhissaṃ, vakkhissāmhe.

Now, the meaning of these forms should be stated by way of 'kathessati, kathessantī,' and so on. And for the root 'vakkha' in the sense of 'to be angry,' having stated forms like 'vakkhati, vakkhanti, vakkhasī,' at the end, in the place of the first person singular, 'vakkhemī' should be stated. But the meaning of these should be stated by way of 'rosati, rosantī,' and so on. This is the method of comparing the forms for the roots 'vac' and 'vakkha' by way of the future and present tenses. Other forms of the root 'vac' combined with the future also exist: vakkhissati, vakkhissanti; vakkhissasi, vakkhissatha; vakkhissāmi, vakkhissāma; vakkhissate, vakkhissante; vakkhissase, vakkhissavhe; vakkhissaṃ, vakkhissāmhe.

Atrāyaṃ pāḷi –

Here is the Pāli text:

“Abhītakappe caritaṃ, ṭhapayitvā bhavābhave;

Imamhi kappe caritaṃ, pavakkhissaṃ suṇohi me”ti.

My conduct in the Fearless Aeon, setting aside existence after existence; my conduct in this aeon, I will declare—listen to me.

Gadratapañhepi [M 0.0033] “rājā tumhehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā gahapati patirūpaṃ āsanaṃ ñatvā nisīdathāti vakkhissatī”ti evamādiaṭṭhakathāpāṭho dissati, tasmāyeva edisī padamālā racitā. Vakkha roseti dhātussapi bhavissantīsahitāni rūpāni “vakkhissati, vakkhissantī”tiādīni bhavanti. Attho panimesaṃ “rosissati, rosissantī”tiādinā vattabbo. Ayaṃ vacavakkhadhātūnaṃ bhavissantīvaseneva rūpasaṃsandanānayo.

Even in the Gadratapañha, a commentary text such as this is seen: 'The king, having exchanged courtesies with you, recognizing a seat suitable for a householder, will say, "Sit down."'; therefore, such a series of forms is composed. Even for the root 'vakkha' in the sense of 'to be angry,' future tense forms such as 'vakkhissati, vakkhissantī' arise. The meaning of these, however, should be explained by way of 'rosissati, rosissantī,' and so on. This is the method of comparing the forms of the roots 'vac' and 'vakkha' by way of the future tense only.

Avacissā, vacissā, avacissaṃsu, vacissaṃsu. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. Idha pana vuttasaddassa atthuddhāraṃ vattabbampi avatvā upariyeva kathessāma ito ativiya vattabbaṭṭhānattā.

Avacissā, vacissā, avacissaṃsu, vacissaṃsu. The rest should all be understood. Here, however, without even giving an explanation of the meaning of the words already stated, we will discuss it further on, since this is a place where a great deal is to be explained.

Cu cavane. Cavati. Kārite “cāvetī”ti rūpaṃ. Devakāyā cuto. Cutaṃ padumaṃ. Cavituṃ, cavitvā.

The root 'cu' is in the sense of falling away. He falls away. In the causative, the form is 'cāveti' (he causes to fall away). 'Devakāyā cuto' (deceased from the realm of gods). 'Cutaṃ padumaṃ' (a fallen lotus). 'Cavituṃ' (to fall away), 'cavitvā' (having fallen away).

Loca dassane. Locati. Locanaṃ.

The root 'loc' is in the sense of seeing. He sees. Seeing.

Seca secane. Secati.

The root 'sec' is in the sense of sprinkling. He sprinkles.

Saca viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Sacati.

The root 'sac' has the meaning of articulation in speech. He articulates.

Kaca bandhane. Kacati.

The root 'kac' has the meaning of binding. He binds.

Maca muci kakkane. Kakkanaṃ sarīre ubbaṭṭanaṃ. Macati. Muñcati. Maci dhāraṇucchāyapūjanesu. Dhāraṇaṃ ucchāyo pūjananti tayo atthā. Tattha ucchāyo malaharaṇaṃ. Mañcati. Mañco, mañcanaṃ. Mañcati puggalaṃ dhāretīti mañco.

The roots 'mac' and 'muc' have the meaning of rubbing. 'Kakkanaṃ' is rubbing on the body. He rubs. He rubs. The root 'maci' has the meanings of holding, raising, and honoring. Holding, raising, honoring—these are the three meanings. Therein, 'ucchāyo' is the removal of impurities. He holds/raises/honors. A bed; the act of honoring. A bed ('mañco') is so called because it holds ('dhāreti') a person.

Paca byattikaraṇe. Pacati. Pāko, paripāko, vipāko, pakkaṃ phalaṃ.

The root 'pac' has the meaning of making manifest. He cooks. Cooking, thorough cooking, result, ripe fruit.

Thuca pasāde. Thocati.

The root 'thuc' has the meaning of making clear. He makes clear.

Vaca vaci dittiyaṃ. Vacati. Vañcati.

The roots 'vac' and 'vaci' have the meaning of shining. It shines. It shines.

Ruca [M 0.0034] dittiyaṃ rocane ca. Ditti sobhā. Rocanaṃ ruci. Rocati. Verocano. Samaṇassa rocate saccaṃ. Tassa te saggakāmassa, ekattamuparocitaṃ. Ayañca divādigaṇe ruciatthaṃ gahetvā “ruccatī”ti rūpaṃ janeti. Tena “gamanaṃ mayha ruccatī”ti pāḷi dissati. Curādigaṇe pana ruciatthaṃ gahetvā “roceti rocayatī”ti rūpāni janeti. Tena “kiṃ nu jātiṃ na rocesī”tiādikā pāḷiyo dissanti. Tegaṇikoyaṃ dhātu.

The root 'ruc' has the meanings of shining and pleasing. 'Ditti' is splendor. 'Rocanaṃ' is liking. It shines/pleases. Verocana. Truth pleases the ascetic. For you, who desire heaven, unity was pleasing. And this root, in the divādi group, taking the meaning of liking, produces the form 'ruccati'. Therefore, the Pāli text 'gamanaṃ mayhaṃ ruccati' (going pleases me) is seen. In the curādi group, however, taking the meaning of liking, it produces the forms 'roceti' and 'rocayati'. Therefore, Pāli texts such as 'kiṃ nu jātiṃ na rocesi' (why do you not delight in birth?) are seen. This root belongs to three groups.

Paca saṃpāke. Pacati, pacanti. Saddasatthavidū pana “attanobhāsā”ti vadanti.

The root 'pac' has the meaning of thorough cooking. He cooks, they cook. Experts in grammar, however, say these are 'attanobhāsā' (forms of the middle voice).

Añca byayagatiyaṃ. Byayagati vināsagati. Añcati.

The root 'añc' has the meaning of going to ruin. 'Byayagati' is going to destruction. It goes to ruin.

Yāca yācanāyaṃ. Brāhmaṇo nāgaṃ maṇiṃ yācati. Nāgo maṇiṃ yācito brāhmaṇena. Te taṃ asse ayācisuṃ. So taṃ rathamayācatha. Devadattaṃ āyācati. Evaṃ suddhakattari rūpāni bhavanti. Brāhmaṇo brāhmaṇena nāgaṃ maṇiṃ yāceti, yācayati, yācāpeti, yācāpayati. Evaṃ hetukattari. Rājā brāhmaṇena dhanaṃ yāciyati, yācayiyati, yācāpiyati, yācāpayiyati. Evaṃ kammani. Yācaṃ, yācanto, yācantī, yācantaṃ kulaṃ. Yācamāno, yācamānā, yācamānaṃ kulaṃ. Yācako, yācanā, yācitabbaṃ, yācituṃ, yācitvāna, yācituna, yāciya, yāciyāna. Evaṃ nāmikapadāni tumantādīni ca bhavanti.

The root 'yāc' has the meaning of begging. A brahmin begs a jewel from a nāga. The nāga is begged for the jewel by the brahmin. They begged him for those horses. He begged for that chariot. He begs from Devadatta. Thus, forms in the active voice arise. A brahmin causes another brahmin to beg a jewel from a nāga; he causes (him) to beg, he has (him) beg, he causes (him) to beg. Thus, in the causative active. Wealth is caused to be begged from a brahmin by the king; it is caused to be begged, it is made to be begged, it is caused to be begged. Thus, in the passive. Begging; he who begs, she who begs, a family that begs. He who is begging, she who is begging, a family that is begging. A beggar, the act of begging, what should be begged, to beg, having begged, having begged, having begged, having begged. Thus, nominal forms and those ending in '-tum', etc., arise.

Paca pāke. Odanaṃ pacati. “Ubhayatobhāsā”ti saddasatthavidū vadanti. Yathā pana sāsane “paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti [M 0.0035] vacadhātussa kammani rūpaṃ pasiddhaṃ, na tathā pacadhātussa. Evaṃ santepi garū “tayā paccate odano”ti tassa kammani rūpaṃ vadanti. Sāsane pana avisesato “paccate”ti vā “paccatī”ti vā vuttassapi padassa akammakoyeva divādigaṇiko payogo icchitabbo “devadatto niraye paccati. Yāva pāpaṃ na paccatī”tiādidassanato. Kecettha vadeyyuṃ “sayameva pīyate pānīyantiādi viya bhūvādigaṇapakkhiko kammakattuppayogo esa, tasmā ‘sayamevā’ti padaṃ ajjhāharitvā ‘sayameva devadatto paccatī’tiādinā attho vattabbo”ti tanna, “sayameva pīyate pānīya”nti ettha hi pānīyaṃ manussā pivanti, na pānīyaṃ pānīyaṃ pivati. Manusseheva taṃ pīyate, na sayaṃ. Evaṃ parassa pānakriyaṃ paṭicca kammabhūtampi taṃ sukarapānakriyāvasena sukarattā attanāva sijjhantaṃ viya hotīti “sayameva pīyate pānīya”nti rūḷhiyā payogo kato.

The root 'pac' has the meaning of cooking. He cooks rice. Grammarians say it is 'ubhayatobhāsā' (having both voices). Just as in the Teaching the passive form of the root 'vac', 'he is called wise' (`paṇḍitoti pavuccatī`), is well-known, this is not so for the root 'pac'. Even so, the teachers state its passive form as 'the rice is cooked by you' (`tayā paccate odano`). In the Teaching, however, for a word stated without distinction as either 'paccate' or 'paccatī', the usage should be understood as active and belonging to the divādi group, from seeing examples such as 'Devadatta is tormented in hell' and 'as long as evil does not ripen'. Some here might say, 'Like 'the water is drunk by itself', this is a usage where the object acts as the agent, belonging to the bhūvādi group; therefore, by supplying the word 'by itself', the meaning should be stated as 'Devadatta torments himself', etc.' That is not so. For in 'the water is drunk by itself', people drink the water; the water does not drink the water. It is drunk by people, not by itself. Thus, although it is the object of another's act of drinking, because the act of drinking it is easy, it is as if it is accomplished by itself. Hence, the idiomatic usage 'the water is drunk by itself' is employed.

“Sayameva kaṭo kariyate”ti etthāpi kaṭaṃ manussā karonti, na kaṭaṃ kaṭo karoti. Manusseheva kaṭo kariyate, na sayaṃ. Evaṃ parassa karaṇakriyaṃ paṭicca kammabhūtopi so sukaraṇa kriyāvasena sukarattā attanāva sijjhanto viya hotīti “sayameva kaṭo kariyate”ti rūḷhiyā payogo kato.

In 'the mat is made by itself'—here too, people make the mat; the mat does not make the mat. The mat is made by people, not by itself. Thus, although it is the object of another's act of making, because the act of making it is easy, it is as if it is accomplished by itself. Hence, the idiomatic usage 'the mat is made by itself' is employed.

Ettha yathā sayaṃsaddo pānīyaṃ pānīyeneva pīyate, na amhehi. Kaṭo kaṭeneva kariyate, na amhehīti sakammakavisayattā payogānaṃ aññassa kriyāpaṭisedhanasaṅkhātaṃ atthavisesaṃ vadati, na tathā “devadatto niraye paccati, kammaṃ paccatī”tiādīsu tumhehi ajjhāharito sayaṃsaddo atthavisesaṃ vadati akammakavisayattā etesaṃ payogānaṃ. Evaṃ [M 0.0036] “devadatto”tiādikassa paccattavacanassa akammakakattuvācakattā kammarahitasuddhakattuvācakattā ca “paccatī”ti idaṃ divādigaṇikarūpanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pacadhātu saddasatthe divādigaṇa vutto natthīti ce? Natthi vā atthi vā, kimettha saddasatthaṃ karissati, pāḷi eva pamāṇaṃ, tasmā mayaṃ lokavohārakusalassa bhagavato pāḷinayaññeva gahetvā imaṃ pacadhātuṃ divādigaṇepi pakkhipissāma. Tathā hi dhammapālācariya anuruddhācariyādīhi abhisaṅkhatā divādigaṇikappayogā dissanti –-

Here, just as the word 'sayaṃ' (by oneself)—because the scope of the usages is the agent itself—conveys a special meaning characterized as the denial of another's action (as if to say, 'water is drunk by water itself, not by us; a mat is made by the mat itself, not by us'), it is not so in cases like 'Devadatta is tormented in hell' and 'kamma ripens', where the word 'sayaṃ' supplied by you does not convey such a special meaning, because the scope of these usages is already the agent itself. Thus, because a personal noun like 'Devadatta' is expressive of an agent whose action is its own, and is expressive of a pure agent devoid of an object, the form 'paccati' should be seen as a form of the divādi group. If it is said that the root 'pac' is not mentioned in the divādi group in the grammatical treatises, we reply: whether it is mentioned or not, what can the grammatical treatises do here? The Pāli text itself is the authority. Therefore, taking the method of the Pāli of the Blessed One, who is skilled in worldly convention, we shall also place this root 'pac' in the divādi group. For indeed, usages belonging to the divādi group composed by teachers such as the Ācariya Dhammapāla and the Ācariya Anuruddha are seen:

Ñāṇayuttavaraṃ tattha, datvā sandhiṃ tihetukaṃ;

Pacchā paccati pākānaṃ, pavatte aṭṭhake duve.

There, having given a three-rooted connection to the excellent one endowed with wisdom; later, of the results, it ripens, in the course of the two octads.

Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāra-vipākāni ca paccati

And the unprompted and prompted results ripen.

Iccevamādayo. Ettha pana tesaṃ idameva pāḷiyā na sameti. Ye curādigaṇamhi sakammakabhāvena bhūvādigaṇe ca akammakabhāvena pavattassa bhūdhātusseva bhūvādigaṇe pavattassa sakamakassapi sato divādigaṇaṃ patvā akammakabhūtassa pacadhātussa sakammakattamicchanti. Etañhi sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane kuto labbhā, tasmā bhagavato pāvacane sotūnaṃ saṃsayasamugghāṭatthaṃ ettha imaṃ nītiṃ paṭṭhapema –

And so on. Here, however, this very view of theirs does not agree with the Pāli. There are those who desire that the root 'pac' becomes intransitive upon reaching the divādi group, by analogy with the root 'bhū' (which is transitive in the curādi group and intransitive in the bhūvādi group). Where can this be found in the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries, the word of the Buddha? Therefore, to dispel the doubts of the listeners regarding the Blessed One's teaching, we shall establish this principle here:

Vināpi upasaggena, gaṇanānattayogato;

Sakammākammakā honti, dhātū pacabhidādayo.

Even without prefixes, due to belonging to various groups, roots such as 'pac' and 'bhid' can be both transitive and intransitive.

Puriso odanaṃ pacati. Sa bhūtapacaniṃ paci. Odano paccati. Kammaṃ paccati. Vīhisīsaṃ paccati. Rukkhaphalāni paccanti. Nāgo pākāraṃ bhindati. Taḷākapāḷi bhijjati. Bhijjanadhammaṃ bhijjati. Ettha ca sayaṃsaddaṃ ajjhāharitvā “sayameva odano paccatī”tiādinā vuttepi “puriso sayameva pāṇaṃ hanati. Bhagavā sayameva [M 0.0037] ñeyyadhammaṃ abujjhī”ti payogesu parassa āṇattisambhūtahananakriyāpaṭisedhamiva paropadesasambhūtabujjhanakriyāpaṭisedhanamiva ca aññassa kriyāpaṭisedhanavasena vuttattā yo sayaṃsaddavasena kammakattubhāvaparikappo, taṃ na pamāṇaṃ. Sayaṃsaddo hi suddhakattuatthepi dissati, na kevalaṃ “sayameva pīyate pānīya”ntiādīsu kammattheyeva, tasmā sāsanānurūpena attho gahetabbo nayaññūhi.

A man cooks rice. He cooked in the Bhūtapācanī hell. The rice cooks. Kamma ripens. The head of paddy ripens. The fruits of the tree ripen. A nāga breaks the wall. The bank of the lake breaks. That which has the nature of breaking, breaks. Here, even when one supplies the word 'sayaṃ' and says, 'The rice cooks by itself,' etc., because this is stated as a denial of another's action—just as in the usages 'The man himself kills a living being' or 'The Blessed One himself understood the knowable Dhamma' it implies a rejection of the act of killing arising from another's command, or a rejection of the act of understanding arising from another's instruction—the supposition of an object-as-agent status based on the word 'sayaṃ' is not an authority. For the word 'sayaṃ' is also seen with the meaning of the agent itself, not only in the passive sense as in 'The drink is drunk by itself.' Therefore, the meaning should be grasped by those skilled in method in accordance with the Teaching.

Vināpi upasaggena, vināpi ca gaṇantaraṃ;

Sakammākammakā honti, atthato divuādayo.

Even without a prefix, and even without belonging to a different group, roots such as 'div' can be transitive or intransitive according to their meaning.

Kāmaguṇehi dibbati. Paccāmitte dibbati. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

One sports with sensual pleasures. One gambles against enemies. Other examples should also be supplied.

Gaṇantarañcopasaggaṃ, vināpi atthanānataṃ;

Payogato sakammā ca, akammā ca gamādayo.

Even without another group or a prefix, due to diversity of meaning and from usage, roots such as 'gam' are both transitive and intransitive.

Puriso maggaṃ gacchati. Gambhīresupi atthesu ñāṇaṃ gacchati. Dhammaṃ carati. Tattha tattha carati.

A man goes on the path. Knowledge penetrates even into deep meanings. He lives the Dhamma. He wanders here and there.

Gaṇantarañcopasaggaṃ, payogañcatthanānataṃ;

Vināpi tividhā honti, disādī rūpabhedato.

Even without a difference of conjugation class, a prefix, or diversity of usage and meaning, they are threefold due to distinctions in form, such as 'disa' and so on.

Pāsādaṃ passati, pāsādaṃ dakkhati pāsādo dissati. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

One sees the palace, will see the palace, the palace is seen. Other forms should also be combined.

Sabhāvato sakammā tu, rudadhātādayo matā;

Sabhāvato akammā ca, nandadhātādayo matā.

By nature, roots such as 'rud' are considered transitive; and by nature, roots such as 'nand' are considered intransitive.

Mataṃ vā amma rodanti, idha nandati pecca nandati.

They weep for the dead, O mother; here one rejoices, and hereafter one rejoices.

Upasaggavaseneke, sakammāpi akammakā;

Sambhavanti tathekacce, akammāpi sakammakā.

Due to prefixes, some verbs, though transitive, become intransitive; and similarly, some verbs, though intransitive, become transitive.

Ekacce [M 0.0038] tupasaggehi, sakammā ca sakammakā;

Akammakā akammā ca, esatthopettha dīpito;

Some, due to prefixes, are both transitive and intransitive; and some intransitive verbs remain intransitive. This meaning is illuminated here.

Puriso gāmā niggacchati, dhanaṃ adhigacchati, puriso pāṇaṃ abhibhavati, himavatā pabhavanti mahānadiyo. Aññānipi payogāni yojetabbāni.

A man leaves the village, acquires wealth, a man overcomes a living being, great rivers originate from the Himalayas. Other applications should also be constructed.

Tattha yadi sāsane pacadhātussa kammani rūpaṃ siyā, “purisena kammaṃ kariyatī”ti payogo viya “purisena odano paciyatī”ti payogo icchitabbo. Ye pana garū “tayā paccate odano”tiādīni icchanti, te saddasatthanayaṃ nissāya vadanti maññe. Evaṃ santepi upaparikkhitvā yuttāni ce, gahetabbāni. Kārite “puriso purisena purisaṃ vā odanaṃ pāceti, pācayati, pācāpeti, pācāpayati. Purisena puriso odanaṃ pāciyati, pācayiyati, pācāpiyati, pācāpayiyatī”ti rūpāni bhavanti. “Yathā daṇḍena gopālo, gāvaṃ pāceti gocara”ntiādīsu aññopi attho daṭṭhabbo.

Here, if in the Dispensation there were a passive form of the root 'pac', the usage 'rice is cooked by a man' should be accepted, just like the usage 'an action is done by a man.' But those teachers who desire forms such as 'the rice is cooked by you,' etc., I think they speak relying on the method of grammar. Even so, having examined them, if they are suitable, they should be accepted. In the causative, the forms are: 'a man has another man cook rice' (puriso purisena purisaṃ vā odanaṃ pāceti, pācayati, pācāpeti, pācāpayati). 'A man is caused to cook rice by another man' (purisena puriso odanaṃ pāciyati, pācayiyati, pācāpiyati, pācāpayiyatī). In examples such as 'Just as a herdsman with a stick makes the cow go to pasture,' another meaning also should be seen.

Pacaṃ, pacanto, pacantī, pacamāno, pacamānā. Pātabbaṃ, pacitaṃ, pacitabbaṃ, pacanīyaṃ, pacituṃ, pacitvā. Ettha ca “imassa maṃsañca pātabba”nti payogo udāharaṇaṃ. “Pacati, pacanti. Pacasī”tiādi padakkamo subodho.

'Cooking' (pacaṃ), 'cooking' (pacanto, pacantī), 'cooking' (pacamāno, pacamānā). 'To be drunk' (pātabbaṃ), 'cooked' (pacitaṃ), 'to be cooked' (pacitabbaṃ), 'to be cooked' (pacanīyaṃ), 'to cook' (pacituṃ), 'having cooked' (pacitvā). Here, the usage 'this meat should also be drunk' (imassa maṃsañca pātabbaṃ) is an example. The verb conjugation 'he cooks, they cook, you cook,' etc., is easily understood.

Sica gharaṇe. Secati, seko, “ubhatobhāsā”ti vadanti.

'Sica' in the sense of sprinkling. 'Secati' (he sprinkles), 'seko' (sprinkling). They say it is 'ubhatobhāsā' (having both voices).

Imāni cakārantadhāturūpāni.

These are forms of roots ending in the letter 'ca'.

Chakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'cha'.

Parassabhāsādibhāvaṃ, sabbesaṃ dhātunaṃ ito;

Paraṃ na byākarissaṃ so, sāsane īrito na hi.

The state of having the active voice and other forms for all roots beyond this I shall not explain, for it is not taught in the Dispensation.

Chu [M 0.0039] chedane. Choti. Chotvāna moḷiṃ varagandhavāsitaṃ. Acchocchuṃvata bho rukkhaṃ.

`Chu` in the sense of cutting. `Choti` (he cuts). `Chotvāna moḷiṃ varagandhavāsitaṃ` (having cut the top-knot, scented with excellent perfumes). `Acchocchuṃvata bho rukkhaṃ` (Indeed, they cut down the tree).

Milecha aviyattāyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Milecchati, milakkhu. Paccantimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti milakkhūsu aviññātāresu.

`Mileccha` in the sense of indistinct speech. `Milecchati` (he speaks indistinctly). `Milakkhu` (a barbarian). `Paccantimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti milakkhūsu aviññātāresu` (he is reborn in the border regions, among barbarians, the uncomprehending ones).

Vachi icchāyaṃ. Vañchati. Vañchitaṃ dhanaṃ.

`Vachi` in the sense of desiring. `Vañchati` (he desires). `Vañchitaṃ dhanaṃ` (desired wealth).

Achi āyāme. Añcati. Dīghaṃ vā añchanto dīghaṃ añchāmīti pajānāti.

`Achi` in the sense of stretching. `Añcati` (he stretches). `Dīghaṃ vā añchanto dīghaṃ añchāmīti pajānāti` (when stretching long, he understands: 'I am stretching long').

Huccha koṭille. Hucchati.

`Huccha` in the sense of crookedness. `Hucchati` (he is crooked).

Muccha mohamucchāsu. Mucchati. Mucchito visavegena, visaññī samapajjatha. Mucchā, mucchitvā.

`Muccha` in the sense of infatuation and stupefaction. `Mucchati` (he is infatuated). `Mucchito visavegena, visaññī samapajjatha` (stupefied by the force of the poison, he became unconscious). `Mucchā` (infatuation, stupefaction). `Mucchitvā` (having been infatuated/stupefied).

Phucha visaraṇe phochati.

`Phucha` in the sense of scattering. `Phochati` (he scatters).

Yucha pamāde. Yucchati.

`Yucha` in the sense of negligence. `Yucchati` (he is negligent).

Uchi uñche. Uñcho pariyesanaṃ. Uñchati. Uñchācariyāya īhatha.

`Uchi` in the sense of gleaning. `Uñcho pariyesanaṃ` (gleaning is seeking). `Uñchati` (he gleans). `Uñchācariyāya īhatha` (strive for the practice of gleaning).

Ucha pipāsāyaṃ. Uchati.

`Ucha` in the sense of thirst. `Uchati` (he thirsts).

Puccha pañhe pucchati. Pucchitā, pucchako, puṭṭho, pucchito, pucchā. Bhikkhu vinayadharaṃ pañhaṃ pucchati. Pucchi, pucchituṃ. Pucchitvā. Ettha ca pañcavidhā pucchā adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā vimaticchedanāpucchā anumatipucchā kathetukamyatāpucchāti. Tāsaṃ nānattaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyādito gahetabbaṃ.

`Puccha` in the sense of questioning. `Pucchati` (he asks). `Pucchitā` (an asker). `Pucchako` (an asker). `Puṭṭho` (asked). `Pucchito` (asked). `Pucchā` (a question, inquiry). `Bhikkhu vinayadharaṃ pañhaṃ pucchati` (a monk asks a Vinaya-holder a question). `Pucchi` (he asked). `Pucchituṃ` (to ask). `Pucchitvā` (having asked). Here, there are five kinds of questions: `adiṭṭhajotanāpucchā` (the question to illuminate what has not been seen), `diṭṭhasaṃsandanāpucchā` (the question to examine what has been seen), `vimaticchedanāpucchā` (the question to cut off doubt), `anumatipucchā` (the question for agreement), and `kathetukamyatāpucchā` (the question from a desire to speak). Their diversity should be understood from the Aṭṭhasālinī and other such works.

Viccha gatiyaṃ. Vicchati. Vicchikā.

`Viccha` in the sense of going. `Vicchati` (he goes). `Vicchikā` (a scorpion).

Vacchu [M 0.0040] chedane. Vucchati. Vuttā, vuttavā, vuttasiro. Vakāragatassa akārassa uttaṃ.

`Vacchu` in the sense of cutting. `Vucchati` (he cuts). `Vuttā` (cut/shaven). `Vuttavā` (one who has cut/shaven). `Vuttasiro` (one with a shaven head). `Vakāragatassa akārassa uttaṃ` (the 'a' sound in the letter 'va' becomes 'u').

Vuttasaddo kesoharaṇepi dissati “kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro”tiādīsu. Ettha ca sirasaddena siroruhā vuttā yathā mañcasaddena mañcaṭṭhā, cakkhusaddena ca cakkhunissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Ropitepi “yathā sāradikaṃ bījaṃ, khette vuttaṃ virūhatī”tiādīsu. Kathitepi “vuttamidaṃ bhagavatā, vuttamarahatā”tiādisu. Atridaṃ vuccati –

The term `vutta` is also seen in the sense of hair removal, as in `kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro` (the young brahmin Kāpaṭika with a shaven head), and so on. Here, by the word `sira`, the hair on the head is meant, just as by the word `mañca`, those on the cot are meant, and by the word `cakkhu`, the consciousness dependent on the eye. It is also seen in the sense of sowing, as in `yathā sāradikaṃ bījaṃ, khette vuttaṃ virūhatī` (just as an autumn seed, sown in a field, sprouts), and so on. And it is seen in the sense of speaking, as in `vuttamidaṃ bhagavatā, vuttamarahatā` (this was spoken by the Blessed One, spoken by the Arahant), and so on. Here, this is said—

Vacchuvapavacavasā, vuttasaddo pavattati;

Kesohāre ropite ca, kathite ca yathākkamanti.

The word `vutta` occurs from the roots `vacchu`, `vapa`, `vaca`, and `vasa`; in hair removal, in sowing, and in speaking, respectively.

Aparo nayo – vuttasaddo “no ca kho paṭivutta”ntiādīsu vāpasamīkaraṇe dissati. “Pannalomo paradattavutto”tiādīsu jīvitavuttiyaṃ. “Paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto”tiādīsu apagame. “Gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samīhita”ntiādīsu pāvacanavasena pavattite. Loke pana “vutto pārāyano”tiādīsu ajjhene dissati, atridaṃ vuccati

Another method: the word `vutta` is seen in the sense of leveling, as in `no ca kho paṭivutta` (but not leveled), and so on. In `Pannalomo paradattavutto` (one whose hair has fallen out, whose livelihood is by means of others' gifts), and so on, it is in the sense of livelihood. In `Paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto` (a withered leaf fallen from its stalk), and so on, it is in the sense of departure. In `Gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samīhita` (the song was sung, performed), and so on, it is in the sense of being performed by way of proclamation. In the world, however, it is seen in the sense of study, as in `vutto pārāyano` (the Pārāyana was studied/recited), and so on. Here, this is said—

“Vāpasamīkaraṇe ca, atho jīvitavuttiyaṃ;

Apagame pāvacana-vasena ca pavattite;

Ajjhene cevametesu, vuttasaddo padissatī”ti.

And in leveling the ground, and also in livelihood; in departure, and in being performed by way of proclamation; and in study—in these meanings, the word `vutta` is seen.

Aparopi nayo – vuttasaddo saupasaggoca anupasaggo ca vapane vāpasamīkaraṇe kesohāre jīvitavuttiyaṃ pamuttabhāve [M 0.0041] pāvacanavasena pavattite ajjhene kathaneti evamādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa –

Yet another method: the word `vutta`, both with and without prefixes, is seen in these and other meanings: in sowing, in leveling the ground, in hair removal, in livelihood, in the state of being freed, in being performed by way of proclamation, in study, and in speaking. Thus it is—

“Gāvo tassa pajāyanti, khette vuttaṃ virūhati;

Vuttānaṃ phalamasnāti, yo mittānaṃ na dubbhatī”ti

His cattle multiply, what is sown in the field sprouts; he enjoys the fruit of what is sown, who is not treacherous to his friends.

Ādīsu vapane āgato. “No ca kho paṭivutta”ntiādīsu aṭṭhadantakādīhi vāpasamīkaraṇe. “Kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro”tiādīsu kesoharaṇe. “Pannalomo paradattavutto migabhūtena cetasā viharatī”tiādīsu jīvitavuttiyaṃ. “Seyyathāpi nāma paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto abhabbo haritatthāyā”tiādīsu bandhanato pamuttabhāve. “Yesamidaṃ etarahi porāṇaṃ mantapadaṃ gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samīhita”ntiādīsu pāvacanabhāvena pavattite. Loke pana “vutto gaṇo, vutto pārāyano”tiādīsu ajjhene. “Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā, dhammadāyādā me bhikkhave bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā”tiādīsu kathane. Atridaṃ vuccati –

In these and other instances, it has come in the sense of sowing. In `no ca kho paṭivutta` (but not leveled), and so on, it is in the sense of leveling the ground with eight-toothed rakes, and so on. In `Kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro` (the young brahmin Kāpaṭika with a shaven head), and so on, it is in the sense of hair removal. In `Pannalomo paradattavutto migabhūtena cetasā viharatī` (one whose hair has fallen out, whose livelihood is by means of others' gifts, who dwells with a mind like a wild animal), and so on, it is in the sense of livelihood. In `Seyyathāpi nāma paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto abhabbo haritatthāyā` (just as a withered leaf fallen from its stalk is incapable of becoming green again), and so on, it is in the state of being freed from bondage. In `Yesamidaṃ etarahi porāṇaṃ mantapadaṃ gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samīhita` (for whom this ancient verse, the word, is now sung, performed, accomplished), and so on, it is in the sense of being performed by way of proclamation. In the world, however, in `vutto gaṇo` (the group is recited), `vutto pārāyano` (the Pārāyana is recited), and so on, it is in the sense of study. In `Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā, dhammadāyādā me bhikkhave bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā` (This, indeed, was spoken by the Blessed One: 'Be heirs of the Dhamma, monks, not heirs of material things'), and so on, it is in the sense of speaking. Here, this is said—

Vapa vatu vacchuvaca-dhātūnaṃ vasato mato;

Sopasaggo nopasaggo, vuttasaddo yathārahaṃ.

The word `vutta` is held to be from the roots `vapa`, `vatu`, `vacchu`, `vaca`, and `vasa`, with or without prefixes, as is appropriate.

Vapane ca vāpasamī-karaṇe muṇḍatāya ca;

Jīvavutyaṃ pamuttatthe, vasā pāvacanassa tu;

Pavattite ca ajjhene, kathane cāti lakkhaye;

And in sowing, and in leveling the ground, and in baldness; in livelihood, in the sense of being freed, and by the power of the teaching; and in being performed, and in study, and in speaking—thus should one discern.

Taccha tanukaraṇe. Tacchati. Tacchako dāruṃ.

The root `taccha` is in the sense of thinning. `Tacchati` (he thins/carves). `Tacchako dāruṃ` (the carpenter carves wood).

Chakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'cha'.

Jakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ja'.

Jijaye. Jeti. Jayati, parājayati. Dhammaṃ caranto sāmikaṃ parājeti. Dhammaṃ caranto parajjati. Rājānaṃ jayāpesuṃ. Jayāpetvā. Ettha jayāpesunti “jayatu bhava”nti āsīsavacanaṃ vadiṃsūti attho. Jayanaṃ, jitaṃ, jayo, vijitaṃ, jino, jetā, jeto, jito māro, māraṃ jito, jitavā, jitāvī, vijitāvī, māraji, lokaji, odhijino, anodhijino, jito. Vijito, jetuṃ, vijetuṃ, jitvā, vijitvā. Imassa pana dhātussa kiyādigaṇaṃ pattassa “jināti jinitvā”tyādīni rūpāni bhavanti.

The root `ji` is in the sense of victory. He conquers. He conquers, he defeats. Practicing the Dhamma, he defeats his master. Practicing the Dhamma, he perishes. They caused the king to conquer. Having caused to conquer. Here, 'they caused the king to conquer' means they spoke words of blessing, saying, 'May you conquer!' The derivatives are: `jayanaṃ`, conquest; `jitaṃ`, the conquered; `jayo`, victory; `vijitaṃ`, the conquered; `jino`, the conqueror; `jetā`, the victor; `jeto`, the victor; `jito māro`, Māra is conquered; `māraṃ jito`, one who has conquered Māra; `jitavā`, one who has conquered; `jitāvī`, victorious; `vijitāvī`, triumphant; `māraji`, conqueror of Māra; `lokaji`, conqueror of the world; `odhijino`, conqueror with limits; `anodhijino`, conqueror without limits; `jito`, conquered. Also: `vijito`, conquered; `jetuṃ`, to conquer; `vijetuṃ`, to conquer; `jitvā`, having conquered; `vijitvā`, having conquered. However, for this root, when it belongs to the Kiyādi group, forms such as `jināti` and `jinitvā` occur.

Ji abhibhavane. Jeti. Jino. Pubbe viya rūpāni. Ettha ca “tumhehi ānanda sappurisehi vijitaṃ, pacchimā janatāsālimaṃsodanaṃ atimaññissatī”ti pāḷi abhibhavanatthasādhakā. Ettha hi vijitanti adhibhūtanti attho.

The root `ji` is in the sense of overcoming. He conquers. The conqueror. The forms are as before. And here, the Pāli passage, 'By you, Ānanda, good persons have been overcome; the later generation will despise rice with meat and broth,' is evidence for the meaning of overcoming. Here, indeed, `vijitaṃ` means 'overcome'.

Ju gatiyaṃ. Ettha sīghagati adhippetā. Javati. Javanaṃ, javo, javaṃ, javanto, javanacittaṃ, javanapañño, javanahaṃso. Manojavaṃ gacchati yenakāmaṃ.

The root `ju` is in the sense of motion. Here, swift motion is intended. He runs. The derivatives are: `javanaṃ`, running; `javo`, speed; `javaṃ`, swiftness; `javanto`, running; `javanacittaṃ`, impulsion-consciousness; `javanapañño`, one of swift wisdom; `javanahaṃso`, a swift goose. He goes with the speed of mind wherever he wishes.

Jekhaye. Jīyati. Ekārassa īyādeso. Sāsanānurūpena “kiṃ maṃ dhanena jīyethā”ti hi pāḷi dissati. Saddasatthavidū pana “jāyatī”ti rūpaṃ vadanti.

The root `ji` is in the sense of wasting away. It wastes away. There is the substitution of `īya` for `e`. In accordance with the teaching, the Pāli passage 'Why should I be overcome by wealth?' is indeed seen. But grammarians say the form is `jāyati`.

Sajja gatiyaṃ. Sajjati.

The root `sajja` is in the sense of motion. It moves.

Kuju khuju theyyakaraṇe. Kojati. Khojati.

The roots `kuju` and `khuju` are in the sense of stealing. He acts crookedly. He acts crookedly.

Vaja gatiyaṃ. Dhaja dhaji ca. Vajati. Abbajati. Manussattañca abbaje. Vajo, vajanaṃ, pavajanaṃ, pabbajjā, pabbajito, pabbājito.

The root `vaja` is in the sense of motion; and also `dhaja` and `dhaji`. He goes. He goes towards. And he might attain the human state. The derivatives are: `vajo`, going; `vajanaṃ`, movement; `pavajanaṃ`, departure; `pabbajjā`, the going forth; `pabbajito`, one who has gone forth; `pabbājito`, one who has been banished.

Sakā raṭṭhā pabbājito, aññaṃ janapadaṃ gato;

Mahantaṃ koṭṭhaṃ kayirātha, duruttānaṃ nidhetave.

Banished from his own country, gone to another district, he should build a large storehouse to deposit his ill-spoken words.

Dhajati. Dhajo. Dhañjati. Dhañjanaṃ. Ettha dhajoti ketu. Dhañjananti gamanaṃ.

He moves. A banner. He moves. Movement. Here, `dhajo` means a banner. And `dhañjanaṃ` means movement.

Aja khepane ca. Gatiapekkhakoyeva cakāro. Ajati. Ajo. Ettha ajoti eḷako. Imāni panassa pariyāyavacanāni “ajo eḷako urabbho avi meṇḍo”ti. Tattha urabbhoti eḷako, yo “ajo”tipi vuccati. Avīti rattalomo eḷako. Meṇḍoti kuṭilasiṅgo eḷako. Tathā hi janakajātake ajarathato meṇḍarathā visuṃ vuttā. Apica ajeḷakanti ajato eḷakassa visuṃ vacanato eḷakasaddena meṇḍopi gahetabbo, mahosadhajātakaṭṭhakathāyañhi meṇḍeḷakānaṃ nibbisesatā vuttāti.

The root `aja` is in the sense of throwing; the particle `ca` implies a connection to motion. He throws. A goat. Here, `ajo` means a goat. These, however, are its synonyms: `ajo`, `eḷako`, `urabbho`, `avi`, `meṇḍo`. Therein, `urabbho` is a ram, which is also called `ajo`. `Avi` is a reddish-haired sheep. `Meṇḍo` is a ram with crooked horns. For thus in the Janaka Jātaka, goat-chariots and ram-chariots are mentioned separately. Moreover, regarding the term `ajeḷakaṃ`, although a goat (`ajo`) is distinct from a ram (`eḷaka`), by the word `eḷaka` a ram (`meṇḍo`) should also be understood, for in the commentary to the Mahosadha Jātaka it is said that rams and goats are indistinguishable.

Ajja sajja ajjane. Ajjanaṃ ajjanakriyā. Ajjati. Sajjati.

The roots `ajja` and `sajja` are in the sense of acquiring. Acquisition, the act of acquiring. He acquires. He acquires.

Kajja byathane. Byathanaṃ hiṃsā. Kajjati.

The root `kajja` is in the sense of affliction. Affliction is harm. He is afflicted.

Khajja majjane ca. Majjanaṃ suddhi. Byathanāpekkho cakāro. Khajjati. Khajjūro.

The root `khajja` is in the sense of cleansing, and also affliction. Cleansing is purification. The particle `ca` implies a connection to affliction. It is cleansed or afflicted. A date-palm.

Khaja manthe. Mantho viloḷanaṃ. Khajati.

The root `khaja` is in the sense of churning. Churning is stirring up. He churns.

Khaji gativekalle. Kissa bhante ayyo khañjatīti. Ubho khañjā. Khañjanaṃ, khañjituṃ, khañjitvā.

The root `khaji` is in the sense of a defect in gait. 'Why, venerable sir, is the noble one limping?' Both are lame. The derivatives are: `khañjanaṃ`, limping; `khañjituṃ`, to limp; `khañjitvā`, having limped.

Khaja kampane. Khajati. Ejā. Ettha ca ejāti lābhādiṃ paṭicca ejati kampatīti ejā, balavataṇhāyetaṃ nāmaṃ.

The root `khaja` is in the sense of trembling. He trembles. Agitation. And here, `ejā` is so called because one trembles and shakes in dependence on gain and so on; this is a name for strong craving.

Buja vajiranibbese. Vajiranigghoseti keci vidū vadanti. Bojati.

The root `buja` is in the sense of the sound of a diamond. Some wise ones say it means 'the roar of a diamond.' It sounds.

Khija [M 0.0044] kuji guji abyattasadde. Khijati. Kuñjati. Guñjati.

The roots `khija`, `kuji`, and `guji` are in the sense of an indistinct sound. It makes an indistinct sound. It coos. It hums.

Laja lāja tajja bhassane. Lajati. Lājati. Tajjati.

The roots `laja`, `lāja`, and `tajja` are in the sense of roasting or scolding. It is roasted. It is roasted. He scolds.

Laji dittiyañca. Bhassanāpekkho cakāro. Lañjati. Tatiyo nayalañjako. Lañjeti pakāseti suttatthanti lañjako.

The root `laji` is in the sense of shining, and also scolding. The particle `ca` implies a connection to scolding. He marks. The third is `nayalañjako`. A `lañjaka` is one who makes clear (`lañjeti`), that is, illuminates (`pakāseti`), the meaning of the suttas.

Jaja jaji yuddhe. Yujjhanaṃ yuddhaṃ. Jajati. Jañjati.

The roots `jaja` and `jaji` are in the sense of battle. Fighting is battle. He fights. He struggles.

Tuja hiṃsāyaṃ. Tojati.

The root `tuj` is in the sense of harming. He harms.

Tuji balane ca. Balanaṃ balanakriyā. Hiṃsāpekkhako cakāro. Tuñjati.

The root `tuj` is in the sense of strengthening, and also harming. Strengthening is the act of making strong. The particle `ca` implies a connection to harming. He pushes.

Gaja kuji muji gajja saddatthā. Gajati. Kuñjati. Muñjati. Gajo gajjati, megho gajjati. Yattha dāso āmajāto, ṭhito thullāni gajjati. Maṇi gajjati. Ñāṇagajjanaṃ gajjati. Gajjituṃ samattho. Gajjitā. Gajjitvā. Tattha gajoti hatthī. Hatthissa hi anekāni nāmāni –

The roots `gaj`, `kuj`, `muj`, and `gajja` are in the sense of sound. It sounds. It coos. It sounds. The elephant roars, the cloud thunders. Where a base-born slave stands, he roars boastfully. The jewel resounds. The roar of wisdom resounds. Able to roar. One who roars. Having roared. Therein, `gajo` means an elephant. Indeed, the elephant has many names:

Hatthī nāgo gajo dantī, kuñjaro vāraṇo karī;

Mātaṅgo dvirado saṭṭhi-hāyano’nekapo ibho.

The one with a trunk (`hatthī`), the great one (`nāgo`), the trumpeter (`gajo`), the tusked one (`dantī`); the forest-dweller (`kuñjaro`), the warder-off (`vāraṇo`), the one with a trunk (`karī`); the `mātaṅga`, the one with two tusks (`dvirado`), the sixty-year-old (`saṭṭhihāyano`), the one that drinks twice (`anekapo`), the elephant (`ibho`).

Thambho rammo dvipo ceva, hatthinī tu kareṇukā;

Hatthipoto hatthicchāpo, bhiṅko ca kalabho bhave.

A tusker elephant is a `thambho`, a `rammo`, and a `dvipo`; but a female elephant is a `hatthinī` or a `kareṇukā`. A young elephant would be a `hatthipoto`, a `hatthicchāpo`, a `bhiṅko`, and a `kalabho`.

Caja cāge. Cajati. Pariccajati. Cāgo. Pariccāgo. Cajanaṃ. Cajaṃ, cajanto. Cajamāno.

The root `caj` is in the sense of relinquishing. He relinquishes. He abandons completely. `Cāgo`, relinquishment; `pariccāgo`, complete abandonment; `cajanaṃ`, relinquishing; `cajaṃ`, relinquishing; `cajanto`, one who relinquishes; `cajamāno`, one who is relinquishing.

Sanja saṅge. Saṅgo laganaṃ. Sañcati. Satto. Sajanaṃ, satti. Āsatti. Sajituṃ. Sajitvā.

The root `sañj` is in the sense of attachment. Attachment is clinging. He is attached. Attached. `Sajanaṃ`, attachment; `satti`, attachment; `āsatti`, clinging; `sajituṃ`, to be attached; `sajitvā`, having been attached.

Īja gatiyaṃ. Ījati.

The root `īj` is in the sense of motion. He moves.

Bhaji bhajjane. Bhajjanaṃ tāpakaraṇaṃ. Tilāni bhajjati. Purisena bhajjamānāni tilāni.

The root `bhajj` is in the sense of roasting. Roasting is the act of heating. He roasts sesame seeds. Sesame seeds being roasted by a man.

Eja [M 0.0045] bheja bhāja dittiyaṃ. Ditti sobhā. Ejati. Bhejati. Bhājati.

The roots `ej`, `bhej`, and `bhāj` are in the sense of radiance. Radiance is beauty. It shines. It shines. It shines.

Tija nisāne, khamāyañca. Nisānaṃ tikkhatākaraṇaṃ. Khamā khanti. Tejati. Titikkhati. Tejano. Tejo. Tattha tejanoti kaṇḍo saro usu. Tejoti sūriyo. Atha vā tejoti tejanaṃ usmā uṇhattaṃ tāpo. Tejoti vā ānubhāvo pabhāvo.

The root `tij` is in the sense of sharpening, and also of patience. Sharpening is the act of making sharp. Patience is forbearance. It is sharp. He endures. An arrow (`tejano`). Splendor (`tejo`). Therein, `tejano` means a shaft, an arrow, a dart. `Tejo` means the sun. Or, `tejo` means heat, warmth, glow, fire. Or, `tejo` means power, majesty.

Sañja parissagge, āliṅganaṃ parissaggo. Sañjati.

The root `sañj` is in the sense of embracing. `Parissagga` is an embrace. He embraces.

Khaji dāne, gatiyañca. Khañjati. Khañjanaṃ.

The root `khaj` is in the sense of giving, and also of motion. He limps. Limping.

Rāja dittiyaṃ bhāja ca. Rājati. Bhājati. Rājā. Rājinī. Vanarāji. Rājitvā. Virājitvā. Atra viññūnamatthavivaraṇe kosallajananatthaṃ silokaṃ racayāma –

The roots `rāj` and `bhāj` are in the sense of shining. He shines. He shines. King. Queen. A forest range. Having shone. Having shone forth. Here, to generate skill for the wise in explaining the meaning, we compose a verse:

Ma’hā’rāja mahārāja, mahārāja mameva’hi;

Ne’tassa iti vatvāna, dve janā kalahaṃ karuṃ.

‘O great one, he shone! O great king! O great king, the snake is mine indeed! It is not his!’—saying thus, two people quarreled.

Ettha ca paṭhamapādassa dutiyapade “me ahi mahī”ti chedo “puttā me atthi puttā matthī”ti viya. “Mahi arāja mahārājā”ti ca chedo “yopi ayaṃ yopāya”nti viya. Ettha arājasaddo “atikaramakarācariyā”ti ettha akarīti atthavācako akarasaddo viya ākhyātaparokkhāvibhattiko daṭṭhabbo. Arāja virocīti attho. Ayaṃ pana gāthāya piṇḍattho “mahārāja me ahi arāja, mama eva ahi arāja, na etassa iti vatvā dve ahituṇḍikajanā kalahaṃ kariṃsū”ti.

Here, in the second part of the first line, the division is ‘me ahi mahī,’ like in ‘puttā me atthi, puttā matthi.’ And the division ‘mahi arāja mahārājā’ is like ‘yo pi ayaṃ, yo’pāyaṃ.’ Here, the word `arāja` should be understood as a perfect tense verb, like the word `akara` meaning ‘he did’ in the phrase ‘atikaram akara acariyā.’ `Arāja` means ‘he shone.’ This, then, is the condensed meaning of the verse: ‘O great king, my snake shone! My snake indeed shone! It is not his!’—saying thus, two snake charmers quarreled.

Ranja rāge. Bhikkhu cīvaraṃ rajati. Satto rūpādīsu rañjati. Rajanaṃ. Rajako. Rāgo. Virāgo. Haliddirāgo. Rājā. Rājinī. Imassa ca divādigaṇaṃ pattassa “rajjati virajjatī”ti rūpāni [M 0.0046] bhavanti. Tattha rajananti rajanavatthu. Rajakoti rajakāro vatthadhovanako. Rāgoti rajjanti sattā tena, sayaṃ vā rañjati, rañjanamattameva vā etanti rāgo, taṇhā. Imāni pana tadabhidhānāni –

The root `rañj` is in the sense of coloring or passion. A bhikkhu dyes a robe. A being is impassioned towards forms and so on. `Rajanaṃ`, dyeing; `rajako`, a dyer; `rāgo`, passion; `virāgo`, dispassion; `haliddirāgo`, the color of turmeric; `rājā`, a king; `rājinī`, a queen. And for this root, when it belongs to the Divādi group, the forms `rajjati` (is colored) and `virajjati` (becomes dispassionate) occur. Therein, `rajanaṃ` means a dyeing substance. `Rajako` means a dyer, a clothes-washer. `Rāgo` is so called because beings are colored by it, or because it itself colors, or because it is the mere act of coloring; it is passion, craving. These, however, are its designations:

Rāgo lobho tasiṇā ca, taṇhā ejā visattikā;

Satti āsatti mucchā ca, lubbhitattañca lubbhanā.

Passion (`rāgo`), greed (`lobho`), thirst (`tasiṇā`), craving (`taṇhā`), agitation (`ejā`), attachment (`visattikā`); a dart (`satti`), clinging (`āsatti`), infatuation (`mucchā`), and greediness (`lubbhitattaṃ`), the state of being greedy (`lubbhanā`).

Kāmo nikāmanā icchā, nikanti ca niyanti ca;

Vanañca vanatho ceva, apekkhā bhavanetti ca.

Sensual desire (`kāmo`), longing (`nikāmanā`), wish (`icchā`), delight (`nikanti`), and attachment (`niyanti`); the jungle (`vanaṃ`) and the jungle of desires (`vanatho`), expectation (`apekkhā`), and the guide to existence (`bhavanetti`).

Anurodho ca sārāgo, saṅgo paṅko ca sibbinī;

Nandīrāgo anunayo, gedho sañjananī tathā;

Janikā paṇidhi ceva, ajjhosānantinekadhā.

Compliance (`anurodho`), lust (`sārāgo`), attachment (`saṅgo`), mire (`paṅko`), and the seamstress (`sibbinī`); delight and passion (`nandīrāgo`), affection (`anunayo`), greed (`gedho`), and the progenitor (`sañjananī`); the generatrix (`janikā`), aspiration (`paṇidhi`), and clinging (`ajjhosānaṃ`) are the many kinds.

Virāgoti maggo nibbānañca. Rājāti pathavissaro. Ettha dhātudvayavasena nibbacanāni niyyante. Nānāsampattīhi rājati dibbati virocatīti rājā. Dānañca piyavacanañca atthacariyā ca samānattatā cāti imehi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi attani mahājanaṃ rañjetītipi rājā. Rājinīti rājabhariyā. Tesaṃ abhidhānāni vuccante sahābhidhānantarehi –

`Virāgo` means the path and Nibbāna. `Rājā` means the lord of the earth. Here, derivations are presented based on two roots. A `rājā` is so called because he shines (`rājati`), sports (`dibbati`), and gleams (`virocati`) with various accomplishments. He is also a `rājā` because he delights (`rañjeti`) the great populace with the four bases of sympathy: giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. `Rājinī` means the king’s wife. Their designations are stated along with other designations:

Rājā bhūpati devo ca, manujindo disampati;

Patthivo jagatipālo, bhūbhujo pathavissaro.

King (`rājā`), lord of the earth (`bhūpati`), deity (`devo`), lord of men (`manujindo`), lord of the quarters (`disampati`); lord of the world (`patthivo`), protector of the world (`jagatipālo`), enjoyer of the earth (`bhūbhujo`), lord of the earth (`pathavissaro`).

Raṭṭhādhipo bhūmipālo, manussindo janādhipo;

Narindo khattiyo ceva, khettassāmi pabhāvako.

Ruler of the nation (`raṭṭhādhipo`), protector of the earth (`bhūmipālo`), lord of men (`manussindo`), lord of the people (`janādhipo`); lord of men (`narindo`), a noble (`khattiyo`), and master of the land (`khettassāmi`), the powerful one (`pabhāvako`).

Muddhābhisitto rājāti, kathito itaro pana;

Rājañño khattiyo cāti, vutto khattiyajātiko.

An anointed one is called a king (`rājā`); but another of the noble caste (`khattiyajātiko`) is called a prince (`rājañño`) and a noble (`khattiyo`).

Muddhābhisitto anurājā, uparājāti bhāsito;

Catuddīpī rājarājā, cakkavattīti bhāsito.

An anointed sub-king is called a viceroy (`anurājā`, `uparājā`); the king of kings of the four continents is called a wheel-turning monarch (`cakkavattī`).

Rājinī [M 0.0047] uparī devī, mahesī bhūbhujaṅganā;

Khattiyā rājapadumī, khattiyānī ca khattiyī;

Itthāgārantu orodho, uparītipi vuccati.

A queen (`rājinī`), chief consort (`uparī`), goddess (`devī`), great consort (`mahesī`), the king's woman (`bhūbhujaṅganā`); a noblewoman (`khattiyā`), a royal lotus (`rājapadumī`), a noblewoman (`khattiyānī`, `khattiyī`). The women's quarters are called the harem (`itthāgāraṃ`, `orodho`), and also `uparī`.

Bhaja sevāyaṃ. Bhajati. Bhajanā. Sambhajanā. Bhatti. Sambhatti. Bhattā.

The root `bhaj` is in the sense of service. He serves. `Bhajanā`, service; `sambhajanā`, association; `bhatti`, devotion; `sambhatti`, close devotion; `bhattā`, a devotee.

Yaja devapūjasaṅgatakaraṇadānadhammesu. Devapūjaggahaṇena buddhādipūjā gahitā. Saṅgatakaraṇaṃ samodhānakaraṇaṃ. Tathā hi adhimuttattheravatthumhi “yadatthi saṅgataṃ kiñci, bhavo vā yattha labbhatī”ti gāthāyaṃ saṅgatasaddena samodhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Dānaṃ pariccāgo. Dhammo jhānasīlādi. Etesvatthesu yajadhātu vattati. Pupphehi buddhaṃ yajati. Devataṃ yajati. Devamanussehi bhagavā yajiyati. Ijjati. Yiṭṭhaṃ. Yañño. Yāgo. Dhammayāgo. Yajamāno sake pure. Yiṭṭhuṃ, yajituṃ. Puthuyaññaṃ yajitvāna. Soḷasaparikkhāraṃ mahāyaññaṃ kattukāmo.

The root `yaj` is in the senses of worship of deities, association, giving, and Dhamma. By the term 'worship of deities,' homage to the Buddha and others is included. `Saṅgatakaraṇa` means making a collection. Thus, in the story of Elder Adhimutta, in the verse `yadatthi saṅgataṃ kiñci, bhavo vā yattha labbhatī` (whatever gathering there may be, or existence wherever it is obtained), the word `saṅgata` is said to mean collection. `Dāna` is relinquishment. `Dhamma` includes jhāna, virtue, and so on. The root `yaj` occurs in these meanings. `Pupphehi buddhaṃ yajati` (he worships the Buddha with flowers). `Devataṃ yajati` (he worships the deity). `Devamanussehi bhagavā yajiyati` (the Blessed One is worshipped by gods and humans). `Ijjati` (it is accomplished). `Yiṭṭhaṃ` (a sacrifice). `Yañño` (a sacrifice). `Yāgo` (a sacrifice). `Dhammayāgo` (a sacrifice of Dhamma). `Yajamāno sake pure` (the sacrificer in his own city). `Yiṭṭhuṃ`, to sacrifice; `yajituṃ`, to sacrifice. `Puthuyaññaṃ yajitvāna` (having performed a great sacrifice of various kinds). `Soḷasaparikkhāraṃ mahāyaññaṃ kattukāmo` (desiring to perform a great sacrifice with the sixteen requisites).

Majja saṃsuddhiyaṃ. Majjati. Bāhiraṃ parimajjati. Bhūmiṃ sammajjati. Majjanaṃ. Sammajjanī.

The root `majj` is in the sense of purification. `Majjati`, he purifies. `Bāhiraṃ parimajjati`, he wipes the exterior. `Bhūmiṃ sammajjati`, he sweeps the ground. `Majjanaṃ`, cleansing. `Sammajjanī`, a broom.

Niñji suddhiyaṃ. Niñjati. Paniñjati. Niñjituṃ. Paniñjituṃ. Niñjitvā. Paniñjitvā. Ayaṃ pana pāḷi “tato tvaṃ moggallāna uṭṭhāyāsanā udakena akkhīni paniñjitvā disā anulokeyyāsī”ti.

The root `niñj` is in the sense of purification. `Niñjati`, he washes. `Paniñjati`, he rinses. `Niñjituṃ`, to wash. `Paniñjituṃ`, to rinse. `Niñjitvā`, having washed. `Paniñjitvā`, having rinsed. This, however, is the Pali passage: `tato tvaṃ moggallāna uṭṭhāyāsanā udakena akkhīni paniñjitvā disā anulokeyyāsī` (Then, Moggallāna, rising from your seat, having rinsed your eyes with water, you should look around the directions).

Niji abyattasadde. Niñjati.

`Niji` is in the sense of indistinct sound. `Niñjati` means it makes an indistinct sound.

Bhaja pāke. Tilāni bhajjati. Bhajjamānā tilāni ca.

`Bhaja` is in the sense of cooking or roasting. `Tilāni bhajjati` means sesame seeds are roasted. `Bhajjamānā tilāni ca` means and sesame seeds are being roasted.

Uju ajjave. Ajjavaṃ ujubhāvo. Ojati. Uju.

`Uju` is in the sense of straightforwardness. `Ajjavaṃ ujubhāvo` means straightforwardness is the state of being straight. `Ojati` means he is straightforward. `Uju` means straightforward.

Saja [M 0.0048] vissaggaparissajjanabbhukkiraṇesu. Sajati. Lokyaṃ sajantaṃ udakaṃ.

`Saja` is in the sense of releasing, embracing, and sprinkling. `Sajati` means he releases or sprinkles. `Lokyaṃ sajantaṃ udakaṃ` means water sprinkling the world.

Ruja bhaṅge. Rujati. Rujā. Rogo. Ettha rujāti byādhi rujanaṭṭhena. Rogoti rujati bhañjati aṅgapaccaṅgānīti rogo, byādhiyeva, yo “ātaṅko”tipi “ābādho”tipi vuccati.

`Ruja` is in the sense of breaking. `Rujati` means it breaks. `Rujā` means pain or sickness. `Rogo` means illness. Here, `rujā` means sickness in the sense of afflicting. `Rogo` means illness because it breaks, it fractures the limbs—thus, illness, which is also called `ātaṅko` (affliction) or `ābādho` (ailment).

Bhuja koṭille. Āvipubbo aññatthesu ca. Urago bhujati. Ābhujati. Bhikkhu pallaṅkaṃ ābhujati, ūrubaddhāsanaṃ bandhatīti attho. Mahāsamuddo ābhujati, āvaṭṭatīti attho. Keci pana “osakkatī”ti atthaṃ vadanti. “Vaṇṇadāna”nti ābhujati, manasi karotīti attho. Mūlāni vibhujatīti mūlavibhujo, ratho. Ettha ca vibhujatīti chindati. Bhogo. Bhogī. Ābhogo. Ābhujitvā. Ettha ca bhogoti bhujayati kuṭilaṃ kariyatīti bhogo, ahisarīraṃ. Bhogīti sappo.

`Bhuja` is in the sense of crookedness. When preceded by `ā`, it is also used in other meanings. `Urago bhujati` means a serpent bends. `Ābhujati` means it coils. `Bhikkhu pallaṅkaṃ ābhujati` means a monk folds his legs cross-legged—the meaning is, he binds his thighs in a seated posture. `Mahāsamuddo ābhujati` means the great ocean coils or swirls—the meaning is, it swirls. Some, however, say the meaning is `osakkati` (it recedes). In the sense of `vaṇṇadāna` (giving attention), `ābhujati` means it bends or considers—the meaning is, it takes to mind. `Mūlāni vibhujatīti mūlavibhujo` means one who severs roots—thus, `mūlavibhujo`, a chariot. Here, `vibhujati` means to cut. `Bhogo` means a serpent's body. `Bhogī` means a serpent. `Ābhogo` means coiling. `Ābhujitvā` means having coiled. Here, `bhoga` is so called because it bends or is made crooked—thus, `bhoga`, a serpent's body. `Bhogī` means a snake.

Raji vijjhane. Nāgo dantehi bhūmiṃ rañjati. Ārañjati. Ettha ca “tathāgatarañjitaṃ itipī”ti nettipāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tassattho “idaṃ sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ tathāgatagandhahatthino mahāvajirañāṇasabbaññutaññāṇadantehi rañjitaṃ ārañjitaṃ, tebhūmakadhammānaṃ ārañjanaṭṭhānantipi vuccatī”ti. Rañjitanti hi rañjati vijjhati etthāti ruñjitaṃ, rañjanaṭṭhānaṃ. “Idaṃ nesaṃ padakkanta”ntiādimhi viya etassa saddassa siddhi veditabbā adhikaraṇatthasambhavato.

`Raji` is in the sense of piercing. `Nāgo dantehi bhūmiṃ rañjati` means the elephant pierces the ground with its tusks. `Ārañjati` means it pierces or marks. Here, the Nettipakaraṇa provides the example `tathāgatarañjitaṃ itipi` (thus pierced or marked by the Tathāgata). Its meaning is: "This holy life of the Dispensation, encompassed by the threefold training, is pierced and marked by the great diamond-wisdom and the all-knowing knowledge of the Tathāgata, which are like the tusks of a fragrant elephant. It is also called the place of piercing or marking for the phenomena of the three planes of existence." For `rañjitaṃ` is so called because one pierces (`vijjhati`) therein (`ettha`); thus it is `ruñjitaṃ`, a place of piercing. The derivation of this word should be understood as in the phrase `idaṃ nesaṃ padakkantaṃ` (this is their going around), and so on, due to the possibility of a locative sense.

Vijī bhayacalanesu. Īkārantoyaṃ dhātu, tenassa saniggahītāgamāni rūpāni na santi. Vejati. Vego. Dhammasaṃvego. Saṃvigo vegena palāyi. Nadīvego. Ūmivego[M 0.0049], vātavego. Ettha dhammasaṃvegoti sahottappaṃ ñāṇaṃ. “Vego, javo, rayo”ti ime ekatthā. Divādigaṇaṃ pana pattassa “vijjati saṃvijjati ubbijjatī”ti rūpāni bhavanti dvigaṇikattā.

`Vijī` is in the sense of fear and trembling. This root ends in `ī`; therefore, it has no forms with an inserted nasal. `Vejati` means he trembles. `Vego` means force or speed. `Dhammasaṃvego` means a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma. `Saṃvigo vegena palāyi` means agitated, he fled with speed. `Nadīvego` means the force of a river. `Ūmivego` means the force of a wave. `Vātavego` means the force of the wind. Here, `dhammasaṃvego` means knowledge accompanied by moral dread. `Vego`, `javo`, and `rayo`—these have the same meaning. But for this root when it belongs to the `divādi` group, forms like `vijjati`, `saṃvijjati`, and `ubbijjati` occur, because of its belonging to two groups.

Lajja lajjane. Lajjati. Lajjā. Lajjāti hirī. Yā “viriḷanā”tipi vuccati.

`Lajja` is in the sense of being ashamed. `Lajjati` means he is ashamed. `Lajjā` means shame. `Lajjā` means `hirī` (moral shame). It is also called `viriḷanā`.

Vaḷaji paribhoge. Vaḷañjati.

`Vaḷaji` is in the sense of using or enjoying. `Vaḷañjati` means he uses or enjoys.

Kujja adhomukhīkaraṇe. Kujjati. Nikujjati. Ukkujjati. Paṭikujjati. Nikujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya. Aññissā pātiyā paṭikujjati. Avakujjo nipajjahaṃ. Tattha kujjati nikujjatīti imāni “carati vicaratī”ti padāni viya samānatthāni, adhomukhaṃ karotīti hi attho. Ukkujjatīti uparimukhaṃ karoti. Paṭikujjatīti mukhe mukhaṃ ṭhapeti.

`Kujja` is in the sense of turning face downward. `Kujjati` means he turns down. `Nikujjati` means he turns down or overturns. `Ukkujjati` means he turns up. `Paṭikujjati` means he turns face to face. `Nikujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya` means he might turn up what was overturned. `Aññissā pātiyā paṭikujjati` means he turns one bowl face to face with another. `Avakujjo nipajjahaṃ` means I was lying face down. Here, `kujjati` and `nikujjati`—these words, like `carati` and `vicarati`, have similar meanings, for the sense is "to make the face downward." `Ukkujjati` means to make the face upward. `Paṭikujjati` means to place face to face.

Mujja osīdane. Mujjati. Nimujjati. Nimuggo. Ummuggo.

`Mujja` is in the sense of sinking. `Mujjati` means he sinks. `Nimujjati` means he submerges. `Nimuggo` means submerged. `Ummuggo` means emerged.

Opuji vilimpane. Gomayena pathaviṃ opuñjati.

`Opuji` is in the sense of smearing. `Gomayena pathaviṃ opuñjati` means he smears the ground with cow dung.

Jakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'ja'.

Jhakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'jh'.

Jhe cintāyaṃ. Jhāyati, nijjhāyati, upanijjhāyati, ujjhāyati, sajjhāyati. Jhānaṃ, nijjhānaṃ, upanijjhānaṃ, ujjhāyanaṃ, sajjhāyanaṃ. Nijjhatti. Upajjhā, upajjhāyo. Jhāyī, ajjhāyako.

`Jhe` is in the sense of thinking. `Jhāyati`, `nijjhāyati`, `upanijjhāyati`, `ujjhāyati`, `sajjhāyati`. `Jhānaṃ`, `nijjhānaṃ`, `upanijjhānaṃ`, `ujjhāyanaṃ`, `sajjhāyanaṃ`. `Nijjhatti`. `Upajjhā`, `upajjhāyo`. `Jhāyī`, `ajjhāyako`.

Tattha jhāyananti duvidhaṃ jhāyanaṃ sobhanamasobhanañca. Tesu sobhanaṃ “jhāyī tapati brāhmaṇo. Jhāyāmi [M 0.0050] akutobhayo”tiādīsu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asobhanaṃ pana “tattha tattha jhāyanto nisīdi. Adhomukho pajjhāyanto nisīdī”tiādīsu daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jhāyīti ārammaṇūpanijjhānena vā lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena vā jhāyanasīlo cintanasīlo. Jhāyī jhānavāti attho. Ajjhāyakoti idaṃ “na dānime jhāyanti, na dānime jhāyantīti kho vāseṭṭha ajjhāyakā ajjhāyakātveva tatiyaṃ akkharaṃ upanibbatta”nti evaṃ paṭhamakappikakāle jhānavirahitānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ garahavacanaṃ uppannaṃ, idāni pana taṃ ajjhāyatīti ajjhāyako, mante parivattetīti iminā atthena pasaṃsāvacanaṃ katvā voharantīti. Ayaṃ panattho “adhipubbassa i ajjhayane”ti dhātussa vasena gahetabbo. Evaṃ adhipubbassa idhātussa vasena imassa dhātussa atthaparivattanaṃ bhavati. Yaṃ sandhāya “ajjhāyako mantadharo”ti vuttaṃ.

Here, `jhāyana` (meditating, thinking) is of two kinds: wholesome and unwholesome. Among these, the wholesome is to be seen in phrases like, 'The meditating brahmin shines,' and 'I meditate, free from fear,' and so on. The unwholesome, however, is to be seen in phrases like, 'Sitting here and there, brooding,' and 'He sat with a downcast face, brooding,' and so on. `Jhāyī` means one who is accustomed to meditating, a thinker, either by way of close attention to an object (`ārammaṇa`) or close attention to characteristics (`lakkhaṇa`). The meaning is a meditator or one who possesses `jhāna`. As for `ajjhāyako`, this term arose as a reproach in the first cosmic age toward brahmins devoid of meditation, as in, 'Nowadays, they do not meditate, they do not meditate, Vāseṭṭha! Thus, the third syllable is applied to them merely as `a-jjhāyakā` (non-meditators).' But now, it is used as a term of praise with the meaning 'one who recites' or 'one who repeats the mantras.' This meaning should be understood based on the root `i` preceded by `adhi` in the sense of 'study' (`ajjhayana`). Thus, by the force of the root `i` preceded by `adhi`, the meaning of this root is transformed. It is in this sense that it is said, 'An `ajjhāyako` is a bearer of mantras.'

Jhe dittiyaṃ. Dīpo jhāyati, dārūni jhāyanti. Ettha jhāyatīti jalati. Jhāyanajalanasaddā hi ekatthā.

`Jhe` is in the sense of shining or blazing. `Dīpo jhāyati` means the lamp blazes. `Dārūni jhāyanti` means the firewood blazes. Here, `jhāyati` means to burn. Indeed, the words `jhāyana` and `jalana` have the same meaning.

Jajjha paribhāsanatajjanesu. Jajjhati.

`Jajjha` is in the sense of reviling and threatening. `Jajjhati`.

Ujjha ussagge. Ussaggo chaḍḍanaṃ. Ujjhati. Ujjhitaṃ.

`Ujjha` is in the sense of abandoning. Abandoning means casting off. `Ujjhati`. `Ujjhitaṃ`.

Jhakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'jh'.

Ñakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ñ'.

Ñā avabodhane. “Ñāti, ñanti, ñāsi. Ñātu, ñantu. Ñeyya, ñeyyu”ntiādīni yathāpāvacanaṃ gahetabbāni. Ñāti, ñātako, añño, ñattaṃ, ñatti, paññatti, viññatti, saññatti, saññā, saññāṇaṃ, paññā, paññāṇaṃ, ñāṇaṃ, viññāṇaṃ.

`Ñā` is in the sense of understanding. `Ñāti, ñanti, ñāsi. Ñātu, ñantu. Ñeyya, ñeyyu,` and so on, should be taken according to usage. `Ñāti`, `ñātako`, `añño`, `ñattaṃ`, `ñatti`, `paññatti`, `viññatti`, `saññatti`, `saññā`, `saññāṇaṃ`, `paññā`, `paññāṇaṃ`, `ñāṇaṃ`, `viññāṇaṃ`.

Tattha [M 0.0051] ñātīti jānāti. Puna ñātīti bandhu. So hi “ayaṃ amhāka”nti ñātabbaṭṭhena ñātīti. Evaṃ ñātako. Aññoti diṭṭhadhammikādayo atthe na ñāti na jānātīti añño, avidvā bāloti attho. Ñattanti jānanabhāvo. “Yāvadeva anatthāya, ñattaṃ bālassa jāyatī”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Saññāṇanti cihanaṃ. Kārite “ñāpeti saññāpeti viññāpayatī”tiādīni bhavanti. Yasmā pana “aññāti paṭivijjhati. Attatthaṃ vā paratthaṃ vā ñassati. Anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ. Ekacce nabbhaññaṃsu, ekacce abbhaññaṃsū”ti pāḷiyo dissanti, tasmā ñātītiādīni ākhyātikapadāni diṭṭhāniyeva honti nayavasena. Tathā hi aññātīti ettha āiti upasaggo, so parassakkharassa saññoguccāraṇicchāya rassaṃ katvā niddiṭṭho. Ñātīti sāsane ākhyātikapadaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, tasmāyeva “ñāti, ñanti. Ñāsī”tiādinā padamālākaraṇe nattheva doso.

Here, `ñāti` means 'he knows.' Again, `ñāti` means 'relative.' For one is called `ñāti` by reason of being known as 'this is ours.' Similarly, `ñātako.` `Añño` is one who, regarding matters of this life and beyond, is not a kinsman and does not know; the meaning is an ignorant person, a fool. `Ñatta` is the state of knowing. The Pāli passage 'Only to his detriment does knowledge arise in a fool' is an illustration. `Saññāṇa` means a sign. In the causative, forms like `ñāpeti,` `saññāpeti,` `viññāpayati,` and so on, occur. Since, however, Pāli passages like 'aññāti paṭivijjhati,' 'Attatthaṃ vā paratthaṃ vā ñassati,' 'Anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ,' 'Ekacce nabbhaññaṃsu, ekacce abbhaññaṃsū' are seen, therefore verbal forms like `ñāti` are indeed seen by way of rule.
