Thus, in `aññāti,` `ā` is a prefix, which is stated with its vowel shortened due to the desire for pronouncing the conjunct consonant. `Ñāti` is seen as a verbal form in the Dispensation; therefore, there is no fault in forming a paradigm like 'ñāti, ñanti, ñāsi,' and so on.

Ñā māraṇatosananisānesu. Māraṇaṃ jīvitindriyupacchedakaraṇaṃ. Tosanaṃ tuṭṭhi. Nisānaṃ tikkhatā. Ñatti. Manuññaṃ. Paññatti.

`Ñā` is in the sense of killing, pleasing, and sharpening. Killing is the act of cutting off the life faculty. Pleasing is satisfaction. Sharpening is keenness. `Ñatti`. `Manuññaṃ`. `Paññatti`.

Ettha ñattīti māretīti vā tosetīti vā nisetīti vā attho. Ayañca ñattisaddo “vatti etāyāti vācā”ti ettha vattisaddo viya ākhyātikapadanti daṭṭhabbo. Tathā ādatteti ettha vibhattibhūtassa tesaddassa viya vibhattibhūtassa tisaddassa saññogabhāvo ca dhātuantassarassa rassattañca. Manuññanti manaṃ ābhuso ñeti tosetīti manuññaṃ. Ayamattho manasaddūpapadassa āpubbassimassa ñādhātussa vasena daṭṭhabbo. Paññattīti nānappakārato pavattinivāraṇena akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ñatti [M 0.0052] māraṇaṃ paññatti. Atha vā dhammaṃ suṇantānaṃ dhammadesanāya citte anekavidhena somanassuppādanaṃ. Atikhiṇabuddhīnaṃ anekavidhena ñāṇatikhiṇakaraṇañca paññatti nāma, tathā sotūnaṃ cittatosanena cittanisānena ca paññāpanaṃ paññattīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, 'ñatti' means to kill, or to please, or to sharpen. This term 'ñatti' should be understood as a verbal form, like the word 'vatti' in 'vatti etāyāti vācā' (speech is that by which one speaks). Similarly, in 'ādatteti,' there is the conjunction of the verbal ending 'ti', like the verbal ending 'te', and the shortening of the final vowel of the root. 'Manuñña' means that which greatly pleases the mind—thus, 'manuñña.' This meaning should be understood based on the root 'ñā' preceded by 'ā' with 'mana' as a prefix. 'Paññatti' is the killing of unwholesome states by preventing their arising in various ways. Alternatively, it is the production of manifold joy in the minds of those who listen to the Dhamma through the teaching of the Dhamma. And for those of keen wisdom, it is the sharpening of their knowledge in various ways that is called 'paññatti.' Thus, it should be understood that 'paññatti' is the making known through the gladdening and sharpening of the listeners' minds.

Iti bhūvādigaṇe cavaggantadhāturūpāni

Thus are the forms of roots ending in the ca-group in the Bhūvādi group.

Samattāni.

Completed.

Ṭakārantadhātu

Verbal roots ending in ṭa

Idāni ṭavaggantadhāturūpāni vuccante –

Now, the forms of verbal roots ending in the ṭa-group are stated:

Soṭu gabbe. Gabbaṃ dabbanaṃ. Soṭati.

'Soṭu' in the sense of covering. 'Gabba' means covering. 'Soṭati' (he/it) covers.

Yoṭu sambandhe. Yoṭati.

'Yoṭu' in the sense of binding. 'Yoṭati' (he/it) binds.

Meṭu mileṭu ummāde. Meṭati. Mileṭati.

'Meṭu' and 'mileṭu' in the sense of madness. 'Meṭati' (he/it) acts madly. 'Mileṭati' (he/it) acts madly.

Kaṭa vassāvaraṇesu. Kaṭati.

'Kaṭa' in the senses of rain and covering. 'Kaṭati' (he/it) covers.

Saṭa paribhāsane. Saṭati.

'Saṭa' in the sense of reviling. 'Saṭati' (he/it) reviles.

Laṭa bālye ca. Pubbāpekkhāya cakāro. Laṭati. Lāṭo.

'Laṭa' also in the sense of childishness. The particle 'ca' refers to the preceding meaning. 'Laṭati' (he/it) acts childishly. 'Lāṭo' (a childish person).

Saṭa rujāvisaraṇagatyāvasānesu. Rujā pīḷā. Visaraṇaṃ vippharaṇaṃ. Gatyāvasānaṃ gatiyā avasānaṃ osānaṃ abhāvakaraṇaṃ, nisīdananti vuttaṃ hoti. Saṭati. Sāṭo vuccati sāṭako.

'Saṭa' in the senses of pain, spreading, and cessation of movement. Pain is affliction. Spreading is diffusion. Cessation of movement is the end of movement, cessation, the bringing about of absence; it is said to mean sitting down. 'Saṭati' (it) rustles/moves. 'Sāṭo' is called a garment.

Vaṭa vedhane. Vaṭati. Vaṭo. Vāṭo.

'Vaṭa' in the sense of piercing. 'Vaṭati' (he/it) pierces. 'Vaṭo' (a banyan tree/enclosure). 'Vāṭo' (an enclosure/fence).

Khiṭa uttāsane. Kheṭati, ākheṭako, kheṭo, ukkheṭito, samukkheṭito.

'Khiṭa' in the sense of frightening. 'Kheṭati' (he/it) frightens. 'Ākheṭako' (a hunter). 'Kheṭo' (the chase/hunt). 'Ukkheṭito' (driven out). 'Samukkheṭito' (completely driven out).

Siṭa anādare. Seṭati.

'Siṭa' in the sense of disrespect. 'Seṭati' (he/it) disrespects.

Jaṭa [M 0.0053] ghaṭa saṅghāte. Jaṭati. Jaṭā, jaṭilo, jaṭī. Antojaṭā bahijaṭā, jaṭāya jaṭitā pajā. Kārite “so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ. Arahattamaggakkhaṇe vijaṭeti nāmā”ti payogo.

'Jaṭa' and 'ghaṭa' in the sense of entangling. 'Jaṭati' (it) becomes entangled. 'Jaṭā' (matted hair), 'jaṭilo' (one with matted hair), 'jaṭī' (one with matted hair). 'Inner tangle, outer tangle; this generation is entangled by a tangle.' In the causative, the usage is: "May he disentangle this tangle." At the moment of the path of arahantship, it is called "disentangling".

Bhaṭa bhattiyaṃ. Bhaṭati. Bhaṭo. Vetanaṃ bhaṭako yathā.

'Bhaṭa' in the sense of wages. 'Bhaṭati' (he) serves for wages. 'Bhaṭo' (a mercenary/servant). As in 'vetanaṃ bhaṭako' (wages for a hireling).

Taṭa ussaye. Ussayo āroho ubbedho. Taṭati. Taṭo, giritaṭo, nadītaṭo, taṭī, taṭaṃ.

'Taṭa' in the sense of elevation. Elevation is an ascent, a height. 'Taṭati' (it) is elevated. 'Taṭo' (a bank/slope), 'giritaṭo' (a mountain slope), 'nadītaṭo' (a river bank), 'taṭī' (a bank), 'taṭaṃ' (a bank).

Khaṭa kaṃse. Khaṭati. Khaṭo.

'Khaṭa' in the sense of desiring. 'Khaṭati' (he/it) desires. 'Khaṭo'.

Naṭa natiyaṃ. Naṭati. Naṭo, nāṭakaṃ.

'Naṭa' in the sense of dancing. 'Naṭati' (he/it) dances. 'Naṭo' (an actor/dancer), 'nāṭakaṃ' (a play/drama).

Piṭa saddasaṅghāṭesu. Peṭati. Peṭako, piṭakaṃ. Piṭakasaddo “mā piṭakasampadānenā”tiādīsu pariyattiyaṃ dissati. “Atha puriso āgaccheyya kudālapiṭakaṃ ādāyā”tiādīsu yasmiṃ kismiñci bhājane.

'Piṭa' in the senses of sound and collection. 'Peṭati' (it) makes a sound/collects. 'Peṭako' (a basket/container), 'piṭakaṃ' (a basket/container). The word 'piṭaka' is seen in the sense of the scriptures, as in "not by the acquisition of the Piṭaka," etc. In phrases like "Then a man might come carrying a hoe and a basket," etc., it refers to any kind of vessel.

Haṭa dittiyaṃ. Haṭati. Hāṭakaṃ, haṭakaṃ. Yaṃ jātarūpaṃ haṭakanti vuccati.

'Haṭa' in the sense of shining. 'Haṭati' (it) shines. 'Hāṭakaṃ' (gold), 'haṭakaṃ' (gold). That which is wrought gold is called 'haṭaka'.

Saṭa avayave. Saṭati.

'Saṭa' in the sense of a part. 'Saṭati' (it) divides into parts.

Luṭa viloṭhane. Loṭati.

'Luṭa' in the sense of rolling. 'Loṭati' (it) rolls.

Ciṭa pesane. Ceṭati. Ceṭako.

'Ciṭa' in the sense of sending. 'Ceṭati' (he/it) sends. 'Ceṭako' (a messenger/servant).

Viṭa sadde. Veṭati. Veṭako.

'Viṭa' in the sense of sound. 'Veṭati' (it) makes a sound. 'Veṭako'.

Aṭa paṭa iṭa kiṭa kaṭa gatiyaṃ. Aṭati. Paṭati. Eṭati. Keṭati. Kaṭati. Paṭo icceva nāmikapadaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. Paṭati jiṇṇabhāvaṃ [M 0.0054] gacchatīti paṭo. Paṭoti vatthaṃ. Vatthassa hi anekāni nāmāni –

'Aṭa, paṭa, iṭa, kiṭa, kaṭa' in the sense of movement. 'Aṭati' (he/it) moves. 'Paṭati' (he/it) moves. 'Eṭati' (he/it) moves. 'Keṭati' (he/it) moves. 'Kaṭati' (he/it) moves. 'Paṭo' is indeed seen as a noun. It is 'paṭo' because it goes (paṭati) to a state of being worn out. 'Paṭo' means cloth. For cloth has many names:

Paṭo coḷo sāṭako ca, vāso vasanamaṃsukaṃ;

Dussamacchādanaṃ vatthaṃ, celaṃ vasani ambaraṃ.

Paṭo, coḷo, and sāṭako; vāso, vasanaṃ, aṃsukaṃ; dussaṃ, acchādanaṃ, vatthaṃ; celaṃ, vasani, ambaraṃ.

Muṭa pamaddane. Moṭati.

'Muṭa' in the sense of crushing. 'Moṭati' (he/it) crushes.

Cuṭa appībhāve. Coṭati.

'Cuṭa' in the sense of becoming small. 'Coṭati' (it) diminishes.

Vaṭi vibhājane. Vaṭati. Vaṇṭo.

'Vaṭi' in the sense of dividing. 'Vaṭati', he divides. 'Vaṇṭo', a share or portion.

Ruṭi luṭi theyye. Ruṇṭati. Luṇṭati. Ruṇṭako. Luṇṭako.

'Ruṭi' and 'luṭi' in the sense of stealing. 'Ruṇṭati', he steals. 'Luṇṭati', he steals. 'Ruṇṭako', a thief. 'Luṇṭako', a thief.

Phuṭa visaraṇe phoṭati. Phoṭo.

'Phuṭa' in the sense of spreading or bursting. 'Phoṭati', it spreads or bursts. 'Phoṭo', a burst or blister.

Ceṭa ceṭāyaṃ. Ceṭati. Ceṭako.

'Ceṭa' in the sense of serving. 'Ceṭati', he serves. 'Ceṭako', a servant.

Ghuṭa parivattane. Ghoṭati.

'Ghuṭa' in the sense of turning or revolving. 'Ghoṭati', it turns or revolves.

Ruṭa luṭa paṭighāte. Roṭati. Loṭati.

'Ruṭa' and 'luṭa' in the sense of striking or resisting. 'Roṭati', he strikes or resists. 'Loṭati', he strikes or resists.

Ghaṭa cetāyaṃ. Ghaṭati. Ghaṭo. Ghaṭo vuccati kumbho. Imāni tadabhidhānāni –

'Ghaṭa' in the sense of striving or exerting. 'Ghaṭati', he strives or exerts. 'Ghaṭo', a pot. 'Ghaṭo' is called a pot. These are its designations:

Ghaṭo kumbho ghaṭī kumbhī, tuṇḍikiro tu ukkhalī;

Mahantabhājanaṃ cāṭi, atikhuddaṃ kuṭṭaṃ bhave;

Ghaṭo, kumbho, ghaṭī, kumbhī, and indeed tuṇḍikiro and ukkhalī. A large vessel is a cāṭi; a very small one would be a kuṭṭa.

Caṭa bhaṭa paribhāsane deṭa ca. Caṭati. Bhaṭati. Deṭati.

'Caṭa', 'bhaṭa', and 'deṭa' in the sense of reviling or scolding. 'Caṭati', he reviles. 'Bhaṭati', he reviles. 'Deṭati', he reviles.

Kuṭa koṭille. Kuṭati. Paṭikuṭati.

'Kuṭa' in the sense of crookedness or bending. 'Kuṭati', it bends or becomes crooked. 'Paṭikuṭati', it bends back.

Puṭa saṃkilesane. Puṭati.

'Puṭa' in the sense of defiling or polluting. 'Puṭati', it defiles or pollutes.

Cuṭa chuṭa kuṭa chedane. Cuṭati. Chuṭati. Kuṭati.

'Cuṭa', 'chuṭa', and 'kuṭa' in the sense of cutting. 'Cuṭati', he cuts. 'Chuṭati', he cuts. 'Kuṭati', he cuts.

Phuṭa vikasane. Phuṭati.

'Phuṭa' in the sense of expanding or blooming. 'Phuṭati', it expands or blooms.

Muṭa aggisaddapakkhepamaddanesu. Muṭati.

'Muṭa' in the senses of fire, sound, throwing, and crushing. 'Muṭati', he crushes.

Tuṭa kalahakammani. Tuṭati.

'Tuṭa' in the sense of quarreling or conflict. 'Tuṭati', he quarrels.

Ghuṭa paṭighāte. Ghuṭati. Ghoṭako.

'Ghuṭa' in the sense of striking or resistance. 'Ghuṭati', he strikes or resists. 'Ghoṭako', a striker or resister.

Ṭakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of verbal roots ending in ṭa.

Ṭhakārantadhātu

Verbal roots ending in ṭha.

Ṭhā [M 0.0055] gatinivattiyaṃ. Gatinivatti uppajjamānassa gamanassupacchedo. Ṭhāti, ṭhanti. Tiṭṭhati. Patiṭṭhāti. Adhiṭṭhāti. Adhiṭṭheti. Saṇṭhāti. Saṇṭhahati. Adhiṭṭhahati. Upaṭṭhahati. Ṭhātu. Tiṭṭhatu. Tiṭṭheyya. Aṭṭha, aṭṭhu. Aṭṭhā, aṭṭhū, aṭṭhāsi, aṭṭhaṃsu. Yāvassa kāyo ṭhassati. Tiṭṭhissati. Upassuti tiṭṭhissatha. Aṭṭhissā, aṭṭhissaṃsu. Atiṭṭhissā, atiṭṭhissaṃsu. Ṭhātuṃ, upaṭṭhātuṃ. Upaṭṭhahituṃ. Adhiṭṭhātuṃ. Adhiṭṭhahituṃ. Ṭhatvā, adhiṭṭhitvā. Upaṭṭhahitvā, adhiṭṭhahitvā. Ṭhānaṃ, ṭhiti, saṇṭhiti, avaṭṭhiti. Saṇṭhānaṃ, paṭṭhānaṃ. Upaṭṭhāko, ṭhito. Pabbataṭṭho bhūmaṭṭho. Upaṭṭhahaṃ iccādīni.

'Ṭhā' in the sense of stopping movement. 'Gatinivatti' is the cutting off of arising movement. 'Ṭhāti', he stands; 'ṭhanti', they stand. 'Tiṭṭhati', he stands. 'Patiṭṭhāti', he is established. 'Adhiṭṭhāti', he resolves or determines. 'Adhiṭṭheti', he resolves or determines. 'Saṇṭhāti', he stands firm. 'Saṇṭhahati', he stands firm. 'Adhiṭṭhahati', he resolves or determines. 'Upaṭṭhahati', he attends or serves. 'Ṭhātu', let him stand. 'Tiṭṭhatu', let him stand. 'Tiṭṭheyya', he should stand. 'Aṭṭha', 'aṭṭhu', he stood. 'Aṭṭhā', 'aṭṭhū', 'aṭṭhāsi', 'aṭṭhaṃsu', he or they stood. 'Yāvassa kāyo ṭhassati', as long as his body will stand. 'Tiṭṭhissati', he will stand. 'Upassuti tiṭṭhissatha', you will stand listening. 'Aṭṭhissā', 'aṭṭhissaṃsu', he or they would have stood. 'Atiṭṭhissā', 'atiṭṭhissaṃsu', he or they would have stood. 'Ṭhātuṃ', to stand; 'upaṭṭhātuṃ', to attend. 'Upaṭṭhahituṃ', to attend. 'Adhiṭṭhātuṃ', to resolve; 'adhiṭṭhahituṃ', to resolve. 'Ṭhatvā', having stood; 'adhiṭṭhitvā', having resolved. 'Upaṭṭhahitvā', having attended; 'adhiṭṭhahitvā', having resolved. 'Ṭhānaṃ', standing, place; 'ṭhiti', standing, state; 'saṇṭhiti', firm standing; 'avaṭṭhiti', fixed state. 'Saṇṭhānaṃ', shape, form; 'paṭṭhānaṃ', origin, starting point. 'Upaṭṭhāko', attendant; 'ṭhito', standing. 'Pabbataṭṭho', standing on a mountain; 'bhūmaṭṭho', standing on the ground. 'Upaṭṭhahaṃ', attending, and so forth.

Tattha ṭhānasaddo issariyaṭhitikhaṇakāraṇesu dissati. “Kiṃ panāyasmā devānamindo kammaṃ katvā imaṃ ṭhānaṃ patto”tiādīsu hi issariye dissati. “Ṭhānakusalo hoti akkhaṇavedhī”tiādīsu ṭhitiyaṃ. “Ṭhānasopetaṃ tathāgataṃ paṭibhātī”tiādīsu khaṇe. “Ṭhānañca ṭhānaso ñatvā aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānaso”tiādīsu kāraṇe. Kāraṇañhi yasmā tattha phalaṃ tiṭṭhati tadāyattavuttibhāvena, tasmā ṭhānanti vuccati.

Herein, the word 'ṭhāna' is seen in the senses of dominion, stability, moment, and cause. For in passages such as, “Having done what kamma, venerable one, did Indra, lord of the gods, attain this station?”, it is seen in the sense of dominion. In passages such as, “He is skilled in standing positions and is an unerring shot”, it is seen in the sense of stability. In passages such as, “The opportunity occurs to the Tathāgata”, it is seen in the sense of moment. In passages such as, “Having known cause as cause, and what is not cause as not cause”, it is seen in the sense of cause. For, because the result stands therein, its existence being dependent on that, it is therefore called 'ṭhāna'.

Issariye ṭhitiyañca, khaṇasmimpi ca kāraṇe;

Catūsvatthesu etesu, ṭhānasaddo pavattatīti.

In dominion and in stability, and also in moment and in cause; in these four meanings the word 'ṭhāna' is used.

Ṭhe saddasaṅkātesu. Ṭhīyati.

'Ṭhe' in the senses of sound and counting. 'Ṭhīyati', it is sounded or counted.

Ṭhe veṭhane. Ṭhāyati.

'Ṭhe' in the sense of wrapping. 'Ṭhāyati', it wraps.

Paṭha [M 0.0056] viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Dhammaṃ paṭhati. Pāṭho, nakkhattapāṭhako, so horapāṭhakaṃ pucchi. Sabbapāṭhī bhavissati. Paṭhituṃ, paṭhitave, paṭhitvā, paṭhitvāna, paṭhituna, paṭhiya, paṭhiyāna.

'Paṭha' in the sense of distinct speech. 'Dhammaṃ paṭhati', he recites the Dhamma. 'Pāṭho', recitation, text; 'nakkhattapāṭhako', an astrologer; 'so horapāṭhakaṃ pucchi', he asked the astrologer. 'Sabbapāṭhī bhavissati', he will be a master of all texts. 'Paṭhituṃ', to recite; 'paṭhitave', to recite; 'paṭhitvā', having recited; 'paṭhitvāna', having recited; 'paṭhituna', having recited; 'paṭhiya', having recited; 'paṭhiyāna', having recited.

Evaṃvidhaṃ tuṃpaccayantādivibhāgaṃ sabbattha yathārahaṃ vattukāmāpi gantha vitthārabhayena na vadāma. Avuttopi īdiso vibhāgo nayānusārena yathāsambhavaṃ sabbattha yojetabbo. Yattha pana pāḷinidassanādiviseso icchitabbo hoti, tatthevetaṃ dassessāma.

Though we wish to explain such distinctions of endings like '-tuṃ', and so forth, everywhere as appropriate, we do not do so for fear of expanding the text. Even when unstated, such distinctions should be applied everywhere as is possible, according to the method. But where a special example from the Pāli canon or the like is desired, we will show it there.

Vaṭha thūliye. Vaṭhati. Vaṭharo. Vaṭharoti thūlaghanasarīrasmiṃ vattabbavacanaṃ. Tathā hi vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vaṭharoti thūlo, thūlo ca ghanasarīro cāyaṃ bhikkhūti vuttaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Vaṭha' in the sense of bulkiness or thickness. 'Vaṭhati', it becomes bulky or thick. 'Vaṭharo', a bulky person. 'Vaṭharo' is a term to be used for a thick and solid body. For so it is said in the Vinaya commentary: “'Vaṭharo' means thick; this means it is said, 'this monk is thick and solid-bodied'.”

Maṭha nivāse. Maṭhati. Maṭho.

'Maṭha' in the sense of dwelling. 'Maṭhati', he dwells. 'Maṭho', a dwelling or hermitage.

Kaṭha kicchajīvane. Kaṭhati. Kaṭho.

'Kaṭha' in the sense of living with difficulty. 'Kaṭhati', he lives with difficulty. 'Kaṭho', a difficult life or a miserable person.

Raṭha paribhāsane. Raṭhati.

'Raṭha' in the sense of reviling or scolding. 'Raṭhati', he reviles or scolds.

Sāṭha balakkāre. Balakkāro nāma attano balena yathājjhāsayaṃ dabbalassa abhibhavanaṃ. Sāṭhati. Sāṭho.

'Sāṭha' in the sense of violence or force. 'Balakkāro' is the overpowering of the weak by one's own strength, according to one's own will. 'Sāṭhati', he acts with violence or force. 'Sāṭho', a violent or deceitful person.

Uṭha ruṭha luṭha upaghāte. Oṭhati. Roṭhati. Loṭhati.

'Uṭha', 'ruṭha', and 'luṭha' in the sense of harming. 'Oṭhati' (he/it) harms. 'Roṭhati' (he/it) harms. 'Loṭhati' (he/it) harms.

Piṭha hiṃsāsaṃkilesesu. Peṭhati. Piṭharo.

'Piṭha' in the sense of harming and defiling. 'Peṭhati' (he/it) harms and defiles. 'Piṭharo' is a pot or vessel.

Saṭha ketave ca. Pubbatthesu cakāro. Saṭhati. Saṭho saṭhoti kerāṭiko vuccati.

'Saṭha' also in the sense of deceit. The particle 'ca' refers to the preceding meanings. 'Saṭhati' (he/it) deceives. 'Saṭho' means a deceiver; a 'saṭho' is called a rogue.

Suṭha gatipaṭighāte. Gamanapaṭihananaṃ gatipaṭighāto. Soṭhati.

'Suṭha' in the sense of obstructing movement. 'Gatipaṭighāto' means the hindering of movement. 'Soṭhati' (he/it) obstructs.

Kuṭhi luṭhi ālassiye ca. Cakāro pubbatthe ca. Kuṇṭhati. Kuṇṭho. Luṇṭhati. Luṇṭho.

'Kuṭhi' and 'luṭhi' also in the sense of laziness. The particle 'ca' also refers to the preceding meanings. 'Kuṇṭhati' (he/it) is lazy or blunted. 'Kuṇṭho' means lazy or blunted. 'Luṇṭhati' (he/it) is lazy or plunders. 'Luṇṭho' means lazy or a plunderer.

Suṭhi [M 0.0057] sosane. Suṇṭhati.

'Suṭhi' in the sense of drying. 'Suṇṭhati' (it) dries.

Ruṭhi luṭhi aṭhi gatiyaṃ. Ruṇṭhati. Luṇṭhati. Aṇṭhati.

'Ruṭhi', 'luṭhi', and 'aṭhi' in the sense of movement. 'Ruṇṭhati' (he/it) moves. 'Luṇṭhati' (he/it) moves. 'Aṇṭhati' (he/it) moves.

Veṭha veṭhane. Veṭhati, nibbeṭhati. Veṭhanaṃ, nibbeṭhanaṃ.

'Veṭha' in the sense of wrapping. 'Veṭhati' (he/it) wraps; 'nibbeṭhati' (he/it) unwraps. 'Veṭhanaṃ' is wrapping; 'nibbeṭhanaṃ' is unwrapping.

Vaṭhi ekacariyāyaṃ. Vaṇṭhati.

'Vaṭhi' in the sense of solitary wandering. 'Vaṇṭhati' (he/it) wanders in solitude.

Maṭha kuṭhi soke. Maṭhati. Kuṇṭhati.

'Maṭha' and 'kuṭhi' in the sense of sorrow. 'Maṭhati' (he/it) grieves. 'Kuṇṭhati' (he/it) grieves.

Eṭha heṭha vibādhāyaṃ. Eṭhati. Heṭhati. Viheṭhati. Viheṭhanaṃ.

'Eṭha' and 'heṭha' in the sense of oppression. 'Eṭhati' (he/it) oppresses. 'Heṭhati' (he/it) oppresses. 'Viheṭhati' (he/it) harasses. 'Viheṭhanaṃ' is harassment.

Luṭha paṭighāte. Loṭhati.

'Luṭha' in the sense of striking against. 'Loṭhati' (he/it) strikes against.

Paṭha vikhyāne. Paṭhati.

'Paṭha' in the sense of proclaiming. 'Paṭhati' (he/it) proclaims.

Luṭha saṃkilese. Loṭhati.

'Luṭha' in the sense of defilement. 'Loṭhati' (he/it) defiles.

Ṭhakārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of roots ending in ṭha.

Ḍakārantadhātu

Roots ending in ḍa.

Ḍi vihāyasagatiyaṃ gamanamatte ca. Ḍeti, ḍayati. Ḍemāno. Ucce sakuṇa ḍemāna. Ye maṃ pure paccuḍḍenti.

'Ḍi' in the sense of moving through the sky and in mere movement. 'Ḍeti', 'ḍayati'. 'Ḍemāno'. 'Ucce sakuṇa ḍemāna'. 'Ye maṃ pure paccuḍḍenti'.

Ḍi khipanuḍḍanesu. Ḍeti. Uḍḍeti.

'Ḍi' in the sense of throwing and flying up. 'Ḍeti'. 'Uḍḍeti'.

Ito bahiddhā pāsaṇḍā, diṭṭhīsu pasīdanti te;

Na tesaṃ dhammaṃ rocemi, na te dhammassa kovidā.

Outside of this, those adhering to other paths delight in their views; I do not approve of their doctrine, nor are they skilled in the Dhamma.

Ettha ca pāsaṇḍāti pāsaṃ ḍentīti pāsaṇḍā, sattānaṃ cittesu diṭṭhipāsaṃ khipantīti attho. Atha vā taṇhāpāsaṃ diṭṭhipāsañca ḍenti uḍḍentīti pāsaṇḍā.

Here, 'pāsaṇḍā' means those who cast (ḍenti) a snare (pāsaṃ)—that is, they cast the snare of views into the minds of beings. Alternatively, 'pāsaṇḍā' means those who cut off (ḍenti) or drive away (uḍḍenti) the snare of craving and the snare of views.

Muḍi [M 0.0058] kaṇḍane. Muṇḍati. Kumāraṃ muṇḍiṃsu. Muṇḍo.

'Muḍi' in the sense of shaving. 'Muṇḍati'. 'Kumāraṃ muṇḍiṃsu'. 'Muṇḍo'.

Cuḍḍa hāvakaraṇe. Cuḍḍati.

'Cuḍḍa' in the sense of dalliance. 'Cuḍḍati'.

Aḍḍa abhiyoge. Aḍḍati.

'Aḍḍa' in the sense of exertion. 'Aḍḍati'.

Gaḍi vadanekadese. Gaṇḍati. Gaṇḍo.

'Gaḍi' in the sense of a part of the face. 'Gaṇḍati'. 'Gaṇḍo'.

Huḍi piḍi saṅghāte. Huṇḍati. Piṇḍati. Piṇḍo.

'Huḍi' and 'piḍi' in the sense of gathering. 'Huṇḍati'. 'Piṇḍati'. 'Piṇḍo'.

Hiḍi gatiyaṃ. Hiṇḍati, āhiṇḍati.

'Hiḍi' in the sense of movement. 'Hiṇḍati', 'āhiṇḍati'.

Kuḍi dāhe. Kuṇḍati. Kuṇḍo.

'Kuḍi' in the sense of burning. 'Kuṇḍati'. 'Kuṇḍo'.

Vaḍi maḍi veṭhane. Vaṇḍati. Maṇḍati. Maṇḍalaṃ.

'Vaḍi' and 'maḍi' in the sense of enclosing. 'Vaṇḍati'. 'Maṇḍati'. 'Maṇḍalaṃ'.

Bhaḍi paribhāsane. Bhaṇḍati. Bhaṇḍanaṃ. Bhaṇḍo.

'Bhaḍi' in the sense of scolding. 'Bhaṇḍati'. 'Bhaṇḍanaṃ'. 'Bhaṇḍo'.

Maḍi majjane. Maṇḍati. Maṇḍanaṃ.

'Maḍi' in the sense of cleansing. 'Maṇḍati'. 'Maṇḍanaṃ'.

Tuḍi toḷane. Tuṇḍati. Tuṇḍo. Tuṇḍenādāya gaccheyya.

Tuḍi: in pecking. Tuṇḍati. Tuṇḍo. Tuṇḍenādāya gaccheyya.

Bhuḍi bharaṇe. Bhuṇḍati.

Bhuḍi: in bearing, supporting. Bhuṇḍati.

Caḍi kope. Caṇḍati. Caṇḍo. Caṇḍālo, caṇḍikkaṃ.

Caḍi: in anger. Caṇḍati. Caṇḍo. Caṇḍālo, caṇḍikkaṃ.

Saḍi rujāyaṃ. Saṇḍati. Saṇḍo.

Saḍi: in sickness. Saṇḍati. Saṇḍo.

Taḍi tāḷane. Taṇḍati. Vitaṇḍā.

Taḍi: in striking. Taṇḍati. Vitaṇḍā.

Paḍi gatiyaṃ. Paṇḍati. Paṇḍā, paṇḍito. Ettha paṇḍāti paññā. Sā hi sukhumesupi atthesu paṇḍati gacchati dukkhādīnaṃ pīḷanādikampi ākāraṃ jānātīti “paṇḍā”ti vuccati. Paṇḍitoti paṇḍāya ito gato pavattoti paṇḍito. Atha vā sañjātā paṇḍā etassāti paṇḍito. Paṇḍati ñāṇagatiyā gacchatītipi paṇḍito. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 0.0059] vuttaṃ “paṇḍantīti paṇḍitā. Sandiṭṭhikasamparāyikatthesu ñāṇagatiyā gacchantīti attho”ti.

Paḍi: in movement. Paṇḍati. Paṇḍā, paṇḍito. Here, 'paṇḍā' means wisdom (paññā). For it penetrates (paṇḍati, gacchati) even the subtlest meanings and knows the nature of afflictions such as suffering, thus it is called 'paṇḍā'. 'Paṇḍito' means one who has gone forth by wisdom (paṇḍāya ito gato) or one in whom wisdom has arisen (sañjātā paṇḍā etassa). Alternatively, 'paṇḍito' means one who moves by the path of knowledge (ñāṇagatiyā gacchati). As stated in the commentary: 'They are paṇḍitā because they penetrate (paṇḍanti). That is, they proceed by the path of knowledge in matters pertaining to both this life and the next.'

Gaḍi made. Gaṇḍati.

Gaḍi: in intoxication. Gaṇḍati.

Khaḍi manthe. Khaṇḍati. Khaṇḍito, khaṇḍo.

Khaḍi: in stirring. Khaṇḍati. Khaṇḍito, khaṇḍo.

Laḍi jivhāmathane. Laṇḍati. Laṇḍo.

Laḍi: in stirring the tongue. Laṇḍati. Laṇḍo.

Ḍakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in the ḍ-sound.

Ḍakārantadhātu

Roots ending in the ḍ-sound.

Vaḍḍha vaḍḍhane. Vaḍḍhati. Sirivaḍḍhako, dhanavaḍḍhako, vaḍḍhito, buḍḍho. Ettha ca vakārassa bakāro, akārassa cukāro.

Vaḍḍha: in growth. Vaḍḍhati. Sirivaḍḍhako, dhanavaḍḍhako, vaḍḍhito, buḍḍho. Here, the 'va' becomes 'ba', and the 'a' becomes 'u'.

Kaḍḍha ākaḍḍhane. Kaḍḍhati, ākaḍḍhati, nikaḍḍhati. Akāmā parikaḍḍhanti, ulūkaññeva vāyasā.

Kaḍḍha: in dragging. Kaḍḍhati, ākaḍḍhati, nikaḍḍhati. Akāmā parikaḍḍhanti, ulūkaññeva vāyasā.

Imāni ḍhakārantadhāturūpāni.

These are the forms of roots ending in the ḍh-sound.

Ṇakārantadhātu

Roots ending in the ṇ-sound.

Aṇa raṇa vaṇa bhaṇa maṇa kaṇa sadde. Aṇati. Aṇako brāhmaṇo. Raṇati. Raṇaṃ. Vaṇati. Vāṇako. Bhaṇati. Bhāṇako. Maṇati. Maṇiko. Kaṇati. Kāṇo. Tattha brāhmaṇoti brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇo, mante sajjhāyatīti attho. Akkharacintakā pana “brahmuno apaccaṃ brāhmaṇo”ti vadanti. Ariyā pana bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇoti.

Aṇa, Raṇa, Vaṇa, Bhaṇa, Maṇa, Kaṇa: in sound. Aṇati. Aṇako. Brāhmaṇo. Raṇati. Raṇaṃ. Vaṇati. Vāṇako. Bhaṇati. Bhāṇako. Maṇati. Maṇiko. Kaṇati. Kāṇo. Here, 'brāhmaṇo' means one who sounds 'brahma' (brahmaṃ aṇati)—that is, one who recites the mantras. The grammarians (akkharacintakā), however, say, 'A brāhmaṇa is the offspring of Brahmā.' But the noble ones (ariyā) say, 'A brāhmaṇa is one who has cast out evil (bāhitapāpattā).'

Brāhmaṇo [M 0.0060] sottiyo vippo, bhovādī brahmabandhu ca;

Brahmasūnu dvijo brahmā, kamalāsanasūnu ca;

A brāhmaṇa is a Vedic scholar, a wise one, a speaker of 'bho', and a kinsman of Brahmā; a son of Brahmā, a twice-born, Brahmā, and a son of the lotus-seated one.

Raṇasaddo “saraṇā dhammā araṇā dhammā”tiādīsu kilesesu vattati. Kilesā hi raṇanti kandanti etehīti raṇāti vuccanti.

The word 'raṇa' applies to defilements in expressions such as 'states with defilements' and 'states without defilements'. Defilements are called 'raṇa' because through them one laments and wails.

“Dhanuggaho asadiso, rājaputto mahabbalo;

Sabbāmitte raṇaṃ katvā, saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamī”ti

The unmatched archer, the prince of great strength, having made war against all enemies, attained restraint.

Ettha yuddhe vattati. Raṇaṃ katvāti hi yuddhaṃ katvāti attho. “Tiṇañca kaṭṭhañca raṇaṃ karontā, dhāviṃsu te aṭṭhadisā samantato”ti ettha cuṇṇavicuṇṇakaraṇe vattati. Raṇaṃ karontāti hi cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karontāti attho. Evaṃ atthavivaraṇampi saddasaṅkhātamatthaṃ antoyeva katvā adhippāyatthavasena kataṃ, na dhātunānatthavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā dhātūnamatthātisayayogopi bhavati, tena evaṃ atthavivaraṇaṃ katantipi daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, it applies in the sense of battle. 'Raṇaṃ katvā' means 'having made battle'. In the phrase, 'Making grass and wood into dust, they rushed about in all eight directions,' it applies in the sense of crushing into fine particles. 'Raṇaṃ karontā' means 'reducing to powder'. Thus, it should be understood that this explanation of meaning is made according to the intended sense, based on the meaning designated by the word itself, and not due to a diversity of root meanings. Alternatively, it should also be understood that roots may have an abundance of meanings, and for that reason this explanation of meaning is made in this way.

Bhaṇa bhaṇane. Parittaṃ bhaṇati, vacanaṃ bhaṇati. Dīghabhāṇako, piyabhāṇī, bhāṇavāro. Ettha bhāṇavāroti –

Bhaṇa: in speaking. Parittaṃ bhaṇati, vacanaṃ bhaṇati. Dīghabhāṇako, piyabhāṇī, bhāṇavāro. Here, 'bhāṇavāro' means –

“Aṭṭhakkharā ekapadaṃ, ekā gāthā catuppadaṃ;

Gāthā cekāmato gantho, gantho bāttiṃsatakkharo;

Eight syllables are one line, one verse has four lines; and one verse is considered a section, a section has thirty-two syllables.

Bāttiṃsakkharaganthānaṃ, paññāsaṃ dvisataṃ pana;

Bhāṇavāro mato eko, svaṭṭhakkharasahassako”ti.

Of sections with thirty-two syllables, two hundred and fifty are considered one recitation section; a recitation section is reckoned as one, with eight thousand syllables.

Evaṃ aṭṭhakkharasahassaparimāṇo pāṭho vuccati.

Thus, a text measuring eight thousand syllables is called a recitation section.

Oṇaṃ apanayane. Oṇati.

Oṇa: in removing. Oṇati.

Soṇa vaṇṇagatīsu. Soṇati, soṇo.

Soṇa: in colors and movements. Soṇati, soṇo.

Soṇa [M 0.0061] siloṇa saṅghāte. Soṇati. Siloṇati.

Soṇa, Siloṇa: in gathering. Soṇati. Siloṇati.

Ghiṇi ghuṇi ghaṇi gahaṇe. Ghiṇṇati. Ghuṇṇati. Ghaṇṇati.

Ghiṇi, Ghuṇi, Ghaṇi: in grasping. Ghiṇṇati. Ghuṇṇati. Ghaṇṇati.

Ghuṇa ghuṇṇa gamane. Ghoṇati. Ghuṇṇati.

Ghuṇa, Ghuṇṇa: in movement. Ghoṇati. Ghuṇṇati.

Paṇa byavahāre, thutiyañca. Paṇati vāṇijo, vohāraṃ karoti iccattho. Saddho buddhaṃ paṇati, thomayati iccattho, āpaṇaṃ, sāpaṇo gāmo.

Paṇa: in trade and in praise. A merchant 'paṇati', meaning he engages in commerce. The faithful 'paṇati' the Buddha, meaning they extol. Āpaṇaṃ, sāpaṇo gāmo.

Gaṇa raṇa gatiyaṃ. Gaṇati. Raṇati.

The roots Gaṇa and Raṇa are in the sense of movement. Gaṇati. Raṇati.

Caṇa saṇa dāne. Caṇati. Saṇati.

The roots Caṇa and Saṇa are in the sense of giving. Caṇati. Saṇati.

Phaṇa gatiyaṃ. Phaṇati. Phaṇaṃ.

The root Phaṇa is in the sense of movement. Phaṇati. Phaṇaṃ.

Veṇu ñāṇacintānisāmanesu. Veṇati.

The root Veṇu is in the sense of knowledge, thought, and examination. Veṇati.

Pīṇa pīṇane. Pīṇanaṃ paripuṇṇatā. Pīṇati. Pīṇo divā na bhuñjati, pīṇorakkhaṃsabāhu.

The root Pīṇa is in the sense of making full. Pīṇanaṃ means fullness. Pīṇati. 'Pīṇo divā na bhuñjati' (A fat person does not eat by day); 'pīṇorakkhaṃsabāhu' (one with a plump chest, shoulders, and arms).

Miṇa hiṃsāyaṃ. Miṇati.

The root Miṇa is in the sense of harming. Miṇati.

Duṇa gatiyañca. Hiṃsāpekkhako cakāro. Duṇati.

The root Duṇa is in the sense of movement; the particle 'ca' also implies harming. Duṇati.

Saṇa abyattasadde. Saṇati. Saṇateva brahmāraññaṃ. Saṇatevāti nadati viya.

The root Saṇa is in the sense of indistinct sound. Saṇati. 'Saṇateva brahmāraññaṃ' (The great forest seems to resound). 'Saṇateva' means 'as if it sounds loudly'.

Tuṇa koṭille. Toṇati.

The root Tuṇa is in the sense of crookedness. Toṇati.

Puṇa nipuṇe. Puṇati, nipuṇati. Nipuṇadhammo. Ettha ca nipuṇasaṇhasukhumasaddā vevacanasaddā kusalachekadakkhasaddā viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The root Puṇa is in the sense of subtlety. Puṇati, nipuṇati. 'Nipuṇadhammo' (one of a subtle nature). Here, it should be understood that the words nipuṇa, saṇha, and sukhuma are synonyms, like the words kusala, cheka, and dakkha.

Muṇa paṭiññāṇe. Muṇati.

The root Muṇa is in the sense of acknowledgment. Muṇati.

Kuṇa saddopakaraṇe. Koṇati.

The root Kuṇa is in the sense of sound-making. Koṇati.

Cuṇa [M 0.0062] chedane. Coṇati.

The root Cuṇa is in the sense of cutting. Coṇati.

Maṇa cāge. Veraṃ maṇatīti veramaṇi.

The root Maṇa is in the sense of abandonment. 'Veramaṇi' (abstinence) is so called because one abandons (maṇati) enmity (veraṃ).

Phuṇa vikiraṇe vidhunane ca. Phuṇati. Aṅgārakāsuṃ apare phuṇanti.

The root Phuṇa is in the sense of scattering and shaking. Phuṇati. 'Aṅgārakāsuṃ apare phuṇanti' (Others scatter embers on the charcoal pit).

Imāni ṇakārantadhāturūpāni.

These are the forms of roots ending in the letter ṇ.

Iti bhūvādigaṇe ṭavaggantadhāturūpāni

Thus, the forms of roots ending in the ṭa-group (ṭavagga) in the Bhūvādi class.

Samattāni.

Completed.

Takārantadhātu

Roots ending in ta

Atha tavaggantadhāturūpāni vuccante –

Now, the forms of roots ending in the ta-group are spoken:

Te pālane. Pālanaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ. Tāyati. Tāṇaṃ, gottaṃ, nakkhattaṃ. Aghassa tātā. Kicchenādhigatā bhogā, te tāto vidhami dhamaṃ. Tattha gottanti gaṃ tāyatīti gottaṃ. “Gotamo kassapo”ti hi ādinā pavattamānaṃ gaṃ vacanaṃ buddhiñca tāyati ekaṃsikavisayatāya rakkhatīti gottaṃ. Yathā hi buddhi ārammaṇabhūtena atthena vinā na vattati, tathā abhidhānaṃ abhidheyyabhūtena, tasmā so gottasaṅkhāto attho tāni tāyati rakkhatīti vuccati. Ko pana soti? Aññakulaparamparāsādhāraṇaṃ tassa kulassa ādipurisasammuditaṃ taṃkulapariyāpannasādhāraṇaṃ sāmaññarūpaṃ.

The root Te is in the sense of protecting. Protecting is guarding. Tāyati. Examples are: Tāṇaṃ, gottaṃ, nakkhattaṃ. 'Aghassa tātā' (A protector from harm). 'Kicchenādhigatā bhogā, te tāto vidhami dhamaṃ' (Wealth gained with difficulty, that father destroyed the Dhamma). Therein, 'gotta' (lineage) is so called because it protects (tāyati) the lineage (gaṃ). For indeed, the lineage (gaṃ), which continues from the beginning as in 'Gotama, Kassapa,' etc., protects both speech and intellect by its specific reference; thus it is 'gotta'. For just as the intellect does not function without an object, so too a designation does not function without its referent. Therefore, that meaning called 'gotta' is said to protect (tāyati) these. But what is that? It is a general characteristic, not common to the lineage of other families, originating from the first man of that family, and common to all who are included within that clan.

Nakkhattanti visamagatiyā agantvā attano vīthiyāva gamanena nakkhanaṃ gamanaṃ tāyati rakkhatīti nakkhattaṃ, taṃ pana assayujādivasena sattavīsatividhaṃ hoti. Tathā hi assayujo [M 0.0063] bharaṇī kattikā rohaṇī migasiro addā punabbasu phusso assaliso māgho pubbaphagguṇī uttaraphagguṇī hattho cittaṃ svāti visākhā anurādhā jeṭṭhā mūlaṃ pubbāsaḷhaṃ uttarāsaḷhaṃ sāvaṇaṃ dhanasiṭṭhā satabhisattaṃ pubbabhaddapadaṃ uttarabhaddapadaṃ revatī cāti sattavīsati nakkhattāni. Tāni pana attano gamanaṭṭhānaṃ īsakampi na vijahanti kiñci sīghaṃ kiñci dandhaṃ, kadāci sīghaṃ, kadāci dandhaṃ, etto ito cāti evaṃ visamagatiyā agantvā yantacakke paṭipāṭiyā yojitāni viya samappamāṇagatiyā attano vīthiyāva gacchantāni maṇḍalākārena sineruṃ parivattanti. Evaṃ imāni nakkhanaṃ gamanaṃ tāyanti rakkhantīti nakkhattānīti vuccanti. Porāṇā pana kharadhātuvasena “nakkharanti na nassantīti nakkhattānī”ti āvocuṃ, “nakkhattaṃ joti rikkhaṃ taṃ” iccetāni nakkhattatārakānaṃ nāmāni. “Uḷu tārā tārakā”ti imāni pana sabbāsampi tārakānaṃ sādhāraṇanāmāni. Osadhīti pana tārakāvisesassa nāmaṃ.

The constellations (nakkhatta) are so called because they protect (tāyati) and guard their movement (gamanaṃ) by not going with irregular motion but by their own path (nakkhanaṃ). They are of twenty-seven kinds, beginning with Assayuja. To elaborate: Assayuja, Bharaṇī, Kattikā, Rohiṇī, Migasira, Addā, Punabbasu, Phussa, Āsilesā, Māgha, Pubbaphagguṇī, Uttaraphagguṇī, Hatthā, Cittā, Svāti, Visākhā, Anurādhā, Jeṭṭhā, Mūla, Pubbāsāḷha, Uttarāsāḷha, Sāvaṇa, Dhaniṭṭhā, Satabhisa, Pubbabhaddapadā, Uttarabhaddapadā, and Revatī—these are the twenty-seven constellations. These constellations never abandon their own place of movement, not even slightly. Some move swiftly, some slowly; sometimes quickly, sometimes leisurely, shifting here and there. Yet, without going with irregular motion, they move with uniform motion along their own paths like spokes fixed in order to a wheel, revolving around Mount Sineru in a circular manner. Thus, because they guard and protect their movement, they are called 'nakkhattāni'. The ancients, however, explained them based on the root 'khar', saying, 'nakkharanti na nassantīti nakkhattāni' (they do not perish, hence they are nakkhattāni). 'Nakkhattaṃ,' 'joti,' and 'rikkhaṃ' are names for the constellations. 'Uḷu,' 'tārā,' and 'tārakā' are common names for all stars. 'Osadhī,' however, is the name of a particular star.

Citi saññāṇe. Saññāṇaṃ cihanaṃ lakkhaṇakaraṇaṃ. Cetati. Cihanaṃ karotīti attho. Īkārantavasena vuttattā asmā dhātuto saki saṅkāyanti dhātuto viya niggahītāgamo na hoti. Esa nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu.

The root Citi is in the sense of cognizing. Saññāṇa means marking or characterizing. Cetati. The meaning is that it performs the act of marking. Because it is stated with an 'i' ending, from this root, like from the root 'sak' in the sense of 'saṅkā' (doubt), there is no nasal augment. This is the method in other such cases as well.

Pata gatiyaṃ. Patati. Papatati papātaṃ, papateyyahaṃ. Pāpattaṃ nirayaṃ bhusaṃ. Ahaṃsaddena yojetabbaṃ, pāpattaṃ papatitosmīti attho. Pāpattha nirayaṃ bhusaṃ, sokumāroti yojetabbaṃ, pāpattha papatitoti attho. Parokkhāpadañhietaṃ dvayaṃ. “Pāvadaṃ pāvadā”tiādīsu viya upasaggapadassa dīghabhāvo, tato aṃsaddassa ttaṃādeso, asaddassa ca tthādeso bhavati. Acinteyyo hi pāḷinayo.

The root Pata is in the sense of going or falling. Patati. 'Papatati papātaṃ' (He falls into a precipice); 'papateyyahaṃ' (I would fall). 'Pāpattaṃ nirayaṃ bhusaṃ' (I have fallen into a terrible hell). This should be connected with the word 'ahaṃ' (I); the meaning is 'papatitosmi' (I have fallen). 'Pāpattha nirayaṃ bhusaṃ' (He has fallen into a terrible hell). This should be connected with 'so kumāro' (that boy); the meaning is 'papatito' (he has fallen). Indeed, these two are forms of the perfect tense. As in 'pāvadaṃ pāvadā' and so on, the prefix is lengthened, and then the substitution of 'tta' for the ending 'aṃ', and 'ttha' for the ending 'a' occurs. Truly, the way of Pāli is inconceivable.

Ata [M 0.0064] sātaccagamane. Sātaccagamanaṃ nirantaragamanaṃ. Atati. Yasmā pana atadhātu sātaccagamanatthavācikā, tasmā bhavābhavaṃ dhāvanto jātijarābyādhimaraṇādibhedaṃ anekavihitaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ atati satataṃ gacchati pāpuṇāti adhigacchatīti attātipi nibbacanamicchitabbaṃ. Atthantaravasena pana “āhito ahaṃmāno etthāti attā, attabhāvo”ti ca “sukhadukkhaṃ adati anubhavatīti attā”ti ca “attamanoti pītisomanassena gahitamano”ti ca attho daṭṭhabbo, yattha yattha yathā yathā attho labbhati, tattha tattha tathā tathā atthassa gahetabbatoti.

The root Ata is in the sense of constant movement. Sātaccagamana means uninterrupted movement. Atati. Since the root 'ata' expresses the meaning of constant movement, therefore, 'attā' should be understood as that which, running through existence and non-existence, constantly goes, reaches, attains, and undergoes the manifold suffering of saṃsāra—such as birth, aging, sickness, and death. However, according to different meanings, it should also be understood as: 'The conceit 'I am' is placed (āhito) here, thus it is 'attā' (self), or 'attabhāva' (individual existence).' Also, 'It eats (adati) or experiences pleasure and pain, thus it is 'attā'.' And, 'One whose mind is seized by joy and satisfaction is called 'attamano' (pleased).' Wherever and in whatever way a meaning is obtained, it should be understood in that particular way.

Cuta āsecane kharaṇe ca. Cotati.

The root Cuta is in the sense of sprinkling and flowing. Cotati.

Ati bandhane. Antati. Antaṃ. Antiyatibandhiyati antaguṇenāti antaṃ. Idha anta saddassa atthuddhāro vuccate “antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariya”nti ettha dvattiṃsākārantogadhaṃ kuṇapantaṃ antaṃ nāma. “Kāyabandhanassa anto jīrati. Haritantaṃ vā”ti ettha antimamariyādanto anto nāma. “Antamidaṃ bhikkhave jīvikāna”nti ettha lāmakanto. “Sakkāyo eko anto”ti ettha koṭṭhāsanto. “Esevanto dukkhassa sappaccayasaṅkhayā”ti ettha koṭanto. Iccevaṃ –

The root Ati is in the sense of binding. Antati. Antaṃ (end, intestine). It is bound (antiyati, bandhiyati) by the intestine (antaguṇa); therefore, it is called antaṃ. Here, the explanation of the meaning of the word 'anta' is given: In 'antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariyaṃ' (intestine, intestinal tract, belly), the foul part included in the thirty-two parts of the body is called 'anta'. In 'Kāyabandhanassa anto jīrati. Haritantaṃ vā' (The end of the body's binding decays. Or the green end), here 'anta' means the final limit. In 'Antamidaṃ bhikkhave jīvikānaṃ' (This, monks, is the lowest of livelihoods), here it means the base end. In 'Sakkāyo eko anto' (The existing body is one extreme), here it means the partial end. In 'Esevanto dukkhassa sappaccayasaṅkhayā' (This is the end of suffering, with the cessation of its cause), here it means the terminal end. Thus—

Kuṇapantaṃ [M 0.0065] antimañca, mariyādo ca lāmakaṃ;

Koṭṭhāso koṭi’me attho, antasaddena bhāsitā.

The foul intestine, the ultimate, the boundary, and the base; the portion and the extreme—these are the meanings spoken by the word 'anta'.

Kita nivāse rogāpanayane ca. Ketati. Sāketaṃ na garaṃ, niketo, niketaṃ pāvisi. Āmodamāno gacchati sanniketaṃ. Tikicchati, cikicchati, cikicchā, cikicchako. Tattha sāketanti sāyaṃ gahitavasanaṭṭhānattā sāketaṃ, yaṃsaddalopo.

The root Kita is in the sense of dwelling and of removing illness. Ketati. Examples for dwelling: 'Sāketaṃ nagaraṃ' (the city of Sāketa); 'niketo' (a dwelling); 'niketaṃ pāvisi' (he entered the dwelling); 'Āmodamāno gacchati sanniketaṃ' (Rejoicing, he goes to his own dwelling). Examples for removing illness: Tikicchati, cikicchati (he treats/heals); cikicchā (treatment); cikicchako (a healer). Therein, Sāketa is so called because it is a place where one takes up residence in the evening (sāyaṃ), with the elision of the syllable 'yaṃ'.

Yata patiyatane. Patiyatanaṃ vāyāmakaraṇaṃ. Yatati. Yati, yatavā, payatanaṃ, āyatanaṃ, lokāyataṃ. Ettha āyatananti āyatanato āyatanaṃ, cakkhurūpādīni. Etāni hi taṃdvārārammaṇacittacetasikā dhammā sena sena anubhavanādikiccena āyatanti uṭṭhahanti ghaṭanti vāyamanti etesūti “āyatanānī”ti vuccanti. Ettha pana nītanudhātūnaṃ vasenapi āyatanasaddattho vattabbo siyā, so uttari āvibhavissati.

The root Yata is in the sense of striving. Patiyatana means making an effort. Yatati. Examples are: Yati, yatavā, payatanaṃ, āyatanaṃ, lokāyataṃ. Here, 'āyatana' is so called because of extending (āyatanato), for example, the eye and forms. For in these spheres, mental states and mental factors, which have those doors as their objects, extend, arise, strive, and exert themselves in their respective functions of experiencing and so on; therefore, they are called 'āyatanas' (spheres). Here, however, the meaning of the word 'āyatana' may also be explained by way of the roots nī (to lead) and tanu (to extend), which will be made clear later.

Āyatanasaddo nivāsaṭṭhāne ākare samosaraṇaṭṭhāne sañjātidese kāraṇe ca. Tathā hi “loke issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatana”ntiādīsu nivāsaṭṭhāne āyatanasaddo vattati. “Suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ rajatāyatana”ntiādīsu ākare. Sāsane pana “manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā”tiādīsu samosaraṇaṭṭhāne. “Dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatana”ntiādīsu sañjātidese. “Tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”tiādīsu kāraṇe vattatīti [M 0.0066] veditabbo. So ca nānāpavattinimittavasena gahetabbo.

The term 'āyatana' is used in the sense of a dwelling place, a source, a gathering place, a place of origin, and a cause. For example, in phrases like 'the dwelling of the lord (issarāyatana)' and 'the dwelling of Vāsudeva (vāsudevāyatana),' the term 'āyatana' denotes a dwelling place. In phrases like 'the golden source (suvaṇṇāyatana)' and 'the silver source (rajatāyatana),' it refers to a source. In the teachings, as in 'in a delightful gathering place (manorame āyatane), birds frequent it,' it signifies a gathering place. In 'the southern region is the place of origin of cows (dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatana),' it indicates a place of origin. And in 'there, in every possible cause (sati satiāyatane), he attains the state of being a witness,' it denotes a cause. Thus it should be understood. And it should be understood based on its various originating causes.

Nivāse ākāre ceva, jātidese ca kāraṇe;

Samosaraṇaṭṭhāne ca, āyatanaravo gato.

In dwelling, and in source, in place of origin, and in cause; and in a gathering place, the word 'āyatana' is used.

Lokāyataṃ nāma “sabbaṃ ucchiṭṭhaṃ, sabbaṃ nucchiṭṭhaṃ. Seto kāko, kāḷo bako iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenā”ti evamādiniratthakakāraṇapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ titthiyasatthaṃ, yaṃ loke “vitaṇḍasattha”nti vuccati, yañca sandhāya bodhisatto asamadhuro vidhurapaṇḍito “na seve lokāyatikaṃ, netaṃ paññāya vaḍḍhana”nti āha. Āyatiṃ hitaṃ tena loko na yatati na īhatīti lokāyataṃ, kintaṃ? Vitaṇḍasatthaṃ. Tañhi ganthaṃ nissāya sattā puññakriyāya cittampi na uppādenti. Aññatthāpi hi evaṃ vuttaṃ “lokāyatasippanti ‘kāko seto, aṭṭhīnaṃ setattā, balākā rattā, lohitassa rattattā’ti evamādinayappavattaṃ paralokanibbānānaṃ paṭisedhakaṃ vitaṇḍasatthasippa”nti.

Lokāyata means a heretical doctrine connected with meaningless arguments based on causes, such as 'Everything is refuse, everything is not refuse. A white crow, a black heron—due to this and that reason,' and so on, which in the world is called 'the doctrine of sophistry (vitaṇḍasattha)'. And referring to which the incomparable and wise Bodhisatta Vidhura said, 'Do not cultivate Lokāyata, for it does not lead to the growth of wisdom.' It is called Lokāyata because people do not strive (yatati) or endeavor (īhati) for future welfare (āyatiṃ hitaṃ) through it; what is it? The doctrine of sophistry. For relying on such a text, beings do not even generate a mind for meritorious action. Elsewhere, it is also said: 'The art of Lokāyata is the sophistry that proceeds on the principle, 'A crow is white because bones are white; a heron is red because blood is red,' and so on—a doctrine of sophistry that denies the afterlife and Nibbāna.'

Yuta juta bhāsane. Bhāsanaṃ udīraṇaṃ. Yotati. Jotati.

The roots 'yuta' and 'juta' are in the sense of speaking. 'Bhāsana' means uttering. It speaks. It speaks.

Jutadittiyaṃ. Jotati, vijjotati. Juti, joti. Kārite “joteti, jotayitvāna saddhamma”nti payogā. Ettha ca jutīti āloko siri vā. Jotīti patāpo. Atha vā jotīti candādīni. Vuttampi ceta sirimāvimāna vatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “jotīti candimasūriyanakkhattatārakānaṃ sādhāraṇanāma”nti. Atha vā “joti jotiparāyaṇo”ti vacanato yo koci jotati khattiyakulādīsu jātattā ca rūpasobhāyuttattā ca, so “jotī”ti vuccati.

The root 'juta' is in the sense of shining. It shines, it illuminates. 'Juti,' 'joti.' In the causative form, there are usages such as 'joteti,' as in 'having illuminated the true Dhamma.' Here, 'juti' means light or splendor, while 'joti' means majesty. Alternatively, 'joti' refers to celestial bodies like the moon and so on. It is also stated in the commentary on the Sirimāvimāna: ''Joti' is the common name for the moon, sun, stars, and constellations.' Or, based on the saying 'joti jotiparāyaṇo' (the shining one whose destination is light), anyone who shines—whether due to being born in a noble family, or because of being endowed with beautiful appearance—is called 'joti'.

Sita [M 0.0067] vaṇṇo. Sitadhātu setavaṇṇe vattati. Kiñcāpettha vaṇṇasāmaññaṃ vuttaṃ, tathāpi idha nīlapītādīsu setavaṇṇoyeva gahetabbo payogadassanavasena. Setati. Setaṃ vatthaṃ. Vāccaliṅgattā pana setasaddo tiliṅgo gahetabbo.

The root 'sita' is in the sense of color. The root 'sita' is used for the color white. Although a general sense of color is stated, nevertheless, here, among blue, yellow, and so on, only the color white should be understood, based on observed usage. It becomes white. White cloth. But because it is an adjective, the word 'seta' should be understood as having three genders.

Setaṃ sitaṃ suci sukkaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ dhavalampi ca;

Akaṇhaṃ goramodātaṃ, setanāmāni honti hi.

Seta, sita, suci, sukka, paṇḍara, and dhavala; akaṇha, gora, odāta—these are indeed names for 'white'.

Vatu vattane. Vattati, pavattati, saṃvattati, anuvattati, parivattati. Pavattaṃ.

The root 'vatu' is in the sense of turning or existing. It turns, proceeds, conduces, conforms, revolves. Proceeded.

Kilota addabhāve. Addabhāvo tintabhāvo. Kilotati, pakilotati, temetīti attho. Kārite pakiloteti, pakilotayati. Uṇhodakasmiṃ pakilotayitvā, temetvāti attho.

The root 'kilota' is in the sense of becoming wet. Becoming wet means becoming moist. 'Kilotati' and 'pakilotati' mean 'it moistens.' In the causative, 'pakiloteti' or 'pakilotayati.' 'Uṇhodakasmiṃ pakilotayitvā' means 'having moistened in warm water.'

Vata yācane. Vatati.

The root 'vata' is in the sense of asking. 'Vatati.'

Kita ñāṇe. Ketati. Ketanaṃ, ketako, saṅketo.

The root 'kita' is in the sense of knowing. 'Ketati.' 'Ketanaṃ,' 'ketako,' 'saṅketo.'

Kati suttajanane. Suttaṃ kantati.

The root 'kati' is in the sense of producing thread. 'Suttaṃ kantati' (he spins thread).

Kati chedane. Maṃsaṃ kantati, vikantati, ayokanto. Sallakanto mahāvīro. Mā no ajja vikantiṃsu, rañño sūdā mahānase.

The root 'kati' is in the sense of cutting. 'Maṃsaṃ kantati' (he cuts flesh), 'vikantati' (he cuts apart), 'ayokanto' (an iron cutter). 'Sallakanto mahāvīro' (the great hero who cuts away barbs). 'Mā no ajja vikantiṃsu, rañño sūdā mahānase' (may the king’s cooks not cut us apart today in the great kitchen).

Catī hiṃsāgandhesu. Īkārantattā imasmā niggahītāgamo na hoti. Catati.

The root 'catī' is in the senses of harming and smelling. Because it ends in 'ī,' there is no niggahīta augment from this root. 'Catati.'

Takārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 't'.

Thakārantadhātu

The root ending in 'th'.

Thā [M 0.0068] gatinivattiyaṃ. Thāti. Avatthā, vavatthānaṃ, vavatthitaṃ, vanatho. “Chetvā vanaṃ vanathañcā”ti ettha hi mahantā rukkhā vanaṃ nāma, khuddakā pana tasmiṃ vane ṭhitattā vanatho nāma vuccanti.

The root 'thā' is in the sense of standing still. 'Thāti.' 'Avatthā,' 'vavatthānaṃ,' 'vavatthitaṃ,' 'vanatho.' In the phrase 'Chetvā vanaṃ vanathañcā' (having cut down the forest and the thicket), large trees are called 'vana,' while the smaller ones, because they stand in that forest, are called 'vanatha.'

Thu thutiyaṃ. Thavati, abhitthavati. Thavanā, abhitthavanā, thuti, abhitthuti.

The root 'thu' is in the sense of praise. 'Thavati,' 'abhitthavati.' 'Thavanā,' 'abhitthavanā,' 'thuti,' 'abhitthuti.'

Yadi hi rūpinī siyā, paññā me vasumatī na sameyya;

Anomadassissa bhagavato, phalametaṃ ñāṇathavanāya.

If my wisdom were embodied, it would not be equal to the earth; this is the fruit of praising the knowledge of the Blessed One Anomadassī.

Tehi thutippasattho so, yenidaṃ thavitaṃ ñāṇaṃ, buddhaseṭṭho ca thomito. Tatra thavanāti pasaṃsanā. Pasaṃsāya hi anekāni nāmāni.

He is praised and extolled by those by whom this knowledge was praised, and the supreme Buddha is honored. Here, 'thavana' means praise. Indeed, there are many names for praise.

Thavanā ca pasaṃsā ca, silāghā vaṇṇanā thuti;

Panuti thomanā vaṇṇo, katthanā guṇakittanaṃ;

Thavanā and pasaṃsā, silāghā, vaṇṇanā, thuti; panuti, thomanā, vaṇṇo, katthanā, guṇakittanaṃ.

The saddasaṅghātesu. Thīyati, patitthīyati. Thī. Atrimā pāḷiyo – abhisajjati kuppati byāpajjati patitthīyati, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti. Thiyo naṃ paribhāsiṃsūti. Tatra “thīyati patitthīyatī”timāni ekārassīyādesavasena sambhūtāni. Thīyati saṅghātaṃ gacchati gabbho etissāti thī. Ācariyā pana itthīsaddasseva evaṃ nibbacanaṃ vadanti, na thīsaddassa.

The root 'the' is in the senses of sound and assemblage. 'Thīyati,' 'patitthīyati.' 'Thī' (woman). The following are Pāli passages: 'abhisajjati kuppati byāpajjati patitthīyati' (he becomes vexed, angry, hostile, and dejected), 'kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti' (he manifests anger, hatred, and displeasure). 'Thiyo naṃ paribhāsiṃsu' (the women reviled him). Here, 'thīyati' and 'patitthīyati' are formed by means of the substitution of 'īya' for the 'e' of the root. 'Thīyati saṅghātaṃ gacchati gabbho etissā' (the embryo goes to assemblage in her), hence 'thī' (woman). But the teachers state this derivation only for the word 'itthī,' not for the word 'thī.'

Gabbho thīyati etissā, iti thī iti no ruci;

Gabbho thīyati etissā, iti itthīti ācariyā.

Because the embryo goes to assemblage in her, therefore 'thī'—this is not our liking. Because the embryo goes to assemblage in her, therefore 'itthī'—so say the teachers.

Tesaṃ sudukkarovāde, “itthī”ti padasambhavo;

Ayaṃ vinicchayo patto, nicchayaṃ bho suṇātha me.

In their teaching, the origin of the word 'itthī' is very difficult; this judgment has been reached. Listen to my determination, sirs.

Thīsaddena [M 0.0069] samānattho, itthīsaddo yato tato;

Thīsadde labbhamānatthaṃ, itthīsaddamhi ropiya.

Because the word 'itthī' has the same meaning as the word 'thī', therefore the meaning obtainable from the word 'thī' is transferred to the word 'itthī'.

Appānaṃ bahutā ñāye, gahite sati yujjati;

Tathā hi “dve duve, taṇhā, tasiṇā”ti nidassanaṃ.

When the principle of the few being many is taken, it is fitting. For example, 'dve duve' (two by two), 'taṇhā' (craving), and 'tasiṇā' (thirst) are illustrations.

Atha vā pana “itthī”ti-idaṃ vaṇṇāgamādito;

Niruttilakkhaṇenāpi, sijjhatīti pakāsaye.

Or else, one may show that this word 'itthī' is also established from the addition of letters and so on, according to the characteristics of etymology.

Icchatīti nare itthī, icchāpetīti vā pana;

Idaṃ nibbacanañcāpi ñeyyaṃ nibbacanatthinā.

'She desires a man (nare icchati), thus she is an itthī'; or else, 'she causes him to desire (icchāpeti)'. This derivation should also be known by one seeking the meaning of the word.

Atrimāni itthīnamabhidhānāni –

The following are the names for women:

Itthī thī vanitā nārī, abalā bhīru sundarī;

Kantā sīmaninī mātu-gāmo piyā ca kāminī.

Itthī, thī, vanitā, nārī; abalā, bhīru, sundarī; kantā, sīmantinī, mātugāma, piyā, and kāminī.

Ramaṇī pamadā dayitā, lalanā mahilā’ṅganā;

Tāsaṃyeva ca nāmāni, avatthāto imānipi.

Delightful, joyous, beloved, charming, woman, lady; these too are their names, according to their state.

Gorī ca dārikā kaññā, kumārī ca kumārikā;

Yuvatī taruṇī māṇa-vikā therī mahallikā.

A fair girl, a girl, a maiden, a young girl, and a little girl; a young woman, a youthful one, a lass, an elder, and an old woman.

Tathā hi aṭṭhavassikā gorītipi dārikātipi vuccati. Dasavassikā kaññāti vuccati. Anibbiddhā vā yobbanitthī kaññāti vuccati. Dvādasavassikā kumārītipi vuccati kumārikātipi. Atho jaraṃ appattā yuvatītipi taruṇītipi māṇavikātipi vuccati. Jaraṃ pattā pana therītipi mahallikātipi vuccati. Purisesupi ayaṃ nayo yathārahaṃ veditabbo.

Thus, an eight-year-old is called a 'gorī' or a 'dārikā.' A ten-year-old is called a 'kaññā.' A young woman who is a virgin is also called a 'kaññā.' A twelve-year-old is called a 'kumārī' or a 'kumārikā.' Furthermore, one who has not reached old age is called a 'yuvatī,' 'taruṇī,' or 'māṇavikā.' But one who has reached old age is called a 'therī' or a 'mahallikā.' This same method should be understood as applicable to men accordingly.

Kiñcāpettha evaṃ niyamo vutto, tathāpi katthaci aniyamavasenapi vohāro pavattati. Tathā hi “rājā kumāramādāya, rājaputtī ca dārika”nti ca “acchā kaṇhājinaṃ kañña”nti ca imāsaṃ dvinnaṃ pāḷīnaṃ vasena yā itthī dārikāsaddena vattabbā, sā kaññāsaddenapi vattabbā jātā. Yāpi [M 0.0070] ca kaññāsaddena vattabbā, sāpi dārikāsaddena vattabbā jātā. Tathā “rājā kumāramādāya, rājaputtī ca dārika”nti ca “kumāriye upaseniye, niccaṃ nigaḷamaṇḍite”ti ca imāsaṃ pana pāḷīnaṃ vasena yā itthī dārikāsadena vattabbā, sā kumārikāsaddenapi vattabbā jātā. Yā ca pana kumārīsaddena vattabbā, sāpi dārikāsaddena vattabbā jātā. Apicettha “rājakaññā rucā nāmā”ti ca “tato maddimpi nhāpesuṃ, sivikaññā samāgatā”ti ca imāsaṃ dvinnaṃ pāḷīnaṃ dassanato yā anibbiddhā vā hotu nibbiddhā vā, yāva jaraṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāva sā kaññāyeva nāmātipi veditabbaṃ.

Although such a rule has been stated here, nevertheless, in some cases, usage proceeds without this restriction. For instance, based on these two Pāli passages: 'The king taking the prince, and the princess the girl,' and 'O maiden with the black antelope skin,' a woman who is to be called by the word 'dārikā' (girl) comes to be called by the word 'kaññā' (maiden). And one who is to be called by the word 'kaññā' also comes to be called by the word 'dārikā.' Similarly, based on these Pāli passages: 'The king taking the prince, and the princess the girl,' and 'O young maiden Upasenī, always adorned with fetters,' a woman who is to be called by the word 'dārikā' comes to be called by the word 'kumārikā' (young maiden). And one who is to be called by the word 'kumārī' also comes to be called by the word 'dārikā.' Moreover, from these two Pāli passages: 'The royal maiden named Rucā,' and 'Then they bathed Maddī, the Sivi maidens having gathered,' it should be understood that whether she is a virgin or not, as long as she does not reach old age, she is indeed named a 'kaññā'.

Kecettha vadeyyuṃ – yaṃ tumhehi “aṭṭhavassikā gorītipi dārikātipi vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ, etasmiṃ pana vacane “yadāhaṃ dārako homi, jātiyā aṭṭhavassiko”ti vacanato aṭṭhavasso dārako hotu, “tatthaddasakumāraṃ so, ramamānaṃ sake pure”ti pāḷiyaṃ pana puttadārehi saṃvaddho vessantaramahārājā kathaṃ “kumāro”ti vattuṃ yujjissati dvādasavassātikkantattā? Yujjateva bhagavato icchāvasena. Bhagavā hi dhammissarattā vohārakusalatāya ca yaṃ yaṃ veneyyajanānurūpaṃ desanaṃ desetuṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ deseti eva, tasmā bhagavatā tassa mātāpitūnaṃ atthitaṃ sandhāya kumāraparihārena vaddhitattañca evaṃ desanā katā. Tathā hi āyasmā kumārakassapo kumāraparihārena vaddhitattā mahallakopi samāno kumārakassapotveva vohariyati. “Na vāyaṃ kumārako mattamaññāsī”ti ettha pana sirasmiṃ palitesu jātesupi āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āyasmā mahākassapo tasmiṃ there adhimattavissāso [M 0.0071] hutvā komāravādena ovadanto kumārakoti avocāti gahetabbaṃ. Udānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sattā jātadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva pañcadasavassaṃ, tāva kumārakā, bālāti ca vuccanti, tato paraṃ vīsativassāni yuvāno”ti vuttaṃ.

Some might say: 'What you have stated, "an eight-year-old is called a gorī or a dārikā," but in this context, from the statement, "When I was a child, eight years old by birth," an eight-year-old is a child. However, in the Pāli text, "there he saw the prince, enjoying himself in his own city," how could King Vessantara, who was established with his wife and children, be called a "prince" when he was over twelve years old?' It is justified by the Buddha’s will. The Blessed One, as the lord of the Dhamma and skilled in expression, teaches whatever instruction suits the disposition of those to be trained. Therefore, the Buddha taught in this way, referring to the presence of his parents and his upbringing as a prince. For example, the Venerable Kumāra-Kassapa, though old, is still called 'Kumāra-Kassapa' because he was raised as a prince. In the phrase, 'This boy did not know his limits,' it should be understood that the Venerable Mahākassapa, having great confidence in that elder, admonished the Venerable Ānanda with the term 'boy' (kumāra), even though grey hairs had appeared on his head. Moreover, in the Udāna commentary, it is said: 'Beings from the day of birth up to fifteen years are called "boys" and "children." Beyond that, for twenty years, they are called "youths."

Mantha mattha viloḷane. Manthati. Manthañca madhupiṇḍikañca ādāya. Abhimatthati dummedhaṃ vajiraṃvamhamayaṃ maṇiṃ. Sineruṃ matthaṃ katvā.

The roots 'manth' and 'math' are in the sense of churning. 'Manthati' (he churns). 'Taking the gruel and a honey-cake.' 'He crushes the foolish one as a diamond crushes a stone gem.' 'Having made Mount Sineru the churning stick.'

Kuthi puthi luthi hiṃsāsaṃkilesesu. Kunthati. Kuntho, kunthakipillikaṃ. Disvāna patitaṃ sāmaṃ, puttakaṃ paṃsukunthitaṃ. Punthati. Lunthati.

The roots 'kuth,' 'puth,' and 'luth' are in the senses of harming and defiling. 'Kunthati.' 'Kuntho' (distress), 'kunthakipillikaṃ' (a species of ant). 'Having seen her own little child fallen and covered in dust.' 'Punthati.' 'Lunthati.'

Nātha yācanopatāpissariyāsīsāsu. Nāthadhātu yācane upatāpe issariye āsīsane cāti catūsvatthesu vattati. Tenāhu porāṇā “nāthatīti nātho, veneyyānaṃ hitasukhaṃ āsīsati pattheti, parasantānagataṃ vā kilesabyasanaṃ upatāpeti, “sādhu bhikkhave bhikkhu kālena kālaṃ attasampattiṃ paccavekkheyyā’tiādinā taṃ taṃ hitapaṭipattiṃ yācatīti attho, paramena cittissariyena samannāgato sabbasatte vā guṇehi īsati abhibhavatīti paramissaro bhagavā ‘nātho’ti vuccatīti nāthatīti nātho”ti. Saddasatthavidū pana tesu catūsu atthesu nātha nādha iti dhātudvayaṃ paṭhanti. Attanobhāsattā pana tassa “nāthate nādhate”ti rūpāni bhavanti.

The root 'nāth' is in the senses of supplication, affliction, lordship, and blessing. The root 'nāth' functions in these four meanings: supplication, affliction, lordship, and blessing. Therefore, the ancients said: 'He is a "nātha" because he "nāthati": he wishes for and desires the welfare and happiness of those to be trained; or he afflicts the calamity of defilements in the mental continuity of others; he requests this and that beneficial practice, saying, "Good, monks, that a monk should from time to time reflect on his own attainment," and so on—this is the meaning; or, endowed with supreme sovereignty of mind, he lords over or overcomes all beings with his virtues—thus the Blessed One, the supreme sovereign, is called "nātha." Therefore, he is a "nātha" because he "nāthati".' Grammarians, however, teach two roots in these four meanings: 'nāth' and 'nādh.' Because they are of the middle voice, their forms are 'nāthate' and 'nādhate'.

Ettha siyā “yadi yācanatthena nāthatīti nātho, evaṃ sante yo koci yācako daliddo, so eva nātho [M 0.0072] siyā. Yo pana ayācako samiddho, so na nāthati na yācatīti anātho siyā”ti? Na, nāthasaddo hi yācanatthādīsu pavattamāno lokasaṅketavasena uttamapurisesu nirūḷho, bhagavā ca uttamesu sātisayaṃ uttamo, tena taṃ taṃ hitapaṭipattiṃ yācatīti nāthasaddassattho vutto. Anāthasaddo pana ittarajanesu nirūḷho, so ca kho “na nāthoti anātho. Natthi nātho etassāti vā anātho”ti dabbapaṭisedhavasena, na pana “na nāthati na yācatīti anātho”ti dhātuatthapaṭisedhavasena. Yo hi aññassa saraṇaṃ gati patiṭṭhā hoti, so nātho, yo ca aññassa saraṇaṃ gati patiṭṭhā na hoti, nāpi attano añño saraṇaṃ gati patiṭṭhā hoti, so anāthoti vuccati saṅketavasena. Tathā hi “saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Imassa panatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne “lokanātho tuvaṃ eko, saraṇaṃ sabbapāṇina”nti ca “anāthānaṃ bhavaṃ nātho”ti ca –

Here, one might argue: 'If "nātha" is so in the sense of asking, then any poor beggar would be a "nātha." And a prosperous person who does not ask would be an "anātha" because they do not ask.' No. The term 'nātha,' while occurring in meanings such as asking, is established by worldly convention for superior persons. The Blessed One is pre-eminently the highest among the highest; therefore, the meaning of the term 'nātha' is explained as 'he asks for this and that beneficial practice.' On the other hand, the term 'anātha' is conventionally applied to common people. This is in the sense of negating the person—'not a protector, thus anātha,' or 'there is no protector for him, thus anātha'—and not in the sense of negating the verbal root's meaning, as in 'he does not ask, thus anātha.' For whoever is a refuge, a resort, or a foundation for others is called a 'nātha'; while one who is neither a refuge, a resort, nor a foundation for others, nor has another as their own refuge, resort, or foundation, is called 'anātha' by convention. As it is said: 'Conventional speech is true, the cause of worldly consensus.' To make this meaning manifest, in this context, there are the passages: 'You alone are the world's protector, the refuge for all beings,' and 'You are the protector of the helpless,' and—

“Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, nekakoṭisataṃ dhanaṃ;

Nāthānāthānaṃ datvāna, himavantamupāgami”nti ca

"Having considered thus, I gave away wealth of many hundred crores to those with protectors and those without, and went to the Himālaya," and—

Pāḷiyo nidassanāni bhavanti. Yasmā pana sāsane ca loke ca yācako “nātho”ti na vuccati, ayācako ca “anātho”ti. Lokassa pana saraṇaṃ “nātho”ti vuccati. Yassa saraṇaṃ na vijjati, so “anātho”ti vuccati, tathā samiddho “nātho”ti vuccati, asamiddho “anātho”ti. Tasmā paññavatā sabbesu ṭhānesu dhātuatthamattena lokasamaññaṃ anatidhāvitvā yathānurūpaṃ attho gahetabbo. Ayañca nīti sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā.

The Pāli passages are illustrations. Because in both the Dispensation and the world, a beggar is not called 'nātha,' nor is one who does not beg called 'anātha.' But a refuge for the world is called 'nātha.' One for whom no refuge exists is called 'anātha.' Similarly, one who is prosperous is called 'nātha,' while one who is not prosperous is called 'anātha.' Therefore, a wise person should, in all instances, grasp the meaning appropriately, not overriding the worldly convention with the mere meaning of the verbal root. And this principle should be carefully borne in mind.

Vithu [M 0.0073] yācane. Vethati.

The root 'vith' is in the sense of asking. 'Vethati' (he asks).

Satha seṭhille. Sathati. Sathalo hi paribbājo, bhiyyo ākirate rajaṃ. Siṭhilotipi pāḷi dissati. Tadā ṭhikāro muddhajo gahetabbo.

The root 'sath' is in the sense of slackness. 'Sathati' (he is slack). 'For a slack wanderer scatters more dust.' The reading 'siṭhilo' is also seen. In that case, the letter 'ṭh' should be understood as a cerebral.

Kathi koṭille. Kanthati.

The root 'kath' is in the sense of crookedness. 'Kanthati' (he is crooked).

Kattha silāghāyaṃ. Katthati, vikatthati. Katthanā, vikatthanā. Tattha katthatīti pasaṃsati. Vikatthatīti virūpaṃ katthati abhūtavatthudīpanato. Ettha ca “bahumpi so vikattheyya, aññaṃ janapadaṃ gato”ti ca “idhekacco katthī hoti vikatthī, so katthati ‘ahamasmi sīlasampannoti vā vattasampannoti vā vikatthatī’ti” ca ādayo payogā.

The root Kattha is used in the sense of praise. It forms katthati (he praises), vikatthati (he boasts), katthanā (praising), and vikatthanā (boasting). Therein, katthati means 'he praises.' Vikatthati means 'he praises in a distorted way,' by revealing that which is not real. And here, the usages are: 'Though he might boast much, having gone to another country,' and 'Here, a certain person is a boaster and an excessive boaster; he boasts, saying, ‘I am accomplished in virtue,’ or ‘I am accomplished in practice’; he boasts excessively.'

Byatha dukkhabhayacalanesu. Byathati. Bhantā byathitamānasā. Tato kumārābyathitā, sutvā luddassa bhāsitaṃ. Itthetaṃ dvayaṃ calañceva byathañca.

The root Byatha is used in the senses of suffering, fear, and agitation. It forms byathati (he is agitated). For example: 'Confused, with agitated minds.' And: 'Then the princes were agitated, having heard the hunter's speech.' Thus, in this context, both agitation and distress are shown.

Sutha kutha katha hiṃsāyaṃ. Sothati. Kothati. Kathati.

The roots Sutha, Kutha, and Katha are used in the sense of harming. They form sothati, kothati, and kathati.

Patha gatiyaṃ. Pathati. Patho. Pathoti maggo. So duvidho mahājanena padasā paṭipajjitabbo pakatimaggo ca paṇḍitehinibbānatthikehi paṭipajjitabbo paṭipadāsaṅkhāto ariyamaggo cāti. Tattha pakatimaggo uppannakiccākiccehi janehi pathiyati gacchiyatīti patho, paṭipadā pana amatamahāpuraṃ gantukāmehi kulaputtehi saddhāpātheyyaṃ gahetvā pathiyati paṭipajjiyatīti patho. Atha vā pātheti kārakaṃ puggalaṃ gameti nibbānaṃ sampāpetīti vā patho[M 0.0074], paṭipadāyeva. Maggābhidhānaṃ curādigaṇe maggadhātukathanaṭṭhāne kathessāma.

The root Patha is used in the sense of going. It forms pathati (he goes). From this comes patho. Patho means a path. It is twofold: the ordinary path, to be traversed on foot by the general public, and the Noble Path, called paṭipadā, to be traversed by the wise who seek Nibbāna. Therein, the ordinary path is called patho because it is traversed (pathiyati, gacchiyati) by people for whom tasks, both necessary and unnecessary, have arisen; but the paṭipadā is called patho because it is traversed (pathiyati, paṭipajjiyati) by clansmen desiring to reach the great city of the Deathless, having taken faith as their provision. Alternatively, patho (which is the paṭipadā itself) leads the agent, the person, to Nibbāna, causing them to attain it. We will discuss the term magga (path) in the context of the curādi group when explaining the root magg.

Katha nippāke. Kathati.

The root Katha is used in the sense of cooking. It forms kathati (he cooks).

Matha vilothane. Mathati.

The root Matha is used in the sense of churning or agitation. It forms mathati (he churns).

Potha pariyāyanabhāve. Pothati. Pothako. Pothetīti ayaṃ curādigaṇepi vattati. Tena “samantā anupariyeyyuṃ, nippothentā catuddisā”ti payogo dissati.

The root Potha is used in the sense of revolving. It forms pothati (he revolves/crushes) and pothako (one who revolves/crushes). The form potheti also occurs in the curādi group. Hence, the usage is seen: 'They would go around on all sides, crushing in the four directions.'

Gottha vaṃse. Gotthati. Gotthulo, gotthu.

The root Gottha is used in the sense of lineage. It forms gotthati (he belongs to a lineage), and the derivatives gotthulo and gotthu.

Puthu vitthāre. Pothati. Puthavī.

The root Puthu is used in the sense of extensiveness. It forms pothati (it extends/spreads), and the derivative puthavī (the earth).

Thakārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of the roots ending in the letter 'tha'.

Dakārantadhātu

Roots ending in the letter 'da'.

Dā dāne. Āpubbo gahaṇe. Saddho dānaṃ dadāti deti, sīlaṃ ādadāti ādeti. Imāni suddhakattupadāni taddīpakattā. Saddho assaddhaṃ dānaṃ dāpeti, sīlaṃ ādapeti, samādapeti. Ye dhammamevādapayanti santo. Imāni kāritapadāni hetukattupadānīti ca vuccanti taddīpakattā. Saddhena dānaṃ dīyati, sīlaṃ ādīyati, samādīyati, imāni kammapadāni taddīpakattā. Ayañca dā dāneti dhātu sāsanānurūpasutivasena divādigaṇaṃ patvā supanakriyaṃ vadanto “dāyati niddāyati niddā”ti sanāmapadāni suddhakattupadāni janayati. Dānamavakhaṇḍanañca vadanto “diyati dānaṃ dātta”nti sanāmapadāni suddhakattupadāni janayati. Suddhiṃvadanto “dāyati vedāyati vodāna”nti sanāmapadāni suddhakattupadāni janayati, imasmiṃ pana bhūvādigaṇe dānaṃ vadanto āpubbavasena gahaṇañca [M 0.0075] vadanto “dadāti deti ādadāti ādeti dānaṃ ādāna”nti sanāmapadāni suddhakattupadāni janayati. Tathā kucchitagamanaṃ vadanto “dāti suddāti suddo suddī”ti sanāmapadāni suddhakattupadāni janayatīti ayaṃ viseso daṭṭhabbo. Yathā cettha, evamaññatrāpi yathāsambhavaṃ viseso upaparikkhitabbo nayaññūhi.

The root Dā is used in the sense of giving. Prefixed with ā, it is in the sense of taking. The faithful one gives a gift (dadāti, deti); he takes up virtue (ādadāti, ādeti). These are pure agent-voice forms, because they indicate the agent. The faithful one causes the faithless one to give a gift; he causes him to take up virtue, he causes him to undertake it thoroughly. 'Those virtuous ones who cause others to take up the Dhamma.' These are causative forms, and are also called causative-agent forms, because they indicate the causative agent. By the faithful one, a gift is given (dīyati); virtue is taken up (ādīyati), is thoroughly undertaken (samādīyati). These are passive (object-voice) forms, because they indicate the object. And this root dā (to give), having entered the divādi group in accordance with the Teaching and the suttas, when expressing the action of sleeping, produces the nominal forms dāyati, niddāyati, and niddā as pure agent-voice forms. And when expressing giving and cutting, it produces the nominal forms diyati, dānaṃ, and dātta as pure agent-voice forms. And when expressing purity, it produces the nominal forms dāyati, vedāyati, and vodāna as pure agent-voice forms. But in this bhūvādi group, when expressing giving, and when expressing taking with ā prefixed, it produces the nominal forms dadāti, deti, ādadāti, ādeti, dānaṃ, and ādāna as pure agent-voice forms. Similarly, when expressing contemptible going, it produces the nominal forms dāti, suddāti, suddo, and suddī as pure agent-voice forms. This distinction should be noted. Just as here, so elsewhere too, those who know the method should examine the distinctions as they arise.

Idānissa nāmapadāni tumantādīni brūma. “Dānaṃ, deyyaṃ, dātabbaṃ, brahmadeyyaṃ, dinnaṃ, dāyako, dāyikā, dakkhiṇā” iccādīni, “dātuṃ, padātuṃ, dātave, padātave, datvā, datvāna, dadātuna, daditvā, daditvāna, dadiya, dajjā, dadiyāna, ādātuṃ, ādāya, ādiya” iccādīni ca yojetabbāni.

Now we will speak of its nominal forms, infinitives, gerunds, and so on. Forms such as dānaṃ, deyyaṃ, dātabbaṃ, brahmadeyyaṃ, dinnaṃ, dāyako, dāyikā, dakkhiṇā, and so on, and forms such as dātuṃ, padātuṃ, dātave, padātave, datvā, datvāna, dadātuna, daditvā, daditvāna, dadiya, dajjā, dadiyāna, ādātuṃ, ādāya, ādiya, and so on, should be connected.

Tattha dānanti dātabbaṃ, dadanti etenāti atthe na deyyadhammo dānacetanā ca vuccati. Kasmā pana tattha dinnasaddoyeva kathiyati, na dattasaddoti? Akathane kāraṇamatthi. “Dānaṃ dinna”ntiādīsu hi dinnasaddaṭṭhāne dattasaddo na dissati, tasmā na kathiyati.

Therein, dāna means 'what is to be given'; in the sense of 'one gives by means of this,' it refers to both the object fit for giving and the volition to give. But why is only the word dinna mentioned there, and not the word datta? There is a reason for not mentioning it. Because in instances such as 'dānaṃ dinna,' the word datta is not seen in place of dinna; therefore, it is not mentioned.

Guṇabhūto dattasaddo, na diṭṭho jinabhāsite;

“Manasā dānaṃ mayā dinnaṃ”, iti dinnapadaṃ viya.

The word datta as an attribute is not seen in the speech of the Jina, unlike the word dinna in the phrase, 'By me a gift was given with the mind.'

“Devadatto yaññadatto, datto” iti ca ādiko;

Paṇṇattivacane diṭṭho, samāsabyāsato pana.

In 'Devadatta, Yaññadatta, Datta,' and so on, it is seen in conventional designation, both in compounded and uncompounded forms.

Tasmā “devadatto”tiādīsu “devena dinno”ti samāsaṃ katvā paṇṇattivacanattā dinnasaddassa dattādeso kātabbo sāsanānurūpena. Upari hi “dinnassa datto kvaci paṇṇattiya”nti lakkhaṇaṃ passissatha. Ayameva hi sāsane nīti avilaṅghanīyā. Idaṃ panettha vavatthānaṃ –

Therefore, in cases like 'Devadatta,' having formed the compound as 'given by a deva,' the substitution of datta for dinna should be made in accordance with the Teaching, because it is a term of designation. For further on, you will see the rule: 'For dinna, datta is sometimes substituted in a designation.' This indeed is the inviolable principle in the Teaching. Herein is the determination:

Sakkaṭe dattasaddova, dinnasaddo na dissati;

Byāsamhi dinnasaddova, dattasaddo na pāḷiyaṃ.

In Sanskrit, only the word datta is seen; the word dinna is not. In an uncompounded form, only the word dinna is seen; the word datta is not found in Pāli.

“Manasā [M 0.0076] dānaṃ mayā dinnaṃ, dānaṃ dinno”tiādisu;

“Dhammadinnā mahāmāyā”, iccādīsu ca pāḷisu.

In such Pāli passages as, 'By me a gift was given with the mind,' 'a gift was given,' and so on; and in 'Dhammadinnā, Mahāmāyā,' and so on.

Iti byāsasamāsānaṃ, vasā dvedhā pavattati;

Dinnasaddoti dīpeyya, na so sakkaṭabhāsite.

Thus one should explain that the word dinna occurs in two ways, according to its use in uncompounded and compounded forms, and that it is not found in the Sanskrit language.

Guṇabhūto dattasaddo, asamāsamhi kevalo;

Na dissati munimate, dinnasaddova kevalo.

In the Sage's view, the word datta as an attribute is not seen by itself in an uncompounded form; only the word dinna is seen by itself.

Teneva dinnasaddassa, dattādeso kato mayā;

“Dattaṃ sirappadāna”nti, kavayo pana abravuṃ.

For that very reason, the substitution of datta for dinna was made by me. Poets, however, have said: 'Dattaṃ sirappadānaṃ' (The giving of the head was given).

Ediso pāḷiyaṃ natthi, nayo tasmā na so varo;

“Datto”ti bhūridattassa, saññā paṇṇattiyaṃ gatā.

Such a method is not found in Pāli, therefore that way is not the best. The name 'Datta' has come to be a designation for Bhūridatta.

“Brahmadatto buddhadatto, datto” iti hi sāsane;

Paṇṇattiyaṃ dattasaddo, asamāsasamāsiko.

For in the Teaching, in cases such as 'Brahmadatta, Buddhadatta, Datta,' the word datta is a designation, used both in uncompounded and compounded forms.

“Paradattabhojana”nti, evamādīsu pāḷisu;

Samāse guṇabhūtoyaṃ, dattasaddo patiṭṭhito.

In Pāli passages such as 'paradattabhojana' (food given by another), and so on, this word datta is established as an attribute within a compound.

“Manasā dānaṃ mayā dinnaṃ, dānaṃ dinno”tiādisu;

Guṇabhūto dinnasaddo, asamāsamhi dissati.

In cases such as, 'By me a gift was given with the mind,' and 'a gift was given,' the word dinna is seen as an attribute in an uncompounded form.

“Dinnādāyī dhammadinnā”, iccevamādīsu pana;

Samāse guṇapaṇṇatti-bhāvenesa padissati.

But in cases such as 'Dinnādāyī' (one who takes what is given) and 'Dhammadinnā,' and so on, it appears in a compound as a qualitative designation.

Koci [M 0.0077] pana saddasatthavidū garu evaṃ saddaracanamakāsi –

But a certain teacher, an expert in the science of words, made a verbal composition thus:

“Yassaṅkurehi jimutambujaloditehi,

Vāteritehi patitehi suṇehi tehi.

By whose sprouts—arisen from clouds, lotuses, and water; agitated by the wind; and fallen—and by those pleasant sounds,

Jenantacīvaramasobhatha brahmadattaṃ,

Vandāmi taṃ caladalaṃ varabodhirukkha”nti.

by which the final robe, a gift from Brahma, was made to shine—I venerate that excellent Bodhi tree with moving leaves.

Ettha ca brahmadattanti idaṃ sakkaṭabhāsāto nayaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ, na pāḷito. Pāḷinayañhipatvā “brahmadattiya”nti vā “brahmadinna”nti vā “devadattiya”nti vā “devadinna”nti vā rūpena bhavitabbaṃ. Tathā hi “bodhisatto ca maddī ca sammodamānā sakkadattiye assame vasiṃsū”ti pāḷinayānurūpo aṭṭhakathāpāṭho dissati. Tasmā etthevaṃ vadāma –

Here, the term 'Brahmadatta' is used, having adopted the style from Sanskrit, not from Pāli. Indeed, according to the Pāli idiom, it should be in the form of 'brahmadattiya' or 'brahmadinna' or 'devadattiya' or 'devadinna.' Thus, for example, the commentary passage 'The Bodhisatta and Maddī, rejoicing together, lived in the hermitage of Sakkadattiya' is seen to conform to the Pāli idiom. Therefore, we say this here—

“Dattasaddassa ṭhānamhi, “dattiya”nti ravo gato;

Devadattiyapatto ca, assamo sakkadattiyo”ti.

“In the place of the word ‘Datta’, the sound ‘dattiya’ occurs; and Devadattiya’s bowl, and the hermitage of Sakkadattiya.”

Ayaṃ nīti sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā. Atra pana paripuṇṇāparipuṇṇavasena yathārahaṃ padakkamo bhavati.

This principle should be carefully borne in mind. Here, however, the sequence of words occurs as is appropriate, according to whether they are complete or incomplete.

Dadāti, dadanti. Dadāsi, dadātha. Dadāmi, dadāma. Dadātu, dadantu. Dadāhi, dadātha. Dadāmi, dadāma, dadāmase. Dadeyya, dade, dajjā. Dajjā sappuriso dānaṃ. Dadeyyuṃ, dajjuṃ. Pitā mātā ca te dajjuṃ. Dadeyyāsi, dajjāsi, dajjesi iccapi. Dajjāsi abhayaṃ mama. Mātaraṃ kena dosena, dajjāsi dakarakkhino. Sīlavantesu dajjesi, dānaṃ maddi yathārahaṃ. Dadeyyātha, dajjātha. Dadeyyāmi, dajjāmi, dadeyyāma, dajjāma. Dadetha, daderaṃ. Dadetho, dadeyyāvho, dajjāvho. Dadeyyaṃ, dajjaṃ. Neva dajjaṃ mahosadhaṃ. Dadeyyāmhe, dajjāmhe. Ayamasmākaṃ khanti. Garūnaṃ pana khanti aññathā bhavati. Tathā hi –

He gives, they give. You give, you all give. I give, we give. Let him give, let them give. Give (you, singular), give (you all). Let me give, let us give, let us give. He should give, he might give, he would give. A good person should give alms. They should give, they would give. Your father and mother would give. You should give, you would give, you would give. You should give me safety. For what fault, mother, would you give me to the water-demons? You should give gifts to the virtuous, Maddi, as is fitting. You all should give. I should give, I would give, we should give, we would give. Give (you all), they would give. Give (you two), you two should give, you two would give. I should give, I would give. I would not give Mahosadha. We should give, we would give. This is our view. But the view of the teachers is otherwise. For thus—

Garū “dajjati dajjanti”, itiādinayena tu;

Aṭṭhannampi vibhattīnaṃ, vasenāhu padakkamaṃ.

The teachers, however, say “dajjati, dajjanti,” and so on, according to this method; they say that the sequence of words is determined by means of the eight sets of verbal endings.

Pāḷiṃ upaparikkhitvā, tañce yujjati gaṇhatha;

Na hi sabbappakārena, pāḷiyo paṭibhanti no.

Having examined the Pāli, if it suits, accept it; for not in every way are the Pāli texts clear to us.

Tattha [M 0.0078] asmākaṃ khantiyā “dajjā dajja”ntiādīni yyakārasahiteyeva sattamiyā padarūpe sijjhanti. “Dajjā sappuriso dāna”nti ettha hi “dajjā idaṃ “dadeyyā”ti padarūpaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā yyakāre pare saralopaṃ katvā tato tiṇṇaṃ byañjanānaṃ saṃyogañca tīsusaññogabyañjanesu dvinnaṃ sarūpānamekassa lopañca dyakārasaññogassa ca jakāradvayaṃ katvā tato dīghavasenuccāritabbattā animittaṃ dīghabhāvaṃ katvā nipphajjati. Evaṃ sāsanassānurūpo vaṇṇasandhi bhavati. Duvidho hi sandhi padasandhi vaṇṇasandhīti. Tesu yattha padacchedo labbhati, so padasandhi. Yathā? Tatrāyaṃ. Yattha pana na labbhati, so vaṇṇasandhi. Yathā? Atrajo. Yathā ca sugato, yathā ca paddhāni. Evaṃ duvidhesu sandhīsu “dajjā”ti ayaṃ vaṇṇasandhi eva.

Here, according to our understanding, forms like “dajjā, dajja,” etc., are correctly established as optative mood forms with the inclusion of the y-sound. In the phrase “dajjā sappuriso dānaṃ,” the word form “dajjā” is accomplished by first establishing the form “dadeyyā,” then, when the y-sound follows, effecting vowel elision, next combining the three consonants, and from the three conjoined consonants, eliding one of the two identical ones and transforming the dy-combination into a double j-sound, and then, because it must be pronounced with a long vowel, effecting lengthening even though no condition requires it. Thus, this phonetic combination is in accordance with the teaching. Indeed, there are two kinds of sandhi: word sandhi and sound sandhi. Among them, where word division is possible, that is word sandhi. For example: “Tatrāyaṃ.” Where, however, it is not possible, that is sound sandhi. For example: “Atrajo.” And just as “sugato” and just as “paddhāni,” so too in these two kinds of sandhi, this “dajjā” is purely sound sandhi.

Aparopi rūpanayo bhavati tvāpaccayantavasena –
