There is also another method of derivation, by way of the tvā suffix—

“Ayaṃ so indako yakkho, dajjā dānaṃ parittakaṃ;

Atirocati amhehi, cando tāragaṇe yathā”ti

“This is that Indaka, the yakkha, who gave a trifling gift; he outshines us, like the moon among the stars.”

Dassanato. Ettha hi dajjāti datvāti attho. Idaṃ pana datvāsaddena samānatthaṃ “dadiyya” iti padarūpaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā yyakāre pare saralopaṃ katvā saññogesu sarūpalopañca tato dyakārasaññogassa jjakāradvayaṃ dīghattañca katvā nipphajjati.

In the sense of ‘having given.’ Here, indeed, ‘dajjā’ means ‘having given.’ This, however, is produced by first establishing the word form ‘dadiyya’ which has the same meaning as the word ‘datvā,’ and then, when the y-sound follows, effecting vowel elision, and also the elision of similar sounds in conjuncts, and then making the dy-combination into a double j-sound and lengthening the preceding vowel.

Athāparopi rūpanayo bhavati kammani yapaccayavasena. Tathā hi “petānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dajjā”ti ca “dakkhiṇā dajjā”ti ca dve pāṭhā dissanti. Tattha pacchimassa dajjāti dātabbāti attho kammani yapaccayavasena. Idha pana dādhātuto yapaccayaṃ katvā dhātussa dvittañca pubbassa rassattañca tato yakāre pare [M 0.0079] saralopaṃ saññogabhāvañca jjakāradvayañca itthiliṅgattā āpaccayādiñca katvā “dajjā”ti nipphajjati. Evaṃ “dajjā dadeyyā”ti ca “dajjā dadiyya datvā”ti ca “dajjā dātabbā”ti ca etāni paccekaṃ pariyāyavacanāni bhavanti. “Dajjuṃ. Dajjāsi, dajjātha. Dajjāmi, dajjāma. Dajjāvho, dajja”nti etānipi “dadeyyuṃ dadeyyāsī”tiādinā padarūpāni patiṭṭhapetvā yyakāre pare saralopaṃ saññogesu sarūpalopaṃ dyakārasamaññogassa jjakāradvayañca katvā nipphajjanti. Etesu dajjāsīti yaṃ rūpaṃ tassāvayavassa ākārassa ekāraṃ katvā aparampi “dajjesī”ti rūpaṃ bhavatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo aññatrāpi yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo.

There is yet another method of derivation, based on the `ya` suffix in the passive voice. For thus, two readings are seen: “petānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dajjā” and “dakkhiṇā dajjā.” In the latter, “dajjā” means “should be given,” based on the `ya` suffix in the passive voice. In this case, the form 'dajjā' is produced from the root `dā` by taking the `ya` suffix, doubling the root, shortening the preceding vowel, then eliding the vowel before the `ya`, forming a conjunct, making a double `jja`, and, because it is feminine, applying the `ā` suffix and so on. Thus, “dajjā” and “dadeyyā”; “dajjā,” “dadiyya,” and “datvā”; and “dajjā” and “dātabbā” are each alternative expressions. Forms like “dajjuṃ, dajjāsi, dajjātha, dajjāmi, dajjāma, dajjāvho, dajja” are also produced by first establishing the word forms “dadeyyuṃ, dadeyyāsī,” etc., then, with `yy` following, applying vowel elision, elision of a similar form in the conjunct, and making a double `jja` from the `dy` combination. Among these, it should be noted that from the form 'dajjāsi', by changing its `ā` component to `e`, another form, 'dajjesi', is also produced. This method should be applied elsewhere as is appropriate.

Acinteyyānubhāvassa hi sammāsambuddhassa pāḷinayo acinteyyoyeva hoti, gambhīro dukkhogāḷho, na yena kenaci lakkhaṇena sādhetabbo, yathātanti viraciteheva lakkhaṇehi sādhetabbo. Tathā hi “khattiyā titthiyā cetiyānī”tiādīsu yakāre pare saralopo bhavati, tena “athetthekasataṃ khatyā. Evampi titthyā puthuso vadanti. Ārāmarukkhacetyānī”ti payogā dissanti. Tathā “sākacchati taccha”nti etthāpi “saha kathayatī”tivā “saṃkathayatī”ti vā “tathya”nti ca padarūpaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā sahasaddassa hakāralopaṃ, saṃsadde ca niggahītalopaṃ katvā sakāragatassa sarassa dīghaṃ katvā yakāre pare saralopaṃ katvā tato thyakārasaññogassa cchayugaṃ katvā visabhāgasaññoge eko ekassa sabhāgattamāpajjati. Tena “sākacchati taccha”nti rūpāni sijjhanti. Tathā hi “aññamaññaṃ sākacchiṃsu. Kālena dhammasākacchā. Bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ. Yathātathiyaṃ viditvāpi dhammaṃ, sammā so loke paribbajeyyā”ti [M 0.0080] savikapāni payogāni dissanti. “Najjā”tiādīsupi “nadiyā”tiādīni padarūpāni patiṭṭhapetvā vaṇṇasandhivasena yakāre pare lopavidhi labbhatiyeva. Vividho hi sāsanānukūlo rūpanipphādanupāyo, upari ca etesaṃ sādhanatthaṃ “saralopo yamanarādīsū”tiādīni lakkhaṇāni bhavissanti. Tattha –

Indeed, the Pāli idiom of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, whose power is inconceivable, is itself inconceivable, profound, difficult to fathom; it is not to be mastered by just any rule, but only by the rules laid down in the tradition. Thus, indeed, in phrases like “khattiyā, titthiyā, cetiyānī,” etc., when a yakāra follows, vowel elision occurs. Therefore, usages like “athetthekasataṃ khatyā,” “evampi titthyā puthuso vadanti,” and “ārāmarukkhacetyānī” are seen. Similarly, in “sākacchati taccha,” here too, by establishing the word forms as “saha kathayatī” or “saṃkathayatī” and “tathya,” the hakāra is elided from “saha,” the niggahīta is elided from “saṃ,” the vowel of the sakāra becomes long, and when a yakāra follows, the vowel is elided. Then, a double ccha is made from the thyakāra combination; in a dissimilar conjunction, one becomes similar to the other. Thus, forms like “sākacchati taccha” are accomplished. For instance, usages such as “aññamaññaṃ sākacchiṃsu,” “kālena dhammasākacchā,” “bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ,” and “yathātathiyaṃ viditvāpi dhammaṃ, sammā so loke paribbajeyyā” with their variations, are seen. Likewise, in cases like “najjā,” by establishing the word forms as “nadiyā,” etc., the elision rule through sound combination can be obtained when a yakāra follows. Indeed, diverse are the means for forming expressions suitable to the Teaching; moreover, for establishing these, rules like “saralopo yamanarādīsū” will be given later. There—

“Dajjā dajju”ntiādīni, sattamīnaṃ vasena me;

Vuttāni yogirājassa, sāsanatthaṃ mahesino.

“Forms like ‘dajjā, dajju,’ etc., were spoken by me with reference to the optative mood, uttered for the purpose of the Dispensation of the Great Sage, the King of Yogis.”

Atridaṃ vattabbaṃ, kiñcāpi aṭṭhakathācariyehi “mātaraṃ tena dosena, dajjāhaṃ dakarakkhino”ti ettha dajjanti padassa “dammī”ti vattamānāvasena vivaraṇaṃ kataṃ, tathāpi sattamīpayogoyeva. Ācariyā hi “sattamīpayogo aya”nti jānantāpi “kadāci aññe parikappatthampi gaṇheyyu”nti āsaṅkāya evaṃ vivaraṇamakaṃsu. Tathā kiñcāpi tehi “anāparādhakammantaṃ, na dajjaṃ dakarakkhino”ti ettha na dajjanti padassa “nāhaṃ dakarakkhassa dassāmī”ti bhavissantīvasena vivaraṇaṃ kataṃ, tathāpi sattamīpayogoyeva, anāgataṃ pana paṭicca vattabbatthattā evaṃ vivaraṇaṃ kataṃ. “Neva dajjaṃ mahosadha”nti ettha pana “na tveva dadeyya”nti sattamīpayogavaseneva vivaraṇaṃ katanti. Evaṃ dajjaṃpadassa vinicchayo veditabbo.

This should be stated herein: Although the commentary teachers explained the word ‘dajjaṃ’ in the phrase ‘mātaraṃ tena dosena, dajjāhaṃ dakarakkhino’ as ‘dammī’ (I give), interpreting it in the sense of the present tense, it is nevertheless a usage of the optative mood. For the teachers, though knowing that it was a usage of the optative mood, gave such an explanation out of concern that ‘perhaps others might take it for a speculative purpose.’ Similarly, although they explained the word ‘na dajjaṃ’ in ‘anāparādhakammantaṃ, na dajjaṃ dakarakkhino’ as ‘nāhaṃ dakarakkhassa dassāmī’ (I will not give to the water-demon), interpreting it in the sense of the future tense, it is nevertheless a usage of the optative mood; however, because the meaning had to be stated with reference to the future, such an explanation was given. But in ‘neva dajjaṃ mahosadha,’ the explanation was made purely in the sense of the optative mood, as ‘na tveva dadeyya’ (one should certainly not give). Thus should the analysis of the word ‘dajjaṃ’ be understood.

Idāni parokkhādivasena padakkamo kathiyati. “Dada, dadū. Dadū”ti ca idaṃ “nārado iti nāmena, kassapo iti maṃ vidū”tiādīsu vidūsaddena samaṃ. Dade, dadittha, dadaṃ, dadimha. Dadittha, dadire. Dadittho, dadivho.

Now, the sequence of forms is explained by way of the perfect tense, etc. “Dada, dadū.” And this “Dadū” is similar to the word ‘vidū’ in such phrases as “Nārado iti nāmena, Kassapo iti maṃ vidū.” Dade, dadittha, dadaṃ, dadimha. Dadittha, dadire. Dadittho, dadivho.

Ettha ca daditthoti idaṃ “sañjagghittho mayā saha. Mā kisittho mayā vinā. Mā naṃ kalale akkamittho”tiādīsu “sañjagghittho”tiādīhi [M 0.0081] samaṃ. Iminā nayena sabbattha labbhamānavasena sadisatā upaparikkhitabbā. Dadaṃ, dadimhe. Parokkhāsahibharūpāni.

Here, ‘dadittho’ is similar to ‘sañjagghittho,’ etc., in phrases like “sañjagghittho mayā saha. Mā kisittho mayā vinā. Mā naṃ kalale akkamittho.” In this manner, similarity should be examined everywhere, to the extent it is found. Dadaṃ, dadimhe. These are perfect tense forms.

Adadā, adadū. Adade, adadattha. Adadaṃ, adadamha. Adadattha, adadatthuṃ. Adadase, adadavhaṃ. Adadiṃ adadamhase. Iti anakārapubbampi rūpaṃ gahetabbaṃ “yesaṃ no na dadamhase”ti dassanato. Hiyyattanīsahitarūpāni.

Adadā, adadū. Adade, adadattha. Adadaṃ, adadamha. Adadattha, adadatthuṃ. Adadase, adadavhaṃ. Adadiṃ, adadamhase. Thus, a form without the augment should also be taken, as exemplified by “yesaṃ no na dadamhase.” These are the hiyyattanī forms.

Adadi, adaduṃ, adadiṃsu. Adado, adadittha. Adadiṃ, adadimhā. Adadā, adadū. Adadase, adadivhaṃ. Adadaṃ, adadimhe. Ajjatanīsahitarūpāni.

Adadi, adaduṃ, adadiṃsu. Adado, adadittha. Adadiṃ, adadimhā. Adadā, adadū. Adadase, adadivhaṃ. Adadaṃ, adadimhe. These are the aorist forms.

“Dadissati, dadissanti” iccādi sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. Bhavissantīsahitarūpāni.

“Dadissati, dadissanti,” etc., all should be inferred. These are forms associated with the future tense.

“Adadisā, dadissā, adadissaṃsu, dadissaṃsu” iccādi ca sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. Kālātipattisahitarūpāni.

“Adadisā, dadissā, adadissaṃsu, dadissaṃsu,” etc., all should be understood. These are forms with a past conditional sense.

Aparānipi vattamānādisahitarūpāni bhavanti. Deti, denti. Desi, detha. Demi, dammi, dema, damma. Detu, dentu. Dehi, detha. Demi, dammi, dema, damma. Attanopadāni appasiddhāni. Sattamīnayo ca parokkhānayo ca appasiddho. Hiyuttanīnayo pana ajjatanīnayo ca koci koci pasiddho pāḷiyaṃ āgatattā, sakkā ca “adā, adū, ado, ada”ntiādinā yojetuṃ. Tathā hi nayo dissati. Adā dānaṃ purindado. Varañceme ado sakka. Brāhmaṇānaṃ adaṃ gajaṃ. Adāsime. Adaṃsu te mamokāsaṃ. Adāsiṃ brāhmaṇe tadāti. “Dassati, dassanti” iccādi sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. “Adassā, dassā, adassaṃsu, dassaṃsu, dassiṃsu” iccādi ca sabbaṃ neyyaṃ.

There are also other forms associated with the present tense, etc. Deti, denti. Desi, detha. Demi, dammi, dema, damma. Detu, dentu. Dehi, detha. Demi, dammi, dema, damma. The middle voice forms are rare. The optative and the perfect are also rare. However, some forms of the hiyyattanī and ajjatanī are well-known since they occur in the Pāli canon, and it is possible to construe them with 'adā, adū, ado, ada,' etc. For indeed, that method is seen: “Adā dānaṃ purindado. Varañceme ado sakka. Brāhmaṇānaṃ adaṃ gajaṃ. Adāsime. Adaṃsu te mamokāsaṃ. Adāsiṃ brāhmaṇe tadā.” “Dassati, dassanti,” etc., all should be inferred. “Adassā, dassā, adassaṃsu, dassaṃsu, dassiṃsu,” etc., all should be inferred.

Tathā [M 0.0082] ādadāti, ādadanti. Ādadāsi, ādadātha. Ādadāmi, ādadāma. Kaccāyanamate “ādatte”ti attanopadaṃ vuttaṃ. Evaṃ “ādadātu, ādadeyya” iccādi sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. Ādetu ādeyya iccādi yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Evameva ca “dāpeti, ādāpetī”tiādīnipi yathārahaṃ yojetabbāni.

Similarly, “ādadāti, ādadanti. Ādadāsi, ādadātha. Ādadāmi, ādadāma.” According to Kaccāyana's system, “ādatte” is stated to be the middle voice. Thus, “ādadātu, ādadeyya,” etc., all should be inferred. “Ādetu, ādeyya,” etc., should be connected as appropriate. Just so, “dāpeti, ādāpeti,” etc., should also be connected as appropriate.

Dākucchite gamane. Dāti. Suddāti. Suddo, suddī. Tattha suddoti suddātīti suddo, parapothanādiluddācārakammunā dārukammādikhuddācārakammunā ca lahuṃ lahuṃ kucchitaṃ gacchatīti attho. Tathā hi su iti sīghatthe nipāto, dā iti garahattho dhātu kucchitagativācakattā. Suddassa bhariyā suddī.

The root Dā, in the sense of contemptuous going. Dāti. Suddāti. Suddo, suddī. Here, 'suddo' means 'suddāti' (one who goes contemptuously). The meaning is: one who goes quickly and lightly in a contemptible manner through actions like striking others, or through petty actions like woodwork. For 'su' is a particle meaning quickness, and 'dā' is a root with the sense of reproach, signifying contemptible movement. The wife of a suddo is a suddī.

Du gatiyaṃ. Davati. Dumo. Ettha ca davati gacchati mūlakkhandhasākhāviṭapapattapallavapupphaphalehi vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇātīti dumo.

The root Du, in the sense of going. Davati. Dumo. Herein, a 'dumo' (tree) is so called because it 'goes' (davati), that is, it attains growth, increase, and abundance by means of its roots, trunk, branches, twigs, leaves, shoots, flowers, and fruits.

Desodhane. Sodhanaṃ pariyodāpanaṃ. Dāyati. Dāyanaṃ. Yathā gāyati, gāyanaṃ. Dāyituṃ, dāyitvā, dhātāvayavassekārassa āyādeso. “Dātuṃ, datvā” iccapi rūpāni.

The root De, in the sense of cleansing. Sodhanaṃ means purification. Dāyati. Dāyanaṃ. Just as gāyati, gāyanaṃ. Dāyituṃ, dāyitvā—there is a substitution of 'āy' for the 'e' of the root element. The forms “Dātuṃ” and “datvā” also exist.

Tatra dātunti sodhetuṃ. Datvāti sodhetvāti attho gahetabbo. Tathā hi “bālo abyatto nappaṭibalo anuyuñjiyamāno anuyogaṃ dātu”nti ettha dātunti padassa sodhetunti attho. Keci “dānattha”nti atthaṃ vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Na hi yo parehi anuyuñjiyati, so anuyogaṃ deti nāmāti. Tasmā “ācariyassa anuyogaṃ datvā bārāṇasiṃ paccāgacchī”tiādīsupi anuyogaṃ datvāti anuyogaṃ sodhetvāti atthoyeva gahetabbo. Tathā [M 0.0083] hi pubbācariyehi “anuyogadāpanattha”nti etasmiṃ padese esoyevattho vibhāvito. Kathaṃ? Anuyogadāpanatthanti anuyogaṃ sodhāpetuṃ. Vimaddakkhamañhi sīhanādaṃ nadanto atthato anuyogaṃ sodheti nāma, anuyuñjanto ca naṃ sodhāpeti nāmāti. Idampi ca tehi vuttaṃ. Dātunti sodhetuṃ. Keci “dānattha”nti atthaṃ vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Na hi yo sīhanādaṃ nadati, so eva tattha anuyogaṃ detīti. Samantapaṭṭhānamahāpakaraṇa saṃvaṇṇanāyampi pubbācariyehi “dānaṃ datvāti taṃ cetanaṃ pariyodāpetvā”ti sodhanattho vutto. Dullabhā ayaṃ nīti sādhukaṃ citte ṭhapetabbā.

Therein, 'dātuṃ' means 'to cleanse'. 'Datvā' means 'having cleansed'—this meaning should be understood. For example, in the phrase “a fool, unskilled, incapable, when questioned, cannot 'dātuṃ' the inquiry,” here the word 'dātuṃ' means 'to cleanse'. Some say the meaning is “for giving,” but this is not correct. For one who is questioned by others does not, so to speak, “give” the inquiry. Therefore, in phrases like “having given the teacher’s inquiry, he returned to Bārāṇasī,” the meaning of “having given the inquiry” should be understood as “having cleansed the inquiry.” Indeed, the ancient teachers explained this very meaning in this instance as “for the purpose of causing the inquiry to be given.” How? “For the purpose of causing the inquiry to be given” means to have the inquiry cleansed. For one roaring a lion's roar capable of crushing opposition truly cleanses the inquiry, and the one questioning causes it to be cleansed. This too was stated by them: 'Dātuṃ' means 'to cleanse'. Some say the meaning is “for giving,” but this is not correct. For one who roars like a lion does not thereby “give” the inquiry. Even in the commentary on the Samantapaṭṭhāna Mahāpakaraṇa, the ancient teachers stated the meaning of cleansing: “having given the gift means having purified that intention.” This principle is hard to find and should be firmly held in mind.

De pālane. Dīyati. Dānaṃ, uddānaṃ dāyituṃ, dāyitvā. Tattha dānanti duggatito dāyati rakkhatīti dānaṃ, dānacetanā. Uddānanti vuttassa atthassa vakkhamānassa vā vippakiṇṇabhāvena nassituṃ adatvā uddhaṃ dānaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ uddānaṃ, saṅgahavacananti attho. Atha vā uddānanti pacchuddānādikaṃ uddānaṃ.

The root De, in the sense of protecting. Dīyati. Dānaṃ, uddānaṃ, dāyituṃ, dāyitvā. Therein, dānaṃ is so called because it protects (dāyati) from misfortune (duggati); it is the intention of giving. Uddānaṃ means the protection of the meaning that has been said or that will be said, preventing it from being lost due to being scattered; the meaning is a summarizing word. Alternatively, uddānaṃ refers to a summary, such as a concluding summary.

Khāda bhakkhane. Khādati. Khādikā, khādanaṃ, aññamaññakhādikā. Pubbaphalakhādikā, khajjaṃ, khādanīyaṃ, khandhā.

The root Khāda, in the sense of eating or devouring. Khādati. Khādikā, khādanaṃ, aññamaññakhādikā. Pubbaphalakhādikā, khajjaṃ, khādanīyaṃ, khandhā.

Tattha khajjanti pūvo. Khādanīyanti pūvaphalāphalādi. “Khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā”ti visuṃ bhojanīyassa vacanato khādanaṃ nāma khajjassa vā khādanīyassa vā bhakkhanaṃ. Apica hiṃsāpi “khādana”nti vuccati. Jātijarābyādhidukkhādīhi khajjantīti khandhā, rūpavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇāni. “Cīvarāni nassantipi ḍayhantipi undūrehipi khajjantī”ti ettha viya khajjanti saddo kammattho.

Therein, `khajjaṃ` is cake. `Khādanīyaṃ` is cakes, fruits, and so on. Because of the phrase “khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā,” which distinguishes “bhojanīya,” khādana means the eating of either khajja or khādanīya. Moreover, harming is also called “khādana.” The aggregates—form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—are so called because they are “eaten” (khajjanti) by birth, aging, sickness, suffering, and so on. Here, the word “khajjanti” is used in a passive sense, as in the phrase “robes are destroyed, burned, or eaten by rats.”

Bada [M 0.0084] theriye. Thirabhāvo theriyaṃ, yathā dakkhiyaṃ. Badati. Badarī, badaraṃ. Atridaṃ vuccati –

The root Bada, in the sense of firmness. Firmness (theriyaṃ) is the state of being firm (thirabhāvo), as in dakkhiyaṃ. Badati. Badarī, badaraṃ. Regarding this, it is said:

Kakkandhu badarī kolī, kolaṃ kulavamiccapi;

Tenilaṃ badarañcāti, nāmaṃ rukkhassa koliyāti.

Kakkandhu, badarī, kolī, kola, and kulava, also tenila and badara, are names for the jujube tree.

Khada dhitihiṃsāsu ca. Theriyāpekkhāya cakāro. Khadati. Khadiro.

The root 'khada' is in the sense of tenacity and harming. The particle 'ca' is with reference to firmness. Khadati. Khadiro.

Gada viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Gadati. Āgadanaṃ, tatho āgado etassāti tathāgato. Suṭṭhu gadatīti sugado.

The root 'gada' is in the sense of articulate speech. Gadati. Āgadanaṃ; from that, 'āgado'; one who possesses this doctrine is a 'Tathāgata'. One who speaks well is a 'Sugado'.

Rada vilekhane. Radati. Radano, rado, dāṭhārado. Atra radanoti danto.

The root 'rada' is in the sense of scraping. Radati. Radano, rado, dāṭhārado. Here, 'radano' means a tooth.

Nada abyattasadde. Sīho nadati, paṇadati. Nādo, nadī. Pabbatesu vanādīsu nadatīti nadī. Nada i iti dhātudvayavasena pana “nadantī gacchatīti nadī”tipi nibbacanaṃ vadanti.

The root 'nada' is in the sense of indistinct sound. A lion roars (nadati, paṇadati). Nādo, nadī. It is called 'nadī' because it roars in mountains, forests, and so on. However, based on the two roots 'nada' and 'i', some also state the derivation: 'roaring, it goes, thus it is a nadī'.

Kecettha vadeyyuṃ yā panesā “nada abyattasadde’ti dhātu tumhehi vuttā, sā kiṃniccamabyattasaddeyeva vattati, udāhu katthaci viyattiyampi vācāyaṃ vattatī”ti? Niccamabyattasaddeyeva vattatīti. Yajjevaṃ “sīho nadatī”tiādīsu tiracchānagatādisaddabhāvena avibhāvitatthatāya nadasaddo abyattasaddo hotu, “sīho viya ayaṃ puriso nadatī”tiādīsu pana manussabhāsāpi abyattasaddo siyāti? Tanna viyattāpi samānā manussabhāsā sīho viyāti evaṃ samupekkhāvasena sīhapadatthassāpekkhanato nadasaddena niddisiyati[M 0.0085], na purisāpekkhanavasena. Yathā hi valāhakūpamāvasena kathitaṃ, “kathañca puggalo gajjitā ca vassitā ca hotī”ti pāḷiyaṃ gajjanaṃ vassanañca puggale alabbhamānampi valāhakassa gajjanavassanasadisatāya bhāsanakaraṇakriyāyūpalabbhanato vattabbameva hoti, evameva nibbhayabhāvena sīhanādasadisiyā vācāya niccharaṇato sīho viya nadatīti avibhāvitatthavantena nadasaddena manussabhāsāpi niddisitabbā hoti.

Some might ask: 'The root 'nada', which you have stated is in the sense of indistinct sound, does it always pertain only to indistinct sound, or does it sometimes also pertain to articulate speech?' It pertains always and only to indistinct sound. 'If so, in cases such as 'the lion roars', let the word 'nada' be an indistinct sound, due to its meaning being unmanifested as the sound of an animal. But in cases such as 'this man roars like a lion', could human speech also be an indistinct sound?' That is not so. Although human speech is articulate, it is indicated by the word 'nada' by way of comparison—'like a lion'—with reference to the meaning of the word 'lion', not with reference to the man. For example, as was said by way of the simile of the cloud in the Pāli text: 'And how is a person one who thunders and rains?' Although thundering and raining are not found in a person, it is still said because the act of speaking is found to be similar to the thundering and raining of a cloud. In the same way, because of the issuing forth of fearless speech similar to a lion's roar, human speech is also to be indicated by the word 'nada'—which has an indistinct meaning—as in 'he roars like a lion'.

Ettha ca ambaphalūpamādayopi āharitvā dassetabbā. Na hi pakkāmakatādīni puggalesu vijjanti, atha kho ambaphalādīsu eva vijjanti, evaṃ santepi bhagavatā aññenākārena sadisattaṃ vibhāvetuṃ ambaphalūpamādayo vuttā, evameva nadasaddo abyattasaddabhāvena tiracchānagatasaddādīsu eva vattabbopi atthantaravibhāvanatthaṃ “sīho viya nadatī”tiādīsu manussabhāsāyampi rūḷhiyā vutto, na sabhāvato. Tathā hi sabhāvato nadasaddenapi vassitasaddādīhipi manussabhāsā niddisitabbā na hotīti. Yadi evaṃ –

Here, similes such as that of the mango fruit should also be brought forth and shown. For qualities like ripeness, rawness, and so on are not found in persons, but rather in things like mango fruits. Even so, the Blessed One used the simile of the mango fruit and others to illustrate similarity in a different way. Likewise, the word 'nada', though it should properly be applied only to indistinct sounds like those of animals, is used for human speech by convention in phrases such as 'he roars like a lion' in order to clarify a different meaning, not by its intrinsic nature. For, by its intrinsic nature, human speech is not to be indicated by words like 'nada', 'vassita', and so on. If so—

“Suvijānaṃ siṅgālānaṃ, sakuṇānañca vassitaṃ;

Manussavassitaṃ rāja, dubbijānataraṃ tato”ti

Easy to understand are the cries of jackals and the calls of birds; the speech of humans, O king, is harder to understand than that.

Ettha kasmā vassitasaddena manussabhāsā niddisiyatīti? Saccaṃ manussabhāsāpi vassitasaddena niddiṭṭhā dissati, evaṃ santepi sā “suvijānaṃ siṅgālānaṃ, sakuṇānañca vassita”nti vassitasaddavasena payogassa vacanato tadanurūpaṃ niddisituṃ arahatīti mantvā vassitasaddasadisī niddiṭṭhā. Na hi “manusso vassatī”tiādinā visuṃ payogā dissanti, “sakuṇo vassati, kūjatī”tiādinā pana payogā dissanti, tasmā “saṅgāmaṃ otaritvāna, sīhanādaṃ nadi kuso”tiādīsu viya yathārahaṃ [M 0.0086] attho gahetabbo. Evaṃ nadadhātu sabhāvato abyattasaddeyeva hoti, na viyattiyaṃ vācāyanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, why is human speech indicated by the word 'vassita'? It is true that human speech is seen to be indicated by the word 'vassita'. Even so, it is indicated as being similar to the word 'vassita', with the thought that, because of the usage of the word 'vassita' in the verse 'Easy to understand are the cries of jackals and the calls of birds...', it is fitting to indicate it accordingly. For usages such as 'a man cries out (vassati)' are not seen separately, whereas usages such as 'a bird cries (vassati), it coos (kūjati)' are seen. Therefore, as in cases like 'Having descended into battle, Kusa roared a lion's roar', the meaning should be understood as is appropriate to the context. Thus, it should be understood that the root 'nada' by its intrinsic nature refers only to indistinct sound, not to articulate speech.

Adda gatiyaṃ yācane ca. Addati.

The root 'adda' is in the sense of going and requesting. Addati.

Nadda gadda sadde. Naddati. Gaddati.

The roots 'nadda' and 'gadda' are in the sense of sound. Naddati. Gaddati.

Tadda hiṃsāyaṃ. Taddati.

The root 'tadda' is in the sense of harming. Taddati.

Kadda kucchite sadde. Kaddati. Kaddamo.

The root 'kadda' is in the sense of a contemptible sound. Kaddati. Kaddamo.

Khadda daṃsane. Daṃsanamiha dantasukatakattikā kriyā abhidhīyate. Sabhāvattā dhātuyā sādhanappayogasamavāyī. Khaddati.

The root 'khadda' is in the sense of biting. Here, biting is defined as the action of teeth made into cutters. By its nature, the root is connected with the application of an instrument. Khaddati.

Adi bandhane. Andati. Andu. Andusaddopanettha itthiliṅgo gahetabbo pāḷiyaṃ itthiliṅgappayogadassanato “seyyathāpi vāseṭṭha ayaṃ aciravatī nadī pūrā udakassa samatittikā kākapeyyā, atha puriso āgaccheyya pāratthiko pāragavesī pāragāmī pāraṃ taritukāmo, so orimatīre daḷhāya anduyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanabandho”ti. Tatra andūti yaṃ kiñci bandhanaṃ vā. “Yathā andughare puriso”ti hi vuttaṃ. Bandhanaviseso vā, “andubandhanādīni chinditvā palāyiṃsū”ti hi vuttaṃ. Apica andanaṭṭhena bandhanaṭṭhena andu viyātipi andu, pañca kāmaguṇā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “ime kho vāseṭṭha pañca kāmaguṇā ariyassa vinaye andūtipi bandhanantipi vuccantī”ti. Niggahītāgamavasenāyaṃ dhātu vuttā. Katthaci pana vigataniggahītāgamopi hoti, taṃ yathā? “Avijjā bhikkhave pubbaṅgamā akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyā anvadeva ahirika”nti pāḷi. Ettha anuandati anubandhatīti anvadi. Anvadi eva anvadevāti kitaviggaho sandhiviggaho ca [M 0.0087] veditabbo. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “anvadevāti anubandhamānamevā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ avijjamahirikaṃ anubandhamānameva hotīti attho.

The root 'adi' is in the sense of binding. Andati. Andu. Here, the word 'andu' should be taken as feminine, as its feminine usage is seen in the Pāli: 'Just as, Vāseṭṭha, this Aciravatī river is full of water to the brim, so a crow could drink from it, and a man comes who wants to cross to the far shore, is seeking the far shore, is heading for the far shore. On this shore, he is bound with a strong bond, with his arms tied behind his back.' Here, 'andu' can mean any kind of bond. For it is said: 'Like a man in a prison house.' Or it can mean a specific kind of bond, for it is said: 'Having cut their fetters and bonds, they fled.' Furthermore, because they bind, the five strands of sensual pleasure are also like a bond, and are thus called 'andu'. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'These five strands of sensual pleasure, Vāseṭṭha, are called a bond and a fetter in the discipline of the noble one.' This root is stated with the addition of a nasal. But in some places it occurs without the added nasal. For instance? In the Pāli: 'Ignorance, monks, is the forerunner for the attainment of unwholesome states, followed by shamelessness.' Here, 'anvadi' means 'it follows' (anu-andati, anubandhati). That 'anvadi eva' becomes 'anvadeva' should be understood as both a primary derivative analysis and a euphonic combination analysis. For in the commentary it is said: 'anvadeva means just following.' The meaning is that it (the unwholesome state) is just following that ignorance and shamelessness.

Idi paramissariye indati. Indanaṃ, indo.

The root 'idi' is in the sense of supreme lordship. Indati. Indanaṃ, indo.

Ettha indoti adhipatibhūto yo koci. So hi indati paresu issariyaṃ pāpuṇātīti indoti vuccati. Apica indoti sakko. Sakkassa hi anekāni nāmāni –

Here, 'indo' means anyone who is an overlord. For he exercises lordship, attaining sovereignty over others—thus he is called 'indo.' Moreover, 'indo' means Sakka. For Sakka has many names—

Sakko purindado indo, vatrabhū pākasāsano;

Sahassanetto maghavā, devarājā sujampati.

Sakka, Purindada, Indo, Vatrabhū, Pākasāsano; Sahassanetto, Maghavā, Devarājā, Sujampati.

Sahassakkho dasasata-locano vajirāvudho;

Hūtapati mahindo ca, kosiyo devakuñjaro.

Sahassakkho, Dasasatalocano, Vajirāvudho; Hūtapati, Mahindo, Kosiyo, Devakuñjaro.

Surādhipo suranātho, vāsavo tidivādhibhū;

Jambāri ceva vajira-hattho asurasāsano;

Gandharājā devindo, surindo asurābhibhūti.

Surādhipo, Suranātho, Vāsavo, Tidivādhibhū; Jambāri, Vajirahattho, Asurasāsano; Gandharājā, Devindo, Surindo, Asurābhibhū.

Evaṃ anekāni nāmāni. Ekopi hi attho anekasaddappavattinimittatāya anekanāmo. Tenāha bhagavā –

Thus, there are many names. For a single meaning, because it is the cause for the application of many words, has many names. Therefore, the Blessed One said—

Sakko mahāli devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno magho nāma māṇavo ahosi, tasmā “maghavā”ti vuccati. Sakko mahāli devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno pure dānaṃ adāsi, tasmā “purindado”ti vuccati. Sakko mahāli devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ adāsi, tasmā “sakko”ti vuccati. Sakko mahāli devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno āvāsaṃ adāsi, tasmā “vāsavo”ti vuccati. Sakko mahāli devānamindo sahassaṃ atthānaṃ muhuttena [M 0.0088] cinteti, tasmā “sahassakkho”ti vuccati. Sakkassa mahāli devānamindassa sujā nāma asurakaññā pajāpati, tasmā “sujampatī”ti vuccati. Sakko mahāli devānamindo devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ issariyādhipaccaṃ rajjaṃ kāreti, tasmā “devānamindo”ti vuccatīti.

Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being, was a young man named Magha, therefore he is called 'Maghavā.' Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being, gave gifts in a city, therefore he is called 'Purindada.' Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being, gave gifts respectfully, therefore he is called 'Sakka.' Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, when he was formerly a human being, gave dwelling places, therefore he is called 'Vāsava.' Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, contemplates a thousand matters in a moment, therefore he is called 'Sahassakkha.' Sujā, the asura maiden, is the consort of Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, therefore he is called 'Sujampatī.' Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the devas, exercises lordship and sovereignty over the devas of the Thirty-Three, therefore he is called 'Devānaminda.'

Evamekassāpi atthassa anekāni saddappavattinimittāni dissanti.

Thus, even for a single meaning, many indicative features for the application of terms are seen.

Tathā hi yena pavattinimittena tāvatiṃsādhipatimhi indasaddo pavatto, na tena tattha sakkādisaddā pavattā, atha kho aññena. Tathā yena sammādiṭṭhiyaṃ paññāsaddo pavatto, na tena tattha vijjādisaddā. Yena sampayuttadhammānaṃ pubbaṅgamabhāvena uppannadhammasmiṃ cittasaddo pavatto, na tena tattha viññāṇādisaddā. Na hi vinā kenaci pavattinimittena saddo pavattatīti. Ekopi attho sammutyattho ca paramattho ca anekasaddappavttinimittatāya anekanāmoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For just as the term 'Inda' arose with reference to the indicative feature associated with the lord of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, the terms 'Sakka' and so on did not arise with that feature, but rather with another. Just as the term 'paññā' arose with reference to right view, the terms 'vijjā' and so on did not arise with that. Just as the term 'citta' arose with reference to a state that arises as the forerunner of associated phenomena, the terms 'viññāṇa' and so on did not arise with that. For indeed, a term does not arise without some indicative feature. Thus, even a single meaning—whether a conventional meaning or an ultimate meaning—should be seen as having many names due to the multiplicity of indicative features giving rise to terms.

Ettha siyā “nāmānīti vadatha, kiṃ nāmaṃ nāmā”ti. Vuccate – īdise ṭhāne atthesu saddappavattinimittaṃ “nāma”nti gahitaṃ, yaṃ “liṅga”ntipi vuccati. Tathā hi “nāma”nti ca “liṅga”nti ca saddopi vuccati, “aññaṃ sobhanaṃ nāmaṃ pariyesissāmi. Liṅgañca nippajjate”tiādīsu viya. Asabhāvadhammabhūtaṃ nāmapaññattisaṅkhātaṃ atthesu saddappavattinimittampi vuccati “nāmagottaṃ na jīrati. Sataliṅgo”tiādīsu viya. Iti nāmasaddenapi liṅgasaddenapi saddappavattinimittassa kathanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddappavattinimittañca nāma lokasaṅketasiddho taṃtaṃvacanatthaniyato sāmaññākāravisesoti gahetabbaṃ. So evaṃbhūtoyeva sāmaññākāraviseso nāma paññattīti pubbācariyā vadanti[M 0.0089]. So hi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe saddaṃ nāmeti tassa tassa atthassa nāmasaññaṃ karotīti nāmaṃ, pakārehi ñāpanato paññatti ca. Saviññattivikārassa pana saddassa sammutiparamatthasaccānaṃ pakārehi ñāpanato paññattibhāve vattabbameva natthi. Saddasseva hi ekantena paññattibhāvo icchitabbo “niruttipaṭisambhidā parittārammaṇā”ti ca “niruttipaṭisambhidā paccuppannārammaṇā”ti ca “niruttipaṭisambhidā bahiddhārammaṇā”ti ca pāḷidassanato. Idha pana saddappavattinimittādhikārattā nāmavasena attho pakāsito. Evaṃ anekavidhassa sāmaññākāravisesoti pubbācariyehi gahitassa nāmapaññattisaṅkhātassa saddappavattinimittassa vasena ekopi ñeyyattho anekaliṅgoti gahetabbo. Tenāha āyasmā suhemanto pabhinnapaṭisambhido –

Here, one might say, 'You speak of 'names,' but what is a name?' It is said: In such contexts, the term 'name' refers to the linguistic signifier for meaning, which is also called a 'mark.' Indeed, both 'name' and 'mark' can refer to a word, as in examples like, 'I will seek another beautiful name,' or 'A mark is produced.' Even that conventional designation called 'name,' which is of the nature of an insubstantial phenomenon, is referred to as the linguistic signifier for meanings, as in phrases like, 'A name-clan does not age,' or 'A hundred marks.' Thus, it should be understood that the linguistic signifier is referred to by both the term 'name' and the term 'mark.' The linguistic signifier is to be understood as a general-specific form established by worldly convention, fixed to express particular meanings. The ancient teachers say that this very general-specific form is what is called 'conceptual designation.' For it inclines a term toward a particular meaning, creating a name-designation for it, and is thus a 'name'; and because it makes things known in various ways, it is a 'designation.' However, concerning the status of communicative sound with its manifestations as designations related to conventional and ultimate truths, there is nothing further to be said. For the nature of designation should be entirely attributed to sound itself, as seen in scriptural passages like, 'The analytical knowledge of language has limited objects,' 'The analytical knowledge of language has present objects,' and 'The analytical knowledge of language has external objects.' Here, however, the meaning is explained in terms of 'name' due to the discussion of the linguistic signifier. Thus, a single object of knowledge, having a diversity of 'marks,' should be understood through the linguistic signifier—called 'name-designation' by the ancient teachers—which takes on various general-specific forms. Therefore, the Venerable Suhemanta, endowed with distinct analytical knowledge, said—

“Sataliṅgassa atthassa, satalakkhaṇadhārino;

Ekaṅgadassī dummedho, satadassīva paṇḍito”ti.

Of an object with a hundred marks, possessing a hundred characteristics: The fool sees only one aspect, but the wise person sees a hundred.

Evaṃ sabbābhidhānesupi iminā nayena yathārahaṃ attho vibhāvetabbo nayaññūhi.

Thus, in all designations, the meaning should be discerned appropriately by those who understand the method, in accordance with this principle.

Vidi avayave. Vindati. Yadi abhidhānamatthi, “vindo”ti dissati. Yathā kaṇḍati. Kaṇḍo.

The root 'Vidi' is in the sense of parts. 'Vindati.' If there is a designation, it is seen as 'vindo.' Just as 'kaṇḍati' (he itches), 'kaṇḍo' (an itch).

Khidi avayaveti candaviduno vadanti. Tesaṃ mate “khindatī”ti rūpaṃ.

The Canda scholars say that the root 'Khidi' is in the sense of parts. According to their view, the form is 'khindati.'

Nidi kucchāyaṃ. Kucchāsaddo garahattho. Nindati. Nindā.

The root 'Nidi' is in the sense of reproach. The word 'kucchā' has the meaning of blame. 'Nindati.' 'Nindā.'

Porāṇametaṃ atula, netaṃ ajjatanāmiva;

Nindanti tuṇhimāsīnaṃ, nindanti bahubhāṇinaṃ;

Mitabhāṇimpi nindanti, natthi loke anindito.

This is an ancient saying, Atula, not one of today only: They blame one who sits silent, they blame one who speaks much, they blame one who speaks in moderation; there is no one in the world who is not blamed.

Avaṇṇo [M 0.0090] aguṇo nindā, garahā ayasopi ca;

Asiloko akitti ca, asilāghā ca atthuti.

Dispraise, lack of virtue, blame, censure, and ill fame; ill report, bad reputation, lack of praise, and non-praise.

Nanda samiddhiyaṃ. Akammikā dhātu. Nandati puttehi puttimā. Nandāya nuna maraṇena. Nandasi sirivāhana. Nandanaṃ vanaṃ. Abhisaddayoge panāyaṃ sakammakopi. Abhinandanti āgataṃ nābhinandanti maraṇaṃ.

The root 'Nanda' is in the sense of prosperity. The root is intransitive. The one with children rejoices because of children. Surely, Nanda, by death. You rejoice, carrier of glory. The Nandana grove. But when combined with the prefix 'abhi', this root is also transitive. They welcome one who has come, they do not welcome death.

Sirīva rūpiniṃ disvā, nanditaṃ āsi taṃ kulaṃ;

Tena nandāti me nāmaṃ, sundaraṃ pavaraṃ ahu.

Seeing the glorious one endowed with beauty, that family was delighted; hence my name became Nandā, lovely and excellent.

Rammaṃ veḷuvanaṃ yena, na diṭṭhaṃ sugatālayaṃ;

Na tena nandanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, iti maññe mahesayaṃ.

By whom the delightful Veḷuvana, the Sugata's abode, has not been seen; by him the Nandana grove has not been seen, so I think, O great sage.

Yena veḷuvanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, naranandananandanaṃ;

Sudiṭṭhaṃ nandanaṃ tena, amarindasunandanaṃ.

By whom Veḷuvana was seen, delighting the delight of men; well seen was Nandana by him, the great delight of the lord of the deathless.

Cadi hilādane dittiyañca. Hilādanaṃ sukhanaṃ. Ditti sobhā. Candati. Candano, cando.

The root 'Cadi' is used in the sense of delight and shining. Delight means pleasantness. Shining means beauty. 'Candati' (it shines/delights). 'Candana' (sandalwood), 'cando' (moon).

Ettha ca candanassapi anekāni nāmāni – candanaṃ, gandhasāro, malayajo, suvaṇṇacandanaṃ, haricandanaṃ, rattacandanaṃ, gosītacandanaṃ. Candayati hilādayati sītaguṇasamaṅgitāya sattānaṃ paliḷāhaṃ vūpasamentaṃ sukhaṃ uppādetīti candanaṃ. Candoti somo, sopi candayati hilādayati sītaguṇasampattiyā attano pabhāya sattānaṃ pariḷāhaṃ vūpasamento sukhaṃ uppādetīti candoti vuccati. Atha vā candati dibbati siriyā virocatīti cando. Āgamaṭṭhakathāsu pana “chandaṃ janetīti cando”ti vuttaṃ. Tassāpi anekāni nāmāni –

Here too, sandalwood has many names: candana, gandhasāra, malayaja, suvaṇṇacandana, haricandana, rattacandana, gosītacandana. It is called 'candana' because it pleases and refreshes, producing happiness by allaying the fever of beings through its cooling properties. 'Canda' is Soma (the moon), and it too pleases and refreshes, producing happiness by allaying the fever of beings through the abundance of its cooling qualities and its own radiance, hence it is called 'canda.' Alternatively, it is called 'cando' because it shines, it gleams, it is radiant with splendor. In the Āgama commentaries, however, it is said, “It generates desire (chanda), thus it is called 'cando.'” It too has many names:

Cando [M 0.0091] nakkhattarājā ca, indu somo nisākaro;

Candimā mā nisānātho, osadhī so nisāpati.

Canda, and the king of stars, Indu, Soma, the night-maker; Candimā, Mā, the lord of the night, the lord of herbs, he the lord of the night.

Uḷurājā sasaṅko ca, himaraṃsi sasīpi ca;

Dvijarājā sasadharo, tārāpati himaṃsu ca.

The king of stars, and the hare-marked; the cool-rayed, and also Sasī; the king of the twice-born, the hare-bearer, the lord of stars, and the cool-rayed.

Kumudabandhavo ceva, migaṅko ca kalānidhi;

Sudhaṃ sudhi dhūpi yūpa-rasmi ceva khamākaro;

Nakkhatteso ca rajanī-karo subbhaṃsu eva ca.

And the friend of the water-lily, and the deer-marked, the treasure of arts; Nectar, the wise one, the incense-bearer, the radiance of the sacrificial post, and the earth-maker; and the lord of stars, the night-maker, and also the bright-rayed.

Tadi cetāyaṃ. Tandati. Tandī.

The root 'Tadi' is in the sense of 'thinking'. (From it are derived) 'tandati' (he is sluggish) and 'tandī' (sluggishness).

Kadi kaladi avhāne rodane ca. Kandati, pakkandati. Pakkanduṃ, kandanto, kalandako.

The roots 'Kadi' and 'Kaladi' are in the sense of calling and weeping. (From them come) 'kandati' (he cries), 'pakkandati' (he cries out). (Also) 'pakkanduṃ' (to cry out), 'kandanto' (crying), 'kalandako' (squirrel).

Kalidi paridevane. Kalindati.

The root 'Kalidi' is in the sense of lamenting. (From it comes) 'kalindati' (he laments).

Khoda paṭighāte. Khodati.

The root 'Khoda' is in the sense of obstruction. (From it comes) 'khodati' (he obstructs).

Khanda gatisosanesu. Khandati. Khando. Khando nāma eko devo, yo “kumāro sattidharo”ti ca vuccati.

The root 'Khanda' is in the sense of going and drying up. (From it come) 'khandati' (it breaks/goes/dries up). (Also) 'khando' (a piece/fragment). Khando is the name of a certain deva, who is also called 'the youth wielding a spear'.

Khudi āpavane. Khundati.

The root 'Khudi' is in the sense of crushing. (From it comes) 'khundati' (he crushes).

Sidi sītiye. Sītiyaṃ sītibhāvo. Sindati. Sosindo, sotatto.

The root 'Sidi' is in the sense of coolness. Coolness means the state of being cool. (From it come) 'sindati' (it flows). (Also) 'sosindo' (dried up), 'sotatto' (scorched).

Vanda abhivādanathutīsu. Vandati, abhivandati. Abhivandanā, vandanaṃ, vandako.

The root 'Vanda' is in the sense of salutation and praise. (From it come) 'vandati' (he salutes), 'abhivandati' (he reveres). (Also) 'abhivandanā' (salutation), 'vandanaṃ' (reverence), 'vandako' (a worshipper).

Ettha pana vandatīti padassa namassati thometi vāti attho. Tathā hi suttantaṭīkākāro “vandeti vandāmi thomemi vā”ti āha.

Here, however, the meaning of the word 'vandati' is 'he pays homage' or 'he praises'. Indeed, the commentator on the Suttantas said: 'vandeti means I pay homage or I praise.'

Bhadi kallāṇe sokhiye ca. Kallāṇaṃ kalyāṇaṃ, sokhiyaṃ sukhino bhāvo, sukhamiccevattho. Bhandati. Bhandako, bhaddo, bhadro.

The root 'bhad' is used in the sense of auspiciousness and happiness. 'Kallāṇa' means auspiciousness; 'sokhiya' is the state of being happy, which is simply happiness. From it are derived 'bhandati' (he shines/behaves), 'bhandako' (a jester/one who behaves), 'bhaddo' (auspicious), and 'bhadro' (auspicious).

Madi [M 0.0092] thutimodamadasupanagatīsu. Mandati. Mando.

The root 'mad' is used in the senses of praise, joy, intoxication, sleeping, and movement. From it are derived 'mandati' (he is sluggish/intoxicated/joyful) and 'mando' (sluggish/foolish/intoxicated).

Ettha pana mandoti aññāṇīpi bāladārakopi vuccati. Tattha aññāṇī mandati aññāṇabhāvena appasaṃsitabbampi puggalaṃ thometīti mando. Mandati amoditabbaṭṭhānepi modatīti mando. Mandati dānasīlādipuññakriyāsu pamajjatīti mando. Mandati attano ca paresañca hitāhitaṃ acintento khādanīyabhojanīyādīhi attano kāyaṃ sañjātamedaṃ kurumāno supatīti mando. Mandati ayuttaṃ paresaṃ kriyaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanena gacchati gaṇhātīti mando. Atha vā mandati punappunaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena gabbhaṃ gacchatīti mando. Vuttañhi bhagavatā “punappunaṃ gabbhamupeti mando”ti. Bāladārako pana mandati yuttāyuttamajānanto uttānaseyyaṃparivattanaseyyaṃ vā supatīti mando. Tathā hi –

Here, 'mando' refers to both the ignorant person and the foolish child. In this context, the ignorant one is called 'mando' because, due to ignorance, he praises even a person who should not be praised. He is called 'mando' because he delights in things in which one should not delight. He is called 'mando' because he is negligent in meritorious deeds like generosity and virtue. He is called 'mando' because, without considering what is beneficial or harmful for himself and others, he makes his body fat with food and drink and sleeps. He is called 'mando' because he follows the improper actions of others, adopting their ways by blindly following what he has seen. Alternatively, he is called 'mando' because he repeatedly goes to the womb by taking rebirth. For the Blessed One has said: 'The fool enters the womb again and again.' As for the foolish child, he is called 'mando' because, not knowing what is proper or improper, he sleeps lying on his back or turning over. Indeed—

“Nonītasukhumālaṃ maṃ, jātapallavakomalaṃ;

Mandaṃ uttānasayanaṃ, pisācabhayatajjitā.

Me, tender as fresh butter, soft as a fresh sprout; sluggishly lying on my back, terrified by fear of demons.

Pādamūle mahesissa, sāyesuṃ dīnamānasā;

Idaṃ dadāma te nātha, saraṇaṃ hohi nāyakā”ti

At the feet of the Great Seer, with saddened hearts they lay down; 'This we give to you, O Lord; be our refuge, O leader!'

Vuttaṃ, iti uttānasayanato paṭṭhāya yāva mandadasakaṃ, tāva “mando”ti “dārako”ti daṭṭhabbo. Appatthavācakopi pana mandasaddo hoti, so pāṭipadikattā idha nādhippeto, atha vā mandati appabhāvena gacchati pavattatīti nipphannapāṭipadikavasenapi gahetabbo.

It is said that from the time of lying on one's back until the 'manda' decade (the first ten years), he should be regarded as 'mando' or 'dārako' (child). However, the word 'manda' can also denote something of little value; that sense is not intended here as it is a primary nominal stem. Alternatively, it can be understood by way of a derived nominal stem, from 'mandati,' meaning 'it proceeds with little power' or 'it occurs weakly.'

Muda hāse. Hasanaṃ hāso tuṭṭhi. Modati, pamodati. Sammodati. Sammodako. Sammodamānā gacchanti muditā. Mudā.

The root 'mud' is used in the sense of joy or laughter. 'Hasanaṃ' means laughter or joy. From it are derived: 'modati' (he delights), 'pamodati' (he greatly delights), 'sammodati' (he rejoices together), and 'sammodako' (one who rejoices together). An example is: 'Sammodamānā gacchanti muditā' (rejoicing, they go, filled with joy). Also derived is 'mudā' (with joy).

Hada [M 0.0093] karīsossagge. Karīsossaggo nāma karīsassa ossajjanaṃ vissajjanaṃ. Hadati. Uhadati. Hadano.

The root 'had' is used in the sense of excreting dung. 'Karīsossagga' means the releasing or discarding of dung. From it are derived: 'hadati' (he excretes), 'uhadati' (he excretes), and 'hadano' (excretion).

Ettha ca “yesaṃ no santhate dārakā uhadantipi ummihantipī”ti ayaṃ pāḷi nidassanaṃ, tatra uhadantipīti vaccampi karonti. Ummihantipīti passāvampi karonti. Pacchimapadassattho miha secaneti dhātuvasena daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ pana curādigaṇepi vattati dvigaṇikattā. Imasmiñhi ṭhāne “mutteti ohadeti cā”ti cariyāpiṭakapāḷippadeso nidassanaṃ. Tattha muttetīti passāvaṃ karoti. Ohadetīti karīsaṃ vissajjeti.

Here, the Pāli passage 'on whose bedding our children excrete and urinate' serves as an example. Therein, 'uhadanti' means they also produce excrement, and 'ummihanti' means they also produce urine. The meaning of the latter word is to be understood by way of the root 'mih' in the sense of 'secana' (discharging). This root 'had', however, also belongs to the Curādi group, as it is a root of two classes. In this instance, the passage from the Cariyāpiṭaka, 'mutteti ohadeti ca,' serves as an example. There, 'mutteti' means to urinate, and 'ohadeti' means to discard excrement.

Uda mode kīḷāyañca. Udati. Udānaṃ. Udaggo.

The root 'ud' is used in the senses of joy and play. From it are derived: 'udati' (he rejoices/plays), 'udānaṃ' (an inspired utterance), and 'udaggo' (elated).

Tattha udānanti kenaṭṭhena udānaṃ? Udānanaṭṭhena. Kimidaṃ udānanaṃ nāma? Pībhivegasamuṭṭhāpito udāhāro. Yathā hi yaṃ telādi minitabbavatthu mānaṃgahetuṃ na sakkoti, vissanditvā gacchati, taṃ “avaseko”ti vuccati. Yañca jalaṃ taḷākaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, ajjhottharitvā gacchati, taṃ “ogho”ti vuccati, evameva yaṃ pītivegasamuṭṭhāpitaṃ vitakkavipphāraṃ hadayaṃ sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti, so adhiko hutvā anto asaṇṭhahitvā vacīdvārena nikkhamanto paṭiggāhakanirapekkho udāhāraviseso “udāna”nti vuccati. Udaggoti sañjātasomanasso.

Therein, 'udāna'—in what sense is it 'udāna'? In the sense of 'udānana' (uttering forth). What is this 'udānana'? It is an utterance produced by the force of joy. Just as oil or a similar substance to be measured, which a measuring vessel is unable to hold, flows out and away, is called 'avaseka' (overflow); and just as water which a pond is unable to hold, overflows and flows away, is called 'ogha' (flood); even so, that expansion of thought produced by the force of joy, which the heart is unable to contain, becomes excessive and, not remaining within, emerges through the door of speech—that special utterance, independent of any recipient, is called 'udāna'. 'Udagga' means one in whom gladness has arisen.

Kuda khuda guda kīḷāyameva. Kodati. Khodati. Godati.

The roots 'kud', 'khud', and 'gud' are used only in the sense of play. From them are derived: 'kodati' (he plays), 'khodati' (he plays), and 'godati' (he plays).

Sūda paggharaṇe. Sūdati. Suttaṃ. Sūdo. Rañño sūdā mahānase.

The root 'sūd' is used in the sense of flowing. From it are derived: 'sūdati' (it flows); also 'suttaṃ' (a discourse) and 'sūdo' (a cook), as in the example: 'Rañño sūdā mahānase' (the king's cooks in the great kitchen).

Ettha [M 0.0094] ca suttanti sūdati dhenu viya khīraṃ atthe paggharāpetīti suttaṃ, tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ. Sakammikadhātuttā pana “paggharāpetī”ti kāritavasena attho kathetuṃ labbhati. Tathā hi “karotī”ti padassa “nipphādetī”ti attho kathetuṃ labbhati. Sūdoti bhattakāro. Yo “āḷāriko, odaniko, sūpakāro, rasako”ti ca vuccati. Sūdati “evañcevañca kate khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā sugandhaṃ manāpaṃ surasañca bhavissatī”ti randhanakriyāya sukusalatāya rasaṃ paggharāpeti abhinibbattetīti sūdo.

Here, 'suttaṃ' (discourse) is so called because it causes the meaning to flow forth, like a cow yielding milk; it refers to the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha. Because the root is transitive, the meaning can be expressed in the causative sense as 'causes to flow forth'. For example, the word 'karoti' can be explained with the meaning 'produces'. 'Sūdo' means a cook, who is also called 'āḷāriko', 'odaniko', 'sūpakāro', or 'rasako'. He is called 'sūdo' because, through his great skill in the art of cooking, he causes flavor to flow forth and brings it into being, thinking, 'If it is made in this and that way, the food will be fragrant, pleasing, and delicious.'

Rahada abyattasadde. Rahadati. Rahado.

The root 'rahad' is used in the sense of indistinct sound. From it are derived: 'rahadati' (it makes an indistinct sound) and 'rahado' (a lake or pool).

Hilādi sukhe ca. Cakāro pubbatthāpekkhako. Hilādati. Hilādanaṃ, hilādo, mettāsahāyakatasattamahāhilādo.

The root 'hilād' is used in the sense of happiness, and also the previous meaning. The particle 'ca' refers to the previous meaning. From it are derived: 'hilādati' (he delights); 'hilādanaṃ' (delight); 'hilādo' (delight), as in 'mettāsahāyakatasattamahāhilādo' (the great delight of beings made friends and companions through loving-kindness).

Sadda kucchite sadde. Saddati.

The root 'sadd' is used in the sense of a contemptible sound. From it is derived 'saddati' (it makes a contemptible sound).

Mida snehe. Sneho nāma vasāsaṅkhāto sneho pītisnehoti duvidho. Idha pana vasāsaṅkhāto sneho adhippeto, medati medo.

The root 'mid' is used in the sense of 'sneha' (unctuousness or affection). 'Sneha' is twofold: the unctuousness known as fat, and the 'sneha' of affection. Here, however, the unctuousness known as fat is intended. From it are derived: 'medati' (it becomes fat) and 'medo' (fat).

Ettha ca medatīti medasahito bhavati ayaṃ purisoti attho. Medo nāma thūlassa sakalasarīraṃ pharitvā kisassa jaṅghamaṃsādīni nissāya ṭhito patthinnasineho, so vaṇṇena haliddivaṇṇo hoti. Kārite “medeti medayatī”ti rūpāni. Tathā hi “te imaṃ kāyaṃ balaṃ gāhenti nāma brūhenti nāma medenti nāmā”ti pāḷi dissati. Tattha medentīti sañjātamedaṃ karontīti attho. Imissā pana dhātuyā divādigaṇaṃ pattāya pītisinehatthe “mejjatī”ti suddhakatturūpaṃ bhavati. Curādigaṇaṃ pana [M 0.0095] pattāya “medeti medayatī”ti suddhakatturūpāni bhavantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, 'medati' means 'this person becomes endowed with fat'. 'Medo' (fat) is the thick unctuousness that pervades the entire body of a stout person and, in a thin person, is established resting on the flesh of the shanks and so on; it is a diffused unctuousness, and its color is that of turmeric. In the causative, the forms are 'medeti' and 'medayati'. For example, the Pāli passage is found: 'They strengthen this body, they nourish it, they fatten it.' There, 'medenti' means 'they cause fat to arise.' However, when this root belongs to the Divādi group, in the sense of the 'sneha' of affection, the form 'mejjati' occurs. But when it belongs to the Curādi group, the forms 'medeti' and 'medayati' occur; this should be noted.

Sida mocane. Sidati. Sedo.

The root 'sid' is used in the sense of release. From it are derived: 'sidati' (it is released/loosened) and 'sedo' (sweat).

Sanda pasavane. Pasavanaṃ sandanaṃ avicchedappavatti. Sandati udakaṃ. Mahanto puññābhisando.

The root 'sand' is used in the sense of flowing forth. 'Pasavana' means streaming, an uninterrupted proceeding. From it is derived 'sandati' (it flows), as in 'sandati udakaṃ' (water flows). Also derived is 'abhisando', as in 'mahanto puññābhisando' (a great flood of merit).

Ettha ca puññābhisandoti puññappavāho, puññanadītipi vattuṃ yujjati.

Here, 'puññābhisando' means a flow of merit; it is also appropriate to call it a river of merit.

Madda maddane. Maddabhi, pamaddati. Mārasenappamaddano. Kaṇṭakaṃ maddati.

The root 'madd' is used in the sense of crushing. From it are derived: 'maddati' (he crushes) and 'pamaddati' (he thoroughly crushes). Examples are: 'Mārasenappamaddano' (the suppressor of Māra's army) and 'Kaṇṭakaṃ maddati' (he crushes a thorn).

Kadi velambe. Vilambabhāvo velambo. Kandati.

The root 'kad' is used in the sense of delay. 'Velambo' is the state of delay. From it is derived 'kandati' (he delays).

Kada avhāne rodane ca. Kadati.

The root 'kad' is used in the senses of calling and weeping. From it is derived 'kadati' (he calls/weeps).

Khadi ujjhane. Chandati.

The root 'khad' is used in the sense of abandoning. From it is derived 'chandati' (he abandons/rejects).

Sada sādane. Sadati. Assādo.

The root 'sad' is used in the sense of accomplishing. From it are derived: 'sadati' (he accomplishes) and 'assādo' (enjoyment).

Sīda visaraṇagatyāvasānesu. Visaraṇaṃ vippharaṇaṃ. Gatyāvasānaṃ gamanassa avasānaṃ osānaṃ abhāvakaraṇaṃ, nisīdananti attho. Sīdati, lābūni sīdanti. Saṃsīdati, osīdati, pasīdati, vippasīdati. Pasādo. Pasanno. Vippasanno. Pasādako. Pasādito. Pāsādo. Osīdāpako. Kusīto. Āsīno. Nisinno. Nisinnako. Sannisīvesu pakkhisu. Nisīdanaṃ, nisinnaṃ. Nisajjā. Gonisādo, upanisā. Sīdeti. Sīdayati. Sīdāpeti. Sīdāpayati. Pasādeti. Nisīdituṃ. Nisīdāpetuṃ, nisādetuṃ, nisīdāpeti, nisīdāpetvā. Ucchaṅge maṃ nisādetvā, pitā atthānusāsati. Nisīditvātipi pāṭho. Nisīditvā. Nisīditvāna. Nisīdituna[M 0.0096]. Nisīdiya. Nisīdiyāna. Saṃsīditvā. Avasīditvā. Osīditvā.

The root 'sīd' is used in the senses of spreading, movement, and cessation. 'Visaraṇa' means pervading. 'Gatyāvasāna' (cessation of movement) means the end of going, termination, bringing to non-existence; its meaning is sitting down. From it are derived: 'sīdati' (it sinks), as in 'lābūni sīdanti' (gourds sink); 'saṃsīdati' (it sinks down); 'osīdati' (it subsides); 'pasīdati' (it becomes clear); 'vippasīdati' (it becomes very clear). Nouns and adjectives include: 'pasādo' (clarity); 'pasanno' (pleased); 'vippasanno' (very pleased); 'pasādako' (one who clarifies); 'pasādito' (clarified); 'pāsādo' (a palace); 'osīdāpako' (one who causes to sink); 'kusīto' (lazy); 'āsīno' (seated); 'nisinno' (sat down); 'nisinnako' (one who is seated), as in 'sannisīvesu pakkhisu' (among birds that have settled down); 'nisīdanaṃ' (a seat; sitting); 'nisinnaṃ' (sitting); 'nisajjā' (sitting); 'gonisādo' (a place where cattle sit); 'upanisā' (a cause). Causative forms include: 'sīdeti', 'sīdayati', 'sīdāpeti', 'sīdāpayati' (it causes to sink); 'pasādeti' (it clarifies). Infinitives include: 'nisīdituṃ' (to sit down); 'nisīdāpetuṃ', 'nisādetuṃ' (to cause to sit down). Causative verbs: 'nisīdāpeti' (he causes to sit down). Gerunds include: 'nisīdāpetvā' (having caused to sit down), as in 'Ucchaṅge maṃ nisādetvā, pitā atthānusāsati' ('Having seated me on his lap, the father instructs me in what is beneficial'); there is also the reading 'nisīditvā'. Other gerunds: 'nisīditvā', 'nisīditvāna', 'nisīdituna', 'nisīdiya', 'nisīdiyāna' (having sat down); 'saṃsīditvā' (having sunk down); 'avasīditvā' (having subsided); 'osīditvā' (having subsided).

Tattha kusītoti vīriyenādhigantabbassa atthassa alābhato kucchitenākārena sīdatīti kusīto. Atha vā sayampi kucchitenākārena sīdati aññepi sīdāpeti taṃ nissāya aññesaṃ sīdanassa sambhavatoti kusīto. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

Herein, one is called 'lazy' (kusīto) because, from not obtaining the goal that should be attained by energy, one sinks (sīdati) in a contemptible manner. Or else, one is called 'lazy' because one sinks in a contemptible manner oneself and causes others to sink; for on account of such a person, the sinking of others occurs. For so it is said:

“Parittaṃ kaṭṭhamārūyha, yathā sīde mahaṇṇave;

Evaṃ kusītamāgamma, sādhajīvīpi sīdatī”ti;

"Just as one, having mounted a small raft, would sink in the great ocean, so too one of good livelihood sinks by associating with a lazy person."

Kusītoti cettha dassa tattaṃ “sugato”ti ettha viya “satasmīti hotī”ti ettha viya ca. Tathā hi sīdatīti sataṃ, aniccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iminā ucchedadiṭṭhi vuttā. Sataiti cettha avibhattiko niddeso. Sannisīvesūti parissamavinodanatthaṃ sabbaso nisīdantesu, vissamamānesūti attho, dakārassa vakāraṃ katvā niddeso. Nisīdananti nisīdanakriyā. Mañcapīṭhādikaṃ vā āsanaṃ. Tañhi nisīdanti etthāti nisīdananti vuccati. Nisinnanti nisīdanakriyā eva. Ettha pana “gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti. Mātugāmena saddhiṃ raho maññe tayā nisinnanti kukkuccaṃ upadahatītiādīsu cassa payogo veditabbo. Ettha hi gamanaṃ gabhaṃ, ṭhānaṃ ṭhitaṃ, nisīdanaṃ nisannaṃ, supanaṃ suttaṃ, jāgaraṇaṃ jāgaritaṃ, bhāsanaṃ bhāsitanti vuccati. Nisajjāti nisīdanā. Gonisādoti gonisajjanā. Upanisāti upanisīdati phalaṃ etthāti upanisā, kāraṇaṃ. Nisādetunti nisīdāpetuṃ. Nisādetvāti nisīdāpetvā.

Here, in kusīto, the change of d to t is to be understood, as in sugato and as in satasmīti hoti. For sīdati means sataṃ, and this is a designation for the impermanent. By this the annihilationist view is expressed. Here sata is a designation without inflection. Sannisīvesu means 'in those who are sitting down completely to relieve fatigue,' that is, 'in those who are resting'; the designation is made by changing the letter d to v. Nisīdanaṃ is the act of sitting, or a seat such as a bed or a stool; for one sits on it, thus it is called nisīdanaṃ. Nisinnaṃ is the act of sitting itself. But its usage should be understood in such passages as: 'He acts with clear comprehension in going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent'; and 'Remorse arises from the thought: “I think you sat in private with a woman.”' For here gamanaṃ (going) is called gataṃ (gone), ṭhānaṃ (standing) is called ṭhitaṃ (stood), nisīdanaṃ (sitting) is called nisinnaṃ (sat), supanaṃ (sleeping) is called suttaṃ (slept), jāgaraṇaṃ (waking) is called jāgaritaṃ (woken), and bhāsanaṃ (speaking) is called bhāsitaṃ (spoken). Nisajjā is sitting. Gonisādo is a place where cattle sit. Upanisā means 'a result is based on this,' hence it means a cause. Nisādetuṃ means to cause to sit down. Nisādetvā means having caused to sit down.

Bhāve [M 0.0097] napuṃsako ñeyyo, nisinnanti ravo pana;

Vāccaliṅgo tiliṅgo so, gatādīsupyayaṃ nayo.

The neuter should be known when expressing the action itself; but the word nisinna is adjectival, having three genders. This same principle applies to gata and other such words.

Cada yācane. Yācanaṃ ajjhesanaṃ. Cadati.

The root cad is used in the sense of asking. Asking means requesting. Cadati: he asks.

Mida meda medhāhiṃsāsu. Midati. Medati.

The roots mid and med are used in the senses of affection and hurting. Midati. Medati.

Nida neda kucchāsannikarisesu. Kucchā garahā. Sannikarisaṃ vohāraviseso. Nidati. Nedati.

The roots nid and ned are used in the senses of reproach and proximity. Reproach means blame. Proximity is a particular kind of intercourse. Nidati. Nedati.

Bundi nisāne. Nisānaṃ tejanaṃ tikkhatā. Bundati. Bondi.

The root bund is used in the sense of sharpening. Sharpening means whetting, sharpness. Bundati. Bondi.

Ettha ca bondīti sarīraṃ. Tañhi bundāni tikkhāni pisuṇapharusavācādīni vā paññāvīriyādīni vā ettha santīti bondīti vuccati, saññogaparattepi ukārassokārādeso, pāpakalyāṇajanavasenesa attho daṭṭhabbo. Bondisaddassa sarīravācakatā pana –

And here, bondi means the body. For sharp things—such as divisive and harsh speech, or such as wisdom and energy—exist in it, thus it is called bondi. The substitution of o for u occurs even when a conjunct consonant follows. This meaning should be understood as relating to either bad or good people. As to the word bondi signifying the body:

“Nāhaṃ puna na ca puna, na cāpi apunappunaṃ;

Hatthibondiṃ pavekkhāmi, tathā hi bhayatajjito”tiādīsu

"'Not again, nor yet again, nor again and again will I enter an elephant’s body, for I am terrified by fear.' In this and other such passages,

Daṭṭhabbā. Imānissa nāmāni –

it is to be seen. These are its names:

Kāyo dehaṃ sarīrañca, vapu bimbañca viggahaṃ;

Bondi gattaṃ tanu ceva, attabhāvo tathūpadhi;

Samussayoti cetāni, dehanāmāni honti hi.

Kāya, deha, sarīra, vapu, bimba, viggaha, bondi, gatta, tanu, attabhāva, upadhi, and samussaya: these are indeed names for the body.

Vada viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Vadati, vajjati. Vadeti, ovadati, ovadeti, paṭivadati. Abhivadati, anuvadati, upavadati, apavadati. Nivadati. Aññānipi yojetabbāni. Tattha “vajjantu bhonto amma”nti pāḷidassanato vajjatīti padaṃ vuttaṃ. Keci pana garū “vajjetī”ti rūpaṃ icchanti, taṃ upaparikkhitvā yuttañce gahetabbaṃ, “upāsako bhikkhuṃ vadeti. Tena yogena janakāyaṃ, ovadeti mahāmunī”ti ca dassanato vadeti ovadetīti ca vuttaṃ. Sabbānetāni suddhakattupadāni.

The root vad is used in the sense of articulate speech. Vadati, vajjati: he speaks. Vadeti: he speaks, he addresses. Ovadati, ovadeti: he advises. Paṭivadati: he replies. Abhivadati: he pays respect. Anuvadati: he repeats or censures. Upavadati: he reproaches. Apavadati: he disparages. Nivadati: he announces. Other forms too should be supplied. Therein, the word vajjati is mentioned on the basis of the Pāli passage: 'Sirs, let them speak!' Some teachers, however, prefer the form vajjeti; this should be examined and accepted if it is correct. And the forms vadeti and ovadeti are mentioned on the basis of the passages: 'A lay follower speaks to a bhikkhu,' and 'By that means the great sage advises the host of people.' All these are words in the active voice.

Ovādeti[M 0.0098], vādayati, vādāpeti, vādāpayati. Vajjento, vajjayanto, imāni hetukattupadāni.

Ovādeti, vādayati, vādāpeti, vādāpayati. Vajjento, vajjayanto. These are words in the causative active voice.

Kamme “vadiyati, ovadiyati, vajjiyati. Vadiyamāno, vajjamāno, ovadiyamāno, ovajjamāno na karoti sāsanaṃ” iccādīni bhavanti. “Vādo, ovādo, paṭivādo, pavādo, abhivādanaṃ, anuvādo, upavādo, apavādo, vivādo, nivādanaṃ, vajjaṃ, vadanaṃ” iccevamādīni nāmikapadāni yojetabbāni.

In the passive voice, there are such forms as vadiyati, ovadiyati, vajjiyati. For example: 'Though being spoken to, being spoken to, being advised, being advised, he does not follow the instruction.' Nominal words such as the following should be supplied: vādo (speech), ovādo (advice), paṭivādo (reply), pavādo (report), abhivādanaṃ (paying respect), anuvādo (censure), upavādo (reproach), apavādo (disparagement), vivādo (dispute), nivādanaṃ (announcement), vajjaṃ (what should be said; fault), vadanaṃ (face; speech).

“Vadituṃ, vaditvā, vivaditvā” iccevamādīni ca tumantādīni padāni.

And words such as the infinitive and gerunds, for example: vadituṃ (to speak), vaditvā (having spoken), vivaditvā (having disputed).

Tattha vādoti kathā. Vaditabbaṃ vattabbanti vajjaṃ, kiṃ taṃ? Vacanaṃ. Etena saccavajjena, samaṅginī sāmikena homīti ettha hi vacanaṃ “vajja”nti vuccati. Vadanti etenāti vadanaṃ, mukhaṃ. Mukhassa hi imāni nāmāni –

Therein, vādo means talk. Vajjaṃ is what should be said or spoken. What is that? A statement. For in the passage, 'By this true statement may I be united with my husband,' a statement is called vajjaṃ. That by which one speaks is the vadanaṃ, the mouth. For these are the names for the mouth:

Vadanaṃ lapanaṃ tuṇḍaṃ, mukha massañca ānanaṃ;

Sūkarādimukhaṃ tuṇḍa-miti ñeyyaṃ visesato.

Vadanaṃ, lapanaṃ, tuṇḍaṃ, mukhaṃ, assaṃ, and ānanaṃ. The mouth of a pig and other such animals is specifically to be known as tuṇḍaṃ.

Tatra vadatīti pitā puttaṃ vadati. Apica vadatīti bherī vadati, nādaṃ muñcatīti attho. Esa nayo vajjatīti etthāpi.

Therein, vadati: a father speaks to his son. Moreover, vadati: a drum sounds; the meaning is that it emits a sound. This same principle applies also to vajjati.

Tatrāyaṃ padamālā, vadati, vadanti. Vadasi, vadatha. Vadāmi, vadāma. Vadate, vadante. Vadase, vadavhe. Vade, vadamhe.

Here is the paradigm: vadati, vadanti; vadasi, vadatha; vadāmi, vadāma. Vadate, vadante; vadase, vadavhe; vade, vadamhe.

Vadatu, vadantu. Vadāhi, vada, vadatha. Vadāmi, vadāma. Vadataṃ, vadantaṃ. Vadassu, vadavho. Vade, vadāmase.

Vadatu, vadantu; vadāhi, vada, vadatha; vadāmi, vadāma. Vadataṃ, vadantaṃ; vadassu, vadavho; vade, vadāmase.

Vajjati, vajjanti. Vajjasi, vajjatha. Vajjāmi, vajjāma. Vajjate, vajjante. Vajjase, vajjavhe. Vajje, vajjamhe.

Vajjati, vajjanti; vajjasi, vajjatha; vajjāmi, vajjāma. Vajjate, vajjante; vajjase, vajjavhe; vajje, vajjamhe.

Vajjatu[M 0.0099], vajjantu. Vajjāhi, vajja, vajjatha. Vajjāmi, vajjāma. Vajjataṃ, vajjantaṃ. Vajjassu, vajjavho. Vajje, vajjāmhase. Imā dve padamālā vadadhātussa vajjādesavasena vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atrāyaṃ sukhumatthavinicchayo, “mānussakā ca dibbā ca, tūriyā vajjanti tāvade”ti pāḷi. Ettha vajjantīti idaṃ suddhakattupadaṃ taddīpakattā. Kiṃ viya?

Vajjatu, vajjantu; vajjāhi, vajja, vajjatha; vajjāmi, vajjāma. Vajjataṃ, vajjantaṃ; vajjassu, vajjavho; vajje, vajjāmhase. It should be understood that these two paradigms are given by way of substituting vajja for the root vad. Here there is this subtle analysis of meaning. In the Pāli passage, 'Then human and divine musical instruments play,' the word vajjanti is in the simple active voice because it indicates that action. Like what?

“Udīrayantu saṅkhapaṇavā, vadantu ekapokkharā;

Nadantu bheī sannaddhā, vaggū vadantu dundubhī”ti

"'Let the conches and small drums sound forth, let the single-headed drums play; let the braced war-drums roar, let the beautiful kettledrums play.'"

Ettha “udīrayantu vadantu”ādīni viya. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vajjantīti vajjiṃsūti atītavacane vattamānavacanaṃ veditabba”nti suddhakattuvasena vivaraṇaṃ kataṃ, tasmā īdisesu ṭhānesu vadadhātussa vajjādeso daṭṭhabbo.

It is like udīrayantu, vadantu, and so on in this passage. For in the commentary the explanation is given in terms of the simple active voice: 'Vajjanti means vajjiṃsu; the present tense should be understood in the sense of the past.' Therefore, in such cases, the substitution of vajja for the root vad is to be seen.

“Saṅkhā ca paṇavā ceva, athopi diṇḍimā bahū;

Antalikkhamhi vajjanti, disvānaccherakaṃ nabhe”ti

"'Conches and small drums, and many kettledrums too, sound in the mid-air, having seen the wonder in the sky.'"

Ettha pana vajjantīti hetukattupadaṃ taddīpakattā. Tañca kho vaṇṇasandhivisayattā vādayantīti kāritapadarūpena siddhaṃ. Tathā hi “vādayantī”ti padarūpaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā yakāre pare saralopo kato, dyakārasaññogassa jjakāradvayaṃ pubbakkharassa rassattañca bhavati. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “vajjantīti vādayantī”ti hetukattuvasena vivaraṇaṃ. Tathā hi “devatā nabhe accherakaṃ bhagavato yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā antalikkhe etāni saṅkhapaṇavādīni tūriyāni vādayantī”ti hetukattuvasena attho gahetabbo bhavati, tasmā īdisesu ṭhānesu vadassa vajjādeso na bhavati.

But here, vajjanti is a word in the causative active voice because it indicates causation. And this is established as the causative form vādayanti by way of euphonic combination. For, having posited the form vādayanti, the vowel is elided before the y, the conjunct dy becomes double jj, and the preceding vowel is shortened. Therefore the commentary gives the explanation in the causative sense: 'Vajjanti means vādayanti (they cause to sound).' Thus the meaning is to be taken in the causative sense: 'The devas, having seen the Blessed One's twin miracle in the sky, cause these musical instruments—conches, small drums, and so on—to sound in the mid-air.' Therefore, in such cases, there is no substitution of vajja for the root vad.

Kecettha vadeyyuṃ “antalikkhamhi vajjanti, disvānaccherakaṃ nabhe”ti etthāpi “vajjantī”ti padaṃ suddhakattupadameva, na hetukattupadaṃ [M 0.0100] “vajjantīti vādayantī”ti vivaraṇe katepi, tathā hi “ye kecime diṭṭhiparibbasānā, “idameva sacca’nti vivādayantī”ti ca “evampi viggayha vivādayantī”ti ca evamādīsu vadantipadena samānatthaṃ “vādayantī”ti padañca sāsane diṭṭha”nti? Tanna, “disvā”ti dassanakriyāvacanato. Na hi saṅkhapaṇavādīnaṃ pāṭihāriyādidassanaṃ upapajjati dassanacittassa abhāvatoti. Saccaṃ, tathāpi –

Some might argue that even in the phrase 'they sound in the sky, having seen the marvel in the heavens,' the word 'vajjantī' is purely an agentive word, not a causative word, despite the explanation 'vajjantī means vādayantī.' They might cite examples such as 'those attached to views, disputing, "This alone is true,"' and 'Thus also, having disputed, they argue,' where in the teachings the word 'vādayantī' is seen with a meaning similar to 'vadanti.' But this is not so, because of the word 'disvā,' which indicates the action of seeing. For the seeing of miracles is not possible for conches and drums, as they lack a mind that sees. True, but—

“Rādante dārake disvā, ubbiddhā vipulā dumā;

Sayamevonamitvāna, upagacchanti dārake”ti

"Seeing the children playing, the great, luxuriant trees bend down of their own accord and approach the children."

Ettha viya upacaritattā upapajjateva dassanavacanaṃ. Tasmā “vajjantīti vādayantī”ti vivaraṇaṃ suddhakattuvasena katanti? Tanna, heṭṭhā –

As in this case, because the term 'seeing' is used metaphorically, it is indeed appropriate. Therefore, is the explanation of 'vajjantī' as 'vādayantī' made in the simple agentive sense? No, because below—

“Saṅgītiyo ca vattanti, ambare anilañjase;

Cammanaddhāni vādenti, disvānaccherakaṃ nabhe”ti

"And musical performances occur in the sky, on the path of the wind; they play the leather-covered instruments, having seen the marvel in the heavens."

Iminnā gāthāya “vādentīti vādayanti devatā”ti sapāṭhasesassa atthavivaraṇassa hetukattuvasena katattā. Athāpi vadeyyuṃ “saṅkhā ca paṇavā ceva, athopi diṇḍimā bahū’ti paccattavacanavasena vuttattā vajjantīti padaṃ kammavācakapada”nti ce? Tampi na, kammavasena vivaraṇassa akatattā, kattuvasena pana katattāti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

By this verse, because the explanation of the meaning of the complete reading, 'vādentīti vādayanti devatā' (they play means the deities cause to sound), is made in the causative sense. And if they were to say, 'Because it is stated in the nominative case, "Conches and drums, and also many kettle-drums," the word "vajjantī" is a word in the passive voice'? That too is not so, because the explanation is not made in the passive voice, but rather is made in the active voice; thus this conclusion should be reached here.

Ayamettha vinicchayo veditabbo. Dvigaṇiko vadadhātu bhūvādigaṇiko ca curādigaṇiko ca. So hi bhūvādigaṇe vattanto “vadati vajjatī”ti suddhakatturūpāni janetvā “vādeti, vādayati, vādāpeti, vādāpayatī”ti cattāri hetukatturūpāni janeti, curādigaṇe pana “vādeti, vādayatī”ti [M 0.0101] suddhakatturūpāni janetvā “vādāpeti, vādāpayatī”ti ca dve hetukatturūpāni janeti, tasmā sāsane “vādenti vādayantī”ti suddhakattupadāni dissanti. “Vadeyya, vadeyyuṃ” iccādi sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. “Vajjeyya, vajjeyyuṃ” iccādi ca sabbaṃ neyyaṃ vajjādesavasena.

Here, this determination should be understood. The root 'vad' belongs to two classes: the Bhūvādi class and the Curādi class. When it occurs in the Bhūvādi class, it generates agentive forms like 'vadati, vajjatī,' and four causative forms like 'vādeti, vādayati, vādāpeti, vādāpayatī.' But in the Curādi class, it generates agentive forms like 'vādeti, vādayatī,' and two causative forms like 'vādāpeti, vādāpayatī.' Therefore, in the teaching, agentive words like 'vādenti, vādayantī' are seen. 'Vadeyya, vadeyyuṃ,' etc., all should be understood accordingly. Similarly, 'vajjeyya, vajjeyyuṃ,' etc., all should be understood accordingly by way of the substitution of 'vajja'.

Atha vā vadeyya, vadeyyuṃ, vajjuṃ. Pitā mātā ca te dajjunti padamiva. Ettha ca “vajjuṃ vā te na vā vajjuṃ, natthi nāsāya rūhanā”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Vadeyyuṃ vāna vadeyyuṃvāti attho. Vadeyyāsi, vajjāsi, vajjesi iccapi. Vutto vajjāsi vandanaṃ. Vajjesi kho tvaṃ vāmūraṃ. Vadeyyātha, vajjātha. Ammaṃ arogaṃ vajjātha. Vadeyyāmi, vajjāmi, vadeyyāma, vajjāma. Vadetha, vaderaṃ. Vadetho, vadeyyāvho, vajjāvho. Vadeyyaṃ, vajjaṃ, vadeyyāmhe, vajjāmhe. Pubbe viya idhāpi yakāre pare saralopo daṭṭhabbo. Aññānipi upaparikkhitvā gahetabbāni.

Alternatively, 'vadeyya, vadeyyuṃ, vajjuṃ.' Like the phrase 'Your father and mother would give.' Here, the Pāli example is: 'Whether they would speak or not, there is no growth for the nose.' The meaning is 'whether they would speak or not speak.' Also, 'vadeyyāsi, vajjāsi, vajjesi' are in the active voice. It is said, 'You should speak a greeting.' And 'Indeed, you spoke ill of the dwarf.' 'Vadeyyātha, vajjātha,' as in 'Mother, you should speak of health.' 'Vadeyyāmi, vajjāmi, vadeyyāma, vajjāma.' 'Vadetha, vaderaṃ. Vadetho, vadeyyāvho, vajjāvho. Vadeyyaṃ, vajjaṃ, vadeyyāmhe, vajjāmhe.' Here too, as before, the elision of a vowel before the following 'ya' should be noted. Other forms should also be examined and understood.

Idāni parokkhādirūpāni kathayāma. Vada, pāvada, yathā babhuva. Dakāralope “pāva” itipi rūpaṃ bhavati, “paṭipaṃ vadehi bhaddante”ti ettha “paṭipa”nti padaṃ viya. Tathā hi “yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāva” iti pāḷi dissati. Ettha pasaddo upasaggo dīghaṃ katvā vutto “pāvadati pāvacana”ntiādīsu viya, pāvāti ca idaṃ atītavacanaṃ, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana atītavacanaṃ idanti jānantopi garu vattamānavacanavasena “pāvāti vadatī”ti vivaraṇamakāsi īdisesu ṭhānesu kālavipallāsavasena atthassa vattabbattā.

Now, we will discuss the forms such as the perfect tense. Vada, pāvada, as in 'yathā babhuva' (as it became). With the elision of the letter 'da', the form 'pāva' also occurs, like the word 'paṭipa' in "paṭipaṃ vadehi bhaddante." For example, the Pāli passage states: "who himself spoke of himself." Here, the prefix 'pa' is stated with lengthening, as in 'pāvadati,' 'pāvacana,' etc. And 'pāva' is a past tense form. In the commentary, although the teacher knew this to be a past tense form, he made the explanation 'pāvāti vadatī' (pāva means he speaks) in the present tense, because in such instances the meaning must be conveyed by way of tense displacement.

Āyasmāpi ca sāriputto niddese “yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāvā”ti padaṃ nikkhipitvā ātumā vuccati attā, sayameva pāvāti sayameva attānaṃ pāvadati, “ahamasmi [M 0.0102] sīlasampanno”ti vā “vatasampanno”ti vāti vattamānavacanena atthaṃ niddisi. Atha vā pāvāti idaṃ na kevalaṃ vadadhātuvaseneva nipphannaṃ, atha kho udhātuvasenapi. Tathā hi idaṃ papubbassa usadde iti dhātussa payoge ukārassa okārādesaṃ katvā tato parokkhābhūte akāre pare okārassa āvādesaṃ tato ca sandhikiccaṃ katvā sijjhati, tasmā udhātussa vadadhātuyā samānatthattā tannipphannarūpassa ca vadadhātuyā nipphannarūpena samānarūpattā “sayameva attānaṃ pāvadatī”ti vadadhātuvasena niddisīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And the Venerable Sāriputta, in the Niddesa, having introduced the phrase 'yo ātumānaṃ sayaṃ eva pāvā,' explained the meaning in the present tense, saying that 'ātumā' means 'attā' (self), and 'sayaṃ eva pāvā' means 'he himself proclaims himself,' saying, 'I am accomplished in virtue' or 'I am accomplished in observance.' Alternatively, 'pāvā' is not only derived from the root 'vad' (to speak), but also from the root 'u' (to sound). For this, when the root 'u' (in the sense of 'sound') is used with the prefix 'pa,' the 'u' is changed to 'o,' and then when the perfect tense affix 'a' is added, the 'o' is changed to 'āva,' and after applying sandhi, it is formed. Therefore, since the root 'u' has the same meaning as the root 'vad,' and since the form derived from it is similar to the form derived from 'vad,' it should be understood that 'he himself proclaims himself' is explained through the root 'vad'.

Idāni vicchinnā padamālā ghaṭīyati. Vada, vaduṃ. Vade, vadittha, vadaṃ, vadimha. Vadittha, vadire. Vadittho, vadivho. Vadiṃ, vadimhe. Pāvada, pāva iccapi. Pāvadu. Pāvade, pāvadittha. Pāvadaṃ, pāvadimha. Pāvadittha, pāvadire. Pāvadittho, pāvadivho. Pāvadiṃ, pāvadimhe. Tathā “vajja, vajju” iccādīni parokkhārūpāni.

Now the interrupted series of verb forms is being connected. Vada, vaduṃ. Vade, vadittha, vadaṃ, vadimha. Vadittha, vadire. Vadittho, vadivho. Vadiṃ, vadimhe. Pāvada, pāva, etc. Pāvadu. Pāvade, pāvadittha. Pāvadaṃ, pāvadimha. Pāvadittha, pāvadire. Pāvadittho, pāvadivho. Pāvadiṃ, pāvadimhe. Similarly, 'vajja, vajju,' etc., are perfect tense forms.

“Avadā, avadū. Avajjā, avajjū” iccādīni hiyyattanīrūpāni.

"Avadā, avadū; avajjā, avajjū," and so on, are imperfect tense forms.

“Avadi, vadi, avaduṃ, vaduṃ, avadiṃsu, vadiṃsu. Avajji, vajji” iccādīni ajjatanīrūpāni.

"Avadi, vadi, avaduṃ, vaduṃ, avadiṃsu, vadiṃsu. Avajji, vajji," and so on—these are aorist forms.

“Vadissati, vadissanti. Vajjissati, vajjissanti” iccādīni bhavissantīrūpāni.

"Vadissati, vadissanti. Vajjissati, vajjissanti," and so on—these are future tense forms.

“Avadissā, vadissā, avajjissā, vajjissā” iccādīni kālātipattirūpāni. Sesāni sabbānipi yathāsambhavaṃ vitthāretabbāni. Yā panettha vadadhātu viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ vuttā, sā katthaci “vadantaṃ ekapokkharā. Bherivādako”tiādīsu abyattasaddepi vattati upacaritavasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

"Avadissā, vadissā, avajjissā, vajjissā," and so on—these are conditional forms. The remaining forms should all be explained in detail as is possible. Furthermore, the verbal root 'vad,' which is stated here in the sense of distinct speech, is sometimes used even with indistinct sounds, as in "vadantaṃ ekapokkharā" (a single drum sounding) or "Bherivādako" (a drum-player); this should be understood as occurring by way of figurative usage.

Vida [M 0.0103] ñāṇe. Ñāṇaṃ jānanaṃ. Vidati. Vedo. Vidū. Kārite “vedeti. Vedayati. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti. Vedayanti ca te tuṭṭhiṃ, devā mānusakā ubho”ti payogā. Tattha pavedetīti bodheti ñāpeti pakāseti. Vedoti vidati sukhumampi kāraṇaṃ ājānātīti vedo, paññāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. “Vedehamunī”ti ettha hi ñāṇaṃ vedoti vuccati. Vedoti vā vedaganthassapi nāmaṃ vidanti jānanti etena uccāritamattena tadādhāraṃ puggalaṃ “brāhmaṇo aya”nti, vidanti vā etena brāhmaṇā attanā kattabbakiccanti vedo. So pana iruvedayajuvedasāmavedavasena tividho. Āthabbaṇavedaṃ pana paṇītajjhāsayā na sikkhanti parūpaghātasahitattā. Tasmā pāḷiyaṃ “tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū”ti vuttaṃ. Eteyeva “chando, manto, sutī”ti ca vuccanti.

The root 'vid' is in the sense of 'knowing.' Knowing is understanding. He knows. Veda. The wise one.
