In the causative, there are usages like 'vedeti' (he causes to know), 'vedayati' (he causes to know). 'Having realized it oneself through direct knowledge, one declares it.' 'And both gods and humans feel satisfaction.' Here, 'pavedeti' means he makes known, he informs, he reveals. 'Veda' is so called because he knows and understands even subtle causes; this is a name for wisdom. Indeed, in 'Vedehamunī' (the sage of Videha), knowledge is called 'Veda.' Or, 'Veda' is also the name of the Vedic texts, because by merely reciting them, people know and recognize the person who relies on them as 'this is a Brahmin'; or, Brahmins know through them what duties they must perform themselves—thus it is 'Veda.' It is threefold, by way of the Rigveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda. But those of refined disposition do not study the Atharva Veda due to its association with harming others. Therefore, in the Pāli texts, it is said, "He has gone beyond the three Vedas." These are also called 'Chanda' (metre), 'Manta' (incantation), and 'Suti' (tradition).

Paññāyaṃ tuṭṭhiyaṃ vede, vedasaddo pavattati;

Pāvakepi ca so diṭṭho, jātasaddapurecaro;

The word 'veda' occurs in the sense of wisdom, satisfaction, and knowledge; and it is also seen in fire, preceded by the word 'jāta'.

Pacchānuge jātasadde, sati tuṭṭhajanepi ca;

“Vedagū sabbadhamme”ti etthāpi viditesu ca.

And when the word 'jāta' follows, and also in the case of a satisfied person; and also in the phrase 'vedagū sabbadhamme' (a knower of all phenomena), and in the sense of 'known'.

Vidūti paṇḍitamanusso. So hi yathāsabhāvato kammañca phalañca kusalādibhede ca dhamme vidatīti “vidū”ti vuccati.

'Vidū' means a wise person. For he understands action and its result according to their true nature, as well as the distinctions among wholesome and other states—thus he is called 'vidū'.

Ruda assuvimocane, sakammikavasenimissā attho gahetabbo. Rodati, rudati iccapi. Ruṇṇaṃ. Ruditaṃ. Rodanaṃ. Rodanto. Rodamāno. Rodantī. Rodamānā. Rudamukhā. Rudaṃ. Rudanto.

The root 'rud' is in the sense of 'shedding tears'; its meaning should be understood in the transitive sense. 'Rodati', 'rudati' (he weeps). 'Ruṇṇaṃ' (weeping). 'Ruditaṃ' (weeping). 'Rodanaṃ' (weeping). 'Rodanto' (weeping, masculine present participle). 'Rodamāno' (weeping, masculine present participle). 'Rodantī' (weeping, feminine present participle). 'Rodamānā' (weeping, feminine present participle). 'Rudamukhā' (with a weeping face). 'Rudaṃ' (weeping, neuter present participle). 'Rudanto' (weeping, masculine present participle).

Tattha [M 0.0104] rodatīti kiṃ rodati? Mataṃ puttaṃ vā bhātaraṃ vā rodati. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi “nāhaṃ bhante etaṃ rodāmi, yaṃ maṃ bhante bhagavā evamāha”. Ayaṃ panettha attho – “yaṃ maṃ bhante bhagavā evamāha, ahaṃ etaṃ bhagavato byākaraṇaṃ na parodāmi na paridevāmi na anutthunāmī’ti evaṃ sakammikavasenattho veditabbo, na assumuñcanamattena.

Here, when it is said 'rodati' (he weeps), what does one weep for? One weeps for a dead son or brother. In this regard, there is this Pāli passage: "Venerable sir, I do not weep for this, that the Blessed One said thus to me." The meaning here is this: "That the Blessed One said thus to me, venerable sir, I do not lament, grieve, or wail over this declaration of the Blessed One." Thus, the meaning should be understood in the transitive sense, not merely as the shedding of tears.

‘Mataṃ vā amma rodanti, yo vā jīvaṃ na dissati;

Jīvantaṃ amma passanti, kasmā maṃ amma rodasī’ti

"Mother, they weep for the dead, or for one who, though living, is not seen. Seeing me alive, mother, why do you weep for me?"

Ayañcettha payogo”ti idamaṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ. Idaṃ pana ṭīkāvacanaṃ – “yathā sakammakā dhātusaddā atthavisesavasena akammakā honti ‘vibuddho puriso vibuddho kamalasaṇḍo’ti, evaṃ atthavisesavasena akammakāpi sakammakā hontīti dassetuṃ ‘na paridevāmi na anutthunāmī’ti āha. Anutthunasaddo sakammakavasena payujjati ‘purāṇāni anutthuna’ntiādīsu. Ayañcettha payogoti iminā gāthāya anutthunanaṃ rudanaṃ adhippetanti dassetī”ti.

“And this is the application here”—this is the commentarial statement. This, however, is the subcommentarial statement: “Just as intransitive verbal roots become transitive due to a difference in meaning, as in ‘the awakened man, the blossomed lotus grove,’ so too, to show that even transitive verbal roots become intransitive due to a difference in meaning, it is said, ‘I do not grieve, I do not wail.’ The word ‘anutthuna’ is used in an intransitive sense in such phrases as ‘lamenting past things.’ ‘And this is the application here’—by this, it is shown that in the verse, weeping is intended to mean lamenting.”

Dalidda duggatiyaṃ. Dukkhassa gati patiṭṭhāti duggatīti ayaṃ attho “apāyaṃ duggatiṃvinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”tiādīsu yujjati, idha pana idaṃ atthaṃ aggahetvā añño attho gahetabbo. Kathaṃ duggatīti? Dukkhena kicchena gati gamanaṃ annapānādilābho duggatīti. Daliddati. Daliddo, daliddī, dāliddiyaṃ. Tattha daliddatīti sabbaṃ icchiticchitaṃ paraṃ yācitvā eva dukkhena adhigacchati, na ayācitvāti attho. Duliddoti duggatamanusso. Daliddīti duggatā nārī. Daliddassa bhāvo dāliddiyaṃ. Ettha ca sabbameva “daliddatī”ti lokikappayogadassanato “daliddatī”ti kriyāpadaṃ vibhāvitaṃ. Sāsane pana [M 0.0105] taṃ kriyāpadaṃ na āgataṃ, “daliddo daliddī”ti nāmapadāniyeva āgatāni. Anāgatampi taṃ “nāthatī”ti padamiva sāsanānulomattā gahetabbameva. Garū pana kaccāyanamatavasena dala duggatimhīti duggativācakadaladhātuto iddapaccayaṃ katvā “daliddo”ti nāmapadaṃ dassesuṃ.

The root 'dalidda' is in the sense of 'duggati' (misfortune). The meaning ‘a destination of suffering is a woeful state’ applies in such phrases as ‘he is reborn in a state of misery, a woeful realm, a place of loss, a hell,’ but here, setting aside that meaning, another meaning should be taken. How is it 'duggati'? 'Duggati' means the difficult, arduous attainment of food, drink, and so on. The verb is 'daliddati'. The nouns are 'daliddo' (a poor man), 'daliddī' (a poor woman), 'dāliddiyaṃ' (poverty). There, 'daliddati' means that one obtains everything desired only by begging from others with difficulty, not without begging. 'Daliddo' is an unfortunate man. 'Daliddī' is an unfortunate woman. 'Dāliddiyaṃ' is the state of being poor. And here, the verb 'daliddati' is explained based on the observation of its usage in worldly language. In the Dispensation, however, that verb form does not appear; only the noun forms 'daliddo' and 'daliddī' appear. Even though it does not appear, it should be accepted as conforming to the Dispensation, like the word 'nāthatī'. The venerable teachers, however, according to Kaccāyana’s view, showed that the noun 'daliddo' is formed by adding the suffix 'idda' to the root 'dala', which signifies 'duggati'.

Tuda byathane. Tudati, vitudati. Kammani “tujjati, vitujjamāno, vedanābhibhunno”ti rūpāni.

The root 'tud' is in the sense of affliction. The verbs are 'tudati', 'vitudati'. In the passive voice, the forms are 'tujjati', 'vitujjamāno', 'vedanābhibhunno'.

Tudanti vācāhi janā asaññatā,

Sarehi saṅgāmagataṃva kuñjaraṃ;

Sutvāna vākyaṃ pharusaṃ udīritaṃ,

Adhivāsaye bhikkhu aduṭṭhacitto;

Unrestrained people torment with words, as with arrows an elephant gone to battle; having heard a harsh word spoken, a bhikkhu should endure with a mind free from malice.

Nuda peraṇe. Peraṇaṃ cuṇṇikaraṇaṃ pisanaṃ, nudati, panudati. Panudanaṃ.

The root 'nuda' is in the sense of impelling. 'Peraṇa' means grinding, crushing, pounding. The verbs are 'nudati', 'panudati'. The noun is 'panudanaṃ'.

Vidi lābhe. Vindati. Uṭṭhātā vindate dhanaṃ. Govindo.

The root 'vid' is in the sense of gain. The verb is 'vindati'. 'Uṭṭhātā vindate dhanaṃ' (An energetic person gains wealth). An example is 'Govindo'.

Khadi parighāte. Parighātaṃ samantato hananaṃ. Khandati.

The root 'khad' is in the sense of destruction. 'Parighāta' means striking all around. The verb is 'khandati'.

Dakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of verbal roots ending in 'da'.

Dhakārantadhātu

Verbal roots ending in 'dha'.

Dhā dhāraṇe. Dadhāti, vidadhāti. Yaṃ paṇḍito nipuṇaṃ saṃvidheti. Nidhiṃ nidheti. Nidhi nāma nidhīyati. Tāva sunihito santo. Yato nidhiṃ parihari. Nidahati. Kuhiṃ deva nidahāmi. Paridahati. Yo vattaṃ paridahissati. Dhassati. Paridhassati. Bāloti paraṃ padahati. Sakyā kho ambaṭṭha rājānaṃ [M 0.0106] ukkākaṃ pitāmahaṃ dahanti. Saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ. Saddhā, saddahanā, saddhātabbaṃ, saddahitabbaṃ, saddhāyiko, paccayiko. Saddheyyavacasā upāsikā. Saddahituṃ, saddahitvā. Visesādhānaṃ. Sotāvadhānaṃ. Sotaṃ odahati. Ohitasoto. Sotaṃ odahitvā. Maccudheyyaṃ, māradheyyaṃ, nāmadheyyaṃ, dhātu, dhātā, vidhātā. Vidhi. Abhidhānaṃ, abhidheyyaṃ, nidhānavatī vācā, ādhānagāhī, sandhi. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

The root 'dhā' is in the sense of holding. The verbs are 'dadhāti', 'vidadhāti'. 'Yaṃ paṇḍito nipuṇaṃ saṃvidheti' (What the wise one skillfully arranges). 'Nidhiṃ nidheti' (He lays down a treasure). 'Nidhi nāma nidhīyati' (A treasure is so called because it is laid down). 'Tāva sunihito santo' (Being so well laid down). 'Yato nidhiṃ parihari' (From where he removed the treasure). 'Nidahati' (He lays down/conceals). 'Kuhiṃ deva nidahāmi' (Where, O lord, shall I lay it down?). 'Paridahati' (He puts on). 'Yo vatthaṃ paridahissati' (Who will put on the cloth?). 'Dhassati'. 'Paridhassati'. 'Bāloti paraṃ padahati' (A fool attacks another). 'Sakyā kho ambaṭṭha rājānaṃ ukkākaṃ pitāmahaṃ dahanti' (The Sakyans, O Ambaṭṭha, burn King Ukkāka, their ancestor). 'Saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ' (One has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata). 'Saddhā' (faith), 'saddahanā' (believing), 'saddhātabbaṃ' (to be believed), 'saddahitabbaṃ' (should be believed), 'saddhāyiko' (faithful), 'paccayiko' (trustworthy). 'Saddheyyavacasā upāsikā' (A laywoman with trustworthy words). 'Saddahituṃ' (to believe), 'saddahitvā' (having believed). 'Visesādhānaṃ' (special attention). 'Sotāvadhānaṃ' (giving ear). 'Sotaṃ odahati' (He gives ear). 'Ohitasoto' (with ear inclined). 'Sotaṃ odahitvā' (having given ear). 'Maccudheyyaṃ' (the realm of death), 'māradheyyaṃ' (the realm of Māra), 'nāmadheyyaṃ' (designation), 'dhātu' (element), 'dhātā' (creator), 'vidhātā' (arranger). 'Vidhi' (rule). 'Abhidhānaṃ' (name), 'abhidheyyaṃ' (what is to be named), 'nidhānavatī vācā' (well-founded speech), 'ādhānagāhī' (one who grasps at support), 'sandhi' (connection). Other forms should also be supplied.

Vipubbo dhā karotyatthe, abhipubbo tu bhāsane;

Nyāsaṃpubbo yathāyogaṃ, nyāsāropanasandhisu.

The root 'dhā' preceded by 'vi' is in the sense of doing; and preceded by 'abhi', in speaking. Preceded by other prefixes, it is used appropriately in the senses of depositing, placing upon, and connecting.

Imasmā pana dhādhātuto pubbassa api iccupasaggassa akāro kvaci niccaṃ lopaṃ pappoti, kvaci niccaṃ lopaṃ na pappoti. Atra lopo vuccate, dvāraṃ pidahati, dvāraṃ pidahanto, pidahituṃ, pidahitvā, evaṃ akāralopo bhavati. Dvāraṃ apidahitvā, evaṃ akāralopo na bhavati. Ettha hi akāro apiupasaggassa avayavo na hoti. Kinti ce? Paṭisedhatthavācako nipātoyeva, upasaggāvayavo pana adassanaṃ gato, ayaṃ niccālopo. Evaṃ dhādhātuto pubbassa api iccupasaggassa akāro kvaci niccaṃ lopaṃ pappoti, kvaci niccaṃ lopaṃ na pappoti. Idaṃ acchariyaṃ idaṃ abbhutaṃ. Yatra hi nāma bhagavato pāvacane evarūpapopi nayo sandissati viññūnaṃ hadayavimhāpanakaro, yo ekasmiṃyeva dhātumhi ekasmiṃyeva upasagge ekasmiṃyevatthe kvaci lopālopavasena vibhajituṃ labbhati. Idāni mayaṃ sotūnaṃ paramakosallajananatthaṃ tadubhayampi ākāraṃ ekajjhaṃ karontā tadākāravatiṃ jinavarapāḷiṃ ānayāma –

From this root 'dhā', the 'a' of the prefix 'api' in some cases is always elided, and in some cases it is never elided. Here, elision is spoken of: in 'dvāraṃ pidahati' (he closes the door), 'dvāraṃ pidahanto' (closing the door), 'pidahituṃ' (to close), 'pidahitvā' (having closed), the elision of 'a' occurs. In 'dvāraṃ apidahitvā' (without closing the door), the elision of 'a' does not occur. For here, the 'a' is not a part of the prefix 'api'. How so? It is a particle signifying negation, while the part of the prefix has disappeared—this is constant elision. Thus, from the root 'dhā', the 'a' of the prefix 'api' in some cases is always elided, and in some cases it is never elided. This is marvelous, this is astonishing! For in the Blessed One’s teaching, such a principle is found, causing wonder in the hearts of the wise, where for a single root, a single prefix, and a single meaning, a distinction can be made based on elision and non-elision. Now, to generate the highest skill in the listeners, bringing both forms together, we shall present the noble Pāli of the Victor containing these forms:

“Gaṅgaṃ [M 0.0107] me pidahissanti, na taṃ sakkomi brāhmaṇa;

Apidhetuṃ mahāsindhuṃ, taṃ kathaṃ so bhavissati;

Na te sakkomi akkhātuṃ, atthaṃ dhammañca pucchito.

“They might dam the Ganges for me, O Brahmin, but that I cannot do; to dam the great ocean—how could that be? I cannot explain to you the meaning and the Dhamma, though you ask.”

Cittatthasādhaniṃ etaṃ, gāthaṃ sambhavajātake;

Paññāsambhavamicchanto, kare citte sumedhaso”ti.

This verse from the Sambhava Jātaka accomplishes the purpose of the mind; one who is wise, desiring the arising of wisdom, should hold it in mind.

Dhu gatitheriyesu. Gati gamanaṃ, theriyaṃ thirabhāvo. Dhavati. Dhuvaṃ.

The root 'dhu' is in the senses of movement and stability. 'Gati' means going; 'theriya' means firmness. The verb is 'dhavati'. The noun is 'dhuvaṃ'.

Ettha ca dhuvanti thiraṃ. “Nicco dhuvo sassato avipariṇāmadhammo”tiādīsu viya, tasmā dhuvanti thiraṃ kiñci dhammajātaṃ. Atha vā dhuvanti idaṃ gatitheriyatthavasena nibbānasseva adhivacanaṃ bhavitumarahati. Tañhi jātijarābyādhimaraṇasokādito muccitukāmehi dhavitabbaṃ gantabbanti dhuvaṃ, uppādavayābhāvena vā niccasabhāvattā dhavati thiraṃ sassataṃ bhavatīti dhuvaṃ. Yañhi sandhāya bhagavatā “dhuvañca vo bhikkhave desessāmi dhuvagāminiñca paṭipada”nti vuttaṃ. Dhuvasaddo “vacanaṃ dhuvasassata”nti ettha thire vattati. “Dhuvañca bhikkhave desessāmī”ti ettha nibbāne. “Dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasī”ti ettha pana ekaṃse nipātapadabhāvena vattatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, `dhuvaṃ` means firm. As in phrases like ‘permanent, stable, eternal, of an unchanging nature,’ thus `dhuvaṃ` refers to something firm, some kind of phenomenon. Alternatively, `dhuvaṃ` here can rightly be considered a term for Nibbāna itself, in the sense of a stable destination. For it is to be pursued and reached by those desiring liberation from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and so forth—hence `dhuvaṃ`. Or, because of the absence of arising and passing away, it is permanent by nature; it endures firmly, eternally—thus `dhuvaṃ`. This is what the Blessed One referred to when he said, ‘Monks, I will teach you the stable and the path leading to the stable.’ The word `dhuva` applies to what is firm, as in ‘a statement is permanent and eternal.’ In ‘Monks, I will teach you the stable,’ it refers to Nibbāna. In ‘Assuredly, you will become a Buddha,’ however, it should be understood as functioning as an indeclinable particle indicating certainty.

Dhū vidhūnane. Ūkārassa ūvattaṃ. Dhūvati. Dhūvitā, dhūvitabbaṃ. Rassatte “dhuto, dhutavā” iccapi rūpāni bhavanti.

The root `dhū` is in the sense of shaking. The long `ū` becomes `ūva`. The verb is `dhūvati`. The forms are `dhūvitā` and `dhūvitabbaṃ`. When shortened, forms like `dhuto` and `dhutavā` also occur.

Dhe pāne. Dhayati, dhīyati. Dhena.

The root `dhe` is in the sense of drinking. The verbs are `dhayati` and `dhīyati`. The noun is `dhena`.

Ettha ca dhenūti dhayati pivati ito khīraṃ potakoti dhenu, “godhenu, assadhenu, migadhenū”ti dhenusaddo sāmaññavasena sapotikāsu tiracchānagatitthīsu vattati, evaṃ santepi yebhuyyena gāviyaṃ vattati. Tathā hi “satta dhenusate datvā”ti pāḷi dissati.

Here, `dhenu` is so called because a calf drinks milk from her. The term `dhenu` applies generally to female animals with offspring, such as `godhenu` (cow), `assadhenu` (mare), and `migadhenu` (doe). Even so, it is mostly used for a cow. Thus, the Pāli text is seen: ‘having given seven hundred cows.’

Sidhu [M 0.0108] gatiyaṃ sedhati, nisedhati, paṭisedhati. Siddho, pasiddho, nisiddho, paṭisiddho, paṭisedhito, paṭisedhako, paṭisedho, paṭisedhituṃ, paṭisedhitvā. Idha acinteyyabalattā upasaggānaṃ taṃyoge sidhudhātussa nānappakārā atthā sambhavanti, aññesampi evameva.

The root `sidh` is in the sense of going. The verbs are `sedhati`, `nisedhati`, and `paṭisedhati`. The forms are `siddho`, `pasiddho`, `nisiddho`, `paṭisiddho`, `paṭisedhito`, `paṭisedhako`, `paṭisedho`, `paṭisedhituṃ`, and `paṭisedhitvā`. Here, due to the inconceivable power of prefixes, the root `sidh` yields various meanings in combination with them. The same applies to other roots as well.

Sidhu satthe maṅgalye ca. Satthaṃ sāsanaṃ, maṅgalyaṃ pāpavināsanaṃ vuddhikāraṇaṃ vā. Sedhati. Siddho, pasiddho, pasiddhi.

The root `sidh` is in the sense of teaching and auspiciousness. `Satthaṃ` means teaching; `maṅgalyaṃ` means the removal of evil or the cause of growth. The verb is `sedhati`. The forms are `siddho`, `pasiddho`, and `pasiddhi`.

Dadha dhāraṇe. Janassa tuṭṭhiṃ dadhateti dadhi. Dhakārassa hakāratte “dahatī”ti rūpaṃ. Ayaṃ itthī imaṃ itthiṃ ayyikaṃ dahati. Ime purisā imaṃ purisaṃ pitāmahaṃ dahanti. Cittaṃ samādahātabbaṃ. Samādahaṃ cittaṃ.

The root `dadh` is in the sense of holding. `Dadhi` (curd) is so called because it holds satisfaction for people. When `dh` becomes `h`, the form is `dahati`. `Ayaṃ itthī imaṃ itthiṃ ayyikaṃ dahati` (This woman cremates this grandmother). `Ime purisā imaṃ purisaṃ pitāmahaṃ dahanti` (These men cremate this grandfather). `Cittaṃ samādahātabbaṃ` (The mind should be composed). `Samādahaṃ cittaṃ` (composing the mind).

Edha vuddhiyaṃ lābhe ca. Edhati. Edho, sukhedhito. Gambhīre gādhamedhati.

The root `edh` is in the sense of growth and gain. The verb is `edhati`. The forms are `edho` and `sukhedhito`. `Gambhīre gādhamedhati` (one gains a firm foothold in the deep).

Ettha ca edhoti edhati. Vaḍḍhati etena pāvakoti edho. Indanaṃ, upādānaṃ. Sukhedhitoti sukhena edhito, sukhasaṃvaḍḍhitoti attho. Gādhamedhatīti gādhaṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ edhati labhati.

Here, `edho` is from `edhati` (it grows). That by which fire grows is `edho` (fuel). It means kindling or fuel. `Sukhedhito` means grown with ease, that is, happily grown. `Gādhamedhati` means one gains or obtains a firm, established footing.

Baddha saṃharise. Saṃhariso vinibaddhakriyā. Baddhati, vinibaddhati. Vinibaddhā.

The root `bandh` is in the sense of binding together. `Saṃhariso` is the act of binding together. The verbs are `baddhati` and `vinibaddhati`. The form is `vinibaddhā`.

Gādha patiṭṭhānissayagandhesu. Gādhati. Gādhaṃ kattā. Gambhīrato agādhaṃ.

The root `gādh` is in the sense of establishing, relying, and smelling. The verb is `gādhati`. `Gādhaṃ kattā` (one who makes firm). `Gambhīrato agādhaṃ` (from the deep, the not-deep).

Bādha viloḷane bādhati, vibādhati. Ābādho. Ābādhati cittaṃ viloḷetīti ābādho.

The root `bādh` is in the sense of agitation. The verbs are `bādhati` and `vibādhati`. The noun is `ābādho`. `Ābādho` is so called because it afflicts and agitates the mind.

Nādha [M 0.0109] yācanādīsu. Nādhati. Nādhanaṃ.

The root `nādh` is in the sense of begging, etc. The verb is `nādhati`. The noun is `nādhanaṃ`.

Bandha bandhane bandhati. Bandhanako, bandho, bandhāpito, paṭibandho, bandhanaṃ, bandho, sambandhanaṃ, sambandho, pabandho, bandhu.

The root `bandh` is in the sense of binding. The verb is `bandhati`. The forms are `bandhanako`, `bandho`, `bandhāpito`, `paṭibandho`, `bandhanaṃ`, `bandho`, `sambandhanaṃ`, `sambandho`, `pabandho`, and `bandhu`.

Tattha bandhananti bandhanti satte etenāti bandhanaṃ, saṅkhalikādi. “Ayaṃ amhākaṃ vaṃso”ti sambandhitabbaṭṭhena bandhu, theragāthāsaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ pana “pemabandhanena bandhū”ti vuttaṃ.

There, `bandhanaṃ` (a bond) is that by which beings are bound, such as a chain and so forth. `Bandhu` (a relative) is so called in the sense of needing to be connected, as in ‘This is our lineage.’ In the commentary to the Theragāthā, however, it is said: ‘Relatives are so called by the bond of affection.’

Dadhi asīghacāre. Asīghacāro asīghappavatti. Dandhati. Dandho, dandhapañño. Yo dandhakāle tarati, taraṇīye ca dandhati.

The root `dandh` is in the sense of slow movement. Slow movement is slow proceeding. The verb is `dandhati` (he is slow). The forms are `dandho` (slow) and `dandhapañño` (slow of wisdom). ‘He who hurries when it is time to be slow, and is slow when it is time to hurry.’

Vaddha vaddhane. Vaddhati. Vaddhi, vuddhi, vaddho, vuddho, jātivuddho, guṇavuddho, vayovuddho.

The root `vaddh` is in the sense of increasing. The verb is `vaddhati`. The forms are `vaddhi` (growth), `vuddhi` (increase), `vaddho` (grown), `vuddho` (elder), `jātivuddho` (senior by birth), `guṇavuddho` (senior by virtue), and `vayovuddho` (senior by age).

Ye vuddhamapacāyanti, narā dhammassa kovidā;

Diṭṭheva dhamme pāsaṃsā, samparāye ca suggatiṃ.

Those persons skilled in the Dhamma who honor the elders are praised in this very life, and in the next, a good destiny awaits.

Sadhu saddakucchiyaṃ. Sadhati.

The root `sadh` is in the sense of `sadda` (sound) and `kucchi` (interior). The verb is `sadhati`.

Piḷadhi alaṅkāre. Piḷandhati. Piḷandhanaṃ.

The root `piḷandh` is in the sense of adornment. The verb is `piḷandhati`. The noun is `piḷandhanaṃ`.

Piḷandhanamalaṅkāro, maṇḍanañca vibhūsanaṃ;

Pasādhanañcābharaṇaṃ, pariyāyā ime matā.

Adornment (`piḷandhana`), decoration (`alaṅkāra`), embellishment (`maṇḍana`), beautification (`vibhūsana`), ornamentation (`pasādhana`), and jewelry (`ābharaṇa`)—these are considered synonyms.

Medha hiṃsāyaṃ saṅgame ca. Medhati. Medhā, medhāvī. Atra medhāti asani viya siluccaye kilese medhati hiṃsatīti medhā. Medhati vā siriyā sīlādīhi ca sappurisadhammehi saha gacchati na ekikā hutvā tiṭṭhatīti medhā, paññāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tathā hi –

The root `medh` is in the sense of harming and of conflict. The verb is `medhati`. The forms are `medhā` (wisdom) and `medhāvī` (the wise one). Here, `medhā` is so called because it slays and harms the defilements like lightning on a mountain. Or, `medhā` is so called because it goes along with prosperity, virtue, and other qualities of noble persons, not standing alone; this is a name for wisdom. For it is said:

“Paññā [M 0.0110] hi seṭṭhā kusalā vadanti,

Nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ;

Sīlaṃ sirī cāpi satañca dhammo,

Anvāyikā paññavato bhavantī”ti

‘Wisdom is indeed declared the best by the skillful, like the king of stars among the constellations. Virtue, prosperity, and the Dhamma of the good—these follow one who is wise.’

Vuttaṃ. Medhāvīti dhammojapaññāya ca samannāgato puggalo.

Thus it is said. `Medhāvī` (a wise one) is a person endowed with wisdom born from the essence of the Dhamma.

Sadhu madhu unde. Sadhati. Madhati. Madhu.

The roots `sadh` and `madh` are in the sense of moistening. The verb is `sadhati`. The verb is `madhati`. The noun is `madhu`.

Budha bodhane. Bodhati. Buddho. Abhisambuddhāno. Sambuddhaṃ. Asambuddhaṃ. Bodhi. Divādigaṇepi ayaṃ dissati. Tatrahi “bujjhatī”ti rūpaṃ, idha pana “bodhatī”ti rūpaṃ. “Yo nindaṃ apabodhatī”ti pāḷi dissati. Kārite pana “bodheti” iccādīni.

The root `budh` is in the sense of awakening. The verb is `bodhati`. The forms are `buddho` (the Awakened One), `abhisambuddhāno` (fully self-awakened), `sambuddhaṃ` (perfectly awakened), `asambuddhaṃ` (unawakened), and `bodhi` (enlightenment). This root is also seen in the Divādi group, where the form is `bujjhati`; but here, the form is `bodhati`. The Pāli text ‘Yo nindaṃ apabodhati’ (Who awakens from blame) is seen. In the causative, however, forms like `bodheti` are found.

Yudha sampahāre. Yodhati. Yodho. Yodhetha māraṃ paññāvudhena. Yuddhaṃ. Caraṇāyudho, caraṇāvudho vā. Āvudhaṃ. Divādigaṇikassa panassa “yujjhatī”ti rūpaṃ.

The root `yudh` is in the sense of battle. The verb is `yodhati`. The forms are `yodho` (a fighter) and `yuddhaṃ` (battle). ‘Fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom.’ Other forms are `caraṇāyudho` or `caraṇāvudho` (one whose weapon is conduct) and `āvudhaṃ` (weapon). For the root belonging to the Divādi group, however, its form is `yujjhati`.

Dīdhi dittivedhanesu. Dīdhati. Dīdhiti. Ettha ca dīdhitīti rasmi. Anekāni hi rasmināmāni.

The root `dīdh` is in the sense of shining and piercing. The verb is `dīdhati`. A derived noun is `dīdhiti`. And here, `dīdhiti` means a ray. For there are many names for rays.

Rasmi ābhā pabhā raṃsi, ditti bhā ruci dīdhiti;

Marīci juti bhāṇva’su, mayūkho kiraṇo karo;

Nāgadhāmo ca āloko, iccete rasmivācakā.

Ray, light, splendor, beam, brightness, luster, glow, radiance; ray of light, brilliance, sun's ray, ray, beam, hand (as a ray); `Nāgadhāmo` and illumination—these are terms that denote rays.

Cakārantarūpāni.

Forms ending in the letter `ca`.

Nakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'n'.

Nī naye. Neti, nayati, vineti. Vineyya hadaye daraṃ. Āneti. Ānayati. Netā. Vinetā. Nāyako. Neyyo[M 0.0111]. Veneyyo. Venayiko. Vinīto puriso. Nīyamāne pisācena, kinnu tāta udikkhati. Nīyanto. Nettaṃ. Netti. Bhavanetti samūhatā. Nettiko. Udakañhi nayanti nettikā. Nettā. Nette ujuṃ gate sati. Nayo. Vinayo. Āyatanaṃ. Netuṃ. Vinetuṃ. Netvā. Vinetvā iccādīni.

The root Nī is in the sense of leading. He leads, he guides, he trains. Having removed fear from the heart. He brings. He brings. A leader. A trainer. A guide. One to be led. One to be trained. Skilled in training. A trained person. When being led by a demon, 'Why, dear one, do you look back?' Being led. The eye. A rein. The cord of existence is uprooted. An irrigator. For irrigators indeed lead the water. A leader. When the eye goes straight. Method. Discipline. Sense base. To lead. To train. Having led. Having trained, and so on.

Tattha nettanti samavisamaṃ dassentaṃ attabhāvaṃ netīti nettaṃ, cakkhu. Nettīti nenti etāya satteti netti, rajju. Bhavanettīti bhavarajju, taṇhāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tāya hi sattā goṇā viya gīvāya bandhitvā taṃ taṃ bhavaṃ niyyanti, tasmā bhavanettīti vuccati. Nettikāti kassakā. Nettāti gavajeṭṭhako yūthapati. Nayoti nayanaṃ gamanaṃ nayo, pāḷigati. Atha vā tattha tattha netabboti nayo, sadisabhāvena netabbākāro. Nīyatīti nayo, tathattanayādi. Nīyati etenāti nayo, antadvayavivajjananayādi.

Herein, 'nettaṃ' is so called because it leads the individual, showing the even and the uneven; it is the eye. 'Netti' is so called because beings are led by it; it is a rein, a rope. 'Bhavanetti' means the rope of existence; this is a name for craving. For by this, beings are led like oxen, bound by the neck, to this or that state of existence; therefore, it is called 'bhavanetti'. 'Nettikā' are farmers. 'Nettā' is the chief bull, the leader of the herd. 'Nayo' is leading, going, a method, the course of the text. Or, it is that which is to be applied in various instances, the mode of application through similarity. 'Nayo' is that which is led, such as the method of suchness. 'Nayo' is that by which one is led, such as the method of avoiding the two extremes.

Tathā hi chabbidho nayo tathattanayo pattinayo desanānayo antadvayavivajjananayo acinteyyanayo adhippāyanayoti. Tesu tathattanayo antadvayavivajjananayena nīyati, pattinayo acinteyyanayena, desanānayo adhippāyanayena nīyati. Etthādimhi tividho nayo kammasādhanena nīyatīti “nayo”ti vuccati, pacchimo pana tividho nayo karaṇasādhanena nīyati etena tathattādinayattayamiti “nayo”ti vuccati. Imasmiṃ atthe papañciyamāne ganthavitthāro siyāti vitthāro na dassito.

Indeed, there are six kinds of methods: the method of suchness, the method of attainment, the method of exposition, the method of avoiding the two extremes, the method of the unthinkable, and the method of intention. Among these, the method of suchness is guided by the method of avoiding the two extremes, the method of attainment by the method of the unthinkable, and the method of exposition by the method of intention. Herein, the first three methods are called 'nayo' as a derivation in the objective sense, as in 'that which is led'. The latter three methods, however, are called 'nayo' as a derivation in the instrumental sense, as in 'that by which the triad of methods beginning with suchness is led'. If this meaning were to be elaborated, the text would become extensive; thus, a detailed explanation is not given.

Aparopi [M 0.0112] catubbidho nayo ekattanayo nānattanayo abyāpāranayo evaṃdhammatānayoti.

There is also another fourfold method: the method of unity, the method of diversity, the method of non-operation, and the method of suchness.

Vineti satte ettha, etenāti vā vinayo. Kāyavācānaṃ vinayanatopi vinayo. Āyatananti anamatagge saṃsāre pavattaṃ atīva āyataṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ yāva na nivattati, tāva nayateva pavattatevāti āyatanaṃ.

'Vinayo' is so called because one trains beings herein, or by this. It is also 'vinayo' from the disciplining of body and speech. 'Āyatanaṃ' is so called because as long as the exceedingly prolonged suffering of saṃsāra, which proceeds in the beginningless cycle, does not cease, it continues to lead and proceed.

Ayaṃ panettha atthuddhāro. “Āyatananti assānaṃ kambojo āyatanaṃ, gunnaṃ dakkhiṇāpatho āyatana”nti ettha sañjātiṭṭhānaṃ āyaanaṃ nāma. “Manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā.

Herein, this is the extraction of meaning. In the phrase, ‘Kamboja is the breeding ground of horses, the southern region is the breeding ground of cattle,’ 'āyatanaṃ' here means a place of origin. ‘In the delightful abode, birds resort to it.

Chāyaṃ chāyatthino yanti, phalatthaṃ phalabhojino”ti ettha samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. “Pañcimāni bhikkhave vimuttāyatanānī”ti ettha kāraṇaṃ. Aññepi pana payogā yata patiyataneti ettha pakāsitā.

‘...those desiring shade go to the shade, and those who eat fruit go for fruit,’ here it means a place of assembly. In, ‘Monks, these are the five bases of liberation,’ here it means cause. Moreover, other usages are shown in the context of 'yata' and 'patiyatane'.

Nī pāpane. Neti, nayati. Nayanaṃ.

The root Nī is in the sense of causing to attain. He leads. Leading.

Nu thutiyaṃ. Noti, navati. Nuto.

The root Nu is in the sense of praise. He praises. Praised.

Thana pana dhana sadde. Thanati. Panati. Dhanati.

The roots Thana, Pana, and Dhana are in the sense of sound. It thunders. It sounds. It resounds.

Kana dittikantīsu. Kanati. Kaññā. Kanakaṃ.

The root Kana is in the sense of shining and beauty. It shines. A maiden. Gold.

Ettha ca yobbanibhāve ṭhitattā rūpavilāsena kanati dippati virocatīti kaññā. Atha vā kaniyati kāmiyabhi abhipatthiyati purisehītipi kaññā, yobbanitthī. Kanakanti kanati, kanīyatīti vā kanakaṃ, suvaṇṇaṃ. Suvaṇṇassa hi anekāni nāmāni.

Herein, a 'kaññā' is so called because, standing in the state of youth, she shines, gleams, and radiates with the charm of her beauty. Or, a 'kaññā' is so called because she is desired and longed for by men; she is a young woman. 'Kanakaṃ' is so called because it shines or is desired; it is gold. For gold indeed has many names.

Suvaṇṇaṃ kanakaṃ hemaṃ, kañcanaṃ haṭakampi ca;

Jātarūpaṃ tapanīyaṃ, vaṇṇaṃ tabbhedakā pana;

Jambunadaṃ siṅgikañca, cāmikaranti bhāsitā.

Suvaṇṇa, kanaka, hema, kañcana, and haṭaka; jātarūpa, tapanīya, and vaṇṇa are said to be names for gold. But its varieties are spoken of as jambunada, siṅgika, and cāmikara.

Vana [M 0.0113] sana sambhattiyaṃ. Vanati. Vanaṃ. Sanati.

The roots Vana and Sana are in the sense of devotion. He is devoted. A forest. He serves.

Tattha vananti. Taṃ sambhajanti mayūrakokilādayo sattāti vanaṃ, araññaṃ. Vanati sambhajati saṃkilesapuggalanti vanaṃ, taṇhā.

Herein, 'vanaṃ' is so called because beings such as peacocks and cuckoos resort to it; it is a forest, a wilderness. That which serves or is devoted to a defiled person is 'vana', that is, craving.

Mana abbhāse. Manati. Mano.

The root Mana is in the sense of repetition. He thinks. The mind.

Māna vīmaṃsāyaṃ, vīmaṃsati. Vīmaṃsā.

The root Māna is in the sense of investigation. He investigates. Investigation.

Jana suna sadde. Janati. Sunati.

The roots Jana and Suna are in the sense of sound. It sounds. It sounds.

Ettha ca “kasmā te eko bhujo janati, eko te na janatī bhujo”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha janatīti sunati saddaṃ karoti.

Herein, the Pāli passage, ‘Why does one of your arms make a sound, while your other arm does not make a sound?’ is an illustration. There, 'janati' means it is heard or it makes a sound.

Khanu avadāraṇe khanati. Sukhaṃ. Dukkhaṃ. Khato āvāṭo.

The root Khanu is in the sense of digging or splitting open. He digs. Happiness. Suffering. A dug pit.

Tattha sukhanti suṭṭhu dukkhaṃ khanatīti sukhaṃ. Duṭṭhu khanati kāyikacetasikasukhanti dukkhaṃ. Aññamaññapaṭipakkhā hi ete dhammā. Dvidhā cittaṃ khanatīti vā dukkhaṃ. Curādigaṇavasena pana “sukhayatīti sukhaṃ, dukkhayatīti dukkha”nti nibbacanāni gahetabbāni. Samāsapaavasena “sukaraṃ khamassāti sukhaṃ, dukkaraṃ khamassāti dukkha”nti nibbacanānipi vividhā hi saddānaṃ byuppatti pavatti nimittañca.

Herein, 'sukhaṃ' is so called because it thoroughly digs up suffering. 'Dukkhaṃ' is so called because it badly digs up bodily and mental happiness; for these states are mutually opposed. Alternatively, 'dukkhaṃ' is that which digs up the mind in two ways. According to the Curādi group of roots, however, the derivations should be taken as 'that which makes happy is sukhaṃ' and 'that which causes suffering is dukkhaṃ'. Based on compound formation, derivations such as 'that which is easy to endure is sukhaṃ' and 'that which is difficult to endure is dukkhaṃ' are also to be taken. For the etymology, usage, and basis of words are indeed diverse.

Dāna avakhaṇḍane. Dānati. Apadānaṃ.

The root Dāna is in the sense of cutting. It cuts. A biographical story.

Sāna tejane. Tejanaṃ nisānaṃ. Sānati.

The root Sāna is in the sense of sharpening. Sharpening, a whetstone. He sharpens.

Hana hiṃsāgatīsu. Ettha pana hiṃsāvacanena pharusāya vācāya pīḷanañca daṇḍādīhi paharaṇañca gahitaṃ, tasmā hana hiṃsāpaharaṇagatīsūti attho gahetabbo. Tathā hi “rājāno coraṃ gahetvā haneyyuṃ vā bandheyyuṃ vā”ti. Pāṭhassa atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇentehi “haneyyunti potheyyuñceva chindeyyuñcā”ti [M 0.0114] vuttaṃ. Ettha ca chedanaṃ nāma hatthapādādichedanaṃ vā sīsacchedavasena māraṇaṃ vā. Hanassa vadhādeso ghātādeso ca bhavati, hanti hanati, hananti. Hanasi, hanatha. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ neyyaṃ.

The root Hana is in the senses of harming and going. Here, however, by the word 'harming,' both oppression with harsh speech and striking with sticks and so forth are included; therefore, the meaning of 'Hana' should be understood as harming, striking, and going. For it is said: 'Kings, having captured a thief, might kill or bind him.' In explaining the meaning of the text, it is said: 'They might kill (haneyyuṃ) means they might strike and cut.' And here, 'cutting' means the cutting off of hands, feet, and so on, or killing by means of cutting off the head. For the root 'han,' the substitutes 'vadha' and 'ghāta' occur. He kills (hanti, hanati); they kill (hananti). You kill (hanasi); you all kill (hanatha). The rest is to be inferred.

Hiṃsādayo cattāro atthā labbhanti. “Hanti hatthehi pādehī”ti ettha pana hantīti paharatīti attho. “Kuddho hi pitaraṃ hanti. Vikkosamānā tibbāhi, hanti nesaṃ varaṃ vara”nti. Ettha hantīti mārentīti attho. “Vadhati, vadheti, ghāteti” iccapi rūpāni bhavanti. Tattha “vadhati na rodati, āpatti dukkaṭassa. Attānaṃ vadhitvā vadhitvā rodatī”tiādīsu vadho paharaṇaṃ. Pāṇaṃ vadheti. Pāṇavadho. “Esa vadho khaṇḍahālassa. Satte ghātetī”ti ca ādīsu vadho māraṇaṃ.

Four meanings, beginning with harming, are found. In the phrase, ‘He strikes with his hands and feet,’ 'hanti' means 'he strikes'. In, ‘Indeed, being angry, he kills his father,’ and ‘Crying out fiercely, she kills their best,’ 'hanti' here means 'he/she kills'. The forms 'vadhati,' 'vadheti,' and 'ghāteti' also occur. Therein, in passages such as, ‘He strikes but does not cry; it is an offense of wrong-doing,’ and ‘Having struck himself again and again, he cries,’ 'vadho' means striking. ‘He slays a living being.’ ‘The slaying of living beings.’ And in passages such as, ‘This is the slaying of Khaṇḍahāla,’ and ‘He slays beings,’ 'vadho' means killing.

“Upāhanaṃ, vadhū”ti ca ettha hanavadhasaddatthogamanaṃ. “Purisaṃ hanati. Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanati” iccādīni kattupadāni. Devadatto yaññadattena haññati. Tato vātātape ghore, sañjāte paṭihaññati. Paccattavacanassekārattaṃ, yathā “vanappagumbe”ti. Vihārenāti padaṃ sambandhitabbaṃ, iccādīni kammapadāni. Hantā. Hato. Vadhako. Vadhū. Āghāto. Upaghāto. Ghātako. Paṭigho. Saṅgho. Byaggho. Sakuṇagghi. Hantuṃ, hanituṃ, hantvā, hanitvā. Vajjhetvā, vadhitvā iccādīni sanāmikāni tumantādipadāni.

And in 'upāhanaṃ' (sandal) and 'vadhū' (bride), the meaning is understood in relation to the roots 'han' (to go) and 'vadha'. ‘He strikes a man,’ ‘He wards off cold and heat,’ and so on are agentive forms. ‘Devadatta is struck by Yaññadatta.’ ‘Then, when fierce wind and heat arise, he is struck down,’ and so on are objective forms. Striker; struck; slayer; bride; assault; injury; slayer; repulsion; assembly; tiger; hawk. To strike/kill (hantuṃ, hanituṃ); having struck/killed (hantvā, hanitvā); having caused to be slain (vajjhetvā); having slain (vadhitvā)—and so on are indeclinable words ending in '-tuṃ', etc.

Tattha upāhananti taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ upahananti upagacchanti tato ca āhananti āgacchanti etenāti upāhanaṃ. Vadhūti kilesavasena sunakhampi upagamanasīlāti vadhū, sabbāsaṃ itthīnaṃ [M 0.0115] sādhāraṇametaṃ. Atha vā vadhūti suṇisā. Tathā hi “tena hi vadhu yadā utunī ahosi, pupphaṃ te uppannaṃ, atha me āroceyyāsī”ti ettha vadhūti suṇisā vuccati. Sā pana “ayaṃ no puttassa bhariyā”ti sassusasurehi adhigantabbā jānitabbāti vadhūti vuccati. Gatyatthānaṃ katthaci buddhiyatthakathanato ayamattho labbhateva. “Suṇhā, suṇisā, vadhū” iccete pariyāyā. Saṅghoti bhikkhusamūho. Samaggaṃ kammaṃ samupagacchatīti saṅgho, suṭṭhu vā kilese hanti tena tena maggāsinā māretītipi saṅgho, puthujjanāriyavasena vuttānetāni. Vividhe satte āhanati bhuso ghātetīti byaggho. So eva “viyaggho, vaggho”ti ca vuccati. Aparampi puṇḍarīkoti tassa nāmaṃ. Dubbale sakuṇe hantīti sakuṇagghi, seno, ayaṃ pana hanadhātu divādigaṇe “paṭihaññatī”ti akammakaṃ kattupadaṃ janeti. Tathā hi “buddhassa bhagavato vohāro lokiye sote paṭihaññatī”tiādikā pāḷiyo dissanti.

Therein, 'upāhana' (sandal) is so called because 'they approach that place' (upahananti, upagacchanti) and 'they return from there' (āhananti, āgacchanti) by means of it. 'Vadhū' (bride/woman) is so called because, due to defilements, she is prone to approaching even a dog; this is common to all women. Alternatively, 'vadhū' means a daughter-in-law. Thus, in the phrase 'Now then, daughter-in-law, when you are in season, and the flower has appeared, you should inform me,' 'vadhū' here is said to mean daughter-in-law. She is called 'vadhū' because she is to be recognized and known by her mother-in-law and father-in-law as 'this is our son’s wife.' This meaning is indeed obtained from the explanation that verbs of motion sometimes have the meaning of understanding. 'Suṇhā,' 'suṇisā,' and 'vadhū'—these are synonyms. 'Saṅgha' means the community of monks. It is called 'saṅgha' because it harmoniously undertakes actions (samaggaṃ kammaṃ samupagacchati), or it is also called 'saṅgho' because it thoroughly destroys defilements (suṭṭhu kilese hanti), killing them with the sword of the respective path. These explanations are stated with reference to ordinary people and noble ones. 'Byaggho' (tiger) is so called because it strikes (āhanati) and fiercely kills (bhuso ghātetī) various beings. It is also called 'viyaggho' or 'vaggha.' Another name for it is 'puṇḍarīka.' 'Sakuṇagghi' (hawk) kills weak birds (dubbale sakuṇe hanti); it is also called 'seno.' However, this root 'han' in the 'divādi' class generates the intransitive, active form 'paṭihaññati.' Thus, passages such as 'The Blessed Buddha’s speech strikes the worldly ear' are seen in the Pāli texts.

Ana pāṇane. Pāṇanaṃ sasanaṃ. Anati. Ānaṃ, pānaṃ. “Tattha ānanti assāso. Pānanti passāso. Etesu assāsoti bahi nikkhamanavāto. Passāsoti anto pavisanavāto”ti vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, suttantaṭṭhakathāsu pana uppaṭipāṭiyā āgataṃ. Tattha yasmā sabbesampi gabbhaseyyakānaṃ mātukucchito nikkhamanakāle paṭhamaṃ abbhantaravāto bahi nikkhamati, pacchā bāhiravāto sukhumaṃ rajaṃ gahetvā abbhantaraṃ pavisanto tāluṃ āhacca nibbāyati, tasmā vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “assāsoti bahi nikkhamanavāto, passāsoti anto pavisanavāto”ti vuttaṃ. Etesu [M 0.0116] dvīsu nayesu vinayanayena anto uṭṭhitasasanaṃ assāso, bahi uṭṭhitasasanaṃ passāso. Suttantanayena pana bahi uṭṭhahitvāpi anto sasanato assāso. Anto uṭṭhahitvāpi bahi sasanato passāso. Ayameva ca nayo “assāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato ajjhattaṃ vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā cā”ti, “passāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato bahiddhā vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā cā”ti imāya pāḷiyā sametīti veditabbaṃ.

The root 'ana' is in the sense of breathing. Breathing is respiration. He breathes. In-breath, out-breath. Therein, 'āna' means in-breath, 'pāna' means out-breath. Of these, 'assāso' means the outgoing breath, and 'passāso' means the incoming breath—this is stated in the Vinaya commentary. However, in the Sutta commentaries, it is given in the reverse order. There, because for all beings lying in the womb, at the time of emerging from the mother's womb, first the internal breath goes out, and afterward the external breath, taking up fine dust, enters and, striking the palate, ceases—therefore, in the Vinaya commentary, it is said: 'Assāso' is the outgoing breath, 'passāso' is the incoming breath. In these two methods, according to the Vinaya method, the respiration that arises internally is the out-breath (assāso), and the respiration that arises externally is the in-breath (passāso). But according to the Sutta method, even when arising externally, because it breathes inward, it is the in-breath (assāso). And when arising internally, because it breathes outward, it is the out-breath (passāso). And this same method should be understood to agree with this Pāli passage: 'For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath with mindfulness, with a mind distracted internally, both body and mind become rigid, agitated, and trembling,' and 'For one who follows the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath with mindfulness, with a mind distracted externally, both body and mind become rigid, agitated, and trembling'.

Dhana dhaññe. Dhananaṃ dhaññaṃ, siripuññapaññānaṃ sampadāti attho. Dhātuattho hi yebhuyyena bhāvavasena kathiyati ṭhapetvā vakkarukkhataceti evamādippabhedaṃ. Yathā bhāvatthe vattamānena yapaccayena saddhiṃ nakārassa yyakāraṃ katvā thenanaṃ theyyanti vuccati, evamidha yapaccayena saddhiṃ nakārassa ññakāraṃ katvā dhananaṃ dhaññanti vuccati. Dhanino vā bhāvo dhaññaṃ, tasmiṃ dhaññe. Dhanti, dhanati. Dhanitaṃ. Dhaññaṃ. Yasmā pana dhaññasaddena siripuññapaññāsampadā gahitā, tasmā “dhaññapuññalakkhaṇasampannaṃ puttaṃ vijāyī”tiādīsu dhaññasaddena siripaññāva gahetabbā puññassa visuṃ vacanato.

The root 'dhana' is in the sense of grain. 'Dhanana' is 'dhañña'; the meaning is the abundance of glory, merit, and wisdom. Indeed, the meaning of a root is mostly explained in the sense of 'state of being,' except for distinctions such as 'vakkarukkhataca' and so forth. Just as, in the sense of 'state of being,' with the suffix 'ya,' and by changing the 'na' sound to 'yya,' 'thenanaṃ' becomes 'theyya' (theft), so here, with the suffix 'ya,' and by changing the 'na' sound to 'ñña,' 'dhananaṃ' becomes 'dhañña' (grain/fortune). Or, the state of being wealthy (dhanino bhāvo) is 'dhañña'; hence, 'in that fortune.' He produces wealth. Wealth produced. Grain/fortune. However, since the word 'dhañña' encompasses the abundance of glory, merit, and wisdom, therefore, in phrases like 'she gave birth to a son endowed with the qualities of fortune and merit,' the word 'dhañña' should be understood as referring to glory and wisdom only, due to the separate mention of merit.

“Nadato parisāyante, vāditabbapahārino;

Ye te dakkhanti vadanaṃ, dhaññā te narapuṅgava.

“Those who see your face as you roar in the assembly, striking those who should be struck, they are blessed, O bull among men.

Dīghaṅgulī tambanakhe, subhe āyatapaṇhike;

Ye pāde paṇamissanti, tepi dhaññā guṇandhara.

With long toes, copper-colored nails, beautiful with long heels; those who will bow to your feet, they too are blessed, O bearer of virtue.

Madhurāni pahaṭṭhāni, dosagghāni hitāni ca;

Yetevākyāni sossanti, tepi dhaññānaruttamā”ti

Sweet, delightful, destructive of faults, and beneficial; those who will hear these words, they too are blessed, O best of men.”

Evamādīsu [M 0.0117] pana dhaññasaddena puññasampadā gahetabbā, puññasampadāya vā saddhiṃ siripaññāsampadāpi gahetabbā. Idamettha nibbacanaṃ “dhaññaṃ siripuññapaññāsampadā etesaṃ atthīti dhaññā”ti. “Dhaññaṃ maṅgalasammata”nti ettha tu “uttamaratanaṃ ida”nti dhanāyitabbaṃ saddhāyitabbanti dhaññaṃ, sirisampannaṃ puññasampannaṃ paññāsampannantipi attho yujjati. “Dhaññaṃ dhanaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpa”nti ca ādīsu “natthi dhaññasamaṃ dhana”nti vacanato dhanāyitabbanti dhaññaṃ, kiṃ taṃ? Pubbaṇṇaṃ. Apica osadhivisesopi dhaññanti vuccati. Dhanasaddassa ca pana samāsavasena “adhano, niddhano”ti ca natthi dhanaṃ etassāti atthena daliddapuggalo vuccati. “Nidhanaṃ yātī”tiettha tu kampanatthavācakassa dhūdhātussa vasena vināso nidhananti vuccatīti.

However, in these and similar contexts, the word 'dhañña' should be understood as the attainment of merit; or, along with the attainment of merit, the attainment of glory and wisdom should also be understood. Here, the etymological explanation is: 'Because they possess the abundance of glory, merit, and wisdom, they are called 'dhaññā'.' Regarding the phrase 'Dhañña is considered auspicious,' here 'dhañña' should be taken to mean 'this is a supreme jewel,' something to be valued and trusted. The meaning of being endowed with glory, merit, and wisdom is also appropriate. And in passages such as 'Grain, wealth, silver, gold,' and from the statement 'There is no wealth equal to grain,' 'dhañña' means something to be valued—what is that? It is staple grain. Moreover, a special type of medicine is also called 'dhañña.' However, as for the word 'dhana' (wealth), in compound formations like 'adhano' (without wealth) and 'niddhano' (destitute), a poor person is said to be one who has no wealth. In the phrase 'goes to destruction,' however, 'nidhana' means destruction, derived from the root 'dhū' (to shake), which signifies trembling.

Muna gatiyaṃ. Munati.

The root 'muna' is in the sense of knowing. He knows.

Cine maññanāyaṃ. Aluttantoyaṃ dhātu, yathā gile, yathā ca mile. Cināyati, ocināyati. “Sabbo taṃ jano ocināyatū”ti idamettha pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Ocināyatati avamaññatūti.

The root 'ci' is in the sense of disrespecting. This root has no elision of its final vowel, like 'gil' and 'mil.' He disrespects, he disrespects. The Pāli illustration here is: 'Let all those people disrespect him.' 'Ocināyatū' means 'let him disrespect'.

Iti bhūvādigaṇe tavaggantadhāturūpāni

Thus, the forms of roots ending in the 'tavagga' within the 'bhū' class.

Samattāni.

Completed.

Pakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'pa'.

Idāni pavaggantadhāturūpāni vuccante –

Now, the forms of roots ending in the 'pavagga' are stated:

Pā pāne. Pānaṃ pivanaṃ. “Pāti, pānti. Pātu, pāntu” iccādi yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

The root 'pā' is in the sense of drinking. 'Pāna' is drinking. 'Pāti, pānti. Pātu, pāntu,' and so on should be applied as appropriate.

Khippaṃ gīvaṃ pasārehi, na te dassāmi jīvitaṃ;

Ayañhite mayā rūḷho, saro pāssati lohitanti.

Quickly stretch out your neck, I will not grant you life; for this arrow, fixed by me, will drink your blood.

Atra [M 0.0118] hi pāssatīti pivissati. “Pāssati, pāssanti. Pāssasi, pāssatha. Pāssāmi, pāssāma” iccādinā, “apassā, apassaṃsu” iccādinā ca nayena sesaṃ sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ nayaññūhi. Ko hi samattho sabbāni buddhavacanasāgare vicitrāni vippakiṇṇarūpantararatanāni uddharitvā dassetuṃ, tasmā sabbāsupi dhātūsu saṅkhepena gahaṇūpāyamattameva dassitaṃ. Pivati, pivanti. Pivaṃ, pivanto, pivamāno, pivaṃ bhāgirasodakaṃ. Kārite kumāraṃ khīraṃ pāyeti. Muhuttaṃ taṇhāsamanaṃ, khīraṃ tvaṃ pāyito mayā. Kamme pīyati, pītaṃ. Tumādīsu “pātuṃ, pivituṃ, pitvā, pivitvā, pāyetvā” iccādīni yojetabbāni. Aññesupi ṭhānesu pāḷinayānurūpena saddarūpāni evameva yojetabbāni.

Here, 'pāssati' means 'will drink'. 'Pāssati, pāssanti. Pāssasi, pāssatha. Pāssāmi, pāssāma,' and similarly 'apassā, apassaṃsu,' etc.—by this method the rest should be applied by those skilled in the method. For who is capable of extracting and showing all the diverse, scattered gems of different forms from the ocean of the Buddha's words? Therefore, for all the roots, only a brief method for comprehension has been shown. Pivati, pivanti. Pivaṃ, pivanto, pivamāno, drinking the water of the Bhagirathi. In the causative: he causes the boy to drink milk. 'For a moment, quenching thirst, you were made by me to drink milk.' In the passive: pīyati, pītaṃ. In the case of the infinitive and absolutive, 'pātuṃ, pivituṃ, pitvā, pivitvā, pāyetvā,' etc., should be applied. In other places as well, word forms should be applied in this way, in accordance with the Pāli method.

Pā rakkhaṇe. Pāti. Nipāti. Pitā, gopo.

The root 'pā' is in the sense of protecting. He protects. He protects thoroughly. Father, guardian.

Pā pūraṇe. Pāti, vippāti. Vippo.

The root 'pā' is in the sense of filling. He fills, he fills completely. A brahmin.

Vippoti brāhmaṇo. So hi vippeti pūreti visiṭṭhena veduccāraṇādinā attano brāhmaṇakammena lokassa ajjhāsayaṃ attano ca hadaye vedānīti vippoti vuccati. “Jāto vippakule aha”nti ettha hi brāhmaṇo “vippo”ti vuccati. Tassa kulaṃ vippakulanti.

A brahmin is a vippo. For by his brahminical actions, such as the distinguished recitation of the Vedas, he gratifies (vippeti) and fills (pūreti) the aspirations of the world and the Vedas in his own heart; thus he is called a vippo. Here, in the phrase 'born in a vippa family,' a brahmin is called a 'vippo.' His family is thus a vippa family.

Pū pavane. Pavati. Putto, puññaṃ. Ettha puttoti attano kulaṃ pavati sodhetīti putto. Kiyādigaṇaṃ pana patvā “punātī”ti vattabbaṃ.

The root Pū, in the sense of purifying. Pavati (he purifies). Putto (son), puññaṃ (merit). Here, a putto is so called because he purifies his own family. But when it belongs to the Kiyādi group, 'punāti' should be said.

Putto’trajo suto sūnu,

Tanujo tanayo’raso;

Puttanattādayo cātha,

Apaccanti pavuccare.

A son is putta, atraja, suta, sūnu, tanuja, tanaya, orasa; and then sons, grandsons, and so forth are called apacca.

Itthiliṅgamhi [M 0.0119] vattabbe, puttīti atrajāti ca;

Vattabbaṃ sesaṭṭhānesu, yathārahamudīraye;

Pāḷiyañhi atrajāti, itthī puttī kathiyati;

When the feminine gender is to be expressed, puttī and atrajā should be said; in the remaining cases, one should utter what is appropriate. For in the Pāli, an atrajā is said to be a female, a daughter.

Ettha pana –

But here –

“Tato dve sattarattassa, vedehassatrajā piyā;

Rājakaññā rucā nāma, dhātimātaramabravī”ti

“Then, after two seven-nights, the beloved daughter of Vedeha, the princess named Rucā, spoke to her nurse-mother.”

Ayaṃ pāḷi nidassanaṃ. “Puttī, dhītā, duhitā, attajā”ti iccete pariyāyā. Evaṃ atrajāti itthivācakassa itthiliṅgassa dassanato sutasaddādīsupi itthiliṅganayo labbhamānālabbhamānavasena upaparikkhitabbo. Tathā hi loke “vesso, suddo, naro, kiṃpuriso” iccādīnaṃ yugaḷabhāvena “vessī, suddī, nārī, kiṃpurisī”tiādīni itthivācakāni liṅgāni dissanti. “Puriso pumā” iccādīnaṃ pana yugaḷabhāvena itthivācakāni itthiliṅgāni na dissanti. Puññanti ettha pana attano kārakaṃ pavati sodhetīti puññaṃ. Kiyādigaṇaṃ pana patvā punātīti puññanti vattabbaṃ.

This Pāli passage is an example. Puttī, dhītā, duhitā, attajā—these are synonyms. Thus, following the example of the feminine gender of atrajā, a word denoting a female, the principle for forming the feminine should also be investigated for words such as suta, according to whether such forms are found or not. For in the world, for pairs such as vesso, suddo, naro, kiṃpuriso, and so on, corresponding feminine gender forms such as vessī, suddī, nārī, kiṃpurisī are seen. However, for pairs such as puriso, pumā, and so on, corresponding feminine gender forms are not seen. Now, regarding puñña, here it is that which purifies its doer; thus it is puñña. But when it belongs to the Kiyādi group, it should be said that puñña comes from punāti.

Añño atthopi vattabbo, niruttilakkhaṇassito;

Tasmā nibbacanaṃ ñeyyaṃ, janapūjādito idha.

Another meaning should also be stated, based on the characteristics of etymology; therefore, the derivation should be understood here from 'veneration by people' and so forth.

Paraṃ pujjabhavaṃ janetīti puññaṃ. Sadā pūjitaṃ vā janetīti puññaṃ. Janaṃ attakāraṃ punātīti puññaṃ. Asesaṃ apuññaṃ punātīti puññaṃ.

That which generates a future state worthy of veneration is puñña. Or, that which always generates what is venerated is puñña. That which purifies the person who performs it is puñña. That which completely purifies demerit is puñña.

Kalyāṇaṃ kusalaṃ puññaṃ, subhamicceva niddise;

Kammassa kusalassādhi-vacanaṃ vacane paṭu.

One should declare kalyāṇa, kusala, puñña, and subha; it is a designation for wholesome action, skillful in expression.

Pe gatiyaṃ. Peti, penti. Pesi, petha. Idha bhikkhave ekacco assakhaḷuṅko pehīti vutto viddho samāno codito sārathinā pacchato paṭisakkati, piṭṭhito rathaṃ paṭivatteti. Ummaggaṃ gaṇhāti, ubbaṭumaṃ rathaṃ karoti.

The root Pe, in the sense of going. Peti (he goes), penti (they go). Pesi (you go), petha (you all go). Here, monks, a certain unbroken horse, when told 'Go!' and struck, urged on by the charioteer, retreats backward, turns the chariot around from behind. It takes the wrong path and overturns the chariot.

Pe [M 0.0120] vuddhiyaṃ payati. Pāyo, apāyo. Ettha apāyoti natthi pāyo vuddhi etthāti apāyo. Ayadhātuvasenapi attho netabbo, ayato vuddhito, sukhato vā apetoti apāyo, nirayatiracchānayonipettivisayaasurakāyā.

The root Pe, in the sense of growth. Payati (he grows). Pāyo (growth), apāyo (decline). Here, apāyo means 'there is no growth (pāyo) here,' thus apāyo. The meaning should also be derived by means of the root aya: apāyo means departed from aya, that is, from growth or happiness; these are the realms of hell, animal birth, the sphere of ghosts, and the host of asuras.

Pe sosane. Pāyati, payati vā. Nipako. Ettha nipako nipayati visoseti paṭipakkhaṃ, tato vā attānaṃ nipāti rakkhatīti nipako, sampajāno.

The root Pe, in the sense of drying up. Pāyati (he dries up), or payati. Nipako (the discerning one). Here, a nipako is one who dries up and withers the opposition, or thereby protects himself; thus he is a nipako, one who is clearly comprehending.

Gupa rakkhaṇe. Gopati. Gopako.

The root Gupa, in the sense of guarding. Gopati (he guards). Gopako (a guardian).

Nagaraṃ yathā paccantaṃ, guttaṃ sāntarabāhiraṃ.

Like a frontier city, guarded within and without.

Evaṃ gopetha attānaṃ, khaṇo ve mā upaccagā.

Thus should you guard yourself; let not the moment pass you by.

Gopethāti gopeyya rakkheyya.

Gopetha means one should guard, one should protect.

Vapa santāne. Vapati.

The root Vapa, in the sense of spreading or sowing. Vapati (he sows).

Sapa samavāye. Sapati.

The root Sapa, in the sense of combination. Sapati (he swears).

Cupa mandagatiyaṃ. Copati.

The root Cupa, in the sense of slow movement. Copati (he moves slowly).

Tupa hiṃsāyaṃ. Topati. Tuppati.

The root Tupa, in the sense of harming. Topati (he harms). Tuppati (he harms).

Gupa gopanajigucchanesu. Gopati, jigucchati. Jigucchaṃ, jigucchamāno. Jegucchī. Jigucchitvā iccādīni.

The root Gupa, in the senses of guarding and feeling disgust. Gopati (he guards), jigucchati (he feels disgust). Jigucchaṃ (disgust), jigucchamāno (feeling disgust). Jegucchī (one who is disgusted). Jigucchitvā (having felt disgust), and so on.

Kapu hiṃsātakkalagandhesu. Kappati. Kappūro.

The root Kapu, in the senses of harming, reasoning, and smelling. Kappati (he harms/reasons/smells). Kappūro (camphor).

Kapu sāmatthiye. Idaṃ amhākaṃ kappati. Netaṃ amhesu kappati.

The root Kapu, in the sense of capability or suitability. Idaṃ amhākaṃ kappati (This is suitable for us). Netaṃ amhesu kappati (This is not suitable for us).

Kapa karuṇāyaṃ. Kapati. Kapaṇo, kāpaññaṃ. Tattha kapatīti karuṇāyati, kāpaññanti kapaṇabhāvo.

The root Kapa, in the sense of compassion. Kapati (he feels compassion). Kapaṇo (wretched, pitiable), kāpaññaṃ (wretchedness, pitiableness). Therein, kapati means 'he feels compassion,' and kāpaññaṃ means 'the state of being pitiable.'

Sapa [M 0.0121] akkose. Sapati. Sapatho, abhisapatho, abhisapito, sapanako.

The root Sapa, in the sense of reviling or cursing. Sapati (he reviles/curses). Sapatho (an oath, a curse), abhisapatho (a solemn oath, a curse), abhisapito (one who is cursed), sapanako (one who curses).

Vapa bījanikkhepe. Bījaṃ vapati. Vāpako. Vāpitaṃ dhaññaṃ. Vuttaṃ bījaṃ purisena. Bījaṃ vappati. Vappamaṅgalaṃ.

The root Vapa, in the sense of depositing seeds. Bījaṃ vapati (he sows seeds). Vāpako (a sower). Vāpitaṃ dhaññaṃ (sown grain). Vuttaṃ bījaṃ purisena (the seed was sown by a person). Bījaṃ vappati (the seed is sown). Vappamaṅgalaṃ (the sowing ceremony).

Supa sayane. Supati. Sukhaṃ supanti munayo, ye itthīsu na bajjhare. Sutto puriso, supanaṃ, suttaṃ.

The root Supa, in the sense of sleeping. Supati (he sleeps). The sages who are not bound to women sleep happily. Sutto puriso (a sleeping man), supanaṃ (sleeping), suttaṃ (sleep).

Khipa peraṇe. Peraṇaṃ cuṇṇikaraṇaṃ pisanaṃ. Khepati. Khepako.

The root Khipa, in the sense of impelling. Peraṇaṃ means grinding, crushing. Khepati (he impels/throws). Khepako (one who impels/throws).

Khipa abyattasadde. Khipati. Khipitasaddo. Yadā ca dhammaṃ desento, khipi lokagganāyako.

The root Khipa, in the sense of an indistinct sound. Khipati (it makes an indistinct sound). Khipitasaddo (an indistinct sound). And when the Leader of the world was teaching the Dhamma, he sneezed.

Khipa chaḍḍano. Khipati, ukkhipati, vikkhipati, avakhipati, saṃkhipati. Khittaṃ, ukkhittaṃ, pakkhittaṃ, vikkhittaṃ iccādīni.

The root Khipa, in the sense of throwing or discarding. Khipati (he throws), ukkhipati (he lifts up, throws up), vikkhipati (he scatters, throws about), avakhipati (he throws down), saṃkhipati (he gathers, summarizes). Khittaṃ (thrown), ukkhittaṃ (lifted up, thrown up), pakkhittaṃ (thrown in, inserted), vikkhittaṃ (scattered), and so on.

Opa niṭṭhubhane. Niṭṭhubhanaṃ kheḷapātanaṃ. Opati. Osadhaṃ saṅkharitvā mukhe kheḷaṃ opi.

The root Opa, in the sense of spitting. Niṭṭhubhanaṃ means the ejection of saliva. Opati (he spits). Having prepared the medicine, he spat saliva into the mouth.

Lipi upalepe. Lepati. Littaṃ paramena tejasā.

The root Lipi, in the sense of smearing or anointing. Lepati (he smears). Littaṃ paramena tejasā (smeared with supreme splendor).

Khipi gatiyaṃ. Khimpati.

The root Khipi, in the sense of movement. Khimpati (he moves).

Ḍipa khepe. Ḍepati.

The root Ḍipa, in the sense of throwing or sending. Ḍepati (he throws, sends).

Nidapi nidampane. Nidampanaṃ nāma sassarukkhādīsu vīhisīsaṃ vā varakasīsaṃ vā acchinditvā khuddakasākhaṃ vā abhañjitvā yathāṭhitameva hatthena gahetvā ākaḍḍhitvā bījamattasseva vā paṇṇamattasseva vā gahaṇaṃ. Puriso vīhisīsaṃ nidampati, rukkhapattaṃ nidampati. Nidampako, nidampitaṃ, nidampituṃ, nidampitvā.

The root Nidapi, in the sense of gleaning. Gleaning means taking a rice ear or a wild rice ear from crops or trees, without cutting it or breaking off a small branch, but grasping it with the hand just as it is and pulling it, grasping only the seed or only the leaf. Puriso vīhisīsaṃ nidampati (a person gleans a rice ear), rukkhapattaṃ nidampati (he gleans a tree leaf). Nidampako (the gleaner), nidampitaṃ (gleaned), nidampituṃ (to glean), nidampitvā (having gleaned).

Tapa [M 0.0122] dittiyaṃ. Ditti virocanaṃ. Divā tapatiādicco.

The root Tapa, in the sense of shining. Ditti means radiance. Divā tapati ādicco (the sun shines by day).

Tapa ubbege. Ubbego utrāso bhīrutā. Tapati, uttapati. Ottappaṃ, ottappiyaṃ dhanaṃ.

The root Tapa, in the sense of agitation. Ubbego means terror, timidity. Tapati (he is agitated), uttapati (he is greatly agitated). Ottappaṃ (moral dread), ottappiyaṃ dhanaṃ (the treasure of moral dread).

Tapa dhūpa santāpe. Tapati. Tapodhanaṃ, ātāpo. Ātāpī. Ātapaṃ. Dhūpati, sandhūpano, kamme tāpiyati. Dhūpiyati. Bhāve tāpanaṃ, tāpo, paritāpo, santāpo. Dhūpanaṃ.

The roots Tapa and Dhūpa, in the sense of heating and tormenting. Tapati (he heats, torments). Tapodhanaṃ (one whose wealth is ascetic practice), ātāpo (ardor, exertion). Ātāpī (the ardent one). Ātapaṃ (sunshine, heat). Dhūpati (it smokes), sandhūpano (smoking, fumigating). In the passive voice, tāpiyati (it is heated, tormented). Dhūpiyati (it is smoked). In the abstract noun form: tāpanaṃ (heating), tāpo (heat), paritāpo (torment), santāpo (intense torment). Dhūpanaṃ (smoking, fumigation).

Pakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'pa'.

Phakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'pha'.

Puppha vikasane. Akammako cāyaṃ sakammako ca. Pupphati. Pupphaṃ, pupphanaṃ, pupphito, pupphituṃ, pupphitvā. Pupphanti pupphino dumā. Thalajā dakajā pupphā, sabbe pupphanti tāvade. Mañjūsako nāma rukkho yattakāni udake vā thale vā pupphāni, sabbāni pupphati.

The root Puppha, in the sense of blooming. This root is both intransitive and transitive. Pupphati (it blooms). Pupphaṃ (flower), pupphanaṃ (blooming), pupphito (bloomed), pupphituṃ (to bloom), pupphitvā (having bloomed). Pupphanti pupphino dumā (Flowering trees bloom). Thalajā dakajā pupphā, sabbe pupphanti tāvade (Land-born and water-born flowers, all bloom then). Mañjūsako nāma rukkho yattakāni udake vā thale vā pupphāni, sabbāni pupphati (The tree called Mañjūsaka causes all flowers, whether in water or on land, to bloom).

Tupha hiṃsāyaṃ. Tophati.

The root Tupha, in the sense of harming. Tophati (it harms).

Dapha daphi vappha gatiyaṃ. Daphati. Damphati. Vapphati.

The roots Dapha, Daphi, and Vappha, in the sense of going. Daphati (it goes). Damphati (it goes). Vapphati (it goes).

Dipha kathanayuddhanindāhiṃsādānesu. Dephati. Depho.

The root Dipha, in the sense of speaking, quarreling, blaming, harming, and taking. Dephati (it speaks). Depho (speech).

Tapha tittiyaṃ. Titti tappanaṃ, taphati.

The root Tapha, in the sense of satisfaction. Titti means gratification. Taphati (it satisfies).

Dupha upakkilese. Upakkilissanaṃ upakkileso. Dophati.

The root Dupha, in the sense of defilement. Upakkilissanaṃ is defilement. Dophati (it defiles).

Gupha ganthe. Gantho ganthikaraṇaṃ. Gophati.

The root Gupha, in the sense of binding. Gantho means the act of tying a knot. Gophati (it binds).

Phakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'pha'.

Bakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ba'.

Bhabba [M 0.0123] hiṃsāyaṃ. Bhabbati. Bhabbo.

The root Bhabba, in the sense of harming. Bhabbati (it harms). Bhabbo (harmful).

Pabba vabba mabba kabba khabba gabba sabba cabba gatiyaṃ. Pabbati. Vabbati. Mabbati. Kabbati. Khabbati. Gabbati. Sabbati. Cabbati.

The roots Pabba, Vabba, Mabba, Kabba, Khabba, Gabba, Sabba, and Cabba, in the sense of going. Pabbati (it goes). Vabbati (it goes). Mabbati (it goes). Kabbati (it goes). Khabbati (it goes). Gabbati (it goes). Sabbati (it goes). Cabbati (it goes).

Abba sabba hiṃsāyañca. Gatyāpekkhāya cakāro. Abbati. Sabbati.

The roots Abba and Sabba, also in the sense of harming. The particle 'ca' is with reference to the sense of going. Abbati (it harms). Sabbati (it harms).

Kubi acchādane. Kubbati.

The root Kubi, in the sense of covering. Kubbati (it covers).

Lubi tubi addane. Lumbati. Tumbati. Lumbinīvanaṃ. Udakatumbo. Athopi dve ca tumbāni.

The roots Lubi and Tubi, in the sense of afflicting. Lumbati (it afflicts). Tumbati (it afflicts). Lumbinīvanaṃ (Lumbinī Grove). Udakatumbo (a water-gourd). Athopi dve ca tumbāni (And also two gourds).

Cubi vadanasaṃyoge. Puttaṃ muddhani cumbati. Mukhe cumbati. Ettha siyā “yadi vadanasaṃyoge cubidhātu vattati, kathaṃ ambudharabinducumbitakūṭoti ettha avadane aviññāṇake pabbatakūṭe ambudharabindūnaṃ cumbanaṃ vutta”nti? Saccaṃ, taṃ pana cumbanākārasadisenākārena sambhavaṃ cetasi ṭhapetvā vuttaṃ, yathā adassanasambhavepi dassanasadisenākārena sambhūtattā “rodante dārake disvā, ubbiddhā vipulā dumā”ti acakkhukānampi rukkhānaṃ dassanaṃ vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi cumbanākārasadisenākārena sambhūtattā avadanānampi ambudharabindūnaṃ cumbanaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabhāvato pana aviññāṇakānaṃ dassanacumbanādīni ca natthi, saviññāṇakānaṃyeva tāni hontīti. Ayaṃ nayo kamu padavikkhepetiādīsupi netabbo.

The root Cubi, in the sense of joining the mouth. Puttaṃ muddhani cumbati (He kisses the child on the head). Mukhe cumbati (He kisses on the mouth). Here one might ask: 'If the root cubi is used in the sense of joining the mouth, how is it that in the phrase ambudharabinducumbitakūṭo (a peak kissed by raindrops), kissing by raindrops is spoken of in relation to an insentient mountain peak, which has no mouth?' It is true, but that is said keeping in mind the occurrence of a form similar to the act of kissing. Just as, although seeing is impossible, seeing is attributed to eyeless trees because of the occurrence of a form similar to seeing, as in: 'Having seen the crying children, the tall trees shot up.' Similarly here, because of the occurrence of a form similar to the act of kissing, kissing is attributed to raindrops, which have no mouths. By nature, however, insentient things do not possess seeing, kissing, and so forth; these belong only to sentient beings. This principle should also be applied in cases such as 'kamu in the sense of stepping,' and so on.

Ubbi tubbi thubbi dubbi dhubbi hiṃsatthā. Ubbati. Tubbati. Thubbati. Dubbati. Dubbā. Dhubbati. Ettha dubbāti dabbatiṇaṃ, yaṃ “tiriyā nāma tiṇajātī”ti pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ. Ettha ca dubbāti itthiliṅgaṃ, dabbanti napuṃsakaliṅganti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The roots Ubbi, Tubbi, Thubbi, Dubbi, and Dhubbi, in the sense of harming. Ubbati (it harms). Tubbati (it harms). Thubbati (it harms). Dubbati (it harms). Dubbā (dabba grass). Dhubbati (it harms). Here, dubbā refers to dabba grass, which is mentioned in the Pāli canon as 'a species of grass called tiriyā'. And here, it should be understood that dubbā is feminine, while dabba is neuter.

Mubbi [M 0.0124] bandhane. Mubbati.

The root Mubbi, in the sense of binding. Mubbati (it binds).

Kubbi uggame. Kubbati.

The root Kubbi, in the sense of rising. Kubbati (it rises).

Pubba pabba sabba pūraṇe. Pubbati. Pabbati. Sabbati. Etta siyā “nanu bho pubbasabbasaddā sabbanāmāni, kasmā panete dhātucintāyaṃ gahitā”ti? Vuccate – sabbanāmesu ca tumantādivirahitesu ca nipātesu upasaggesu ca dhātucintā nāma natthi, imāni pana sabbanāmāni na honti. Kevalaṃ sutisāmaññena sabbanāmāni viya upaṭṭhahanti, tena te tabbhāvamuttattā dhātucintāyaṃ pubbācariyehi gahitā “pubbati sabbatī”ti payogadassanatoti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā buddhavacane etāni rūpāni na santīti? Anāgamanabhāvena na santi, na avijjamānabhāvena. Kiñcāpi buddhavacanesu etāni rūpāni na santi, tathāpi porāṇehi anumatā purāṇabhāsāti gahetabbāni, yathā “nāthatīti nātho”ti ettha “nāthatī”ti rūpaṃ buddhavacane avijjamānampi gahetabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ imānipi. Tasmā vohāresu viññūnaṃ kosallatthāya sāsane avijjamānāpi sāsanānurūpā lokikappayogā gahetabbāti “pubbati sabbatī”ti rūpāni gahitāni. Esa nayo aññesupi ṭhānesu veditabbo.

The roots Pubba, Pabba, and Sabba, in the sense of filling. Pubbati (it fills). Pabbati (it fills). Sabbati (it fills). Here, one might ask: 'Sir, are not the words pubba and sabba pronouns? Why then are they included in the analysis of roots?' It is replied: In pronouns, in particles lacking endings such as -tum, and in prefixes, there is no analysis of roots. These, however, are not pronouns. They merely appear to be like pronouns due to a similarity in sound. Therefore, because they are free from that nature, they were included in the analysis of roots by the ancient teachers to show the usage pubbati and sabbatī. If so, why are these forms not found in the word of the Buddha? They are not found due to non-transmission, not due to non-existence. Although these forms are not found in the word of the Buddha, they should still be accepted as ancient speech approved by the ancients, just as in the phrase 'nāthatīti nātho' (a lord is one who helps), the form 'nāthatī' is to be accepted even though it is not found in the word of the Buddha; so too are these. Therefore, for the sake of the skill of the wise in worldly usage, worldly expressions not found in the Teaching but conforming to it should be accepted—hence, the forms pubbati and sabbatī are included. This principle should be understood in other cases as well.

Camba adane. Cambati.

The root Camba is in the sense of eating. It eats.

Kabba khabba gabba dabbe. Dabbo ahaṅkāro. Kabbati. Khabbati. Gabbati.

The roots Kabba, Khabba, and Gabba are in the sense of pride. Dabba is egoism. It is proud. It is proud. It is proud.

Abi dabi sadde. Ambati. Ambā, ambu. Dambati.

The roots Abi and Dabi are in the sense of sound. It sounds. Ambā (mother), ambu (water). It sounds.

Labi avasaṃsane. Avasaṃsanaṃ avalambanaṃ. Lambati, vilambati, byālambati. Nīce co’lambate sūriyo. Ālambati[M 0.0125]. Ālambanaṃ, tadālambanaṃ, tadālambaṇaṃ, tadālambaṃ vā. Lābu. Alābu vā, akāro hi tabbhāve.

The root Labi is in the sense of hanging down. Avasaṃsana is avalambana (hanging, support). It hangs, it dangles, it hangs down. The sun also hangs low. It clings to. Support, object of attention, that as support, that as object of attention. Lābu (gourd). Or alābu (bottle gourd), for the letter 'a' is indeed in that sense.

Bakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'ba'.

Bhakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'bha'.

Bhā dittiyaṃ. Cando bhāti, pañhā maṃ paṭibhāti. Ratti vibhāti. Bhāṇu, paṭibhānaṃ. Vibhātā ratti.

The root Bhā is in the sense of shining. The moon shines. A question occurs to me. The night brightens. Bhāṇu (sun), paṭibhānaṃ (ready wit). The night has dawned.

Bhī bhaye. Bhāyati. Bhayaṃ, bhayānako, bhīmo, bhīmaseno, bhīru, bhīruko, bhīrukajātiko. Kārite “bhāyeti, bhāyayati, bhāyāpeti, bhāyāpayatī”ti rūpāni.

The root Bhī is in the sense of fear. He fears. Fear, fearful, dreadful, Bhīmasena, timid, timid, of a timid nature. In the causative, the forms are 'bhāyeti, bhāyayati, bhāyāpeti, bhāyāpayati'.

Sabhu sambhu hiṃsāyaṃ. Sabhati. Sambhati.

The roots Sabhu and Sambhu are in the sense of harming. He harms. He harms.

Sumbha bhāsane ca. Cakāro hiṃsāpekkhako. Sumbhati. Sumbho. Kusumbho.

The root Sumbha is in the sense of speaking, and also. The particle 'ca' refers to harming. He crushes. Sumbho. Kusumbho.

Ettha sumbhoti āvāṭo. “Sumbhaṃ nikkhanāhī”ti idamettha nidassanaṃ. Kusumbhoti khuddakaāvāṭo, “pabbatakandarapadarasākhāparipūrā kusumbhe paripūrentī”ti idamettha nidassanaṃ.

Here, 'sumbha' means a pit. 'Dig a pit'—this is an example here. 'Kusumbha' means a small pit. '[Streams] full of [debris from] mountain caves, rock fissures, and branches fill the small pits'—this is an example here.

Abbha vabbha mabbha gatiyaṃ. Abbhati. Abbho. Vabbhati. Mabbhati.

The roots Abbha, Vabbha, and Mabbha are in the sense of movement. It moves. Abbho (a cloud). It moves. It moves.

Ettha abbhoti megho. So hi abbhati anekasatapaṭalo hutvā gacchatīti “abbho”ti vuccati. “Vijjumālī satakkakū”ti vuttaṃ. Satakkakūti ca anekasatapaṭalo. Ettha ca abbhasaddo tiliṅgiko daṭṭhabbo. Tathā [M 0.0126] hi ayaṃ “abbhuṭṭhitova sa yāti, sa gacchaṃ na nivattatī”ti ettha pulliṅgo. “Abbhā, mahikā, dhūmo, rajo, rāhū”ti ettha itthiliṅgo. “Abbhāni candamaṇḍalaṃ chādentī”ti ettha napuṃsakaliṅgo.

Here, 'abbha' means a cloud. For it moves, becoming of many hundred layers, and thus it is called 'abbha'. It is said, 'Vijjumālī satakkakū' (having garlands of lightning, with a hundred peaks). And 'satakkakū' means having many hundred layers. Here, the word 'abbha' should be understood as being of three genders. For example, in the phrase 'abbhuṭṭhitova sa yāti, sa gacchaṃ na nivattatī,' it is masculine. In 'Abbhā, mahikā, dhūmo, rajo, rāhū,' it is feminine. And in 'Abbhāni candamaṇḍalaṃ chādentī,' it is neuter.

Imāni pana meghassa nāmāni –

These, moreover, are the names for a cloud:

Megho valāhako laṅghi, jīmūto ambudo ghano;

Dhārādharo ambudharo, pajjunno himagabbhako.

The cloud, the rain cloud, the overspreading one, the thundercloud, the water-giver, the dense one; the stream-bearer, the water-bearer, the rain-god, the one with snow in its womb.

Yabha methune. Mithunassa janadvayassa idaṃ kammaṃ methūnaṃ, tasmiṃ methune yabhadhātu vattati. Yabhati. Yābhassaṃ.

The root Yabha is in the sense of sexual intercourse. This action of a couple, of a pair of beings, is sexual intercourse; in that sexual intercourse, the root Yabh operates. He copulates. Yābhassaṃ (sexual intercourse).

Ettha ca “methuna”nti esā sabbhivācā, lajjāsampannehi puggalehi vattabbabhāsābhāvato. Tathā hi “methuno dhammo na paṭisevitabbo”ti ca “na me rājā sakhā hoti, na rājā hoti methuno”ti ca sobhane vācāvisaye ayaṃ bhāsā āgatā. “Yabhatī”tiādikā pana bhāsā “sikharaṇī”tiādikā bhāsā viya asambhivācā. Na hi hirottappasampanno lokiyajanopi īdisiṃ vācaṃ bhāsati. Evaṃ santepi adhimattukkaṃsagatahirottappopi bhagavā mahākaruṇāya sañcoditahadayo lokānukampāya parisamajjhe abhāsi. Aho tathāgatassa mahākaruṇāti.

Herein, the term 'methuna' is a civil expression, unlike a word that is not to be spoken by individuals possessed of shame. For instance, phrases like 'the sexual act should not be practiced' and 'the king is not my friend, nor is the king my partner in sexual intercourse' are found in contexts of refined speech. On the other hand, expressions like 'yabhati' and similar terms, as well as phrases like 'sikharaṇī', are uncivil expressions. Indeed, not even a worldly person endowed with shame and moral dread speaks such a word. Yet, even so, the Blessed One, though possessing extremely elevated shame and moral dread, his heart stirred by great compassion, out of pity for the world, spoke in the midst of the assembly. Oh, the great compassion of the Tathāgata!

Imāni pana methunadhammassa nāmāni –

Moreover, these are the names for the act of sexual intercourse:

Saṃvesanaṃ niddhuvanaṃ, methunaṃ sūrataṃ rataṃ;

Byathayo gāmadhammo ca, yābhassaṃ mohanaṃ rati.

Cohabitation, intercourse, sexual union, amorous sport, pleasure; affliction, vulgar behavior, copulation, delusion, enjoyment.

Asaddhammo ca vasala-dhammo mīḷhasukhampi ca;

Dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti, dvando gammo’dakantiko.

And the ignoble practice, the outcast's practice, and also pleasure in filth; the union of two by two, coupling, the vulgar, that which ends in fluid.

Sibha vibha katthane. Sibhati. Vibhati.

The roots Sibha and Vibha are in the sense of boasting. He boasts. He boasts.

Debha [M 0.0127] abhi dabhi sadde. Debhati. Ambhati. Ambho. Dambhati.

The roots Debha, Abhi, and Dabhi are in the sense of sound. It sounds. It sounds. Ambho (sound). It sounds.

Ettha ca ambho vuccati udakaṃ. Tañhi nijjīvampi samānaṃ oghakālādīsu vissandamānaṃ ambhati saddaṃ karotīti ambhoti vuccati.

Here, 'ambho' is called water. For though it is lifeless, when flowing during times of flood and so on, it makes a sound, hence it is called 'ambho'.

Imānissa nāmāni –

These are its names:

Pānīyaṃ udakaṃ toyaṃ, jalaṃ pāto ca ambu ca;

Dakaṃ kaṃ salilaṃ vāri, āpo ambho papampi ca.

Pānīyaṃ, udakaṃ, toyaṃ, jalaṃ, and pāto, and ambu; dakaṃ, kaṃ, salilaṃ, vāri, āpo, ambho, and also papaṃ.

Nīrañca kepukaṃ pāni, amataṃ elameva ca,

Āponāmāni etāni, āgatāni tato tato.

And nīraṃ, kepukaṃ, pāni, amataṃ, and also elaṃ; these are names for water, come from various sources.

Ettha ca “vālaggesu ca kepuke. Pivitañca tesaṃ bhusaṃ hoti pānī”tiādayo payogā dassetabbā.

And here, usages such as 'on the tips of hairs and in the foam' and 'and for them, the drinking of water is abundant' and so on should be shown.

Thabhi khabhi paṭibaddhe thambhati, vitthambhati. Khambhati, vikkhambhati. Thambho. Thaddho, upatthambho. Upatthambhinī. Vikkhambho. Vikkhambhitakileso.

The roots Thabhi and Khabhi are in the sense of being obstructed. He is stiff or obstructs (thambhati, khambhati); he supports or paralyzes (vitthambhati); he suppresses (vikkhambhati). Thambho (pillar, obstruction). Thaddho (stiff), upatthambho (support). Upatthambhinī (supporting). Vikkhambho (suppression). Vikkhambhitakileso (one whose defilements are suppressed).

Jabha jabhi gattavināme. Jabhati. Jambhati, vijambhati. Vijambhanaṃ, vijambhitā. Vijambhanto, vijambhamāno, vijambhito.

The roots Jabha and Jabhi are in the sense of bending the body. He yawns (jabhati, jambhati); he stretches or yawns (vijambhati). Yawning (vijambhanaṃ, vijambhitā). Yawning (vijambhanto, vijambhamāno), yawned or stretched (vijambhito).

Sabbha kathane. Sabbhati.

The root Sabbha is in the sense of speaking. He speaks.

Vabbha bhojane. Vabbhati.

'Vabbha' in the sense of eating. He eats.

Gabbha dhāraṇe. Gabbhati. Gabbho.

'Gabbha' in the sense of holding or containing. He holds or contains. Womb, embryo, interior.

Ettha gabbhoti mātukucchipi vuccati kucchigataputtopi. Tathā hi “yamekarattiṃ paṭhamaṃ, gabbhe vasati māṇavo”ti ettha mātukucchi “gabbho”ti vuccati. “Gabbho me deva patiṭṭhito. Gabbho ca patito chamā”ti ca ettha pana kucchigataputto. Apica gabbhoti āvāsaviseso. “Gabbhaṃ [M 0.0128] paviṭṭho”tiādīsu hi ovarako “gabbho”ti vuccati.

Here, 'gabbha' refers both to the mother's womb and to the child in the womb. For example, in the phrase, "On that first night, the young one dwells in the gabbha," here 'gabbha' means the mother's womb. Again, in the phrases, "O king, a gabbha has been established in me," and "The gabbha has fallen to the ground," here 'gabbha' refers to the child in the womb. Furthermore, 'gabbha' can also denote a particular dwelling. In phrases like, "He entered the gabbha," here 'gabbha' means an inner chamber.

Rabha rābhasse. Āpubbo rabha hiṃsākaraṇavāyamanesu. Rābhassaṃ rābhasabhāvo. Taṃsamaṅgino pana pāḷiyaṃ “caṇḍā ruddhā rabhasā”ti evaṃ āgatā.

'Rabha' in the sense of impetuosity or violence. With the prefix 'ā', 'rabha' is in the sense of harming, doing, and striving. 'Rābhassaṃ' is the state of impetuosity or violence. Those endowed with that quality are found in the Pāli as 'fierce, angry, impetuous'.

Tattha rabhasāti karaṇuttariyā. Rabhati, ārabhati, samārabhati, ārambhati. Rabhaso. Ārambho. Samārambho, ārabhanto. Samārabhanto. Āraddhaṃ me vīriyaṃ. Sārambhaṃ. Anārambhaṃ. Sārambho te na vijjati. Pakāraṇārambho. Vīriyārambho. Ārabhituṃ. Ārabhitvā. Ārabbha.

Here, 'rabhasā' means 'supreme in action'. He acts, he undertakes, he intensely undertakes, he initiates. Impetuosity. Undertaking. Intense undertaking, one who undertakes. One who intensely undertakes. My energy has been aroused. With undertaking. Without undertaking. No undertaking is found in you. Undertaking for a reason. Undertaking of energy. To undertake. Having undertaken. Having undertaken.

Ettha vīriyārambhoti vīriyasaṅkhāto ārambho. Ārambhasaddo kamme āpattiyaṃ kriyāya vīriye hiṃsāya vikopaneti anekesu atthesu āgato.

Here, 'vīriyārambha' means the undertaking reckoned as energy. The word 'ārambha' occurs in many meanings, such as action, offense, deed, energy, harming, and agitation.

“Yaṃ kiñci dukkhaṃ sambhobhi, sabbaṃ ārambhapaccayā;

Ārambhānaṃ nirodhena, natthi dukkhassa sambhavo”ti
