"Whatever suffering arises, all arises from undertaking; with the cessation of undertakings, there is no arising of suffering."

Ettha hi kammaṃ ārambhoti āgataṃ. “Ārambhati ca vippaṭisārī ca hotī”ti ettha āpatti. “Mahāyaññā mahārambhā, na te honti mahapphallā”ti ettha yūpussāpanādikriyā. “Ārambhatha nikkamatha, yuñjatha buddhasāsane”ti ettha vīriyaṃ. “Samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ uddissa pāṇaṃ ārambhantī”ti ettha hiṃsā. “Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirato hotī”ti ettha chedanabhañjanādikaṃ vikopanaṃ. Iccevaṃ –

Here indeed, 'ārambha' means action. In 'He undertakes and regrets,' here it means offense. In 'Great sacrifices, great undertakings, they do not bear great fruit,' here it refers to actions like setting up sacrificial posts. In 'Undertake, set forth, strive in the Buddha's teaching,' here it means energy. In 'They undertake killing living beings intending it for the ascetic Gotama,' here it means harming. In 'He abstains from injuring seed-germination and plant-growth,' here it refers to disturbance or injury such as cutting and breaking. Thus indeed—

Kamme [M 0.0129] āpattiyañceva, vīriye hiṃsākriyāsu ca;

Vikopane ca ārambha-saddo hotīti niddise;

In action and also in offense, in energy and in acts of harming, and in disturbance, the word 'ārambha' occurs, thus one should specify.

Labha lābhe. Labhati, labbhati. Lābho, laddhaṃ, alattha, alatthuṃ.

'Labha' in the sense of gain. He gains, it is gained. Gain, obtained, he obtained, they obtained.

Subha dittiyaṃ. Sobhati. Sobhā, sobhanaṃ, sobhito.

'Subha' in the sense of shining. It shines. Splendor, beautiful, shining.

Khubha sañcalane. Khobhati, saṅkhobhati. Hatthināge padinnamhi, khubbhittha nagaraṃ tadā. Khobhā, saṅkhobho.

'Khubha' in the sense of agitation. It agitates, it disturbs. When the elephant-king was let loose, the city was then agitated. Agitation, disturbance.

Nabha tubha hiṃsāyaṃ. Nabhati. Tubhati.

'Nabha' and 'tubha' in the sense of harming. He harms. He harms.

Sambha vissāse. Sambhati. Sambhatti, sambhatto.

'Sambha' in the sense of trust. He trusts. Trust, trusted.

Lubha vimohane. Lobhati, palobhati. Thullakumārīpalobhanaṃ. Kārite pana “lobheti, palobheti, palobhetvā”ti rūpāni bhavanti. Divādigaṇaṃ pana patvā giddhiyatthe “lubbhatī”ti rūpaṃ bhavati.

'Lubha' in the sense of deluding. He deludes, he allures. The alluring of a plump young woman. But in the causative, forms like 'lobheti, palobheti, palobhetvā' occur. However, having entered the Divādi class, in the sense of greed, the form 'lubbhati' occurs.

Dabhi ganthane. Dambhati. Dambhanaṃ.

'Dabhi' in the sense of binding. He binds. Binding.

Rubhi nivāraṇe. Rumbhati, sannirumbhati. Sannirumbho, sannirumbhitvā.

'Rubhi' in the sense of obstructing. It obstructs, it completely obstructs. Complete obstruction, having completely obstructed.

Ubha ubbha umbha pūraṇe. Ubhati. Ubbhati. Umbhati. Ubhanā. Ubbhanā. Umbhanā. Obho. Keṭubhaṃ. Ubbhaṃ. Kumbho. Kumbhī. Kārite “obheti. Ubbheti. Umbhetī”ti rūpāni bhavanti.

'Ubha', 'ubbha', and 'umbha' in the sense of filling. It fills. It fills or raises. It fills or swells. Filling. Raising. Swelling. Overflow. Keṭubha. Raised. A pot. A pitcher. In the causative, forms like 'obheti, ubbheti, umbheti' occur.

Tattha keṭubhanti kriyākappavikappo kavīnaṃ upakāriyasatthaṃ. Idaṃ panettha nibbacanaṃ kiṭeti gameti kriyādivibhāgaṃ, taṃ vā anavasesapariyādānato keṭento gamento obheti pūretīti keṭutaṃ kiṭaubhadhātuvasena. Ubbhati ubbheti [M 0.0130] pūretīti ubbhaṃ, pūraṇanti attho. Cariyāpiṭakepi hi īdisī saddagati dissati, taṃ yathā? “Mahādānaṃ pavattesi, accubbhaṃ sāgarūpama”nti. Tattha ca accubbhanti ativiya yācakānaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ pūraṇaṃ. Akkhumbhantipi pāṭho. Kumbhoti kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena ubbhetabboti kumbho, so eva itthiliṅgavasena kumbhī. Ettha ca “kumbhī dhovati onato”ti payogo.

Here, 'keṭubha' refers to a treatise that aids poets with the arrangement and variations of actions. Herein, this is the etymology: it 'kiṭeti' (collects or arranges) or 'gameti' (leads to) the divisions of actions; or, 'keṭento' (collecting or arranging) or 'gamento' (leading to) completely, it 'obheti' (fills) or 'pūreti' (fills), thus 'keṭubha' from the roots 'kiṭ' and 'ubha'. Because it fills ('ubbhati', 'ubbheti', 'pūreti'), it is 'ubbhaṃ'; the meaning is 'fulfilling'. Indeed, such a usage of the word is seen in the Cariyāpiṭaka, for example: "He set forth a great almsgiving, exceedingly abundant, like the ocean." And there, 'accubbhaṃ' means excessively fulfilling the intention of beggars. 'Akkhumbhaṃ' is also a reading. 'Kaṃ' is said to be water; that which is to be filled with it is 'kumbho'; that same word in the feminine gender is 'kumbhī'. And here, the usage is: "Bent over, he washes the pitcher."

Kumbhasaddo ghaṭe hatthi-siropiṇḍe dasambaṇe;

Pavattatīti viññeyyo, viññunā nayadassinā.

The word 'kumbha' should be understood as occurring in the sense of a pot, a lump on an elephant's head, and a ten-ambaṇa measure; this should be recognized by the wise who see the method.

Bhakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'bha'.

Makārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ma'.

Mā māne sadde ca. Māti. Mātā. Ettha mātāti janikā vā cūḷamātā vā mahāmātā vā.

The root 'Mā' is used in the sense of pride and sound. It forms 'Māti'. 'Mātā' (mother). Here, 'mātā' means either a birth mother, a foster mother, or a great mother.

Mū bandhane. Mavati. Kiyādigaṇassa panassa “munātī”ti rūpaṃ.

The root 'Mū' is used in the sense of binding. It forms 'Mavati'. But for this root in the Kiyādi group, the form is 'munāti'.

Me paṭidānaādānesu. Meti, mayati. Medhā.

The root 'Me' is used in the sense of giving back and taking. It forms 'Meti', 'mayati'. 'Medhā' (wisdom).

Ettha medhāti paññā. Sā hi sukhumampi atthaṃ dhammañca khippameva meti ca dhāreti cāti medhāti vuccati. Ettha pana metīti gaṇhāti. Tathā hi aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ vuttaṃ “asani viya siluccaye kilese medhati hiṃsatīti medhā, khippaṃ gahaṇadhāraṇaṭṭhena vā medhā”ti. Saṅgamatthavācakassa pana medhadhātussa vasena medhati sīlasamādhiādīhi saddhammehi siriyā ca saṅgacchatīti medhāti attho gahetabbo. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Here, 'medhā' means wisdom. For it quickly comprehends ('meti') and retains ('dhāreti') even subtle meanings and teachings, hence it is called 'medhā'. Here, however, 'meti' means 'to grasp'. As stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī: "'Medhā' is so called because it harms ('medhati'), that is, destroys ('hiṃsati'), the defilements like a thunderbolt on a rocky mountain; or it is 'medhā' because of its swiftness in grasping and retaining." Alternatively, based on the root 'medha,' which conveys the meaning of 'association,' the meaning of 'medhā' should be understood as: it associates with good qualities such as morality and concentration, and with glory. Thus, it is said:

“Dvidhātuyekadhātuyā[M 0.0131], dviratthavatiyāpi ca;

Medhāsaddassa nipphattiṃ, jaññā sugatasāsane”ti.

"In the Sugata's Dispensation, one should know the derivation of the word 'medhā'—from two roots, from one root, and also as having two meanings."

Omā sāmatthiye. Sāmatthiyaṃ samatthabhāvo. Aluttantoyaṃ dhātu, omāti, omanti.

The root 'Omā' is used in the sense of ability. 'Sāmatthiyaṃ' means the state of being capable. This root does not elide its final vowel; it forms 'omāti', 'omanti'.

Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “omāti bhante bhagavā iddhiyā manomayena kāyena brahmalokaṃ upasaṅkamitu”nti. Tattha omātīti pahoti sakkoti.

Here is the Pāli text: "Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is able to approach the Brahma-world with a mind-made body by means of psychic power." In this context, 'omāti' means 'is able' or 'can'.

Timu addabhāve. Addabhāvo tintabhāvo. Temati. Tinto, temiyo. Temitukāmā temiṃsu.

The root 'Timu' is used in the sense of being moist. 'Addabhāvo' means the state of being moist. It forms 'Temati'. 'Tinto', 'temiyo'. 'Temitukāmā temiṃsu' (they, desiring to moisten, moistened).

Ettha temiyoti evaṃnāmako kāsirañño putto bodhisatto. So hi rañño ceva mahājanassa ca hadayaṃ temento addabhāvaṃ pāpento sītalabhāvaṃ janento jātoti “temiyo”ti vuccati.

Here, 'Temiya' refers to the Bodhisatta, son of the king of Kāsi, so named. He was called 'Temiya' because, having been born, he moistened the hearts of the king and the populace, bringing them to a state of tenderness and generating coolness.

Nitami kilamane. Nitammati. Hadayaṃ dayhate nitammāmi.

The root Nitami is used in the sense of weariness. It forms Nitammati (it becomes weary). 'Hadayaṃ dayhate nitammāmi' (my heart burns, I am weary).

Camu chamu japu jhamu umu jimu adane. Camati. Camū. Camūti senā. Chamati. Jamati. Jhamati. Umati. Jemati.

The roots Camu, Chamu, Japu, Jhamu, Umu, and Jimu are used in the sense of eating. They form: Camati. Camū. 'Camū' means an army. Chamati. Jamati. Jhamati. Umati. Jemati.

Kamu padavikkhepe. Padavikkhepo padasā gamanaṃ. Idaṃ pana vohārasīsamattaṃ vacanaṃ, tasmā “nāssa kāye aggi vā visaṃ vā satthaṃ vā kamatī”tiādīsu apadavikkhepatthopi gahetabbo. Kamati. Caṅkamati, atikkamati. Abhikkamati. Paṭikkamati. Pakkamati. Parakkamati. Vikkamati. Nikkamati. Saṅkamati. Saṅkamanaṃ. Saṅkanti. Kamanaṃ. Caṅkamanaṃ. Atikkamo. Abhikkamo. Paṭikkamo. Pakkamo. Vikkamo. Nikkamo. Atikkanto puriso. Abhikkantā ratti. Nikkhamati. Abhinikkhamati. Kārite [M 0.0132] nikkhāmeti. Aññānipi yojetabbāni. Yasmā panāyaṃ dhātu curādigaṇaṃ patvā icchākanti yatthesu vattati, tasmā tepi atthe upasaggavisesite katvā idha abhikkantasaddassa atthuddhāraṃ vattabbampi avatvā upari curādigaṇeyeva kathessāma.

The root Kamu is used in the sense of stepping. 'Padavikkhepo' means going by foot. This, however, is merely a conventional expression; therefore, in instances such as 'fire, poison, or a weapon does not enter his body,' a meaning other than the movement of the feet should also be taken. It forms: Kamati (he goes, moves). Caṅkamati (he walks back and forth). Atikkamati (he transgresses, surpasses). Abhikkamati (he advances, approaches). Paṭikkamati (he retreats, returns). Pakkamati (he departs, goes away). Parakkamati (he exerts himself, strives). Vikkamati (he strides, walks powerfully). Nikkamati (he goes out, exits). Saṅkamati (he passes on, transmigrates). Saṅkamanaṃ (passing on, transmigration). Saṅkanti (a transition, passing over). Kamanaṃ (going, movement). Caṅkamanaṃ (walking back and forth). Atikkamo (transgression, surpassing). Abhikkamo (advance, approach). Paṭikkamo (retreat, return). Pakkamo (departure, going away). Vikkamo (stride, powerful walk). Nikkamo (going out, exit). Atikkanto puriso (a man who has transgressed). Abhikkantā ratti (the night has advanced). Nikkhamati (he goes out, exits). Abhinikkhamati (he goes forth, renounces). In the causative, it forms nikkhāmeti (he causes to go out). Other forms should also be construed accordingly. Since this root, upon entering the curādi class, also functions with the meanings of wishing and desiring, therefore, having distinguished those meanings with specific prefixes, we will not state the analysis of the meaning of the word 'abhikkanta' here, but will speak of it later, in the curādi section itself.

Yamu uparame. Uparamo viramanaṃ. Yamabhi. Yamo. “Pare ca na vijānanti, mayamettha yamāmase”ti idamettha nidassanaṃ. Tattha yamāmaseti uparamāma, nassāma, marāmāti attho.

The root Yamu is used in the sense of ceasing. 'Uparamo' means desisting. It forms: Yamabhi, Yamo. The example here is: 'Others do not know that we shall perish here.' Here, 'yamāmase' means 'we cease, we perish, we die'—this is the meaning.

Nama bahutte sadde. Bahutto saddo nāma uggatasaddo. Namati.

The root Nama is used in the sense of abundant sound. 'Bahutto saddo' means a loud sound. It forms: Namati (it sounds).

Ama dama hamma mima chama gatimhi. Amati. Damati. Hammati. Mimati. Chamati. Chamā.

The roots Ama, Dama, Hamma, Mima, and Chama are used in the sense of going. They form: Amati (he goes). Damati (he tames). Hammati (he strikes). Mimati (he measures). Chamati (he goes). Chamā (the earth).

Chamāti pathavī. Chamāsaddo itthiliṅgo daṭṭhabbo, “na chamāyaṃ nisīditvā āsane nisinnassa agilānassa dhammaṃ desessāmīti sikkhā karaṇīyā”ti ca “chamāyaṃ parivattāmi vāricarova ghamme”ti ca payogadassanato. So ca kho sattahi aṭṭhahi vā vibhattīhi dvīsu ca vacanesu yojetabbo. Chamanti gacchanti etthāti chamā.

'Chamā' means the earth. The word 'chamā' should be regarded as feminine, as seen from its usage in: 'A training rule should be undertaken: I will not teach the Dhamma to one seated on a seat if I am not ill and am myself sitting on the ground,' and 'I toss about on the ground like a fish in the heat.' And it should be construed with seven or eight cases and in the two numbers. 'They go on it' (chamanti), hence 'chamā' (the earth).

Dhama saddaggisaṃ yogesu. Dhamadhātu sadde ca mukhavātena saddhiṃ aggisaṃyoge ca vattati. Tattha paṭhamatthe “saṅkhaṃ dhamati. Saṅkhadhamako. Bheriṃ dhamati. Bheridhamako. Dhame dhame nātidhame”ti payogo. Dutiyatthe “aggiṃ dhamati. Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ, aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhama”nti payogo.

The root Dhama is used in the senses of sound and connection with fire. The root Dhama applies to sound and, along with blowing with the mouth, to connection with fire. In the first sense, the usage is: 'He blows the conch. A conch-blower. He beats the drum. A drum-beater. Blow, blow, do not overblow.' In the second sense, the usage is: 'He blows on the fire. He stirs himself up, like fanning a tiny flame.'

Bhāma kodhe. Bhāmati.

The root Bhāma is used in the sense of anger. It forms: Bhāmati (it rages).

Namu [M 0.0133] namane. Namati. Namo. Nataṃ, namanaṃ. Nati. Namaṃ. Namamāno. Namanto. Namito. Nāmaṃ. Nāmitaṃ. Namituṃ. Natvā, natvāna. Namitvā, namitvāna, namituna. Kārite “nāmeti, nāmayati. Nāmetvā. Nāmayitvā”ti rūpāni bhavanti. Tatra hi “namati namitvā”ti evaṃpakārāni padāni namanatthe vandanāyañca daṭṭhabbāni, “namo natvā”ti evaṃpakārāni pana vandanāyameva. Atrāyamupalakkhaṇamattā payogaracanā –

The root Namu is used in the sense of bending. It forms: Namati (he bends). Namo (homage). Nataṃ (bent), namanaṃ (bending). Nati (inclination). Namaṃ (bending). Namamāno (bending). Namanto (bending). Namito (bent). Nāmaṃ (name). Nāmitaṃ (caused to bend). Namituṃ (to bend). Natvā, natvāna (having bent). Namitvā, namitvāna, namituna (having bent). In the causative, forms like 'nāmeti, nāmayati (he causes to bend); nāmetvā, nāmayitvā (having caused to bend)' arise. Here, words of the type 'namati, namitvā' should be understood in the sense of bending and of paying homage, while words of the type 'namo, natvā' refer solely to homage. Here is merely an illustrative example of usage:

Rukkho phalī phalabhāragarutāya namitvāna bhijjati;

Vuddho jarājajjaratāya namati namitvā gacchati;

Saddho buddhaṃ namati namitvā gacchati;

Namo buddhassa satthāraṃ natvāna agamāsīti;

A fruit-bearing tree, from the weight of its fruit-burden, having bent, breaks; The old man, worn by decay, bends; having bent, he passes away; The faithful one reveres the Buddha; having revered, he departs; 'Homage to the Buddha'; having paid homage to the Teacher, he went.

Ettha namoti padaṃ nipātesupi labbhati. Tena hi paccattopayogavacanāni abhinnarūpāni dissanti “devarāja namo tyatthu. Namo katvā mahesino”ti. Upasaggehipi ayaṃ yojetabbā “paṇamati, paṇāmo, uṇṇamati, uṇṇati” iccādinā.

Here, the word 'namo' is also found among particles. Thus, expressions of personal usage like 'Homage to you, King of Gods,' and 'having paid homage to the great sage,' appear with unchanging forms. This root should also be combined with prefixes, as in 'paṇamati (he bows down), paṇāmo (bowing down); uṇṇamati (he rises up), uṇṇati (rising up),' etc.

Khamu sahane. Khamati. Khanti. Khamo, khamanaṃ, evaṃ bhāve. Kattari pana “khantā. Khamitā. Khamo hoti sītassapi uṇhassapī”ti payogā.

The root Khamu is used in the sense of forbearance. It forms: Khamati (he endures). Khanti (patience). Khamo (forbearing), khamanaṃ (endurance), thus in the sense of state. In the agent sense, however, the usages are: 'khantā (she is forbearing). Khamitā (he is forbearing). Khamo hoti sītassapi uṇhassapī (he is able to endure both cold and heat).'

Sama adassane. Samati, vūpasamati aggi.

The root Sama is used in the sense of disappearing. It forms: Samati (it is calmed), vūpasamati aggi (the fire goes out).

Yama parivesane. Yamati. Yamo. Yamarājā.

The root Yama is used in the sense of serving. It forms: Yamati (he serves). Yamo (the server). Yamarājā (King Yama).

Sama sadde. Samati.

The root Sama is used in the sense of sound. It forms: Samati (it sounds).

Sama thama velambe. Samati. Thamati.

The roots Sama and Thama are used in the sense of delaying. They form: Samati (it delays). Thamati (it delays).

Vāyama īhāyaṃ. Vāyamati. Vāyāmo.

The root Vāyama is used in the sense of exertion. It forms: Vāyamati (he strives). Vāyāmo (effort).

Gamu [M 0.0134] gatiyaṃ. Gacchati. Gamako. Gato. Gati. Gamanaṃ. Kārite “gameti, gamayati, gacchāpetī”tiādīni bhavanti.

The root Gamu is used in the sense of going. It forms: Gacchati (he goes). Gamako (one who goes). Gato (gone). Gati (going, destination). Gamanaṃ (the act of going). In the causative, forms such as 'gameti, gamayati, gacchāpeti (he causes to go),' etc., occur.

Ramu kīḷāyaṃ. Ramati. Viramati. Paṭiviramati. Uparamati. Ārati. Virati. Paṭivirati. Uparati. Veramaṇi. Viramaṇaṃ. Rati. Ramaṇaṃ. Rato. Ārato virato paṭivirato. Uparato, uparamo. Ārāmo.

The root Ramu is used in the sense of delighting. It forms: Ramati (he delights). Viramati (he abstains). Paṭiviramati (he refrains completely). Uparamati (he ceases). Ārati (abstinence). Virati (abstinence). Paṭivirati (complete restraint). Uparati (cessation). Veramaṇi (abstinence). Viramaṇaṃ (abstinence). Rati (delight). Ramaṇaṃ (enjoyment). Rato (one who delights). Ārato (one who has desisted), virato (one who has abstained), paṭivirato (one who has refrained completely). Uparato (one who has ceased), uparamo (cessation). Ārāmo (a park).

Vamu uggiraṇe. Vamati. Vamathu. Vammiko.

The root Vamu is used in the sense of emitting. It forms: Vamati (he vomits). Vamathu (vomiting). Vammiko (an anthill).

Dhīratthu taṃ visaṃ vantaṃ, yamahaṃ jīvitakāraṇā;

Vantaṃ paccāvamissāmi, mataṃ me jīvitā varaṃ.

Fie on that vomited poison, which I, for the sake of life, would swallow again. Death is better for me than life.

Tattha vammikoti vamatīti, vantakoti, vantussayoti, vantasinehasambandhoti vammiko. So hi ahinakulaundūragharagoḷikādayo nānappakāre pāṇake vamatīti vammiko. Upacikāhi vantakoti vammiko. Upacikāhi vamitvā mukhatuṇḍakena ukkhittapaṃsucuṇṇena kaṭippamāṇenapi porisappamāṇenapi ussitoti vammiko. Upacikāhi vantakheḷasinehena ābaddhatāya sattasattāhaṃ deve vassantepi na vippakirayati, nidāghepi tato paṃsumuṭṭhiṃ gahetvā tasmiṃ muṭṭhinā pīḷiyamāne sinehova nikkhamati, evaṃ vantasinehasambandhoti vammiko.

Here, 'vammika' means 'that which emits' (vamatīti), 'that which is emitted' (vantakoti), 'a heap of what is emitted' (vantussayoti), or 'that which is connected with emitted stickiness' (vantasinehasambandhoti), hence 'vammiko'. For it is an anthill because it emits various kinds of creatures like snakes, mongooses, rats, house lizards, and so forth. It is an anthill because it is emitted by termites. It is an anthill because, having been emitted by them, the termites raise it, whether waist-high or a man's height, with dust particles from their mouthparts. Because it is bound by the sticky saliva emitted by termites, even when the gods rain for seven weeks, it does not scatter; and even in the hot season, when a handful of dust is taken from it and squeezed in the hand, the stickiness itself comes out—thus, it is connected with emitted stickiness.

Ettha pana “bhagavā, himavā”tiādīni padāni na kevalaṃ vantupaccayavaseneva nipphādetabbāni, atha kho vamudhātuvasenapi nipphādetabbāni, tenāha visuddhimaggakārako “yasmā pana tīsu bhavesu taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ gamanamanena vantaṃ, tasmā “bhavesu vantagamano’ti vattabbe bhavasaddato bhakāraṃ, gamanasaddato gakāraṃ, vantasaddato vakārañca dīghaṃ katvā ādāya bhagavāti vuccati, yathā loke ‘mehanassa [M 0.0135] khassa mālā’ti vattabbe mekhalā”ti vadatā niruttinayena saddasiddhi dassitā.

Here, however, words like 'Bhagavā,' 'Himavā,' etc., are to be derived not only by means of the vantu suffix, but also by means of the root vamu. Therefore, the author of the Visuddhimagga says: 'Because by him the 'going' known as craving in the three existences is vomited out, therefore, instead of saying 'bhavesu vantagamano' (one whose going in existences is vomited out), taking the syllable 'bha' from 'bhava,' the syllable 'ga' from 'gamana,' and taking the syllable 'va' from 'vanta' and making it long, it is called 'Bhagavā,' just as in the world, instead of saying 'mehanassa khassa mālā' (a garland of the stream of urine), it is said 'mekhalā.'' Thus, the formation of the word is shown by the method of etymology.

Ettha, siyā “visamamidaṃ nidassanaṃ, yena ‘mehanassa khassa mālā’ti ettha mekārakhakāralākārānaṃ kamato gahaṇaṃ dissati, “bhavesu vantagamano’ti ettha pana bhakāravakāragakārānaṃ kamato gahaṇaṃ na dissatī”ti? Saccaṃ, idha pana “aggāhito, vijjācaraṇasampanno”tiādīsu viya guṇasaddassa paranipātavasena “bhavesu gamanavanto”ti vattabbepi evamavatvā saddasatthe yebhuyyena guṇasaddānaṃ pubbanipātabhvassa icchitattā saddasatthavidūnaṃ kesañca viññūnaṃ manaṃ tosetuṃ “bhagavā”ti pade akkharakkamaṃ anapekkhitvā atthamattanidassanavasena “āhitaggi, sampannavijjācaraṇo”tiādīni viya pubbanipātavasena “bhavesu vantagamano”ti vuttaṃ. Īdisasmiñhi ṭhāne “āhitaggī”ti vā “aggāhito”ti vā “chinnahattho”ti vā “hatthacchinno”ti vā padesu yathā tathā ṭhitesupi atthassa ayutti nāma natthi aññamaññaṃ samānatthattā tesaṃ saddānaṃ.

Here, one might say: "This is an inconsistent illustration. In 'the garland of dung's dung,' the sequence of the letters 'me,' 'kha,' and 'la' is seen to be taken in order, but in 'one who has abandoned going in existences,' the sequence of the letters 'bha,' 'va,' and 'ga' is not seen to be taken in order." True. However, in this case, just as in phrases like 'aggāhito' (fire-maintained one) and 'vijjācaraṇasampanno' (accomplished in knowledge and conduct), where the qualifying word is placed after, it could have been stated as 'bhavesu gamanavanto' (one possessing going in existences). But without stating it thus, because in the science of language the prior placement of qualifying words is generally preferred, in order to please the minds of some wise persons skilled in the science of language, the word 'Bhagavā' is explained as 'bhavesu vantagamano' (one who has abandoned going in existences) with prior placement, without regard to the sequence of letters and merely to illustrate the meaning, just like 'āhitaggi' (one who has maintained the fire) and 'sampannavijjācaraṇo' (accomplished in knowledge and conduct). For in such a case, whether in the words 'āhitaggī' or 'aggāhito,' or 'chinnahattho' (one with a cut hand) or 'hatthacchinno' (one whose hand is cut), however they may be placed, there is no inappropriateness in the meaning, since those words are synonymous with each other.

Vedajātotiādīsu pana ṭhānesu atthevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ visuddhimagge “bhagavā”ti padassa vamudhātuvasenapi nipphatti dassitā, taṭṭīkāyampi ca dassitā “bhage vamīti bhagavā. Bhāge vamīti bhagavā”ti. Nibbacanaṃ pana evaṃ veditabbaṃ – bhagasaṅkhātaṃ siriṃ issariyaṃ yasañca vami uggiri kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya anapekkho chaḍḍayīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhāni nāma nakkhattāni, tehi samaṃ gacchanti pavattantīti bhagā, sineruyugandharauttarakuruhimavantādibhājanalokā, visesasannissayasobhākappaṭṭhiyabhāvato. Tepi bhagavā vami tannivāsisattāvāsasamatikkamanato tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena pajahīti bhagavā.

In instances such as 'Vedajāto,' however, it should be understood that there is indeed meaning. Thus, in the Visuddhimagga, the derivation of the word 'Bhagavā' is also shown by way of the root 'vam,' and in its commentary as well it is shown: "Bhage vamīti bhagavā. Bhāge vamīti bhagavā." The etymology, however, should be understood thus: he vomited, spat out, and discarded without attachment, like a ball of phlegm, the glory, sovereignty, and fame designated as 'bhaga'; thus, he is Bhagavā. Or else, 'bhāni' are the constellations. The receptacle worlds such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and Himavantā are called 'bhagā' because they proceed or move along with them, due to their being distinguished by special foundations, splendor, and aeon-long stability. The Bhagavā also vomited and abandoned even these by transcending the abodes of the beings dwelling therein and by relinquishing the sensual desire and passion connected with them; thus, he is Bhagavā.

Cakkavattisiriṃ [M 0.0136] yasmā, yasaṃ issariyaṃ sukhaṃ;

Pahāsi lokacittañca, sugato bhagavā tato.

Since the Sugata, the Bhagavā, abandoned the glory of a universal monarch, fame, sovereignty, happiness, and the worldly mind, therefore is he so called.

Tathā khandhāyatanadhātādibhede dhammakoṭṭhāse sabbaṃ papañca sabbaṃ yogaṃ sabbaṃ ganthaṃ sabbaṃ saṃyojanaṃ samucchinditvā amataṃ dhātuṃ samadhigacchanto vami uggiri anapekkho chaḍḍayi na paccāvamīti bhagavā. Atha vā sabbepi kusalākusale sāvajjānavajje hīnappaṇīte kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme ariyamaggañāṇamukhena vami uggiri anapekkho pariccaji pajahīti bhagavā.

Likewise, in the divisions of phenomena such as the aggregates, sense bases, and elements, having cut off all proliferation, all yokes, all bonds, and all fetters, while attaining the deathless element, he vomited, spat out, discarded without attachment, and did not take up again; thus he is Bhagavā. Or else, by means of the knowledge of the noble path, he vomited, spat out, forsook, and abandoned without attachment all wholesome and unwholesome states, the blameable and blameless, the inferior and superior, the dark and bright with their counterparts; thus he is Bhagavā.

Khandhāyatanadhātādī, dhammabhedā mahesinā;

Kaṇhasukkā yato vantā, tatopi bagavā mato.

Since the divisions of Dhamma—aggregates, sense bases, elements, and so on, both dark and bright—were relinquished by the great sage, therefore he is considered Bhagavā.

Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana himavāti padassa vamudhātuvasenapi nipphatti dassitā. Tathā hi sambhavajātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “himavāti himapātasamaye himayuttoti himavā. Gimhakāle himaṃ vamatīti himavā”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “himavā”ti padassa vamudhātuvasenapi nipphatti dassitā, ayaṃ nayo īdisesu ṭhānesupi netabbo. “Guṇavāgaṇavā”tiādīsu pana na netabbo. Yadi nayeyya, “guṇavā gaṇavā”ti padānaṃ “nigguṇo parihīnaguṇo”ti evamādiattho bhaveyya, tasmā ayaṃ nayo sabbatthapi na netabbo. Ettha siyā “yadi “bhagavā’tiādipadānaṃ vamudhātuvasena nipphatti hoti, kathaṃ “bhagavanto, bhagavanta”ntiādīni sijjhantī”ti? Yathā “bhagavā”ti padaṃ niruttinayena sijjhati, tathā tānipi teneva sijjhanti. Acinteyyo hi niruttinayo kevalaṃ atthayuttipaṭibandhamattova, atthayuttiyaṃ sati nipphādetumasakkuṇeyyānipi rūpāni aneneva sijjhanti. Ettha ca [M 0.0137] yaṃ niruttilakkhaṇaṃ āharitvā dassetabbaṃ siyā, taṃ upari rūpanipphādanādhikāre udāharaṇehi saddhiṃ pakāsessāma.

In the Jātaka commentary, however, the derivation of the word 'himavā' is also shown by way of the root 'vam.' For instance, in the commentary on the Sambhava Jātaka, it is said: "'Himavā' is so called because it is connected with snow (himayutta) during the time of snowfall. In the summer, it 'vomits snow' (himaṃ vamati), hence 'himavā.'" Thus, in the Jātaka commentary, the derivation of the word 'himavā' is also shown by way of the root 'vam,' and this method should be applied in similar instances. However, it should not be applied to words like 'guṇavā' and 'gaṇavā.' If it were applied, the words 'guṇavā' and 'gaṇavā' would have meanings such as 'devoid of virtue' and 'lacking virtue.' Therefore, this method should not be applied everywhere. Here, one might ask: "If words like 'Bhagavā' are derived by way of the root 'vam,' how then are forms like 'bhagavanto' and 'bhagavanta' established?" Just as the word 'Bhagavā' is established by the method of etymology, so too are those forms established by the same method. For the method of etymology is indeed inconceivable, being bound only by the appropriateness of meaning. When there is appropriateness of meaning, even forms that are impossible to derive by other means are established by this very method. And here, whatever etymological characteristic should be brought forth and shown, we shall explain that later in the chapter on the formation of forms, along with examples.

Idha sāramate munirājamate,

Paramaṃ paṭutaṃ sujano pihayaṃ;

Vipulatthadharaṃ dhaninītimimaṃ,

Satataṃ bhajataṃ matisuddhakaraṃ.

Let the good person, aspiring to the highest skill in this essential doctrine, the doctrine of the King of Sages, constantly resort to this Saddanīti, which bears a vast meaning and purifies the mind.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññunaṃ

Thus, for the wise in the paths of expression within the ninefold Teaching, with its commentaries, in the three Piṭakas,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the treatise Saddanīti, composed for the sake of proficiency,

Saravaggapañcakantiko nāma dhātuvibhāgo

the Division of Roots, named 'Ending with the Fifth of the Vowel Group',

Pannarasamo paricchedo.

the Fifteenth Chapter.

16. Bhūvādigaṇikapariccheda

16. The Chapter on the Bhū-group

Ito paraṃ avaggantā, missakā ceva dhātuyo;

Vakkhāmi dhātubhedādi-kusalassa matānugā.

Henceforth, following the opinion of one skilled in the divisions of roots and so on, I shall explain the roots with unclassified final consonants and the mixed roots.

Yakārantadhātu

Roots Ending in 'ya'

Yā gatipāpuṇesu. Yāti, yanti. Yātu, yantu. Yeyya, yeyyuṃ, anupariyeyyuṃ. Yathāsambhavaṃ padamālā yojetabbā. Yanto puriso. Yantī itthī. Yantaṃ kulaṃ. Yānaṃ, upayānaṃ, uyyānaṃ iccādīni. Divādigaṇikassa panassa “yāyati, yāyantī”tiādīni rūpāni bhavanti.

The root Yā is used in the senses of going and attaining. Yāti, yanti. Yātu, yantu. Yeyya, yeyyuṃ, anupariyeyyuṃ. The paradigm of forms should be supplied as appropriate. Yanto puriso. Yantī itthī. Yantaṃ kulaṃ. Yānaṃ, upayānaṃ, uyyānaṃ, and so on. For this root belonging to the Divādi group, however, there are forms such as yāyati and yāyanti.

Tatra yānantiādīsu yanti etenāti yānaṃ, rathasakaṭādi. Upayanti etena issarassa vā piyamanāpassa vā santikaṃ gacchantīti upayānaṃ, paṇṇākāraṃ. “Upayānāni me dajjuṃ, rājaputta tayi gate”ti ettha hi paṇṇākārāni “upayānānī”ti [M 0.0138] vuccanti. Sampannadassanīyapupphaphalāditāya uddhaṃ olokentā yanti gacchanti etthāti uyyānaṃ.

Therein, regarding yānaṃ and so on: that by which one goes (yanti etena) is a yānaṃ, a chariot, cart, etc. That by which one approaches or goes near a lord or a dear and beloved one is an upayānaṃ, a gift. For in the line, 'They should give me gifts (upayānāni) when you, O prince, have gone,' gifts are called upayānāni. A place where people go looking upwards because of the abundance of beautiful flowers, fruits, and so on to be seen, is an uyyānaṃ, a park.

Byā ummīsane. Byāti, byanti. Byāsi, byātha. Byāmi, byāma. Yathāsambhavaṃ padamālā yojetabbā. Tatra panāyaṃ pāḷi “yāva byāti nimmīsati, tatrāpi rasatibbayo”ti. Tattha yāva byātīti yāva ummīsati, purāṇabhāsā esā, ayañhi yasmiṃ kāle bodhisatto cūḷabodhiparibbājako ahosi, tasmiṃ kāle manussānaṃ vohāro.

The root Byā is used in the sense of opening the eyes. Byāti, byanti. Byāsi, byātha. Byāmi, byāma. The paradigm of forms should be supplied as appropriate. In this regard, there is this Pāli passage: "In the time it takes to open and close the eyes, even then there is a passing away of essence." In this context, 'yāva byāti' means 'as long as one opens the eyes'—this is an ancient expression; for this was the common parlance of people at the time when the Bodhisatta was the wanderer Cūḷabodhi.

Yu missane gatiyañca. Yoti, yavati. Āyu, yoni.

The root Yu is used in the senses of mingling and motion. Yoti, yavati. Āyu, yoni.

Tattha “āyū”ti āsaddo upasaggo. Āyavanti missībhavanti sattā etenāti āyu. Atha vā āyavanti āgacchanti pavattanti tasmiṃ sati arūpadhammāti āyu. Tathā hi aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ vuttaṃ “āyavanaṭṭhena āyu. Tasmiñhi sati arūpadhammā āyavanti āgacchanti pavattanti, tasmā āyūti vuccatī”ti. “Āyu, jīvitaṃ, pāṇo” iccete pariyāyā lokavohāravasena. Abhidhammavasena pana “ṭhiti yapanā yāpanā jīvitindriyaṃ” iccetepi teheva saddhiṃ pariyāyā. Yonīti aṇḍajādīnaṃ aṇḍajādīhi saddhiṃ yāya missībhāvo hoti, sā yoni. Idaṃ panettha nibbacanaṃ “yavanti ettha sattā ekajātisamanvayena aññamaññaṃ missakā hontīti yoni” iti. Ettha ca yonisaddassa atthuddhāro nīyate. Yonīti khandhakoṭṭhāsassapi kāraṇassapi passāvamaggassapi nāmaṃ. “Catasso nāgayoniyo. Catasso supaṇṇayoniyo”ti ettha hi khandhakoṭṭhāso yoni nāma. “Yoni [M 0.0139] hesā bhūmija phalassa adhigamāyā”ti ettha kāraṇaṃ. “Na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brūmi, yonijaṃ mattisambhava”nti ettha passāvamaggo. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Here, regarding 'āyu', the particle 'ā' is a prefix. Beings come together and mingle through this, hence it is called āyu. Alternatively, when this exists, formless phenomena approach, arise, and persist—thus it is called āyu. As stated in the Aṭṭhasālinī: 'Āyu means 'coming together.' For when this exists, formless phenomena approach, arise, and persist; therefore, it is called āyu.' 'Āyu, jīvitaṃ, pāṇo'—these are synonyms in worldly usage. From the Abhidhamma perspective, 'ṭhiti, yapanā, yāpanā, jīvitindriyaṃ' are also synonyms with those. Yoni is that by which oviparous beings and so forth mingle with other oviparous beings. Here, the derivation is: 'Because beings here mingle with each other through a common birth-class, it is called yoni.' And here, the meaning of the word 'yoni' is derived. Yoni is also a term for a division of aggregates, a cause, and the urinary passage. For instance: 'Four kinds of nāga-yonis, four kinds of supaṇṇa-yonis'—here, yoni refers to a division of aggregates. 'This is the yoni, Bhūmija, the cause for the attainment of the fruit'—here, it refers to the cause. 'I do not call one a brahmin who is born from a yoni, sprung from a mother'—here, it refers to the urinary passage. Thus it is said:

Khandhānañcāpi koṭṭhāse, muttamagge ca kāraṇe;

Imesu tīsu atthesu, yonisaddo pavattati.

The word 'yoni' applies in these three senses: in the divisions of the aggregates, in the urinary passage, and in the cause.

Bye saṃvaraṇe. Byāyati.

The root 'bye' is used in the sense of restraining. Byāyati.

Bye pavattiyaṃ. Byeti sahabyo.

The root 'bye' is used in the sense of occurrence. Byeti, sahabyo.

Ettha sahabyoti saha byeti saha pavattatīti sahabyo, sahāyo, ekabhavūpago vā. Tathā hi “tāvatiṃsānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapanno”tiādīsu ekabhavūpago “sahabyo”ti vuccati.

Here, 'sahabyo' means 'one who goes together,' 'one who occurs together,' thus 'sahabyo,' a companion, or one who has attained the same existence. For example, in phrases like 'he was reborn into the companionship of the Tāvatiṃsa devas,' one who shares the same existence is called 'sahabyo.'

Haya gatiyaṃ. Hayati. Hayo. Hayoti asso. So hi hayati sīghaṃ gacchatīti hayoti vuccati. Imāni panassa nāmāni –

The root 'haya' is used in the sense of motion. Hayati. Hayo. 'Hayo' means a horse. For it moves swiftly, hence it is called 'hayo.' Moreover, these are its names:

Asso turaṅgo turago, vājī vāho hayopi ca;

Tabbhedā sindhavo ceva, gojo assataropi ca.

Asso, turaṅgo, turago, vājī, vāho, and also hayo; its varieties are the Sindh horse, the goja, and also the mule.

Kāraṇākāraṇaññū tu, ājānīyo hayuttamo;

Ghoṭako tu khaḷuṅkasso, vaḷavoti ca vuccati;

Assapoto kisoroti, khaḷuṅkotipi vuccati;

However, the one who knows what is proper and improper is the noble thoroughbred, the most excellent horse. A 'ghoṭaka' is an unruly horse, and a 'vaḷavā' is a mare. A foal is called a 'kisora' and also a 'khaḷuṅka'.

Hariya gatigelaññesu. Hariyati.

The root 'hariya' is used in the senses of motion and sickness. Hariyati.

Aya vaya paya maya taya caya raya gatiyaṃ. Ayati. Vayati. Payati. Mayati. Tayati. Cayati. Rayati. Ayo, samayo, vayo, payo, rayo. Mayatayacayadhātūnaṃ nāmikapadāni upaparikkhitabbāni.

The roots 'aya', 'vaya', 'paya', 'maya', 'taya', 'caya', 'raya' are used in the sense of motion. Ayati. Vayati. Payati. Mayati. Tayati. Cayati. Rayati. Ayo, samayo, vayo, payo, rayo. The nominal forms of the roots 'maya', 'taya', 'caya' should be examined.

Tattha [M 0.0140] ayoti kāḷalohaṃ, ayati nānākammārakiccesu upayogaṃ gacchatīti ayo. Vayoti paṭhamavayādiāyukoṭṭhāso, vayati parihāniṃ gacchatīti vayo. Payoti khīrassapi udakassapi nāmaṃ, payati janena pātabbabhāvaṃ gacchatīti payo. Rayoti vego, yo “javo”tipi vuccati, tasmā rayanaṃ javanaṃ rayo. Ettha samayasaddassa atthuddhāro vuccate aha nibbacanena. Samayasaddo –

Here, 'ayo' means black iron; it goes to use in various blacksmith's tasks, hence 'ayo.' 'Vayo' means the portion of life such as the first stage of life; it goes to decline, hence 'vayo.' 'Payo' is a name for milk and also water; it goes to the state of being drinkable by people, hence 'payo.' 'Rayo' means speed, which is also called 'javo'; therefore, 'rayana' is 'javana,' hence 'rayo.' Here, the derivation of the meaning of the word 'samaya' is stated. The word 'samaya' is:

Samavāye khaṇe kāle, samaye hetudiṭṭhisu;

Paṭilābhe pahāne ca, paṭivedhe ca dissati.

It is seen in the sense of conjunction, moment, time, assembly, cause, views, acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.

Tathā hi “appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāma kālañca samayañca upādāyā”ti evamādīsu samavāyo attho. “Ekova kho bhikkhave khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu khaṇo. “Uṇhasamayo pariḷāhasamayo”tiādīsu kālo. “Mahāsamayo pavanasmi”ntiādīsu samūho. “Samayopi kho te bhaddāli appaṭividdho ahosī”tiādīsu hetu. “Tena samayena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasatī”tiādīsu diṭṭhi.

For example: In phrases like 'Perhaps tomorrow we will approach, considering the time and occasion,' the meaning is conjunction. In phrases like 'Monks, there is only one moment and occasion for living the holy life,' it means moment. In phrases like 'The hot season, the scorching season,' it means time. In phrases like 'A great assembly in the forest,' it means multitude. In phrases like 'Even the reason, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you,' it means cause. In phrases like 'At that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāno, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was dwelling in Mallikā's park, at the single-hall debating ground on the Tinduka strip,' it means view.

“Diṭṭhe dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti

He who understands the goal in this very life and the goal in the future, through that full understanding of the goal, the wise one is called a sage.

Ādīsu [M 0.0141] paṭilābho. “Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”tiādīsu pahānaṃ. “Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”tiādīsu paṭivedho. Ettha ca upasaggānaṃ jotakamattattā tassa tassa atthassa vācako samayasaddo evāti samayasaddassa atthuddhārepi saupasaggo abhisamayasaddo vutto.

In (phrases) like these, it means acquisition. In phrases like 'Through the complete overcoming of conceit, he made an end of suffering,' it means abandonment. In phrases like 'The meaning of suffering is oppression, the conditioned, affliction, and penetration,' it means penetration. And here, because prefixes merely illuminate meaning, the word 'samaya' itself is the designator of that particular meaning. Thus, even in deriving the meaning of 'samaya', the word 'abhisamaya' is mentioned with its prefix.

Tattha sahakārīkāraṇatāya sannijjhaṃ sameti samavetīti samayo, samavāyo. Sameti samāgacchati maggabrahmacariyaṃ ettha tadādhārapuggaloti samayo, khaṇo. Samenti ettha, etena vā saṅgacchanti dhammā sahajātadhammehi uppādādīhi vāti samayo, kālo. Dhammappavattimattatāya atthato abhūtopi hi kālo dhammappavattiyā adhikaraṇaṃ karaṇaṃ viya ca parikappanāmattasiddhena rūpena vohariyatīti. Samaṃ, saha vā avayavānaṃ ayanaṃ pavatti avaṭṭhānanti samayo, samūho, yathā “samudāyo”ti. Avayavasahāvaṭṭhānameva hi samūho. Paccayantarasamāgame eti phalaṃ etasmā uppajjati pavattati cāti samayo, hetu, yathā “samudayo”ti. Sameti saṃyojanabhāvato sambandhā eti attano visaye pavattati, daḷhaggahaṇabhāvato vā saṃyuttā ayanti pavattanti sattā yathābhinivesaṃ etenāti samayo, diṭṭhi. Diṭṭhisaṃyojanena hi sattā ativiya bajjhanti. Samiti saṅgati samodhānanti samayo, paṭilābho. Samassa nirodhassa yānaṃ, sammā vā yānaṃ apagamo appavattīti samayo, pahānaṃ. Ñāṇena abhimukhaṃ sammā etabbo adhigantabboti samayo, dhammānaṃ aviparīto sabhāvo, abhimukhabhāvena sammā eti gacchati bujjhatīti samayo. Yathābhūtasabhāvāvabodho. Evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe samayasaddassa pavatti veditabbā.

Here, because it comes together and converges fittingly due to its nature as a co-operating cause, it is 'samaya', a conjunction. Because the path and the holy life converge here, and the individuals who are its basis, it is 'samaya', a moment. Because phenomena coincide here, or because through this they associate with co-nascent phenomena, arising, and other conditions, it is 'samaya', time. For though time is ultimately unreal, being merely the occurrence of phenomena, it is conventionally spoken of as a basis and instrument for the occurrence of phenomena, like a mere conceptual designation established by a nominal form. Because it is the equal or simultaneous going, occurrence, or establishment of parts, it is 'samaya', a collection, just as in 'samudāya' (assemblage). For a collection is simply the co-establishment of parts. Because the result comes, arises, and proceeds from this when other conditions meet, it is 'samaya', a cause, just as in 'samudaya' (origin). Because it comes together and, due to its nature as a fetter, it proceeds connectedly and persists in its own object; or because beings, connected by the nature of firm grasping, move and proceed through this according to their inclination, it is 'samaya', a view. For beings are deeply bound by the fetter of views. Because it is a coming together, a meeting, an integration, it is 'samaya', acquisition. Because it is the going to the cessation of the whole, or the proper going, departure, and non-arising, it is 'samaya', abandonment. Because it is the unperverted nature of phenomena, to be properly approached and realized directly by knowledge; or because, by being directly faced, one correctly goes, understands, and awakens, it is 'samaya', the comprehension of things as they truly are. In this way, the application of the term 'samaya' should be understood in each of these senses.

Nanu [M 0.0142] ca atthamattaṃ pati saddā abhinivisantīti na ekena saddena aneke atthā abhidhīyantīti? Saccametaṃ saddavisese apekkhite. Saddavisese hi apekkhamāne ekena saddena anekatthābhidhānaṃ na sambhavati. Na hi yo kālattho samayasaddo, soyeva samūhādiatthaṃ vadati. Ettha pana tesaṃ tesaṃ atthānaṃ samaya saddavacanīyatā sāmaññamupādāya anekatthatā samayasaddassa vuttā. Evaṃ sabbattha atthuddhāre adhippāyo veditabbo.

Is it not the case that words adhere only to a single meaning, so that multiple meanings are not expressed by a single word? This is true when a specific word is considered. For when one considers a specific word, the expression of multiple meanings by a single word is not possible. Indeed, the word 'samaya' that means time does not express the meaning of a group and so forth. But here, the manifold meaning of the word 'samaya' is stated by taking into account the commonality of the expressibility of those various meanings by the word 'samaya.' Thus, in all cases of deriving meaning, the intention should be understood.

Ito yāto ayato ca, nipphattiṃ samudīraye;

Viññū samayasaddassa, samavāyādivācino.

From the roots 'yā' and 'aya', the discerning one should declare the derivation of the word 'samaya', which expresses conjunction and so forth.

Ito yāto ayato ca, samānatthehi dhātuhi;

Evaṃ samānarūpāni, bhavantīti ca īraye.

From the roots 'yā' and 'aya', and from roots with similar meanings, one should state that thus similar forms arise.

Naya rakkhaṇe ca. Cakāro gatipekkhako. Nayati. Nayo. Nayoti nayanaṃ gamananti nayo, pāḷigati. Nayanti vā rakkhanti atthaṃ etenāti nayo, tathattanayādi.

The root 'naya' is used in the sense of protection and so on. The particle 'ca' implies motion. Nayati. Nayo. 'Nayo' means leading, going; thus, 'nayo' refers to the way of the Pāli text. Or, they lead or protect the meaning by this, hence 'nayo', as in 'tathattanaya' (the method of reality) and so forth.

Daya dānagatihiṃsādānarakkhāsu. Dayati. Dayā.

The root 'day' is in the sense of giving, going, harming, taking, and protecting. It gives, goes, harms, takes, or protects. Hence, 'dayā'.

Dayāti mettāpi vuccati karuṇāpi. “Dayāpanno”ti ettha hi mettā “dayā”ti, mettacittataṃ āpannoti hi attho. “Adayāpanno”ti ettha pana karuṇā “dayā”ti vuccati. Nikkaruṇataṃ āpannoti hi attho. Evaṃ dayāsaddassa mettākaruṇāsu pavatti veditabbā. Tathā hi abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ “dayāsaddo yattha yattha pavattati, tattha tattha adhippāyavasena yojetabbo. Dayāsaddo hi anurakkhaṇatthaṃ antonītaṃ katvā pavattamāno mettāya ca karuṇāya ca pavattatī”ti.

The term 'dayā' is also said to be mettā and also karuṇā. Here, in 'dayāpanno', 'dayā' refers to mettā, for the meaning is 'endowed with a mind of mettā'. Conversely, in 'adayāpanno', 'dayā' is said to be karuṇā, for the meaning is 'devoid of karuṇā'. Thus, the application of the word 'dayā' in relation to mettā and karuṇā should be understood. Indeed, as stated in the Abhidhammaṭīkā: 'Wherever the word "dayā" occurs, it should be applied according to the intended meaning. For the word "dayā," when occurring with the sense of inward protection, applies to both mettā and karuṇā.'

Vacanattho panettha evaṃ veditabbo – dayati dadāti sattānaṃ abhayaṃ etāyāti dayā. Dayati gacchati vibhāgaṃ akatvā [M 0.0143] pāpakalyāṇajanesu samaṃ vattati, sītena samaṃ pharantaṃ rajomalañca pavāhentaṃ udakamivātipi dayā, mettā. Dayati vā hiṃsati kāruṇikaṃ yāva yathādhippetaṃ parassa hitanipphattiṃ na pāpuṇāti, tāvāti dayā. Dayati anuggaṇhāti pāpajanampi sajjano etāyātipi dayā. Dayati attano sukhampi pahāya khedaṃ gaṇhāti sajjano etāyāti dayā. Dayanti gaṇhanti etāya mahābodhisattā buddhabhāvāya abhinīhārakaraṇakāle hatthagatampi arahattaphalaṃ chaḍḍetvā saṃsārasāgarato satte samuddharitukāmā anassāsakaraṃ atibhayānakaṃ mahantaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ, pacchimabhave ca saha amatadhātupaṭilābhena anekaguṇasamalaṅkataṃ sabbaññutaññāṇañcātipi dayā, karuṇā. Karuṇāmūlakā hi sabbe buddhaguṇā.

Here, the meaning of the word should be understood thus: By this, one gives fearlessness to beings; hence, 'dayā'. Or, it goes, proceeding equally among evil and good people without making distinctions, like cool water that pervades equally and washes away dust and impurities; this too is 'dayā,' which is mettā. Or, it harms or afflicts the compassionate one for as long as the intended benefit for another is not attained; this too is 'dayā'. Or, by this, a virtuous person helps even wicked people; this too is 'dayā'. Or, by this, a virtuous person, abandoning even their own happiness, takes on weariness; this too is 'dayā'. Or, by this, the Great Bodhisattas, at the time of making their aspiration for Buddhahood, abandoning even the fruit of arahantship that was within their grasp, desiring to uplift beings from the ocean of saṃsāra, take hold of the unbearable, extremely terrifying, immense suffering of saṃsāra; and in their final existence, together with the attainment of the deathless element, they also take hold of the all-knowing wisdom adorned with countless virtues; this too is 'dayā,' which is karuṇā. For all the virtues of the Buddhas are rooted in karuṇā.

Aparo nayo – dayanti anurakkhanti satte etāya, sayaṃ vā anudayati, anudayamattameva vā etanti dayā, mettā ceva karuṇā ca. Kiñci payogamettha kathayāma “seyyathāpi gahapati gijjho vā kaṅko vā kulalo vā maṃsapesiṃ ādāya dayeyya. Puttesu maddī dayesi, sassuyā sasuramhi ca. Dayitabbo rathesabha”. Tattha dayeyyāti uppatitvā gaccheyya, gatyatthavasenetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dayesīti mettacittaṃ kareyyāsi. Dayitabboti piyāyitabbo. Ubhayampetaṃ vivaraṇaṃ rakkhaṇatthaṃ antogadhaṃ katvā adhippāyatthavasena katanti veditabbaṃ.

Another method: By this, they protect beings, or one has compassion oneself, or it is simply compassion; this is 'dayā,' which is both mettā and karuṇā. Here, we will state some usages: 'Just as, householder, a vulture or a heron or a hawk might take a piece of meat and fly away (dayeyya). Maddī had compassion (dayesi) for her children, and for her mother-in-law and father-in-law. The noble bull should be treated with compassion (dayitabbo).' Here, 'dayeyya' means 'it would fly up and go'; this should be understood in the sense of motion. 'Dayesi' means 'you should cultivate a mind of mettā'. 'Dayitabbo' means 'should be loved'. Both of these explanations should be understood as having been made according to the intended meaning, by including them within the sense of protection.

Ūyī tantasantāne. Ūyati. Ūto, ūtavā.

The root 'ūy' is in the sense of weaving a continuous thread. It weaves. Woven; one who has woven.

Pūyī visaraṇe duggandhe ca. Pūyati. Pūto, pūtavā. Pūtimacchaṃ kusaggena, yo naro upanayhati.

The root 'pūy' is in the sense of spreading and foul smell. It spreads or stinks. Spread or stunk; one who has spread or stunk. 'The man who wraps a putrid fish with a blade of kusa grass.'

Kanuyī [M 0.0144] sadde. Kanuyati. Kanuto, kanutavā.

The root 'kanuy' is in the sense of sound. It sounds. Sounded; one who has sounded.

Khamāya vidhūnane. Khamāyati. Khamāto, khamātavā.

The root 'khamā' is in the sense of shaking off. It shakes off. Shaken off; one who has shaken off.

Phāyi pāyi vuddhiyaṃ. Phāyati. Phīto, phatavā.

The roots 'phāy' and 'pāy' are in the sense of growth. It grows. Grown; one who has grown.

Tattha tatavantupaccayā, yakāralopo, dhātvantassa sarassa ikārādeso ca daṭṭhabbo. Esa nayo “pūto pūtavā”tiādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ daṭṭhabbo. Pāyati. Pāyo. Apāyo. Ettha ca natthi pāyo vuddhi etthāti apāyo. Atha vā pana ayato sukhato apetoti apāyotipi nibbacanīyaṃ. Apāyoti ca nirayo tiracchānayoni pettivisayo asurakāyoti cattāro apāyā.

Here, on account of the suffixes -ta and -tavant, the elision of 'y' and the substitution of 'i' for the final vowel of the root should be noted. This principle should be observed similarly, as appropriate, in cases like 'pūto, pūtavā'. It grows. Hence, 'pāyo'. Hence, 'apāyo'. And here, 'apāyo' means 'there is no growth (pāyo) here'. Alternatively, 'apāyo' can also be explained as 'devoid of gain (aya) and happiness (sukha)'. And 'apāyo' refers to the four woeful states: hell, the animal realm, the sphere of spirits, and the host of asuras.

Tāyu santānapālanesu. Tāyati. Tāyanaṃ. Divādigaṇe pana tā pālaneti dhātuṃ passatha, tassa “tāyati tāṇa”nti rūpāni. Ubhayesaṃ kriyāpadaṃ samaṃ. Akārayakārapaccayamatteneva nānattaṃ, nāmikapadāni pana visadisāni “tāyanaṃ, tāṇa”nti.

The root 'tāy' is in the sense of continuity and protection. It protects or continues. Hence, 'tāyanaṃ'. However, in the Divādi group, you see the root 'tā' in the sense of protection, and its forms are 'tāyati' and 'tāṇa'. The verb form is the same for both. The difference is only in the suffix, 'a' or 'ya'. The nominal forms, however, are dissimilar: 'tāyanaṃ' and 'tāṇa'.

Cāyu pūjānisāmanesu. Pūjā pūjanā. Nisāmanaṃ olokanaṃ savanañca vuccati. “Iṅgha maddi nisāmehi. Nisāmayatha sādhavo”ti ca ādīsu hi olokanasavanāni nisāmanasaddena vuttāni. Apica ñāṇena upaparikkhaṇampi nisāmanamevāti gahetabbaṃ. Cāyati, apacāyati. Anagāre pabbajite, apace brahmacāriye. Ye vuddhamapacāyanti. Apacitiṃ dasseti. Niccaṃ vuddhāpacāyino.

The root 'cāy' is in the sense of honoring and observing. Honoring is 'pūjā'. 'Nisāmana' is said to be looking and listening. Indeed, in passages like 'Come, Maddī, observe!' and 'Good people, listen!', looking and listening are expressed by the word 'nisāmana'. Moreover, examination by means of knowledge should also be taken as 'nisāmana'. It honors; it reveres. For example: 'the homeless renunciants, the celibate ones, should be revered'; 'Those who revere the elders'; 'He shows reverence'; 'Always revering the elders'.

Yakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'y'.

Rakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'r'.

Rā [M 0.0145] ādāne. Rāti.

The root 'rā' is in the sense of taking. It takes.

Ri santāne. Reti. Reṇu. Reṇūti rajo.

The root 'ri' is in the sense of continuation or flowing. It flows. Hence, 'reṇu'. 'Reṇu' means dust.

Ru gatiyaṃ rosane ca. Ravati, viravati.

The root 'ru' is in the sense of movement and displeasure. It moves or is displeased; it cries out.

Ru sadde. Roti, ravati. Ravo, uparavo. Rutamanuññaṃ ruciyā ca piṭṭhi. Rutanti ravanaṃ rutaṃ, saddo.

The root 'ru' is in the sense of sound. It sounds, it cries out. Hence, 'ravo' (sound), 'uparavo' (clamor). An example: 'a pleasant sound and a delightful surface'. 'Rutanti' means they sound; 'ravanaṃ' and 'rutaṃ' mean sound.

Re sadde. Rāyati. Rā. Ratti. Ettha ca rāti saddo. Rattīti nisāsaṅkhāto sattānaṃ saddassa vūpasamakālo. Rā tiyyati ucchijjati etthāti ratti.

The root 're' is in the sense of sound. It sounds. Hence, 'rā' (sound) and 'ratti' (night). Here, 'rā' means sound. 'Ratti' is designated as night, the time when the sound of beings subsides. It is 'ratti' because sound (rā) is cut off or ceases therein.

Brū viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Api hantvā hato brūti.

The root 'brū' is in the sense of clear speech. For example: 'Though having struck, say you were struck.'

Bravīti, brunti. Brūsi, brūtha. Brūmi, brūma. Brūte, bruvante. Brūse, bruvhe. Bruve, brumhe.

Active voice: He says, they say. You (sg.) say, you (pl.) say. I say, we say. Middle voice: He says, they say. You (sg.) say, you (pl.) say. I say, we say.

Brūtu, bruvitu, bruvantu. Brūhi, brūtha. Brūmi, brūma. Brūtaṃ, bruvantaṃ.

Imperative, Active: Let him say, let them say. Say (you sg.), say (you pl.). Let me say, let us say. Middle: Let him say, let them say.

Ettha ca ambaṭṭhasutte “puna bhavaṃ gotamo bruvitū”ti pāḷidassanato “bruvitū”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbatthāpi upaparikkhitvā nayo gahetabbo.

Here, the form 'bruvitū' is given based on the Pāli reading in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta: 'puna bhavaṃ gotamo bruvitū' (Let the venerable Gotama speak again). In this way, the principle should be understood by examining all such cases.

Bruveyya, bruve, bruveyyuṃ. Bruveyyāsi, bruveyyātha. Bruveyyāmi, bruveyyāma. Bruvetha, bruveraṃ. Bruvetho, bruveyyāvho. Bruveyyaṃ. Bruveyyāmhe.

Optative, Active: He should say, they should say. You (sg.) should say, you (pl.) should say. I should say, we should say. Middle: He should say, they should say. You (sg.) should say, you (pl.) should say. I should say, we should say.

Pabrūti. Anubrūti. Pabrūtu, anubrūtu. Pabruveyya, anubruveyya. Evaṃ sabbattha paanuupasaggehipi yathāsambhavaṃ padamālā yojetabbā.

He proclaims. He repeats. Let him proclaim, let him repeat. He should proclaim, he should repeat. Thus, in all cases, the paradigms should be formed as appropriate with prefixes such as 'pa' and 'anu'.

Āha, āhu. Brave, bravittha, bravire. Bravittho, bravivho. Braviṃ, bravimhe. Parokkhāvasena vuttāni.

He said, they said. He spoke, you (pl.) spoke, they spoke. You (sg.) spoke, you (pl.) spoke. I spoke, we spoke. These are stated in the perfect tense.

Abravā[M 0.0146], abravū. Abravo, abravattha. Abravaṃ, abravamhā. Abravattha, abravatthuṃ. Abravase, abravhaṃ. Abraviṃ, abravimhase. Hiyyattanīvasena vuttāni.

Active: He said, they said. You (sg.) said, you (pl.) said. I said, we said. Middle: He said, they said. You (sg.) said, you (pl.) said. I said, we said. These are stated in the imperfect tense.

Abravi, abravuṃ. Abravo, abravittha. Abraviṃ, abravimhā. Abravā, abravū. Abravase, abravivhaṃ. Abravaṃ, abravimhe. Ajjatanīvasena vuttāni.

Active: He said, they said. You (sg.) said, you (pl.) said. I said, we said. Middle: He said, they said. You (sg.) said, you (pl.) said. I said, we said. These are stated in the aorist tense.

Bruvissati, bruvissanti. Abravissā, abravissaṃsu. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ netabbaṃ. Kammapadaṃ appasiddhaṃ. Sace pana siyā, “brūyatī”ti siyā “luyati, lūyatī”ti padāni viya.

He will say, they will say. He would have said, they would have said. All the remaining forms should be inferred. The passive form is not found. But if it were to exist, it would be 'brūyatī,' like the forms 'luyati' and 'lūyatī'.

Jīra brūhane. Brūhanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ. Jīrati. Jīraṃ. Jīramāno. Jīraṇaṃ. Appassutāyaṃ puriso, balibaddova jīrati.

The root 'jīra' is in the sense of growing old (brūhana). 'Brūhana' means growing. It grows old. Old age. Growing old. The process of growing old. 'This man of little learning grows old like an ox.'

Pūra pūraṇe. Pūrati. Pūratova mahodadhi. Sabbe pūrentu saṅkappā. Pūrituṃ, pūritvā, pūraṃ, pūritaṃ. Puṇṇaṃ, paripuṇṇaṃ. Sampuṇṇaṃ, pūraṇaṃ. Pūraṇo kassapo. Kārite “pāramiyo pūreti, pūrayati, pūrāpeti, pūrāpayati. Pūretvā, pūrayitvā, pūrāpetvā, pūrāpayitvā, paripūretvā” iccādīni bhavanti.

Pūra: in the sense of filling. Pūrati. Pūratova mahodadhi: The great ocean is ever filling. Sabbe pūrentu saṅkappā: May all aspirations be fulfilled. Pūrituṃ, pūritvā, pūraṃ, pūritaṃ. Puṇṇaṃ, paripuṇṇaṃ. Sampuṇṇaṃ, pūraṇaṃ. Pūraṇo Kassapo. In the causative, such forms as: pāramiyo pūreti, pūrayati, pūrāpeti, pūrāpayati; pūretvā, pūrayitvā, pūrāpetvā, pūrāpayitvā, paripūretvā, and so on, occur.

Ghora gatipaṭighāte. Gatipaṭighātaṃ gatipaṭihananaṃ. Ghorati.

Ghora: in the sense of obstructing movement. Obstructing movement is striking against movement. Ghorati.

Dhora gaticāturiye. Gaticāturiyaṃ gatichekabhāvo. Dhoreti.

Dhora: in the sense of skill in movement. Skill in movement is the state of being an expert in movement. Dhoreti.

Sara gatiyaṃ. Sarati, visarati, ussarati. Ussāraṇā. Saro. Saṃsāro iccādīni. Tattha saroti rahado. Saṃsāroti vaṭṭaṃ, yo “bhavo”tipi vuccati.

Sara: in the sense of movement. Sarati, visarati, ussarati. Ussāraṇā. Saro. Saṃsāro, and so on. Therein, saro means a lake. Saṃsāro means the round of rebirth, which is also called 'becoming.'

Cara caraṇe. Carati, vicarati, anucarati, sañcarati.

Cara: in the sense of moving. Carati, vicarati, anucarati, sañcarati.

Cara [M 0.0147] gatibhakkhanesu. Carati, vicarati, anucarati, sañcarati, paṭicarati. Cariyā. Caritā. Cāro. Vicāro. Anuvicāro. Upavicāro. Caraṇaṃ. Cārako. Ocarako. Brahmacariyaṃ iccādīni.

Cara: in the senses of movement and eating. Carati, vicarati, anucarati, sañcarati, paṭicarati. Cariyā. Caritā. Cāro. Vicāro. Anuvicāro. Upavicāro. Caraṇaṃ. Cārako. Ocarako. Brahmacariyaṃ, and so on.

Tattha caratīti gacchati, bhakkhati vā. Tathā hi caranti padassa gacchanto khādanto cāti atthaṃ vadanti garū. Paṭicaratīti paṭicchādeti. Cārakoti taṃpavesitānaṃ sattānaṃ sukhaṃ carati bhakkhatīti cārako, rodho. Ocarakoti adhocārī. Brahmacariyanti dānampi veyyāvaccampi sikkhāpadampi brahmavihāropi dhammadesanāpi methunaviratipi sadārasantosopi uposathopi ariyamaggopi sakalaṃ sāsanampi ajjhāsayopi vuccati.

Therein, carati means to go or to eat. Thus, the teachers explain that the word caranti means one who goes or eats. Paṭicarati means to conceal. A cāraka is a prison, because it consumes the happiness of beings who have entered there. An ocaraka is one who moves below. Brahmacariya is said to mean: giving, service, moral precepts, the divine abidings, teaching the Dhamma, abstaining from sexual intercourse, contentment with one's own wife, the Uposatha, the Noble Path, the entire dispensation, and also inclination.

Kinte vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Kissa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhijutibalavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca te nāga mahāvimānaṃ.

What was your observance, what indeed your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result? This attainment of psychic power, radiance, strength, and energy, and this great celestial mansion of yours, O Nāga?

Ahañca bhariyā ca manussaloke,

Saddhā ubho dānapatī ahumhā;

Opānabhūtaṃ me gharaṃ tadāsi,

Santappitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca.

My wife and I in the human world, were both faithful, masters of giving. My house then was like a well, and ascetics and brahmins were well satisfied.

Taṃ me vataṃ taṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Tassa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhijutibalavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca me dhīra mahāvimāna”nti

That was my observance, that indeed my holy life; of that well-practiced deed, this is the result; this attainment of psychic power, radiance, strength, and energy, and this great celestial mansion of mine, O wise one.

Imasmiñhi puṇṇakajātake dānaṃ “brahmacariya”nti vuttaṃ.

For in this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, giving is called 'brahmacariya.'

“Kena [M 0.0148] pāṇi kāmadado, kena pāṇi madhussavo;

Kena te brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhati.

By what is the hand a giver of desires, by what does the hand flow with honey? By what holy life of yours does merit prosper in the hand?

Tena pāṇi kāmadado, tena pāṇi madhussavo;

Tena me brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhatī”ti

By that is the hand a giver of desires, by that the hand flows with honey; by that holy life of mine, merit prospers in my hand.

Imasmiṃ aṅkurapetavatthumhi veyyāvaccaṃ “brahmacariya”nti vuttaṃ. “Idaṃ kho taṃ bhikkhave tittiriyaṃ nāma brahmacariyaṃ ahosī”ti imasmiṃ tittirajātake sikkhāpadaṃ “brahmacariya”nti vuttaṃ. “Taṃ kho pana pañcasikha brahmacariyaṃ neva nibbidāya na virāgāya…pe… yāvadeva brahmalokūpapattiyā”ti imasmiṃ mahāgovindasutte brahmavihārā “brahmacariya”nti vuttā. “Ekasmiṃ brahmacariyasmiṃ, sahassaṃ maccuhāyino”ti ettha dhammadesanā “brahmacariya”nti vuttā. “Pare abrahmacārī bhavissanti, mayamettha brahmacārino bhavissāmā”ti sallekhasutte methunavirati “brahmacariya”nti vuttā.

In this Aṅkurapetavatthu, service is called 'brahmacariya.' 'This, monks, was the holy life called Tittiriya'; in this Tittira Jātaka, a precept is called 'brahmacariya.' 'But, Pañcasikha, that holy life was neither for disenchantment nor for dispassion… but only for rebirth in the Brahma-world'; in this Mahāgovinda Sutta, the divine abidings are called 'brahmacariya.' 'In one holy life, a thousand are conquerors of death'; here the teaching of the Dhamma is called 'brahmacariya.' 'Others will be unchaste, but here we will be chaste'; in the Sallekha Sutta, abstinence from sexual intercourse is called 'brahmacariya.'

Mayañca bhariyā nātikkamāma,

Amhe ca bhariyā nātikkamanti;

Aññatra tāha brahmacariyaṃ carāma;

Tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare”ti

We do not transgress against our wives, and our wives do not transgress against us; apart from them, we live the holy life; therefore our young ones do not die.

Mahādhammapālajātake sadārasantoso “brahmacariya”nti vutto.

In the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, contentment with one's own wife is called 'brahmacariya.'

Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devesu, uttamena visujjhatī”ti

Through an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the khattiyas; through a middling one, among the devas; through the highest, one is purified.

Evaṃ nimijātake avītikkamavasena kato uposatho “brahmacariya”nti vutto. “Idaṃ kho pana pañcasikha brahmacariyaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya…pe… ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti [M 0.0149] mahāgovindasuttasmiṃyeva ariyamaggo “brahmacariya”nti vutto. “Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāvadeva manussehi suppakāsita”nti pāsādikasutte sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ “brahmacariya”nti vuttaṃ.

Thus, in the Nimi Jātaka, the Uposatha undertaken without transgression is called 'brahmacariya.' 'And this, Pañcasikha, is the holy life leading solely to disenchantment, to dispassion… this very Noble Eightfold Path'; in the Mahāgovinda Sutta, the Noble Path itself is called 'brahmacariya.' 'This holy life is successful, thriving, widespread, known to many, has become popular, and is well proclaimed among humans'; in the Pāsādika Sutta, the entire dispensation, encompassing the threefold training, is called 'brahmacariya.'

“Api ataramānānaṃ, phalāsāva samijjhati;

Vipakkabrahmacariyosmi, evaṃ jānāhi gāmaṇī”ti

Even for those not hurrying, the hope for the fruit succeeds; I am one with a ripened holy life, know this, village headman.

Ettha ajjhāsayo “brahmacariya”nti vutto. Iccevaṃ –

Here, inclination is called 'brahmacariya.' Thus:

Dānaṃ veyyāvaṭiyañca, sikkhā brahmavihārakā;

Dhammakkhānaṃ methunatā-virati ca uposatho.

Giving and service, training and the divine abidings; teaching the Dhamma, abstaining from sexual intercourse, and the Uposatha.

Sadāresu ca santoso, ariyamaggo ca sāsanaṃ;

Ajjhāsayo cime brahma-cariyasaddena vuccare.

Contentment with one's own wife, the Noble Path, and the Dispensation; and inclination—these are called by the word 'brahmacariya.'

Hura koṭille. Hurati.

Hura: in the sense of crookedness. Hurati.

Sara saddopatāpesu. Sarati. Saro, saraṇaṃ.

Sara: in the senses of sound and torment. Sarati. Saro, saraṇaṃ.

Ettha ca saroti saddopi vuccati usupi. Saraṇanti sarati upatāpeti hiṃsati saraṇagatānaṃ teneva saraṇagamanena bhayaṃ santāpaṃ dukkhaṃ duggatiṃ parikilesañcāti saraṇaṃ, buddhādiratanattayaṃ. Atha vā saddhā pasannā manussā “amhākaṃ saraṇamida”nti saranti cintenti, taṃ tattha ca vācaṃ niccharanti gacchanti cātipi saraṇaṃ.

And here, saro is said to mean sound and also arrow. Saraṇaṃ means that it destroys, afflicts, and harms the fear, distress, suffering, bad destinations, and defilements of those who have gone to it for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge; this refuge is the Triple Gem, beginning with the Buddha. Or, faithful and devoted people remember and think, 'This is our refuge,' and they utter words concerning it and go to it; therefore, it is also called refuge.

Sara cintāyaṃ. Sarati, susarati iccapi payogo. Appakkharānañhi bahubhāvo aññathābhāvo ca hoti, yathā “dve, duve, taṇhā tasiṇā, pamhaṃ, pakhuma”nti. Anussarati, paṭissarati. Saranti etāya sattā, sayaṃ vā sarati, saraṇamattameva vā etanti sati. Anussati, paṭissati. Saratīti sato. Punappunaṃ saratīti paṭissato.

Sara: in the sense of thinking. Sarati, susarati—this is the usage. For few syllables become many and also change, as in 'dve, duve; taṇhā, tasiṇā; pamhaṃ, pakhumaṃ.' Anussarati, paṭissarati. Beings remember by this, or one remembers oneself, or it is merely the act of remembering—thus, sati (mindfulness). Anussati, paṭissati. Because one remembers, one is mindful (sato). Because one remembers again and again, one is repeatedly mindful (paṭissato).

Dvara [M 0.0150] saṃvaraṇe. Saṃvaraṇaṃ rakkhaṇā. Dvarati. Dvāraṃ. Dvisaddūpapadaaradhātuvasenapi idaṃ rūpaṃ sijjhati. Tatrimāni nibbacanāni – dvaranti saṃvaranti rakkhanti etenāti dvāraṃ, atha vā dve kavāṭā aranti gacchanti pavattanti etthātipi dvāranti. Gehadvārampi kāyadvārādīnipi upāyopi dvāranti vuccati. Pāḷiyaṃ tu “dvāraṃ dvārā”ti ca itthinapuṃsakavasena dvārasaddo vutto. Tathā hi “dvārampi surakkhitaṃ hotī”ti ca “dvārāpesā”ti ca tassa dviliṅgatā vuttā.

Dvara: in the sense of restraint. Restraint is protection. Dvarati. Dvāraṃ. This form is also accomplished by means of the root ara with the word dvi as a prefix. Here are the etymologies: they restrain (dvaranti), guard (saṃvaranti), or protect (rakkhanti) by this—thus, dvāraṃ (door). Or, two panels go, move, or function here—thus, dvāraṃ. A house door, the sense doors, and a means are also called dvāraṃ. In the Pāli canon, the word dvāra is stated to be of both feminine and neuter gender, as dvāraṃ and dvārā. For example, in 'the door is well-guarded' (dvāraṃpi surakkhitaṃ hoti) and 'door-panels' (dvārāpesā), its two genders are stated.

Gara ghara secane. Garati. Gharati. Gharaṃ.

Gara, ghara: in the sense of sprinkling. Garati. Gharati. Gharaṃ.

Dhūra hucchane. Hucchana koṭillaṃ. Dhūrati.

Dhūra: in the sense of deception. Deception is crookedness. Dhūrati.

Tara plavanasaraṇesu. Tarati. Taraṇaṃ. Titthaṃ. Tiṇṇo. Uttiṇṇo. Otiṇṇo iccādīni. Tattha taraṇaṃ vuccati nāvā, tarati udakapiṭṭhe plavati, taranti uttaranti vā nadiṃ etenāti atthena.

Tara: in the senses of floating and crossing. Tarati. Taraṇaṃ. Titthaṃ. Tiṇṇo. Uttiṇṇo. Otiṇṇo, and so on. Therein, taraṇaṃ is called a boat, with the meaning that one floats on the surface of the water, or that they cross or go beyond a river by means of this.

Nāvā plavo taraṃ poto, taraṇaṃ uttaraṃ tathā;

Jalayānanti etāni, nāvānāmāni honti tu.

Nāvā: boat; plavo: raft; taraṃ: ferry; poto: vessel; taraṇaṃ: crossing; uttaraṃ: going beyond; jalayānaṃ: water-vehicle—these are indeed names for boats.

Tara sambhame. Sambhamo anavaṭṭhānaṃ. Tarati. Tarito. Turaṅgo.

Tara: in the sense of haste. Sambhamo: haste is instability. Tarati: he hastens. Tarito: swift. Turaṅgo: horse.

Ettha ca “so māsakhettaṃ tarito avāsari”nti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha taritoti turito sambhamanto. Avāsarinti upagacchiṃ upavisiṃ vā.

Here, the Pāli example is: 'So māsakhettaṃ tarito avāsari' (He swiftly descended to the bean field). There, 'tarito' means swift, hurrying. 'Avāsari' means he approached or sat down.

Jara roge. Ettha jararogoyeva “rogo”ti adhippeto payogavasena. Jarasaddassa hi jararoge pavattaniyamanatthaṃ “roge”ti vuttaṃ. Tena añño rogo idha rogasaddena na vuccati. Jarati. Jaro. Sajjaro. Pajjararogo. Jarena pīḷitā manussā. Yattha tu ayaṃ vayohānivācako[M 0.0151], tattha payoge “jīrati, jarā”ti cassa rūpāni bhavanti.

Jara: in the sense of disease. Here, by force of usage, the term 'disease' is intended specifically to mean the disease of old age. Indeed, the word 'disease' is stated to restrict the meaning of the word 'jara' to the disease of old age. Therefore, no other disease is referred to by the term 'disease' here. Jarati: it decays. Jaro: old age. Sajjaro: subject to old age. Pajjararogo: the disease of decrepitude. Jarena pīḷitā manussā: people afflicted by old age. But where this denotes the decline of life, there its forms 'jīrati' (it ages) and 'jarā' (aging) occur in usage.

Dara bhaye. Darati. Darī. “Bīlāsayā darīsayā”ti nidassanaṃ. Tattha darīti bhāyitabbaṭṭhena darī.

Dara: in the sense of fear. Darati: he fears. Darī: cave. 'Bīlāsayā darīsayā' (dwelling in holes, dwelling in caves) is an illustration. Herein, a cave is called 'darī' in the sense that it is to be feared.

Dara ādarānādaresu. Darati, ādarati, anādarati. Ādaro, anādaro.

Dara: in the sense of regard and disregard. Darati: he fears; ādarati: he regards; anādarati: he disregards. Ādaro: regard; anādaro: disregard.

Ettha ca daratīti daraṃ karotīti ca anādaraṃ karotīti ca attho. Yathā hi ārakāsaddo dūrāsannavācako, tathāyampi daradhātu ādarānādaravācako daṭṭhabbo. Darasaddo ca kāyadarathe cittadarathe kilesadarathe ca vattati. Ayañhi –

Here, 'daratīti' means it causes fear, and it also means it causes disregard. Just as the word 'āraka' denotes both far and near, so too should this root 'dara' be understood to denote both regard and disregard. And the word 'dara' applies to bodily distress, mental distress, and the distress of defilements. This is—

Ādittaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñci, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye dara”nti

Alas, though peaceful, I am burning, like a fire sprinkled with ghee; sprinkle me as with water, and extinguish all this distress.

Ettha kāyadarathe cittadarathe ca vattati. “Vītaddaro vītasoko vītasallo, sayaṃ abhiññāya abhāsi buddho”ti ettha pana kilesadarathe vattati. Vītaddaroti hi aggamaggena sabbakilesānaṃ samucchinnattā vigatakilesadarathoti attho.

Here, it applies to bodily distress and mental distress. In 'Vītaddaro vītasoko vītasallo, sayaṃ abhiññāya abhāsi buddho' (Free from distress, free from sorrow, free from darts, the Buddha spoke having directly known it himself), here, however, it applies to the distress of defilements. For 'Vītaddaro' means 'one whose distress of defilements has vanished,' because of the complete eradication of all defilements by the highest path.

Nara nayane. Narati. Naro, nārī.

Nara: in the sense of leading. Narati: he leads. Naro: man; nārī: woman.

Ettha naroti puriso. So hi narati netīti naro. Yathā paṭhamapakatibhūto satto datarāya pakatiyā seṭṭhaṭṭhena puri uccāṭṭhāne seti pavattatīti purisoti vuccati, evaṃ nayanaṭṭhena naroti vuccati. Puttabhātubhūtopi hi puggalo mātujeṭṭhabhaginīnaṃ netuṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati, pageva itaro itarāsaṃ. Nārīti narena yogato, narassāyanti vā nārī. Aparampettha narasaddassa nibbacanaṃ, nariyati sakena [M 0.0152] kammena niyyatīti naro, satto manusso vā. “Kammena niyyateo loko”ti hi vuttaṃ. Tattha narasaddassa tāva purisavacane “narā ca atha nāriyo”ti nidassanaṃ. Sattamanussavacane pana “buddho ayaṃ edisako naruttamo. Āmoditā naramarū”ti ca nidassanaṃ, tasmā “naroti puriso, naroti satto, naroti manusso”ti tattha tattha yathāsambhavaṃ attho saṃvaṇṇetabbo.

Here, 'nara' means a man. For he is called 'nara' because he leads (neti). Just as the first primordial being, due to his nature as a giver and his excellence, dwells and operates in a high position in the city, and thus is called 'purisa,' so too is he called 'nara' in the sense of leading. Indeed, a person who is a son or brother stands in the position of leader to his mother and elder sisters—how much more so with others. 'Nārī' (woman) is derived from connection with 'nara' (man), or meaning 'belonging to a man.' Here is another explanation of the word 'nara': 'He is led (nariyati) by his own actions,' thus he is called 'nara'—a being or a human. For it is said, 'The world is led by action.' In this context, firstly, the word 'nara' in the sense of man is illustrated by the example: 'narā ca atha nāriyo' (men and women). However, when referring to beings or humans, it is illustrated by examples like: 'buddho ayaṃ edisako naruttamo' (This Buddha is such a supreme man), and 'Āmoditā naramarū' (Delighted are the men and gods). Therefore, depending on the context, 'nara' should be understood as 'a man,' 'a being,' or 'a human.'

Hara haraṇe. Haraṇaṃ pavattanaṃ. Harati. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Vihāsi. Vihaṃsu. Viharissati. Appamatto vihissati. Voharati. Saṃvoharati. sabbo harati vā. Rūpiyasaṃvohāro, rūpiyasabbohāro vā. Pāṭihāriyaṃ. Pītipāmojjahāro. Vihāro. Vohāro. Abhihāro. Cittaṃ abhinīharati. Sāsane viharaṃ, viharanto, viharamāno. Vihātabbaṃ, viharituṃ. Viharitvā. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

Hara: in the sense of carrying or removing. Haraṇaṃ: removal or causing to proceed. Harati: he carries/removes. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati: he dwells in Sāvatthī. Vihāsi: he dwelt. Vihaṃsu: they dwelt. Viharissati: he will dwell. Appamatto vihissati: the heedful one will dwell. Voharati: he conducts/speaks. Saṃvoharati: he transacts. Or from `sabbaṃ harati` (he removes all). Rūpiyasaṃvohāro: transaction of money; or rūpiyasabbohāro. Pāṭihāriyaṃ: a miracle. Pītipāmojjahāro: bearing of joy and delight. Vihāro: a dwelling. Vohāro: conduct/speech. Abhihāro: an offering. Cittaṃ abhinīharati: he directs the mind. Sāsane viharaṃ, viharanto, viharamāno: dwelling in the Dispensation, dwelling, abiding. Vihātabbaṃ: it should be dwelt in; viharituṃ: to dwell. Viharitvā: having dwelt. Other connections should also be applied.

Tattha pāṭihāriyanti samāhite citte vigatūpakkilese katakiccena pacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti pāṭihāriyaṃ. Paṭīti hi ayaṃ saddo “pacchā”ti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu viya. Vihāroti ṭhānanisajjādinā viharanti etthāti vihāro, bhikkhūnaṃ āvāso. Viharaṇaṃ vā vihāro, viharaṇakriyā. Vohāroti byavahāropi paṇṇattipi vacanampi cetanāpi. Tattha

Here, 'pāṭihāriyaṃ' means that with the mind concentrated and free from defilements, after the task is done, it should be brought about and manifested afterward. For the word 'paṭi' here conveys the meaning of 'after,' as in 'tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo' (after he had entered, another brahmin came), and similar instances. 'Vihāro' means that monks reside here by standing, sitting, and so on; it is the abode of monks. Or 'vihāra' is the act of dwelling, the activity of abiding. 'Vohāro' means conventional usage, designation, speech, and intention. Here,

Yo hi koci manussesu, vohāraṃ upajīvati;

Evaṃ vāseṭṭha jānāti, vāṇijo so nabrāhmaṇo”ti.

Whoever among humans lives by a trade; thus, Vāseṭṭha, know him as a merchant, not a brahmin.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0153] byavahāravohāro nāma. “Saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro”ti ayaṃ paṇṇattivohāro nāma. Tathā tathā voharanti parāmasantīti ayaṃ vacanavohāro nāma. “Aṭṭha ariyavohārā, aṭṭha anariyavohārā”ti ayaṃ cetanāvohāro nāma. Iccevaṃ –

This is called conventional usage (byavahāravohāro). 'Saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro' (Designation, term, concept, usage)—this is called usage in designation (paṇṇattivohāro). Because they speak and refer to things in various ways (tathā tathā voharanti parāmasantīti), this is called usage in speech (vacanavohāro). 'Aṭṭha ariyavohārā, aṭṭha anariyavohārā' (Eight noble usages, eight ignoble usages)—this is called usage in intention (cetanāvohāro). Thus—

Byavahāre vacane ca, paṇṇatticetanāsu ca;

Vohārasaddo catūsu, imesvatthesu dissati.

The word 'vohāra' is seen in these four meanings: in conventional usage and speech, and in designation and intentions.

Hara apanayane. Apanayanaṃ nīharaṇaṃ. Dosaṃ harati. Nīharati. Nīhāro, pariharati. Parihāro. Rajoharaṇaṃ. Sabbadosaharo dhammo. Bhagavato ca sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhe titthiye haratīti pāṭihāriyaṃ. Mattāvaṇṇabhedenettha “pāṭiheraṃ pāṭihīraṃ pāṭihāriya”nti tīṇi padarūpāni, bhavanti.

Hara: in the sense of taking away. Apanayanaṃ: taking away is removing. Dosaṃ harati: he removes faults. Nīharati: he removes. Nīhāro: removal; pariharati: he avoids. Parihāro: avoidance. Rajoharaṇaṃ: the removal of dust. Sabbadosaharo dhammo: the Dhamma that removes all faults. It removes the opponents, the heretics, of the Blessed One and his Dispensation; therefore, it is a miracle (pāṭihāriyaṃ). Here, due to variations in meter and letters, three word-forms occur: 'pāṭiheraṃ, pāṭihīraṃ, pāṭihāriyaṃ.'

Hara ādāne. Adinnaṃ harati. Harissati. Hāhiti iccapa. “Kharājinaṃ para suñca, khārikājañca hāhitī”ti idamettha nidassanaṃ. Āharati, avaharati, saṃharati, apaharati, upaharati, paharati, sampaharati, samāharati. Manoharo pāsādo. Parassaharaṇaṃ. Āhāro, avahāro, saṃhāro, upahāro, sampahāro, samāhāro. Hariyyati, āhariyyati. Āhariyyanti. Āhaṭaṃ, harituṃ, āharituṃ, āharitvā, āharitvāna. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

Hara: in the sense of taking. Adinnaṃ harati: he takes what is not given. Harissati: he will take. Hāhiti: he will take. 'Kharājinaṃ para suñca, khārikājañca hāhitī' (Give up the other's rough hide, and he will take the carrying-pole)—this is an example here. Āharati: he brings; avaharati: he steals; saṃharati: he gathers; apaharati: he takes away; upaharati: he offers; paharati: he strikes; sampaharati: he prepares; samāharati: he collects. Manoharo pāsādo: a delightful palace. Parassaharaṇaṃ: taking from another. Āhāro: food; avahāro: theft; saṃhāro: gathering; upahāro: offering; sampahāro: preparation; samāhāro: collection. Hariyyati: it is taken; āhariyyati: it is brought. Āhariyyanti: they are brought. Āhaṭaṃ: brought; harituṃ: to take; āharituṃ: to bring; āharitvā: having brought; āharitvāna: having brought. Other connections should also be applied.

Dhara dharaṇe. Dharaṇaṃ vijjamānatā. Dharati. Dharate satthusāsanaṃ.

Dhara: in the sense of bearing. Dharaṇaṃ: bearing is existence. Dharati: he bears. Dharate satthusāsanaṃ: he bears the Teacher's Dispensation.

Dhara aviddhaṃsane. Nibbānaṃ niccaṃ dharati.

Dhara: in the sense of non-perishing. Nibbānaṃ niccaṃ dharati: Nibbāna is eternally enduring.

Khara khaye. Kharati. Kharaṇaṃ. Nakkharanti na khiyyantīti akkharāni. Nakkharanti na nassantīti nakkhattānīti porāṇā.
