Khara: in the sense of destruction. Kharati: it is destroyed. Kharaṇaṃ: destruction. Nakkharanti na khiyyantīti akkharāni: they do not decay or waste away, therefore they are called 'letters.' Nakkharanti na nassantīti nakkhattānīti porāṇā: they do not decay or perish, therefore the ancients called them 'constellations.'

Jāgaraniddakkhaye [M 0.0154] jāgarati. Jāgaro, jāgaraṇaṃ, jāgaraṃ. Dīghā jāgarato ratti. Jāgaramāno. Ayañca dhātu tanādigaṇaṃ patvā “jāgaroti, paṭijāgarotī”ti rūpāni janeti.

Jāgara: in the sense of cessation of sleep. Jāgarati: he is awake. Jāgaro: wakeful; jāgaraṇaṃ: wakefulness; jāgaraṃ: being awake. Dīghā jāgarato ratti: long is the night for one who is awake. Jāgaramāno: staying awake. And this root, having entered the tanādi class, produces forms such as 'jāgaroti' (he is awake) and 'paṭijāgaroti' (he is fully awake).

Īra vacane gatikampanesu ca. Īrati. Īritaṃ. Eritaṃ. Samīraṇo. Jinerito dhammo. Kuppanti vātassapi eritassa.

Īra: in the sense of speaking, moving, and shaking. Īrati: it moves. Īritaṃ: stirred. Eritaṃ: agitated. Samīraṇo: wind. Jinerito dhammo: the Dhamma proclaimed by the Conqueror. Kuppanti vātassapi eritassa: they are agitated by the stirred-up wind.

Tattha samīraṇoti vāto. So hi samīrati vāyati, samīreti ca rukkhasākhāpaṇṇādīni suṭṭhu kampetīti “samīraṇo”ti vuccati.

Here, 'samīraṇa' means wind. For it blows (samīrati vāyati), and it thoroughly shakes (samīreti) the branches and leaves of trees, hence it is called 'samīraṇa.'

Hare lajjāyaṃ. Aluttantoyamekāranto dhātu, gile pītikkhayeti dhātu viya. Harāyati. Harāyanaṃ. Aṭṭīyāmi harāyāmi.

Hare: in the sense of shame. This is a root ending in 'e' whose final vowel is not elided, like the root 'gil' in the sense of 'consuming, drinking, and decaying'. He is ashamed. Shame. I am disgusted, I am ashamed.

Ettha harāyatīti lajjati, hiriṃ karotīti attho.

Here, 'harāyati' means 'is ashamed', that is, 'acts with shame'.

Para pālanapūraṇesu. “Parati, paramo”timassa rūpāni, nara nayaneti dhātussa “narati naro”ti rūpāni viya.

Para: in the sense of protecting and fulfilling. Its forms are 'parati' and 'paramo', just as the forms of the root 'nar' in the sense of 'leading' are 'narati' and 'naro'.

Tattha paratīti pāleti, pūrati vā. Suddhakattuvasenidaṃ padaṃ vuttaṃ. Hetukattuvasena hi “pāreti pārayatī”tiādīni rūpāni bhavanti. Paramoti pālako pūrako vā. Ettha ca “pāramī”ti padaṃ etassatthassa sādhakaṃ. Tathā hi pāramīti parati, pāreti cāti paramo, dānādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ pālako pūrako ca mahābodhisatto. Paramassa idaṃ, paramassa vā bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramī, dānādikriyā. Garūhi pana “pūretīti paramo, dānādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ pūrako pālako cā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ vīmaṃsitabaṃ.

Here, 'parati' means 'protects' or 'fulfills'. This word is stated in the sense of a simple agent. For in the causative sense, forms like 'pāreti' and 'pārayati' occur. 'Paramo' means 'protector' or 'fulfiller'. And here, the word 'pāramī' establishes this meaning. Thus, because he protects (parati) and causes to protect (pāreti), he is a 'paramo'; the Great Bodhisatta is the protector and fulfiller of virtues such as generosity. That which belongs to the 'paramo', or the state of the 'paramo', or the action of the 'paramo' is 'pāramī', namely, the practice of generosity and so forth. However, the teachers have said, "Because one fulfills (pūreti), therefore he is 'paramo', the fulfiller and protector of virtues such as generosity"; that should be examined.

Vara varaṇe. Varati. Vāraṇo, varuṇo.

The root 'var' is in the sense of choosing. It chooses. 'Vāraṇa', 'Varuṇa'.

Gira [M 0.0155] niggiraṇo. Niggiraṇaṃ paggharaṇaṃ. Girati, giri.

The root 'gir' is in the sense of swallowing. 'Niggiraṇa' means 'dripping forth'. It swallows. 'Giri'.

Ettha girīti pabbatā, yo ‘selo”tiādīhi anekehi nāmehi kathiyati. So hi sandhisaṅkhātehi pabbehi citattā pabbamassa atthīti pabbato. Himavamanādivasena jalassa sārabhūtānaṃ bhesajjādivatthūnañca giraṇato girīti vuccati.

Here, 'giri' refers to mountains, which are spoken of by many names such as 'sela' and so forth. Indeed, because it is composed of segments called 'joints', it is called 'pabbata' (having segments). And because it absorbs water and essential substances like medicines, in the manner of the Himalayas, it is called 'giri'.

Imāni panassa nāmāni –

These, moreover, are its names:

Pabbato acalo selo, nago giri mahīdharo;

Addi siluccayo cāti, giripaṇṇattiyo imā.

Pabbata, acala, sela, naga, giri, mahīdhara; addi, siluccaya—these are the designations for a mountain.

Sura issariyadittīsu. Surati. Suro, asuro.

The root 'sur' is in the sense of lordship and radiance. It shines. 'Sura', 'Asura'.

Tatra saroti surati īsati devissariyaṃ pāpuṇāti virocati cāti suro. Sundarā rā vācā assāti vā suro, devo. Devābhidhānāni divādigaṇe pakāsessāma. Asuroti devo viya na surati na īsati na virocati cāti asuro. Surānaṃ vā paṭipakkho mittapaṭipakkhā amittā viyāti asuro, dānavo, yo “pubbadevo”tipi vuccati. Tathā hi kumbhajātake vuttaṃ –

There, 'suro' is so called because he shines, rules, attains divine sovereignty, and radiates. Or, 'suro' is so called because he has beautiful speech; he is a deity. We will explain the designations of deities in the 'divādi' group. 'Asuro' is so called because, though like a deity, he does not shine, does not rule, and does not radiate. Or, 'asuro' is so called because he is the opponent of the suras, just as enemies are the opponents of friends; he is a dānava, who is also called 'pubbadevo' (former deity). For so it is said in the Kumbha Jātaka—

“Yaṃ ve pivitvā pubbadevā pamattā,

Tidivā cutā sassatiyā samāyā;

Taṃ tādisaṃ majjamimaṃ niratthaṃ,

Jānaṃ mahārāja kathaṃ piveyyā”ti.

“Indeed, having drunk that, the former deities became heedless, fallen from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, from an eternal state. Knowing such worthless liquor as this, great king, how could you drink it?”

Sagāthāvaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ pana “na suraṃ pivimha, na suraṃ pivimhā’ti āhaṃsu, tato paṭṭhāya asurā nāma jātā”ti vuttaṃ.

However, in the commentary on the Sagāthāvagga, it is said: "'We will not drink sura, we will not drink sura,' they said, and from that time on they came to be called asuras."

Imāni [M 0.0156] tadabhidhānāni –

These are its designations:

Asuro pubbadevo ca, dānavo devatāri tu;

Nāmāni asurānanti, imāni niddise vidū.

Asura, pubbadeva, and dānava, and foe of the deities; these are the names of the asuras, the wise declare.

Pāko iti tu yaṃ nāmaṃ, ekassa asurassa tu;

Paṇṇattītipi ekacce, garavo pana abravuṃ.

The name 'Pāka', indeed, is of one asura. Some also say it is a designation, but the venerable ones have stated otherwise.

Kura sadde akkose ca. Kurati. Kuraro, kurarī. Kummo, kummī.

The root 'kur' is in the sense of sound and abuse. It makes a sound. 'Kurara', 'kurarī'. 'Kumma', 'kummī'.

Khura chedane vilekhane ca. Khurati. Khuro.

The root 'khur' is in the sense of cutting and scraping. It scrapes. 'Khura'.

Mura saṃveṭhane. Murati. Muro, moro.

The root 'mur' is in the sense of enveloping. It envelops. 'Mura', 'mora'.

Ghura abhimatta saddesu. Ghurati. Ghoro.

The root 'ghur' is in the sense of excessive sounds. It makes a sound. 'Ghora'.

Pura aggagamane. Aggagamanaṃ nāma padhānagamanaṃ, paṭhamameva gamanaṃ vā. Purati. Puraṃ, purī. Avāpurati. Avāpuretaṃ amatassa dvāraṃ. Avāpuraṇaṃ ādāya gacchati.

The root 'pur' is in the sense of going foremost. Going foremost means principal going, or going first of all. It goes foremost. 'Pura', 'purī'. He opens. 'Open the door to the Deathless.' He takes the key and goes.

Tattha puranti rājadhānī. Tathā hi “nagaraṃ puraṃ purī rājadhānī”ti ete pariyāyā. “Eso āḷāriko poso, kumārī puramantare”tiādīsu pana gehaṃ “pura”nti vuccati. Padhānatāya purato purato gamanena gantabbanti puraṃ, rājadhānī ceva gehañca. Avāpuraṇanti avāpuranti vivaranti dvāraṃ etenāti avāpuraṇaṃ, yaṃ “kuñcikā”tipi “tāḷo”tipi vuccati. Avāpuratītiādīsu ava āiccubho upasaggāti daṭṭhabbā.

There, 'pura' means 'royal capital'. Thus, 'nagara', 'pura', 'purī', 'rājadhānī'—these are synonyms. However, in phrases like 'eso āḷāriko poso, kumārī puramantare' and so forth, 'pura' is said to mean 'house'. Due to its prominence, and because it is to be gone to by proceeding ever forward, it is 'pura', both a royal capital and a house. 'Avāpuraṇa' is so called because by it they open, they unlock a door; it is also called 'kuñcikā' or 'tāḷa'. In 'avāpurati' and so forth, it should be understood that 'ava' and 'ā' are both prefixes.

Phara pharaṇe. Pharaṇaṃ nāma byāpanaṃ gamanaṃ vā. Samaṃ pharati sītena. Āhāratthaṃ pharati. Pharaṇaṃ.

The root 'phar' is in the sense of spreading. Spreading means pervading or going. It spreads evenly with coolness. It goes about for the sake of food. Spreading.

Gara uggame. Garati. Garu.

The root 'gar' is in the sense of rising. It rises. 'Garu'.

Garūti [M 0.0157] mātāpitādayo gāravayuttapuggalā. Te hi garanti uggacchanti uggatā pākaṭā hontīti garūti vuccanti. Apica pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya bhāriyaṭṭhena garūti vuccanti. Garusaddo “idamāsanaṃ atra bhavaṃ nisīdatu, bhavañhi me aññataro garūna”nti ettha mātāpitūsu dissati. “Sanarāmaralokagaru”nti ettha sabbalokācariye sabbaññumhi. Apica garusaddo aññesvatthesupi dissati. Sabbametaṃ ekato katvā atridaṃ vuccati –

'Garu' refers to individuals worthy of respect, such as parents and so forth. Indeed, they are called 'garu' because they rise, they ascend, they become prominent. Furthermore, they are called 'garu' due to their weightiness, like a stone canopy. The word 'garu' is seen in the sense of parents in the passage, 'Let your honor sit on this seat here, for your honor is one of my revered ones'. In the phrase 'sanarāmaralokagaru' (teacher of the world with its humans and deities), it refers to the All-knowing One, the teacher of all worlds. Moreover, the word 'garu' is also seen in other meanings. Having brought all this together, it is said here:

Mātāpitācariyesu, dujjare alahumhi ca;

Mahante cuggate ceva, nichekādikaresu ca;

Tathā vaṇṇavisesesu, garusaddo pavattati.

The word 'garu' occurs in the sense of parents and teachers, the difficult to bear and the not-light; in the great and the eminent, and in experts and so forth; and likewise in distinctions of syllables.

Keci panācariyā “garu garū”ti ca dvidhā gahetvā bhāriyavācakatte garusaddo ṭhito. Ācariyavācakatte pana gurusaddoti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Pāḷivisaye hi sabbesampi yathāvuttānaṃ atthānaṃ vācakatte garusaddoyeva icchitabbo, akārassa ākārabhāve “gārava”nti savuddhikassa taddhitantapadassa dassanato. Sakkaṭabhāsāvisaye pana gurusaddoyeva icchitabbo, ukārassa vuddhibhāve aññathā taddhitantapadassa dassanato.

Some teachers, however, say that the word 'garu' stands for expressing heaviness, while the word 'guru' is used for expressing the meaning of a teacher. That should not be accepted. For in the domain of Pāli, the word 'garu' alone should be preferred for expressing all the meanings mentioned, because the formation of the derivative word 'gārava' with vowel strengthening is seen. However, in the domain of Sanskrit, the word 'guru' alone should be preferred, because the derivative word is formed differently through the strengthening of the vowel 'u'.

Mara pāṇacāge. Marati. Mattuṃ. Maritvā. Hetukattari “puriso purisaṃ māreti, mārayati. Puriso purisena purisaṃ mārāpeti, mārāpayati. Puriso purisaṃ māretuṃ māretvā” iccādīni rūpāni. Macco. Maru. Maraṇaṃ, maccu. Maṭṭu. Māro.

The root 'mar' is in the sense of abandoning life. He dies. To die. Having died. In the causative active voice, the forms are: 'A man kills a man, causes a man to kill. A man has a man killed by a man, causes a man to have a man killed. A man, to kill, having killed,' and so forth. 'Macco'. 'Maru'. 'Maraṇa', 'maccu'. 'Maṭṭu'. 'Māra'.

Tattha mattunti marituṃ. Tathā hi alīnasattujātake “yo mattumicche pituno pamokkhā”ti pāḷi dissati. Maccoti maritabbasabhāvatāya “macco”ti laddhanāmo satto[M 0.0158]. Marūti dīghāyukopi samāno maraṇasīloti maru, devo. Maraṇanti cuti.

There, 'mattuṃ' means 'to die'. Thus, in the Alīnasattujātaka, the Pāli passage 'yo mattumicche pituno pamokkhā' is found. 'Macco' is a being who has obtained the name 'macco' due to its nature of being subject to death. 'Maru' means that even one who is long-lived is of a nature to die; thus 'maru' (a deity). 'Maraṇa' means 'passing away'.

Maraṇaṃ antako maccu, hindaṃ kālo ca maṭṭu ca;

Nikkhepo cuti cetāni, nāmāni maraṇassa ve.

Maraṇa, antaka, maccu, hinda, kāla, and maṭṭu; nikkhepa, cuti—these, indeed, are names for death.

Māroti sattānaṃ kusalaṃ māretīti māro, kāmadevo.

'Māra' is so called because he destroys the wholesome states of beings; he is the god of sensual pleasure.

Imānissa nāmāni –

These are his names:

Māro namuci kaṇho ca, vasavatti pajāpati;

Pamattabandhu maddano, pāpimā dabbakopi ca;

Kandappo ca ratipati, kāmo ca kusumāyudho.

Māra, Namuci, and Kaṇha, Vasavatti, Pajāpati; Pamattabandhu, Maddana, and Pāpimā, Dabbakopi; Kandappa and Ratipati, Kāma and Kusumāyudha.

Aññe aññānipi nāmāni vadanti, tāni sāsanānulomāni na hontīti idha na dassitāni. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana “māro, namuci, kaṇho, pamattabandhū”ti cattārova nāmāni āgatāni.

Others mention other names, but since they are not in accordance with the teaching, they are not shown here. However, in the commentaries, only four names are found: 'Māra', 'Namuci', 'Kaṇha', 'Pamattabandhu'.

Ettha ca māroti devaputtamārena saddhiṃ pañca mārā kilesamāro khandhamāro abhisaṅkhāramāro maccumāro devaputtamāroti.

And here, 'Māra' refers to the five Māras, along with Devaputta-Māra: the Māra of defilements, the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of volitional formations, the Māra of death, and Devaputta-Māra.

Dhara avatthāne. Dharati.

The root 'dhara' is in the sense of establishing. It establishes.

Bhara posane. Bharati. Bharito, bhattā.

The root 'bhara' is in the sense of nourishing. It nourishes. 'Bharita', 'bhattā'.

Thara santharaṇe. Tharati, santharati. Santharaṇaṃ.

The root 'thara' is in the sense of spreading out. It spreads. It spreads out. Spreading out.

Dara vidāraṇe. Bhūmiṃ darati. Kudālo.

The root 'dara' is in the sense of splitting. It splits the earth. 'Kudāla'.

Dara dāhe. Kāyo darati. Daro, daratho.

The root 'dara' is in the sense of burning. The body burns. 'Daro', 'daratha'.

Tira adhogatiyaṃ. Tirati. Tiracchāno, tiracchā vā.

The root 'tira' is in the sense of oblique motion. It goes obliquely. An animal, or obliquely.

Ara gatiyaṃ. Arati. Atthaṃ, attho, utu.

The root 'ara' is in the sense of motion. It moves. Meaning, purpose, season.

Ettha [M 0.0159] atthaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ. Taṃ taṃ sattakiccaṃ arati vattetīti utu.

Here, 'attha' is said to be Nibbāna. That which moves and carries on the respective work of beings is called 'utu'.

Rakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'ra'.

Lakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'la'.

Lā ādāne. Lāti. Lānaṃ, garuḷo, sīhaḷo, rāhulo, kusalaṃ, bālo, mahallako, mahallikā.

The root 'lā' is in the sense of taking. It takes. Taken, a garuḍa, a Sinhalese, Rāhula, wholesome, a fool, an old man, an old woman.

Tatra garuḷoti garuṃ lāti ādadāti gaṇhātīti garuḷo, yo “supaṇṇo, dijādhipo, nāgāri, karoṭī”ti ca vuccati. Sīhaḷoti sīhaṃ lāti ādadāti gaṇhātīti sīhaḷo, pubbapuriso. Tabbaṃse jātā etarahi sabbepi sīhaḷā nāma jātā.

There, 'garuḍa' means one who takes, accepts, or seizes what is heavy—thus, a garuḍa, who is also called 'supaṇṇa', 'lord of birds', 'nāgāri', and 'karoṭī'. 'Sīhaḷa' means one who takes, accepts, or seizes a lion—thus, Sīhaḷa, the forefather. Those born in that lineage are now all called Sinhalese.

Rāhulotiādīsu pana rāhu viya lāti gaṇhātīti rāhulo, ko so? Sikkhākāmo āyasmā rāhulabhaddo buddhaputto. Tassa hi jātadivase suddhodanamahārājā “puttassa me tuṭṭhiṃ nivedethā”ti uyyāne kīḷantassa bodhisattassa sāsanaṃ pahiṇi. Bodhisatto taṃ sutvā “rāhu jāto bandhanaṃ jāta”nti āha. Puttassa hi jāyanaṃ rāhuggaho viya hoti. Taṇhākilissanatāpādanato bāḷhena ca saṅkhalikādibandhanena bandhaṃ viya hoti muccituṃ appadānatoti “rāhu jāto bandhanaṃ jāta”nti āha. Rājā “kiṃ me putto avacā”ti pucchitvā taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “ito paṭṭhāya me nattā ‘rāhulo’ tveva hotū”ti āha, tato paṭṭhāya kumāro rāhulo nāma jāto.

In the case of 'Rāhula' and similar terms, it means one who seizes like Rāhu—thus, Rāhula. Who is he? The Venerable Rāhulabhadda, the Buddha’s son, who was desirous of the training. On the day of his birth, King Suddhodana sent a message to the Bodhisatta, who was playing in the garden, saying, 'Announce to me the joy of my son.' Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said, 'A rāhu is born, a bond is born.' For the birth of a son is like being seized by Rāhu. Because it produces the torment of defilement from craving, and is like being bound by strong chains and other bonds, giving little opportunity to be freed, he said, 'A rāhu is born, a bond is born.' The king asked, 'What did my son say?' and upon hearing those words, declared, 'From now on, my grandson shall be called ‘Rāhula’.' From then on, the prince was named Rāhula.

Mahāpadānasuttaṭīkāyañhi [M 0.0160] “rāhu jāto”ti ettha “rāhūti rāhuggaho”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ pana “rāhulo”ti vacanassatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ adhippāyatthavasena vuttaṃ. Na hi kevalo “rāhū”ti saddo “rāhuggaho”ti atthaṃ vadati, atha kho jātasaddasambandhaṃ labhitvā vadati. Tathā hi “rāhu jāto”ti bodhisattena vuttavacanassa “rāhuggaho jāto”ti atthौ bhavati, tasmā suddhodanamahārājā “mama nattā rāhu viya lātīti rāhuloti vattabbo”ti cintetvā “rāhulotveva hotū”ti āhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Indeed, in the subcommentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta, concerning 'rāhu jāto', it is said, 'rāhu means seizure by Rāhu.' This, however, was stated in terms of its intended meaning in order to clarify the meaning of the word 'Rāhula'. For the word 'Rāhu' alone does not convey the meaning 'seizure by Rāhu,' but rather conveys it after obtaining a connection with the word 'born.' Thus, the meaning of the statement uttered by the Bodhisatta, 'A rāhu is born,' is 'A seizure by Rāhu is born.' Therefore, it should be understood that King Suddhodana, thinking, 'My grandson seizes like Rāhu, therefore he should be called ‘Rāhula,’' declared, 'He shall indeed be called ‘Rāhula’.'

Keci pana “rāhulo jāto bandhanaṃ jāta”nti paṭhanti, katthaci potthake ca likhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ, atthassa ayuttito ṭīkāya ca saddhiṃvirocato. Na hi “rāhulo”ti kumārassa nāmaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppannaṃ, pacchāyeva pana uppannaṃ ayyakena dinnattā, tasmā tadā bodhisattena “rāhulo jāto”ti vattuṃ na yujjati. Yathā hi anabhisitte arājini puggale “mahārājā”ti vohāro nappavattati. Ṭīkāyañca “rāhūti rāhuggaho”ti vuttaṃ. Athāpi tesaṃ siyā “rāhulo jāto bandhanaṃ jāta”nti padassa vijjamānattā eva ṭīkāyaṃ “rāhuggaho”ti bhāvavasena lāsaddena samānattho ādānattho gahasaddo vuttoti evampi nupapajjati, “rāhulānaṃ jātaṃ bandhanaṃ jāta”nti pāṭhassa vattabbattā. Rāhuloti hi idaṃ padaṃ “sīhaḷo”ti padaṃ viya dabbavācakaṃ, na kadācipi bhāvavācakaṃ, tasmā “rāhulo jāto bandhanaṃ jāta”nti etaṃ ekaccehi duropitaṃ pāṭhaṃ aggahetvā “rāhu jāto bandhanaṃ jāta”nti ayameva pāṭho gahetabbo, sārato ca paccetabbo suparisuddhesu anekesu potthakesu diṭṭhattā, porāṇehi ca gambhīrasukhumañāṇehi ācariyapacāriyehi paṭhitattā.

However, some recite, 'Rāhula is born, a bond is born,' and write it thus in some books, but this is not proper, as it is inconsistent with the meaning and conflicts with the subcommentary. For the name 'Rāhula' did not arise for the prince at first—it was only bestowed later by his grandfather. Therefore, it would not be fitting for the Bodhisatta to say, 'Rāhula is born,' at that time. Just as the designation 'great king' is not applied to a person who is unanointed and not a king. Moreover, the subcommentary states, 'Rāhu means seizure by Rāhu.' Even if they were to argue that because the phrase 'Rāhula is born, a bond is born' exists, the word 'gaha' (seizure) is stated in the subcommentary as having the same meaning as the word 'lā' (taking) in the sense of an abstract state—even this is untenable, because the reading would have to be 'The state of being Rāhula is born, a bond is born.' For this word 'Rāhula', like the word 'Sīhaḷa', denotes a substance, not ever an abstract state. Therefore, rejecting the reading 'Rāhula is born, a bond is born,' which has been wrongly introduced by some, this very reading, 'A rāhu is born, a bond is born,' should be accepted. It should be relied upon as the essence, for it is found in many very pure manuscripts and was recited by the ancient teachers and their pupils, who possessed profound and subtle wisdom.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0161] panettha sādhippāyā atthappakāsanā – rāhu jātoti bodhisatto puttassa jātasāsanaṃ sutvā saṃvegappatto “idāni mama rāhu jāto”ti vadati, muccituṃ appadānavasena mama gahaṇatthaṃ rāhu uppannoti hi attho. Bandhanaṃ jātanti iminā “mama bandhanaṃ jāta”nti vadati. Tathā hi ṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ “rāhūti rāhuggaho”ti. Tattha rāhuggahoti gaṇhātīti gaho, rāhu eva gaho rāhuggaho, mama gāhako rāhu jātoti attho. Atha vā gahaṇaṃ gaho, rāhuno gaho rāhuggaho, rāhuggahaṇaṃ mama jātanti attho. Putto hi rāhusadiso. Pitā candasadiso puttarāhunā gahitattā.

Herein is the explanation of the meaning with its intention: 'A rāhu is born' means the Bodhisatta, upon hearing the news of his son's birth, was struck with a sense of urgency and said, 'Now my rāhu is born.' The meaning is that a rāhu has arisen to seize me, by way of giving no opportunity to be freed. By 'A bond is born,' he conveys, 'My bond has been born.' Thus it is stated in the subcommentary: 'Rāhu means seizure by Rāhu.' There, 'rāhuggaho' means 'one who seizes' (gaṇhātīti gaho); Rāhu himself is the seizer, thus 'rāhuggaho'. The meaning is, 'My seizer, Rāhu, is born.' Alternatively, 'seizure' (gahaṇaṃ) is 'gaho'; Rāhu's seizure is 'rāhuggaho'. The meaning is, 'A seizure by Rāhu has been born for me.' For the son is like Rāhu, and the father is like the moon, having been seized by his son, the rāhu.

Ekacce pana “rāhulotveva hotū”ti imaṃ padesaṃ disvā “rāhu jāto”ti vutte iminā na sameti, “rāhulo jāto”ti vutteyeva pana sametīti maññamānā evaṃ pāṭhaṃ paṭhanti likhanti ca, tasmā so anupaparikkhitvā paṭhito duropito pāṭho na gahetabbo, yathāvutto porāṇako porāṇācariyehi abhimato pāṭhoyeva āyasmantehi gahetabbo atthassa yuttito, ṭīkāya ca saddhiṃ avirodhatoti.

However, some, seeing the passage, 'He shall indeed be called Rāhula,' and thinking, 'When "A rāhu is born" is said, it does not fit with this, but when "Rāhula is born" is said, it does fit,' thus recite and write the text in this way. Therefore, that unexamined, wrongly introduced reading should not be accepted. The ancient reading, as stated and approved by the ancient teachers, should be accepted by the venerable ones because of the coherence of the meaning and its non-contradiction with the subcommentary.

Tattha kusalanti kucchitānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ sānato tanukaraṇato ñāṇaṃ kusaṃ nāma, tena kusena lātabbaṃ pavattetabbanti kusalaṃ. Bāloti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikasaṅkhāte dve anatthe devadattakokālikādayo viya lāti ādadātīti bālo. Imāni pana taṃnāmāni –

Therein, 'wholesome' (kusala) is so called because wisdom, which cuts and thins contemptible, evil states, is called 'kusa'; and because it is to be taken up and set in motion by that 'kusa', it is 'kusala'. 'Fool' (bāla) refers to one who, like Devadatta, Kokālika, and others, takes up and accepts the two kinds of harm designated as pertaining to the present life and to the future life. These, however, are its names:

Bālo avidvā añño ca, aññāṇī avicakkhaṇo;

Apaṇḍito akusalo, dummedho kumati jaḷo.

A fool, ignorant, and unknowing, unwise, undiscerning; unlearned, unskilled, dull-witted, misguided, sluggish.

Eḷamūgo [M 0.0162] ca nippañño, dummedhī avidū mago;

Aviññū andhabālo ca, duppañño ca aviddasu.

Dumb and witless, dull-witted, an ignoramus, a beast; unintelligent, a blind fool, of little wisdom, and unlearned.

Mahallakoti mahattaṃ lāti gaṇhātīti mahallako, jiṇṇapuriso. Imānissa nāmāni –

'Mahallaka' is so called because he takes or grasps greatness, thus 'mahallaka'; an aged man. These are his names:

Jiṇṇo mahallako vuddho, buddho vuḍḍho ca kattaro;

Thero cāti ime saddā, jiṇṇapaññattiyo siyuṃ.

Aged, old, venerable, elderly, senior, and decrepit; and elder—these words are designations for an old person.

Tathā hi –

For thus:

“Dure apassaṃ therova, cakkhuṃ yācitumāgato”;

Evamādīsu daṭṭhabbo, therasaddo mahallake.

'Though not seeing from afar, he came like an elder to ask for eyesight'; in such instances, the word 'thera' should be understood as 'an old man'.

Imāni pana nāmāni itthiyā itthiliṅgavasena vattabbāni –

These names, however, are to be stated for a woman in the feminine gender:

Jiṇṇā mahallikā vuddhī, buddhī vuḍḍhī ca kattarā;

Therī cāti ime saddā, nāmaṃ jiṇṇāya itthiyā;

Aged, old, venerable, elderly, senior, and decrepit; and an elder nun—these words are names for an old woman.

Dala phala visaraṇe. Dalati. Phalati. Dalito rukkho. Phalito bhūmibhāgo.

The roots 'dala' and 'phala' are in the sense of splitting or bursting open. It splits. It bursts open. A tree is split. A portion of the earth is burst open.

Ala bhūsane. Alati. Alaṅkāro, alaṅkato, alaṅkataṃ. “Sālaṅkānanayogepi, sālaṅkānanavajjitā”ti imissañhi kavīnaṃ kabbaracanāyaṃ alaṅkasaddo bhūsanavisesaṃ vadati. Keci panettha ala bhūsanapariyāpanavāranesūti dhātuṃ paṭhanti, “alatī”ti ca rūpaṃ icchanti. Mayaṃ pana aladhātussa pariyattinivāraṇatthavācakattaṃ na icchāma payogādassanato. Nipātabhūto pana alaṃsaddo pariyattinivāraṇatthavācako dissati “alametaṃ sabbaṃ. Alaṃ me tena rajjenā”tiādīsu.

The root 'ala' is in the sense of adorning. It adorns. Ornament; adorned; that which is adorned. Indeed, in the poetic compositions of poets, such as, “Even with an adorned face, she is without an adorned face,” the word 'alaṅka' denotes a special ornament. Some, however, read the root 'ala' here as meaning 'to adorn, to obtain, or to prevent,' and wish the form to be 'alatī'. We, however, do not accept that the root 'ala' signifies obtaining or preventing, due to lack of usage. But the particle 'alaṃ' is seen to signify 'sufficiency' or 'prevention' in examples such as: “Enough of all this. Enough of that kingdom for me.”

Mīla nimelane. Mīlati, nimīlati, ummīlati. Nimīlanaṃ.

The root 'mīla' is in the sense of closing the eyes. It closes; it shuts; it opens. The act of closing.

Bila patitthambhe. Bilati.

The root 'bila' is in the sense of supporting. It supports.

Nīla [M 0.0163] vaṇṇe. Nīlavatthaṃ.

The root 'nīla' is in the sense of color. Blue cloth.

Sīla samādhimhi. Sīlati. Sīlaṃ, sīlanaṃ.

The root 'sīla' is in the sense of concentration. It concentrates. Virtue; the act of observing virtue.

Ettha sīlanti sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ visuddhimagge “sīlanti kenaṭṭhena sīlaṃ? Sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ, kimidaṃ sīlanaṃ nāma? Samādhānaṃ vā kāyakammādīnaṃ susīlyavasena avippakiṇṇatāti attho. Upadhāraṇaṃ vā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhānavasena ādhārabhāvoti attho. Etadeva hi ettha atthadvayaṃ saddalakkhaṇavidū anujānanti. Aññe pana ‘siraṭṭho sīlaṭṭho, sītalaṭṭho sīlaṭṭho’ti evamādinā nayenettha atthaṃ vaṇṇentī”ti. Tattha “atthadvayaṃ saddalakkhaṇa vidū anujānantī”ti idaṃ “sīla samādhimhi sīla upadhāraṇe”ti dvigaṇikassa sīladhātussa atthe sandhāya vuttaṃ. Imassa hi curādigaṇaṃ pattassa upadhāraṇe “sīleti, sīlayatī”ti rūpāni bhavanti, upadhāretītipi tesaṃ attho. Idha pana bhūvādigaṇikattā samādhānatthe “sīlatī”ti rūpaṃ bhavati, samādhiyatīti tassa attho. Punapi ettha sotūnaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ nibbacanāni vuccante. Sīlati samādhiyati kāyakammādīnaṃ susīlyavasena na vippakiratīti sīlaṃ. Atha vā sīlanti samādahanti cittaṃ etenāti sīlaṃ. Imāni bhūvādigaṇikavasena nibbacanāni. Curādigaṇikavasena pana sīleti kusale dhamme upadhāreti patiṭṭhābhāvena bhuso dhāretīti sīlaṃ. Sīlenti vā etena kusale dhamme upadhārenti bhuso dhārenti sādhavoti sīlanti nibbacanāni.

Herein, 'sīla' is so called in the sense of composing. For it is said in the Visuddhimagga: “In what sense is 'sīla' called 'sīla'? It is called 'sīla' in the sense of composing. What is this composing? It means the composing, or the non-scattering, of bodily actions, etc., by way of good conduct. Or it means the upholding, the supporting of wholesome states as a foundation. Indeed, here, those skilled in the science of words acknowledge these two meanings. Others, however, explain the meaning here by such methods as 'the meaning of head is the meaning of sīla, the meaning of coolness is the meaning of sīla,' and so on.” Therein, the statement, “those skilled in the science of words acknowledge these two meanings,” is said with reference to the meanings of the 'sīla' root which belongs to two groups, namely, “'sīla' in the sense of composing” and “'sīla' in the sense of upholding.” For in the case of this root belonging to the curādi group, when it means upholding, forms like 'sīleti' and 'sīlayati' arise, and their meaning is “upholds.” Here, however, because it belongs to the bhūvādi group, in the sense of composing, the form 'sīlati' arises, and its meaning is “is composed.” Furthermore, here, etymologies are stated for the sake of easy comprehension by listeners. 'Sīla' is so called because it composes, is composed, and does not scatter bodily actions, etc., by way of good conduct. Or, 'sīla' is so called because by means of it, they compose the mind. These are the etymologies according to the bhūvādi group. According to the curādi group, however, 'sīla' is so called because it upholds wholesome states, firmly holding them as a foundation. Or, 'sīla' is so called because by means of it, the virtuous uphold wholesome states, firmly holding them—these are the etymologies.

Kila bandhe. Kilati. Kilaṃ.

The root 'kila' is in the sense of binding. It binds. A stake.

Kūla āvaraṇe. Kulati. Kūlaṃ. Vahe rukkhe pakūlaje. Kūlaṃ bandhati. Nadīkūle vasāmahaṃ. Kūlati āvarati udakaṃ bahi nikkhamituṃ na detīti kūlaṃ.

The root 'kūla' is in the sense of obstructing. It obstructs. A bank. As in: “Trees grown on the bank.” “He binds the bank.” “I dwell on the riverbank.” It is called 'kūla' because it obstructs, it prevents water from flowing outward.

Sūla [M 0.0164] rujāyaṃ. Sūlati. Sūlaṃ. Kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti.

The root 'sūla' is in the sense of pain. It pains. A pain, a stake. As in: “He does not cause ear-ache.”

Tūla nikkarīse. Nikkarīsaṃ nāma karīsamattenapi aminetabbato lahubhāvoyeva. Tūlati. Tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃva māluto.

The root 'tūla' is in the sense of lightness. Lightness means a state of being light, from being unmeasurable even by a measure of dung. It is light. As in: “Cotton, as if blown by the wind.”

Pula saṅghāte. Pulati. Pañcapuli.

The root 'pula' is in the sense of assembling. It assembles. A collection of five.

Mūla patiṭṭhāyaṃ mūlati. Mūlaṃ. Mūlasaddo “mūlāni uddhareyya antamaso ussīranāḷimattānipī”tiādīsu mūlamūle dissati. “Lobho akusalamūla”ntiādīsu asādhāraṇahetumhi. “Yāvamajjhanhike kāle chāyā pharati, nivāte paṇṇāni patanti, ettāvatā rukkhamūla”ntiādīsu samīpe. Atridaṃ vuccati –

The root 'mūla' is in the sense of establishing. It establishes. A root. The word 'mūla' is seen in the primary sense of root in passages like, “one should uproot the roots, even if they are only the size of usīra grass stalks,” and so on. It is seen in the sense of a specific cause, as in, “greed is the root of the unwholesome,” and so on. It is seen in the sense of proximity, as in, “as long as the shade spreads at midday, and leaves fall in a windless place, that much is the base of the tree,” and so on. Here, this is said:

Mūlamūle mūlasaddo, padissati tatheva ca;

Asādhāraṇahetumhi, samīpamhi ca vattati.

The word 'mūla' appears in the primary sense of root, and likewise, it is used in the sense of a specific cause, and also in the sense of proximity.

Phala nibbattiyaṃ. Rukkho phalati. Rukkhaphalāni bhuñjantā. Mahapphalaṃ mahānisaṃsaṃ. Sotāpattiphalaṃ. Tattha phalanti mahānibbattikaṃ.

The root 'phala' is in the sense of production. The tree bears fruit. Eating the fruits of the tree. Great fruit, great benefit. The fruit of stream-entry. Therein, it means 'yielding a great result'.

Phala bhede. Phalati. Muddhā te phalatu sattadhā. Pādā phaliṃsu. Tattha phalatūti bhajjitu.

The root 'phala' is in the sense of breaking. It breaks. “May your head split into seven pieces.” “The feet split.” There, 'phalatu' means 'may it be broken'.

Phala abyattasadde. Asanī phalati. Dveme bhikkhave asaniyā phalantiyā na santasanti. Phalantiyāti saddaṃ karontiyā.

The root 'phala' is in the sense of an indistinct sound. Lightning strikes with a sound. “These two, monks, are not frightened when lightning strikes.” 'Phalantiyā' means 'making a sound'.

Culla hāvakaraṇe. Hāvakaraṇaṃ vilāsakaraṇaṃ. Cullati.

The root 'culla' is in the sense of making coquettish gestures. Making coquettish gestures means making alluring movements. It makes alluring movements.

Phulla [M 0.0165] vikasanabhedesu. Phullati. Phullaṃ. Phullito kiṃsuko. Suphullitamaravindavanaṃ.

The root 'phulla' is in the senses of blooming and breaking open. It blooms or breaks open. Bloomed, broken. A blooming kiṃsuka tree. A grove of lotuses in full bloom.

Asītihatthamubbedho, dīpaṅkaro mahāmuni;

Sobhati dīparukkhova, sālarājāva phullito.

The great sage Dīpaṅkara, eighty cubits high, shines like a lamp-tree, like a blossoming king of sāla trees.

Khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ.

The restoration of what is broken and dilapidated.

Cilla seṭhille. Siṭhilabhāvo seṭhillaṃ. Cillati.

The root 'cilla' is in the sense of slackness. Slackness is the state of being loose. It becomes slack.

Velu celu kelu khelu pelu belu selu sala tila gatiyaṃ. Velati. Celati. Kelati. Khelati. Pelati. Belati. Selati. Salati. Tilati. Celaṃ, belako. Ettha celanti vatthaṃ. Pelakoti saso.

The roots 'velu, celu, kelu, khelu, pelu, belu, selu, sala, tila' are in the sense of movement. It moves (velati). It moves (celati). It moves (kelati). It moves (khelati). It moves (pelati). It moves (belati). It moves (selati). It moves (salati). It moves (tilati). Cloth; a hare. Herein, 'celaṃ' means cloth, and 'pelako' means a hare.

Khala calane. Khalati. Khalo. Khaloti dujjano asādhu asappuriso pāpajano.

The root 'khala' is in the sense of stirring. It stirs. A wicked person. 'Khalo' means a wicked person, an unvirtuous one, an evil person, a bad person.

Khala sañcinane. Khalati. Khalaṃ. Khalanti vīhiṭṭhapanokāsabhūtaṃ bhūmimaṇḍalaṃ. Tañhi khalanti sañcinanti rāsiṃ karonti ettha dhaññānīti khalanti vuccati. “Khalaṃ sālaṃ pasuṃ khettaṃ, gantā cassa abhikkhaṇa”nti payogo.

The root 'khala' is in the sense of gathering. It gathers. A threshing floor. 'Khalaṃ' is a circular piece of ground that is a place for putting paddy. Indeed, it is called 'khalaṃ' because here they gather, collect, and make piles of grain. The usage is: “He goes frequently to the threshing floor, the hall, the cattle, the field.”

Gila ajjhoharaṇe. Gilati. Gilamakkhaṃ puriso na bujjhati.

The root 'gila' is in the sense of swallowing. It swallows. “A person does not understand the stain of swallowing.”

Gala adane. Galati. Galo. Galanti adanti ajjhoharanti etenāti galo. Galoti gīvā vuccati.

The root 'gala' is in the sense of eating. It eats. The throat. It is called 'galo' because by means of it, they eat, consume, and swallow. 'Galo' is called the neck.

Sala salla āsugatiyaṃ. Āsugati sīghagamanaṃ. Salati. Sallati. Sallaṃ. Ettha ca “sallaṃ usu saro sallo kaṇḍo tejano”ti pariyāyā ete.

The roots 'sala, salla' are in the sense of swift movement. Swift movement means rapid motion. It moves swiftly. It moves swiftly. A dart. And here, 'sallaṃ, usu, saro, sallo, kaṇḍo, tejano' are synonyms for this.

Khola gatipaṭighāte. Kholati.

The root 'khola' is in the sense of obstructing movement. It obstructs.

Gile [M 0.0166] pītikkhaye. Gilāyati. Gilāno, gelaññaṃ. Gilānoti akallako. Vinayepi hi vuttaṃ “nāhaṃ akallako”ti. Aṭṭhakathāyañca “nāhaṃ akallakoti nāhaṃ gilāno”ti vuttaṃ.

The root 'gile' is in the sense of wasting away from sickness. It wastes away, is sick. A sick person; sickness. 'Gilāno' means 'unwell.' Indeed, it is said in the Vinaya, “I am not unwell.” And in the commentary, it is said, “‘I am not unwell’ means ‘I am not sick.’”

Mile gattavināme. Milāyati. Milāyano, milāyanto, milāyamāno.

The root 'mile' is in the sense of the withering of the body. It withers. Withering; one who is withering; while withering.

Kele mamāyane. Mamāyanaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhivasena “mama ida”nti gahaṇaṃ. Kelāyati. Tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyati.

The root 'kele' is in the sense of possessiveness. Possessiveness is the grasping of 'this is mine' by way of craving and views. It clings or is possessive. 'To what are you possessive?'

Sala calane saṃvaraṇe ca, vala valla calane ca. Saṃvaraṇāpekkhāyaṃ cakāro. Salati. Kusalaṃ. Valati. Vallati. Vallūro.

The root 'sala' is in the sense of movement and restraint, and 'vala, valla' are in the sense of movement. The particle 'ca' is with reference to restraint. It moves or restrains. 'Kusalaṃ' (skillful). It moves. It moves. 'Vallūro' (dried flesh).

Tattha kusalanti kucchite pāpadhamme salayati calayati kampeti viddhaṃsetīti kusalaṃ. Kucchitaṃ apāyadvāraṃ salanti saṃvaranti pidahanti sādhavo etenāti kusalaṃ. Vallanti saṃvaranti rakkhanti ito kākasenādayo satte akhādanatthāyāti vallūro.

Herein, 'kusala' is so called because it shakes, agitates, makes tremble, and destroys despicable, evil states. It is called 'kusala' because by means of it, the virtuous restrain and close off the despicable doors to the lower realms. It is called 'vallūro' because it restrains and protects, preventing beings such as crows and their flocks from eating other beings.

Mala malla dhāraṇe. Malati. Malaṃ. Mallati. Mallo.

The roots 'mala, malla' are in the sense of holding or bearing. It holds or bears. 'Malaṃ' (dirt, impurity). It holds or bears. 'Mallo' (a wrestler).

Bhala bhalla paribhāsanahiṃsādānesu. Bhalati. Bhallati.

The roots 'bhala, bhalla' are in the senses of abusing, harming, and giving. It abuses, harms, or gives. It abuses, harms, or gives.

Kala saṅkhyāne. Kalati. Kalā, kālo.

The root 'kala' is in the sense of counting or reckoning. It counts or reckons. 'Kalā' (a part, an art), 'kālo' (time).

Ettha kalāti soḷasabhāgādibhāgo. Kāloti “ettako atkkanto”tiādinā kalitabbo saṅkhātabboti kālo, pubbaṇhādisamayo.

Herein, 'kalā' means a division, such as a sixteenth part, and so on. 'Kālo' is that which is to be counted or reckoned by such thoughts as 'so much has passed,' and so on; it is a period of time, such as the forenoon.

Kalla asadde. Asaddo. Nissaddo. Kallati.

The root 'kalla' is in the sense of being without sound. Without sound. Silent. It is silent.

Jala dittiyaṃ. Jalati. Jalaṃ, jalanto, pajjalanto, jalamāno.

The root 'jala' is in the sense of shining. It shines. 'Jalaṃ' (water), 'jalanto' (shining), 'pajjalanto' (blazing forth), 'jalamāno' (shining).

Ko [M 0.0167] eti siriyā jalaṃ. Jalaṃva yasasā aṭṭhā, devadattoti me sutaṃ. Saddhammapajjoto jalito.

Who comes shining with splendor? He stood shining with fame like a flame—so have I heard of Devadatta. The lamp of the True Dhamma is lit.

Hula calane. Hulati. Halo. Haloti phālo, so hi holeti bhūmiṃ bhindanto mattikakhaṇḍaṃ cāletīti “halo”ti vuccati ukārassa akāraṃ katvā.

The root 'hula' is in the sense of movement. It moves. 'Halo' (a plow). 'Halo' means a plowshare, for it is called 'halo'—by changing 'u' to 'a'—because it moves the earth, breaking it and stirring the clods of soil.

Cala kampane. Calati. Calito, acalo. Mahanto bhūmicālo. Calanaṃ, cālo.

The root 'cala' is in the sense of shaking. It shakes. 'Calito' (shaken), 'acalo' (unshaken). A great earthquake. 'Calanaṃ' (shaking), 'cālo' (tremor).

Jala dhaññe. Jalati. Jalaṃ.

The root 'jala' is in the sense of grain. It produces grain. 'Jalaṃ' (grain).

Ṭala ṭula velambe. Ṭalati. Ṭulati.

The roots 'ṭala, ṭula' are in the sense of swinging or delaying. It swings or delays. It swings or delays.

Thala ṭhāne. Thalati. Thalo. Thaloti nirudakappadeso. Pabbajjānibbānesupi taṃsadisattā tabbohāro. Yathā hi loke udakoghena anottharaṇaṭṭhānaṃ “thalo”ti vuccati, evaṃ kilesoghena anottharaṇīyattā pabbajjā nibbānañca “thalo”ti vuccati, “tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo”ti hi vuttaṃ.

The root 'thala' is in the sense of a place. It stands. 'Thalo' (dry land). 'Thalo' refers to a waterless region. The same term is applied to renunciation and Nibbāna because of their similarity. Just as in the world a place not submerged by a flood of water is called 'thalo,' so too, because they cannot be submerged by the flood of defilements, renunciation and Nibbāna are called 'thalo.' For it is said: 'The brahmin has crossed over, gone to the far shore, and stands on dry land.'

Phāla vilekhane. Phālati bhūmiṃ vilekhati bhindatīti phālo.

The root 'phāla' is in the sense of splitting. It splits, scratches, and breaks the earth—thus it is a 'phālo' (plowshare).

Nala ganthe. Nalati.

The root 'nala' is in the sense of binding. It binds.

Bala pāṇane. Iha pāṇanaṃ jīvanaṃ sasanañca. Balati. Balaṃ, bālo.

The root 'bala' is in the sense of living. Here, living means life and breathing. It lives. 'Balaṃ' (strength), 'bālo' (a fool).

Ettha balanti jīvitaṃ kappenti etenāti balaṃ, kāyabalabhogabalādikaṃ balaṃ. Atha vā balanti sammājīvanaṃ jīvanti etenāti balaṃ, saddhādikaṃ balaṃ. Āgamaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “assaddhiye na kampatīti saddhābala”ntiādi vuttaṃ, taṃ daḷhaṭṭhena balanti vattabbānaṃ saddhādīnaṃ akampanabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttanti [M 0.0168] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā dhātūnaṃ atthātisayayogato assaddhiyādīnaṃ abhibhavanena saddhādibalānaṃ abhibhavanatthopi gahetabbo “abalā naṃ baliyantī”ti ettha viya. Bāloti balati assasati ceva passasati cāti bālo, assasitapassasitamattena jīvati, na seṭṭhena paññājīvitenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ “balantīti bālā, assasitapassasitamattena jīvanti, na paññājīvitenāti attho”ti. Paññājīvinoyeva hi jīvitaṃ seṭṭhaṃ nāma. Tenāha bhagavā “paññājīviṃ jīvitamāhu seṭṭha”nti.

Herein, 'balaṃ' (strength) is that by which they live or sustain life, such as physical strength, the strength of possessions, and so on. Or, 'balaṃ' is that by which they live a right life, such as the strength of faith and so on. In the commentary on the Āgamas, however, it is said, "Faith is a strength because one does not waver in the face of faithlessness," and so on. This should be understood as being said to show the unshakable nature of faith and other qualities, which are called strength due to their firmness. Alternatively, due to the connection with an extended meaning of the root, the sense of overcoming should also be taken for the strengths of faith and so on, by their overcoming of faithlessness and the like, just as in the phrase, "The weak are overcome by them." 'Bālo' (a fool) is so called because he lives by merely breathing in and out; that is to say, he lives only by breathing in and out, not by the superior life of wisdom. Thus, in the commentary it is said: "They are called 'bālā' (fools) because they live merely by breathing in and out; the meaning is that they do not live by the life of wisdom." For indeed, the life of one who lives by wisdom is truly the best. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "They declare the life lived by wisdom to be the best."

Pula mahatte. Pulati. Vipulaṃ.

The root 'pula' is in the sense of greatness. It becomes great. 'Vipulaṃ' (vast).

Kula saṅkhāne bandhumhi ca. Kolati. Kulaṃ, kolo.

The root 'kula' is in the sense of reckoning and kinship. It reckons or binds. 'Kulaṃ' (family), 'kolo' (a jujube).

Sala gamane. Salati.

The root 'sala' is in the sense of going. It goes.

Kila pītiya kīḷanesu. Pītassa bhāvo pītiyaṃ yathā dakkhiyaṃ. Kīḷanaṃ kīḷāyeva. Kilati.

The root 'kila' is in the senses of joy and playing. The state of being joyful is 'pītiyaṃ', just as 'dakkhiyaṃ' is the state of being skilled. 'Kīḷanaṃ' is indeed 'kīḷā' (play). It plays.

Ila kampane. Ilati. Elaṃ, elā. Ettha elaṃ vuccati doso. Kenaṭṭhena? Kampanaṭṭhena. Dosoti cettha aguṇo veditabbo, na paṭigho. “Nelaṅgo setapacchādo”ti idamettha nidassanaṃ.

The root 'ila' is in the sense of shaking. It shakes. 'Elaṃ', 'elā'. Here, 'elaṃ' is said to be a fault. In what sense? In the sense of shaking. Here, 'doso' should be understood as a defect, not as aversion. "Nelaṅgo setapacchādo" (without blemish, with a white covering) is an example here.

Apica elaṃ vuccati udakaṃ. Tathā hi “elambujaṃ kaṇṭakiṃ vārijaṃ yathā”ti imissā pāḷiyā atthaṃ niddisanto āyasmā sāriputto “elaṃ vuccati udaka”nti āha. Elāti lālā vuccati “elamūgo”ti ettha viya. Apica elāti kheḷo vuccati “sutvā nelapatiṃ vācaṃ, vāḷā panthā apakkamu”nti ettha viya. Ettha nelapatiṃ vācanti kheḷabindunipātavirahitaṃ [M 0.0169] vacananti attho. Lālākheḷavācakassa tu elāsaddassa aññaṃ pavattinimittaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ. Anekappavattinimittā hi saddā. Kiṃ vā aññena pavattinimittena, ila kampaneti evaṃ vuttaṃ kampanaṃ eva lālākheḷavācakassa elāsaddassa pavattinimittaṃ, tasmā ilanti jigucchitabbabhāvena kampenti hadayacalanaṃ pāpuṇanti janā etthāti elāti attho gahetabbo. Samānapavattinimittāyeva hi saddā lokasaṅketavasena nānāpadatthavācakāpi bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? Hinoti gacchatīti hetu, sappati gacchatīti sappo, gacchatīti goti. Tathā asamānappavattinimittāyeva samānapadatthavācakāpi bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? Rañcatīti rājā, bhūmiṃ pāletīti bhūmipālo, nare indatīti narindoti. Esa nayo sabbatthāpi vibhāvetabbo.

Moreover, 'elaṃ' is said to be water. Thus, when explaining the meaning of the Pāli passage "elambujaṃ kaṇṭakiṃ vārijaṃ yathā" (like a thorny water-born lotus), the Venerable Sāriputta said, "'elaṃ' is said to be water." 'Elā' is said to be saliva, as in the example "elamūgo" (one who is dumb from excessive saliva). Furthermore, 'elā' is said to be phlegm, as in the phrase "sutvā nelapatiṃ vācaṃ, vāḷā panthā apakkamu" (having heard speech without phlegm, the wild beasts departed from the path). Here, "nelapatiṃ vācaṃ" means speech devoid of the falling of phlegm-drops. However, for the word 'elā', which denotes saliva and phlegm, another derivational basis must be sought. Indeed, words have multiple derivational bases. Or rather, what other derivational basis is there? The shaking mentioned in the rule "ila is in the sense of shaking" is itself the derivational basis of the word 'elā' which denotes saliva and phlegm. Therefore, the meaning of 'elā' should be taken as that in which people shake, due to its disgusting nature, and experience agitation of the heart. For indeed, words with the same derivational basis can also denote different meanings according to worldly convention. How so? 'It goes (hinoti), therefore it is a cause (hetu)'; 'it creeps (sappati), therefore it is a snake (sappo)'; 'it goes (gacchati), therefore it is a cow (go)'. Similarly, words with different derivational bases can denote the same meaning. How so? 'He delights (rañcati), therefore he is a king (rājā)'; 'he protects the earth (bhūmiṃ pāleti), therefore he is an earth-protector (bhūmipālo)'; 'he is lord over men (nare indati), therefore he is a lord of men (narindo)'. This method should be applied everywhere.

Ila gatiyaṃ. Ilati.

The root 'ila' is in the sense of going. It goes.

Hila hāvakaraṇe. Helati.

The root 'hila' is in the sense of amorous gesturing. It makes amorous gestures.

Sila uñche. Silati.

The root 'sila' is in the sense of gleaning. It gleans.

Tila sinehane. Tilati. Tilaṃ, telaṃ, tilo.

The root 'tila' is in the sense of oiling. It oils. 'Tilaṃ' (sesame), 'telaṃ' (oil), 'tilo' (a sesame plant).

Cila vasane. Cilati.

The root 'cila' is in the sense of dressing. It dresses.

Vala vilāsane. Valati.

'Vala' is in the sense of displaying charm. Valati means it displays charm.

Pila gahaṇe. Pilati.

'Pila' is in the sense of grasping. Pilati means it grasps.

Mila sinehane. Milati.

'Mila' is in the sense of anointing or uniting. Milati means it anoints or unites.

Phula sañcale pharaṇe ca. Phulati.

'Phula' is in the sense of moving and spreading. Phulati means it moves or spreads.

Lakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'l'.

Vakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'v'.

Vā [M 0.0170] gatigandhanesu. Vāti. Vāto.

'Vā' is in the sense of going and smelling. Vāti means it goes or smells. Vāto means wind.

Vī pajanakanti asanakhādana gatīsu. Pajanaṃ calanaṃ. Kanti abhiruci. Asanaṃ bhattaparibhogo. Khādanaṃ pūvādibhakkhanaṃ. Gati gamanaṃ. Veti.

'Vī' is in the senses of movement, delighting, eating, consuming, and going. Pajanaṃ is movement. Kanti is delight. Asanaṃ is the partaking of food. Khādanaṃ is the eating of cakes and so on. Gati is going. The form is veti.

Ve tantasantāne. Vāyati. Tantavāyo.

'Ve' is in the sense of stretching threads. Vāyati means he weaves. Tantavāyo means a weaver.

Ve sosane. Vāyati.

'Ve' is in the sense of drying. Vāyati means it dries.

Dhivu khivu nidassane. Dhevati. Khevati.

'Dhivu' and 'khivu' are in the sense of displaying. Dhevati means it displays. Khevati means it displays.

Thivu dittiyaṃ. Thevati. Madhumadhukā thevanti.

'Thivu' is in the sense of shining. Thevati means it shines. An example is: Madhumadhukā thevanti, the honey-makers drip.

Jīva pāṇadhāraṇe. Jīvati. Jīvitaṃ, jīvo, jīvikā. Atthi no jīvikā deva, sā ca yādisakīdisā. Jīvitaṃ kappeti.

'Jīva' is in the sense of sustaining life. Jīvati means he lives. Derived forms are jīvitaṃ (life), jīvo (a living being), and jīvikā (livelihood). An example is: "Atthi no jīvikā deva, sā ca yādisakīdisā" (We have a livelihood, lord, and it is of a meager sort). Jīvitaṃ kappeti means he makes a living.

Piva miva tiva niva thūliye. Pivati. Pivaro. Mivati. Tivati. Nivati.

'Piva', 'miva', 'tiva', and 'niva' are in the sense of being thick. Pivati means it is thick. A derivative is pivaro (a stout person). Mivati means it is thick. Tivati means it is thick. Nivati means it is thick.

Ettha ca pivaroti kacchapo, yo koci vā thūlasarīro. Tathā hi “pivaro kacchape thūle”ti pubbācariyehi vuttaṃ.

Here, pivaro means a turtle, or any stout-bodied creature. Indeed, it has been said by the ancient teachers: "Pivaro is used for a turtle or a stout one."

Ava pālane. Avati. Buddho mama avataṃ.

'Ava' is in the sense of protecting. Avati means he protects. An example is: Buddho mama avataṃ (May the Buddha protect me).

Bhava gatiyaṃ. Savati.

'Sava' is in the sense of going or flowing. Savati means it flows.

Kava vaṇṇe. Kavati.

'Kava' is in the sense of describing or praising. Kavati means he describes or praises.

Khivu made. Khivati.

'Khivu' is in the sense of intoxication or pride. Khivati means he is intoxicated or proud.

Dhovu dhovane. Dhovati.

'Dhovu' is in the sense of washing. Dhovati means he washes.

Devu [M 0.0171] deva devane. Devati ādevati, paridevati, ādevo, paridevo, ādevanā, paridevanā, ādevitattaṃ, paridevitattaṃ.

'Devu' is in the sense of playing and lamenting. The forms are devati (he plays or laments), ādevati (he laments), and paridevati (he laments). Derived nouns are ādevo (lamentation), paridevo (lamentation), ādevanā (lamenting), paridevanā (lamenting), ādevitattaṃ (the state of lamenting), and paridevitattaṃ (the state of lamenting).

Sevu kevu khevu gevu gilevu mevu milevu secane. Sevati. Kevati. Khevati. Gevati. Gilevati. Mevati milevati.

'Sevu', 'kevu', 'khevu', 'gevu', 'gilevu', 'mevu', and 'milevu' are in the sense of sprinkling. Sevati means he sprinkles. Kevati means he sprinkles. Khevati means he sprinkles. Gevati means he sprinkles. Gilevati means he sprinkles. Mevati means he sprinkles. Milevati means he sprinkles.

Devu plutagatiyaṃ. Plutagati pariplutagamanaṃ. Devati.

'Devu' is in the sense of leaping motion (plutagati). Plutagati means unsteady movement (pariplutagamanaṃ). Devati means he leaps or moves unsteadily.

Dhātu gatisuddhiyaṃ. Dhāvati, vidhāvati. Ādhāvati, paridhāvati. Dhāvako.

'Dhāvu' is in the sense of motion and purification. Dhāvati means he runs. Vidhāvati means he runs about. Ādhāvati means he runs towards. Paridhāvati means he runs around. Dhāvako means a runner.

Civu ādānasaṃvaresu. Civati.

'Civu' is in the sense of taking and restraining. Civati means he takes or restrains.

Cevi cetanātulye. Cevati.

'Cevi' is in the sense of being equal in intention. Cevati.

Vakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'v'.

Sakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 's'.

Sā pāke. Sāti.

'Sā' is in the sense of cooking. Sāti means he cooks.

Si sevāyaṃ. Sevati. Sevanā, sevako, sevito, sivo, sivaṃ.

'Si' is in the sense of serving. The form is sevati. Derived forms are sevanā (service), sevako (servant), sevito (one who is served), sivo (auspicious), and sivaṃ (that which is auspicious).

Nihīyati puriso nihīnasevī,

Na ca hāyetha kadāci tulyasevī;

Seṭṭhamupagamaṃ udeti khippaṃ,

Tasmā attano uttaritaraṃ bhajetha;

A person who associates with the inferior declines; one who associates with equals would never decline; approaching the superior, one rises quickly. Therefore, one should associate with those better than oneself.

Si gatibuddhīsu. Seti, atiseti. Atisituṃ, atisitvā, setu.

Si (root) in the sense of 'movement' and 'knowledge'. Seti (he moves/knows), atiseti (he surpasses/excels). Atisituṃ (to surpass/excel), atisitvā (having surpassed/excelled). Setu (a bridge).

Sī [M 0.0172] saye. Sayo supanaṃ. Seti. Sayati. Senaṃ. Sayanaṃ.

Sī (root) in the sense of 'to lie down'. Sayo (lying down) is supanaṃ (sleeping). Seti (he lies down). Sayati (he lies down). Senaṃ (a bed/lying down). Sayanaṃ (a bed/lying down).

Su gatiyaṃ. Savati. Pasavati. Pasuto, suto.

Su (root) in the sense of 'movement'. Savati (he moves/flows). Pasavati (he flows forth/brings forth). Pasuto (flowed forth/brought forth), suto (moved/flowed).

Ettha sutoti dūto, “vittiñhi maṃ vindati suta disvā”ti “devasuto ca mātalī”ti ca imāni tattha payogāni.

Here, 'suta' means a messenger, as in 'For he finds joy in me, having seen the messenger,' and 'and Mātali, the divine messenger'—these are its usages there.

Su savane. Savanaṃ sandanaṃ. Savati. Āsavo.

Su (root) in the sense of 'hearing'. Savanaṃ (hearing) is sandanaṃ (flowing). Savati (he hears/flows). Āsavo (outflow/canker).

Sū pasave. Pasavo jananaṃ. Savati, pasavati. Suttaṃ.

Sū (root) in the sense of 'producing'. Pasavo (production) is jananaṃ (generation). Savati (he produces), pasavati (he produces/begets). Suttaṃ (a thread/discourse).

Ettha pana suttanti atthe savati janetīti suttaṃ, tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ, tadaññampi vā hatthisuttādi suttaṃ.

Here, however, 'suttaṃ' means that which flows with or generates meaning; it refers to the Buddha's word in the Tipiṭaka, or other discourses such as the Hatthisutta and so forth.

Sū pāṇagabbhavimocanesu. Sūti. Pasūti. Pasūto.

Sū (root) in the sense of 'releasing a living being from the womb'. Sūti (birth). Pasūti (birth/offspring). Pasūto (born).

Su peraṇe. Suti.

Su (root) in the sense of 'impelling'. Suti (impelling).

Se khaye. Sīyati. Ekārassīyādeso.

Se (root) in the sense of 'decay'. Sīyati (it decays/wastes away). The substitution of 'sīya' for the vowel 'e'.

Se pāke. Seti.

Se (root) in the sense of 'cooking'. Seti (he cooks).

Se gatiyaṃ. Seti. Setu.

Se (root) in the sense of 'movement'. Seti (he moves). Setu (a bridge).

Hiṃsa hiṃsāyaṃ. Hiṃsati. Hiṃsako, hiṃsanā, hiṃsā.

Hiṃsa (root) in the sense of 'harming'. Hiṃsati (he harms). Hiṃsako (a harmer), hiṃsanā (harming), hiṃsā (harm).

Issa issāyaṃ. Issati. Purisaparakkamassa devā na issanti. Issā, issāyanā.

Issa (root) in the sense of 'envy'. Issati (he envies). The gods do not envy a man's effort. Issā (envy), issāyanā (the act of envying).

Namassa vandanānatiyaṃ. Vandanānati nāma vandanāsaṅkhātaṃ namanaṃ, sakammakoyevāyaṃ dhātu, na namudhātu viya sakammako ceva akammako ca. Namassati.

Namassa (root) in the sense of 'bowing in reverence'. Vandanānati is bowing, reckoned as reverence; this root is indeed transitive, not like the root 'namu,' which is both transitive and intransitive. Namassati (he pays homage).

Ghusa sadde. Ghusati, ghosati. Paṭighoso, nigghoso, vacīghoso.

Ghusa (root) in the sense of 'sound'. Ghusati (he sounds), ghosati (he proclaims). Paṭighoso (echo), nigghoso (loud sound/roar), vacīghoso (vocal sound).

Cusa [M 0.0173] pāne. Cusati.

Cusa (root) in the sense of 'drinking'. Cusati (he drinks/sucks).

Pusa buddhiyaṃ. Pusati. Poso. Sampīḷe mama posanaṃ. Posananti vaḍḍhanaṃ.

Pusa (root) in the sense of 'intellect'. Pusati (he understands/nourishes). Poso (a man). 'Sampīḷe mama posanaṃ' (My nourishment in affliction). Posanaṃ means growth.

Musa theyye. Thenanaṃ theyyaṃ corikā. Musati. Duddikkho cakkhumusano. Musalo.

Musa (root) in the sense of 'theft'. Thenanaṃ (stealing) is theyyaṃ (theft), corikā (robbery). Musati (he steals/deceives). Duddikkho (hard to see), cakkhumusano (eye-deceiving). Musalo (a pestle).

Pusa pasave. Pusati.

Pusa (root) in the sense of 'producing'. Pusati (he/she produces).

Vāsi bhūsa alaṅkāre. Vāsati. Bhūsati, vibhūsati. Bhūsanaṃ, vibhūsanaṃ.

Vāsi and Bhūsa (roots) in the sense of 'adornment'. Vāsati (he adorns). Bhūsati (he adorns), vibhūsati (he embellishes). Bhūsanaṃ (ornament), vibhūsanaṃ (embellishment).

Usa rujāyaṃ. Usati.

Usa (root) in the sense of 'pain'. Usati (it pains/afflicts).

Isa ucche. Esati. Isi.

Isa (root) in the sense of 'seeking'. Esati (he seeks). Isi (a seer/sage).

Ettha pana sīlādayo guṇe esantīti isayo, buddhādayo ariyā tāpasapabbajjāya ca pabbajitā narā. “Isi tāpaso jaṭilo jaṭī jaṭādharo”ti ete tāpasapariyāyā.

Here, however, 'isayo' (sages) are those who seek virtues such as morality; they are the Buddhas and other noble ones, and men who have gone forth into the ascetic life. 'Isi, tāpaso, jaṭilo, jaṭī, jaṭādharo'—these are synonyms for ascetics.

Kasa vilekhane. Kasati, kassati. Kassako, ākāso.

Kasa (root) in the sense of 'plowing'. Kasati, kassati (he plows). Kassako (a farmer), ākāso (the sky).

Ettha kassakoti kasikārako. Ākāsoti nabhaṃ. Tañhi na kassatīti ākāso. Kasituṃ vilekhituṃ na sakkāti attho. Imāni tadabhidhānāni –

Here, 'kassako' means one who plows. 'Ākāso' means the sky. Indeed, it is called 'ākāso' because it is not plowed—meaning it is impossible to plow or scratch. These are its appellations:

Ākāso ambaraṃ abbhaṃ, antalikkha’maghaṃ nabhaṃ;

Vehāso gaganaṃ devo, kha’mādiccapathopi ca.

Ākāso, ambaraṃ, abbhaṃ, antalikkhaṃ, aghaṃ, nabhaṃ; vehāso, gaganaṃ, devo, khaṃ, and also ādiccapatho.

Tārāpatho ca nakkhatta-patho ravipathopi ca;

Vehāyasaṃ vāyupatho, apatho anilañjasaṃ.

Tārāpatho, nakkhattapatho, and also ravipatho; vehāyasaṃ, vāyupatho, apatho, anilañjasaṃ.

Kasa [M 0.0174] sisa jasa jhasa vasa masa disa jusa yusa hiṃsatthā. Kasati. Sisati. Jasati. Jhasati. Vasati. Masati. Masako. Omasati, omasavādo. Disati. Jusati. Yūsati.

Kasa, sisa, jasa, jhasa, vasa, masa, disa, jusa, yusa—these roots are in the sense of 'harming'. Kasati. Sisati. Jasati. Jhasati. Vasati. Masati. Masako (a mosquito). Omasati (he touches/insults), omasavādo (offensive speech). Disati. Jusati. Yūsati.

Tattha omasatīti vijjhati. Omasavādoti paresaṃ sūciyā viya vijjhanavādo. Masakoti makaso.

Herein, 'omasati' means 'to pierce'. 'Omasavādo' refers to speech that pierces others like a needle. 'Masako' means a mosquito.

Bhassa bhassane. Bhassanti kathanaṃ vuccati “āvāso gocaro bhassaṃ. Bhassakāraka”ntiādīsu viya. Bhassati. Bhaṭṭhaṃ. Bhaṭṭhanti bhāsitaṃ, vacananti attho. Ettha pana –

The root bhassa is in the sense of 'speaking' or 'falling'. 'Bhassanti' is said to be speaking, as in 'āvāso, gocaro, bhassaṃ, bhassakāraka' and so forth. Bhassati. Bhaṭṭhaṃ. 'Bhaṭṭhaṃ' means spoken; the meaning is 'utterance'. Here, however –

“Subhāsitā atthavatī, gāthāyo te mahāmuni;

Nijjhattomhi subhaṭṭhena, tvañca me saraṇaṃ bhavā”ti

Well-spoken and meaningful are your verses, O great sage; I am convinced by what is well-spoken, and be my refuge.

Pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha nijjhattoti nijjhāpito dhammojapaññāya paññattigato amhi. Subhaṭṭhenāti subhāsitena.

A Pāli example. Therein, 'nijjhatto' means: I have been made to comprehend; I have attained understanding through wisdom born of the Dhamma. 'Subhaṭṭhena' means 'by that which is well-spoken'.

Jisu nisu visu misu vassa secane. Jesati. Nesati. Vesati. Mesati. Devo vassati.

The roots jisu, nisu, visu, misu, and vassa are in the sense of 'sprinkling' or 'raining'. Jesati. Nesati. Vesati. Mesati. Devo vassati (the god rains).

Marisu sahane ca. Cakāro secanāpekkhako. Marisati.

The root marisu is in the sense of 'enduring'. The particle 'ca' refers back to 'sprinkling'. Marisati.

Pusa posane. Posati. Poso. Kammacittautuāhiārehi posiyatīti poso. “Aññepi devo posetī”ti dassanato pana curādigaṇepi imaṃ dhātuṃ vakkhāma.

The root pusa is in the sense of 'nourishing'. Posati. Poso. Poso means 'one who is nourished by kamma, mind, season, and nutriment.' However, in reference to the phrase 'Aññepi devo posetī' (A deva also nourishes others), we will also explain this root in the curādi group.

Pisu silisu pusu palusu usu upadāhe. Pesati. Silesati. Sileso. Posati. Palosati. Osati. Usu.

The roots pisu, silisu, pusu, palusu, and usu are in the sense of 'burning'. Pesati. Silesati. Sileso. Posati. Palosati. Osati. Usu.

Ghasu saṃharise. Saṃhariso saṅghaṭṭanaṃ. Ghassati.

The root ghasu is in the sense of 'friction'. Saṃhariso means 'rubbing' or 'friction'. Ghassati.

Hasu āliṅge. Āliṅgo upagūhanaṃ. Hassati.

The root hasu is in the sense of 'embracing'. Āliṅgo means 'an embrace'. Hassati.

Hasa [M 0.0175] hasane. Hasati. Assā hasanti, ājānīyā hasanti, pahasati, uhasati. Kārite “hāseti”iccādi, uhasiyamāno, hāso, pahāso, hasanaṃ, pahasanaṃ, hasitaṃ. Hakāralopena mandahasanaṃ “sita”nti vuccati “sitaṃ pātvākāsī”tiādīsu.

The root hasa is in the sense of 'laughing'. Hasati. Assā hasanti (horses laugh), ājānīyā hasanti (thoroughbreds laugh), pahasati, uhasati. In the causative, there are forms like 'hāseti', and so on: uhasiyamāno, hāso, pahāso, hasanaṃ, pahasanaṃ, hasitaṃ. With the elision of the letter 'ha', a gentle laugh is called 'sita', as in 'sitaṃ pātvākāsi' and so on.

Tattha uhasatīti avahasati. Udasiyamānoti avahasiyamāno. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi “idha bhikkhuṃ araññagataṃ vā rukkhamūlagataṃ vā suññāgāragataṃ vā mātugāmo upasaṅkamitvā uhasati” iti ca “so mātugāmena uhasiyamāno” iti ca. Hāsoti hasanaṃ vā somanassaṃ vā “hāso me upapajjathā”tiādīsu viya.

Therein, 'uhasati' means 'to mock'. 'Udasiyamāno' means 'being mocked'. In this regard, the Pāli passage states: 'Here, a bhikkhu gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, is approached by a woman who mocks him,' and also, 'he, being mocked by the woman.' 'Hāso' means 'laughter' or 'joy', as in phrases like 'may joy arise in me' and so on.

Tusa hasa hisa rasa sadde. Tusati, hasati, hisati, rasati, rasitaṃ. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “bheriyo sabbā vajjantu, vīṇā sabbā rasantu tā” iti.

The roots tusa, hasa, hisa, and rasa are in the sense of 'sounding'. Tusati, hasati, hisati, rasati, rasitaṃ. In this regard, the Pāli passage states: 'Let all drums be struck, let all lutes sound.'

Rasa assādane. Rasati. Raso.

The root rasa is in the sense of 'tasting'. Rasati. Raso.

Rasa assādasinehesu. Rasati. Raso.

The root rasa is in the sense of 'savoring' and 'affection'. Rasati. Raso.

Rasa hāniyaṃ. Rasati. Rasanaṃ, raso.

The root rasa is in the sense of 'decline'. Rasati. Rasanaṃ, raso.

Atrāyaṃ pāḷi –

In this regard, the Pāli passage is as follows:

“Naheva ṭhita nā’sīnaṃ, na sayānaṃ na paddhaguṃ;

Yāva byāti nimīsati, tatrāpi rasatibbayo”ti.

Neither when standing, nor sitting, nor lying down, nor walking; for as long as one blinks, even then age declines.

Tattha rasatibbayoti so so vayo rasati parihāyati, na vaḍḍhatīti attho.

Therein, 'rasatibbayo' means 'that each age declines and perishes, and does not increase'—this is the meaning.

Lasa silesanakīḷanesu. Lasati. Lāso. Lasī ca te nippalitā. Lasi vuccati matthaluṅgaṃ. Nippalitāti nikkhantā.

The root lasa is in the sense of 'clinging' and 'playing'. Lasati. Lāso. 'Lasī ca te nippalitā'. 'Lasi' is said to be the brain. 'Nippalitā' means 'emerged'.

Nisa [M 0.0176] samādhimhi. Samādhi samādhānaṃ cittekaggatā. Nesati.

The root nisa is in the sense of 'concentration'. Samādhi means 'concentration' or 'one-pointedness of mind'. Nesati.

Misa masa sadde rose ca. Mesati. Masati. Meso. Masako.

The roots misa and masa are in the sense of 'sounding' and 'anger'. Mesati. Masati. Meso. Masako.

Pisi pesu gatiyaṃ. Pisati. Pesati.

The roots pisi and pesu are in the sense of 'movement'. Pisati. Pesati.

Sasu hiṃsāyaṃ. Sasati. Satthaṃ. Satthaṃ vuccati asi.

The root sasu is in the sense of 'harming'. Sasati. Satthaṃ. 'Satthaṃ' means a sword (asi).

Saṃsa thutiyañca. Cakāro hiṃsāpekkhāya. Saṃsati, pasaṃsati. Pasaṃsā, pasaṃsanā. Pasattho bhagavā. Pasaṃsamāno, pasaṃsito, pasaṃsako, pasaṃsitabbo, pasaṃsanīyo, pāsaṃso, pasaṃsitvā iccādīni.

The root saṃsa is in the sense of 'praising'. The particle 'ca' refers back to 'harming'. Saṃsati, pasaṃsati. Pasaṃsā, pasaṃsanā. Pasattho bhagavā. Pasaṃsamāno, pasaṃsito, pasaṃsako, pasaṃsitabbo, pasaṃsanīyo, pāsaṃso, pasaṃsitvā and so on.

Disa pekkhane. Etissā pana nānārūpāni bhavanti – “dissati padissati” iccādi akammakaṃ. “Passati dakkhati”iccādi sakammakaṃ.

The root disa is in the sense of 'looking'. However, it has various forms: 'dissati, padissati' and so on are intransitive; 'passati, dakkhati' and so on are transitive.

Dissatu, passatu, dakkhatu. Disseyya, passeyya, dakkheyya. Disse, passe, dakkhe. Dissa, passa, dakkha. Adissā, apassā. Addā sīdantare nage. Addakkhā, addakkhuṃ, adassuṃ. Adassi, apassi, adakkhi.

Let him see, let him look, let him perceive. He might see, he might look, he might perceive. I might see, I might look, I might perceive. See! Look! Perceive! `Adissā, apassā`. He saw in the Sīdantara mountain. I saw, they saw, they saw. He saw, he looked, he perceived.

Dassissati, passissati, dakkhissati. Adassissā, apassissā, dakkhissā. Evaṃ vattamānapañcamiyādivasena vitthāretabbāni. Kārite “dasseti dassayatī”ti rūpāni. Kamme “passiyati” iccādīni.

Dassissati, passissati, dakkhissati. Adassissā, apassissā, dakkhissā. These should be elaborated according to the present tense, imperative mood, and so on. In the causative, forms like 'dasseti, dassayati' occur. In the passive, forms like 'passiyati' and so on occur.

Disā. Passo. Passaṃ. Passitā. Dassetā. Dassanaṃ. Vipassanā, ñāṇadassananti nāmikapadāni. Tadatthe pana tumatthe ca “dakkhitāye”ti rūpaṃ. “Āgatāmha imaṃ dhammasamayaṃ, dakkhitāye aparājitasaṅgha”nti hi pāḷi. Imasmiṃ pana pāḷippadese “dakkhitāye”ti idaṃ tadatthe tumatthe vā catutthiyā rūpaṃ. Tathā [M 0.0177] hi dakkhitāyeti imassa dassanatthāyāti vā passitunti vā attho yojetabbo. Disātiādīsu pana puratthimādibhedāpi disāti vuccati. Yathāha –

Disā. Passo. Passaṃ. Passitā. Dassetā. Dassanaṃ. Vipassanā, ñāṇadassana—these are nominal forms. In that sense, and in the sense of the infinitive (tum), the form 'dakkhitāye' occurs. For example, the Pāli passage states: 'We have come to this assembly of the Dhamma, to see the invincible Sangha.' In this particular Pāli passage, 'dakkhitāye' is a dative form used in that sense or in the sense of the infinitive. Thus, the meaning of 'dakkhitāye' should be construed as 'for the purpose of seeing' or 'to see.' As for 'disā' and so on, directions such as east and so on are also called 'disā.' As it is said—

“Disā catasso vidisā catasso,

Uddhaṃ adho dasa disatā imāyo;

Katamaṃ disaṃ tiṭṭhati nāgarājā,

Yamaddasā supine chabbisāṇa”nti.

The four directions, the four intermediate directions, above, below—these are the ten directions. In which direction does the Nāga king stand, whom you saw in a dream with six tusks?

Mātāpitādayopi. Yathāha –

Also parents and so on. As it is said—

“Mātāpitā disā pubbā, ācariyā dakkhiṇā disā;

Puttadārā disā pacchā, mittāmaccā ca uttarā;

Parents are the eastern direction, teachers the southern direction; children and wife are the western direction, and friends and companions the northern;

Dāsakammakarā heṭṭhā, uddhaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇā;

Etā disā namasseyya, alamatto kule gihī”ti;

Servants and workers are below, ascetics and brahmins above; these directions a capable householder in his family should venerate.

Paccayadāyakāpi. Yathāha – “agārino annadapānavatthadā, avhāyikā nampi disaṃ vadantī”ti.

Also supporters. As it is said: 'Householders are givers of food, drink, and clothing; those who invite also call them a direction.'

Nibbānampi. Yathāha –

Also Nibbāna. As it is said—

“Etādisā paramā setaketu,

Yaṃ patvā niddukkhā sukhino bhavantī”ti;

Such is the supreme white banner, having attained which, they become free from suffering and happy.

Evaṃ disāsaddena vuccamānaṃ attharūpaṃ ñatvā idānissa nibbacanamevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dissati candāvaṭṭanādivasena “ayaṃ purimā ayaṃ pacchimā”tiādinā nānappakārato paññāyatīti disā, puratthimadisādayo. Tathā “ime amhākaṃ garuṭṭhāna’ntiādinā passitabbāti disā, mātāpitādayo. Dissanti sakāya puññakriyāya ime dāyakāti paññāyantīti disā, paccayadāyakā. Dissati uppādavayābhāvena niccadhammattā sabbakālampi vijjatīti disā, nibbānaṃ. Passoti kāraṇākāraṇaṃ [M 0.0178] passatīti passo. Evaṃ passatīti passaṃ. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi –

Thus, having known the form of the meaning expressed by the word 'disā', its explanation should now be understood as follows. It is seen, that is, it is discerned in various ways, such as by the turning of the moon, with 'this is the east,' 'this is the west,' and so on—thus, 'disā' (direction), such as the eastern direction and so on. Similarly, they are to be regarded with 'these are our venerable ones,' and so on—thus, 'disā' (parents and the like). They are seen, that is, they are discerned as 'these are donors' through their own meritorious action—thus, 'disā' (supporters who give requisites). It is seen, that is, it exists at all times due to the absence of arising and passing away, being of a permanent nature—thus, 'disā' (Nibbāna). 'Passo' is one who sees cause and non-cause. Thus, one who sees in this way is a 'passaṃ.' Herein, this is the Pāli text—

“Passati passo passantaṃ, apassantampi passati;

Apassanto apassantaṃ, passantampi na passatī”ti.

One who sees, sees one who is seeing; one sees even one who is not seeing. One who does not see, does not see one who is not seeing; and does not see even one who is seeing.

Passatīti passitā. Dassetīti dassitā. Dassananti dassanakriyā. Apica dassananti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tañhi rūpārammaṇaṃ passatīti dassananti vuccati. Tathā “dassanena pahātabbā dhammā”ti vacanato dassanaṃ nāma sotāpattimaggo. Kasmā sotāpattimaggo dassanaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato. Nanu gotrabhū paṭhamataraṃ passatīti? No na passati, disvā kattabbakiccaṃ pana na karoti saṃyojanānaṃ appahānato, tasmā “passatī”ti na vattabbo. Yattha katthaci rājānaṃ disvāpi paṇṇākāraṃ datvā kiccanipphattiyā adiṭṭhattā ajjāpi rājānaṃ na passāmīti vadanto gāmavāsī nidassanaṃ.

'Passitā' is one who sees. 'Dassitā' is one who shows. 'Dassanaṃ' is the act of seeing. Moreover, 'dassanaṃ' is eye-consciousness, for it is called 'dassanaṃ' because it sees a form-object. Likewise, from the statement, 'states to be abandoned by seeing,' 'dassanaṃ' refers to the path of stream-entry. Why is the path of stream-entry called 'dassanaṃ'? Because it is the first seeing of Nibbāna. But does not the change-of-lineage consciousness see it first? No, it does not see; or rather, having seen, it does not perform the task that should be done, due to the non-abandonment of the fetters. Therefore, it cannot be said to 'see.' An illustration is the villager who, though having seen the king somewhere and offered tribute, still says, 'I have not yet seen the king,' because his purpose was not accomplished.

Vipassanāti aniccādivasena khandhānaṃ vipassanakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Ñāṇadassananti dibbacakkhupi vipassanāpi maggopi phalampi paccavekkhaṇañāṇampi sabbaññutaññāṇampi vuccati. “Appamatto samāno ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādhetī”ti ettha hi dibbacakkhu ñāṇadassanaṃ nāma. “Ñāṇadassanāya cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmetī”ti ettha vipassanāñāṇaṃ. “Abhabbā te ñāṇadassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāyā”ti ettha maggo, “ayamañño uttarimanussadhammo alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso adhigato phāsuvihāro”ti ettha phalañāṇaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi, akuppā me cetovimutti, ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti ettha paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. “Ñāṇañca [M 0.0179] pana me dassanaṃ udapādi sattāhakālaṅkato āḷāro kālāmo”ti ettha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Etthetaṃ bhavati –

'Vipassanā' is the knowledge that sees the aggregates in various ways as impermanent and so on. 'Ñāṇadassana' is said to be the divine eye, insight, the path, the fruit, reviewing knowledge, and omniscient knowledge. For instance, in the phrase 'The diligent one attains knowledge and vision,' 'ñāṇadassana' here means the divine eye. In 'He directs and inclines his mind towards knowledge and vision,' it refers to insight knowledge. In 'They are incapable of the knowledge and vision for unsurpassed supreme enlightenment,' it means the path. In 'This other state beyond the human, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision, has been attained, a pleasant abiding,' it refers to fruition knowledge. In 'And knowledge and vision arose in me: "Unshakeable is my liberation of mind, this is the last birth, there is now no further becoming,"' it refers to reviewing knowledge. In 'And knowledge and vision arose in me: "Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago,"' it refers to omniscient knowledge. Herein it is as follows—

“Dibbacakkhupi maggopi, phalañcāpi vipassanā;

Paccavekkhaṇañāṇampi, ñāṇaṃ sabbaññutāpi ca;

Ñāṇadassanasaddena, ime atthā pavuccare”ti.

The divine eye, the path, the fruit, and insight; reviewing knowledge, and also omniscient knowledge; by the word 'ñāṇadassana', these meanings are expressed.

Daṃsa daṃsane. Daṃsati, vidaṃsati. Danto. Kārite ālokaṃ vidaṃseti.

The root `daṃs` is in the sense of biting. Forms are `daṃsati`, `vidaṃsati`, and `danto`. In the causative, `ālokaṃ vidaṃseti` means 'to illuminate'.

Esa buddhiyaṃ. Esati.

The root `es` is in the sense of seeking. A form is `esati`.

Saṃsa kathane. Saṃsati. Yo me saṃse mahānāgaṃ.

The root `saṃs` is in the sense of speaking. A form is `saṃsati`. For example: 'Who will tell me of the great nāga?'

Kilisa bādhane. Kilisati. Kileso.

The root `kilis` is in the sense of afflicting. Forms are `kilisati` and `kileso`.

Ettha bādhanaṭṭhena rāgādayopi “kilesā”ti vuccanti dukkhampi. Etesu dukkhavasena –

Here, in the sense of 'afflicting', both lust and so on and also suffering are called 'kilesā'. Among these, in the sense of suffering—

“Idañca paccayaṃ laddhā, pubbe kilesamattano;

Ānandiyaṃ vicariṃsu, ramaṇīye giribbaje”ti

And having obtained this condition, formerly they roamed in delight, with their own suffering, in lovely Giribbaja.

Payogo veditabbo. Divādigaṇaṃ pana pattassa “kilissatī”ti rūpaṃ.

The usage should be understood. However, for the root when it belongs to the Divādi group, the form is 'kilissati'.

Vasa sinehane. Vasati. Vasā.

The root `vas` is in the sense of affection or grease. Forms are `vasati` and `vasā`.

Ettha ca vasā nāma vilīnasineho. Sā vaṇṇato nāḷikeratelavaṇṇā. Ācāme āsittatelavaṇṇātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

And here, 'vasā' means dissolved grease. In color, it has the color of coconut oil. It is also possible to say it has the color of oil poured into rice gruel.

Īsa hiṃsāgatidassanesu. Īsati. Īso.

The root `īs` is in the senses of harming, going, and showing. Forms are `īsati` and `īso`.

Bhāsabyattāyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Bhāsati. Bhāsā, bhāsitaṃ, bhātā. Paribhāsati. Paribhāsā, paribhāsako.

The root `bhās` is in the sense of articulate speech. Forms are `bhāsati`, `bhāsā`, `bhāsitaṃ`, and `bhātā`. Also `paribhāsati`, `paribhāsā`, and `paribhāsako`.

Tatra [M 0.0180] bhāsanti atthaṃ etāyāti bhāsā, māgadhabhāsādi. Bhāsitanti vacanaṃ. Vacanattho hi bhāsitasaddo niccaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgo daṭṭhabbo. Yathā “sutvā luddassa bhāsita”nti. Vāccaliṅgo pana bhāsitasaddo tiliṅgo daṭṭhabbo. Yathā “bhāsito dhammo, bhāsitaṃ catusaccaṃ, bhāsitā vācā”ti. Pubbe bhāsatīti bhātā, jeṭṭhabhātāti vuttaṃ hoti. So hi pubbe jātattā evaṃ vattuṃlabhati. Kiñcāpi bhātusaddo “bhātikasataṃ, sattabhātaro. Bhātaraṃ kena dosena, dujjāsi dakarakkhino”tiādīsu jeṭṭhakaniṭṭhabhātūsu vattati, tathāpi yebhuyyena jeṭṭhake nirūṭṭho, “bhātā”ti hi vutte jeṭṭhabhātāti viññāyati, tasmā katthaci ṭhāne “kaniṭṭhabhātā”ti visesetvā vuttaṃ.

Herein, `bhāsā` (language) is that by which they speak meaning, such as the Māgadhī language and so on. `Bhāsitaṃ` means speech. The word `bhāsita`, when it means speech, should be understood as always being in the neuter gender. For example: 'having heard the hunter's speech.' However, the word `bhāsita`, when it agrees with what is spoken, should be understood as having three genders. For example: 'the Dhamma was spoken' (masc.), 'the four truths were spoken' (neut.), 'the word was spoken' (fem.). `Bhātā` is one who speaks first; this means 'elder brother'. For he, having been born first, gets to speak in this way. Although the word `bhātu` (brother) applies to both elder and younger brothers—as in 'a hundred brothers,' 'seven brothers,' and 'Brother, for what fault are you hostile to the water-guardian?'—it is nevertheless predominantly established as meaning the elder. For when `bhātā` is said, it is understood as 'elder brother.' Therefore, in some places, it is specified as 'younger brother'.

Nanu ca bho katthaci “jeṭṭhabhātā”ti visesetvā vuttanti? Saccaṃ, taṃ pana bhātāsaddassa kaniṭṭhepi vattanato pākaṭīkaraṇatthaṃ “jeṭṭhabhātā”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā hi hariṇesu vattamānassa migasaddassa kadāci avasesacatuppadesupi vattanato “hariṇamigo”ti visesetvā vācaṃ bhāsanti, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca gohatthimahiṃsaacchasūkarasasabiḷārādīsu sāmaññavasena migasadde vattamānepi “migacammaṃ migamaṃsa”nti āgataṭṭhāne “hariṇassā”ti visesanasaddaṃ vināpi “hariṇamigacammaṃ hariṇamigamaṃsa”nti visesatthādhigamo hoti, ettha na gohatthiādīnaṃ cammaṃ vā maṃsaṃ vā viññāyati. Tathā “migamaṃsaṃ khādantī”ti vacanassa gohatthiādīnaṃ maṃsaṃ khādantīti attho na sambhavati, evameva katthaci vināpi jeṭṭhakaiti visesanasaddaṃ “bhātā”ti vutteyeva “jeṭṭhakabhātā”ti attho viññāyatīti. Nanu ca bho “migacammaṃ, migamaṃsa”nti ettha cammamaṃsasaddeheva [M 0.0181] visesatthādhigamo hotīti? Na hoti, migasaddassa iva cammamaṃsasaddānaṃ sāmaññavasena vattanato, evañca sati kena visesatthādhigamo hotīti ce? Lokasaṅketavasena, tathā hi migasadde ca cammasaddādīsu ca sāmaññavasena vattamānesupi lokasaṅketena paricchinnattā gohatthiādīnaṃ cammādīni na ñāyanti lokena, atha kho hariṇacammādīniyeva ñāyanti. “Saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammuti kāraṇa”nti hi vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

But, sir, is it not said somewhere 'elder brother' with specification? True, but 'elder brother' is said to clarify that the word 'brother' also applies to the younger. Just as, for example, although the word 'miga' (animal) applies to deer, it is sometimes also applied to other quadrupeds; therefore, to distinguish it, they say 'hariṇamigo' (deer-animal). So, too, should this be understood. And just as, although the word 'miga' is used generally for cows, elephants, buffaloes, bears, pigs, rabbits, cats, and so on, in contexts where 'animal hide' or 'animal flesh' are mentioned, the specific meaning of 'deer hide' or 'deer flesh' is understood even without the specifying word 'of a deer'; here, the hide or flesh of cows, elephants, and so on is not understood. Similarly, for the statement 'they eat animal flesh,' the meaning 'they eat the flesh of cows, elephants, etc.' is not possible. In the same way, in certain contexts, even without the specifying word 'elder', when 'brother' is said, the meaning 'elder brother' is understood. But, sir, in the phrases 'animal hide' or 'animal flesh,' is the specific meaning derived from the words 'hide' and 'flesh' themselves?
