No, it is not, for just like the word 'animal', the words 'hide' and 'flesh' are used generally. If that is the case, then by what means is the specific meaning understood? By worldly convention. For even though the words 'animal', 'hide', and so on are used generally, because they are defined by worldly convention, the hides of cows, elephants, and so on are not recognized by people; rather, only the hides of deer are known. It should be seen that it is said: 'Conventional speech is true, for worldly consensus is the cause.'

Gilesu anvicchāyaṃ. Punappunaṃ icchā anvicchā. Gilesati.

The root Gilesu is in the sense of seeking. Repeated desire is anvicchā. Gilesati.

Yesu payatane. Yesati.

The root Yesu is in the sense of striving. Yesati.

Jesu nesu esu hesu gatiyaṃ. Jesati. Nesati. Esati. Hesati. Dhātvantassa pana saññogavasena “jessati, nessatī”tiādīnipi gahetabbāni. Jessamāno. Jessaṃ, jessanto. Ettha ca –

The roots Jesu, Nesu, Esu, and Hesu are in the sense of going. Jesati. Nesati. Esati. Hesati. However, due to the conjunction at the end of the root, forms like "jessati, nessati," and so on, should also be taken. Jessamāno. Jessaṃ, jessanto. And here—

“Yathā āraññakaṃ nāgaṃ, dantiṃ anveti hatthinī;

Jessantaṃ giriduggesu, samesu visamesu cā”ti

Just as a cow elephant follows a wild elephant, a tusker; going in rugged mountains, and in level and uneven places.

Pāḷi nidassanaṃ.

This is a Pāli example.

Desu hesu abyattasadde. Desati. Hesati.

The roots Desu and Hesu are in the sense of inarticulate sound. Desati. Hesati.

Kāsa saddakucchāyaṃ. Kāsati, ukkāsati. Kāso. Kāsaṃ sāsaṃ daraṃ balyaṃ, khīṇamedho nigacchati.

The root Kāsa is in the sense of sound and illness. Kāsati, ukkāsati. Kāso. Kāsaṃ sāsaṃ daraṃ balyaṃ, khīṇamedho nigacchati.

Kāsu bhāsu dittiyaṃ. Dittīti pākaṭatā, virājanatā vā. Kāsati, pakāsati. Pakāsati tejo. Dūre santo pakāsenti. Bhāsati. Pabhāsati midaṃ byamhaṃ. Pakāso. Kāsu obhāso.

The roots Kāsu and Bhāsu are in the sense of shining. Ditti means clearness or radiance. Kāsati, pakāsati. Fire illuminates. The virtuous shine forth from afar. Bhāsati. This Brahma-world shines forth. Pakāso. Kāsu obhāso.

Tatra [M 0.0182] pakāsatīti pakāso, pākaṭo hotīti attho. Tucchabhāvena puñjabhāvena vā kāsati pakāsati pākaṭā hotīti kāsu. “Kāsu” iti āvāṭopi vuccati rāsipi.

Here, 'pakāso' is from 'pakāsati,' which means it becomes manifest. Kāsu is that which shines, becomes manifest, or becomes evident, either by being empty or by being heaped. The term 'kāsu' is also called a pit and a heap.

“Kiṃnu santaramānova, kāsuṃ khanasi sārathi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃkāsuyā karissasī”ti

Why indeed, as if hurrying, do you dig a pit, charioteer? Asked by me, friend, tell me, what will you do with this pit?

Ettha hi āvāṭo kāsu nāma. “Aṅgārakāsuṃ apare phuṇanti, narā rudantā paridaḍḍhagattā”ti ettha rāsi. Kārite – pakāsetīti pakāsako. Obhāsetīti obhāsako. Kamme pakāsiyatīti pakāsito. Evaṃ bhāsito. Bhāve – kāsanā. Saṅkāsanā. Pakāsanā. Tumantāditte “pakāsituṃ, pakāsetuṃ, obhāsituṃ, obhāsetuṃ. Pakāsitvā, pakāsetvā, obhāsitvā, obhāsetvā”ti rūpāni bhavanti. Taddhite bhāsu etassa atthīti bhāsuro, pabhassaro yo koci. Bhāsuroti vā kesarasīho. Imasmiṃ atthe bhāsusaddo “rāja dittiya”nti ettha rājasaddo viya virājanavācako siyā, tasmā rūpasiriyā virājanasampannatāya bhāsu virājanatā etassa atthīti bhāsuroti nibbacanaṃ ñeyyaṃ.

Here, indeed, a pit is called a 'kāsu.' In "Some make a heap of charcoal, weeping men with scorched limbs," here it means a heap. In the causative: one who makes known from 'pakāseti' is 'pakāsako.' One who illuminates from 'obhāseti' is 'obhāsako.' In the passive: that which is made known from 'pakāsiyati' is 'pakāsito.' Similarly, 'bhāsito.' In the abstract sense: 'kāsanā,' 'saṅkāsanā,' 'pakāsanā.' In the infinitive and so on, forms like 'pakāsituṃ, pakāsetuṃ, obhāsituṃ, obhāsetuṃ; pakāsitvā, pakāsetvā, obhāsitvā, obhāsetvā' arise. In derivation: from 'bhāsu,' 'bhāsuro' (radiant one) is formed in the sense of 'it has this,' or 'pabhassaro' (shining), whoever it may be. Or 'bhāsuro' means a maned lion. In this sense, the word 'bhāsu' could be a word signifying radiance, like the word 'rāja' (king) in "rāja dittiyaṃ" (royal splendor). Therefore, the etymology of 'bhāsuro' should be understood as: 'it has bhāsu (radiance),' due to being endowed with the radiance of beauty of form.

Nāsu rāsu sadde. Nāsati. Rāsati. Nāsā, nāsikā.

The roots Nāsu and Rāsu are in the sense of sound. Nāsati. Rāsati. Nāsā, nāsikā.

Tatra nāsāti hatthisoṇḍāpi nāsāti vuccati “sace maṃ nāganāsūrū, olokeyya pabhāvatī”tiādīsu viya. Manussādīnaṃ nāsikāpi nāsāti vuccati “yo te hatthe ca pāde ca, kaṇṇanāsañca chedayī”tiādīsu viya. Nāsanti abyattasaddaṃ karonti etāyāti nāsā. Nāsā eva nāsikā. Yattha nibbacanaṃ na vadāma, tattha taṃ suviññeyyattā appasiddhattā [M 0.0183] vā na vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, avuttampi payogavicakkhaṇehi upaparikkhitvā yojetabbaṃ. Atridaṃ vuccati –

Here, 'nāsā' is also used for an elephant's trunk, as in instances such as, "If the radiant one with thighs like a nāga's trunk were to look at me." Similarly, the nose of humans and others is called 'nāsā', as in instances such as, "He who cut off your hands and feet, ears and nose." They produce an inarticulate sound with it, therefore it is 'nāsā'. 'Nāsā' is the same as 'nāsikā'. Where we do not state the etymology, it should be understood that it is not stated either because it is easily understood or because it is unexpressed. Even what is not stated should be analyzed and applied by those skilled in usage. Here it is said:

Nāsā soṇḍā karo hattho,

Hatthidabbe samā matā;

Nāsā ca nāsikā ca dve,

Narādīsu samā matā”ti.

The trunk (nāsā), the trunk (soṇḍā), the trunk (kara), and the trunk (hattha) are considered the same in matters concerning elephants. And nāsā and nāsikā, these two, are considered the same among humans and so on.

Nasa koṭille. Nasati.

The root Nasa is in the sense of crookedness. Nasati.

Bhisi bhaye. Bhiṃsati. Bhiṃsanako. Tadāsi yaṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ. Bhesmākāyo.

The root Bhisi is in the sense of fear. Bhiṃsati. Bhiṃsanako. That was what was terrifying. Bhesmākāyo.

Āsisi icchāyaṃ. Āpubbo sisi icchāyaṃ vattati. Āsisati. Āsisateva puriso. Āsisanā. Āsisattaṃ. Āsisanto, āsisamāno, āsamāno. “Suggatimāsamānā”ti pāḷi ettha nidassanaṃ.

The root Āsisi is in the sense of desiring. Sisi, preceded by Ā, functions in the sense of desiring. Āsisati. A man indeed desires. Āsisanā. Āsisattaṃ. Āsisanto, āsisamāno, āsamāno. The Pāli 'Suggatimāsamānā' is an example here.

Gasu adane. Gasati.

The root Gasu is in the sense of eating. Gasati.

Ghusī kantikaraṇe. Īkārantoyaṃ, tena ito na niggahītāgamo. Ghusati.

The root Ghusī is in the sense of making beautiful or making a sound. This ends in 'ī', therefore there is no augment of the nasal consonant from this. Ghusati.

Paṃsu bhaṃsu avasaṃsane. Paṃsati. Bhaṃsati.

The roots Paṃsu and Bhaṃsu are in the sense of falling down. Paṃsati. Bhaṃsati.

Dhaṃsu gatiyaṃ. Dhaṃsati. Rajo nuddhaṃsati uddhaṃ.

The root Dhaṃsu is in the sense of going. Dhaṃsati. Dust is scattered upwards.

Pasa vitthāre. Pasati. Pasu.

The root Pasa is in the sense of spreading. Pasati. Pasu.

Kusa avhāne rodane ca. Kosati, pakkosati. Pakkosako, pakkosito, pakkosanaṃ.

The root Kusa is in the sense of calling and lamenting. Kosati, pakkosati. Pakkosako, pakkosito, pakkosanaṃ.

Kassa gatiyaṃ. Kassati, parikassati. Paṭikassati. Mūlāya paṭikasseyya. Paṭikasseyyāti ākaḍḍheyya, mūlāpattiyaṃyeva patiṭṭhāpeyyāti attho.

The root Kassa is in the sense of going. Kassati, parikassati. Paṭikassati. He should be drawn back to the root. "He should be drawn back" means he should be pulled back; the meaning is that he should be established in the root offense itself.

Asa [M 0.0184] dityādānesu ca. Cakāro gatipekkhako. Asati.

The root Asa is in the sense of shining, taking, and so on. The particle 'ca' also indicates going. Asati.

Disa ādānasaṃvaraṇesu. Dissati puriso.

The root Disa is in the sense of taking and restraining. Dissati puriso.

Dāsu dāne. Dāsati.

The root Dāsu is in the sense of giving. Dāsati.

Rosa bhaye. Rosati. Rosako.

The root Rosa is in the sense of fear. Rosati. Rosako.

Bhesu calane. Bhesati.

The root Bhesu is in the sense of moving. Bhesati.

Pasa bādhanaphassanesu. Pasati. Pāso, nāgapāso, hatthapāso.

The root Pasa is in the sense of afflicting and touching. Pasati. Pāso, nāgapāso, hatthapāso.

Lasa kantiyaṃ. Lasati, abhilasati, vilasati. Lāso, vilāso, vilasanaṃ.

The root Lasa is used in the sense of beauty. Lasati, abhilasati, vilasati. Lāso, vilāso, vilasanaṃ.

Casa bhakkhaṇe. Casati.

The root Casa is used in the sense of eating. Casati.

Kasa hiṃsāyaṃ. Kasati.

The root Kasa is used in the sense of harming. Kasati.

Tisa tittiyaṃ. Titti tappanaṃ paripuṇṇatā suhitatā. Tisati. Titti.

The root Tisa is used in the sense of satisfaction. Titti means satisfaction, contentment, fullness, and satiation. Tisati. Titti.

Vasa nivāse. Vasati, vasiyati, vacchati. Vatthu, vatthaṃ, parivāso, nivāso, āvāso, upavāso, uposatho, vippavāso, cirappavāsī, cirappavuttho, vasitvā, vattuṃ, vasituṃ iccādīni.

The root Vasa is used in the sense of dwelling. Vasati, vasiyati, vacchati. Vatthu, vatthaṃ, parivāso, nivāso, āvāso, upavāso, uposatho, vippavāso, cirappavāsī, cirappavuttho, vasitvā, vattuṃ, vasituṃ, and so forth.

Atra upavāsoti annena vajjito vāso upavāso. Uposathoti upavasanti etthāti uposatho, upavasanti sīlena vā anasanena vā upetā hutvā vasantīti attho. Ayaṃ panettha atthuddhāro – “āyāmāvuso kappina uposathaṃ gamissāmā”tiādīsu pātimokkhuddeso [M 0.0185] uposatho. “Evaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgato kho visākhe uposatho upavuttho”tiādīsu sīlaṃ. “Suddhassa ve sadā phaggu, suddhassuposatho sadā”tiādīsu upavāso. “Uposatho nāma nāgarājā”tiādīsu paññatti. “Na bhikkhave tadahuposathe sabhikkhukā āvāsā”tiādīsu upavasitabbadivasoti.

Here, 'upavāso' means dwelling while abstaining from food; that dwelling is called 'upavāso'. 'Uposatho' is where they observe; it means they dwell, having undertaken virtue or fasting. This is the analysis of meaning here: in 'Come, friend Kappina, we will go to the Uposatha,' etc., 'Uposatha' refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. In 'Thus, Visākha, the Uposatha observed with the eight factors,' etc., it refers to virtue. In 'For the pure, it is always Phaggu; for the pure, Uposatha is constant,' etc., it refers to fasting. In 'Uposatha is the name of a nāga king,' etc., it refers to a designation. In 'Monks, on that Uposatha day, from a residence with monks…' etc., it refers to the day of observance.

Vasa kantiyaṃ. Vacchati. Jinavacchayo.

The root Vasa is used in the sense of beauty. Vacchati. Jinavacchayo.

Sasa susane. Sasati. Saso.

The root Sasa is used in the sense of the charnel ground. Sasati. Saso.

Sasa pāṇane. Sasati. Satova assasati, satova passasati. Saso, sasanaṃ. Assāso passāso assasanto passasanto.

The root Sasa is used in the sense of breathing. Sasati. Mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out. Saso, sasanaṃ. Assāso, passāso, assasanto, passasanto.

Asa bhuvi. Atthi. Asa.

The root Asa is used in the sense of being. Atthi. Asa.

Ettha atthīti ākhyātapadaṃ. Na atthi khīrā brāhmaṇī. Atthitā, atthibhāvo, “yaṃ kiñci ratanaṃ atthī”tiādīsu viya nipātapadaṃ. Tasmā atthīti padaṃ ākhyātanipātavasena duvidhanti veditabbaṃ. Asaiti avibhattikaṃ nāmikapadaṃ. Ettha ca “asasmīti hotī”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha atthīti asa, niccassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Iminā sassatadiṭṭhi vuttā.

Here, 'atthi' is a finite verb. For example, 'Na atthi khīrā brāhmaṇī.' 'Atthitā' and 'atthibhāvo' refer to existence or being. And in phrases like 'whatever treasure there is,' 'atthi' is a particle. Therefore, the word 'atthi' should be understood as twofold: as a finite verb and as a particle. 'Asa' is an uninflected nominal form. And here, the Pāli example is 'asasmīti hoti.' There, 'atthi' is synonymous with 'asa', a designation for permanence. By this, the eternalist view is stated.

Tatrāyaṃ padamālā – “atthi, santi. Asi, attha. Asmi, asma, amhi, amha” iccetāni pasiddhāni. “Atthu, santu. Āhi, attha. Asmi, asma amhi, amha” iccetāni ca, “siyā, assa, siyuṃ, assu, siyaṃsu. Assa, assatha. Siyaṃ, assa, assāma” iccetāni ca pasiddhāni.

Here is the paradigm: 'atthi, santi; asi, attha; asmi, asma, amhi, amha'—these are well-known. And 'atthu, santu; āhi, attha; asmi, asma, amhi, amha'—these too; and 'siyā, assa, siyuṃ, assu, siyaṃsu; assa, assatha; siyaṃ, assa, assāma'—these are also well-known.

Ettha pana “tesañca kho bhikkhave samaggānaṃ sammodamānānaṃ…pe… siyaṃsu dve bhikkhū abhidhamme nānāvādā”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ[M 0.0186]. Tattha siyaṃsūti bhaveyyuṃ. Abhidhammeti visiṭṭhe dhamme.

Here, however, the Pāli passage 'tesañca kho bhikkhave samaggānaṃ sammodamānānaṃ…pe… siyaṃsu dve bhikkhū abhidhamme nānāvādā' is an example. There, 'siyaṃsu' means 'they might be.' 'Abhidhamme' means 'in the higher doctrine.'

Idāni siyāsaddassa atthuddhāro pabhedo ca vuccate. Siyāti ekaṃse ca vikappane ca “pathavīdhātu siyā ajjhattikā, siyā bāhirā”ti ekaṃse. “Siyā aññatarassa bhikkhuno āpattivītikkamo”ti vikappane.

Now, the meaning and divisions of the word 'siyā' are explained. 'Siyā' is used in the sense of certainty (ekaṃse) and in the sense of option (vikappane). 'The earth element is sometimes internal, sometimes external' is an example of certainty. 'There might be a transgression of a rule by a certain monk' is an example of option.

Siyāti ekamārakhyātapadaṃ, ekamabyayapadaṃ. Ākhyātatte ekavacanantaṃ, abyayatte yathāpāvacanaṃ. “Puttā matthi dhanā matthī”ti ettha atthīti abyayapadamiva ekavacanantampi bahuvacanantampi bhavati. Tassākhyātatte payogoviditova. Abyayatte pana “sukhaṃ na sukhasahagataṃ, siyā pītisahagata”nti “ime dhammā siyā parittārammaṇā”ti ca ekavacanabahuvacanappayogā veditabbā. Ettha dhātuyā kiccaṃ natthi. Parokkhāyaṃ “itiha asa itiha asā”ti dassanato asa iti padaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Hiyyattanīrūpāni appasiddhāni. Ajjataniyā pana “āsi, āsiṃsu, āsuṃ. Āsi, āsittha. Āsiṃ, āsimhā” iccetāni pasiddhāni. Bhavissantiyā “bhavissati, bhavissanti” iccādīni. Kālātipattiyā “abhavissā, abhavissaṃsu” iccādīni bhavanti.

'Siyā' is a single word, being a finite verb and an indeclinable. As a finite verb, it is in the singular number; as an indeclinable, its number is according to usage. In 'puttā m'atthi, dhanā m'atthi,' the indeclinable 'atthi' is used with a plural subject. The usage of 'siyā' as a finite verb is known from convention. But as an indeclinable, as in 'sukhaṃ na sukhasahagataṃ, siyā pītisahagataṃ' and 'ime dhammā siyā parittārammaṇā,' its singular and plural usages should be understood. Here, the root has no function. For the perfect tense, in 'itiha asa, itiha asā,' the word 'asa' should be taken as an example. The aorist forms are established. The imperfect forms, however, are well-known: 'āsi, āsiṃsu, āsuṃ; āsi, āsittha; āsiṃ, āsimhā.' Forms of the future include 'bhavissati, bhavissanti,' etc. Forms of the conditional include 'abhavissā, abhavissaṃsu,' etc.

Sāsa anusiṭṭhiyaṃ. Sāsati, anusāsati. Kammantaṃ vo sāsati, sāsanaṃ, anusāsanaṃ, anusāsanī, anusiṭṭhi, satthā, satthaṃ, anusāsako, anusāsikā.

The root Sāsa is used in the sense of instruction. Sāsati, anusāsati. 'He instructs you in work.' Sāsanaṃ, anusāsanaṃ, anusāsanī, anusiṭṭhi, satthā, satthaṃ, anusāsako, anusāsikā.

Tatra sāsananti adhisīlādisikkhattayasaṅgahitasāsanaṃ, pariyattipaṭipattipaṭivedhasaṅkhātaṃ vā sāsanaṃ. Tañhi sāsati etena, ettha vāti “sāsana”nti pavuccati. Apica sāsananti “rañño [M 0.0187] sāsanaṃ pesetī”tiādīsu viya pāpetabbavacanaṃ. Tathā sāsananti ovādo, yo “anusāsanī”ti ca, “anusiṭṭhī”ti ca vuccati. Satthāti tividhayānamukhena sadevakaṃ lokaṃ sāsatīti satthā, diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ satte anusāsatīti attho. Satthanti sadde ca atthe ca sāsati ācikkhati etenāti satthaṃ. Kiṃtaṃ? Byākaraṇaṃ.

Here, 'sāsana' means the Teaching, which comprises the threefold training of higher virtue and so forth, or the Teaching known as scripture, practice, and realization. For one instructs by means of this, or in this, therefore it is called 'sāsana.' Furthermore, 'sāsana' means a message to be delivered, just as in 'he sends the king's message.' Similarly, 'sāsana' means advice, which is also called 'anusāsanī' and 'anusiṭṭhī.' 'Satthā' means a teacher, because he instructs the world with its devas through the three kinds of vehicles; that is, he instructs beings appropriately with regard to their welfare in this life, in the next life, and in the ultimate sense. 'Satthaṃ' means a treatise, because by it one instructs and explains sounds and meanings. What is that? Grammar.

Īsa issariye. Issariyaṃ issarabhāvo. Īsati. Vaṅgīso, janapadeso, manujeso.

The root Īsa is used in the sense of mastery. Issariyaṃ is the state of being a master. Īsati. Vaṅgīso, janapadeso, manujeso.

Tatra vaṅgīsoti vācāya īso issaroti vaṅgīso. Ko so? Āyasmā vaṅgīso arahā. Āha ca sayameva –

There, 'Vaṅgīsa' means master of speech, one who is a lord of words. Who is that? The Venerable Vaṅgīsa, the Arahant. And he himself said:

“Vaṅge jātoti vaṅgīso, vacane issaroti ca;

‘Vaṅgīso’ iti me nāmaṃ, abhavī lokasammata”nti;

“Because I was born in Vaṅga I am Vaṅgīsa, and because I am a master in speech; thus my name ‘Vaṅgīsa’ became honored in the world.”

Āsa upavesane. Upavesanaṃ nisīdanaṃ “āsane upaviṭṭho saṅgho”ti ettha viya. Āsati. Acchati. Āsīno. Āsanaṃ. Upāsati. Upāsako.

The root Āsa is used in the sense of sitting. Upavesanaṃ means sitting, as in 'āsane upaviṭṭho saṅgho' (the Saṅgha is seated on a seat). Āsati. Acchati. Āsīno. Āsanaṃ. Upāsati. Upāsako.

Tattha āsananti āsati nisīdati etthāti āsanaṃ, yaṃ kiñci nisīdanayoggaṃ mañcapīṭhādi.

There, 'āsana' is so called because one sits (āsati, nisīdati) on it (ettha); it is any object suitable for sitting, such as a couch, stool, and so forth.

Kasī gatisosanesu. Īkārantoyaṃ dhātu, tenito na niggahītāgamo. Kasati.

The root Kasī is used in the sense of going and drying. This is an ī-ending root, therefore it is not augmented with a niggahīta. Kasati.

Nisī cumbane. Nisati.

The root Nisī is used in the sense of kissing. Nisati.

Disī appītiyaṃ. Dhammaṃ dessati. Diso. Diṭṭho. Dessī. Desso. Dessiyo.

The root Disī is used in the sense of aversion. He hates the Dhamma. Diso (an enemy). Diṭṭho (an enemy). Dessī (hateful). Desso (hated). Dessiyo (hateful).

Tatra disoti ca diṭṭhoti ca paccāmittassādhivacanametaṃ. So hi pare dessati nappiyāyati, parehi vā dessiyati piyo [M 0.0188] na kariyatīti “diso”ti ca “diṭṭho”ti ca vuccati. Atha vā disoti coro vāpaccāmitto vā. Diṭṭhoti paccāmittoyeva. Atrime payogā –

There, 'diso' and 'diṭṭho' are terms for an enemy. For he hates others and is not fond of them, or he is hated by others and not held dear—thus he is called 'diso' and 'diṭṭho.' Alternatively, 'diso' means a thief or an enemy. 'Diṭṭho' means an enemy specifically. Here are some usages:

“Diso disaṃ yaṃ taṃ kayirā, verī vā pana verinaṃ;

Micchāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, pāpiyo naṃ tato kare”ti ca.

'Whatever an enemy might do to an enemy, or a hater to one who is hated; a wrongly directed mind can do one even greater harm.'

“Disā hi me dhammakathaṃ suṇantū”ti ca, “disā hi me te manusse bhajantu ye dhammamevādapayanti santo”ti ca,

'May those in all directions hear my Dhamma talk,' and 'May those in all directions attend to those people who, being at peace, teach only the Dhamma.'

“Yassete caturo dhammā, vānarinda yathā tava;

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, diṭṭhaṃ so ativattatī”ti ca.

'Whoever has these four qualities, O king of monkeys, just as you do—truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity—he overcomes his enemy.'

Dessīti dessanasīlo appiyāyanasīloti dessī. “Dhammakāmo bhavaṃ hoti, dhammadessī parābhavo”ti idamettha payoganidassanaṃ. Dessoti appiyo, tathā dessiyoti. Ettha ca –

'Dessī' means one of a hating nature, one inclined to dislike. 'One who loves the Dhamma prospers; one who hates the Dhamma declines'—this illustrates the usage here. 'Desso' means disliked, and likewise 'dessiyo.' Here also:

“Na me dessā ubho puttā, maddīdevī na dessiyā;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā piye adāsaha”nti ca,

Neither of my two sons is hateful to me, nor is Queen Maddī hateful; omniscience is dear to me, therefore I gave away what was dear.

“Na me sā brāhmaṇī dessā, napi me balaṃ na vijjatī”ti ca,

That brahmin woman is not hateful to me, nor do I lack strength.

“Mātā pitā na me dessā, napi dessaṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā vatamadhiṭṭhahi”nti ca

Neither mother nor father are hateful to me, nor is great fame hateful; omniscience is dear to me, therefore I undertook this vow.

Payogā. Sabbattha meti ca mayhanti ca sāmivacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

These are the usages. Everywhere, 'me' and 'mayhaṃ' should be understood as a term of ownership.

Imāni pana paccāmittassa nāmāni –

These, however, are the names of an enemy:

“Paccamitto ripu diṭṭho, diso verī ca satva’ri;

Amitto ca sapatto ca, evaṃ paṇṇattikārisū”ti.

Adversary, foe, opponent, enemy, hostile one, and rival; unfriend and competitor—thus are the terms for an enemy.

Esu gatiyaṃ. Esati.

Esu: in going. He goes.

Bhassa [M 0.0189] bhassanadittīsu. Bhassanaṃ vacanaṃ. Ditti sobhā. Bhassati. Bhassaṃ, pabhassaraṃ.

Bhassa: in speaking and shining. Bhassanaṃ: speech. Ditti: radiance. He speaks, he shines. Bhassaṃ, pabhassaraṃ.

Dhisa sadde. Dhisati.

Dhisa: in sounding. He sounds.

Disa atisajjane. Disati, upadisati, sandisati, niddisati, paccādisati, paṭisandisati, uddisati. Deso, uddeso iccādīni.

Disa: in pointing out. He points out, he instructs, he indicates, he specifies, he rejects, he reconciles, he points out. A region, an outline, etc.

Pisu avayave. Pisati.

Pisu: in component parts. He grinds, he crushes.

Isi gatiyaṃ. Isati.

Isi: in going. He goes.

Phusa samphasse. Phusati. Phasso, phusanā, samphusanā, samphusitattaṃ. Evarūpo kāyasamphasso ahosi. Phoṭṭhabbaṃ, phusitaṃ. Devo ca ekamekaṃ phusāyati. Phuṭṭhuṃ, phusituṃ, phusitvā, phusitvāna, phusiya, phusiyāna. Phussa phussa byantiṃ karoti.

Phusa: in contact. He touches. Contact, touching, mutual touching, the state of having been touched. Such was the bodily contact. Tangible object, touched. And the god causes it to rain down one by one. To touch, to touch, having touched, having touched, touching, while touching. Repeatedly touching, he brings it to an end.

Tatra phassoti ārammaṇaṃ phusanti etena, sayaṃ vā phusati, phusanamattameva vā etanti phasso, ārammaṇe phusanalakkhaṇo dhammo.

Here, 'contact' means that by which one touches an object, or that which touches of itself, or merely the act of touching—thus, contact is a phenomenon characterized by touching an object.

Rusa risa hiṃsāyaṃ. Rosati. Risati. Puriso.

Rusa, risa: in harming. He is angry. He harms. A person.

Ettha ca “puṃ vuccati nirayo, taṃ risatīti puriso”ti ācariyā vadanti.

Moreover, here the teachers say: "'Puṃ' is called hell; he who harms it is 'puriso' (a person)."

Risa gatiyaṃ. Resati.

Risa: in going. He goes.

Visa pavesane. Visati, pavisati. Paveso, pavesanaṃ, nivesanaṃ, pavisaṃ. Ettha nivesanaṃ vuccati gehaṃ.

Visa: in entering. He enters, he enters. Entrance, entering, dwelling, entering. Here, 'dwelling' is called a house.

Masa āmasane. Masati, āmasati, parāmasati. Parāmāso, parāmasanaṃ.

Masa: in touching. He touches, he touches, he grasps. Grasping, the act of grasping.

Ettha [M 0.0190] parāmāsoti parato āmasatīti parāmāso, aniccādidhamme niccādivasena gaṇhātīti attho. “Parāmāso micchādiṭṭhi kummaggo micchāpatho”tiādīni bahūni vevacanapadāni abhidhammato gahetabbāni.

Here, 'grasping' (parāmāsa) is so called because one grasps perversely; the meaning is that one takes impermanent phenomena and so forth as permanent and so forth. "Grasping is wrong view, the wrong path, the wrong way"—many such synonymous terms are to be taken from the Abhidhamma.

Isu icchāyaṃ. Icchati, sampaṭicchati. Sampaṭicchanaṃ, icchā, abhicchā, icchaṃ, icchamāno.

Isu: in desiring. He desires, he accepts. Acceptance, desire, craving, wish, wishing.

Vesu dāne. Vecchati, pavecchati, paveccheti. Pavecchaṃ, pavecchanto.

Vesu: in giving. He gives, he bestows, he causes to give. Bestowing, while bestowing.

Nisa baddhāyaṃ. Baddhāti vinibaddho, ahaṅkārassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Nisati.

Nisa: in binding. 'Bound' means thoroughly bound; this is a designation for egoism. It binds.

Jusi pītisevanesu. Josati.

Jusi: in enjoying pleasure. He enjoys.

Isa pariyesane. Esati. Isi, iṭṭhaṃ, aniṭṭhaṃ, esaṃ, esamāno.

Isa: in seeking. He seeks. Seeker, desirable, undesirable, seeking, while seeking.

Saṃkase acchane. Acchanaṃ nisīdanaṃ. Saṅkasāyati.

Saṃkase: in sitting. Acchanaṃ: sitting. He sits down.

Sakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'sa'.

Hakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ha'.

Hā cāge. Jahati, vijahati. Vijahanaṃ, jahituṃ, jahātave, jahitvā, jahāya.

Hā: in abandoning. He abandons, he forsakes. Abandoning, to abandon, for abandoning, having abandoned, having abandoned.

Mhī īsaṃhasane. Mhayate, umhayate vimhayate.

Mhī: in slight smiling. He smiles, he smiles joyfully, he is astonished.

Tattha mhayateti sitaṃ karoti. Umhayateti pahaṭṭhākāraṃ dasseti. Vimhayateti vimhayanaṃ karoti. Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi “na naṃ umhayate disvā. Pekkhitena mhitena ca. Mhitapubbaṃva [M 0.0191] bhāsati. Yadā umhayamānā maṃ, rājaputtī udikkhati. Umhāpeyya pabhāvatī. Pamhāpeyya pabhāvatī”ti.

Here, 'mhayati' means to make a smile. 'Umhayati' means to display a delighted appearance. 'Vimhayati' means to cause astonishment. In this regard, the Pali passage is: "Seeing him, she does not smile joyfully. With a glance and a smile. She speaks as if having smiled beforehand. When the princess looks at me, smiling joyfully. Pabhāvatī might cause me to smile. Pabhāvatī might cause me to laugh heartily."

Tattha umhayamānāti pahaṭṭhākāraṃ dassetvā hasamānā. Umhāpeyyāti sitavasena pahaṃseyya. Pamhāpeyyāti mahāhasitavasena parihāseyya.

Here, 'umhayamānā' means showing a delighted appearance and laughing. 'Umhāpeyya' means to amuse with a smile. 'Pamhāpeyya' means to make one laugh heartily.

Hu dāne. Havati. Huti.

The root 'hu' is in the sense of 'giving'. He gives. An offering.

Hu pasajjakaraṇe. Pasajjakaraṇaṃ pakārena sajjanakriyā. Havati. Huto, hutavā, hutāvī, āhuti.

The root 'hu' is in the sense of 'sacrificing'. Sacrificing is the act of preparing in a particular way. He sacrifices. Sacrificed, having sacrificed, a sacrificer, an offering.

Hū sattāyaṃ. Hoti, honti. Hosi, hotha. Homi, homa. Pahoti, pahonti. Pahūtaṃ, pahūtā, kuto pahūtā kalahā vivādā. Honto, hontā, hontaṃ, pahonto. Pacchāsamaṇena hotabbaṃ. Hotuṃ hotuye, pahotuṃ, hutvāna. Vattamānāvibhattirūpādīni. Ettha pasiddharūpāneva gahitāni.

The root 'hū' is in the sense of 'being' or 'existence'. He is, they are. You are, you all are. I am, we are. He is able, they are able. Abundant, plentiful; whence come abundant quarrels and disputes? Being, being, being, being able. It is to be by a junior ascetic. To be, to be, to be able, having been. Forms of the present tense conjugations, and so forth. Here, only well-known forms are taken.

Hotu, hontu. Hosi, hotha. Homi, homa. Pañcamīvibhattirūpāni. Etthāpi pasiddharūpāneva gahitāni.

Let it be, let them be. You be, you all be. I be, we be. Forms of the imperative mood. Here too, only well-known forms are taken.

Huveyya, huveyyuṃ. Huveyyāsi, huveyyātha. Huveyyāmi, huveyyāma. Huvetha, huveraṃ. Huvetho, huveyyāvho. Huveyyaṃ, huveyyāmhe. Sattamiyā rūpāni. Ettha pana “upako ājīvako ‘huveyya pāvuso’ti vatvā sīsaṃ okampetvā ummaggaṃ gahetvā pakkamī”ti pāḷiyaṃ huveyyāti padassa dassanato nayavasena ‘huveyya, huveyyu”ntiādīni vuttāni. Hupeyyātipi pāṭho dissati, yathā paccapekkhaṇā. Tabbasena “hupeyya, hupeyyuṃ[M 0.0192]. Hupeyyāsī”tiādinā vakārassa pakārādesabhūtāni rūpānipi gahetabbāni.

May it be, may they be. May you be, may you all be. May I be, may we be. May you be, may they be. May you two be, may you all be. May I be, may we be. These are the forms of the optative mood. Here, however, in the Pali passage, "The ascetic Upaka, saying, 'It may be so, friend,' shaking his head and taking a wrong path, departed," forms such as "may it be, may they be," and so forth, are mentioned, illustrating the meaning of the word "huveyya." The reading "hupeyyāti" is also seen, as in the reflection. Therefore, forms such as "hupeyya, hupeyyuṃ, hupeyyāsi," and so forth, where 'p' replaces 'v,' should also be included.

Aparo nayo – heyya, heyyuṃ. Heyyāsi, heyyātha. Heyyāmi, heyyāma. Hetha, heraṃ. Hetho, heyyāvho. Heyyaṃ, heyyāmhe. Imāni aṭṭhakathānayena gahitarūpāni. Ettha pana “na ca uppādo hoti. Sace heyya, uppādassāpi uppādo pāpuṇeyyā”ti idampi nidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Another method – may it be, may they be. May you be, may you all be. May I be, may we be. May you be, may they be. May you two be, may you all be. May I be, may we be. These forms are taken according to the commentary method. Here, however, this example should also be seen in the passage: "And there is no arising. If it were to be, the arising of arising would also be reached."

Huva, huvu. Huve, huvittha. Huvaṃ, huvimha. Huvittha, hotha iccapi saññogatakāralopena ahosīti attho. Tathāhi “kasirā jīvikā hothā”ti padassatthaṃ vaṇṇentehi “dukkhā no jīvikā ahosī”ti attho vutto. huvire. Huvittho, huvivho. Huviṃ, huvimhe. Parokkhāya rūpāni.

He was, they were. You were, you all were. I was, we were. Huvittha, hotha – with the elision of the connecting sound, the meaning is 'it was'. For example, in explaining the meaning of the passage: "Difficult was our livelihood," the commentators say the meaning is "our livelihood was suffering." They were. You two were, you all were. I was, we were. These are forms of the perfect tense.

Ahuvā, ahuvū. Ahuvo, ahuvattha. Ahuvaṃ, ahuvamha. Ahuvattha, ahuvatthuṃ. Ahuvase, ahuvavhaṃ. Ahuviṃ, ahuvamhase. Hiyyattanīrūpāni.

He was, they were. You were, you all were. I was, we were. You all were, they were. You were, you two were. I was, we were. These are forms of the imperfect tense.

Ettha ahuvamhaseti mayaṃ bhavamhaseti attho. “Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ, yaṃ balaṃ ahuvamhase”ti pāḷiyaṃ pana “ahuva amhase” iti vā padacchedo kātabbo “ahu amhase”ti vā. Pacchimanaye vakārāgamo “ahuvā”ti ca “ahū”ti ca dvinnampi ahosīti attho. Amhanti amhākaṃ. Seti nipātamattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – amhākaṃ yaṃ balaṃ ahosi, mayaṃ tena balena tava kiccaṃ akaramhāti.

Here, 'ahuvamhaseti' means 'mayaṃ bhavamhase', that is, 'we were'. However, in the Pali phrase, "We did your work, whatever strength we had," the word division should be either "ahuva amhase" or "ahu amhase". In the latter method, the insertion of 'v' gives 'ahuvā' and 'ahū', both meaning 'it was'. 'Amhanti' means 'for us'. 'Seti' is merely a particle. This is what is said: 'Whatever strength we had, with that strength we did your work for you.'

Ahosi, ahuṃ, ahesuṃ. Ahuvo, ahuvittha. Ahositthaiccapi. Ahosiṃ, ahuvāsiṃ iccapi, ahosimhā, ahumhā[M 0.0193]. Ahuvā, ahuvu, ahuvase, ahuvivhaṃ. Ahuvaṃ, ahuṃ iccapi. Ahuvimhe. Ajjataniyā rūpāni.

He was, they were, I was. You were, you all were. Also 'ahosittha'. I was, also 'ahuvāsiṃ', we were, we were. He was, they were, you were, you two were. I was, also 'ahuṃ'. We were. These are forms of the aorist tense.

Ettha “ahaṃ kevaṭṭagāmasmiṃ, ahuṃ kevaṭṭadārako”ti dassanato “ahu”nti vuttaṃ, ahosinti attho. “Ahaṃ bhadante ahuvāsiṃ pubbe sumedhanāmassa jinassa sāvako”ti dassanato “ahuvāsi”nti iccevattho. Tathā hi anekavaṇṇavimānavatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ imissā pāḷiyā atthaṃ vaṇṇentehi ahuvāsinti ahosinti attho pakāsito.

Here, in the example "I was in the village of fishermen, I was a fisherman's boy," the word 'ahuṃ' is stated, meaning 'ahosiṃ'. In the example "Venerable sir, I was formerly a disciple of the Jina named Sumedha," the word 'ahuvāsiṃ' has this very meaning. Thus, in the commentary on the Anekavaṇṇavimānavatthu, the meaning of this Pali passage is explained by showing that 'ahuvāsiṃ' means 'ahosiṃ'.

“Hessati, hehissati, hehiti, hohitī”ti imāni cattāri bhavissantiyā mātikāpadāni veditabbāni.

"Hessati, hehissati, hehiti, hohiti" – these four should be understood as the principal terms for the future tense.

Idāni tāni vibhajissāmi – hessāti, hessanti. Hessasi, hessatha. Hessāmi, hessāma. Hessate, hessante. Hessase, hessavhe. Hessaṃ, hessāmhe. Imāni “anāgatamhi addhāne, hessāma sammukhā ima”nti dassanato vuttāni.

Now I will analyze them: He will be, they will be. You will be, you all will be. I will be, we will be. He will be, they will be. You will be, you all will be. I will be, we will be. These are stated with reference to the future, as in the example: "In the future time, we will be present here."

Hehissati, hehissanti. Hehissasi. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

He will be, they will be. You will be. The rest should be expanded accordingly.

Hohissati, hohissanti. Hohissasi. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

He will be, they will be. You will be. The rest should be expanded similarly.

Hehiti, hehinti. Hehisi. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

He will be, they will be. You will be. The rest is to be expanded.

Hohiti, hohinti. Hohisi. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Bhavissantiyā rūpāni.

He will be, they will be. You will be. The rest should be expanded accordingly. These are forms of the future tense.

Ahuvissā, ahuvissaṃsu. Ahuvissase, ahuvissatha. Ahuvissaṃ, ahuvissamhā. Ahuvissatha, ahuvissisu. Ahuvissase[M 0.0194], ahuvissavhe. Ahuvissiṃ, ahuvissāmhase. Kālātipattirūpāni.

He would have been, they would have been. You would have been, you all would have been. I would have been, we would have been. You would have been, they would have been. You would have been, you two would have been. I would have been, we would have been. These are forms of the conditional tense.

Vhe avhāyane baddhāyaṃ sadde ca. Avhāyanaṃ pakkosanaṃ. Baddhāti ahaṅkāro, ghaṭṭanaṃ vā sārambhakaraṇaṃ vā. Saddo ravo. Vheti, vhāyati, avheti, avhāyati, avhāsi iccapi. Kaccāyano māṇavakosmi rāja, anūnanāmo iti mavhayanti. Āsaddo upasaggova, so saññogaparattā rasso jāto. Avhito. Anavhito tato āgā. Avhā, avhāyanā. Vāraṇavhayanā rukkhā. Kāmavhe visaye. Kumāro candasavhayo.

The root 'vhe' is in the sense of 'calling', 'binding', and 'sound'. Calling is summoning. 'Binding' refers to egoism, or striking, or inciting. Sound is noise. 'Vheti', 'vhāyati', 'avheti', 'avhāyati', 'avhāsi', and so on, are forms. "O king, I am the young man Kaccāyana; they call me by a complete name." The sound 'ā' is a prefix; it becomes short because it is followed by a conjunct consonant. Called. Uncalled, he came from there. Calling, calling. Trees named Vāraṇa. In the realm called 'kāma'. The prince is named Candasavhayo.

“Sattatantiṃ sumadhuraṃ,

Rāmaṇeyyaṃ avācayiṃ;

So maṃ raṅgamhi avheti,

Saraṇaṃ me hohi kosiyā”ti.

I played the sweet, delightful seven-stringed lute; he challenges me on the stage. Be my refuge, O Kosiya!

Ettha avhetīti sārambhavasena attano visayaṃ dassetuṃ saṅghaṭṭatīti attho. “Samāgate ekasataṃ samagge, avhettha yakkho avikampamāno”ti etthāpi sārambhavasena ghaṭṭanaṃ avhāyanaṃ nāma.

Here, 'avheti' means he clashes in order to show his own domain by way of provocation. In the passage, 'When a hundred gathered together, united, the yakkha called, unperturbed,' here too, clashing by way of provocation is called 'calling'.

“Tattha naccanti gāyanti, avhāyanti varāvaraṃ;

Accharā viya devesu, nāriyo samalaṅkatā”ti

There they dance and sing, challenging one another; women, beautifully adorned, like celestial nymphs among the devas.

Ettha pana avhāyanti varāvaranti varato varaṃ naccañca gītañca karontiyo sārambhaṃ karontīti attho daṭṭhabbo.

Here, however, 'avhāyanti varāvaraṃ' means that by performing dances and songs in a competitive manner, they are making a provocation—this meaning should be understood.

Pañha pucchāyaṃ. Bhikkhu garuṃ pañhaṃ pañhati. Pañho. Ayaṃ pana pāḷi “paripucchati paripañhati idaṃ bhante kathaṃ imassa ko attho”ti. Pañhasaddo pulliṅgavasena gahetabbo. “Pañho maṃ [M 0.0195] paṭibhāti, taṃ suṇā”ti yebhuyyena pulliṅgappayogadassanato. Katthaci pana itthiliṅgopi bhavati napuṃsakaliṅgopi. Tathā hi “pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā. Koṇḍañña pañhāni viyākarohī”ti taddīpikā pāḷiyo dissanti, liṅgavipallāso vā tattha daṭṭhabbo.

The root 'pañh' is in the sense of questioning. A monk asks a teacher a question. A question. This Pali passage, however, reads: 'He asks, he questions: "Venerable sir, how is this? What is its meaning?"' The word 'pañha' should be taken as masculine, as the masculine usage is mostly seen in 'A question occurs to me, listen to it.' Sometimes, however, it is also feminine or neuter. For example, such illustrative Pali passages are seen as 'These questions were pondered by the wise. Koṇḍañña, explain the questions,' or a gender shift should be noted there.

Pañha icchāyaṃ. Pañhati. Pañho. Ettha ca pañhoti ñātuṃ icchito attho. Idaṃ panettha nibbacanaṃ pañhiyati ñātuṃ icchiyati soti pañhoti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “vissajjitamhi pañhe”ti imissā nettipāḷiyā atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇentena “pañheti ñātuṃ icchite atthe”ti.

The root pañh is in the sense of desiring. He desires. A question. And here, 'pañho' means a matter desired to be known. This is its derivation: 'it is questioned, it is desired to be known,' thus it is a 'pañho.' For so it was said by the one explaining the meaning of this Netti Pāḷi passage, 'When the question is answered,' that 'pañhe' means 'in the matter desired to be known.'

Miha secane. Mihati, ummihati. Megho, mehanaṃ.

The root mih is in the sense of sprinkling. He sprinkles, he urinates. A cloud, the urinary organ.

Tattha ummihatīti passāvaṃ karoti. Meghoti mihati siñcati lokaṃ vassadhārāhīti megho, pajjunno. Mehananti itthīnaṃ guyhaṭṭhānaṃ.

Therein, 'ummihati' means to make urine. 'Megho' is so called because it sprinkles, it waters the world with streams of rain—thus 'megho,' a rain-cloud. 'Mehanaṃ' is the private place of women.

Daha bhasmīkaraṇe dhāraṇe ca. Āgārāni aggi dahati. Ayaṃ puriso imaṃ itthiṃ ayyikaṃ dahati, mama ayyikāti dhāretīti attho. Imassa purisassa ayaṃ itthī ayyikā hotīti adhippāyo. Atra panāyaṃ pāḷi “sakyā kho ambaṭṭha rājānaṃ ukkākaṃ pitāmahaṃ dahantī”ti. Agginā daḍḍhaṃ gehaṃ, dayhati, dayhamānaṃ. Dassa ḍādese “ḍahatī”ti rūpaṃ. “Ḍahantaṃ bālamanveti, bhasmāchannova pāvako”tiādayo payogā ettha nidassanāni bhavanti.

The root dah is in the sense of reducing to ashes and of holding. Fire burns houses. This man 'holds' this woman as his grandmother, meaning he considers her as 'my grandmother.' The intention is that this woman is this man's grandmother. Here, however, is this Pāḷi passage: 'Indeed, O Ambaṭṭha, the Sakyans hold King Ukkāka as their forefather.' A house burned by fire; it is burned, being burned. With the substitution of ḍ for d, the form is 'ḍahati.' Usages such as, 'Folly follows the one who burns, like a fire covered with ashes,' are illustrations here.

Caha parisakkane. Cahati.

The root cah is in the sense of striving. He strives.

Raha cāge. Rahati. Raho, rahito.

The root rah is in the sense of abandoning. He abandons. Seclusion, devoid.

Rahi gatiyaṃ. Rahati. Raho, rahaṃ.

The root rah is in the sense of going. He goes. Seclusion, privately.

Dahi [M 0.0196] bahi vuddhiyaṃ. Dahati. Bahati.

The roots dah and bah are in the sense of increase. He increases. He increases.

Bahi saddhe ca. Cakāro vuddhāpekkho. Bahati.

The root bah is in the sense of faith, and also. The particle 'ca' refers to 'increase'. He has faith; he increases.

Tuhi duhi addane. Tuhati. Duhati.

The roots tuh and duh are in the sense of harming. He harms. He milks.

Araha maha pūjāyaṃ. Arahati. Arahaṃ, arahā. Mahati.

The roots arah and mah are in the sense of veneration. He is worthy. A worthy one, an Arahant. He venerates.

Mahanaṃ, maho. Vihāramaho. Cetiyamaho.

Veneration, a festival. A monastic festival. A shrine festival.

Tatra nikkilesattā ekantadakkhiṇeyyabhāvena attano katapūjāsakkārādīnaṃ mahapphalabhāvakaraṇena arahaṇīyo pūjanīyoti arahā, khīṇāsavo.

Therein, because he is without defilements, because he is exclusively worthy of offerings, and because he causes the worship, honor, and so forth done to himself to be of great fruit, he is worthy of veneration, worthy of homage—thus he is an 'arahā,' one whose taints are destroyed.

Īha cetāyaṃ. Īhati. Īhā. Īhā vuccati vīriyaṃ.

The root īh is in the sense of striving. He strives. Striving. Striving is called energy.

Vaha maha buddhiyaṃ. Vahati, mahati.

The roots vah and mah are in the sense of understanding. He understands. He understands.

Ahi pilahi gatiyaṃ. Ahati. Pilahati, ahi.

The roots ah and pilah are in the sense of going. He goes. He goes, a snake.

Ettha ca ahīti nippādopi samāno ahati gacchati gantuṃ sakkotīti ahi.

And here, 'ahi' (snake), although being without feet, is so called because 'it goes,' 'it moves,' 'it is able to go'—thus 'ahi.'

Garaha kalaha kucchane. Garahati. Garahā, kalahati, kalaho.

The roots garah and kalah are in the sense of blaming. He blames. Blame. He quarrels. A quarrel.

Varaha valaha padhāniye paribhāsanahiṃsādānesu ca. Varahati. Valahati. Varāho.

The roots varah and valah are in the sense of pre-eminence, and also of reviling, harming, and giving. He acts accordingly. He acts accordingly. A boar.

Ettha ca varāhoti sūkaropi hatthīpi vuccati. Tathā hi “eneyyā ca varāhā ca. Mahāvarāhova nivāpapuṭṭho”tiādīsu sūkaro “varāho”ti nāmena vuccati. “Mahāvarāhassa nadīsu jaggato, bhisaṃ ghasamānassā”tiādīsu pana hatthī “varāho”ti nāmena vuccati. Mahāvarāhassāti hi mahāhatthinoti attho.

And here, 'varāha' is said of both a pig and an elephant. For so, in passages such as 'Eneyya deer and boars,' and 'like a great boar nourished by offerings,' the pig is called by the name 'varāha.' But in passages such as 'Of the great varāha watching in the rivers, eating lotus stalks,' the elephant is called by the name 'varāha.' For 'mahāvarāhassa' means 'of the great elephant.'

Vehu jehu vāhu payatane. Vehati, jehati. Vāhati. Vāhano.

The roots veh, jeh, and vāh are in the sense of exertion. He exerts. He exerts. He exerts. A mount.

Vāhano [M 0.0197] vuccati asso. So hi vāhanti saṅgāmādīsu kicce uppanne payatanti vīriyaṃ karonti, etenāti vāhanoti vuccati.

'Vāhana' is said of a horse. For when a duty such as battle arises, it exerts itself, it strives, it makes an effort; for this reason it is called a 'vāhana'.

Dāhu niddakkhaye. Dāhati.

The root dāh is in the sense of consuming fuel. He burns.

Ūha vitakke. Ūhati, āyūhati, viyūhati, byūhati apohati. Ūhanaṃ, āyūhanaṃ, byūho, apoho.

The root ūh is in the sense of reasoning. He reasons, he strives, he arranges, he arranges, he removes. Reasoning, striving, arrangement, removal.

Tattha ūhatīti vitakketi, āyūhatīti vāyamati, viyūhatīti paṃsuṃ uddharati. Evaṃ byūhatīti etthāpi. Apohatīti chaḍḍeti, atha vā viveceti.

Therein, 'ūhati' means to reason; 'āyūhati' means to strive; 'viyūhati' means to remove dust. Likewise also for 'byūhati.' 'Apohati' means to cast aside, or alternatively, to discriminate.

Gāhu viloḷane. Gāhati. Gāho, candaggāho, sūriyaggāho, nakkhattaggāho.

The root gāh is in the sense of agitating. He plunges. Seizure; a lunar eclipse, a solar eclipse, a planetary eclipse.

Gaha gahaṇe. Gahati, paggahati. Āhutiṃpaggahissāmi. Paggaho, paggāho.

The root gah is in the sense of grasping. He grasps, he holds forth. 'I will take up the offering.' Support, exertion.

Paggahoti patto. Paggāhoti vīriyaṃ.

'Paggaho' means a bowl. 'Paggāho' means energy.

Saha parisahane. Parisahanaṃ khanti. Sahati. Saho, asaho, asayho.

The root sah is in the sense of enduring. Endurance is patience. He endures. Enduring, not enduring, unbearable.

Ruha cammani pātubhāve. Ruhati. Rukkho.

The root ruh is in the sense of appearing on the skin. It grows. A tree.

Mātu māne. Māhati.

In the sense of honoring or measuring. He honors or measures.

Guhū saṃvaraṇe. Guhati nigguhati. Guho, guyhako.

In the sense of concealing. He conceals, he hides. A cave, a secret.

Vaha pāpuṇe. Vahati. Vārivaho.

In the sense of conveying. He conveys. A water-carrier.

Duha papūraṇe. Duhati, dohati. Duyhamānā gāvī.

In the sense of filling or milking. He milks. The cow being milked.

Diha upacaye. Dehati. Deho. Dehoti sarīraṃ.

In the sense of accumulation. It accumulates. The body. 'Deho' means the body.

Liha [M 0.0198] assādane. Lehati, palehati. Lehanīyaṃ. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “sunakhā himassa palihiṃsu pāde”ti. Ayaṃ panattho – sunakhā imassa kumārassa pādatale attano jivhāya palihiṃsūti.

In the sense of tasting. He licks, he licks thoroughly. That which is to be licked. Herein, this is the Pāli text: 'The dogs licked his feet.' And this is the meaning: The dogs licked the soles of this boy's feet with their tongues.

Oha cāge. Ohati. Sabbamanatthaṃ apohati. Apoho.

In the sense of abandoning. He abandons. He casts off all misfortune. Abandoning.

Brahma uggame. Brahati. Brahā.

In the sense of rising. He grows. The Great One.

Daha thaha hiṃsatthā. Dahati. Thahati.

The roots Daha and Thaha are in the sense of harming. He burns. He harms.

Brūha vaḍḍhane. Uparūpari brūhatīti brahmā. Kārite “vivekamanubrūhetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti payogo.

In the sense of increasing. Because he increases ever higher, he is called Brahmā. In the causative, there is the usage: 'It is fitting to cultivate seclusion.'

Brahmāti tehi tehi guṇavisesehi brūhitoti brahmā. Brahmāti mahābrahmāpi vuccati tathāgatopi brāhmaṇopi mātāpitaropi seṭṭhampi. “Sahasso brahmā dvisahasso brahmā”tiādīsu hi mahābrahmā “brahmā”ti vuccati. “Brahmāti kho bhikkhave tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti ettha tathāgato.

He is called Brahmā because he is augmented by those various special qualities. The term Brahmā is also used for Mahābrahmā, the Tathāgata, a brahmin, parents, and that which is best. Indeed, in phrases such as 'a thousand Brahmās, two thousand Brahmās,' Mahābrahmā is called 'Brahmā.' In 'Monks, “Brahmā” is a designation for the Tathāgata,' it refers to the Tathāgata.

“Tamonudo buddho samantacakkhu,

Lokantagū sabbabhavātivatto;

Anāsavo sabbadukkhappahīno,

Saccavhayo brahme upāsito me”ti

The Buddha, dispeller of darkness, all-seeing,

The one who has reached the end of the world, transcending all existence;

Without taints, having abandoned all suffering,

O brahmin, the Truth-named one is revered by me.

Ettha brāhmaṇo. “Brahmāti mātāpitaro, pubbācariyāti vuccare”ti ettha mātāpitaro. “Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetī”ti ettha seṭṭhaṃ. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Here, it refers to a brahmin. In 'Parents are called Brahmā, the first teachers,' it refers to parents. In 'He sets the Brahma-wheel in motion,' it refers to that which is best. Herein it is said:

“Mahābrahmani [M 0.0199] vippe ca, atho mātāpitūsu ca;

Tathāgate ca seṭṭhe ca, brahmasaddo pavattatī”ti.

The word 'brahma' is used for Mahābrahmā and for a sage, and also for mother and father; and for the Tathāgata and for that which is best.

Aparo nayo – brahmāti tividhā brahmāno sammutibrahmāno upapattibrahmāno visuddhibrahmānoti.

Another method: Brahmās are of three kinds—conventional brahmās, brahmās by rebirth, and brahmās by purity.

“Sampannaṃ sālikedāraṃ, suvā bhuñjanti kosiya;

Paṭivedemi te brahme, na ne vāretumussahe,

Paribbaja mahābrahme, pacantaññepi pāṇino”ti ca

A rice field is fully ripe, Kosiya, and the parrots are eating it. I declare to you, O brahmin, I cannot restrain them. Go forth, O great brahmin, for other beings too are cooking.

Evamādīsu hi brahmasaddena sammutibrahmāno vuttā.

Indeed, in such instances, conventional brahmās are spoken of by the word 'brahma'.

“Apārutā tesaṃ amatassa dvārā,

Ye sotavanto pamuñcantu saddhaṃ;

Vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ,

Dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme,

Open for them are the doors to the Deathless, let those with ears release faith. Perceiving it as a vexation, O Brahmā, I did not speak the sublime and excellent Dhamma among humans.

Atha kho brahmā sahampatī”ti ca evamādīsu brahmasaddena upapattibrahmā. “Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetī”tiādivacanato brahmanti ariyadhammo vuccati. Tato nibbattā avisesena sabbepi ariyā visuddhibrahmāno nāma paramatthabrahmatāya. Visesato pana “brahmāti kho bhikkhave tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti vacanato sammāsambuddho uttamabrahmā nāma sadevake loke brahmabhūtehi guṇehi ukkaṃsapāramippattito. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

And in 'Then Brahmā Sahampati,' and so on, by the word 'brahma' is meant a brahmā by rebirth. From the statement beginning 'He sets rolling the Brahma-wheel,' the noble Dhamma is called Brahmā. Arisen from that, all noble ones without distinction are called purified Brahmās on account of their ultimate Brahmā-nature. But especially, from the saying 'Monks, “Brahmā” is a designation for the Tathāgata,' the Perfectly Enlightened One is called the supreme Brahmā in the world with its gods, because of his reaching the peak of excellence in qualities that are Brahmā-like. Herein it is said:

“Sammutiyupapattīnaṃ, visuddhīnaṃ vasena ca;

Brahmāno tividhā honti, uttamena catubbidhā”ti.

Brahmās are of three kinds by way of convention, rebirth, and purity; with the supreme one, they are fourfold.

Dhimha [M 0.0200] niṭṭhubhane. Dhimheti. “Paṭivāmagataṃ sallaṃ, passa dhimhāmi lohita”nti pāḷi nidassanaṃ.

In the sense of spitting out. He spits out. The Pāli example is: 'See the dart that has turned back, I spit out the blood.'

Tattha dhimhāmīti niṭṭhubhāmīti attho.

Therein, 'dhimhāmi' means 'I spit out.'

Hakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in -ha.

Ḷakārantadhātu

Roots ending in -ḷa.

Biḷa akkose. Beḷati. Biḷāro.

In the sense of abusing. He abuses. A cat.

Kīḷa vihāre. Kīḷati. Kīḷā.

In the sense of playing. He plays. Play.

Aḷa uggame. Aḷati. Vāḷo.

In the sense of rising. He rises. A beast of prey.

Laḷa vilāse. Laḷati. Laḷito asso.

In the sense of dalliance. He dallies. A playful horse.

Kaḷa made kakkasse ca. Kakkassaṃ kassasiyaṃ pharusabhāvo. Kaḷati.

In the sense of intoxication and harshness. 'Kakkassaṃ' is harshness, a harsh nature. He is intoxicated or is harsh.

Tuḷa toḷane. Toḷati.

In the sense of weighing. He weighs.

Huḷa hoḷa gatiyaṃ. Huḷati. Hoḷati.

The roots Huḷa and Hoḷa are in the sense of motion. It moves. It moves.

Roḷa anādare. Roḷati.

The root Roḷa is in the sense of disregarding. It disregards.

Loḷa ummāde. Loyati.

The root Loḷa is in the sense of derangement. It is agitated.

Heḷa hoḷa anādare. Heḷati. Hoḷati.

The roots Heḷa and Hoḷa are in the sense of disrespect. It disrespects. It disrespects.

Vāḷa ālape. Vāḷati.

The root Vāḷa is in the sense of addressing. It addresses.

Dāḷa dhāḷa visaraṇe. Dāḷati. Dhāḷati.

The roots Dāḷa and Dhāḷa are in the sense of scattering. It scatters. It scatters.

Haḷa silāghāyaṃ. Haḷati.

The root Haḷa is in the sense of praising. It praises.

Hīḷa anādare. Hīḷati. Hīḷā, hīḷiko, hīḷito.

The root Hīḷa is in the sense of disregarding. It disregards. Disregard, one who disregards, disregarded.

Kaḷa [M 0.0201] secane. Kaḷati. Kaḷanaṃ.

The root Kaḷa is in the sense of sprinkling. It sprinkles. Sprinkling.

Heḷa veṭhane. Heḷati.

The root Heḷa is in the sense of wrapping. It wraps.

Īḷa thutiyaṃ. Īḷati.

The root Īḷa is in the sense of praising. It praises.

Juḷa gatiyaṃ. Juḷati, joḷati.

The root Juḷa is in the sense of motion. It moves, it moves.

Puḷa muḷa sukhane. Puḷati. Muḷati.

The roots Puḷa and Muḷa are in the sense of drying. It dries. It dries.

Guḷa rakkhāyaṃ. Guḷati. Guḷo.

The root Guḷa is in the sense of protecting. It protects. A ball.

Juḷa bandhane. Juḷati.

The root Juḷa is in the sense of binding. It binds.

Kuḷa ghasane. Kuḷati.

The root Kuḷa is in the sense of eating. It eats.

Khuḷa bālye ca. Cakāro ghasanāpekkhako. Khuḷati.

The root Khuḷa is in the sense of childishness; the particle 'ca' indicates it is also in the sense of eating. It acts childishly.

Suḷa buḷa saṃvaraṇe. Suḷati. Buḷati.

The roots Suḷa and Buḷa are in the sense of restraining. It restrains. It restrains.

Puḷa saṅghāte. Puḷati. Puḷinaṃ.

The root Puḷa is in the sense of gathering. It gathers. A sandbank.

Saḷa abyattasadde. Saḷati. Sāḷiko, sāḷikā.

The root Saḷa is in the sense of indistinct sound. It makes an indistinct sound. Myna bird (male), myna bird (female).

“Usabhova mahī nadati,

Migarājāva kūjati;

Susumārova saḷati,

Kiṃ vipāko bhavissatī”ti nidassanaṃ;

“The earth roars like a bull; it cries like a king of beasts; it makes an indistinct sound like a crocodile. What will be the result?”—this is an illustration.

Imāni ḷakārantadhāturūpāni.

These are the forms of the roots ending in ḷ.

Iti bhūvādigaṇe avaggantadhāturūpāni samattāni. Ettāvatā sabbāpi bhūvādigaṇe dhātuyo pakāsitā.

Thus, the forms of roots in the Bhū-group ending in a consonant are complete. By this, all the roots in the Bhū-group have been explained.

Idāni bhūvādigaṇikadhātūnaṃyeva kāci asamānasutikā, kāci asamānantikā. Tāsu kāci samānatthavasena samodhānetvā pubbācariyehi vuttā, tāyeva dhātuyo ekadesena rūpavibhāvanādīhi saddhiṃ pakāsayissāma. Taṃ yathā?

Now, among the roots belonging to the Bhū-group, some are not uniform in their sound, and some are not uniform in their endings. Among these, some roots have been grouped together by the ancient teachers due to similarity of meaning. We will explain these same roots in part, along with form-analysis and so on. What are they?

Hū [M 0.0202] bhū sattāyaṃ hoti, bhavati. Pahoti, pabhavati. Huveyya pāvuso. Sace uppādo heyya. Ajesi yakkho naravīraseṭṭhaṃ, tatthappanādo tumulo bahūva. Ambā’yaṃ ahuvā pure. Ahu rājā videhānaṃ. Pahūtaṃ me dhanaṃ sakka. Pahūtamariyo pakaroti puññaṃ. Pahūtavitto puriso. Pahūtajivho bhagavā. Piyappabhūtā kalahā vivādā. Pacchāsamaṇena hotabbaṃ. Bhavitabbaṃ. Hotuṃ, hetuye, bhavituṃ. Hutvā, hutvāna. Bhavitvā, bhavitvāna.

The roots Hū and Bhū are in the sense of existence. Hoti, bhavati. Pahoti, pabhavati. Huveyya pāvuso. Sace uppādo heyya. Ajesi yakkho naravīraseṭṭhaṃ, tatthappanādo tumulo bahūva. Ambā’yaṃ ahuvā pure. Ahu rājā videhānaṃ. Pahūtaṃ me dhanaṃ sakka. Pahūtamariyo pakaroti puññaṃ. Pahūtavitto puriso. Pahūtajivho bhagavā. Piyappabhūtā kalahā vivādā. Pacchāsamaṇena hotabbaṃ. Bhavitabbaṃ. Hotuṃ, hetuye, bhavituṃ. Hutvā, hutvāna. Bhavitvā, bhavitvāna.

Ettha pana “atthi hehiti so maggo, na so sakkā na hetuye”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha nahetuyeti abhavituṃ. Hūdhātuto tuṃpaccayassa tavepaccayassa vā tuye ādeso, ūkārassa ca ekārādeso katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā hetubhāvāya na na sakkātipi attho. Ayaṃ panattho idha nādhippeto, purimoyevattho adhippeto hotissa dhātuno payogabhāvāya udāharitapadassatthabhāvato. Tattha pahotīti idaṃ vatthaṃ vipulabhāvena cīvaraṃ kātuṃ pahoti, no nappahoti. Pahotīti vā puriso arayo jetuṃ sakkoti. Atha vā pahotīti hoti. Pabhavatīti sandati. Pahūtanti vipulaṃ, mahantanti attho. Pahūtavittoti vipulavitto mahaddhano. Pahūtajivhoti suputhulasudīghasumudukajivho, piyappabhūtāti piyato nibbattā.

Here, however, the Pāli passage is an illustration: “There is that path, it will be; it is not possible not to be.” There, “na hetuye” means “not to be.” From the root Hū, it should be understood that the substitution of ‘tuye’ for the suffix ‘tuṃ’ or ‘tave’, and the substitution of ‘e’ for ‘ū’ have been made. Or, the meaning is also: “it is not possible for it not to be a cause.” But this meaning is not intended here; the former meaning is intended, because the meaning of the example word is for the purpose of showing the usage of the root ‘hoti’. There, “pahoti” means this cloth is able to be made into a large robe due to its ample size; it is not unable. Or, “pahoti” means a man is able to conquer enemies. Or, “pahoti” means “hoti” (exists/is). “Pabhavati” means “it flows.” “Pahūtaṃ” means “ample,” “great” is the meaning. “Pahūtavitto” means “one with ample wealth,” “very rich.” “Pahūtajivho” means “one with a very broad, very long, very soft tongue.” “Piyappabhūtā” means “arisen from affection.”

Gamu sappa gatiyaṃ. Gacchati, gamati, ghammati, āgacchati, uggacchati, atigacchati, paṭigacchati, avagacchati, adhigacchati, anugacchati, upagacchati, apagacchati, vigacchati, nigacchati, niggacchati. Aññānipi yojetabbāni. “Samuggacchatī”tiādinā upasaggadvayavasenapi [M 0.0203] yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbāni. Sappati, saṃsappati, parisappati. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

The roots Gamu and Sappa are in the sense of going. Gacchati, gamati, ghammati, āgacchati, uggacchati, atigacchati, paṭigacchati, avagacchati, adhigacchati, anugacchati, upagacchati, apagacchati, vigacchati, nigacchati, niggacchati. Others should also be combined. They should also be combined as appropriate with double prefixes, such as “samuggacchati,” etc. Sappati, saṃsappati, parisappati. Others should also be combined.

Tattha gamatīti gacchati. Kārite “devadattaṃ gameti gamayatī”ti rūpāni bhavanti. “Apāyaṃ gametīti apāyagamanīya”nti idamettha nidassanaṃ. Curādigaṇaṃ pattassa āpubbassa imassa “āgameti, āgamayati, āgamento, āgamayamāno”ti suddhakatturūpāni bhavanti.

There, “gamati” means “gacchati.” In the causative, forms like “gameti” and “gamayati” (he makes Devadatta go) arise. “Apāyaṃ gameti” (he leads to the lower realms) means “apāyagamanīya” (leading to the lower realms)—this is the example here. For this root, which has entered the Curādi group with the prefix ‘ā-’, forms like “āgameti,” “āgamayati,” “āgamento,” “āgamayamāno” arise.

Tattha āgametīti muhuttaṃ adhivāsetīti attho. Ghammatīti gacchati. Āgacchatīti āyāti. Uggacchatīti uyyāti uddhaṃ gacchati. Atigacchatīti atikkamitvā gacchati. Paṭigacchatīti puna gacchati. Avagacchatīti jānāti. Adhigacchatīti labhati jānāti vā. Anugacchatīti pacchato gacchati. Upagacchatīti samīpaṃ gacchati. Apagacchatīti apeti. Vigacchatīti vigamati. Nigacchatīti labhati. “Yasaṃ poso nigacchatī”ti idaṃ nidassanaṃ. Niggacchatīti nikkhamati. Sappatīti gacchati. Saṃsappatīti saṃsaranto gacchati. Parisappatīti samantato gacchati.

There, “āgameti” means “to wait for a moment,” that is the meaning. “Ghammati” means “gacchati” (goes). “Āgacchati” means “āyāti” (comes). “Uggacchati” means “uyyāti” (rises) or “uddhaṃ gacchati” (goes upwards). “Atigacchati” means “atikkamitvā gacchati” (goes having transgressed). “Paṭigacchati” means “puna gacchati” (goes again). “Avagacchati” means “jānāti” (knows). “Adhigacchati” means “labhati” (obtains) or “jānāti” (knows). “Anugacchati” means “pacchato gacchati” (goes after). “Upagacchati” means “samīpaṃ gacchati” (goes near). “Apagacchati” means “apeti” (goes away). “Vigacchati” means “vigamati” (goes away). “Nigacchati” means “labhati” (obtains). The example is: “Yasaṃ poso nigacchati” (A man obtains glory). “Niggacchati” means “nikkhamati” (goes out). “Sappati” means “gacchati” (goes). “Saṃsappati” means “saṃsaranto gacchati” (goes wandering). “Parisappati” means “samantato gacchati” (goes all around).

Idāni pana viññūnaṃ sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane paramakosallajananatthaṃ sappayogaṃ padamālaṃ kathayāma. Seyyathidaṃ? So gacchati, te gacchanti, gacchare. Tvaṃ gacchasi, tumhe gacchatha. Ahaṃ gacchāmi, mayaṃ gacchāma. So gacchate, te gacchante. Tvaṃ gacchase, tumhe gacchavhe. Ahaṃ gacche, mayaṃ gacchāmhe. Vattamānāya rūpāni.

Now, for the purpose of generating supreme skill in the Buddha’s words, which are accompanied by commentaries and are in the Tipiṭaka, for the wise, we shall explain the word forms with their usage. Such as: So gacchati, te gacchanti, gacchare. Tvaṃ gacchasi, tumhe gacchatha. Ahaṃ gacchāmi, mayaṃ gacchāma. So gacchate, te gacchante. Tvaṃ gacchase, tumhe gacchavhe. Ahaṃ gacche, mayaṃ gacchāmhe. These are the forms of the present tense.

So gacchatu, te gacchantu. Tvaṃ gacchāhi, gaccha, gacchassu, tumhe gacchatha. Ahaṃ gacchāmi, mayaṃ gacchāma. So gacchataṃ, te gacchantaṃ. Tvaṃ gacchassu, tumhe gacchavho. Ahaṃ gacche, mayaṃ gacchāmase. Pañcamiyā rūpāni.

So gacchatu, te gacchantu. Tvaṃ gacchāhi, gaccha, gacchassu, tumhe gacchatha. Ahaṃ gacchāmi, mayaṃ gacchāma. So gacchataṃ, te gacchantaṃ. Tvaṃ gacchassu, tumhe gacchavho. Ahaṃ gacche, mayaṃ gacchāmase. These are the forms of the imperative mood.

So [M 0.0204] gaccheyya, gacche, te gaccheyyuṃ. Tvaṃ gaccheyyāsi, tumhe gaccheyyātha. Ahaṃ gaccheyyāmi, mayaṃ gaccheyyāma, gacchemu. So gacchetha, te gaccheraṃ. Tvaṃ gacchetho, tumhe gaccheyyāvho. Ahaṃ gaccheyyaṃ, mayaṃ gaccheyyāmhe. Sattamiyā rūpāni.

So gaccheyya, gacche, te gaccheyyuṃ. Tvaṃ gaccheyyāsi, tumhe gaccheyyātha. Ahaṃ gaccheyyāmi, mayaṃ gaccheyyāma, gacchemu. So gacchetha, te gaccheraṃ. Tvaṃ gacchetho, tumhe gaccheyyāvho. Ahaṃ gaccheyyaṃ, mayaṃ gaccheyyāmhe. These are the forms of the optative mood.

So gaccha, te gacchu. Tvaṃ gacche, tumhe gacchittha, gañchittha. Ahaṃ gacchaṃ, mayaṃ gacchimha, gañchimha. So gacchittha, gañchittha, te gacchire. Tvaṃ gacchittho, tumhe gacchivho. Ahaṃ gacchiṃ, gañchiṃ, mayaṃ gacchimhe. Parokkhāya rūpāni.

So gaccha, te gacchu. Tvaṃ gacche, tumhe gacchittha, gañchittha. Ahaṃ gacchaṃ, mayaṃ gacchimha, gañchimha. So gacchittha, gañchittha, te gacchire. Tvaṃ gacchittho, tumhe gacchivho. Ahaṃ gacchiṃ, gañchiṃ, mayaṃ gacchimhe. These are the forms of the perfect tense.

So agacchā, te agacchū. Tvaṃ agacche, tumhe agacchatha. Ahaṃ agacchaṃ, mayaṃ agacchamhā. So agacchatha, te agacchatthuṃ. Tvaṃ agacchase, tumhe agacchivhaṃ. Ahaṃ agacchaṃ, mayaṃ agacchimhe. Ajjataniyā rūpāni.

So agacchā, te agacchū. Tvaṃ agacche, tumhe agacchatha. Ahaṃ agacchaṃ, mayaṃ agacchamhā. So agacchatha, te agacchatthuṃ. Tvaṃ agacchase, tumhe agacchivhaṃ. Ahaṃ agacchaṃ, mayaṃ agacchimhe. These are the forms of the aorist.

So gacchissati, te gacchissanti. Tvaṃ gacchissasi, tumhe gacchissatha. Ahaṃ gacchissāmi, mayaṃ gacchissāma. So gacchissate, te gacchissante. Tvaṃ gacchissase, tumhe gacchissavhe. Ahaṃ gacchissaṃ, mayaṃ gacchissāmhe. Bhavissantiyā rūpāni.

So gacchissati, te gacchissanti. Tvaṃ gacchissasi, tumhe gacchissatha. Ahaṃ gacchissāmi, mayaṃ gacchissāma. So gacchissate, te gacchissante. Tvaṃ gacchissase, tumhe gacchissavhe. Ahaṃ gacchissaṃ, mayaṃ gacchissāmhe. These are the forms of the future tense.

So agacchissā, te agacchissaṃsu. Tvaṃ agacchisse, tumhe agacchissatha. Ahaṃ agacchissaṃ, mayaṃ agacchissāmhā. So agacchissatha, te agacchissisu. Tvaṃ agacchissase, tumhe agacchissavhe. Ahaṃ agacchissaṃ, mayaṃ agacchissāmhase. Kālātipattiyā rūpāni.

So agacchissā, te agacchissaṃsu. Tvaṃ agacchisse, tumhe agacchissatha. Ahaṃ agacchissaṃ, mayaṃ agacchissāmhā. So agacchissatha, te agacchissisu. Tvaṃ agacchissase, tumhe agacchissavhe. Ahaṃ agacchissaṃ, mayaṃ agacchissāmhase. These are the forms of the conditional mood.

Tattha ajjataniyā kālātipattiyā ca akārāgamaṃ sabbesu purisesu sabbesu vacanesu labbhamānampi sāsane aniyataṃ hutvā labbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi “agacchi, gacchi, agacchissā, gacchissā”tiādinā dve dve rūpāni dissanti. Gamati, gamanti. Gamatu, gamantu. Gameyya. Gameyyuṃ. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

Herein, it should be understood that even though the augment ‘a’ is found in all persons and all numbers for the aorist and conditional, in the teaching it is found to be optional. Thus, two forms each are seen, such as “agacchi, gacchi, agacchissā, gacchissā,” and so on. Gamati, gamanti. Gamatu, gamantu. Gameyya. Gameyyuṃ. All the rest should be elaborated.

Idāni [M 0.0205] parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanīsu viseso vuccate – so puriso maggaṃ ga, sā itthī ghara’māga. Te maggaṃ gu, tā ghara’māgu. Ekārassa akārādesaṃ tvaṃ maggaṃ ga, tvaṃ ghara”māga. Tumhe maggaṃ guttha, tumhe ghara’māguttha. Ahaṃ maggaṃ gaṃ, ahaṃ ghara’māgaṃ. Ahaṃ taṃ purisaṃ anvagaṃ, mayaṃ maggaṃ gumha, mayaṃ gharaṃ āgumha, mayaṃ taṃ purisaṃ anvagumha. Ayaṃ tāva parokkhāya viseso.

Now, the distinction among the perfect, imperfect, and aorist is stated: so puriso maggaṃ ga, sā itthī ghara’māga. Te maggaṃ gu, tā ghara’māgu. Substitution of 'a' for 'e': tvaṃ maggaṃ ga, tvaṃ ghara’’māga. Tumhe maggaṃ guttha, tumhe ghara’māguttha. Ahaṃ maggaṃ gaṃ, ahaṃ ghara’māgaṃ. Ahaṃ taṃ purisaṃ anvagaṃ, mayaṃ maggaṃ gumha, mayaṃ gharaṃ āgumha, mayaṃ taṃ purisaṃ anvagumha. This, for now, is the distinction for the perfect tense.

“So maggaṃ agamā, te maggaṃ agamū” iccādi hiyyattaniyā rūpaṃ. “So agami, te agamuṃ, te guṃ” iccādi ajjataniyā rūpaṃ.

“So maggaṃ agamā, te maggaṃ agamū,” etc., is the form of the imperfect tense. “So agami, te agamuṃ, te guṃ,” etc., is the form of the aorist tense.

Idāni tesaṃ padarūpāni pākaṭīkaraṇatthaṃ kiñci suttaṃ kathayāma – “sopāgā samitiṃ vanaṃ. Athettha pañcamo āgā. Āguṃ devā yasassino. Māhaṃ kākova dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvagaṃ. Agamā rājagahaṃ buddho. Vaṅkaṃ agamu pabbataṃ. Brāhmaṇā upagacchu ma”nti evamādīni bhavanti.

Now, to make the forms of these words clear, we shall state some textual passages: “sopāgā samitiṃ vanaṃ. Athettha pañcamo āgā. Āguṃ devā yasassino. Māhaṃ kākova dummedho, kāmānaṃ vasamanvagaṃ. Agamā rājagahaṃ buddho. Vaṅkaṃ agamu pabbataṃ. Brāhmaṇā upagacchu maṃ”—such are the examples.

Ga gu ga guttha gaṃ gumha, agu agamu agamuṃ;

Agamā’gami gacchanti, ādibhedaṃ mane kare.

Ga, gu, ga, guttha, gaṃ, gumha; agu, agamu, agamuṃ; agamā, agami, gacchanti—one should keep the initial distinctions in mind.

Idāni nāmikapadāni vuccante – gato, gantā, gacchaṃ, gacchantī, gacchantaṃ kulaṃ, sahagataṃ, gati, gamanaṃ, gamo, āgamo, avagamo, gantabbaṃ, gamanīyaṃ, gammaṃ, gammamānaṃ, gamiyamānaṃ, go, mātugāmo, hiṅgu, jagu, indagū, medhago iccādīni, kārite – gacchāpeti, gacchāpayati, gaccheti, gacchayati, gammeti. Kamme – gammati, gamiyati, adhigammati, adhigamiyati. Tumantāditte “gantuṃ, gamituṃ, gantvā, gantvāna, gamitvā, gamitvāna, gamiya, gamiyāna, gamma, āgamma, āgantvā, adhigamma, adhigantvā” iccādīni[M 0.0206]. Sappadhātussa pana “sappo, sappinī, pīṭhasappī, sappi” iccādīni rūpāni bhavanti.

Now the nominal forms are stated: gato (gone), gantā (goer), gacchaṃ (going, masc.), gacchantī (going, fem.), gacchantaṃ kulaṃ (the going family), sahagataṃ (accompanied by), gati (course), gamanaṃ (going), gamo (movement), āgamo (approach), avagamo (understanding), gantabbaṃ (should be gone), gamanīyaṃ (to be gone), gammaṃ (to be gone), gammamānaṃ (being gone to), gamiyamānaṃ (being gone to), go (cow), mātugāmo (woman), hiṅgu (asafoetida), jagu (leg), indagū (Indra's cow), medhago (Medhaga), and so forth. In the causative: gacchāpeti, gacchāpayati, gaccheti, gacchayati, gammeti (makes go, causes to go). In the passive: gammati, gamiyati, adhigammati, adhigamiyati (is gone to, is attained). In the infinitives and absolutives: gantuṃ, gamituṃ (to go), gantvā, gantvāna, gamitvā, gamitvāna, gamiya, gamiyāna, gamma, āgamma, āgantvā, adhigamma, adhigantvā (having gone, having approached, having attained), and so forth. For the root sappa, however, the forms are: sappo (snake), sappinī (she-snake), pīṭhasappī (one who crawls on a seat), sappi (clarified butter), and so forth.

Tattha sahagatasaddo tabbhāve vokiṇṇe nissaye ārammaṇe saṃsaṭṭheti imesu atthesu dissati. Tattha “yāyaṃ taṇhā ponobbhavikā nandirāgasahagatā”ti tabbhāve veditabbo, nandirāgabhūtāti attho. “Yāyaṃ bhikkhave vīmaṃsā kosajjasahagatā kosajjasampayuttā”ti vokiṇṇe veditabbo, antarantarā uppajjamānena kosajjena vokiṇṇāti ayamettha attho. “Aṭṭhikasaññāsahagataṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetī”ti nissaye veditabbo, aṭṭhikasaññaṃ nissāya aṭṭhikasaññaṃ bhāvetvā paṭiladdhanti attho. “Lābhī hoti rūpasahagatānaṃ vā samāpattīnaṃ arūpasahagatānaṃ vā”ti ārammaṇe, rūpārūpārammaṇānanti attho. “Idaṃ sukhaṃ imāya pītiyā sahagataṃ sahajātaṃ sampayutta”nti saṃsaṭṭhe, imissā pītiyā saṃsaṭṭhanti attho. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Therein, the word sahagata is seen in these meanings: 'nature,' 'mixed,' 'dependence,' 'object,' and 'association.' Therein, “This craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust” is to be understood in the sense of 'nature,' meaning it is of the nature of delight and lust. “Monks, this investigation accompanied by laziness, associated with laziness” is to be understood in the sense of 'mixed,' meaning it is interspersed with laziness arising from time to time. “One develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor accompanied by the perception of bones” is to be understood in the sense of 'dependence,' meaning it is obtained by depending on the perception of bones, having developed the perception of bones. “One obtains attainments accompanied by form or formless (realms)” is to be understood in the sense of 'object,' meaning they have form or formless (realms) as their object. “This pleasure, accompanied by this joy, co-arisen, associated” is to be understood in the sense of 'association,' meaning it is associated with this joy. Herein, this is said:

Tabbhāve ceva vokiṇṇe, nissayārammaṇesu ca;

Saṃsaṭṭhe ca sahagata-saddo dissati pañcasu;

In 'nature' and 'mixed,' in 'dependence' and 'object,' and in 'association'—the word sahagata is seen in these five.

Gatīti gatigati nibbattigabhi ajjhāsayagati vibhavagati nipphattigati ñāṇagatīti bahuvidhā gati nāma.

The word gati is of many kinds, namely: course as destination, course as origination, course as inclination, course as dissolution, course as accomplishment, and course as knowledge.

Tattha “taṃ gatiṃ pecca gacchāmī”ti ca “yassa gatiṃ na jānanti, devā gandhabbamānusā”ti ca ayaṃ gatigatināma. “Imesaṃ [M 0.0207] kho ahaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ neva jānāmi gatiṃvā agatiṃvā”ti ayaṃ nibbattigati nāma. “Evaṃ kho te ahaṃ brahme gatiñca jānāmi jutiñca jānāmī”ti ayaṃ ajjhāsayagati nāma. “Vibhavo gati dhammānaṃ, nibbānaṃ arahato gatī”ti ayaṃ vibhavagati nāma. “Dve gatiyo bhavanti anaññā”ti ayaṃ nipphattigati nāma. “Taṃ tattha gatimā dhibhimā”ti ca “sundaraṃ nibbānaṃ gato”ti ca ayaṃ ñāṇagati nāma. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Therein, “After death, I go to that destination” and “Whose destination neither devas, gandhabbas, nor humans know”—this is called gatigati. “Indeed, of these virtuous monks, I do not know their destination or non-destination”—this is called nibbattigati. “Thus, O Brahma, I know your destination and your radiance”—this is called ajjhāsayagati. “Non-existence is the destination of phenomena, Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant”—this is called vibhavagati. “There are two destinations, no others”—this is called nipphattigati. “One who is wise and steadfast goes there” and “Gone to the beautiful Nibbāna”—this is called ñāṇagati. Herein, this is said:

Gatigatyañca nibbatyaṃ, vibhavajjhāsayesu ca;

Nipphattiyañca ñāṇe ca, gatisaddo pavattati.

In destination and origination, in dissolution and inclination, and in accomplishment and knowledge—the word gati occurs.

Gacchatīti go. Mātuyā samabhāvaṃ missībhāvañca gacchati pāpuṇātīti mātugāmo. Rogaṃ hiṃsantaṃ gacchatīti hiṅgu.

Because it goes, it is a go (cow). Because one attains the state of a mother and the state of being mixed, one is a mātugāma (woman). Because it goes while harming illness, it is hiṅgu (asafoetida).

Imāni tassa nāmāni

These are its names:

Hiṅgu hiṅgujatucceva, tathā hiṅgusipāṭikā;

Hiṅgujātīti kathitā, vinayaṭṭhakathāya hi.

Hiṅgu, and hiṅgujatu, and also hiṅgusipāṭikā—these are called the hiṅgu species, as indeed stated in the Vinaya commentary.

Jagūti cutito jātiṃ gacchatīti jagu. Indriyena gacchatīti indagū. Atha vā indabhūtena kammunā gacchatīti indagu. “Hindagū”tipi pāḷi. Tattha hindanti maraṇaṃ. Taṃ gacchatīti hindagū. Sabbametaṃ sattādhivacanaṃ, liṅgato pulliṅgaṃ. Medhagoti attano nissayañca parañca medhamāno hiṃsamāno gacchati pavattatīti medhago, kalaho. “Tato sammanti medhagā”ti ettha hi kalaho medhagasaddena bhagavatā vutto. Gamitvāti ettha –

One who goes to birth after passing away is `jagu`. One who goes by means of a faculty is `indagū`. Alternatively, one who goes by action that has become like Indra is `indagu`. There is also the reading `hindagū`. Here, `hinda` means death. One who goes to that is `hindagū`. All these are terms for beings, masculine in gender. One who, harming oneself and others, goes forward is `medhago`, a quarrel. In the phrase, 'Then quarrels subside,' the Blessed One indeed used the word `medhaga` to refer to a quarrel. Here, regarding `gamitvā`—

“Isivhayaṃ gamitvāna, vinitvā pañcavaggiye;

Tato vinesi bhagavā, gantvā gantvā tahiṃ tahi”nti

“Having gone to Isipatana and trained the group of five, then the Blessed One trained others, going here and there.”

Ayaṃ [M 0.0208] pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Sappoti sappatīti sappo, saṃsappanto gacchatīti attho. Tenāha āyasmā sāriputto “yo kāme parivajjeti, sappasseva padāsiro”ti imissā pāḷiyā niddese “sappo vuccati ahi. Kenaṭṭhena sappo? Saṃsappanto gacchatīti sappo. Bhujanto gacchatīti bhujago. Urena gacchatīti urago. Pannasiro gacchatīti pannago. Sarīrena sappatīti sarīsapo. Bile sayatīti bilāsayo. Dāṭhā tassa āvudhoti dāṭhāvudho. Visaṃ tassaghoranti ghoraviso. Jivhā tassa duvidhāti dujivho. Dvīhi jivhāhi rasaṃ sāyatīti dvirasaññū”ti. Sappinīti uragī. Pīṭhasappīti pīṭhena sappati gacchatīti pīṭhasappī, paṅguḷo. Sappīti yo na paribhuñjati, tassa balāyuvaḍḍhanatthaṃ sappati gacchati pavattatīti sappi, ghataṃ.

One who creeps is `sappo`, meaning one who goes by creeping. Therefore, the Venerable Sāriputta said in the explanation of this Pali passage, 'One who would avoid sensual pleasures, as one would a snake's head with the foot': '`Sappo` is called `ahi`. In what sense is it `sappo`? It is `sappo` because it goes by creeping. One who goes crookedly is `bhujago`. One who goes by the chest is `urago`. One who goes with head lowered is `pannago`. One who creeps with the body is `sarīsapo`. One who lies in holes is `bilāsayo`. One whose fangs are its weapon is `dāṭhāvudho`. One whose poison is dreadful is `ghoraviso`. One whose tongue is twofold is `dujivho`. One who tastes flavor with two tongues is `dvirasaññū`.' `Sappinī` means a female serpent. One who creeps or goes by means of a seat is `pīṭhasappī`, a cripple. That which proceeds for the purpose of increasing strength and longevity for one who does not consume it is `sappi`, ghee.

Sakka ṭeka laṅgha gatyattā. Sakkati, nisakkati, parisakkati. Nisakko, parisakkanaṃ. Ṭekati. Ṭīkā. Laṅghati, ullaṅghati, olaṅghati, laṅghako, ullaṅghikā pīti.

The roots `sakka`, `ṭeka`, and `laṅgha` are in the sense of 'going.' From `sakka`: `sakkati` (is able), `nisakkati` (withdraws), `parisakkati` (moves around); `nisakko` (withdrawal), `parisakkanaṃ` (moving around). From `ṭeka`: `ṭekati` (supports); `ṭīkā` (commentary). From `laṅgha`: `laṅghati` (leaps), `ullaṅghati` (jumps up), `olaṅghati` (crosses over); `laṅghako` (a leaper), `ullaṅghikā pīti` (uplifting joy).

Ke re ge sadde. Kāyati. Rāyati. Gāyati. Jātakaṃ. Rā. Gītaṃ. Kāyituṃ. Rāyituṃ, gāyituṃ. Kāyitvā. Rāyitvā. Gāyitvā.

The roots `ke`, `re`, and `ge` are in the sense of 'sound.' From `ke`: `kāyati` (sounds). From `re`: `rāyati` (resounds). From `ge`: `gāyati` (sings). `Jātakaṃ` (Jātaka). `Rā` (sound). `Gītaṃ` (song). `Kāyituṃ` (to sound). `Rāyituṃ` (to resound), `gāyituṃ` (to sing). `Kāyitvā` (having sounded). `Rāyitvā` (having resounded). `Gāyitvā` (having sung).

Tattha jātakanti jātaṃ bhūtaṃ atītaṃ attano caritaṃ kāyati katheti bhagavā etenāti jātakaṃ. Jātakapāḷi hi idha jātakanti vuttaṃ. Aññatra pana jātaṃ evaṃ jātakanti gahetabbā. Tathā hi jātakasaddo pariyattiyampi vattati “itivuttakaṃ jātakaṃ abbhutadhamma”ntiādīsu, jātiyampi vattati “jātakaṃ samodhānesī”tiādīsu. Rā vuccati saddo. Gītanti gāyanaṃ.

Here, `jātaka` means that by this the Blessed One relates or narrates his own past conduct that was born, existed, and passed away; therefore, it is called `jātaka`. Indeed, the Jātaka Pāḷi is here called `jātaka`. Elsewhere, however, what is born should be understood simply as `jātaka`. Thus, the word `jātaka` also occurs in the sense of scripture, as in phrases like 'Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma,' and also in the sense of birth, as in 'He brought together the birth story.' `Rā` is called a sound. `Gīta` means singing.

Khe [M 0.0209] je se khaye. Khāyati. Jāyati. Sāyati. Khayaṃ gacchatīti attho.

The roots `khe`, `je`, and `se` are in the sense of 'destruction.' From `khe`: `khāyati`. From `je`: `jāyati`. From `se`: `sāyati`. The meaning is that it goes to destruction.

Ettha pana siyā “nanu ca bho khāyatīti padassa khādatīti vā paññāyatīti vā attho bhavati, tathā jāyatīti padassa nibbattatīti attho, sāyatīti padassa rasaṃ assādetīti attho, evaṃ sante bho kasmā idha evaṃ attho tumhehi kathiyatī”ti? Saccaṃ, dhātūnantu anekatthattā evaṃ attho kathetuṃ labbhati. Tathā hi “appassutāyaṃ puriso, balibaddova jīratī”ti ettha jīratīti ayaṃ saddo jaraṃ pāpuṇātīti atthaṃ avatvā vaḍḍhatīti atthameva vadati, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, however, one might object: 'But, sirs, does not the word `khāyati` have the meaning of 'eats' or 'is known'? Similarly, does not the word `jāyati` have the meaning of 'is produced'? And does not the word `sāyati` have the meaning of 'tastes a flavor'? If that is so, sirs, why is the meaning explained by you here in this way?' It is true; because verbal roots have multiple meanings, it is permissible to explain the meaning in this way. For instance, in the phrase 'This unlearned man grows old like an ox,' the word `jīrati` does not convey the meaning 'reaches old age' but rather speaks only of the meaning 'grows fat.' This should be seen as similar.

Gu ghu ku u sadde. Gavati. Ghavati. Kavati. Avati.

The roots `gu`, `ghu`, `ku`, and `u` are in the sense of 'sound.' From `gu`: `gavati` (lows). From `ghu`: `ghavati` (shines). From `ku`: `kavati` (praises). From `u`: `avati` (protects).

Khu ru ku sadde. Khoti. Roti. Koti.

The roots `khu`, `ru`, and `ku` are in the sense of 'sound.' From `khu`: `khoti`. From `ru`: `roti`. From `ku`: `koti`.

Cu ju pu plu gā se gatiyaṃ. Cavati. Javati. Pavati. Plavati. Gāti. Seti. Cavanaṃ, cuti. Javanaṃ, javo. Pavanaṃ, plavanaṃ. Gānaṃ. Setu. Poto. Plavo.

The roots `cu`, `ju`, `pu`, `plu`, `gā`, and `se` are in the sense of 'going.' From `cu`: `cavati` (moves); `cavanaṃ` (movement), `cuti` (decease). From `ju`: `javati` (speeds); `javanaṃ` (speed), `javo` (swiftness). From `pu`: `pavati` (flows); `pavanaṃ` (flowing), `poto` (a boat). From `plu`: `plavati` (floats); `plavanaṃ` (floating), `plavo` (a float). From `gā`: `gāti` (sings); `gānaṃ` (singing). From `se`: `seti` (lies); `setu` (a bridge).

Ettha gānanti gamanaṃ. Pototi pavati gacchati udake etenāti poto, nāvā. Tathā plavati na sīdatīti plavo, nāvā eva. “Bhinnaplavo sāgarasseva majjhe”ti hi jātakapāḷi dissati. “Nāvā, poto, plavo, jalayānaṃ, taraṇa”nti nāvābhidhānāni.

Here, `gānaṃ` means 'going.' `Poto` means that by this one flows or goes on water; hence, `poto`, a boat. Similarly, that which floats and does not sink is `plavo`, which is also a ship. Indeed, in the Jātaka Pāḷi, the phrase 'Like a broken raft in the midst of the ocean' is seen. `Nāvā`, `poto`, `plavo`, `jalayānaṃ`, `taraṇa`—these are synonyms for a ship.

Dhe the saddasaṅghātesu. Dhāyati. Thāyati. Bhāve – dhiyati, thiyati. Itthī. Thī.

The roots `dhe` and `the` are in the sense of 'sound-clusters.' From `dhe`: `dhāyati` (suckles). From `the`: `thāyati` (stands). In the passive voice: `dhiyati` (is placed), `thiyati` (is fixed). `Itthī` (a woman). `Thī` (a female).

De te pālane. Dāyati. Dayā. Tāṇaṃ.

The roots `de` and `te` are in the sense of 'protecting.' From `de`: `dāyati` (protects); `dayā` (compassion). From `te`: `tāṇaṃ` (refuge).

Rā lā ādāne. Rāti. Lāti.

The roots `rā` and `lā` are in the sense of 'taking.' From `rā`: `rāti` (takes). From `lā`: `lāti` (takes).

Ati adi bandhane. Antati. Andati. Antaṃ. Andu.

The roots `at` and `ad` are in the sense of 'binding.' From `at`: `antati` (binds); `antaṃ` (an end). From `ad`: `andati` (binds); `andu` (a fetter).

Jutasubha [M 0.0210] ruca dittiyaṃ. Jotati. Sobhati. Rocati, virocati.

The roots `jut`, `subh`, and `ruc` are in the sense of 'shining.' From `jut`: `jotati` (shines). From `subh`: `sobhati` (is beautiful, shines). From `ruc`: `rocati` (pleases, shines), `virocati` (shines forth).

Aka aga kuṭilāyaṃ gatiyaṃ. Akati. Agati.

The roots `ak` and `ag` are in the sense of 'crooked movement.' From `ak`: `akati`. From `ag`: `agati`.
