Kupa kope. Kuppati. Kuppanti vātassapi eritassa. Kopo, pakopo. Vacīpakopaṃ rakkheyya.

The root 'kupa' is in the sense of agitation. 'Kuppati' means 'it is agitated.' 'Kuppanti vātassapi eritassa' means 'even the wind, when stirred, becomes agitated.' 'Kopo' and 'pakopo' mean 'agitation.' 'Vacīpakopaṃ rakkheyya' means 'one should guard against verbal agitation.'

Tapa santāpe. Tappati, santappati. Santāpo.

The root 'tapa' is in the sense of torment. 'Tappati' and 'santappati' mean 'it torments' or 'it burns.' 'Santāpo' means 'torment' or 'burning.'

Tapa pīṇane. Tappati. Tappanaṃ.

The root 'tapa' is in the sense of satisfying. 'Tappati' means 'it is satisfied.' 'Tappanaṃ' means 'satisfaction.'

Dapa hāse. Dappati.

The root 'dapa' is in the sense of pride. 'Dappati' means 'he is proud.'

Dīpa dittiyaṃ. Dippati. Dīpo.

The root 'dīpa' is in the sense of shining. 'Dippati' means 'it shines.' 'Dīpo' means 'lamp.'

Lupa adassane. Luppanaṃ, lopo, lutti.

The root 'lupa' is in the sense of disappearing. 'Luppanaṃ' means 'disappearance'; 'lopo' means 'elision'; 'lutti' means 'cutting off.'

Khipa peraṇe. Khippati. Khippaṃ.

The root 'khipa' is in the sense of throwing. 'Khippati' means 'it is thrown.' 'Khippaṃ' means 'swiftly.'

Lubha giddhiyaṃ. Lubbhati. Attanoyeva jaṇṇukaṃ olubbha tiṭṭhati. Lubbhanaṃ, lobho, lubbhitvā, lubbhitvāna, lubbhiya, lubbhiyāna, olubbhitvā, olubbhitvāna, olubbhiya, olubbhiyāna, lubbhituṃ, olubbhituṃ.

The root 'lubha' is in the sense of greed. 'Lubbhati' means 'he is greedy.' 'Attanoyeva jaṇṇukaṃ olubbha tiṭṭhati' means 'he stands clinging even to his own knee.' 'Lubbhanaṃ' means 'craving'; 'lobho' means 'greed'; 'lubbhitvā' and 'lubbhitvāna' mean 'having craved'; 'lubbhiya' and 'lubbhiyāna' also mean 'having craved'; 'olubbhitvā' and 'olubbhitvāna' mean 'having clung to'; 'olubbhiya' and 'olubbhiyāna' also mean 'having clung to'; 'lubbhituṃ' means 'to crave'; 'olubbhituṃ' means 'to cling to.'

Tattha lobhoti lubbhanti tena sattā, sayaṃ vā lubbhati, lubbhanamattameva vā tanti lobho. Ettha pana “lobho lubbhanā [M 0.0236] lubbhitattaṃ rāgo taṇhā tasiṇā mucchā ejā vanaṃ vanatho” iccādīni lobhassa bahunāmāni veditabbāni.

Therein, 'lobho' (greed) is that by which beings are greedy, or by which one is greedy oneself, or it is merely the state of greed. In this context, 'lobho,' 'lubbhanā,' 'lubbhitattaṃ,' 'rāgo,' 'taṇhā,' 'tasiṇā,' 'mucchā,' 'ejā,' 'vanaṃ,' 'vanatho,' and so on, are to be understood as the many names for greed.

Khubha sañcalane. Khubbhati, saṃkhubbhati. Khubbhitthanagaraṃ. Saṅkhobho. Kārite – khobheti, khobhayati.

The root 'khubha' is in the sense of shaking. 'Khubbhati' means 'it shakes'; 'saṃkhubbhati' means 'it is thoroughly shaken.' 'Khubbhitthanagaraṃ' means 'a city that was shaken.' 'Saṅkhobho' means 'disturbance.' In the causative: 'khobheti' and 'khobhayati' mean 'to cause to shake' or 'to agitate.'

Samu upasame. Cittaṃ sammati, upasammati, vūpasammati, samaṇo, santi, santo.

The root 'samu' is in the sense of calming. 'Cittaṃ sammati, upasammati, vūpasammati' means 'the mind is calmed, is stilled, is completely stilled.' 'Samaṇo' means 'a recluse'; 'santi' means 'peace'; 'santo' means 'peaceful.'

Ettha samaṇoti sammati santacitto bhavatīti samaṇo. Kāritavasena pana kilese sameti upasametīti samaṇoti nibbacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi “yaṃ sametīti idaṃ ariyaṃ. Samayatītidha sattāna”nti dve kāritarūpāni.

Herein, 'samaṇo' is so called because 'he is calmed, he becomes one of peaceful mind.' But in the causative sense, the definition should be understood as 'samaṇo' because 'he calms or pacifies the defilements.' For thus, 'that which calms is noble' and 'he calms beings here' are two causative forms.

Samu khede nirodhe ca. Khedo. Kilamanaṃ. Nirodho abhāvagamanaṃ. Addhānamaggappaṭipannassa kāyo sammati. Aggi sammati. Santo.

The root 'samu' is also in the sense of exhaustion and cessation. 'Khedo' means 'exhaustion.' 'Kilamanaṃ' means 'weariness.' 'Nirodho' means 'cessation,' a going to non-existence. 'Addhānamaggappaṭipannassa kāyo sammati' means 'the body of one traveling a long road becomes exhausted.' 'Aggi sammati' means 'a fire ceases.' 'Santo' means 'exhausted' or 'ceased.'

Santasaddo “dīghaṃ santassa yojana”ntiādīsu kilantabhāve āgato. “Ayañca vitakko ayañca vicāro santā honti samitā”tiādīsu niruddhabhāve. “Adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo gambhīro duddaso duranubodho santo paṇīto”tiādīsu santañāṇagocaratāyaṃ. “Upasantassa sadā satīmato”tiādīsu kilesavūpasame. “Santo have sabbhi pavedayantī”tiādīsu sādhūsu. “Pañcime bhikkhave mahācorā santo saṃvijjamānā”tiādīsu atthibhāve. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

The word 'santa' appears in contexts like 'a yojana is long for the weary' to denote weariness. In 'this thought and this reflection are stilled and calmed,' it denotes cessation. In 'this Dhamma I have attained is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime,' it refers to being the domain of peaceful knowledge. In 'for one always mindful and completely calmed,' it refers to the complete stilling of defilements. In 'the good indeed make things known among the good,' it refers to good people. In 'these five great thieves, bhikkhus, being existent,' it denotes existence. Thus it is said:

“Kilantatte [M 0.0237] niruddhatte, santadhīgocarattane;

Kilesūpasame ceva, atthibhāve ca sādhusu;

Imesu chasu ṭhānesu, santasaddo panāgato”ti.

In weariness, in cessation, in being the domain of peaceful attainment; in the stilling of defilements, in existence, and among the good; in these six instances the word 'santa' is found.

Damu damane. Dammati. Danto, damo, damanaṃ. Kārite “cittaṃ dameti, damayatī”ti rūpāni.

The root 'damu' is in the sense of taming. 'Dammati' means 'he is tamed.' 'Danto' means 'tamed'; 'damo' means 'taming'; 'damanaṃ' means 'restraint.' In the causative, the forms are 'cittaṃ dameti' and 'damayati,' meaning 'he tames the mind.'

Tattha damoti indriyasaṃvarādīnaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. “Saccena danto damasā upeto. Vedantagū vusitabrahmacariyo”ti ettha hi indriyasaṃvaro “damo”ti vutto. “Yadi saccā damā cāgā, khantyā bhiyyodha vijjatī”ti ettha paññā “damo”ti vuttā. “Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjenā”ti ettha uposathakammaṃ “damo”ti vuttaṃ. “Damupasamenā”ti ettha khanti “damo”ti vuttā. Iccevaṃ –

Therein, 'dama' is a name for restraint of the senses and so on. In 'tamed by truth, endowed with restraint, one who has gone to the end of knowledge, who has lived the holy life,' restraint of the senses is called 'dama.' In 'if through truth, restraint, generosity, and patience, one here excels,' wisdom is called 'dama.' In 'by giving, by restraint, by self-control, by truthful speech,' the Uposatha observance is called 'dama.' In 'by taming and calming,' patience is called 'dama.' Thus:

“Indriyasaṃvaro paññā, khanti cāpi uposatho;

Ime atthā pavuccanti, damasaddena sāsane”ti.

Restraint of the senses, wisdom, patience, and also the Uposatha—these meanings are spoken of by the word 'dama' in the Teaching.

Yā gatipāpuṇesu. Yāyati, yāyanti. Pariyāyo. Yāyamāno mahārājā, addā sīdantare nage. Yāyanto. Yāyantamanuyāyati. Yātānuyāyī. Yāyituṃ, yāyitvā iccādīni.

The root 'yā' is in the senses of going and reaching. 'Yāyati' means 'he goes'; 'yāyanti' means 'they go.' 'Pariyāyo' means 'way' or 'method.' 'Yāyamāno mahārājā, addā sīdantare nage' means 'the great king, while traveling, saw a sinking-place in the mountain.' 'Yāyanto' means 'going.' 'Yāyantamanuyāyati' means 'he follows one who is going.' 'Yātānuyāyī' means 'a follower of one who has gone.' 'Yāyituṃ' means 'to go'; 'yāyitvā' means 'having gone,' and so on.

Ettha pariyāyasaddassa atthuddhāro vuccate, pariyāyasaddo vāradesanākāraṇesu samantato gantabbaṭṭhāne ca sadise ca vattati. “Kassa nu kho ānanda ajja pariyāyo bhikkhuniyo ovaditu”ntiādīsu hi vāre vattati. “Madhupiṇḍikapariyāyotinaṃ dhārehī”tiādīsu desanāyaṃ. “Imināpi kho te rājañña pariyāyena evaṃ hotū”tiādīsu [M 0.0238] kāraṇe. “Pariyāyapatho”tiādīsu samantato gantabbaṭṭhāne. “Kopasaddo khobhapariyāyo”tiādīsu sadise vattati. Iccevaṃ –

Here, the explanation of the meaning of the word 'pariyāya' is given. The word 'pariyāya' is used in the senses of turn, discourse, reason, a place to be gone around, and synonym. In 'Whose turn is it today, Ānanda, to advise the bhikkhunīs?' and so on, it is used in the sense of turn. In 'Bear in mind this Madhupiṇḍika discourse' and so on, it is used in the sense of discourse. In 'By this reason too, O prince, let it be so for you' and so on, it is used in the sense of reason. In 'pariyāyapatho' (a path around) and so on, it is used in the sense of a place to be gone around. In 'The word 'kopa' is a synonym for 'khobha'' and so on, it is used in the sense of synonym. Thus:

Pariyāyaravo vāra-desanākāraṇesu ca;

Samantatova gantabba-ṭṭhāne ca sadise siyā.

The word 'pariyāya' may be used for turn, discourse, and reason; and for a place to be gone around, and for a synonym.

Ri vasane. Riyati.

The root 'ri' is in the sense of clinging. 'Riyati' means 'it clings.'

Vilī vilīnabhāve. Sappi vilīyati. Kārite vilāpayati.

The root 'vilī' is in the sense of dissolving. 'Sappi vilīyati' means 'ghee dissolves.' In the causative: 'vilāpayati' means 'he causes to dissolve.'

Vā gatigandhanesu. Vāyati. Vāyo, vāto.

The root 'vā' is in the senses of going and smelling. 'Vāyati' means 'it blows' or 'it smells.' 'Vāyo' and 'vāto' mean 'wind.'

Sivu tantasantāne. Sibbati, saṃsibbati. Sibbaṃ, sibbanto. Kārite – sibbeti, sibbayati, sibbāpeti, sibbāpayati.

The root 'sivu' is in the sense of continuing a thread. 'Sibbati' means 'he sews'; 'saṃsibbati' means 'he sews together.' 'Sibbaṃ' means 'sewn'; 'sibbanto' means 'sewing.' In the causative: 'sibbeti,' 'sibbayati,' 'sibbāpeti,' and 'sibbāpayati' mean 'he causes to sew.'

Sivu gatisosanesu. Sibbati.

The root 'sivu' is in the senses of going and drying. 'Sibbati' means 'it goes' or 'it dries.'

Dhivu khivu nidassane. Dhibbati. Khibbati.

The roots 'dhivu' and 'khivu' are in the sense of pointing out. 'Dhibbati' means 'he points out.' 'Khibbati' means 'he points out.'

Sā tanukaraṇe. Siyati, siyanti.

The root 'sā' is in the sense of making thin. 'Siyati' means it thins; 'siyanti' means they thin.

Sā antakammani. Siyati anavasesato mānaṃ siyati samucchindatīti aggamaggo mānasanti hi vuttaṃ.

The root 'sā' is in the sense of ending. 'Siyati' means it ends or destroys. Because it completely destroys and uproots conceit, the highest path is indeed called 'mānasanta', the ender of conceit.

Sā assādane. Rasaṃ sāyati. Sāyitaṃ, sāyanaṃ.

The root 'sā' is in the sense of tasting. 'Rasaṃ sāyati' means one tastes the flavor. 'Sāyitaṃ' means tasted; 'sāyanaṃ' means tasting.

Si pāṇippasave. Sūyati, pasūyati. Pasūtā gāvī.

The root 'si' is in the sense of giving birth. 'Sūyati' and 'pasūyati' mean she gives birth. 'Pasūtā gāvī' means a cow that has calved.

Kusu haraṇadittīsu. Kusayati.

The root 'kusu' is in the senses of plucking and shining. 'Kusayati' means one plucks or shines.

Silisa āliṅgane. Silissati. Sileso.

The root 'silisa' is in the sense of embracing. 'Silissati' means one embraces. 'Sileso' means an embrace.

Kilisa upatāpe. Kilissati, saṃkilissati. Kileso, saṃkileso. Ikāralope klissati kleso [M 0.0239] iccādīni. Apica malīnatāpi kilisasaddena vuccati, kiliṭṭhavatthaṃ paridahati. “Cittena saṃkiliṭṭhena, saṃkilissanti māṇavā”tiādīsu dhātūnaṃ anekatthatāya.

The root 'kilisa' is in the sense of torment. 'Kilissati' means one is afflicted; 'saṃkilissati' means one is thoroughly defiled. 'Kileso' means defilement; 'saṃkileso' means corruption. With the elision of the vowel 'i', forms such as 'klissati' and 'kleso' arise. Moreover, impurity is also denoted by the word 'kilisa', as in 'one wears a soiled garment'. In passages such as, 'With a defiled mind, young men are defiled,' this is due to the multiple meanings of roots.

Masa appībhāve khamāyañca. Massati.

The root 'masa' is in the senses of diminishing and of forgiveness. 'Massati' means it diminishes or forgives.

Līsa appībhāve. Lissati. Leso. “Lisa lesane”tipi paṭhanti ācariyā.

The root 'līsa' is in the sense of becoming meager. 'Lissati' means it sticks. 'Leso' means stickiness. Some teachers also read, 'The root "lisa" is in the sense of sticking.'

Tasa pipāsāyaṃ. Tassati, paritassati. Paritassanā, tasiṇā, tasito.

The root 'tasa' is in the sense of thirst. 'Tassati' means one thirsts; 'paritassati' means one thirsts intensely. 'Paritassanā' means intense thirst; 'tasiṇā' means thirst; 'tasito' means thirsty.

Dusa dosane. Dussati. Doso, dosanaṃ, dosito.

The root 'dusa' is in the sense of malice. 'Dussati' means one is malicious. 'Doso' means malice; 'dosanaṃ' means corrupting; 'dosito' means corrupted.

Dusa appītiyaṃ. Dussati, padussati. Doso, padoso, duṭṭho, paduṭṭho, dūsako, dūsito, dūsanā.

The root 'dusa' is in the sense of displeasure. 'Dussati' means one is displeased; 'padussati' means one is greatly displeased. 'Doso' means anger; 'padoso' means great anger; 'duṭṭho' means corrupted; 'paduṭṭho' means greatly corrupted; 'dūsako' means one who corrupts; 'dūsito' means corrupted; 'dūsanā' means corruption.

Asu khepe. Khepo khipanaṃ. Assati. Nirassatiādiyati ca dhammaṃ. Issāso.

The root 'asu' is in the sense of throwing. 'Khepo' means throwing; 'khipanaṃ' means casting. 'Assati' means one throws. 'Nirassati' means one rejects, and 'ādiyati' means one takes up the Dhamma. 'Issāso' means an archer.

Ettha ca nirassatīti chaḍḍeti satthāraṃ tathā dhammakkhānādīni. Issāsoti usuṃ assati khipatīti issāso, dhanuggaho.

Here, 'nirassati' means to discard, to reject the Teacher, likewise the exposition of the Dhamma, and so forth. 'Issāso' is one who shoots or casts an arrow, thus an archer, a bowman.

Yasu payatane. Yassati. Niyasakammaṃ.

The root 'yasu' is in the sense of striving. 'Yassati' means one strives. 'Niyasakammaṃ' means an act of reliance or dismissal.

Ettha ca yena vinayakammena “nissāya te vatthabba”nti niyassiyati bhajāpiyatīti niyaso bālaṃ, taṃ niyasakammaṃ nāma. “Karohi me yakkha niyasakamma”nti ettha pana niggahakammaṃ niyasakammaṃ nāma.

Here, that disciplinary act by which an immature person is made to rely upon and associate with support, according to the rule, 'You must live in dependence,' is called 'niyaso'. That is the 'act of reliance' (niyasakamma). However, in the phrase, 'Perform for me, O yakkha, the niyasakamma,' here 'niyasakamma' means an act of restraint.

Bhassa bhassane. Bhassati. Bhassaṃ, bhassakārako.

The root 'bhassa' is in the sense of chattering. 'Bhassati' means one chatters. 'Bhassaṃ' means chatter; 'bhassakārako' means a chatterer.

Vasa sadde. Sakuṇo vassati. Adhamo migajātānaṃ, siṅgālo tāta vassati. Maṇḍūko vassati.

The root 'vasa' is in the sense of making a sound. 'Sakuṇo vassati' means the bird cries out. 'Adhamo migajātānaṃ, siṅgālo tāta vassati' means the lowest of the beast-kind, the jackal, cries out, my dear. 'Maṇḍūko vassati' means the frog cries out.

Nasa [M 0.0240] adassane. Nassanadhammaṃ nassati. Panassati. Vinassati. Nassa vasali, cara pire vinassa. Naṭṭho, vinaṭṭho. Kārite – nāseti, nāsayati.

The root 'nasa' is in the sense of disappearance. 'Nassanadhammaṃ nassati' means that which is of a perishable nature perishes. 'Panassati' means it perishes. 'Vinassati' means it is utterly destroyed. 'Nassa vasali, cara pire vinassa' means begone, outcast; go away, you wretch, and perish! 'Naṭṭho' means lost; 'vinaṭṭho' means destroyed. In the causative: 'nāseti' and 'nāsayati' mean one causes to perish or destroys.

Susa sosane. Paṇṇaṃ sussati. Kārite – vāto paṇṇaṃ soseti, sosayati. Kamme – vātena paṇṇaṃ sosiyati. Bhāve kriyāpadamappasiddhaṃ. Soso, sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ. Sussaṃ, sussanto. Sussamāno dahado.

The root 'susa' is in the sense of drying. 'Paṇṇaṃ sussati' means a leaf dries up or withers. In the causative: 'vāto paṇṇaṃ soseti' means the wind dries a leaf; 'sosayati' means it causes to dry. In the passive: 'vātena paṇṇaṃ sosiyati' means a leaf is dried by the wind. In the impersonal construction, the verb form is not common. 'Soso' means dryness; 'sukkhaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ' means dry wood. 'Sussaṃ' and 'sussanto' mean drying. 'Sussamāno dahado' means a wasting fever.

Tusa tuṭṭhiyaṃ. Tussati, santussati. Santuṭṭhi, santoso, tosanaṃ, tuṭṭhabbaṃ, tussitabbaṃ, tusitā. Kārite “toseti” iccādīni.

The root 'tusa' is in the sense of satisfaction. 'Tussati' means one is pleased; 'santussati' means one is content. 'Santuṭṭhi' means contentment; 'santoso' means satisfaction; 'tosanaṃ' means pleasing. 'Tuṭṭhabbaṃ' and 'tussitabbaṃ' mean fit to be pleased with. 'Tusitā' means the satisfied ones. In the causative: 'toseti', meaning one pleases, and so forth.

Hā parihāniyaṃ. Hāyati, parihāyati. Hāyanti tattha vaḷavā. Bhāve “bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā, so pahīyissatī”ti ca “rāgo pahīyatī”ti ca rūpaṃ. Kamme kriyāpadamappasiddhaṃ. “Rāgo pahīyatī”ti idaṃ pana “hā cāge”ti vuttassa bhūvādigaṇikadhātussa rūpaṃ “rāgaṃ pajahatī”ti kattupadassa dassanato.

The root 'hā' is in the sense of decline. 'Hāyati' means one declines; 'parihāyati' means one deteriorates. 'Hāyanti tattha vaḷavā' means there, the mares decline. In the impersonal construction, the forms are seen in 'fear or trembling or hair-raising, that will be abandoned,' and 'lust is abandoned.' In the passive voice, the verb form is not common. However, the form 'rāgo pahīyati' (lust is abandoned) is from the root 'hā' meaning to abandon, which belongs to the Bhūvādi group, because the corresponding active form 'rāgaṃ pajahati' (one abandons lust) is found.

Naha bandhane. Nayhati. Upanayhati. Sannayhati. Sannāho. Sannaddho.

The root 'naha' is in the sense of binding. 'Nayhati' means one binds. 'Upanayhati' means one ties to. 'Sannayhati' means one ties together or puts on armor. 'Sannāho' means armor. 'Sannaddho' means armored.

Muha vecitte. Muyhati, sammuyhati, pamuyhati. Moho, pamoho. Mūḷho. Momūho puriso. Momūhaṃ cittaṃ. Kārite – moheti. Pamohako. Ettha ca momūhoti avisadatāya momūho, mahāmūḷhoti attho.

The root 'muha' is in the sense of confusion or delusion. 'Muyhati' means one is deluded; 'sammuyhati' means one is utterly deluded; 'pamuyhati' means one is greatly deluded. 'Moho' means delusion; 'pamoho' means great delusion. 'Mūḷho' means deluded. 'Momūho puriso' means a very deluded man. 'Momūhaṃ cittaṃ' means a very deluded mind. In the causative: 'moheti' means one deludes. 'Pamohako' means a deluder. Here, 'momūho' means greatly deluded due to a lack of clarity; the meaning is 'very confused'.

Saha suha sattiyaṃ. Sayhati. Suyhati.

The roots 'saha' and 'suha' are in the sense of power or endurance. 'Sayhati' means one endures. 'Suyhati' means one endures.

Nhā [M 0.0241] soceyye. Nhāyati, appakkharānaṃ bahubhāve nahāyati. Nahāyitvā, nhāyitvā. Nahānaṃ, nhānaṃ. Sīsaṃ nhāto. Ettha ca sīsaṃ nhātoti sīsaṃ dhovitvā nhātoti attho gahetabbo porāṇehi anumatattā.

The root 'nhā' is in the sense of cleansing. 'Nhāyati' means one bathes; the form 'nahāyati' also occurs for euphonic reasons. 'Nahāyitvā' and 'nhāyitvā' mean having bathed. 'Nahānaṃ' and 'nhānaṃ' mean bathing. 'Sīsaṃ nhāto' means one with head bathed. Here, 'sīsaṃ nhāto' should be understood to mean 'having washed one's head, one has bathed,' this being approved by the ancients.

Siniha pītiyaṃ. Siniyhati. Sinehako, sinehito, siniddho. Putte sineho ajāyatha. Ikāralopena sneho. Tathā hi “nisnehamabhikaṅkhāmī”ti pāḷi dissati.

The root 'siniha' is in the sense of affection. 'Siniyhati' means one feels affection. 'Sinehako' means affectionate; 'sinehito' means beloved; 'siniddho' means smooth or affectionate. 'Putte sineho ajāyatha' means affection for a son arose. By the elision of the vowel 'i', the form 'sneho' arises. Indeed, the Pāli text, 'nisnehamabhikaṅkhāmī' (I desire the absence of affection), is found.

Viriḷa lajjāyaṃ codane ca. Viriḷito. Lajjāvasena attho pasiddho, na codanāvasena. Tathā hi “viriḷitoti lajjito”ti atthasaṃvaṇṇakā garū vadanti “lajjanākārappatto”ti ca.

The root 'viriḷa' is in the senses of shame and of reproach. 'Viriḷito' means one is ashamed. The meaning is established by way of shame, not by way of reproach. Indeed, the venerable commentators on the meaning say that 'viriḷito' means 'ashamed,' and also 'one who has attained the state of shame.'

Divādī ettakā diṭṭhā, dhātavo me yathābalaṃ;

Suttesvaññepi pekkhitvā, gaṇhavho atthayuttitoti.

These many roots of the Divādi group have been presented by me according to my ability; having examined them in the discourses and elsewhere, you should grasp them as being connected with the meaning.

Divādigaṇoyaṃ.

Here ends the Divādi group.

Svādigaṇika

Svādigaṇika (belonging to the svādi group).

Su savane. “Suṇoti, suṇāti. Suṇiṃsu. Paṭissuṇi, paṭissuṇiṃsu. Assosi, assosuṃ. Paccassosi, paccassosuṃ” iccādīni, “suṇissati, sossati” iccādīni ca bhavanti. Abbhāsavisaye “sussūsati, sussūsā” iccādīni. Anabbhāsavisaye – sāvako, soto, suṇaṃ, suṇanto, suṇamāno, suyyamāno, savanaṃ, sutaṃ. Asuyitthāti vā sutaṃ. Sutavā, sotaṃ, soṇo, suṇituṃ, sotuṃ. Suṇitvā, suṇiya, suṇiyāna, sutvā, sutvāna. Kārite – sāveti, sāvayati. Kamme – saddo suyyati, sūyati ca. Bhāve padarūpamappasiddhaṃ.

The root Su is in the sense of hearing. ‘Suṇoti’ (he hears), ‘suṇāti’ (he hears). ‘Suṇiṃsu’ (they heard). ‘Paṭissuṇi’ (he promised), ‘paṭissuṇiṃsu’ (they promised). ‘Assosi’ (he heard), ‘assosuṃ’ (they heard). ‘Paccassosi’ (he replied), ‘paccassosuṃ’ (they replied), and so forth. ‘Suṇissati’ (he will hear), ‘sossati’ (he will hear), and so forth, also occur. In the context of reduplication: ‘sussūsati’ (he desires to hear), ‘sussūsā’ (desire to hear), and so forth. In the context of non-reduplication: sāvako (disciple), soto (ear), suṇaṃ (hearing), suṇanto (hearing), suṇamāno (hearing), suyyamāno (being heard), savanaṃ (the act of hearing), sutaṃ (heard). Or, ‘asuyitthā’ means ‘sutaṃ’ (heard). Sutavā (one who has heard), sotaṃ (the ear), soṇo (a dog), suṇituṃ (to hear), sotuṃ (to hear). Suṇitvā (having heard), suṇiya (having heard), suṇiyāna (having heard), sutvā (having heard), sutvāna (having heard). In the causative: sāveti (he causes to hear), sāvayati (he causes to hear). In the passive: saddo suyyati (the sound is heard), and sūyati (it is heard). In the abstract sense, the word-form is not well-established.

Tattha [M 0.0242] sāvakoti antevāsiko, so duvidho āgatapphalo anāgatapphalo ca, tattha āgatapphalo savanante ariyāya jātiyā jātoti “sāvako”ti vuccati, itaro garūnaṃ ovādaṃ suṇātīti “sāvako”ti. Sāvako, antevāsiko, sissoti pariyāyā.

Herein, ‘sāvako’ means a student (antevāsiko). He is of two kinds: one who has attained the fruit and one who has not yet attained the fruit. Among them, the one who has attained the fruit is called ‘sāvako’ because he is born into the noble lineage at the end of hearing. The other is called ‘sāvako’ because he listens to the advice of his teachers. ‘Sāvako’ (disciple), ‘antevāsiko’ (student), and ‘sisso’ (pupil) are synonyms.

Ettha sutasaddassa atthuddhāraṃ vadāma saddhiṃ sotasaddassa atthuddhārena. Sutasaddo saupasaggo anupasaggo ca anupapadena, sutasaddo ca –

Here we shall explain the extraction of the meaning of the word ‘suta’, together with the extraction of the meaning of the word ‘sota’. The word ‘suta’ is found with a prefix, without a prefix, and without a preceding word; and the word ‘suta’:

Gamane vissute tinte, niyogo’pacitepi ca;

Sadde ca sotadvārānu-sārañātesu dissati.

It is seen in the sense of going, in the well-known, in the defiled, in appointment, and in the accumulated; and in sound, and in what is known by following the ear-door.

Tathā hi “senāya pasuto”tiādīsu gacchantoti attho. “Sutadhammassa passato”tiādīsu vissutadhammassāti attho. “Avassutā avassutassa purisapuggalassā”tiādīsu tintassāti attho. “Ye jhānappasutā dhīrā”tiādīsu anuyuttāti attho. “Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappaka”ntiādīsu upacitanti attho. “Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññāta”ntiādīsu saddoti attho. “Bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo”tiādīsu sotadvārānusāraviññātadhammadharoti attho.

For example, in phrases like ‘senāya pasuto’ (gone forth with the army), the meaning is ‘gacchanto’ (going). In ‘sutadhammassa passato’ (of one who sees the heard doctrine), the meaning is ‘vissutadhammassā’ (of one whose doctrine is renowned). In ‘avassutā avassutassa purisapuggalassā’ (defiled, for a defiled person), the meaning is ‘tintassā’ (moistened/defiled). In ‘ye jhānappasutā dhīrā’ (those wise ones devoted to jhāna), the meaning is ‘anuyuttā’ (devoted). In ‘tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ’ (much merit has been generated by you), the meaning is ‘upacitaṃ’ (accumulated). In ‘diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ’ (seen, heard, sensed, cognized), the meaning is ‘saddo’ (sound). In ‘bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo’ (he is very learned, a bearer of what is heard, an accumulator of what is heard), the meaning is ‘sotadvārānusāraviññātadhammadharo’ (a bearer of the doctrine known by following the ear-door).

Sotasaddopi anekatthappabhedo. Tathā hesa –

The word ‘sota’ also has various kinds of meanings. Thus it is:

Maṃsaviññāṇañāṇesu, taṇhādīsu ca dissati;

Dhārāyaṃ ariyamagge, cittasantatiyampi ca.

It is seen in the physical ear, consciousness, and knowledge, and in craving and so forth; in a current, in the Noble Path, and also in the continuity of consciousness.

“Sotāyatanaṃ[M 0.0243], sotadhātu, sotindriya”ntiādīsu sotasaddo maṃsasote dissati, “sotena saddaṃ sutvā”tiādīsu sotaviññāṇe. “Dibbāya sotadhātuyā”tiādīsu ñāṇasote. “Yāni sotāni lokasminti, yāni etāni sotāni mayā kittitāni pakittitāni ācikkhitāni desitāni paññapitāni paṭṭhapitāni vivaritāni vibhattāni uttānīkatāni pakāsitāni. Seyyathidaṃ? Taṇhāsoto diṭṭhisoto kilesasoto duccaritasoto avijjāsoto”tiādīsu pañcasu dhammesu. “Addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamāna”ntiādīsu udakadhārāyaṃ. “Ariyassetaṃ āvuso aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ soto”tiādīsu ariyamagge. “Purisassa ca viññāṇasotaṃ pajānāti ubhayato abbocchinnaṃ idhaloke patiṭṭhitañca paraloke patiṭṭhitañcā”tiādīsu cittasantatiyanti.

In phrases like ‘sotāyatanaṃ’ (ear-base), ‘sotadhātu’ (ear-element), ‘sotindriyaṃ’ (ear-faculty), and so forth, the word ‘sota’ is seen in the sense of the physical ear. In ‘sotena saddaṃ sutvā’ (having heard a sound with the ear), and so forth, it is in the sense of ear-consciousness. In ‘dibbāya sotadhātuyā’ (by the divine ear-element), and so forth, it is in the sense of the stream of knowledge. In ‘yāni sotāni lokasmin’ (whatever streams there are in the world), and so forth, it is in the sense of five things: the stream of craving, the stream of views, the stream of defilements, the stream of misconduct, and the stream of ignorance. In ‘addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamānaṃ’ (the Blessed One saw a great log being carried by the current of the river Ganges), and so forth, it is in the sense of a current of water. In ‘ariyassetaṃ āvuso aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ soto’ (this, friend, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path, namely, the stream), and so forth, it is in the sense of the Noble Path. In ‘purisassa ca viññāṇasotaṃ pajānāti ubhayato abbocchinnaṃ idhaloke patiṭṭhitañca paraloke patiṭṭhitañca’ (he knows the stream of consciousness of a person, unbroken on both sides, established in this world and established in the other world), and so forth, it is in the sense of the continuity of consciousness.

Soṇoti sunakho. So hi sāmikassa vacanaṃ suṇātīti soṇoti vuccati.

‘Soṇo’ means a dog (sunakho). It is called ‘soṇo’ because it listens (suṇāti) to its master’s words.

Imāni tadabhidhānāni –

These are its designations:

Sunakho sārameyyo ca, suṇo sūno ca kukkuro;

Soṇo svāno suvāno ca, sāḷuro migadaṃsano.

Sunakho, sārameyyo, suṇo, sūno, and kukkuro; soṇo, svāno, and suvāno; sāḷuro, migadaṃsano.

Sā sunidhāti’me saddā, pumānesu pavattare;

Sunakhī kukkurī sī’ti, ime itthīsu vattare.

These words, ‘sā,’ ‘sunidhā,’ and so forth, are used for males; ‘sunakhī,’ ‘kukkurī,’ ‘sī,’ and so forth, are used for females.

Sunakhā sārameyyāti, ādi bahuvaco pana;

Pavattati pumitthīsu, aññatrāpi ayaṃ nayo;

However, the plural forms like ‘sunakhā,’ ‘sārameyyā,’ and so forth, apply to both males and females. This principle applies elsewhere as well.

Kukkuroti [M 0.0244] ayaṃ tattha, bālakāle ravena ve;

Mahallakepi sunakhe, rūḷhiyā sampavattati.

The term ‘kukkuro’ is used for dogs in their youth due to their sound; however, by convention it applies even to old dogs.

Tathā hi aṭṭhakathācariyā kukkurajātake “ye kukkurā rājakulamhi vaḍḍhā, koleyyakā vaṇṇabalūpapannā”tiimasmiṃpadese evamatthaṃ vaṇṇayiṃsu “ye kukkurāti ye sunakhā. Yathā hi taruṇopi passāvo pūtimuttanti tadahujātopi siṅgālo “jarasiṅgālo’ti, komalāpi gaḷācīlatā ‘pūtilatā’ti, suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi kāyo ‘pūtikāyo’ti vuccati, evameva vassasatikopi sunakho ‘kukkuro’ti vuccati, tasmā mahallakā kāyūpapannāpi te ‘kukkurā’tveva vuttā”ti.

Indeed, the commentary teachers on the Kukkura Jātaka, regarding the passage, ‘ye kukkurā rājakulamhi vaḍḍhā, koleyyakā vaṇṇabalūpapannā’ (those dogs who grew up in the royal family, of high breed, endowed with beauty and strength), explained the meaning thus: ‘“ye kukkurā” means “ye sunakhā” (those dogs). Just as even fresh urine is called “pūtimuttaṃ” (foul urine), a newborn jackal is called “jarasiṅgālo” (an old jackal), a tender gaḷācīlatā creeper is called “pūtilatā” (rotten creeper), and a golden-hued body is called “pūtikāyo” (a foul body), so too even a hundred-year-old dog is called “kukkuro” (a puppy). Therefore, even those that are old and well-built are called “kukkurā”.’

Ki hiṃsāyaṃ. Kiṇoti, kiṇāti, kiṇanti.

The root Ki is in the sense of harming. Kiṇoti, kiṇāti, kiṇanti.

Saka sāmatthiye. Samatthabhāvo sāmatthiyaṃ, yathā dakkhiyaṃ. Sakkuṇāti, sakkuṇanti. Asakkhi. Sakkhissati. Sakko. Sakkī.

The root Saka is in the sense of capability. The state of being capable (samatthabhāvo) is capability (sāmatthiyaṃ), just as there is skillfulness (dakkhiyaṃ). Sakkuṇāti (he is able), sakkuṇanti (they are able). Asakkhi (he was able). Sakkhissati (he will be able). Sakko (able). Sakkī (able).

Ettha sakkoti devarājā. So hi parahitaṃ sakahitañca kātuṃ sakkuṇātīti sakko. Apica sakyakulajāto yo kocipi. Tathā hi “atha kho mahānāmo sakko”tiādi vuttaṃ. “Bhagavantañca piṅgiyo maṃ sakka samuddharāhīti ālapi. Sakyā vata bho kumārā paramasakyā vata bho kumārā”ti vacanamupādāya sabbepi sakyakule jātā “sakyā”ti ca “sākiyā”ti ca “sakkā”ti ca vuccanti. Ettha svādittepi anekassaradhātuto ekova uṇāpaccayo hoti, na ṇu ṇāpaccayāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, 'Sakko' means the king of the gods. For he is capable (sakkuṇāti) of doing good for others and for himself, hence 'Sakko.' Moreover, it means anyone born in the Sakya clan. As it is said: 'Then Mahānāma the Sakyan...' and so on. And Piṅgiya addressed the Blessed One, 'O Sakyan, lift me up!' Taking the statement 'Indeed, O young men of the Sakyas, most excellent young men of the Sakyas,' all born in the Sakya clan are called 'Sakyas,' 'Sākiyas,' and 'Sakkas.' Here, although this root belongs to the svādi group, from a root with many vowels only the uṇā-suffix occurs, not the ṇu or ṇā suffixes—this should be understood.

Khī [M 0.0245] khaye. Khīṇoti. Khīṇāti. Khīṇā jāti. Khīṇo. Ayogā bhūrisaṅkhayo.

The root Khī is in the sense of destruction. Khīṇoti. Khīṇāti. ‘Khīṇā jāti’ means birth is destroyed. ‘Khīṇo’ means destroyed. ‘Ayogā bhūrisaṅkhayo’ means from the yokes, a great destruction.

Ge sadde. Giṇoti, giṇāti.

The root Ge is in the sense of sound. Giṇoti, giṇāti.

Ci caye. Ṇakārassa nakārattaṃ. Pākāraṃ cinoti. Citaṃ kusalaṃ. Ceto puggalo.

The root Ci is in the sense of accumulation. The letter 'ṇ' becomes 'n.' ‘Pākāraṃ cinoti’ means he builds a wall. ‘Citaṃ kusalaṃ’ means accumulated merit. ‘Ceto puggalo’ means a person of mind.

Ru upatāpe. Ruṇoti, ruṇāti.

The root Ru is in the sense of affliction. Ruṇoti, ruṇāti.

Rādha sādha saṃsiddhiyaṃ. Rādhuṇāti. Sādhuṇāti. Rādhanaṃ. Ārādhanaṃ. Sādhanaṃ.

The roots Rādha and Sādha are in the sense of accomplishment. Rādhuṇāti. Sādhuṇāti. Rādhanaṃ. Ārādhanaṃ. Sādhanaṃ.

Pī pītiyaṃ. Pīṇoti, pīṇāti. Pīti, piyo.

The root Pī is in the sense of joy. Pīṇoti, pīṇāti. Pīti (joy), piyo (dear).

Apa pāpuṇe sambhu ca. Pāpuṇoti, pāpuṇāti. Patto. Sabbaññutaṃ satthā patto. Sampatto yamasādhanaṃ. Sambhuṇāti, na kiñci atthaṃ abhisambhuṇāti. Sambhuṇanto, abhisambhuṇamāno.

The root Āp is in the sense of reaching and accomplishing. Pāpuṇoti, pāpuṇāti. Patto. ‘Sabbaññutaṃ satthā patto’ means the Teacher has attained omniscience. ‘Sampatto yamasādhanaṃ’ means he has reached the abode of Yama. Sambhuṇāti. ‘Na kiñci atthaṃ abhisambhuṇāti’ means he does not fully comprehend any matter. Sambhuṇanto, abhisambhuṇamāno.

Tattha pattoti pasaddo upasaggo “pappotī”ti ettha pasaddo viya. Tathā hi “patto”ti ettha pāpuṇīti atthe papubbassa apadhātussa pakāre lutte tapaccayassa dvibhāvo bhavati. Tattha na abhisambhuṇātīti na sampāpuṇāti, na sādhetīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, in ‘patto’, the sound ‘pa’ is a prefix, like the sound ‘pa’ in ‘pappoti.’ For, in the word ‘patto’, in the sense of ‘pāpuṇāti’, from the root ‘ap’ preceded by ‘pa’, when the letter ‘p’ of the root is elided, the suffix ‘ta’ is doubled. Herein, ‘na abhisambhuṇāti’ means ‘he does not attain,’ ‘he does not achieve’—this is what is said.

Khipa khepe. Khipuṇāti. Khippaṃ. Khippanti macchapañjaro.

The root Khipa is in the sense of throwing. Khipuṇāti. ‘Khippaṃ’ means quickly. ‘Khippanti macchapañjaro’ means they throw the fish-trap.

Āpa byāpane. Āpuṇāti. Āpo.

The root Āpa is in the sense of pervading. Āpuṇāti. ‘Āpo’ means water.

Mi pakkhepane. Minoti. Mitto.

The root Mi is in the sense of placing or depositing. Minoti. ‘Mitto’ means friend.

Ettha ca sabbaguyhesu nimiyati pakkhipiyatīti mitto. “Mitto have sattapadena hotī”ti vacanaṃ pana vohāravasena vuttaṃ, na atthavasena. Vucceyya ce, yo koci avissāsiko [M 0.0246] attano paṭiviruddhopi ca mitto nāma bhaveyya, na cevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañca pana daṭṭhabbaṃ “sattapadavītihāramattenapi saha gacchanto saha gacchantassa piyavācānicchāraṇena aññamaññaṃ ālāpasallāpakaraṇamattena mitto nāma hotīti vattabbaṃ. Kiṃkāraṇā? Daḷhavissāso mitto nāma na bhaveyyāti mittassa guṇapasaṃsāvasena evaṃ vutta”nti.

Herein, 'mitto' (a friend) is so called because one is 'placed' or 'deposited' (nimiyati pakkhipiyati) in all secrets. The statement, 'A friend is indeed made by seven steps,' is said conventionally, not in terms of its ultimate meaning. If it were said that anyone untrustworthy or even opposed to oneself could be called a friend, it should not be regarded thus. Rather, it should be regarded in this way: 'One is called a friend merely by walking together for the space of seven steps, by uttering kind words while walking together, and merely by engaging in mutual conversation and polite talk.' For what reason? Because a friend who inspires strong trust would not be made thus; this is said in praise of a friend’s qualities.

Vu saṃvaraṇe. Vuṇoti, vuṇāti, saṃvuṇoti, saṃvuṇāti. Paṇḍito sīlasaṃvuto.

The root 'vu' is in the sense of restraining. Vuṇoti, vuṇāti, saṃvuṇoti, saṃvuṇāti. 'Paṇḍito sīlasaṃvuto' means 'the wise one is restrained by virtue.'

Su abhisave. Abhisavo nāma pīḷanaṃ manthanaṃ sandhānaṃ sinhānaṃ vā. Suṇoti, suṇāti.

The root 'su' is in the sense of pressing out. 'Abhisavo' means pressing, churning, combining, or flowing. Suṇoti, suṇāti.

Si bandhane. Sinoti.

The root 'si' is in the sense of binding. Sinoti.

Si nisāne. Siṇoti, siṇāti. Nisitasatthaṃ.

The root 'si' is in the sense of sharpening. Siṇoti, siṇāti. 'Nisitasatthaṃ' means 'a sharpened weapon.'

Na hi nūnāyaṃ sā khujjā, labhati jivhāya chedanaṃ;

Sunisitena satthena, evaṃ dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇaṃ;

Surely this hunchbacked woman, speaking such ill-spoken words, receives the cutting of her tongue with a well-sharpened knife.

Ettha bhaṇanti bhaṇantī.

Herein, 'bhaṇanti' is 'they speak,' and 'bhaṇantī' is 'speaking (feminine).'

Vusa pāgabbiye. Pāgabbiyaṃ nāma kāyavācāmanehi pagabbabhāvo. Vusuṇāti.

The root 'vusa' is in the sense of boldness. 'Pāgabbiyaṃ' is the state of being bold in body, speech, and mind. Vusuṇāti.

Asu byāpane. Asuṇāti. Assu.

The root 'asu' is in the sense of pervading. Asuṇāti. 'Assu' means 'a tear.'

Hi gatibuddhīsu upatāpe ca. Hinoti.

The root 'hi' is in the sense of movement, understanding, and affliction. Hinoti.

Ettha pana asamānantattepi samānatthānaṃ samodhānaṃ vuccati.

Herein, however, even when there is no immediate contiguity, the connection of things having a similar meaning is called 'samodhāna.'

Tika tiga sagha dikkha kivi ciri jiri dāsa du hiṃsāyaṃ. Tikuṇāti. Tiguṇāti. Saghuṇāti. Dikkhuṇāti. Kivuṇāti[M 0.0247]. Ciruṇāti. Jiruṇāti. Dāsuṇāti. Duṇoti, duṇātīti rūpāni hiṃsāvācakāni bhavanti.

The roots 'tika,' 'tiga,' 'sagha,' 'dikkha,' 'kivi,' 'ciri,' 'jiri,' 'dāsa,' and 'du' are in the sense of harming. Tikuṇāti, tiguṇāti, saghuṇāti, dikkhuṇāti, kivuṇāti, ciruṇāti, jiruṇāti, dāsuṇāti, duṇoti, and duṇāti—these forms are expressive of harming.

Suvādī ettakā diṭṭhā, dhātavo me yathābalaṃ;

Suttesvaññepi pekkhitvā, gaṇavho atthayuttito.

So many roots of the Suvādi group have been seen by me according to my ability; having also examined other texts, you should grasp the grouping in accordance with the meaning.

Svādigaṇoyaṃ.

This is the Svādi group.

Kiyādigaṇika

The Kiyādi Group

Kī dabbavinimaye. Dabbavinimayo kayavikkayavasena bhaṇḍassa parivattanaṃ. Kiṇāti, kiṇanti. Vikkiṇāti, vikkiṇanti. Ketuṃ, kiṇituṃ. Vikketuṃ, vikkiṇituṃ. Kiṇitvā, vikkiṇitvā. Kītaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ. Kayo, vikkayo. Vikkiṇeyya haneyya vā.

The root 'kī' is in the sense of exchanging goods. 'Dabbavinimayo' is the exchange of merchandise by way of buying and selling. Kiṇāti, kiṇanti. Vikkiṇāti, vikkiṇanti. Ketuṃ, kiṇituṃ. Vikketuṃ, vikkiṇituṃ. Kiṇitvā, vikkiṇitvā. 'Kītaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ' means 'purchased goods.' 'Kayo' is buying; 'vikkayo' is selling. 'Vikkiṇeyya haneyya vā' means 'one might sell or kill.'

Khi gatiyaṃ. Khiṇāti. Atikhiṇo saro. Khaṃ, khāni. Nakārassa ṇakārattaṃ.

The root 'khi' is in the sense of movement. Khiṇāti. 'Atikhiṇo saro' means 'a sound that has gone beyond.' Khaṃ, khāni. 'Nakārassa ṇakārattaṃ' means 'the letter ‘na’ becomes ‘ṇa’.'

Tattha khiṇātīti gacchati. Atikhinoti atigato. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “senti cāpātikhiṇāva, purāṇāni anutthuna”nti. Tattha cāpātikhiṇā’ti cāpato atikhiṇā atigatā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “cāpātikhiṇāti cāpato atikhiṇā cāpā vinimuttāti attho”ti padatthavivaraṇaṃ kataṃ, tampi gatatthaññeva sandhāya adhippāyatthavasena katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tatra khanti saggo. So hi katapuññehi gantabbattā “kha”nti vuccati. Khānīti saggā.

Therein, 'khiṇāti' means 'one goes.' 'Atikhinoti' means 'one has gone beyond.' Herein, this is the Pāli text: 'Senti cāpātikhiṇāva, purāṇāni anutthuna' ('They lie like arrows gone from the bow, lamenting not their former state'). Therein, 'cāpātikhiṇā' means 'gone beyond from the bow, surpassed.' In the commentary, however, the explanation of the word's meaning is given as: 'cāpātikhiṇā means gone beyond from the bow, that is, released from the bow.' It should be understood that this too is stated according to the intended meaning, with reference to the sense already conveyed. There, 'kha' means heaven. It is called 'kha' because it is to be gone to by those who have performed meritorious deeds. 'Khāni' means heavens.

Ci caye. Puññaṃ cināti. Pākāraṃ cināti. Pāramiyo vicināti, vicinati ca. Pupphaṃ ocināti, ocinati vā. Pacināti. Pacinitvā. Citaṃ kusalaṃ. Cayo sañcayo. Cito pākāro. Cinātīti ceto, iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī. Yo satto puññasañcayo[M 0.0248]. “Sañcayo rāsi samūho piṇḍo gaṇo saṅgho kadambo vaggo karo ghaṭā”iccevamādayo pariyāyā.

The root 'ci' is in the sense of accumulating. 'Puññaṃ cināti' means 'one accumulates merit.' 'Pākāraṃ cināti' means 'one builds a wall.' 'Pāramiyo vicināti, vicinati ca' means 'one investigates or selects the perfections.' 'Pupphaṃ ocināti, ocinati vā' means 'one plucks or gathers a flower.' 'Pacināti' means 'one gathers.' 'Pacinitvā' means 'having gathered.' 'Citaṃ kusalaṃ' means 'accumulated skillfulness.' 'Cayo, sañcayo' both mean 'accumulation.' 'Cito pākāro' means 'a built wall.' 'Cinātīti ceto' means 'one who builds is a ceto, a brick-mason.' 'Yo satto puññasañcayo' means 'that being who is an accumulator of merit.' 'Sañcayo, rāsi, samūho, piṇḍo, gaṇo, saṅgho, kadambo, vaggo, karo, ghaṭā' and so forth are synonyms.

Ji jaye. Jināti, vijināti, jiniyati. Jetā, jino. Jito māro. Māraṃ jito. Jitavā, jitāvī, jitabbo, jeyyo, jayanaṃ, jitaṃ, vijitaṃ, jayo, parājayanaṃ, parājayo. Yassa jitaṃ nāvajīyati. Jitamassa noyāti koci loke. Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ, mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo.

The root 'ji' is in the sense of conquering. Jināti, vijināti, jiniyati. Jetā, jino. Jito māro. Māraṃ jito. Jitavā, jitāvī, jitabbo, jeyyo, jayanaṃ, jitaṃ, vijitaṃ, jayo, parājayanaṃ, parājayo. 'Yassa jitaṃ nāvajīyati' means 'whose victory is not undone.' 'Jitamassa noyāti koci loke' means 'no one in the world surpasses his victory.' 'Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ, mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo' means 'for this is the victory of the glorious Buddha, and the defeat of the evil Māra.'

Tattha jetāti jinātīti jetā, yo koci puggalo. Ajinīti jino, sabbaññū dhammarājā. Kiṃ so ajini? Pāpake akusale dhamme mārādiarayo ca. Iti pāpake akusale dhamme mārādayo ca arayo ajinīti jino. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Therein, 'jetā' means 'one who conquers,' any person whatsoever. 'Jino' means 'conqueror,' the All-Knowing King of Dhamma, because he conquered. What did he conquer? Evil, unskillful states and enemies such as Māra. Thus, because he conquered evil, unskillful states and enemies such as Māra, he is called 'jino.' And this is said:

“Mādisā ve jinā honti, ye pattā āsavakkhayaṃ;

Jitā me pāpakā dhammā, tasmāhaṃ upaka jino”ti,

'Conquerors are indeed like me, those who have attained the destruction of the taints. Evil states have been conquered by me; therefore, Upaka, I am a conqueror.'

“Tathāgato bhikkhave abhibhū anabhibhūto”ti ca.

and, 'The Tathāgata, monks, is the conqueror, the unconquered.'

Jinasaddo hi kevalo sabbaññumhi pavattati, sopapado pana paccekabuddhādīsu tamhi ca yathārahaṃ pavattati. “Paccekajino, odhijino, anodhijino, vipākajino, avipākajino”ti imānettha nidassanapadāni.

The word 'Jina' by itself applies only to the All-Knowing One; however, with a prefix, it applies to Paccekabuddhas and others, and also to him, as is appropriate. 'Paccekajino, odhijino, anodhijino, vipākajino, avipākajino'—these herein are illustrative terms.

Ji jāniyaṃ. Jināti, na jināti na jāpaye, jino rathassaṃ maṇikuṇḍale ca, putte ca dāre ca tatheva jino. Jino dhanañca dāse ca.

The root 'ji' is in the sense of knowing. Jināti, na jināti, na jāpaye. 'Jino rathassaṃ' means 'a master of a chariot,' 'maṇikuṇḍale ca' means 'and of jeweled earrings,' 'putte ca dāre ca tatheva jino' means 'and likewise a master of sons and wives.' 'Jino dhanañca dāse ca' means 'a master of wealth and of slaves.'

Ñā [M 0.0249] avabodhane. Jānāti, ñāyati, nāyati. Animittā na nāyare. Jaññā so yadi hāpaye. Mā maṃ jaññūti icchati. “Ime amhāka”nti ñātabbaṭṭhena ñāti, ñātako. Ñātimittā suhajjā ca. Ñātako no nisinnoti. Ñātabbaṃ ñeyyaṃ, saṅkhāravikāralakkhaṇanibbānapaññattidhammā. Īdisesu ṭhānesu ñeyyasaddo ekantena napuṃsako, vāccaliṅgatte sabbaliṅgiko, yathā? Ñeyyo phasso. Ñeyyā vedanā. Ñeyyaṃ cittaṃ. Ñeyyo puriso, ñeyyā itthī, ñeyyaṃ dhananti ca.

The root 'ñā' is in the sense of understanding. Jānāti, ñāyati, nāyati. 'Animittā na nāyare' means 'the signless are not known.' 'Jaññā so yadi hāpaye' means 'he would know if he were to abandon.' 'Mā maṃ jaññūti icchati' means 'he wishes, “Let them not know me.”' Because they are to be known as 'these are ours,' they are called 'ñāti' (a relative) or 'ñātako' (a kinsman). 'Ñātimittā suhajjā ca' means 'relatives, friends, and companions.' 'Ñātako no nisinnoti' means 'our kinsman sits down.' 'Ñātabbaṃ' is 'ñeyyaṃ' (what is to be known, the knowable), which are the phenomena of formations, derivatives, characteristics, Nibbāna, and concepts. In such contexts, the word 'ñeyya' is exclusively neuter, but when it qualifies a noun, it takes any gender, for example: 'ñeyyo phasso' (knowable contact), 'ñeyyā vedanā' (knowable feeling), 'ñeyyaṃ cittaṃ' (knowable mind), 'ñeyyo puriso' (a knowable man), 'ñeyyā itthī' (a knowable woman), and 'ñeyyaṃ dhanaṃ' (knowable wealth).

Thu abhitthave. Thunāti. Abhitthunāti. Thuti, abhitthuti. Thavanā, abhitthavanā, thuto, abhitthuto.

The root 'thu' is in the sense of praising. Thunāti. Abhitthunāti. 'Thuti, abhitthuti' mean praise, laudation. 'Thavanā, abhitthavanā' mean praising, extolling. 'Thuto, abhitthuto' mean praised, extolled.

Thu nitthunane. Thunāti.

The root 'thu' is in the sense of lamenting. Thunāti.

Uṭṭhehi revate supāpadhamme,

Apārutadvāre adānasīle;

Nessāma taṃ yattha thunanti duggatā,

Samappitā nerayikā dukkhena;

Purāṇāni anutthuna”nti ca payogo.

Arise, Revata, of evil nature, with unguarded doors, of ungenerous character! We will lead you where the unfortunate lament, hell-beings given over to suffering. And 'Purāṇāni anutthuna' ('lamenting not their former state') is an example.

Du hiṃsāyaṃ. Dunāti. Mittaddu. Dumo.

The root 'du' is in the sense of harming. Dunāti. 'Mittaddu' means 'a treacherous friend.' 'Dumo' means 'a tree.'

Ettha mittaddūti mittaṃ dunāti hiṃsati dubbhatīti mittaddu. Atra “vedā na tāṇāya bhavanti tassa, mittadduno bhūnahuno narassā”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Dumoti duniyati gehasambhārādiatthāya hiṃsiyati chindiyati, paṇṇapupphādiatthikehi vā paṇṇapupphādiharaṇena pīḷiyatīti dumo.

Herein, 'mittaddu' means one who harms, injures, or betrays a friend, hence 'mittaddu'. Here, the Pāli passage 'For him, the betrayer of friends, the slayer of beings, the Vedas are no protection' is an illustration. 'Dumo' means that which is harmed or cut down for the sake of household materials and so on; or, it is that which is afflicted by those who desire leaves and flowers, through the removal of leaves and flowers.

Dhū kampane. Dhunāti. Dhūmo, dhonā, dhono, dhuto. Dhunanto vākacīrāni, gacchāmi ambare tadā.

The root 'dhū' is in the sense of shaking. It shakes. Smoke, cleansed (feminine), cleansed (masculine), shaken. 'Shaking the bark robes, then I go in the sky.'

Tattha [M 0.0250] dhūmoti dhunāti kampatīti dhūmo. Dhūmasaddo kodhe taṇhāya vitakke pañcasu kāmaguṇesu dhammadesanāyaṃ pakatidhūmeti imesu atthesu vattati. “Kodho dhūmo bhasmāni mosavajja”nti ettha hi kodhe vattati. “Icchā dhūmāyito sadā”ti ettha taṇhāyaṃ. “Tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhu bhagavato avidūre dhūmāyanto nisinno hotī”ti ettha vitakke.

Herein, 'dhūma' is so called because it shakes, it trembles. The word 'dhūma' is used in these senses: anger, craving, thought, the five strands of sensual pleasure, Dhamma teaching, and natural smoke. For instance, in 'Anger is smoke, lying is ashes,' it refers to anger. In 'Always smoldering with desire,' it refers to craving. In 'At that time, a certain bhikkhu was sitting not far from the Blessed One, agitated with thought,' it refers to thought.

“Paṅko ca kāmā palipo ca kāmā,

Bhayañca metaṃ timulaṃ pavuttaṃ;

Rajo ca dhūmo ca mayā pakāsito,

Hitvā tuvaṃ pabbaja brahmadattā”ti

Sensual pleasures are mud, and sensual pleasures are mire; and this fear has been declared a thicket. Dust and smoke have been revealed by me; abandoning them, go forth, O Brahmadatta.

Ettha pañcasu kāmaguṇesu. “Dhūmaṃ kattā hotī”ti ettha dhammadesanāyaṃ. “Dhajo rathassa paññāno, dhūmo paññānamaggino”ti ettha pakatidhūme. Iccevaṃ –

Herein, it refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. In 'One who makes smoke,' it refers to the Dhamma teaching. In 'The banner is the sign of the chariot, smoke is the sign of fire,' it refers to natural smoke. Thus:

Kodhataṇhāvitakkesu, pañcakāmaguṇesu ca;

Desanāyañca pakati-dhūme dhūmo pavattati.

In anger, craving, and thoughts, and in the five strands of sensual pleasure; and in teaching and natural smoke, the word 'dhūma' occurs.

Dhonāti paññā. Vuttañhetaṃ niddese “dhonā vuccati paññā, yā paññā pajānanā sammādiṭṭhi, kiṃkāraṇā dhonāti vuccati paññā? Yaṃ tāya paññāya kāyaduccaritaṃ dhutañca dhotañca sandhotañca niddhotañca, vacīduccaritaṃ manoduccaritaṃ dhutañca dhotañca sandhotañca niddhotañca. Taṃkāraṇā dhonā vuccati paññā. Atha vā sammādiṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhiṃ dhutā ca dhotā ca sandhotā ca niddhotā ca, taṃkāraṇā dhonā vuccati paññā”ti. “Dhonassa hi natthi kuhiñci loke, pakappitā diṭṭhi bhavābhavesū”ti ayamettha pāḷi nidassanaṃ[M 0.0251]. Atra dhonā assa atthīti dhono, tassa dhonassāti nibbacanaṃ. Dhātūnamanekatthatāya dhūdhātu kampanatthepi dhovanatthepi vattati.

Wisdom is 'dhonā' (the cleanser). As stated in the Niddesa: 'Wisdom is called 'dhonā,' that wisdom which is understanding, right view. For what reason is wisdom called 'dhonā'? Because through that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely purified; verbal misconduct and mental misconduct are shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely purified. For that reason, wisdom is called 'dhonā.' Alternatively, right view shakes off, washes, thoroughly washes, and completely purifies wrong view. For that reason, wisdom is called 'dhonā'.' The Pāli passage 'For the purified one there is nowhere in the world any fabricated view concerning various states of existence' is the illustration here. Herein, 'dhono' means 'one who possesses 'dhonā',' and 'dhonassa' is its derivation. Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root 'dhū' is used in the sense of shaking and also in the sense of washing.

Muna ñāṇe. Munāti. Monaṃ, muni. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne dhātuyā ākhyātatte ekantena antalopo bhavati. Sobhitattheragāthāyaṃ pana anāgatavacane ukārassa vuddhivasena “ahaṃ monena monissa”nti rūpantarañca dissati. Tattha monissanti jānissaṃ. Nāmatte antalopo na hoti. Tattha monanti kiñcāpi “na monena muni hotī”ti ettha tuṇhībhāvo “mona”nti vuccati, tathāpi idha “ñāṇe”ti vacanato na so adhippeto, ñāṇamevādhippetaṃ, tasmā moneyyapaṭipadāsaṅkhātaṃ maggañāṇamonampi gahetabbaṃ. Munīti munāti jānāti hitāhitaṃ paricchindatīti muni. Atha vā khandhādiloke tulaṃ āropetvā minanto viya “ime ajjhattikā khandhā, ime bāhirā”tiādinā nayena ime ubho atthe munātīti muni. Tenāha bhagavā –

The root 'muna' is in the sense of knowing. It knows. Knowledge, a sage. In this context, when the root is used as a verb, the final vowel is entirely elided. However, in the verse of Elder Sobhita, in the future tense, due to the strengthening of the vowel 'u,' a variant form 'ahaṃ monena monissa' is also seen. There, 'monissa' means 'I will know.' In nouns, the final vowel is not elided. Although 'mona' in 'na monena muni hoti' (a sage is not made by silence) refers to silence, here, due to the statement 'in knowledge,' that is not the intended meaning; only knowledge is intended. Therefore, the knowledge of the path, designated as the practice of sagacity (moneyyapaṭipadā), should also be taken as 'mona.' 'Muni' means one who knows, who discerns what is beneficial and harmful, hence 'muni.' Alternatively, like one who weighs on a scale in the world of aggregates and so on, distinguishing thus: 'These are internal aggregates, these are external,' and so forth—he knows these two things, hence 'muni.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Na monena muni hoti, mūḷharūpo aviddasu;

Yo ca tulaṃva paggayha, varamādāya paṇḍito.

Not by silence does one become a sage, being deluded and unlearned; but the wise one who, as if holding a scale, takes the excellent,

Pāpāni parivajjeti, sa muni tena so muni;

Yo munāti ubho loke, muni tena pavuccatī”ti.

avoids evils—he is a sage, by that he is a sage. He who knows both worlds, by that he is called a sage.

Aparāpettha bhavati atthavibhāvanā. Munīti monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, kāyamoneyyādīsu vā aññataraṃ, tena samannāgatattā puggalo “munī”ti vuccati. So panesa agāriyamuni anagāriyamuni sekkhamuni asekkhamuni paccekamuni munimunīti anekavidho[M 0.0252]. Tattha agāriyamunīti gihipi āgataphalo viññātasāsano. Anagāriyamunīti tathārūpova pabbajito. Sekkhamunīti satta sekkhā. Asekkhamunīti khīṇāsavo. Paccekamunīti paccekabuddho. Munimunīti sammāsambuddho. Tathā hi āyasmāpi sāriputto āha “munīti vuccati tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti.

Herein, there is another explanation of the meaning. 'Mona' is said to be knowledge (ñāṇa), or one of the kinds of sagacity, such as bodily sagacity (kāyamoneyya); a person is called 'muni' because of being endowed with that. This muni is of many kinds: a householder muni, a homeless muni, a trainee muni, a perfected muni, a Paccekamuni, and the Muni of munis. Herein, a 'householder muni' is a layperson who has attained the fruit and understood the Teaching. A 'homeless muni' is one who has gone forth in such a way. A 'trainee muni' refers to the seven trainees. A 'perfected muni' is one whose cankers are destroyed. A 'Paccekamuni' is a Paccekabuddha. The 'Muni of munis' is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Indeed, the Venerable Sāriputta also said: 'The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is called 'Muni.''

Pū pavane. Pavanaṃ sodhanaṃ. Punāti. Puññaṃ, putto, dantapoṇaṃ.

The root 'pū' is in the sense of purifying. Purifying is cleansing. It purifies. Merit, a son, a tooth-cleaner.

Ettha ca puññanti attano kārakaṃ punāti sodhetīti puññaṃ. Atha vā yattha sayaṃ uppannaṃ taṃsantānaṃ punāti visodhetīti puññaṃ. Kintaṃ? Sucaritaṃ kusalakammaṃ. Sakammikattā dhātussa kāritavasena atthavivaraṇaṃ labbhati. Puttoti attano kulaṃ punāti sodhetīti putto. Evañca sati hīnajaccānaṃ caṇḍālādīnaṃ putto nāma na bhaveyyāti na vattabbaṃ saddānamatthakathanassa nānappakārena pavattito, tasmā attano pitu hadayaṃ pūretīti puttoti evamādināpi nibbacanaṃ gahetabbameva. Nānādhātuvasenapi hi padāni siddhiṃ samupagacchanti.

Herein, 'puñña' (merit) means that which purifies and cleanses its doer, hence 'puñña'. Alternatively, it is 'puñña' because it purifies and cleanses the mental continuum in which it arises. What is that? Good conduct, wholesome action. Because the root is transitive, the explanation of meaning is obtained in a causative sense. 'Putta' (son) is so called because he purifies and cleanses his own family. Even so, it should not be said that low-caste people like outcastes would not have a 'son,' for explanations of the meaning of words proceed in various ways. Therefore, derivations such as 'he fills his father's heart, thus he is a son' should also be accepted. Indeed, words attain their validity through various verbal roots.

Putto ca nāma atrajo khetrajo antevāsiko dinnakoti catubbidho. Tattha attānaṃ paṭicca jāto atrajo nāma. Sayanapīṭhe pallaṅke ureti evamādīsu nibbatto khetrajo nāma. Santike sippuggaṇhanako antevāsiko nāma. Posāpanatthāya dinno dinnako nāma dantapoṇanti dante punanti visodhenti etenāti dantapoṇaṃ, dantakaṭṭhaṃ.

A son is of four kinds: one born of oneself, one born of the field, a resident pupil, and one given. Herein, 'atraja' is one born dependent on oneself. 'Khetraja' is one produced on a bed, chair, couch, lap, and so on. 'Antevāsika' is one who learns a craft in close proximity. 'Dinnaka' is one given for the purpose of being raised. As for 'dantapoṇa,' it is so called because they purify and cleanse the teeth with it; it is a tooth-stick.

Pī tappanakantīsu. Piṇātīti pīti. Ettha ca pītīti pīṇanaṃ pīti, tappanaṃ kantīti ca vuttaṃ hoti. Idaṃ bhāvavasena nibbacanaṃ. Idaṃ [M 0.0253] pana hetukattuvasena piṇayatīti pīti, tappetīti attho.

The root 'pī' is in the sense of satisfying and delighting. 'Pīti' is so called because it satisfies. Herein, 'pīti' is said to be satisfaction (pīṇana) and delight (kanti). This is an explanation in terms of state. However, in terms of causative derivation, 'pīti' means 'it causes to satisfy,' that is, 'it delights.'

Sā panesā khuddakāpīti khaṇikāpīti okkantikāpīti ubbegāpīti pharaṇāpītīti pañcavidhā hoti. Tattha khuddakāpīti sarīre lomahaṃsanamattameva kātuṃ sakkoti. Khaṇikāpīti khaṇe khaṇe vijjuppādasadisā hoti. Okkantikāpīti samuddatīraṃ vīci viya kāyaṃ okkamitvā okkamitvā bhijjati. Ubbegāpīti balavatī hoti kāyaṃ uddhaggaṃ katvā ākāse laṅghāpanappamāṇā hoti. Pharaṇāpītiyā pana uppannāya sakalasarīraṃ dhamitvā pūritavatthi viya mahatā udakoghena pakkhandapabbatakucchi viya ca anupariphuṭaṃ hoti, evaṃ pañcavidhā pīti, sā sampiyāyanalakkhaṇattā “piṇātī”ti pītīti suddhakattuvasenapi vattuṃ yujjati. Ettha “piyāyati, pitā, piyo, pemo”tiādīni pīdhātuyā eva rūpāni. Tattha “puttaṃ piyāyatīti pitā”ti vadanti. Piyāyitabboti piyo. Pemanaṃ pemo.

This joy is of five kinds: minor joy (khuddakā pīti), momentary joy (khaṇikā pīti), flooding joy (okkantikā pīti), uplifting joy (ubbegā pīti), and pervading joy (pharaṇā pīti). Herein, minor joy is only capable of making the hairs of the body stand on end. Momentary joy is like flashes of lightning occurring moment by moment. Flooding joy breaks over the body again and again like waves on the seashore. Uplifting joy is powerful, making the body rise up, so that it is capable of leaping into the air. When pervading joy has arisen, the entire body is suffused, like a bladder filled by blowing, or like the interior of a mountain cave inundated by a great gush of water. Thus, joy is fivefold. Because it has the characteristic of making one delighted, it is also appropriate to say 'pīti' (joy) as 'it satisfies' in the sense of a pure agent. Herein, terms like 'piyāyati' (he loves), 'pitā' (father), 'piyo' (beloved), and 'pemo' (love) are all forms derived from the root 'pī'. Among these, they say 'pitā' (father) because he cherishes his son ('puttaṃ piyāyati'). 'Piyo' means worthy of being cherished. 'Pemo' means loving.

Mā parimāṇe. Mināti. Mānaṃ, parimāṇaṃ, mattaṃ, mattā, mano, vimānaṃ, minitabbaṃ, metabbaṃ, chāyā metabbā. Īdisesu ṭhānesu anīyapaccayo na labbhati.

The root 'mā' is in the sense of measuring. It measures. Measure, measurement, limit, measure, mind, celestial mansion, what should be measured, what should be measured, the shadow should be measured. In such cases, the suffix 'anīya' is not found.

Ettha manoti ekāya nāḷiyā ekāya ca tulāya minamāno viya ārammaṇaṃ mināti paricchindatīti mano. Visesato miniyate paricchindiyateti vimānaṃ, devānaṃ puññabalena nibbattabyamhaṃ devaniketaṃ. Yaṃ vimānaṃ upasobhitaṃ, pabhāsatimidaṃ byamhanti ca ādinā thomiyati.

Here, 'mano' (mind) is so called because it measures and defines its object, like one measuring with a single reed or a single balance. 'Vimāna' (celestial mansion) is so called because it is specifically measured and defined; it is a divine abode, a celestial mansion, produced by the power of the gods' merit. It is praised with phrases such as 'that celestial mansion is adorned, this celestial mansion shines,' and so forth.

Mī hiṃsāyaṃ. Mināti. Mīno, kumīnaṃ.

The root 'mī' is in the sense of harming. It harms. A fish, a fish trap.

Ettha [M 0.0254] mīnoti maccho. Macchassa hi “mīno maccho ambujo vārijo vāricaro”ti anekāni nāmāni. Visesanāmāni pana “amaro khaliso candakulo kandaphali indaphali indavalo kuliso vāmi kuṅkutalo kaṇḍiko sakulo maṅguro siṅgī satavaṅko rohito pāṭhīno kāṇo savaṅko pāvuso” iccevamādīni, “timi timiṅgalo” iccevamādīni ca bhavanti. Kumīnanti kucchitenākārena macche minanti hiṃsanti etenāti kumīnaṃ, macchabandhanapañjaro. So pana pāḷiyaṃ kumīnasaddena vuccati. Tathā hi –

Here, 'mīna' means fish. Indeed, a fish has many names, such as 'mīna,' 'maccha,' 'ambuja,' 'vārija,' and 'vāricara.' Specific names, however, include 'amara,' 'khalisa,' 'candakula,' 'kandaphali,' 'indaphali,' 'indavala,' 'kulisa,' 'vāmi,' 'kuṅkutala,' 'kaṇḍika,' 'sakula,' 'maṅgura,' 'siṅgī,' 'satavaṅka,' 'rohita,' 'pāṭhīna,' 'kāṇa,' 'savaṅka,' 'pāvusa,' and so on, as well as 'timi,' 'timiṅgala,' and the like. 'Kumīna' is so called because by this they harm or injure fish in a despicable way; it is a fish trap. In the Pāli texts, it is called by the term 'kumīna.' Thus:

“Vārijasseva me sato, bandhassa kumināmukhe;

Akkosati paharati, piye putte apassato”ti

Like a water-creature that I am, bound at the mouth of a fish-trap, he scolds and strikes me, who cannot see my beloved son.

Pāḷi dissati.

The Pāli text is seen.

Mū bandhane. Munāti. Muni.

The root 'mū' is in the sense of binding. Munāti. Muni.

Ettha munīti attano cittaṃ munāti mavati bandhati rāgadosādivasaṃ gantuṃ na detīti muni.

Here, a sage is called 'muni' because he understands, comprehends, and binds his own mind, not allowing it to go under the sway of passion, hatred, and so forth.

Ri gatidesanesu. Rikāti. Reṇu. Nakārassa ṇattaṃ.

The root 'ri' is in the sense of going and teaching. Rikāti. Reṇu. The letter 'n' is changed to 'ṇ'.

Lī silese. Lināti, nilināti. Līnaṃ, sallīnaṃ, paṭisallānaṃ.

The root 'lī' is in the sense of adhering. Lināti, nilināti. Līnaṃ, sallīnaṃ, paṭisallānaṃ.

Vī tantasantāne. Vatthaṃ vināti. Iminā suttena cīvaraṃ vināhi. Kamme – idaṃ kho āvuso cīvaraṃ maṃ uddissa viyyati. Vītaṃ. Suvītaṃ. Appakaṃ hoti vetabbaṃ. Kārite “vāyāpeti, tantavāyehi cīvaraṃ vāyāpessāmā’ti cīvaraṃ vāyāpesuṃ” iccevamādīni bhavanti.

The root 'vī' is in the sense of extending threads, i.e., weaving. He weaves the cloth. Weave the robe with this thread. In the passive voice: 'Friends, this robe is being woven for me.' Woven. Well-woven. Little remains to be woven. In the causative: 'He causes to weave'; 'We will have a robe woven by weavers,' thus they caused the robe to be woven,' and so on, are the forms.

Vī hiṃsāyaṃ. Vināti. Veṇu. Veṇūti vaṃso.

The root 'vī' is in the sense of harming. Vināti. Veṇu. Veṇu means bamboo.

Lū [M 0.0255] chedane. Lunāti. Loṇaṃ, kusalaṃ, bālo, lūto.

The root 'lū' is in the sense of cutting. Lunāti. Loṇaṃ, kusalaṃ, bālo, lūto.

Ettha ca loṇanti lunāti vītarasabhāvaṃ vināseti sarasabhāvaṃ karotīti loṇaṃ, lavaṇaṃ. Kuso viya hatthappadesaṃ akusaladhamme lunātīti kusalaṃ, anavajjaiṭṭhavipākalakkhaṇo dhammo. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyike dve atthe lunātīti bālo, avidvā. Lūtoti makkaṭako vuccati. Tassa hi suttaṃ “lūtasutta”nti vadanti. Yūsaṃ pātuṃ paṭaṅgamakkhikādīnaṃ jīvitaṃ lunātīti lūto.

Here, 'loṇa' (salt) is so called because it cuts, destroys the tasteless quality, and produces a tasteful quality; it is also called 'lavaṇa.' Just as kusa grass cuts the hand, 'kusala' (wholesome) cuts off unwholesome states; it is a quality characterized by blamelessness and desirable results. A 'bālo' (fool) is so called because he cuts off the two benefits pertaining to this life and the next; he is ignorant. 'Lūta' refers to a spider. Indeed, its thread is called 'lūtasutta' (spider's thread). It is also called 'lūta' because it cuts off the life of moths, flies, and other insects that come to drink broth.

Si bandhane. Sināti. Sīmā, sīsaṃ.

The root 'si' is in the sense of binding. Sināti. Sīmā, sīsaṃ.

Ettha sīmāti sinīyate samaggena saṅghena kammavācāya bandhiyateti sīmā. Sā duvidhā baddhasīmā abaddhasīmāti. Tāsu abaddhasīmā mariyādakaraṇavasena “sīmā”ti veditabbā. Sināti bandhati kese moḷikaraṇavasena etthāti sīsaṃ. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

Here, 'sīmā' (boundary) is so called because it is bound or demarcated by the unified Sangha through a formal act. It is of two kinds: the established boundary and the unestablished boundary. Among these, the unestablished boundary should be understood as a 'sīmā' by way of establishing limits. 'Sīsaṃ' (head) is so called because it binds the hair by way of making a topknot. Other similar derivations should also be applied.

Sā pāke. Sināti.

The root 'sā' is in the sense of cooking. Sināti.

Su hiṃsāyaṃ. Suṇāti. Parasu. Paraṃ suṇanti hiṃsanti etenāti parasu.

The root 'su' is in the sense of harming. Suṇāti. Parasu. Because they harm others with this, it is called 'parasu' (axe).

Asa bhojane. Vuttānaṃ phalamasnāti. Asanaṃ.

The root 'asa' is in the sense of eating. He experiences the fruit of what has been said. Asanaṃ.

Ettha asananti āhāro. So hi asiyati bhuñjiyatīti “asana”nti vuccati. “Asnātha khādatha pivathā”ti idamettha nidassanaṃ.

Here, 'asana' means food. For it is eaten, consumed, therefore it is called 'asana.' 'Eat, chew, drink,' is an example here.

Kilisa vibādhane. Kilisnāti. Kileso.

The root 'kilisa' is in the sense of afflicting. Kilisnāti. Kileso.

Ettha ca kilesoti rāgādayopi dukkhampi vuccati.

Here, by 'kilesa' is meant lust and so forth, and also suffering.

Uddhasa uñche. Uñcho pariyesanaṃ. Uddhasnāti.

The root 'uddhasa' is in the sense of gleaning. Gleaning is seeking. Uddhasnāti.

Isa [M 0.0256] abhikkhaṇe. Isnāti.

The root 'isa' is in the sense of repetition. Isnāti.

Visa vippayoge. Visnāti. Visaṃ.

The root 'visa' is in the sense of separation. Visnāti. Visaṃ.

Pusa sinehasavanapūraṇesu. Pusnāti.

The root 'pusa' is in the senses of affection, flowing, and filling. Pusnāti.

Pusa posane. Pusnāti.

The root 'pusa' is in the sense of nourishing. Pusnāti.

Musa theyye. Musnāti. Musalo.

The root 'musa' is in the sense of stealing. Musnāti. Musalo.

Kiyādī ettakā diṭṭhā, dhātavo me yathābalaṃ;

Suttesvaññepi pekkhitvā, gaṇhavho atthayuttito.

So many roots of the Kiyādi group have been presented by me according to my ability; having observed others in the scriptures, you should accept them in accordance with the suitability of their meaning.

Sāsanā lokato cete,

Dassitā tesu lokato;

Sāsanassopakārāya,

Vuttā tadanurūpakā.

And these roots, from the Dispensation and from the world, are shown. Among them, those from the world are spoken of for the benefit of the Dispensation in a suitable manner.

Kiyādigaṇoyaṃ.

This is the Kiyādi group.

Gahādigaṇika

The Gahādi Group

Idāni gahādigaṇo vuccate. Ettheke evaṃ maññanti.

Now the Gahādi group is spoken of. Here some think thus:

Gahādīnaṃ gaṇo nāma, paccekaṃ nupalabbhati;

Athameko gahadhātu, gahādīnaṃ gaṇo siyā.

The group named Gahādi is not found individually; but if there were a single root 'gaha', then it would be the Gahādi group.

Yato ppaṇhā parā heyyuṃ, dhātuto jinasāsane;

Tepi aññe na vijjanti, aññatra gahadhātuyā.

Since the affix ṇhā would be inapplicable to other roots in the Dispensation of the Conqueror, and those others are not found, except for the root gaha.

Iti cintāya ekacce, gahadhātuṃ kiyādinaṃ;

Pakkhipiṃsu gaṇe evaṃ, na vadiṃsu gahādikaṃ.

Thinking thus, some included the root gaha in the Kiyādi group; thus, they did not speak of a Gahādi group.

Na tesaṃ gahaṇaṃ dhīro, gaṇheyya suvicakkhaṇo;

Yato kaccāyane vutto, gahādīnaṃ gaṇo visuṃ.

A wise and discerning person should not accept their view, since in Kaccāyana's grammar, the Gahādi group is stated separately.

“Gahādito ppaṇhā” iti, lakkhaṇaṃ vadatā hi so;

Kaccāyanena garunā, dassito nanu sāsane.

Indeed, by stating the characteristic 'from the Gahādi group, the affix ṇhā,' was it not shown in the Dispensation by the venerable Kaccāyana?

Sace [M 0.0257] visuṃ gahādīnaṃ, gaṇo nāma na labbhati;

Gahādidīpake sutte, hitvāna bāhiraṃ idaṃ.

If the group named Gahādi is not accepted as distinct, then in the Sutta illuminating the Gahādi group, having abandoned this external matter,

“Gahato ppaṇhā” icceva, vattabbaṃ atha vā pana;

“Kiyādito nāppaṇhā”ti, kātabbaṃ ekalakkhaṇaṃ.

it should be said only, 'from gaha, the affix ṇhā,' or else a single characteristic should be made: 'from the Kiyādi group, not the affix ṇhā.'

Yasmā tathā na vuttañca, na katañcekalakkhaṇaṃ;

Tasmā ayaṃ visuṃyeva, gaṇo icceva ñāyati.

Since it is not said thus, nor is a single characteristic made, therefore it is known that this group is indeed distinct.

“Sarā sare lopa”miti-ādīni lakkhaṇāniva;

Gambhīraṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etaṃ, dujjānaṃ takkagāhinā.

Like such characteristics as 'A vowel is elided before a vowel,' this characteristic is profound, difficult to understand for one who relies on logic.

Usādayopi sandhāya, ādiggaho kato tahiṃ;

Tathā hi “uṇhāpetī”ti, ādirūpāni dissare.

The inclusion of 'ādi' (etc.) was made there with reference also to roots such as 'usa'; for thus, initial forms such as 'uṇhāpeti' are seen.

Idāni pākaṭaṃ katvā, ādisaddaphalaṃ ahaṃ;

Sappayogaṃ gahādīnaṃ, gaṇaṃ vakkhāmi me suṇa.

Now, having made clear the fruit of the word 'ādi' (etc.), I will explain the Gahādi group with its applications; listen to me.

Gaha upādāne. Upādānaṃ gahaṇaṃ, na kilesupādānaṃ. Upasaddo hettha na kiñci atthavisesaṃ vadati. Atha vā kāyena cittena vā upagantvā ādānaṃ gahaṇaṃ upādānanti samīpattho upasaddo. Katthaci hi upasaddo ādānasaddasahito daḷhaggahaṇe vattati “kāmupādāna”ntiādīsu. Idha pana daḷhaggahaṇaṃ vā hotu sithilaggahaṇaṃ vā, yaṃ kiñci gahaṇaṃ upādānameva, tasmā gahadhātu gahaṇe vattatīti attho gahetabbo. Gheppati, gaṇhāti vā. Pariggaṇhāti, paṭiggaṇhāti, adhigaṇhāti, paggaṇhāti, niggaṇhāti. Padhānagaṇhanako. Gaṇhituṃ, uggaṇhituṃ. Gaṇhitvā, uggaṇhitvā. Aññathāpi rūpāni bhavanti. Ahaṃ jāliṃ gahessāmi. Gahetuṃ. Gahetvā. Uggāhako, saṅgāhako, ajjhogāḷho. Kārite “gaṇhāpeti, gaṇhāpayati, aññataraṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhāpenti, saddhiṃ amaccasahassena gaṇhāpetvā. Upajjhaṃ gāhāpetabbo. Upajjhaṃ gāhāpetvā[M 0.0258]. Gāheti, gāhayati, gāhāpessati. Gāhāpayanti sabbhāvaṃ. Gāhako, gāhetvā” iccādīni. Kammani – gayhati, saṅgayhati, gaṇhiyati vā. Tathā hi “gaṇhiyanti uggaṇhiyantī”ti niddesapāḷi dissati. “Gehaṃ, gāho, pariggaho, saṅgāhako, saṅgahetā” iccādīni yojetabbāni.

The root gah is in the sense of grasping (upādāna). Upādāna is grasping, not the clinging that is defilement. Here, the prefix upa does not convey any special meaning. Alternatively, approaching and taking hold with body or mind is upādāna; thus, the prefix upa has the sense of proximity. In some cases, the prefix upa combined with the word ādāna (taking) functions in the sense of firm grasping, as in kāmupādāna (clinging to sensual pleasures) and so forth. Here, however, whether the grasping is firm or loose, any act of grasping is simply upādāna; therefore, the meaning to be understood is that the root gah functions in the sense of grasping. Gheppati (it is grasped), or gaṇhāti (one grasps). Pariggaṇhāti (he seizes), paṭiggaṇhāti (he receives), adhigaṇhāti (he attains), paggaṇhāti (he lifts), niggaṇhāti (he subdues). Padhānagaṇhanako (one who is intent on grasping). Gaṇhituṃ (to grasp), uggaṇhituṃ (to take up). Gaṇhitvā (having grasped), uggaṇhitvā (having taken up). There are also other forms: 'I will take the net' (Ahaṃ jāliṃ gahessāmi). Gahetuṃ (to take). Gahetvā (having taken). Uggāhako (one who learns), saṅgāhako (one who collects), ajjhogāḷho (one who is immersed). In the causative: gaṇhāpeti, gaṇhāpayati (he causes to take); 'they cause one to learn a certain foundation of mindfulness' (aññataraṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhāpenti); 'having caused to be taken along with a thousand ministers' (saddhiṃ amaccasahassena gaṇhāpetvā). 'A preceptor should be caused to be taken' (Upajjhaṃ gāhāpetabbo). 'Having caused a preceptor to be taken' (Upajjhaṃ gāhāpetvā). Gāheti, gāhayati (he causes to take); gāhāpessati (he will cause to take). 'They cause the true nature to be grasped' (Gāhāpayanti sabbhāvaṃ). Gāhako (one who causes to take), gāhetvā (having caused to take), and so on. In the passive: gayhati, saṅgayhati (it is grasped), or gaṇhiyati. For thus the text of the Niddesa is seen: 'gaṇhiyanti uggaṇhiyantī' (they are grasped, they are learned). Forms such as gehaṃ (house), gāho (seizure), pariggaho (possession), saṅgāhako (one who collects), saṅgahetā (a collector) should be connected.

Tatra akārānantaratyantapadānaṃ “gheppati, gheppanti. Gheppasī”ti ca “gaṇhati, gaṇhanti. Gaṇhasī”ti ca ādinā nayena sabbāsu vibhattīsu sabbathā padamālā yojetabbā. Ākārekārānantaratyantapadānaṃ “gaṇhāti gaṇhāpetī”tiādinā yathāsambhavaṃ padamālā yojetabbā vajjetabbaṭṭhānaṃ vajjetvā.

Therein, for verbal forms ending in '-ti' preceded by the vowel 'a', the paradigm should be constructed in all inflections and in every way according to the method beginning with gheppati, gheppanti, gheppasi and gaṇhati, gaṇhanti, gaṇhasi. For verbal forms ending in '-ti' preceded by the vowels 'ā' or 'e', the paradigm should be constructed as far as possible, beginning with gaṇhāti, gaṇhāpeti, and so on, avoiding the places that should be avoided.

Imāni pana pasiddhāni kānici ajjatanīrūpāni “aggahī mattikāpattaṃ. Aggahuṃ, aggahiṃsu, aggahesu”nti. Bhavissantīādīsu gahessati, gahessanti. Sesaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ kātabbaṃ. Aggahissā, aggahissaṃsu. Sesaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ kātabbaṃ.

However, these are some well-known aorist forms: 'he took the clay bowl' (aggahī mattikāpattaṃ). Aggahuṃ, aggahiṃsu, aggahesu (they took). In the future tense and so on: gahessati (he will take), gahessanti (they will take). The rest should be completed. In the conditional: aggahissā (he would have taken), aggahissaṃsu (they would have taken). The rest should be completed.

Usa dāhe. Dāho uṇhaṃ. Usati dahatīti uṇhaṃ. Uṇhasaddo “uṇhaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjatī”tiādīsu dabbamapekkhati, “sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanatī”tiādīsu pana guṇaṃ uṇhabhāvassa icchitattā. Uṇhabhāvo hi sītabhāvo ca guṇo.

The root us is in the sense of burning. Burning is heat. Because it burns (usati) and consumes (dahati), it is called uṇha (hot/heat). The word uṇha refers to a substance in phrases like 'he eats hot food,' but in phrases like 'it repels cold and heat,' it denotes a quality, because the state of being hot is intended. Indeed, the state of being hot and the state of being cold are qualities.

Tasa vipāsāyaṃ. Taṇhā. Kenaṭṭhena taṇhā? Tassati paritassatīti atthena.

The root tas is in the sense of thirsting. Craving. In what sense is it craving? In the sense that one thirsts (tassati), one is parched (paritassati).

Jusi pītisevanesu. Juṇho samayo. Kāḷe vā yadi vā juṇhe, yadā vāyati māluto.

The root jus is in the sense of delighting and enjoying. The bright season. 'Whether in the dark or in the bright, whenever the wind blows.'

Tattha juṇhoti joseti lokassa pītiṃsomanassañca uppādetīti juṇho.

Therein, it is called juṇha because it delights (juṇhoti), pleases (joseti), and generates joy and gladness for the world.

Juta [M 0.0259] dittiyaṃ. Juṇhā ratti. Jotati sayaṃ nippabhāpi samānā candatārakappabhāsenapi dibbati virocati sappabhā hotīti juṇhā.

The root jut is in the sense of shining. A bright night. It is called juṇhā because it shines (jotati); though being itself without radiance, with the light of the moon and stars it shines forth (dibbati), radiates (virocati), and becomes luminous.

Sā tanukaraṇe. Saṇhavācā. Siyati tanukariyati, na pharusabhāvena kakkasā kariyatīti saṇhā.

The root sā is in the sense of making subtle. Gentle speech. It is called saṇhā because it is made subtle (siyati), made thin (tanukariyati); it is not made harsh or coarse by a rough nature.

So antakammani. Saṇhaṃ, ñāṇaṃ. Siyati sayaṃ sukhumabhāvena atisukhumampi atthaṃ antaṃ karoti nipphattiṃ pāpetīti saṇhaṃ.

The root so is in the sense of ending. Subtle knowledge. It is called saṇhaṃ because it brings to an end (siyati); by its own subtle nature, it brings even the most subtle meaning to a conclusion, leading it to completion.

Tija nisāne. Nisānaṃ tikkhatā. Tiṇho parasu. Titikkhatīti tiṇho.

The root tij is in the sense of sharpening. Sharpening is keenness. A sharp axe. Because it is keen (titikkhati), it is tiṇho.

Si sevāyaṃ. Attano hitamāsīsantehi seviyateti sippaṃ, yaṃ kiñci jīvitahetu sikkhitabbaṃ sippāyatanaṃ. Apica sippanti aṭṭhārasa mahāsippāni – suti sūramati byākaraṇaṃ chandoviciti nirutti jotisatthaṃ sikkhā mokkhañāṇaṃ kriyāvidhi dhanubbedo hatthisikkhā kāmatantaṃ assalakkhaṇaṃ purāṇaṃ itihāso nīti takko vejjakañcāti.

The root si is in the sense of serving. That which is practiced by those who desire their own welfare is sippa (skill); whatever is to be learned for the sake of livelihood is a basis of skill. Moreover, sippa refers to the eighteen great skills: listening, heroism, grammar, prosody, etymology, astrology, training, knowledge of liberation, ritual procedures, archery, elephant-training, the art of love, horse-lore, ancient lore, history, policy, logic, and medicine.

Ku kucchāyaṃ. Kucchā garahā. Kaṇhā dhammā. Kaṇho puriso.

The root ku is in the sense of reviling. Reviling is blame. Dark qualities. A dark person.

Tattha kaṇhāti apabhassarabhāvakaraṇattā paṇḍitehi kucchitabbā garahitabbāti kaṇhā, akusaladhammā. Kāḷavaṇṇattā suvaṇṇavaṇṇādikaṃ upanidhāya kucchitabbo ninditabboti kaṇho, kāḷavaṇṇo. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Therein, kaṇhā (dark qualities) are so called because, by causing a state of non-luminosity, they are to be reviled and censured by the wise; these are unwholesome states. Due to his black color, being reviled and censured in comparison to golden or other colors, he is kaṇho (dark), black-colored. And this has also been said:

“Kaṇho vatāyaṃ puriso, kaṇhaṃ bhuñjati bhojanaṃ;

Kaṇhe bhūmippadesasmiṃ, na mayhaṃ manaso piyo”ti ca,

“Dark, indeed, is this person, dark is the food he eats; in a dark region of the earth, he is not dear to my mind,” and,

“Na [M 0.0260] kaṇho tacasā hoti,

Antosāro hi brāhmaṇo;

Yasmiṃ pāpāni kammāni,

Sa ve kaṇho sujampatī”ti ca.

“One is not dark because of one's skin; a brahmin has substance within. He in whom there are evil deeds, he, indeed, is dark, O Sujampati.”

Iccevaṃ –

Thus indeed.

Gahādike dhātugaṇe, sandhāya tasiādayo;

Ādiggaho kato ppaṇhā, gahādīsu yathārahaṃ.

In the group of roots beginning with gah, referring to tas and so forth, the initial inclusion is made with ppa and ṇhā, as is appropriate in the gahādi group.

Gahato dhātuto hi ppo,ākhyātattevadissati;

Ākhyātatte ca nāmatte, ṇhāsaddo usato tathā.

Indeed, from the root gah, the suffix ppa is seen only in verbal forms; and in verbal forms and nominal forms, the suffix ṇhā is likewise seen from the root us.

Usagahehi aññasmā, nāmatteva duve matā;

Evaṃ visesato ñeyyo, gahādigaṇanicchayo.

From roots other than us and gah, the two suffixes are considered to be only in nominal forms. Thus, the determination of the gahādi group should be especially understood.

Ettha pana kiñcāpi sāsane “taṇhāyatī”ti kriyāpadampi dissati, tathāpi tassa “pabbatāyati, mettāyatī”tiādīni viya nāmasmā vihitassa āyapaccayassa vasena siddhattā kriyāpadattepi ṇhāpaccayo mukhyato labbhatīti na sakkā vattuṃ. “Taṇhāyatī”ti hi idaṃ ṇhāpaccayavatā tasadhātuto nipphannataṇhāsaddasmā parassa āyapaccayassa vasena nipphannaṃ. Tathā kiñcāpi rūpiyasaṃvohārasikkhāpadavaṇṇanāyaṃ “vāsiphalaṃ tāpetvā udakaṃ vā khīraṃ vā uṇhāpetī”ti imasmiṃ padese “uṇhāpetī”ti hetukattuvācakaṃ kriyāpadaṃ dissati, tathāpi tassa ṇhāpaccayavatā usadhātuto nipphannauṇhāsaddato vihitassa kāritasaññassa ṇāpepaccayassa vasena nipphannattā kriyāpadattepi ṇhāpaccayo mukhyato labbhatīti na sakkā vattuṃ. “Uṇhāpetī”ti idaṃ vuttappakārauṇhāsaddato ṇāpepaccayavasena nipphannaṃ, etasmiṃ diṭṭhe “uṇhāpayatī”ti padampi diṭṭhameva hoti.

Here, although the verb form taṇhāyati is also seen in the Dispensation, nevertheless, because it is formed by means of the suffix āya prescribed after a noun, like pabbatāyati (he acts like a mountain), mettāyati (he acts with loving-kindness), etc., it cannot be said that the suffix ṇhā is primarily obtained even in the verb form. For this taṇhāyati is formed by means of the suffix āya which is after the word taṇhā, which is itself formed from the root tas with the suffix ṇhā. Similarly, although in the commentary on the training rule regarding transactions in silver, in this passage, 'having heated an adze-blade, he heats water or milk,' the causative verb uṇhāpeti is seen, nevertheless, because it is formed by means of the suffix ṇāpe, which has the designation 'causative', prescribed after the word uṇha, which is itself formed from the root us with the suffix ṇhā, it cannot be said that the suffix ṇhā is primarily obtained even in the verb form. This uṇhāpeti is formed by means of the suffix ṇāpe from the word uṇha of the aforementioned type; when this is seen, the form uṇhāpayati is also seen as well.
