Kiñca [M 0.0261] bhiyyo vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “uṇhāpetī”ti kāritapadassa diṭṭhattāyeva “uṇhatī”ti kattupadampi nayato diṭṭhameva hoti kattukāritapadānaṃ ekadhātumhi upalabbhamānattā, yathā? Gaṇhati, gaṇhāpeti, gacchati, gacchāpetīti, tasmā “usa dāhe”ti dhātussa “uṇhatī”ti rūpaṃ upalabbhatīti mantvā “uṇhatīti uṇha”nti nibbacanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Iti ppapaccayo gahato ca aññato ca ekadhā labbhati, ṇhāpaccayo pana gahato usato ca dvidhā aññato ekadhā labbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñcāpettha evaṃ niyamo vutto, tathāpi sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane aññānipi ekekassa dhātussa nāmikapadāni dve dve kriyāpadāni vicinitabbāni. Yena pana buddhavacanānurūpena nayena gahādigaṇe ādisaddena tasadhātādayo amhehi gahitā, imasmā nayā añño nayo pasatthataro natthi, ayameva pasatthataro, tasmā ayaṃ nīti sāsanaṭṭhitiyā āyasmantehi sādhukaṃ dhāretabbā vācetabbā ca.

Moreover, since the causative form uṇhāpeti is seen in the Vinaya commentary, the active form uṇhati is also seen by implication, as active and causative forms are found for a single root. For example: gaṇhati (he takes), gaṇhāpeti (he causes to take); gacchati (he goes), gacchāpeti (he causes to go). Therefore, considering that the form uṇhati is found from the root us in the sense of 'burning', the etymological explanation 'uṇha is that which burns' should be made. Thus, it should be understood that the suffix ppa is obtained in one way from gah and from another, while the suffix ṇhā is obtained in two ways from gah and us, and in one way from another. Although such a rule is stated here, nevertheless, in the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries, other nominal forms and two verbal forms for each single root should be investigated. However, by the method consistent with the word of the Buddha, we have included roots like tas and so forth in the gahādi group by the word ādi. There is no method more excellent than this; this indeed is the most excellent. Therefore, this principle should be well preserved and taught by the venerable ones for the stability of the Dispensation.

Gahādī ettakā diṭṭhā, dhātavo me yathābalaṃ;

Suttesvaññepi pekkhitvā, gaṇhavho atthayuttito.

These many gahādi roots have been seen by me according to my ability. Having also looked for others in the suttas, you should grasp them according to their appropriate meaning.

Gahādigaṇoyaṃ.

This is the Gahādi group.

Tanādigaṇika

The Tanādi Group

Tanu vitthāre. Tanoti. Āyatanaṃ, tanu. Kammani “taniyyati, taniyyanti. Vitaniyyatī”ti rūpāni. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “yathā hi āsabhaṃ cammaṃ, pathabyā vitaniyyatī”ti. Garū pana “patāyate, pataññatī”ti rūpāni vadanti. Tanituṃ, tanitvāna. Tumantādirūpāni.

The root tanu is in the sense of 'spreading.' It forms tanoti. Āyatana and tanu are derived from it. In the passive voice, the forms are taniyyati, taniyyanti, vitaniyyatī. Here is a Pāli text: 'Just as a bull's hide is stretched out on the earth.' But some teachers say the forms are patāyate, pataññatī. Tanituṃ and tanitvāna are forms beginning with the infinitive.

Tattha [M 0.0262] āyatananti āyabhūte dhamme tanoti vitthāretīti āyatanaṃ. Tanūti sarīraṃ. Tañhi kalalato paṭṭhāya kammādīhi yathāsambhavaṃ taniyyati vitthāriyati mahattaṃ pāpiyatīti “tanū”ti vuccati. “Tanu vapu sarīraṃ puṃ kāyo deho”tiādayo sarīravācakā saddā. Sarīraṃ khandhapañcakaṃ. Yañhi mahājano sarīranti vadati, taṃ paramatthato khandhapañcakamattameva, na tato attā vā attaniyaṃ vā upalabbhati. “Kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ tanuttakaraṃ sakadāgāmimaggacitta”ntiādīsu pana tanusaddo appatthavācako, appatthavācakassa ca tassa kriyāpadaṃ na passāma, tasmā nipātapadena tena bhavitabbaṃ. Tanusaddo nipātapadanti vuttaṭṭhānampi na passāma, nicchayena pana anipphannapāṭipadikoti gahetabbo.

Therein, āyatana is so called because it spreads out (tanoti, vitthāreti) the phenomena (dhamme) that are the basis of influx (āyabhūte). Tanu means the body. For, beginning from the embryo stage, it is stretched (taniyyati), expanded (vitthāriyati), and brought to greatness by kamma and other factors as may be—thus it is called tanu. Words such as tanu, vapu, sarīra, puṃ, kāya, and deha are words denoting the body. The body is the five aggregates. For what ordinary people call the body is, in the ultimate sense, merely the five aggregates; beyond that, neither a self (attā) nor anything belonging to a self (attaniyaṃ) is found. However, in phrases like 'the once-returner path-consciousness that makes sensual lust and ill will thin (tanuttakaraṃ)', the word tanu denotes 'smallness'. But we do not find a verb for it when it denotes 'smallness'; therefore, it must be a particle. We do not see a place where it is stated that the word tanu is a particle, but it should definitely be taken as an underived nominal stem.

Tanoti, tanonti. Tanosi, tanotha. Tanomi, tanoma. Tanute, tanunte. Tanuse, tanuse, tanuvhe. Tane, tanumhe. Sesaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

He stretches, they stretch. You stretch, you (pl.) stretch. I stretch, we stretch. He stretches (for himself), they stretch (for themselves). You (sg.) stretch, you (sg.) stretch, you (pl.) stretch. I stretch (for myself), we stretch (for ourselves). The rest should be elaborated as is possible.

Tanotu, tanontu. Taneyya, tane, taneyyuṃ. Vitana, vitanu. Atanā, atanu. Ammāya patanu kesā. Atani, ataniṃsu. Tanissati, tanissanti. Atanissā, atanissaṃsu. Kammani “taniyyati, taniyyanti. Taniyyasī”tiādinā vitthāretabbaṃ.

Let him stretch, let them stretch. He might stretch, he might stretch (for himself), they might stretch. Spread out, spread out (pl.). He stretched (for himself), they stretched (for themselves). 'Mother, let the hair be spread out.' He stretched, they stretched. He will stretch, they will stretch. He would have stretched, they would have stretched. In the passive voice, it should be elaborated with 'it is stretched,' 'they are stretched,' 'you are stretched,' and so on.

Saka sattiyaṃ. Satti samatthabhāvo. Sakkoti sakko. Viññāpetuṃ asakkhi. Sakkhissasi. Sakkhati. Tvampi amma pabbajituṃ sakkhissasi. Sakkate jarāya paṭikammaṃ kātunti pāḷi.

The root saka is in the sense of 'power.' Power (satti) is capability (samatthabhāva). He is able (sakkoti); he is capable (sakko). He was unable to inform. You will be able. He is able. 'You too, mother, will be able to go forth.' The Pāli text is: 'Is it possible to make a remedy for old age?'

Tattha [M 0.0263] sakkoti devarājā. So hi atthānaṃ sahassampi muhuttena cintanasamatthatāya saparahitaṃ kātuṃ sakkotīti “sakko”ti vuccati. Aññatra pana dhātūnaṃ avisaye taddhitavasena sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ adāsīti sakkoti evampi atthaṃ gahetvā sakkasaddo niruttinayena sādhetabbo. Vuttañhi bhagavatā “sakko mahāli devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ adāsi, tasmā ‘sakko’ti vuccatī”ti. Sakkonto. Sakkontī. Sakkontaṃ kulaṃ.

Therein, Sakko is the king of the gods. For he is called Sakko because, due to his ability to consider even a thousand matters in a moment, he is able (sakkoti) to act for his own and others' welfare. Elsewhere, however, outside the domain of roots, by way of a secondary derivative, taking the meaning thus, 'he gave a gift respectfully' (sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ adāsi), the word Sakko should be derived by etymological method. For it was said by the Blessed One: 'Sakka, Mahāli, the lord of the gods, having been a human being in a former existence, gave gifts respectfully; therefore he is called Sakko.' Being able (masc.), being able (fem.), a capable family (neut.).

Khuṇu khiṇu hiṃsāyaṃ. Khuṇoti. Khiṇoti.

The roots khuṇu and khiṇu are in the sense of 'harming.' They form khuṇoti and khiṇoti.

Iṇu gatiyaṃ. Iṇoti. Iṇaṃ iṇāyiko.

The root iṇu is in the sense of 'going.' It forms iṇoti. Iṇa (debt) and iṇāyika (debtor) are derived from it.

Tiṇu adane. Tiṇoti. Tiṇaṃ. Ettha tiṇanti yavasaṃ. Tañhi tiṇiyate tiṇabhakkhehi goṇādīhi adiyate khādiyateti tiṇaṃ.

The root tiṇu is in the sense of 'eating.' It forms tiṇoti. Tiṇa (grass) is derived from it. Here, tiṇa means fodder. For it is called tiṇa because it is eaten (tiṇiyate), consumed (adiyate, khādiyate) by grass-eating creatures such as cattle.

Ghiṇu dittiyaṃ. Ghiṇoti.

The root ghiṇu is in the sense of 'shining.' It forms ghiṇoti.

Hanu apanayane. Apanayanaṃ anālāpakaraṇaṃ nibbacanatākaraṇaṃ. Hanoti. Hanute.

The root hanu is in the sense of 'removing.' Removal (apanayana) is the act of not mentioning (anālāpakaraṇa) or the act of making something disappear (vivassanatākaraṇa). It forms hanoti and hanute.

Panu dāne panoti. Panute.

The root panu is in the sense of 'giving.' It forms panoti and panute.

Manu bodhane. Manoti. Manute. Mano. Manaṃ. Mānasaṃ. Manusso. Mānavo. Māṇavo.

The root manu is in the sense of 'understanding.' It forms manoti and manute. Derived from this are mano (mind), mana (mind), mānasa (mental), manussa (human being), mānava (man), and māṇava (youth).

Ettha manoti manute bujjhatīti mano, evaṃ manaṃ. Imesaṃ pana dvinnaṃ manasaddānaṃ “yasmiṃ mano nivisati. Santaṃ tassa manaṃ hotī”tiādīsu punnapuṃsakaliṅgatā daṭṭhabbā. Mānasanti rāgopi cittampi arahattampi. “Antalikkhacaro pāso, yvāyaṃ [M 0.0264] carati mānaso”ti ettha hi rāgo mānasaṃ. “Cittaṃ mano mānasa”nti ettha cittaṃ. “Appattamānaso sekkho, kālaṃ kayirā jane suto”ti ettha arahattaṃ. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Herein, mano is so called because one knows (manute, bujjhati); likewise mana. For these two words for mind, their masculine and neuter genders should be seen in phrases such as 'in which the mind (mano) settles' and 'peaceful is his mind (manaṃ).' Mānasa can mean lust, mind, or Arahantship. For in 'the snare that moves in the sky, that which moves mentally (mānaso)', here mānasa is lust. In 'cittaṃ mano mānasaṃ', here mānasa means mind (citta). In 'a learner whose goal has not been attained (appattamānaso) might die, so it is heard among people', here it means Arahantship. Regarding this, it is said:

Rāgo cittaṃ arahattañca, “mānasa”nti samīritaṃ;

Satthuno sāsane pāpa-sāsane’khilasāsane.

Lust, mind, and Arahantship are called 'mānasa' in the Teacher's Dispensation, in the evil dispensation, and in every dispensation.

Tattha sampayuttamanasi bhavoti rāgo mānaso. Mano eva mānasanti katvā cittaṃ mānasaṃ. Anavasesato mānaṃ siyati samucchindatīti aggamaggo mānasaṃ. Tannibbattattā pana arahattassa mānasatā daṭṭhabbā. Manūti satto. “Yena cakkhupasādena, rūpāni manu passatī”ti ettha hi “manū”ti satto vutto. Atha vā manūti paṭhamakappikakāle manussānaṃ mātāpibhuṭṭhāne ṭhito manunāmako puriso, yo sāsane “mahāsammatarājā”ti vutto. So hi sakalalokassa hitaṃ kātuṃ manute jānātīti “manū”ti vuccati. Yathābalaṃ attano hitaṃ manute jānātīti manusso, manassa vā ussannattā manusso. Atha vā vuttappakārassa manuno apaccaṃ manusso. Evaṃ mānavo māṇavo ca, nakārassa hi ṇakāre kate “māṇavo”ti rūpaṃ sijjhati. Keci panāhu “dantajanakārasahito mānavasaddo sabbasattasādhāraṇavacano, muddhajaṇakārasahito pana māṇavasaddo kucchitamūḷhāpaccavacano”ti, taṃ vīmaṃsitvā yuttañce, gahetabbaṃ, na panettha vattabbaṃ “māṇavasaddassa atthuddhāravacane idaṃ vacanaṃ virujjhatī”ti antarasaddassa atthuddhāre antaraantarikāsaddānampi āharaṇassa dassanato.

Here, lust is mānasa because it is present in the mind (sampayuttamanasi bhava). Taking the mind itself as mānasa, citta is mānasa. Because it utterly destroys conceit (māna), the supreme path (aggamagga) is mānasa. However, due to its arising therefrom, the state of an Arahant should be seen as mānasatā. Manū refers to a being. For in 'By which visual sensitivity, the being sees forms,' here manū indeed refers to a being. Alternatively, manū refers to a man named Manu, who stood in the place of mother and father of humans in the first cosmic age, who is called 'Mahāsammatarājā' in the Dispensation. For he intends (manute), that is, knows, how to benefit the whole world; thus he is called manū. A human (manussa) is so called because he intends (manute), that is, knows, his own benefit according to his strength, or because his mind is pre-eminent (ussannattā). Alternatively, a human is the descendant of that aforementioned Manu. Thus, mānava and māṇava are derived; for when the dental 'n' is changed to a retroflex 'ṇ', the form māṇava is established. Some, however, say: 'The term mānava, with a dental 'n', is a term common to all beings, while māṇava, with a retroflex 'ṇ', is a term for a base, deluded offspring.' This should be examined, and if found valid, it should be accepted. But here, it should not be said that 'this statement contradicts the explanation of the meaning of the term māṇava,' for in explaining the meaning of the term antara, the citation of the terms antara and antarikā is also seen.

Tatra [M 0.0265] panāyaṃ vīmaṃsanā – cūḷakammavibhaṅgasuttasmiñhi “subho māṇavotodeyyaputto”ti imasmiṃ padese aṭṭhakathācariyehi “subhoti so kira dassanīyo ahosi pāsādiko, tenassa aṅgasubhatāya ‘subho’tveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. ‘Māṇavo’ti pana taṃ taruṇakāle vohariṃsu, so mahallakakālepi teneva vohārena vohariyatī”ti evaṃ muddhajaṇakārassa māṇavasaddassa attho pakāsito, taṭṭīkāyampi garūhi “yaṃ apaccaṃ kucchitaṃ muddhaṃ vā, tattha loke māṇavavohāro, yebhuyyena ca sattā daharakāle muddhadhātukā hontīti vuttaṃ ‘taruṇakāle vohariṃsū”ti, evaṃ muddhajaṇakārassa māṇavasaddassa attho pakāsito. Idāni māṇavasaddassa atthuddhāro bhavati, māṇavoti sattopi coropi taruṇopi vuccati. “Coditā devadūtehi, ye pamajjanti māṇavā”tiādīsu hi satto “māṇavo”ti vutto. “Māṇavehi saha gacchanti katakammehipi akatakammehipī”tiādīsu coro. “Ambaṭṭho māṇavo”tiādīsu taruṇo “māṇavo”ti vutto.

Here, this examination is as follows: In the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta, concerning the passage 'Subha the māṇava, son of Todeyya,' the commentary teachers explain thus: 'Subha' means that he was attractive and pleasing to behold; therefore, due to the beauty of his body, they gave him the name 'Subha.' Māṇava, however, was used to refer to him in his youth, and even in old age he was still referred to by that term. Thus, the meaning of the word māṇava, with a retroflex 'ṇ', is explained. In the ṭīkā (subcommentary) also, the teachers state: 'Wherever there is an offspring that is base (kucchita) or deluded (muddha), in the world the term māṇava is used; and generally, beings in their youth are of a deluded nature, hence it is said, 'they called him that in his youth.' Thus, the meaning of the word māṇava, with a retroflex 'ṇ', is explained. Now, an exposition of the meaning of the word māṇava follows: māṇava can refer to a being, a thief, or a youth. For instance, in passages like 'Reproved by the divine messengers, those beings (māṇavā) who are heedless,' a being is called māṇava. In phrases like 'They go with thieves (māṇavehi), whether their deeds are done or undone,' a thief is referred to as māṇava. And in statements like 'Ambaṭṭha the māṇava,' a youth is called māṇava.

Appa pāpuṇe. Appoti. Āpo.

The root appa is in the sense of 'attaining.' It forms appoti (he attains). From this is derived āpo (water).

Ettha āpoti appoti taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ vissaratīti āpo.

Here, āpo (water) is so called because it attains (appoti) and spreads (vissarati) to various places.

Mā parimāṇe. Minoti. Upamā, upamānaṃ, vimānaṃ. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

The root mā is in the sense of 'measuring.' It forms minoti (he measures). From this are derived upamā (simile), upamāna (comparison), and vimāna (celestial mansion). Others should also be connected.

Ettha ca yā accantaṃ na minoti na vicchindati, sā mānassa samīpe vattatīti upamā yathā “goṇo viya gavajo”ti. Upamānanti [M 0.0266] upamā eva. Tathā hi “vītopamānamappamāṇamanāthanātha”nti. Ettha vītopamānanti imassa vītopamaṃ, nirupamanti attho. Atha vā upamānanti upametabbākāro “sīho viya bhagavā”ti. Ettha hi sīho upamā, bhagavā upameyyo tejoparakkamādīhi upametabbattā, tejoparakkamādayo upametabbākāro. Ettha pana sātisayattā kiñcāpi sīhassa tejādīhi bhagavato tejādiupametabbākāro natthi, tathāpi hīnūpamāvasena “sīho viya bhagavā”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vimānanti utusamuṭṭhānattepi kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānattā kammena visesato miniyati paricchindiyatīti vimānaṃ.

Here, that which does not measure (minoti) or sever (vicchindati) entirely, but exists near the measure (māna), is called a simile (upamā), as in 'like an ox, a gavaya.' Upamāna is indeed upamā. Thus, 'freed from comparison, immeasurable, a refuge for the refuge-less.' Here, 'freed from comparison' means this is without comparison, unequalled. Alternatively, upamāna refers to the aspect to be compared, as in 'the Blessed One is like a lion.' Here, the lion is the simile (upamā), the Blessed One is the subject of comparison (upameyyo) because he is to be compared in terms of splendor and energy, etc., and splendor, energy, etc., are the aspects to be compared. However, here, due to the Blessed One's superiority, although there is no aspect for comparing his splendor, etc., with that of a lion, still, it should be understood that 'the Blessed One is like a lion' is said by way of an inferior comparison. Vimāna is that which is specially measured or defined by kamma; for, although arising from the seasons, it arises from seasons that are conditioned by kamma.

Kara karaṇe. “Karoti, kayirati, kubbati, krubbati, pakaroti, upakaroti, apakaroti, paṭikaroti, nirākaroti, paṭisaṅkharoti, abhisaṅkharoti” iccevamādīni kattari bhavanti. Kamme pāḷinayavasena ikārāgamaṭṭhāne yakārassa dvebhāvo. Tasmiṃyevaṭhāne rayakārānaṃ vipariyāye sati na dvebhāvo. Tathā īkārāgamaṭṭhāne “kariyyati, kayirati, karīyati, kayyati, pakarīyati, pakariyyati, paṭisaṅkhariyyati, abhisaṅkhariyyati” iccevamādīni kammani bhavanti.

The root kara is in the sense of 'doing' or 'making.' Forms such as karoti (does), kayirati (does), kubbati (does), krubbati (does), pakaroti (accomplishes), upakaroti (assists), apakaroti (harms), paṭikaroti (counteracts), nirākaroti (rejects), paṭisaṅkharoti (repairs), abhisaṅkharoti (forms) occur in the active voice. In the passive voice, according to Pāli grammatical rules, where 'i' is added, the 'y' becomes doubled. In that same place, when 'r' and 'y' are interchanged, there is no doubling. Similarly, where 'ī' is added, forms such as kariyyati, kayirati, karīyati, kayyati, pakarīyati, pakariyyati, paṭisaṅkhariyyati, abhisaṅkhariyyati occur in the passive voice.

Ettha ca kayiratīti padaṃ dvīsu ṭhānesu dissati kattari kamme ca. Tesa kattuvasena “puriso kammaṃ kayiratī”ti yojetabbaṃ, kammavasena pana ayaṃ pāḷi “kuṭi me kayirati adesitavatthukā”ti. Tattha ca kattuvasena vuttaṃ kattupadaṃ yirapaccayena siddhaṃ. Kammavasena pana vuttaṃ kammapadaṃ ikārāgamassa ādiantabhūtānaṃ rayakārānaṃ vipariyāyenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Kāreti, kārayati, kārāpeti, kārāpayatī”ti cattāri kāritarūpāni, yāni “hetukatturūpānī”ti vuccanti taddīpakattā.

Here, the word 'kayirati' appears in two instances, in both the active and passive voices. Of these, in the active sense, it should be construed as 'a person does an action' (puriso kammaṃ kayiratī). But in the passive sense, this Pāli phrase is 'a hut is made for me without designated materials' (kuṭi me kayirati adesitavatthukā). There, the active word mentioned is formed with the suffix 'yira'. However, the passive word mentioned is to be understood as formed by the inversion of the letters 'r' and 'y', which are at the beginning and end of the 'i' augment. 'Kāreti, kārayati, kārāpeti, kārāpayatī'—these are the four causative forms, which are called 'forms of the causative agent' because they indicate that.

Idāni [M 0.0267] pana padamālā vattabbā, tatra paṭhamaṃ “kubbatī”ti padasseva padamālaṃ yojessāma sabbāsu vibhattīsu ekākārena yojetabbattā. “Karotī”ti okārānantaratyantapadassa pana “kāretī”ti ekārānantaratyantapadassa ca padamālaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ pacchā yojessāma ekākārena ayojetabbattā.

Now, however, the paradigms should be stated. Therein, first, we will present the paradigm of the word 'kubbatī' itself, because it is to be presented uniformly in all inflections. But the paradigms of the word 'karotī', a word ending in '-ti' preceded by 'o', and the word 'kāretī', a word ending in '-ti' preceded by 'e', we will present later as is suitable, since they are not to be presented uniformly.

Tatra kubbati, kubbanti. Kubbasi, kubbatha. Kubbāmi, kubbāma. Kubbate, kubbante. Kubbase, kubbavhe. Kubbe, kubbamhe. Vattamānāvasena vuttarūpāni.

Therein: kubbati, kubbanti; kubbasi, kubbatha; kubbāmi, kubbāma. Kubbate, kubbante; kubbase, kubbavhe; kubbe, kubbamhe. These are the forms stated according to the present tense.

Pañcamiyādīnaṃ vasena pana kubbatu, kubbantu. Kubbeyya, kubbeyyuṃ. Sesaṃ “bhavati, bhavantī”ti vuttanayānusārena sabbattha vitthāretabbaṃ.

And according to the imperative mood and so on: kubbatu, kubbantu. Kubbeyya, kubbeyyuṃ. The rest should be elaborated everywhere according to the manner stated for 'bhavati, bhavanti'.

“Kariyatī”tiādīnipi a kārānantaratyantapadāni evameva yojetabbāni. Ettha ca “kubbati, kubbanti. Kubbasī”tiādinā vuttā ayaṃ padamālā pāḷinayadassanato edisī vuttā. Saddasatthavidū pana sāsanikā saddasattheyeva ādaraṃ katvā “kubbati, kubbasī”ti evaṃpakārāni rūpāni pāḷiyaṃ natthīti maññantā na icchanti. Tehi saddasatthe viya pāḷiyampi “asanto nānukubbantī”tiādīsu okārapaccayassādesabhūto ukāro sareyeva pare vakāraṃ pappotīti maññamānā “kubbanti, kubbante”tiādīniyeva rūpāni icchanti, parasarassābhāvato “kubbati, kubbasī”tiādīni pāḷiyaṃ natthīti na icchanti. Mayaṃ pana pāḷinayadassanato tāni rūpāni icchāma. Atra sotārānaṃ kaṅkhāvinodanatthaṃ kiñci pāḷinayaṃ vadāma – “sīlavanto na kubbanti, bālo sīlāni kubbatī”ti ca, “kasmā bhavaṃ vijanamaraññanissito, tapo idha krubbatī”ti ca, “pharusāhi vācāhi pakrubbamāno”ti ca. Īdisesu pana ṭhānesu akārāgamo kātabbo[M 0.0268]. Acinteyyo hi pāḷinayo, yebhuyyena saddasatthanayavidūro ca. Tathā hi yathā “agginiṃ sampajjalitaṃ pavisantī”ti pāḷigatidassanato “aggini, agginī, agginayo. Agginiṃ, agginī, agginayo. Aggininā”ti padamālā kātabbā hoti, evameva “bālo sīlāni kubbatī”ti pāḷigatidassanato “kubbati, kubbanti. Kubbasī”ti padamālāpi yojetabbāva.

Words such as 'kariyatī' ending in 'tya' preceded by the vowel 'a' should be formed in this same way. Here, this paradigm stated with 'kubbati, kubbanti, kubbasī,' etc., is given as such according to the Pāli method. However, grammarians, though adherents of the teaching, have regard only for the science of grammar and, believing that such forms as 'kubbati, kubbasī' do not exist in Pāli, do not accept them. They think that in Pāli, just as in the science of grammar, in phrases such as 'asanto nānukubbantī,' the vowel 'u', being a substitute for the suffix 'o', becomes 'v' only when followed by a vowel. Thus, they prefer only forms like 'kubbanti, kubbante,' etc., and, due to the absence of a subsequent vowel, do not accept that 'kubbati, kubbasī,' etc., exist in Pāli. We, however, following the Pāli method, do accept those forms. Here, to dispel the doubts of the listeners, we cite some Pāli examples: 'sīlavanto na kubbanti, bālo sīlāni kubbatī,' and 'kasmā bhavaṃ vijanamaraññanissito, tapo idha krubbatī,' and 'pharusāhi vācāhi pakrubbamāno.' In such cases, the augment of the vowel 'a' should be made. For the Pāli method is indeed inconceivable and mostly far removed from the method of the science of grammar. Just as, according to the Pāli usage of 'agginiṃ sampajjalitaṃ pavisantī,' the paradigm 'aggini, agginī, agginayo; agginiṃ, agginī, agginayo; aggininā' should be formed, so too, according to the Pāli usage of 'bālo sīlāni kubbatī,' the paradigm 'kubbati, kubbanti, kubbasī' must also be formed.

Yathā ca “bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātavedā”ti pāḷigatidassanato “santo sabbhīhi saddhiṃ sataṃ dhammo na jaraṃ upetīti pavedayantī”ti aṭṭhakathāgatidassanato ca “sabbhi, sabbhī, sabbhayo. Sabbhiṃ, sabbhī, sabbhayo. Sabbhinā”ti padamālā yojetabbā hoti, evameva “bālo sīlāni kubbatī”ti pāḷigatidassanato “kubbati, kubbanti. Kubbasī”ti padamālāpi yojetabbāva. Tathā “krubbati, krubbanti. Krubbasī”tiādi sabbaṃ sabbattha yojetabbaṃ.

And just as, according to the Pāli usage in 'bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātavedā' and according to the commentary usage in 'santo sabbhīhi saddhiṃ sataṃ dhammo na jaraṃ upetīti pavedayantī,' the paradigm 'sabbhi, sabbhī, sabbhayo; sabbhiṃ, sabbhī, sabbhayo; sabbhinā' should be formed, even so, according to the Pāli usage in 'bālo sīlāni kubbatī,' the paradigm 'kubbati, kubbanti, kubbasī' must also be formed. Likewise, all such forms as 'krubbati, krubbanti, krubbasī,' etc., should be formed everywhere.

Idāni yathāpaṭiññātā padamālā anuppattā. Karoti, karonti. Karosi, karotha. Karomi, kummi, karoma, kumma. Kurute, kubbante. Kuruse, kuruvhe. Kare, karumhe. Vattamānāvasena vuttarūpāni.

Now the promised paradigm has arrived. Karoti, karonti; karosi, karotha; karomi, kummi, karoma, kumma. Kurute, kubbante; kuruse, kuruvhe; kare, karumhe. These are the forms stated by way of the present tense.

Karotu, kurutu, karontu. Karohi, karotha. Karomi, kummi, karoma, kumma. Kurutaṃ, kubbantaṃ. Karassu, kurussu, kuruvho. Kare, kubbāmase. Pañcamīvasena vuttarūpāni.

Karotu, kurutu, karontu; karohi, karotha; karomi, kummi, karoma, kumma. Kurutaṃ, kubbantaṃ; karassu, kurussu, kuruvho; kare, kubbāmase. These are the forms stated by way of the imperative mood.

Ettha pana koci vadeyya –

Here, however, someone might say:

“Na no vivāho nāgehi, katapubbo kudācanaṃ;

Taṃ vivāhaṃ asaṃyuttaṃ, kathaṃ amhe karomase”ti

“No marriage with Nāgas has ever been performed by us at any time. How shall we undertake that unsuitable marriage?”

Pāḷidassanato [M 0.0269] “karomase”ti padaṃ kasmā idha na vuttaṃ, nanu karadhātuto paraṃ okāraṃ paṭicca āmasevacanassāvayavabhūto ākāro lopaṃ pappotīti? Tanna, “karomase”ti ettha “āmase”ti vacanassa abhāvato mavacanassa sabbhāvato. Ettha hi sekāro āgamo, tasmā “karomā”ti vattamānāvacanavasena attho gahetabbo, na pana pañcamīvacanavasena. Evaṃbhūto ca sekāro katthaci nāmikapadato paro hoti “ye keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse. Yaṃ balaṃ ahuvamhase”tiādīsu. Katthaci panākhyātikapadato sādesanirādesavasena –

Based on the Pāli example, why is the word 'karomase' not mentioned here? Is it not that the vowel 'ā', which is a component of the 'āmase' ending, undergoes elision after the vowel 'o' following the root 'kar'? That is not so, because in 'karomase,' the ending 'āmase' is absent, and the ending 'ma' is present. For here, 'se' is an augment. Therefore, the meaning should be taken in the sense of the present tense form 'karomā,' not in the sense of the imperative mood. Such a 'se' augment is found elsewhere after nominal words, as in 'ye keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse' and 'yaṃ balaṃ ahuvamhase.' In other cases, it occurs after verbal words, either with or without substitution—

“Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ; Okkantāmasi bhūtāni;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase”ti

“We have done for you what was to be done; we have overcome beings; this has not been heard repeatedly, therefore we speak thus.”

Ādīsu.

And so on.

Kareyya, kareyyuṃ. Kareyyāsi, kareyyātha. Kareyyāmi, kareyyāma. Kubbetha, kubberaṃ. Kubbetho, kubbeyyavho. Kareyyaṃ, kare, kareyyāmhe. Sattamīvasena vuttarūpāni.

Kareyya, kareyyuṃ; kareyyāsi, kareyyātha; kareyyāmi, kareyyāma. Kubbetha, kubberaṃ; kubbetho, kubbeyyavho; kareyyaṃ, kare, kareyyāmhe. These are the forms stated by way of the optative mood.

Kara, karu. Kare, karittha. Karaṃ, karimha. Karittha, karire. Karittho, karivho. Kariṃ, karimhe. Parokkhāvasena vuttarūpāni.

Kara, karu; kare, karittha; karaṃ, karimha. Karittha, karire; karittho, karivho; kariṃ, karimhe. These are the forms stated by way of the perfect tense.

Ettha karāti puriso kammaṃ karīti paṭhamapurisayojanāya yojetabbaṃ. “Āguṃ kara mahārāja, akaraṃ kammadukkaṭa”nti etthāpi “mahārāja bhavaṃ āguṃ karī”ti paṭhamapurisayojanāya yojetabbaṃ. Evañhi sati ayaṃ payogo “maññe bhavaṃ patthayati, rañño bhariyaṃ patibbata”ntiādayo viya paṭhamapurisappayogo bhavati.

Here, 'kara' and 'kari' should be construed with a third-person construction, as in 'a person does an action'. In 'Āguṃ kara mahārāja, akaraṃ kammadukkaṭa' as well, it should be construed with a third-person construction as 'mahārāja bhavaṃ āguṃ karī' (Your Majesty, the king, committed a fault). For when this is so, this usage becomes a third-person usage, like 'maññe bhavaṃ patthayati, rañño bhariyaṃ patibbata,' and so on.

Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ [M 0.0270] pana majjhimapurisappayogo vutto “āguṃ karāti mahārāja tvaṃ mahāparādhaṃ mahāpāpaṃ kari. Dukkaṭanti yaṃ kataṃ dukkaṭaṃ hoti,taṃ lāmakaṃ kammaṃ akara”nti, tasmā jātakaṭṭhakathāvasenāpi kadāci karaiti ca karīti ca akaranti ca majjhimapurisappayogo bhavatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yebhuyyavasena pana “puriso kammaṃ kara, puriso kammaṃ kari, ahaṃ kammaṃ akara”nti paṭhamuttamapurisappayogo daṭṭhabbo. Ettha ca karaiti yathāvuttavibhattivasena, karīti ajjatanīvasena, akaranti hiyyattanīvasena vuttaṃ. Tattha “karittho”ti padaṃ “aññaṃ bhattāraṃ pariyesa, mā kisittho mayā vinā”ti ettha “kisittho”ti padena samaṃ parokkhāyattanopadamajjhimapurisekavacanavasena, ediso pana nayo aññatrāpi yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo.

In the Jātaka commentary, however, a second-person usage is stated: 'O great king, you have committed a fault, a great offense, a great evil. As for "wrongly done," what is done is wrongly done; that base deed you did.' Therefore, it should be understood that according to the Jātaka commentary, 'kara,' 'kari,' and 'akara' are sometimes found as second-person usages. Generally, however, 'puriso kammaṃ kara,' 'puriso kammaṃ kari,' and 'ahaṃ kammaṃ akara' should be understood as third and first-person usages. Here, 'kara' is stated according to the aforementioned inflection (the perfect), 'kari' in the aorist tense, and 'akara' in the imperfect tense. In this context, the word 'karittho' is comparable to the word 'kisittho' in the phrase 'Seek another husband; do not grieve without me,' in the sense of the second person singular of the perfect tense, middle voice. This same principle should be applied elsewhere as appropriate.

Akā, akarā, akara iti rassapāṭhopi. Akaru. Ettha “sabbārivijayaṃ akā”ti padaṃ nidassanaṃ. Akarāti puriso kammaṃ akāsīti atītakriyāvācako paṭhamapurisappayogo daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi “rajjassa kira so bhīto, akarā ālaye bahū”ti pāḷi dissati. “Mā metaṃ akarā kammaṃ, mā me udakamāharī”ti ettha pana santepi atītavācakapaṭṭhamapurisappayogabhāve māsaddayogato hiyyattanajjatanīvibhattiyo pañcamīvibhattiatthe anuttakālikā hutvā “tvaṃ mā karosi, mā āharasī”ti majjhimapurisappayogārahā bhavanti.

Akā, akarā; 'akara' is also a reading with a short vowel. Akaru. Here, the phrase 'sabbārivijayaṃ akā' is an example. 'Akarā,' meaning 'a person did an action' (akāsi), should be understood as a third-person usage indicating past action. Thus, the Pāli text is seen: 'Indeed, fearing for the kingdom, he made many dwellings.' In 'Mā metaṃ akarā kammaṃ, mā me udakamāharī' (Do not do this deed for me, do not bring me water), however, even though there is a third-person usage indicating past tense, due to the connection with the particle 'mā', the imperfect and aorist inflections become non-temporal in the sense of the imperative mood, and are thus suitable for second-person usage, as in 'tvaṃ mā karosi, mā āharasī' (you, do not do; you, do not bring).

Kiñca bhiyyo “jarādhammaṃ mā jīrīti alabbhaneyyaṃ ṭhāna”ntiādīsupi santepi atītavācakapaṭhamapurisappayogabhāve māsaddayogato ajjatanīvibhattipañcamīvibhattiatthe anuttakālikā hutvā “mā jīratū”tiādinā paṭhamapurisappayogārahā [M 0.0271] bhavanti. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā “jarādhammaṃ mā jīrīti yaṃ mayhaṃ jarāsabhāvaṃ, taṃ mā jīritu. Esa nayo sesesupī”ti. Yaṃ panamhehi “akara iti rassapāṭhopī”ti vuttaṃ, tassa “atikara’makarā’cariya, mayhampetaṃ na ruccatī”ti imāya pāḷiyā vasena atthitā veditabbā. Tassāyamattho “ācariya bhavaṃ atikkantakaraṇaṃ akarā”ti paṭhamapurisavasena gahetabbo. Apica “bhava”nti vattabbe atthe “tva”nti vacanaṃ vattabbamevāti adhippāyavasena “ācariya tvaṃ atikkantakaraṇaṃ karosī”ti yojanāpi kātabbāva.

What more? Even in phrases such as “It is impossible for what is subject to aging not to age” (jarādhammaṃ mā jīrīti alabbhaneyyaṃ ṭhāna), although there is the use of a past-tense verb in the third person, due to the connection with mā and the sense of the Aorist and Imperative moods, becoming timeless, they become suitable for third-person usage, as in “May it not age” (mā jīratu). Therefore, the commentary teachers said: “What is subject to aging, may it not age” (jarādhammaṃ mā jīrīti), meaning “may my nature of aging not age” (yaṃ mayhaṃ jarāsabhāvaṃ, taṃ mā jīritu). This is the method for the rest as well. But what we said, “akara, even with the short reading,” should be understood as existing based on this passage: “Teacher, you did an excessive deed; this does not please me either” (atikara’makarā’cariya, mayhampetaṃ na ruccatī). Its meaning is: “Teacher, you did an excessive deed” (ācariya bhavaṃ atikkantakaraṇaṃ akarā), to be taken in the third person. Moreover, where “bhavaṃ” (venerable sir) ought to be said, the word “tvaṃ” (you) is used, implying that it must be said. Thus, the construction “Teacher, you do an excessive deed” (ācariya tvaṃ atikkantakaraṇaṃ karosī) should also be made.

Akaro, akattha, akarotha. Akaraṃ, akaṃ, akaramha, akamha. Ettha “saṃvaḍḍhayitvā puḷinaṃ, akaṃ puḷinacetiya”nti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Akattha, akatthuṃ. Akuruse, akaravhaṃ. Akariṃ, akaraṃ, akaramhase. Hiyyattanīvasena vuttarūpāni.

He did, you (sg.) did, you (pl.) did. I did, I did, we did, we did. Here, the Pali example is given: “Having piled up the sand, I made a sand shrine” (saṃvaḍḍhayitvā puḷinaṃ, akaṃ puḷinacetiyaṃ). You (sg.) did, they did. You (sg.) did, you (pl.) did. I did, I did, we did. These forms are stated in the Aorist tense.

Ettha ca pañcavidho sekāro āharitvā dassetabbo. Tathā hi pañcavidho sekāro padāvayava apadāvayavaanekantapadāvayava sosaddattha ādesavasena. Tattha padāvayavo sekāro “tvaṃ kammaṃ kuruse, tvaṃ atthakusalo abhavase”tiādīsu daṭṭhabbo. Apadāvayavo pana “tasmā evaṃ vademase. Mūlā akusalā samūhatāse”tiādīsu daṭṭhabbo. Anekantapadāvayavo “arogā ca bhavāmase. Maṇiṃ tāta gaṇhāmase”ādīsu daṭṭhabbo. Ettha hi sekāro yadi pañcamīvibhattiyaṃ āmasevacanassāvayavo, tadā pañcamīvibhattiyuttānaṃ patthanāsīsanatthānaṃ “bhavāmase, gaṇhāmase”ti padānaṃ avayavo hoti. Yadi pana āgamo, pañcamīvibhattiyuttānaṃ patthanāsīsanatthānaṃ “bhavāma, gaṇhāmā”ti padānaṃ avayavo na hoti, evaṃ “bhavāmase”tiādīsu [M 0.0272] sekārassa anekantapadāvayavattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sosaddattho “esese eke ekaṭṭhe”ti ettha daṭṭhabbo. Eseseti imassa hi “esoso eko ekaṭṭho”ti attho. Ādeso “akaramhasa te kicca”nti ettha, “okkantāmasi bhūtānī”ti cettha daṭṭhabbo ekārassa akārikārādesakaraṇavasena. Tattha “akaramhasa te kicca”nti imassa “akaramhase te kicca”nti attho. “Akaramhase”ti cettha sace sekāro āgamo, tadā “karamhā”ti padaṃ hiyyattanīparassapade uttamapurisabahuvacanantaṃ. Sace pana mhasevacanassāvayavo, tadā “akaramhase”ti padaṃ hiyyattanīattanopade uttamapurisabahuvacanantaṃ. Evaṃ pañcavidho sekāro bhavatīti avagantabbaṃ.

Here, the fivefold nature of the sound 'sa' should be explained by bringing examples. That is, the fivefold nature of 'sa' is: as a part of a word (padāvayava), as not a part of a word (apadāvayava), as an indefinite part of a word (anekantapadāvayava), in the sense of the word 'so' (sosaddattha), and as a substitute (ādesavasena). Among these, the 'sa' as a part of a word is seen in phrases like “you do the deed” (tvaṃ kammaṃ kuruse), “you were skilled in meaning” (tvaṃ atthakusalo abhavase), etc. The 'sa' not a part of a word is seen in phrases like “therefore we speak thus” (tasmā evaṃ vademase), “the roots of unwholesomeness have been uprooted” (Mūlā akusalā samūhatāse), etc. The 'sa' as an indefinite part of a word is seen in phrases like “may we be free from illness” (arogā ca bhavāmase), “father, let us take the jewel” (Maṇiṃ tāta gaṇhāmase), etc. Here, if the 'sa' is considered a part of the imperative ending `āmase`, then in expressions like “may we be” (bhavāmase) and “let us take” (gaṇhāmase), it forms part of the word. But if it is considered an augment, then in the same expressions, it does not form part of the word. Thus, in phrases like “may we be,” etc., the 'sa' should be understood as having an indefinite word-part status. The 'sa' in the sense of the word 'so' is seen in “esese eke ekaṭṭhe”. For the meaning of “esese” is “esoso eko ekaṭṭho” (this one, that one, is one, with one meaning). The substitution is seen in phrases like “we have done your duty” (akaramhasa te kiccaṃ), and “we have entered among beings” (okkantāmasi bhūtānī), by means of the substitution of 'a' and 'i' for 'e'. In the phrase “we have done your duty,” the meaning is “we have done your duty.” Here, if the 'sa' is considered an augment, then the word “karamhā” is a verb in the Aorist, active voice, first person plural. But if it is considered part of the ending `mhase`, then the word “akaramhase” is a verb in the Aorist, middle voice, first person plural. Thus, the fivefold nature of the sound 'sa' should be understood.

Akari, kari, akāsi, akaruṃ, akariṃsu, akaṃsu, akaṃsuṃ. Akaro, akarittha, akāsittha.

He did, he did, he did, they did, they did, they did, they did. You (sg.) did, you (sg.) did, you (sg.) did.

Ettha ca akaroti tvaṃ akaroti yojetabbaṃ. “Akaro” iti hi padaṃ “varañce me ado sakkā”ti ettha majjhimapurisekavacanatthaṃ “ado”ti padamiva daṭṭhabbaṃ pāḷiyaṃ avijjamānattepi nayavasena gahetabbattā. Garū pana “akaro”ti vuttaṭṭhāne “akāsī”ti majjhimapurisavacanaṃ icchanti. Tādisañhi padaṃ yebhuyyena paṭhamapurisavacanameva hoti. Tathā hi “adāsi me, akāsi me”ti paṭhamapurisapāḷiyo bahū sandissanti. “Mākāsi mukhasā pāpaṃ, mā kho sūkaramukho ahū”tiādīsu pana māsaddayogato “tvaṃ pāpaṃ mā akāsi, mā sūkaramukho ahosī”ti padayojanā kātabbā hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, 'akaro' should be construed as 'tvaṃ akaro' (you did). For the word 'akaro,' in the phrase “if you would grant me a boon, Sakka” (varañce me ado sakkā), it should be seen as equivalent to the word 'ado' (you granted) in the sense of the second person singular, even though such a word is not found in the Pali texts, because it must be taken by way of reasoning. However, the teachers prefer the second person singular form 'akāsī' in places where 'akaro' is used. For such a word is mostly in the third person singular. Thus, many Pali passages like “he gave to me, he did for me” (adāsi me, akāsi me) refer to the third person. But in phrases like “Do not commit evil by mouth, do not be pig-faced” (mākāsi mukhasā pāpaṃ, mā kho sūkaramukho ahū), due to the association with mā, the sentence construction should be understood as “you should not commit evil by mouth, you should not be pig-faced” (tvaṃ pāpaṃ mā akāsi, mā sūkaramukho ahosī).

Akariṃ[M 0.0273], kariṃ, akāsiṃ, akarimha, karimha, akāsimha. Akarā, akarū. Akaruse, akarivhaṃ. Akaraṃ, akarimhe. Ajjatanīvasena vuttarūpāni.

I did, I did, I did, we did, we did, we did. You (sg.) did, they did. You (sg.) did, you (pl.) did. I did, we did. These forms are stated in the Aorist tense.

Karissati, karissanti. Karissasi, karissatha. Karissāmi, karissāma. Karissate, karissante. Karissase, karissavhe. Karissaṃ, kassaṃ iccapi. Tathā hi pāḷi dissati “kassaṃ purisakāriya”nti. Karissamhe. Tathā kāhati, kāhanti. Kāhasi, kāhatha. Kāhāmi, kāhāma. Kāhiti, kāhinti. Kāhisi iccevamādinā yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Bhavissantīvasena vuttarūpāni.

He will do, they will do. You (sg.) will do, you (pl.) will do. I will do, we will do. He will do (for himself), they will do (for themselves). You (sg.) will do (for yourself), you (pl.) will do (for yourselves). I will do, I will do—thus also. For in Pali, it is seen: “I will do the work of a man” (kassaṃ purisakāriyaṃ). We will do (for ourselves). Similarly, he will do, they will do. You (sg.) will do, you (pl.) will do. I will do, we will do. He will do, they will do. You (sg.) will do—and so on, as appropriate, they should be connected. These forms are stated in the future tense.

Akarissā, akarissa, akarissaṃsūti sesaṃ sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Kālātipattivasena vuttarūpāni.

He would have done, you would have done, they would have done—and so on, the rest should all be connected accordingly. These forms are stated in the Conditional mood.

Kayirati, kayiranti. Kayirasi, kayirātha. Kayirāmi, kayirāma. Kayirate. Sesaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Vattamānāvasena vuttarūpāni.

It is done, they are done. You (sg.) are done, you (pl.) are done. I am done, we are done. It is done (for itself). The rest should be connected accordingly. These forms are stated in the Present tense.

Kayiratu, kayirantu. Sesaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Pañcamīvasena vuttarūpāni.

Let it be done, let them be done. The rest should be connected accordingly. These forms are stated in the Imperative mood.

Kayirā, kuyirā. Kayiruṃ. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “kumbhimhipa’ñjaliṃ kuyirā, cātañcāpi padakkhiṇa”nti. Tattha kumbhimhipi añjalinti chedo. Kayirāsi, kayirātha. Kayirāmi, kayirāma. Kayiretha, kayireraṃ. Kayiretho, kayirāvho. Kayiraṃ, kayirāmhe. Sattamīvasena vuttarūpāni.

It should be done, it should be done. They should be done. Here, the Pali reads: “One should make a gesture of reverence even to a pot, and also respectfully circumambulate it” (kumbhimhipa’ñjaliṃ kuyirā, cātañcāpi padakkhiṇaṃ). In this, the division is “kumbhimhipi añjaliṃ” (even to a pot, a gesture of reverence). You (sg.) should be done, you (pl.) should be done. I should be done, we should be done. It should be done (for itself), they should be done (for themselves). You (sg.) should be done (for yourself), you (pl.) should be done (for yourselves). I should be done, we should be done. These forms are stated in the Optative mood.

Tattha kayirāti idaṃ “puññañce puriso kayirā”ti dassanato paṭhamapurisavasena yojetabbaṃ, “adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā”ti etthāpi “sārathi bhavaṃ adhammaṃ kareyyā”ti [M 0.0274] paṭhamapurisavasena yojetabbaṃ, na majjhimapurisavasena. Atha vā “kayirāsī”ti vattabbe sikāralopaṃ katvā “kayirā”ti majjhimapurisavacanaṃ vuttanti gahetabbaṃ.

Here, 'kayirā' in the example “if a person were to do merit” (puññañce puriso kayirā) should also be construed in the third person. Similarly, in “were the charioteer to do unrighteousness” (adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā), here too, it should be construed in the third person as “were the charioteer, venerable sir, to do unrighteousness” (sārathi bhavaṃ adhammaṃ kareyyā), not in the second person. Or, alternatively, it should be understood that 'kayirā' is said as a second person form, having dropped the 'si' from what should have been 'kayirāsī'.

Ettha pana siyā – yathā “puttaṃ labhetha varada”nti pāḷiyaṃ “labhethā”ti imassa padassa “sabbhireva samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhava”ntiādīsu “samāsethā”tiādīnaṃ viya paṭhamapurisavasena atthaṃ aggahetvā purisavipallāsaṃ katvā “labheyya”nti uttamapurisavasenattho aṭṭhakathācariyehi gahito, tathā tumhehipi “adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā”ti ettha “kayirā”ti padassa purisavipallāsaṃ katvā “kareyyāsī”ti majjhimapurisavasenattho vattabbo, aṭṭhakathācariyehipi “kareyyāsī”ti tadattho vuttoti? Saccaṃ, evaṃ santepi aṭṭhakathācariyehi vohāratthesu paramakosallasamannāgatattā “tva”nti vattabbe atthe bhavaṃsaddo pavattati, “bhava”nti vattabbe atthe tvaṃsaddo pavattatīti cintetvā adhippāyatthavasena “kareyyāsī”ti attho vutto, na purisavipallāsavasena. Tathā hi “puttaṃ labhetha varada”nti imassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “labhethā”ti ulliṅgitvā “labheyya”nti purisavipallāsavasena vivaraṇaṃ kataṃ. “Adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā”ti imassa pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “kayirā”ti ulliṅgitvā “kareyyāsī”ti vivaraṇaṃ kataṃ, tasmā “adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā”ti ettha purisavipallāso na cintetabbo. Atha vā yathā “puttaṃ labhetha varada”nti ettha ca “kāye rajo na limpethā”tiādīsu ethavacanaṃ gahitaṃ, evaṃ ethavacanaṃ aggahetvā “labhe athā”ti padacchedo karaṇīyo. Evañhi sati purisavipallāsena kiccaṃ natthi. Tattha labheti sattamiyā [M 0.0275] uttamapurisavacanaṃ “vajjhañcāpi pamocaye”ti padamiva. Athāti adhikārantare nipāto padapūraṇe vā. Ettha ca adhikārantaravasena aparampi varaṃ puttaṃ labheyyanti attho. Yasmā panettha dvinnamatthānaṃ uppatti dissati, yasmā cetesu dvīsu dujjāno bhagavato adhippāyo, tasmā dvepi atthā gahetabbāva.

Here, it might be said: Just as in the Pāli phrase “puttaṃ labhetha varada” (may one obtain a son, O giver of boons), the word “labhethā” is interpreted by the commentary teachers as “labheyya” (may I obtain) in the sense of the first person by altering the person, not taking the meaning in the sense of the third person as in phrases like “sabbhireva samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhava” (one should associate with the good, one should make friends with the good), where “samāsethā” and similar terms are used—similarly, you too should interpret “kayirā” in “adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā” (were the charioteer to do unrighteousness) by altering the person to “kareyyāsi” (you should do) in the sense of the second person, as the commentary teachers have explained its meaning as “kareyyāsi”. This is true, yet even so, because the commentary teachers are supremely skilled in conventional usage, they considered that the term “bhavaṃ” (venerable sir) is used where “tvaṃ” (you) should be said, and “tvaṃ” is used where “bhavaṃ” should be said. Thus, considering the intended meaning, the sense is stated as “kareyyāsi”, not by way of altering the person. For instance, in the commentary on the phrase “puttaṃ labhetha varada,” “labhethā” is cited and explained as “labheyya” through a change of person. However, in the commentary on “adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā,” “kayirā” is cited and explained as “kareyyāsi.” Therefore, in “adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā,” a change of person should not be considered. Alternatively, just as in “puttaṃ labhetha varada” and in phrases like “kāye rajo na limpethā” (dust should not adhere to the body), the `etha` termination is taken, so too, without taking the `etha` termination, the word division should be made as “labhe atha.” In this case, there is no need for a change of person. Here, “labhe” is a first-person optative form, like the word in “vajjhañcāpi pamocaye” (one should release even the condemned). “Atha” is a particle indicating a transition to another topic or is a mere expletive. And here, in the sense of a transition to another topic, the meaning is “may I obtain yet another boon, a son.” Since two meanings arise here, and since the Blessed One’s intention in these two instances is difficult to discern, both meanings should be accepted.

Ettha pana kiñcāpi liṅgavipallāso vibhattivipallāso vacanavipallāso kālavipallāso purisavipallāso akkharavipallāsoti chabbidho vipallāso āharitvā dassetabbo, tathāpi so upari āvibhavissatīti na dassito. Tatra kayirāthāti padaṃ sattamiyā parassapadavasena attanopadavasena ca dvidhā bhijjati, tathā majjhimapurisabahuvacanavasena paṭhamapurisekavacanavasena ca. Tathā hi “yathā puññāni kayirātha, dadantā aparāpara”nti ettha “kayirāthā”ti idaṃ sattamiyā parassapadavasena majjhimapurisabahuvacanavasena ca vuttaṃ. Yathānurūpaṃ puññāni kareyyāthayevāti hi attho. “Kayirātha dhīro puññānī”ti ettha pana “kayirāthā”ti idaṃ sattamiyā attanopadavasena paṭhamapurisekavacanavasena ca vuttaṃ. Kareyyāti hi attho. Idha parokkhādivasena yirapaccayasahitāni rūpāni yebhuyyena sāsane appasiddhānīti na dassitāni.

Here, although the interchange of gender, the interchange of case, the interchange of number, the interchange of tense, the interchange of person, and the interchange of letters—these six types of interchange—should be brought forth and shown, they are not shown, as they will become clear later on. Therein, the word “kayirātha” is divided in two ways: as a parassapada (active voice) form in the optative mood and as an attanopada (middle voice) form; and likewise as a second-person plural and a third-person singular. For example, in the phrase “yathā puññāni kayirātha, dadantā aparāpara” (that you should perform meritorious deeds, giving again and again), the word “kayirātha” is used as a parassapada form in the optative mood and as a second-person plural. For the meaning is: “You should indeed perform meritorious deeds as is fitting.” On the other hand, in the phrase “kayirātha dhīro puññānī” (the wise one should perform meritorious deeds), the word “kayirātha” is used as an attanopada form in the optative mood and as a third-person singular. For the meaning is: “One should perform.” Here, forms with the `yira` suffix, such as in the perfect tense, are not shown, as they are for the most part not established in the Teaching.

Attano phalaṃ karotīti kāraṇaṃ. Karotīti kattā, evaṃ kārako kārakaṃ vā. Ettha hi kārakasaddo yattha kattukārakakammakārakādivācako, tattha pulliṅgopi hoti, yebhuyyena napuṃsakaliṅgopi. Yattha pana rajatakārakammakāralohakārādivācako, tattha pulliṅgo eva. Kārāpetīti kārāpako. Karaṃ, kubbaṃ, krubbaṃ, karonto, kubbanto, kubbāno, kurumāno, pakruṃbbamāno[M 0.0276]. Kārikā, kārāpikā. Karontī, kubbantī. Kārakaṃ kulaṃ. Kārāpakaṃ, karontaṃ, kubbantaṃ, kurumānaṃ. Saṅkhāro, parikkhāro, parikkhato, purakkhato, karaṇaṃ, kriyā. Akkharacintakā pana “kriyā” iccapi padamicchanti. Ettha kriyāsaddo kiñcāpi “aphalā hoti akrubbato”tiādīsu kakārarakārasaṃyogavantāni padāni dissanti, tathāpi klesasaddo viya pāḷiyaṃ na dissati, adissamānopi so aṭṭhakathācariyādīhi garūhi gahitattā gahetabbova. Tathā hi “kriyākriyāpattivibhāgadesako”tiādikā saddaracanā dissati.

That which produces its own result is a `kāraṇa` (cause). One who does (`karoti`) is an agent (`kattā`); similarly, a doer (`kāraka`) can be masculine (`kārako`) or neuter (`kārakaṃ`). Here, indeed, the term “kāraka,” when it denotes the agent-case (`kattukāraka`), object-case (`kammakāraka`), etc., can be masculine, but is mostly neuter. But when it refers to a silversmith (`rajatakāra`), a worker (`kammakāra`), a coppersmith (`lohakāra`), etc., it is exclusively masculine. One who causes to be done (`kārāpeti`) is a causer (`kārāpako`). `Karaṃ`, `kubbaṃ`, `krubbaṃ`, `karonto`, `kubbanto`, `kubbāno`, `kurumāno`, `pakruṃbbamāno` (present participles). `Kārikā` (female doer), `kārāpikā` (female causer). `Karontī`, `kubbantī` (feminine present participles). `Kārakaṃ kulaṃ` (a family of doers). `Kārāpakaṃ`, `karontaṃ`, `kubbantaṃ`, `kurumānaṃ` (neuter present participles). `Saṅkhāro` (formation), `parikkhāro` (requisite), `parikkhato` (furnished), `purakkhato` (placed in front), `karaṇaṃ` (doing), `kriyā` (action). The grammarians, however, prefer the term “kriyā”. Here, although words with the `k-r` consonant cluster are seen in phrases like “aphalā hoti akrubbato” (it is fruitless for one who does not act), the word “kriyā” itself is not found in the Pāli Canon, like the word “klesa”. Nevertheless, as it has been adopted by venerable teachers such as the commentators, it should be accepted. For indeed, verbal constructions like “kriyākriyāpattivibhāgadesako” (a teacher of the division of offenses of commission and omission) are found.

Kātuṃ, kattuṃ. Kātave, kāretuṃ. Katvā, katvāna, kātuna, karitvā, karitvāna, kacca, adhikacca, kariya, kariyāna, purakkhitvā, kāretvā. Aññānipi tumantādīni yojetabbāni.

`Kātuṃ`, `kattuṃ` (infinitives: 'to do'). `Kātave` (infinitive: 'to do'), `kāretuṃ` (causative infinitive: 'to cause to do'). `Katvā`, `katvāna`, `kātuna`, `karitvā`, `karitvāna`, `kacca`, `adhikacca`, `kariya`, `kariyāna`, `purakkhitvā`, `kāretvā` (absolutives: 'having done', 'having caused to do'). Other similar forms, such as those ending in `-tuṃ`, should also be supplied.

Tatra kaccāti katvā. Adhikaccāti adhikaṃ katvā. Akkharacintakā pana saddasatthanayaṃ nissāya “adhikicca” iti rūpaṃ icchanti, mayaṃ panetādisaṃ rūpaṃ pāḷiyā anukūlaṃ na hotīti na icchāma. Tathā hi therikāgāthāyaṃ gotamiyā parinibbānavacane “padakkhiṇaṃ kacca nipacca pāde”ti pāḷi dissati. Tattha hi padakkhiṇaṃ katvāti attho. Kaccāti padassa dassanena adhikaccāti padampi diṭṭhameva hoti, esa nayo aññatrāpi yathārahaṃ veditabbo.

Therein, “kacca” means “having done.” “Adhikacca” means “having done excessively.” The grammarians, however, relying on the principles of grammar, prefer the form “adhikicca.” But we do not prefer such a form because it is not in accordance with the Pāli Canon. For instance, in the Therīgāthā, in the words of Gotamī on her final extinguishment, the Pāli text is seen: “padakkhiṇaṃ kacca nipacca pāde” (having circumambulated and bowed down at the feet). Here, the meaning is “having performed a circumambulation.” Since the word “kacca” is seen, the word “adhikacca” is also considered established. This principle should be understood appropriately elsewhere as well.

Idāni karotissa dhātussa appamattakaṃ atthātisayayogaṃ kathayāma – taṇhaṅkaro. Kāraṇā. Pharusāhi vācāhi pakrubbamāno. Sante na kurute piyanti.

Now we shall speak a little about the connection of the root `karoti` with extended meanings: `Taṇhaṅkaro`. `Kāraṇā`. `Pharusāhi vācāhi pakrubbamāno`. `Sante na kurute piyaṃ`.

Tatra [M 0.0277] taṇhaṅkaroti veneyyānaṃ taṇhaṃ lobhaṃ karoti hiṃsatīti taṇhaṅkaro. Atha vā rūpakāyadhammakāyasampattiyā attani sakalalokassa taṇhaṃ sinehaṃ karoti janetīti taṇhaṅkaro. Kāraṇāti hiṃsanā. Pakrubbamānoti hiṃsamāno. Sante na kurute piyanti sappurise attano piye iṭṭhe kante manāpe na karotīti attho. Atha vā piyaṃ piyāyamāno tussamāno modamāno sante na kurute na sevatīti attho. Yathā “rājānaṃ sevatī”ti etasmiṃ atthe rājānaṃ piyaṃ kuruteti saddasatthavidū mantenti, dullabhāyaṃ nīti sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā.

Therein, `Taṇhaṅkara` is so named because for those who can be trained, he makes (`karoti`) an end of, that is, he harms (`hiṃsati`), their craving and greed. Or alternatively, through the accomplishment of his form-body and Dhamma-body, he makes (`karoti`), that is, he generates (`janeti`), craving and affection for himself in the entire world; therefore he is called `Taṇhaṅkara`. `Kāraṇā` means harming. `Pakrubbamāno` means harming. `Sante na kurute piyaṃ` means he does not make virtuous people dear, agreeable, pleasing, or delightful to himself. Or alternatively, the meaning is that, while cherishing, delighting in, and rejoicing in what is dear, he does not cultivate (`na kurute`), that is, does not associate with (`na sevati`), the good. Just as for the phrase “rājānaṃ sevati” (he serves the king), experts in grammar explain the meaning as “rājānaṃ piyaṃ kurute” (he makes the king dear to himself). This is a rare principle and should be carefully borne in mind.

Ettha ca parikkhārasaddassa atthuddhāro nīyate, “parikkhāroti sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhittaṃ hotī”tiādīsu parivāro vuccati. “Ratho setaparikkhāro, jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”tiādīsu alaṅkāro. “Ye cime pabbajitena jīvitaparikkhārā samudānetabbā”tiādīsu sambhāro. Etthetañhi vuccati –

And here the meaning of the word `parikkhāra` is set forth. In passages such as “parikkhāroti sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhittaṃ hoti” (it is well-fortified with the seven city fortifications), it is said to mean `parivāra` (surroundings). In passages such as “Ratho setaparikkhāro, jhānakkho cakkavīriyo” (a chariot with white adornments, with the axle of jhāna, and the wheel of energy), it means `alaṅkāra` (adornment). In passages such as “Ye cime pabbajitena jīvitaparikkhārā samudānetabbā” (and these requisites of life to be procured by one who has gone forth), it means `sambhāra` (equipment). In this regard, it is said:

Sāsanaññūhi viññūhi, parikkhāroti sāsane;

Parivāro alaṅkāro, sambhāro ca pavuccati.

By the wise who know the Teaching, in the Teaching, the word `parikkhāra` is said to mean: surroundings, adornment, and equipment.

Jāgara niddakkhaye. Jāgaroti. Jāgaraṃ. Dīghā jāgarato ratti.

The root `jāgara` is used in the sense of the ending of sleep. `Jāgaroti` (he is awake). `Jāgaraṃ` (wakefulness). `Dīghā jāgarato ratti` (Long is the night for one who is awake).

Tanādī ettakā diṭṭhā, dhātavo me yathābalaṃ;

Suttesvaññepi pekkhitvā, gaṇhavho atthayuttitoti.

These roots, beginning with 'tan', as many as have been seen by me according to my ability. Having examined others also in the suttas, you should grasp what is meaningful.

Tanādigaṇoyaṃ.

This is the Tanādi group.

Rudhādichakkaṃ [M 0.0278] vividhatthasāraṃ,

Matiṅkaraṃ viññujanādhirāmaṃ;

Uḷārachandehi susevanīyaṃ,

Suvaṇṇahaṃsehi suciṃva ṭhānaṃ.

The sixfold group beginning with 'rudh', rich in diverse meanings, producing wisdom, delighting the wise; worthy of being resorted to by those with noble aspirations, like a pure place frequented by golden swans.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise in the ways of expression within the ninefold Teaching with its commentary and the three Piṭakas,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe rudhādichakkaṃ

the section on the sixfold group beginning with 'rudh' in the grammatical treatise called Saddanīti, composed for the sake of skill,

Nāma

is named

Sattarasamo paricchedo.

The Seventeenth Chapter.

18. Curādigaṇaparidīpana

18. The Elucidation of the Group Beginning with Cura

Ito paraṃ pavakkhāmi, pacuratthahitakkaraṃ;

Curādikagaṇanāmaṃ, nāmato aṭṭhamaṃ gaṇaṃ.

Henceforth, I will declare the eighth group by name, called the Curādi group, which is conducive to much benefit and welfare.

Cura theyye. Thenanaṃ theyyaṃ, corikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ theyye curadhtu vattati. Coreti, corayati, coro, corī, corikā, coretu, corayituṃ, coretvā, corayitvā. Kattutthesu ṇeṇayatā curādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Kārite – corāpeti, corāpayati, corāpetuṃ, corāpayituṃ, corāpetvā, corāpayitvā. Kammedhanaṃ corehi coriyati, coritaṃ dhanaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Cura is in the sense of theft. Stealing is theft, which is also called 'corikā'. In this sense of theft, the root 'cura' is used. Forms include: coreti, corayati (he steals), coro (a thief), corī (a female thief), corikā (theft), coretu (may he steal), corayituṃ (to steal), coretvā, corayitvā (having stolen). In the active sense, the characteristic of the Curādi group is the suffixes ṇe and ṇaya. In the causative: corāpeti, corāpayati (he causes to steal), corāpetuṃ, corāpayituṃ (to cause to steal), corāpetvā, corāpayitvā (having caused to steal). In the passive: dhanaṃ corehi coriyati (wealth is stolen by thieves); coritaṃ dhanaṃ (stolen wealth). This method applies everywhere.

Kakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ka'

Loka dassane. Loketi, lokayati, oloketi, olokayati, ulloketi, ullokayati, apaloketi, apalokayati, āloketi, ālokayati, viloketi, vilokayati. Loko, āloko, lokanaṃ, olokanaṃ, ullokanaṃ, ālokanaṃ, vilokanaṃ, apalokanaṃ, avalokanaṃ. Oloketuṃ, olokayituṃ, oloketvā, olokayitvā. Kārite pana “olokāpeti, olokāpayati, olokāpetuṃ, olokāpayituṃ, olokāpetvā[M 0.0279], olokāpayitvā” iccevamādīni yojetabbāni. Esa nayo sabbatthāpi.

Loka is in the sense of seeing. Forms include: loketi, lokayati (he sees), oloketi, olokayati (he looks at), ulloketi, ullokayati (he looks up), apaloketi, apalokayati (he glances at), āloketi, ālokayati (he illuminates), viloketi, vilokayati (he examines). Nouns include: loko (world), āloko (light), lokanaṃ (seeing), olokanaṃ (looking at), ullokanaṃ (looking up), ālokanaṃ (illuminating), vilokanaṃ (examining), apalokanaṃ (glancing at), avalokanaṃ (looking down at). Infinitives and gerunds: oloketuṃ, olokayituṃ (to look at), oloketvā, olokayitvā (having looked at). In the causative, however, forms such as ‘olokāpeti, olokāpayati (he causes to look at), olokāpetuṃ, olokāpayituṃ (to cause to look at), olokāpetvā, olokāpayitvā (having caused to look at)’ should be applied. This method applies everywhere.

Tattha lokoti tayo lokā saṅkhāraloko sattaloko okāsalokoti. Tattha “eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā”ti āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhāraloko veditabbo. “Sassato loko’ti vā ‘asassato loko’ti vā”ti āgataṭṭhāne sattaloko.

Therein, 'loka' refers to three worlds: the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), the world of beings (sattaloka), and the world of space (okāsaloka). Therein, in the passage, 'One world: all beings subsist on food,' the 'world of formations' is to be understood. In the passage, 'The world is eternal' or 'the world is not eternal,' the 'world of beings' is meant.

“Yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharanti,

Disā bhanti virocamānā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko,

Ettha te vattate vaso”ti

'As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining, they illuminate the directions; so far extends the thousandfold world, herein your power prevails.'

Āgataṭṭhāne okāsaloko.

In this passage, it is the world of space.

Atha vā lokoti tividho loko kilesaloko bhavaloko indriyalokoti. Tattha rāgādikilesabahulatāya kāmāvacarasattā kilesaloko. Jhānābhiññāparibuddhiyā rūpāvacarasattā bhavaloko. Āneñjasamādhibahulatāya visadindriyattā arūpāvacarasattā indriyaloko. Atha vā kilissanaṃ kileso, vipākadukkhanti attho. Tasmā dukkhabahulatāya apāyesu sattā kilesaloko. Tadaññe sattā sampattibhavabhāvato bhavaloko. Tattha ye vimuttiparipācakehi indriyehi samannāgatā sattā, so indriyalokoti veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, 'loka' is a threefold world: the world of defilements (kilesaloka), the world of existence (bhavaloka), and the world of faculties (indriyaloka). Therein, due to the abundance of defilements such as greed, beings in the desire realm are the world of defilements. Due to the perfection of jhānas and higher knowledges, beings in the form realm are the world of existence. Due to the abundance of imperturbable concentration and the clarity of their faculties, beings in the formless realm are the world of faculties. Alternatively, 'kilesa' is defiling, meaning the suffering of its result. Therefore, due to the abundance of suffering, beings in the woeful states are the world of defilements. Other beings, due to their state of prosperous existence, are the world of existence. Therein, those beings who are endowed with faculties that lead to the ripening of liberation should be understood as the world of faculties.

Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

In the Jātaka commentary, however:

“Saṅkhāraloko sattaloko okāsaloko khandhaloko āyatanaloko dhātulokoti [M 0.0280] anekavidho loko. Ettha ‘eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā…pe… aṭṭhārasa lokā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo’ti ettha saṅkhāraloko vutto. Khandhalokādayo tadantogadhāyeva. ‘Ayaṃ loko paro loko brahmaloko sadevako’tiādīsu pana sattaloko vutto. ‘Yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharanti, disā bhanti virocamānā. Tāva sahassadhā loko, ettha tevattate vaso’ti ettha okāsaloko vutto”ti vuttaṃ.

'The world is of many kinds: the world of formations, the world of beings, the world of space, the world of aggregates, the world of sense bases, and the world of elements. Here, where it is said, “One world: all beings are sustained by nutriment… up to… eighteen worlds are eighteen elements,” the world of formations is spoken of. The world of aggregates and the others are included within that. But in phrases like “this world, the other world, the world of Brahmā with its gods,” the world of beings is spoken of. Where it is said, “As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining, they illuminate the directions; so far extends the thousandfold world, herein your power prevails,” here, the world of space is spoken of.' Thus it is said.

Atthato pana indriyabaddhānaṃ khandhānaṃ samūho santāno ca sattaloko, rūpādīsu sattavisattatāya satto, lokiyati ettha kusalākusalaṃ tabbipāko cāti. Anindriyabaddhānaṃ rūpānaṃ samūho santāno ca okāsaloko, lokiyanti ettha tasā thāvarā ca, tesañca okāsabhūtoti, tadādhāraṇatāya hesa “bhājanaloko”tipi vuccati. Duvidhopi cesa rūpādidhamme upādāya paññattattā upādāpaññattibhūto aparamatthasabhāvo sappaccaye pana rūpārūpadhamme upādāya paññattattā tadubhayassāpi upādānānaṃ vasena pariyāyato paccayāyattavuttitā upacaritabbā, tadubhaye khandhā saṅkhāraloko, paccayehi saṅkhariyanti, lujjanti palujjanti cāti ettha paccayāyattavuttitāya maggaphaladhammānampi satipi lujjanapalujjanatte tebhūmikadhammānaṃyeva “loko”ti adhippetattā natthi lokatāpajjanaṃ. Tathā hi te “lokuttarā”ti vuttā.

In meaning, however, the world of beings (sattaloka) is the collection and continuity of aggregates bound to the faculties; a being (satta) is so called because of attachment (satta) and clinging to form, etc.; herein, wholesome and unwholesome actions and their results are experienced (lokiyati). The world of space (okāsaloka) is the collection and continuity of forms not bound to the faculties; herein, moving and stationary beings are seen (lokiyanti), and it is the space for them; because it is their support, it is also called the 'receptacle-world' (bhājanaloka). This twofold world, being designated in dependence on phenomena such as form, is a derivative concept (upādāpaññatti) and has no ultimate nature. However, since it is designated in dependence on conditioned form and formless phenomena, the fact that both have an existence dependent on conditions by way of their substrata should be figuratively understood. Both these aggregates are the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), for they are formed (saṅkhariyanti) by conditions, and they decay (lujjanti) and disintegrate (palujjanti). Here, due to their existence being dependent on conditions, even though the path and fruition states also decay and disintegrate, since only the phenomena of the three planes of existence are intended as 'world', they do not attain the state of being 'world'. For this reason, they are called 'transcendent' (lokuttarā).

Ālokoti rasmi, ālokenti etena bhuso passanti janā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ vāti āloko. Olokananti [M 0.0281] heṭṭhā pekkhanaṃ. Vilokananti uddhaṃ pekkhanaṃ. Ālokananti purato pekkhanaṃ. Vilokananti dvīsu passesu pekkhanaṃ, vividhā vā pekkhanaṃ. Apalokananti “saṅghaṃ apaloketvā”tiādīsu viya jānāpanaṃ. Avalokananti “nāgāvalokitaṃ avaloketvā”tiādīsu viya purimakāyaṃ parivattetvā pekkhanaṃ. “Ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hotī”ti etthāpi bhāvavasena ālokanaṃ ālokitaṃ vilokanaṃ vilokitanti attho gahetabbo.

'Āloka' is radiance; it is called 'āloka' because by it people see clearly, or it is eye-consciousness. 'Olokana' is looking down. 'Ullokana' is looking up. 'Ālokana' is looking forward. 'Vilokana' is looking to both sides, or looking in various ways. 'Apalokana' is informing, as in 'having informed the Saṅgha.' 'Avalokana' is looking back by turning the front of the body, as in 'having looked back with an elephant's glance.' In the phrase 'one acts with clear comprehension when looking forward or looking around,' the meaning should be understood that 'ālokita' is the act of looking forward and 'vilokita' is the act of looking around.

Thaka paṭighāte. Thaketi, thakayati dvāraṃ puriso.

Thaka is in the sense of obstructing. Thaketi, thakayati: a person bolts the door.

Takka vitakke. Takketi, vitakketi, vitakkayati. Takko, vitakko, vitakkitā.

Takka is in the sense of applied thought. Takketi, vitakketi, vitakkayati (he applies thought, he reflects). Takko, vitakko (applied thought), vitakkitā (one who applies thought).

Tattha takkanaṃ takko, ūhananti vuttaṃ hoti, evaṃ vitakko. Atha vā vitakkenti etena, sayaṃ vā vitakketi, vitakkanamattameva vā etanti vitakko. “Takko, vitakko, appanā, byappanā, cetaso abhiniropanā”ti abhidhamme pariyāyasaddā vuttā. Vitakketīti vitakkitā, puggalo. “Avitakkitā maccumupabbajantī”ti pāḷi.

Here, 'takka' is the act of thinking, which is said to be pondering; similarly 'vitakka.' Alternatively, 'vitakka' is that by which one thinks, or one thinks by oneself, or it is merely the act of thinking. In the Abhidhamma, 'takka, vitakka, appanā, byappanā, cetaso abhiniropanā' are given as synonyms: reasoning, applied thought, absorption, application, and placing of the mind. One who applies thought is called 'vitakkitā,' a person. The Pāli passage is: 'The unthinking approach death.'

Aki lakkhaṇe. Lakkhaṇaṃ saññāṇaṃ, sañjānanakāraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Atridaṃ sallakkhitabbaṃ. Ye imasmiṃ curādigaṇe anekassarā asaṃyogantā ikārānubandhavasena niddiṭṭhā dhātavo, te evaṃvuttehi imehi tīhi lakkhaṇehi samannāgatā ākhyātattaṃ nāmikattañca pāpuṇantā ekantato niggahītāgamena nipphannarūpāyeva bhavanti, na katthacipi vigataniggahītāgamarūpāni bhavanti. Aṅketi, aṅkayati. Aṅkanaṃ, aṅko[M 0.0282]. Samāse pana “sasaṅko, cakkaṅkitacaraṇo”tiādīni rūpāni bhavanti.

Aki is in the sense of marking. A mark (lakkhaṇa) is a sign (saññāṇa); it is said to be a cause of recognition. This should be carefully noted here. Those roots in this Curādi group which are specified by means of an i-anubandha, have multiple vowels, and do not end in a conjunct consonant—these, being endowed with these three characteristics thus stated, attain the state of a verb and a noun, and are invariably forms produced with the insertion of a niggahīta; they never occur as forms without the insertion of a niggahīta. Aṅketi, aṅkayati (he marks). Aṅkanaṃ (marking), aṅko (a mark). In compounds, however, forms like sasaṅko (one with a mark, i.e., the moon) and cakkaṅkitacaraṇo (one whose feet are marked with wheels) occur.

Sakka vakka bhāsane. Sakketi, sakkayati. Vakketi, vakkayati.

Sakka and vakka are in the sense of speaking. Sakketi, sakkayati (he speaks). Vakketi, vakkayati (he speaks).

Nakka vakka nāsane. Nakketi, nakkayati. Vakketi, vakkayati.

Nakka and vakka are in the sense of destroying. Nakketi, nakkayati (he destroys). Vakketi, vakkayati (he destroys).

Cakka cukka byathane. Cakketi, cakkayati. Cukketi, cukkayati. Cakkaṃ. Cakkanti kenaṭṭhena cakkaṃ? Cakketi byathati hiṃsatīti atthena cakkaṃ. Cakkasaddo –

Cakka and cukka are in the sense of afflicting. Cakketi, cakkayati (he afflicts). Cukketi, cukkayati (he afflicts). Cakkaṃ (a wheel). In what sense is it a wheel (cakka)? It is a wheel in the sense that it afflicts, torments, and harms. The word 'cakka'—

Sampattiyaṃ lakkhaṇe ca, rathaṅge iriyāpathe;

Dāne ratnadhammakhura-cakkādīsu padissati;

In prosperity, in characteristics, in chariot parts, in deportment; in giving, in the jewel-wheel, Dhamma-wheel, razor-wheel, and so forth, it is evident.

“Cattārimāni bhikkhave cakkāni yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussāna”ntiādīsu hi ayaṃ sampattiyaṃ dissati. “Pādatalesu cakkāni jātānī”ti ettha lakkhaṇe. “Cakkaṃva vahato pada”nti ettha rathaṅge. “Catucakkaṃ navadvāra”nti ettha iriyāpathe. “Dada bhuñja ca mā cappamādo, cakkaṃ vattassu pāṇina”nti ettha dāne. “Dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti ettha ratanacakke. “Mayā pavattitaṃ cakka”nti ettha dhammacakke. “Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti ettha khuracakke. “Khurapariyantena cepi cakkenā”ti ettha paharaṇacakke. “Asanivicakka”nti ettha asanimaṇḍaleti.

Indeed, in passages like 'These four wheels, O monks, are possessed by gods and men,' this word is seen in the sense of prosperity. In 'Wheels are born on the soles of the feet,' here it is in the sense of a mark. In 'like the wheel of one moving,' here it is in the sense of a chariot part. In 'Four-wheeled, nine-gated,' here it is in the sense of deportment. In 'Give, enjoy, and do not be heedless; turn the wheel for beings,' here it is in the sense of giving. In 'The divine wheel-treasure appeared,' here it is in the sense of the jewel-wheel. In 'The wheel set in motion by me,' here it is in the sense of the Dhamma-wheel. In 'For a man consumed by desire, the wheel turns on his head,' here it is in the sense of a razor-wheel. In 'Even if with a wheel edged with razors,' here it is in the sense of a weapon-wheel. In 'the thunderbolt wheel,' here it is in the sense of a thunderbolt circle.

Taki [M 0.0283] bandhane. Taṅketi, taṅkayati.

Taki is in the sense of binding. Taṅketi, taṅkayati (he binds).

Akka thavane. Thavanaṃ thuti. Akketi, akkayati. Akko. Akkoti sūriyo. So hi mahājutitāya akkiyati abhitthaviyati tappasannehi janehīti akko. Tathā hi tassa “natthi sūriyasamā ābhā. Udetayaṃ cakkhumā ekarājā”tiādinā abhikkhuti dissati.

Akka is in the sense of praising. Praising (thavana) is eulogy (thuti). Akketi, akkayati (he praises). Akko (the sun). The sun is called 'Akko' because, due to its great radiance, it is praised and extolled by people who are pleased by it. Thus, its praise is seen in passages like: 'There is no light equal to the sun. This eye of the world, the sole king, rises...'

Hikka hiṃsāyaṃ. Hikketi, hikkayati.

Hikka is in the sense of harming. Hikketi, hikkayati (he harms).

Nikka parimāṇe. Nikketi, nikkayati.

Nikka is in the sense of measuring. Nikketi, nikkayati (he measures).

Bukka bhassane. Ettha sunakhabhassanaṃ bhassananti gahetabbaṃ, na vācāsaṅkhātaṃ bhassanaṃ. Bukketi, bukkayati. Ettha ca “bukkayati sā core” iti lokiyappayogo veditabbo. Bhūvādigaṇe pana “bukkati sā”ti rūpaṃ bhavati. Añño tu “bukka paribhāsane” iti paṭhati, evaṃ paṭhantepi sunakhabhassanamevādhippetaṃ.

Bukka is in the sense of barking. Here, 'bhassana' should be taken as the barking of a dog, not speech. Bukketi, bukkayati (he barks). Here, the common usage 'bukkayati sā core' (it barks at the thief) should be understood. But in the Bhūvādi group, the form 'bukkati sā' (it barks) occurs. Another reads 'bukka paribhāsane' (bukka is in the sense of reviling), but even when read thus, the intended meaning is still the barking of a dog.

Daka laka assādane. Daketi, dakayati. Laketi, lakayati.

Daka and laka are in the sense of tasting. Daketi, dakayati (he tastes). Laketi, lakayati (he tastes).

Takka loka bhāsāyaṃ. Takketi, takkayati. Loketi, lokayati.

Takka and loka are in the sense of speaking. Takketi, takkayati (one thinks, one reasons). Loketi, lokayati (one observes, one sees).

Cika sika āmasane. Ciketi, cikayati. Siketi, sikayati.

Cika and sika are in the sense of touching. Ciketi, cikayati (one touches, one causes to touch). Siketi, sikayati (one touches, one causes to touch).

Kakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'ka'.

Khakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'kha'

Lakkha dassanaṅkesu. Dassanaṃ passanaṃ. Aṅko lañjanaṃ. Lakkheti, lakkhayati. Sallakkheti, sallakkhayati. Lakkhaṃ vijjhati usunā, lakkhaṃ karoti.

Lakkha is in the sense of seeing and marking. Seeing is observing. Marking is a sign. Lakkheti, lakkhayati (one marks, one causes to mark). Sallakkheti, sallakkhayati (one discerns, one causes to discern). One pierces a target with an arrow, one makes a mark.

Gaṅgāya [M 0.0284] vālukā khīye, udakaṃ khīye mahaṇṇave;

Mahiyā mattikā khīye, lakkhe na mama buddhiyā.

The sands of the Ganges may be exhausted, the water in the great ocean may be exhausted, the soil of the earth may be exhausted, but not my wisdom by a fraction.

Kappalakkhaṇaṃ. Golakkhaṇaṃ. Itthilakkhaṇaṃ. Dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ. Sallakkhanā. Upalakkhanā. Paccupalakkhanā. Lakkhadhātuyā yupaccayantāya samādipubbānaṃ rūpānaṃ nakāro dantajo.

The characteristic of an aeon. The characteristic of a cow. The characteristic of a woman. The characteristic of phenomena. Discernment. Inference. Specific discernment. In forms from the root 'lakkha' with the suffix 'yu' and preceded by 'sam' and so forth, the letter 'n' is dental.

Bhakkha adane. Bhakkheti, bhakkhayati. Bhakkho no laddho. Bhakkhayanti migādhamā. Bhūvādigaṇe pana “bhakkhatī”ti rūpaṃ.

Bhakkha is in the sense of eating. Bhakkheti, bhakkhayati (one eats, one causes to eat). Food was not obtained. Hunters eat [or wild beasts eat]. In the Bhūvādi group, however, the form 'bhakkhati' occurs.

Nakkha sambandhe. Nakkheti, nakkhayati.

Nakkha is in the sense of connecting. Nakkheti, nakkhayati (one connects, one causes to connect).

Makkha makkhane. Makkheti, makkhayati. Makkho, makkhī. Tattha makkhoti parehi kataguṇaṃ makkheti pisatīti makkho, guṇadhaṃsanā. “Makkhaṃ asahamāno”ti ettha pana attani parehi kataṃ avamaññanaṃ makkhoti vuccati.

Makkha is in the sense of smearing. Makkheti, makkhayati (one smears, one causes to smear). Makkho, makkhī. Here, 'makkho' means one who smears over or crushes merits done by others, thus a smearer, a destroyer of merits. However, in 'unable to endure the smear,' the term 'makkho' refers to the contempt shown by others towards oneself.

Yakkha pūjāyaṃ. Yakkheti, yakkhayati. Yakkho. Yakkhoti mahānubhāvo satto. Tathā hi “pucchāmi taṃ mahāyakkha, sabbabhūtānamissarā”ti ettha sakko devarājā “yakkho”ti vutto. Atha vā yakkhoti yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbattasatto. Sabbepi vā sattā “yakkhā”ti vuccanti. “Paramayakkhavisuddhiṃ paññāpentī”ti ettha hi yakkhasaddo satte vattati. Tathā hi yakkhopi sattopi devopi sakkopi khīṇāsavopi yakkhoyeva nāma, mahānubhāvatāya yakkhiyati saraṇagatehi janehi nānāpaccayehi nānābalīhi ca pūjiyatīti yakkho.

Yakkha is in the sense of worshipping. Yakkheti, yakkhayati (one worships, one causes to worship). Yakkho. 'Yakkha' means a being of great power. Thus, in 'I ask you, great yakkha, lord of all beings,' Sakka, the king of gods, is called 'yakkha.' Or, 'yakkha' means a being born in the yakkha realm. Or, all beings are called 'yakkhas.' Indeed, in 'declaring the supreme purification of a being,' the word 'yakkha' refers to beings. Thus, a yakkha, a being, a god, Sakka, or even one whose taints are destroyed—all are called 'yakkha,' because due to their great power, they are worshipped by people who have gone for refuge with various necessities and various offerings; therefore they are 'yakkhas'.

Satte deve ca sakke ca, khīṇāsave ca rakkhase;

Pañcasvetesu atthesu, yakkhasaddo pavattati.

The term 'yakkha' is applied to beings, gods, Sakka, those whose taints are destroyed, and ogres.

Lakkha [M 0.0285] ālocane. Lakkheti, lakkhayati. Lakkhaṃ vijjhati usunā.

Lakkha is in the sense of considering. Lakkheti, lakkhayati (one considers, one causes to consider). One pierces a target with an arrow.

Mokkha āsane. Mokkheti, mokkhayati.

Mokkha is in the sense of releasing. Mokkheti, mokkhayati (one releases, one causes to release).

Rukkha phārusse. Phārussaṃ pharusabhāvo. Rukkheti, rukkhayati. Samāse “rukkhakeso, atirukkhavacano”ti rūpāni. Ettha ca “samaṇo ayaṃ pāpo atirukkhavāco”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha atirukkhavācoti atipharusavacanoti attho.

Rukkha is in the sense of harshness. Harshness is the state of being harsh. Rukkheti, rukkhayati (one is harsh, one causes to be harsh). In compounds, forms like 'rukkhakeso' (rough-haired) and 'atirukkhavacano' (excessively harsh-spoken) occur. And here, the Pali phrase 'samaṇo ayaṃ pāpo atirukkhavāco' (this wicked ascetic is excessively harsh-spoken) is an example. There, 'atirukkhavāco' means 'one of excessively harsh speech'.

Khakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'kha'.

Gakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ga'

Liṅga cittīkaraṇe. Cittīkaraṇaṃ vicitrabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Liṅgeti, liṅgayati, liṅgaṃ. Ettha liṅgaṃ nāma dīgharassakisathūlaparimaṇḍalādibhedaṃ saṇṭhānanti gahaṇe atīva yujjati. Tañhi nānappakārehi vicitraṃ hoti, liṅgīyati vicittaṃ kariyati avijjātaṇhākammehi utunā vā cuṇṇādīhi vā sarīramiti liṅgaṃ, ajjhattasantānatiṇarukkhādikuṇḍalakaraṇḍakādīsu pavattasaṇṭhānavasenetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Liṅgasaddo sadde saddappavattinimitte itthibyañjane purisabyañjane saññāṇe ākāre cāti imesu atthesu dissati. Ayañhi “rukkhoti vacanaṃ liṅga”nti ettha sadde dissati. “Sataliṅgassa atthassā”ti ettha saddappavattinimitte. “Tena kho pana samayena aññatarassa bhikkhuno itthiliṅgaṃ pātubhavatī”ti ettha itthibyañjane. “Purisaliṅganimittakuttākappāna”nti ettha purisabyañjane. “Tena liṅgena jānāma, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissatī”ti ettha saññāṇe[M 0.0286]. “Tehi liṅgehi tehi nimittehi tehi ākārehi āgantukabhāvo jānitabbo “āgantukā ime”ti ettha ākāre dissati.

Liṅga is in the sense of marking. Marking is making variegated. Liṅgeti, liṅgayati (one marks, one causes to be marked); liṅgaṃ (a sign). Here, the term 'liṅga' is very appropriately used in the sense of 'form,' which has distinctions such as long, short, thin, thick, round, etc. For it becomes variegated in various ways; the body is made variegated, or marked, by ignorance, craving, and kamma, or by the seasons, or by powders, etc.—thus it is 'liṅga.' This should be understood in terms of the forms occurring in internal continuities, in grass, trees, etc., or in things like earrings and caskets. The term 'liṅga' is seen in these meanings: a word, the cause of the application of a word, the female organ, the male organ, a sign, and appearance.
