The root kanda is in the sense of continuity. Continuity is a state of being constant, a state of being uninterrupted. It forms kandeti, kandayati.

Muda saṃsagge. Ekatokaraṇaṃ saṃsaggo. Modeti, modayati sattūni sappinā.

The root muda is in the sense of mixing. Mixing is the act of making into one. It forms modeti, modayati. For example: modeti sattūni sappinā, 'he mixes barley groats with ghee.'

Nada bhāsāyaṃ. Nādeti, nādayati. Hetukatturūpānīti na vattabbāni pāḷidassanato “sīho ca sīhanādena, daddaraṃ abhinādayī”ti. Aññatrāpi saṃsayo na kātabbo. Imasmiṃ curādigaṇe hetukatturūpasadisānampi suddhakatturūpānaṃ sandissanato.

The root nada is in the sense of sounding. It forms nādeti, nādayati. These should not be called causative forms, as shown by the Pāli example: 'And the lion with its lion's roar made the Daddara mountain resound.' One should not have doubt in other cases either, because in this curādi group, forms that resemble causative forms are also seen as simple active forms.

Sada assādane. Sādeti, sādayati. Assādeti, assādayati. Ettha āupasaggo rassavasena ṭhito.

The root sada is in the sense of enjoying. It forms sādeti, sādayati. With the prefix ā-, it forms assādeti, assādayati. Here the prefix ā- stands in its short form.

Gada devasadde. Devasaddo vuccati meghasaddo. Gadeti, gadayati.

The root gada is in the sense of a 'divine sound.' A 'divine sound' refers to the sound of a cloud, that is, thunder. It forms gadeti, gadayati.

Pada [M 0.0314] gatiyaṃ. Padeti, padayati. Padaṃ. Imissā divādigaṇe “pajjatī”ti rūpaṃ bhavati, idha pana īdisāni.

The root pad is in the sense of going. It goes; it causes to go. A step. For this root, in the divādi group the form is pajjati, but here there are forms such as these.

Chidda kaṇṇabhede. Chiddeti, chiddayati. Chiddaṃ.

The root chidd is in the sense of piercing the ear. It pierces; it causes to pierce. A hole.

Chida dvedhākaraṇe. Nanu bho yo catudhā vā pañcadhā vā anekasatadhā vā chindati, tassa taṃ chedanaṃ dvedhākaraṇaṃ nāma na hoti, evaṃ sante kasmā sāmaññena avatvā “dvedhākaraṇe”ti dvidhā gahaṇaṃ katanti? Dvidhākaraṇaṃ nāma na hotīti na vattabbaṃ, anekasatadhā chedanampi dvidhākaraṇaṃyeva. Aparassa hi aparassa chinnakoṭṭhāsassa pubbena ekena koṭṭhāsena saddhiṃ apekkhanavasena dvidhākaraṇaṃ hotiyeva. Chedeti, chedayati.

The root chid is in the sense of dividing in two. Surely, sir, when someone cuts something into four, five, or even a hundred pieces, is that cutting not called 'dividing in two'? If so, why is the specification 'in dividing in two' made, instead of stating it generally? It should not be said that it is not 'dividing in two.' Even cutting into a hundred pieces is indeed a dividing in two, for in relation to the one previous part, each subsequent severed portion constitutes a division in two. It cuts; it causes to cut.

Yo te hatthe ca pāde ca, kaṇṇanāsañca chedayi;

Tassa kujjha mahāvīra, mā raṭṭhaṃ vinassa idaṃ;

“He who cut off your hands and feet, your ears and nose—be angry with him, O great hero, lest this kingdom of yours perish!”

Yo me hatthe ca pāde ca, kaṇṇanāsañca chedayi;

Ciraṃ jīvatu so rājā, na hi kujjhanti mādisāti.

“He who cut off my hands and feet, my ears and nose—long may that king live! For those like me do not become angry.”

Chada apavāraṇe. Chādeti, chādayati. Chattaṃ. Purisassa bhattaṃ chādayati.

The root chad is in the sense of covering. It covers; it causes to cover. An umbrella. He covers the man's food.

Īdī sandīpane. Īdeti, īdayati. Īkārantavasena niddiṭṭhattā saniggahītāgamāni rūpāni na bhavanti.

The root īdī is in the sense of kindling. It kindles; it causes to kindle. Because it is specified as ending in long ī, forms with an inserted niggahīta do not occur.

Adda hiṃsāyaṃ. Addeti, addayati.

The root add is in the sense of harming. It harms; it causes to harm.

Vada bhāsāyaṃ. Vādeti, vādayati. Vādo.

The root vad is in the sense of speaking. It speaks; it causes to speak. Speech.

Tattha “vādeti, vādayatī”ti imesaṃ “vadatī”ti suddhakattuvaseneva attho daṭṭhabbo, na hetukattuvasena. Tathā hi “saṅketaṃ katvā visaṃvādeti. Ovadeyyānusāseyya. Idameva saccanti ca vādayanti. Avisaṃvādako lokassā”ti suddhakattudīpakapāḷinayā dissanti[M 0.0315], saddasatthe ca “vādayatī”ti suddhakattupadaṃ dissati. Tattha visaṃvādetīti musā vadeti, atha vā vippalambheti, vādoti vacanaṃ. “Vādo jappo vitaṇḍā”ti evaṃvidhāsu tīsu kathāsu vādasaṅkhātā kathā. “Vādāpeti, vādāpayatī”ti dveyeva hetukattupadāni bhavanti.

Here, the forms vādeti and vādayati should be understood as having the meaning of the simple agent form vadati, not in the causative sense. For in Pāli passages that illustrate their usage, such as: 'Having made an agreement, he deceives'; 'He should advise and instruct'; 'They declare, "This alone is the truth"'; and 'not deceptive to the world,' they are seen as simple agent verbs. And in grammar, vādayati is seen as a simple agent verb. Here, visaṃvādeti means 'he speaks falsely' or 'he deceives'; vādo means 'speech.' Among the three kinds of talk—'speech, murmuring, and wrangling'—the one designated as vāda is speech. Only the two forms vādāpeti and vādāpayati are causative agent verbs.

Chadī icchāyaṃ. Īkārantoyaṃ dhātu, tasmā saniggahītāgamānissa rūpāni na bhavanti. Purisassa bhattaṃ chādeti, chādayati, ruccatīti attho. Purisassa bhattaṃ chādayamānaṃ tiṭṭhati chādentaṃ vā.

The root chadī is in the sense of desire. This root ends in long ī; therefore its forms do not have an inserted niggahīta. The forms are chādeti and chādayati, meaning 'it is pleasing' (ruccati), as in: 'The food is pleasing to the man.' The participle forms are chādayamānaṃ or chādentaṃ.

Vadī abhivādanathutīsu. Ayampi īkāranto dhātu, tasmā imassapi saniggahītāgamāni rūpāni na bhavanti. Vādeti, vādayati, vandati, thometi vāti attho. Imāni anupasaggāni rūpāni. Saddasatthepi ca “vādayatī”ti anupasaggavandanathutiatthaṃ padaṃ vuttaṃ, sāsane pana “abhivādeti, abhivādayati, abhivādanaṃ, bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā”tiādīni sopasaggāni rūpāni dissanti.

The root vadī is in the sense of respectful greeting and praise. This root also ends in long ī; therefore its forms also do not have an inserted niggahīta. The forms are vādeti and vādayati, meaning 'he salutes' (vandati) or 'he praises' (thometi). These are forms without a prefix. And in grammar, the word vādayati is said to have the meaning of saluting and praising without a prefix, but in the Dispensation, prefixed forms are seen, such as abhivādeti, abhivādayati, abhivādanaṃ, and 'having paid respects to the Blessed One.'

Tattha abhivādetvāti vanditvā, thometvā vā, ayamasmākaṃ ruci. Āgamaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “abhivādetvāti ‘sukhī arogo hotū’ti vadāpetvā, vandanto hi atthato evaṃ vadāpeti nāmā”ti hetukattuvasena abhivādanasaddattho vutto, amhehi pana vandanasaddaṃ saddasatthanayamaggahetvā suddhakattuvasena attho kathito. Abhivādanañhi vandanaṃyeva, na vadāpanaṃ abhisaddena sambandhitattā “abhivādanasīlissā”ti ettha viya. Idañhi “abhivādāpanasīlissā”ti na vuttaṃ. Yadi ca saddasatthe vadāpanamadhippetaṃ siyā, “vadī vadāpanathutīsū”ti nissandehavacanaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā[M 0.0316], evañca na vuttaṃ, evaṃ pana vuttaṃ “vadī abhivādanathutīsū”ti, tena vadāpanamanadhippetanti ñāyati.

Here, abhivādetvā means 'having venerated' or 'having praised'—this is our preference. In the scriptural commentary, however, the meaning of the word abhivādana is given in the causative sense: 'abhivādetvā means having caused another to say, "May you be happy and free from illness," for one who venerates, by that very act, causes this to be said.' But we, following the method of grammar, have explained the meaning in the simple agent sense. For abhivādana is indeed veneration, not causing to speak, because it is connected with the prefix abhi, as in the phrase 'of one who is habitually respectful' (abhivādanasīlissa). For this is not stated as 'of one who habitually causes respect' (abhivādāpanasīlissa). And if 'causing to speak' were intended in the grammar, the unambiguous statement 'the root vadī is in the sense of causing to speak and praise' would have had to be made. But it was not stated thus; rather, it was stated as 'the root vadī is in the sense of respectful greeting and praise.' From this it is understood that 'causing to speak' is not intended.

Athāpi siyā “kassaci vuddhena visiṭṭhaṃ vadāpanaṃ abhivādana”nti, evampi nupapajjati kāritavasena dhātuatthassa akathetabbato. Tathā hi “paca pāke, chidi dvidhākaraṇe”tiādinā bhāvavasena atthappakāsanamatteyeva “pacati, paccati, pāceti. Chindati, chijjati, chedāpetī”tiādīni sakammakāni ceva akammakāni ca sakāritāni ca rūpāni nipphajjanti, na ca tadatthāya visuṃ visuṃ dhātuniddeso kariyati. Tasmā “vadī abhivādanathutīsū”ti ettha kāritavasena dhātuattho kathitotipi vattuṃ na sakkā kriyāsabhāvattā dhātūnaṃ. Yathā pana “takketi, vitakketi. Takko, vitakko”tiādīni samānatthāni, tathā “vādeti, abhivādetī”tiādīni samānatthāni. Ato saddasatthepi saddasatthavidūhi “takka vitakke, vadī abhivādanathutīsū”tiādīnaṃ dhātūnaṃ “takkayati, vādayatī”tiādīni anupasaggāniyeva rūpāni dassitāni, tāni ca kho suddhakattupadāniyeva, na hetukattupadāni, tasmā “abhivādanathutīsū”ti etassa “vadāpanathutīsū”ti attho nupapajjati.

Further, it might be said: 'Veneration (abhivādana) is causing someone to speak a special utterance to an elder.' Even this is not proper, because the meaning of a root should not be stated in a causative sense. For when the meaning is expressed simply in terms of the action, as in 'the root pac is in the sense of cooking,' 'the root chid is in the sense of dividing in two,' etc., then simple agent, passive, and causative forms are all produced, such as pacati (he cooks), paccate (it is cooked), pāceti (he causes to cook); chindati (he cuts), chijjati (it is cut), chedāpeti (he causes to cut), etc. And a separate definition of the root is not made for each of these. Therefore, it cannot be said that the meaning of the root in 'the root vadī is in the sense of respectful greeting and praise' is stated in a causative sense, because the nature of roots is to express an action. Just as takketi (he thinks), vitakketi (he thinks), takko (thought), and vitakko (thought) are synonymous, so too are vādeti (he venerates) and abhivādeti (he venerates). Thus, in grammar, the grammarians have shown only unprefixed forms like takkayati and vādayati for roots such as 'takka in the sense of thinking' and 'vadī in the sense of respectful greeting and praise.' And these are simple agent verbs, not causative agent verbs. Therefore, the meaning 'causing to speak and praise' is not proper for 'respectful greeting and praise.'

Kiñca bhiyyo – “abhivādeti, abhivādayati. Abhivādetvā, abhivādayitvā”tiādīni samānatthāni, ṇeṇayamattena hi savisesāni. Yadi “abhivādetvā”ti imassa padassa “sukhī arogo hotū’ti vadāpetvā”ti attho siyā, “sirasā abhivādayi”nti ettha “sirasā”ti padaṃ na vattabbaṃ siyā vadāpanena asambandhattā. Yasmā vuttaṃ taṃ padaṃ, tena ñāyati “abhivādetvā”tiādīsu vadāpanattho na icchitabbo, vandanattho icchitabbo thomanattho ca. Yasmā bhūvādigaṇe “vanda abhivādānathutīsū”ti imassa dhātussa “vandatī”ti [M 0.0317] padarūpassa “abhivandati, thometi cā”ti atthoyeva icchitabbo, na vadāpanattho. Tathā hi “vande sugataṃ gativimutta”nti padānamatthaṃ vadantena ṭīkācariyenapi “vandeti vandāmi, thomemi cā”ti vandanathomanatthoyeva dassito, na abhivādanasaddatthaṃ paṭicca vadāpanattho, tasmā “abhivādetvā”ti etthāpi vandanathomanatthāyeva icchitabbā, na vadāpanattho.

Furthermore: forms such as abhivādeti, abhivādayati, abhivādetvā, and abhivādayitvā are synonymous, differing only by the ṇe or ṇaya suffix. If the meaning of the word abhivādetvā were 'having caused another to say, "May you be happy and free from illness,"' then in the phrase 'he venerated with his head' (sirasā abhivādayi), the word sirasā ('with his head') should not have been used, as it has no connection with causing to speak. Since that word was used, it is understood that for abhivādetvā and similar forms, the meaning 'causing to speak' is not to be accepted, but the meanings of venerating and praising are to be accepted. For in the bhūvādi group, for the root vand in 'the root vand is in the sense of respectful greeting and praise,' the meaning of the verb form vandati must be 'he venerates and praises,' not 'he causes to speak.' Indeed, when explaining the meaning of the words 'I venerate the Well-Farer, freed from all destinations' (vande sugataṃ gativimuttaṃ), the subcommentary teacher has shown only the meaning of venerating and praising—'vande means I venerate and I praise'—not the meaning of causing to speak with reference to the word abhivādana. Therefore, for abhivādetvā too, only the meanings of venerating and praising should be accepted, not the meaning of causing to speak.

Athāpi siyā “vande’ti pade kāritapaccayo natthi, ‘abhivādetvā’ti imasmiṃ pana atthi, tasmā tattha vadāpanattho na labbhati, idha pana labbhatī”ti. Tanna, “karotī”tisuddhakattupadassapi “nipphādetī”ti hetukattupadavasena vivaraṇassa viya “vande”ti padassapi “sukhī arogo hotū’ti vadāpetvā”ti vivaraṇassa vattabbattā. “Abhivādetvā”ti idañca “vande”ti padamiva kāritapaccayantaṃ na hoti. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā “cinteti, cintayati. Manteti, mantayatī”tiādīnaṃ curādigaṇikānaṃ suddhakattupadānaṃ “cintāpeti, cintāpayatī”tiādīniyeva hetukattupadāni dissanti, tasmā yadi hetukattupadaṃ adhippetaṃ siyā, “abhivādāpetvā”ti vā “abhivādāpayitvā”ti vā vattabbaṃ siyā, yasmā panevaṃ na vuttaṃ, tasmā taṃ kāritapaccayantaṃ na hotīti siddhaṃ.

Again, it might be said: 'In the word vande there is no causative suffix, but in abhivādetvā there is one. Therefore the meaning of causing to speak is not found in the former, but is found in the latter.' That is not so. For just as the simple agent verb karoti is sometimes explained by way of the causative agent verb nipphādeti, so too the word vande would have to be explained as 'having caused to say, "May you be happy and free from illness."' And this word abhivādetvā, like the word vande, is not a form with a causative suffix. If you ask why, it is because for simple agent verbs of the curādi group, such as cinteti, cintayati, manteti, and mantayati, only forms like cintāpeti and cintāpayati are seen as causative agent verbs. Therefore, if a causative agent verb were intended, it would have to be stated as abhivādāpetvā or abhivādāpayitvā. Since it was not stated thus, it is established that it is not a form with a causative suffix.

Imassatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne sāṭṭhakathaṃ vidhurajātakappadesaṃ vadāma.

To make the meaning of this clear, at this point we will cite a passage from the Vidhura Jātaka along with its commentary.

“Kathaṃ no abhivādeyya, abhivādāpayetha ve;

Yaṃ naro hantumiccheyya, taṃ kammaṃ nupapajjatī”ti

“How could one pay respect to, or cause respect to be paid to, a person one wishes to kill? Such an action is not fitting.”

Ayaṃ tāva jātakapāḷi. Ayaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāpāṭho “yañhi naro hantumiccheyya, so taṃ kathaṃ nu abhivādeyya, kathaṃ vā [M 0.0318] tena attānaṃ abhivādāpayetha ve. Tassa hi taṃ kammaṃ na upapajjatī”ti. Tattha pāḷiyaṃ abhivādeyyāti suddhakattupadaṃ tabbācakattā. Abhivādāpayetha veti hetukattupadaṃ tabbācakattā. Evaṃ vibhāgaṃ pana ñatvā pāḷiyā aṭṭakathāya ca adhippāyo gahetabbo “naro yaṃ puggalaṃ hantuṃ iccheyya, so hantā taṃ vajjhaṃ puggalaṃ kathaṃ nu abhivādeyya, so vā hantā, tena vajjhena maṃ vandāhīti attānaṃ kathaṃ vandāpeyyā”ti. Ettha pana “rājāno coraṃ sunakhehipi khādāpentī”tiādīsu viya karaṇavasena “tena vajjhenā”ti padaṃ yojitaṃ, attho pana “taṃ vajjha”nti upayogavacanavasena daṭṭhabbo dvikammakattā sakāritapaccayassa sakammakadhātuyāti. Nanu evaṃ sante “aṭṭhakathācariyā passitabbaṃ na passanti, atitthe pakkhandantī”ti tesaṃ doso hotīti? Na hoti, suṇātha asmākaṃ sodhanaṃ, tathā hi aṭṭhakathācariyehi “abhivādetvā”ti ettha “vadī abhivādanathutīsū”ti dhātuyā atthamaggahetvā vohāravisaye kosallasamannāgatattā saṇhasukhumamatthaṃ sotūnaṃ bodhetuṃ “vada viyattiyaṃ vācāya”nti dhātuyevatthaṃ gahetvā kāritapaccayaparikappanena kāritatthamādāya “abhivādetvāti ‘sukhī arogo hotū’ti vadāpetvā, vandanto hi atthato evaṃ vadāpeti nāmā”ti hetukattuvasena abhivādanasaddattho vuttoti na koci tesaṃ doso. Pūjārahā hi te āyasmanto, namoyeva tesaṃ karoma, idampi ṭhānaṃ sukhumaṃ sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ. Evañhi karoto paññā vaḍḍhatīti.

This, first, is the Jātaka text. This, however, is the commentary passage: 'For if a person should wish to kill another, how indeed could he pay respect to him? Or how could he have himself paid respect to by that person? For such an action is not suitable for him.' Therein, in the Pāli text, abhivādeyya is a simple agentive verb, being indicative of that. And abhivādāpayetha is a causative agentive verb, being indicative of that. Having understood this distinction, the intention of both the Pāli text and the commentary should be grasped thus: 'If a person should wish to kill another person, how indeed could that killer pay respect to the person to be killed? Or how could that killer have himself paid homage to by the one to be killed, thinking, "Pay homage to me"?' Here, however, like in such examples as 'kings have thieves devoured by dogs,' the word tena vajjhena is construed in the instrumental case, but the meaning should be understood in the objective case as taṃ vajjhaṃ because the root takes two objects when the causative suffix is applied. Now, this being so, might one object: 'Is it not a fault of the commentators that they do not see what should be seen and plunge into a wrong ford?' It is not so. Listen to our clarification. For the commentators, being skilled in the domain of usage and wishing to explain a subtle and fine meaning to the listeners, did not take the meaning here for abhivādetvā from the root vadī in the sense of 'paying homage and praise.' Rather, taking the meaning from the very root vada in the sense of 'articulate speech,' and adopting a causative meaning by constructing it with a causative suffix, they stated the meaning of the word abhivādana by means of a causative construction, thus: 'abhivādetvā means having caused to say, "May you be happy and free from illness," for one who pays homage indeed, in effect, causes this to be said.' Therefore, there is no fault on their part. For those venerable ones are worthy of veneration; we pay homage to them. This point, too, being subtle, should be well borne in mind. For wisdom increases for one who does so.

Dakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in d.

Dhakārantadhātu

Roots ending in dh.

Randha [M 0.0319] pāke. Sūdo bhattaṃ randheti, randhayati. Kākaṃ sokāya randhehi. Randhako. Sūdena odano randhiyati. Randhito. Randhanaṃ. Puriso sūdaṃ sūdena vā odanaṃ randhāpeti, randhāpayati. Randhetuṃ, randhayituṃ. Randhitvā, randhayitvā, randhiya iccādīni.

The root randh is in the sense of 'cooking.' Sūdo bhattaṃ randheti, randhayati: The cook cooks food. Kākaṃ sokāya randhehi: Cook the crow for sorrow. Randhako: A cook. Sūdena odano randhiyati: Rice is cooked by the cook. Randhito: Cooked. Randhanaṃ: Cooking. Puriso sūdaṃ sūdena vā odanaṃ randhāpeti, randhāpayati: A man has the cook cook the rice, or has the rice cooked by the cook. Randhetuṃ, randhayituṃ: To cook. Randhitvā, randhayitvā, randhiya: Having cooked, etc.

Dhū kampane. Dhāveti, dhāvayati.

The root dhū is in the sense of 'shaking.' Dhāveti, dhāvayati: He makes shake; he causes to shake.

Gandha sūcane addane ca. Sūcanaṃ. Pakāsanaṃ. Addanaṃ pariplutā. Gandheti, gandhayati, gandho.

The root gandh is in the sense of 'indicating' and 'harming.' Indicating is making known. Harming is assailing. Gandheti, gandhayati: He indicates; he causes to indicate. Gandho: Scent.

Ettha gandhoti gandheti attano vatthuṃ sūcayati pakāsetīti gandho. Paṭicchannaṃ vā pupphaphalādiṃ “idamettha atthī”ti pesuññaṃ upasaṃharanto viya pakāsetīti gandho. Gamudharadhātudvayavasenapi gandhasaddattho vattabbo “gacchanto dhariyatīti gandho” iti, āha ca “gacchanto dhariyatīti gandho, sūcanatopi vā”ti. Gandhasaddo ca “uppalagandhatheno”ti ettha chedane vattatīti daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, gandho (scent) is so called because it indicates (gandheti), that is, it indicates or reveals its own source. Or, it is called gandho because it reveals a hidden thing such as a flower or fruit, announcing, 'This is here,' as if one were delivering a slanderous report. The meaning of the word gandha is also explained by means of the two roots gam and dhar, thus: 'It is carried (dhariyati) while going (gacchanto), therefore it is gandho.' And it is said: 'Gandho is so called because it is carried while going, or from indicating.' And it should be understood that the word gandha is used in the sense of 'cutting' here in the phrase uppalagandhatheno.

Vadha saṃyame. Vadheti, vadhayati.

The root vadh is in the sense of 'restraining.' Vadheti, vadhayati: He restrains; he causes to restrain.

Budhi hiṃsāyaṃ. Bundheti, bundhayati. Palibundheti, palibundhayati. Palibodho, parisaddo upasaggo, so vikāravasena aññathā jāto. Tattha palibodhoti āvāsapalibodhādi. Apica palibodhoti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhittayañca.

The root budh is in the sense of 'harming.' Bundheti, bundhayati: He harms; he causes to harm. Palibundheti, palibundhayati: He obstructs; he causes to obstruct. Palibodho: The word pari is a prefix; it has become otherwise by way of modification. Therein, palibodho means the hindrances concerning a dwelling, etc. Moreover, palibodho also means the triad of craving, conceit, and wrong view.

Vaddha chedanapūraṇesu. Vaddheti, vaddhayati. Vaddhakī. Vaddhakīti gahakārako.

The root vaddh is in the senses of 'cutting' and 'filling.' Vaddheti, vaddhayati: He cuts; he fills. Vaddhakī: A carpenter. Vaddhakī means a house-maker.

Gaddha abhikaṅkhāyaṃ. Gaddheti, gaddhayati. Gaddho. Gaddhoti gijjho. “Gaddhabādhipubbo”ti idamettha nidassanaṃ.

The root gaddh is in the sense of 'longing for.' Gaddheti, gaddhayati: He longs for; he causes to long for. Gaddho: Greedy. Gaddho also means a vulture. Here, Gaddhabādhipubbo is the example.

Sadhu [M 0.0320] pahaṃsane. Sadheti, sadhayati.

The root sadh is in the sense of 'delighting.' Sādheti, sādhayati: He accomplishes; he causes to accomplish.

Vaddha bhāsāyaṃ. Vaddheti, vaddhayati.

The root vaddh is in the sense of 'speaking.' Vaddheti, vaddhayati: He speaks; he causes to speak.

Andha diṭṭhūpasaṃhāre. Diṭṭhūpasaṃhāro nāma cakkhusaññitāya diṭṭhiyā upasaṃhāro apanayanaṃ vināso vā. Cakkhu hi passanti etāyāti diṭṭhīti vuccati. Yaṃ sandhāya aṭṭhakathāsu “sasambhāracakkhuno setamaṇḍalaparikkhittassa kaṇhamaṇḍalassa majjhe abhimukhaṃ ṭhitānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattidesabhūte diṭṭhimaṇḍale”ti vuttaṃ. Ṭīkāyampi ca “diṭṭhimaṇḍaleti abhimukhaṭṭhitānaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattidesabhūte cakkhusaññitāya diṭṭhiyā maṇḍale”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃbhūtāya diṭṭhiyā upasaṃhāre andhadhātu vattati. Andheti, andhayati. Cakkhūni andhayiṃsu, andho. Andhoti andhetīti andho. Dvinnaṃ cakkhūnaṃ ekassa vā vasena naṭṭhanayano, evamidha andhadhātu vutto. Kaccāyane pana “khādāmagamānaṃ khandhandhagandhā”ti vacanena amadhātussa andhādesakaraṇavasena rūpanipphatti dassitā.

The root andh is in the sense of 'the removal of sight.' 'Removal of sight' means the removal, elimination, or destruction of sight, which is termed 'eye.' Indeed, the eye is called diṭṭhi because 'they see with it' (passanti etāya). With reference to this, it is said in the commentaries: 'in the circle of sight (diṭṭhimaṇḍala), which is the place where the forms of bodies standing opposite appear, in the middle of the black pupil, which is surrounded by the white circle, of an eye complete with its components.' And in the subcommentary too it is said: 'diṭṭhimaṇḍale means in the circle of sight, termed 'eye,' which is the place where the forms of bodies standing opposite appear.' The root andh is used in the sense of the removal of such sight. Andheti, andhayati: He blinds; he causes to blind. Cakkhūni andhayiṃsu: They blinded the eyes. Andho: Blind. Andho is so called because it blinds (andheti). Thus the root andh is spoken of here in the sense of one whose eye(s) are destroyed, with respect to one or both eyes. In Kaccāyana's grammar, however, the formation of the word is shown by means of making andh a substitute for the root am, by the rule khādāmagamānaṃ khandhandhagandhā.

Badha bandhane. Migaṃ bādheti, bādhayati. Baddho migo, baddhosi mārapāsena.

The root badh is in the sense of 'binding.' Migaṃ bādheti, bādhayati: He binds a deer; he causes a deer to be bound. Baddho migo: The deer is bound. Baddhosi mārapāsena: You are bound by Māra's snare.

Tattha bādhetīti bandhatīti suddhakattuvasena attho gahetabbo. Evaṃ bādhayatīti etthāpi. Tathā hi “vātaṃ jālena bādhesi, yo anicchantimicchasī”ti ettha bādhesīti bandhasīti suddhakattuvasena attho. Bhūvādigaṇe pana “bādha baddhāya”nti bādhadhātussa vasena “bādhatī”ti kattupadaṃ “bādheti, bādhayatī”ti hetukattupadaṃ bhavati. Baddhoti bādhiyate bandhiyate soti baddho.

Therein, bādheti means 'he binds'; the meaning should be taken in the simple active sense. Likewise also for bādhayati. For example, in the phrase 'You bind the wind with a net, you who desire one who is unwilling,' here bādhesi means 'you bind,' in the simple active sense. However, in the Bhūvādi group, from the root bādh in the sense of 'obstructing,' the active verb is bādhati and the causative verbs are bādheti, bādhayati. Baddho is so called because he is obstructed (bādhiyate) or bound (bandhiyate).

Dhakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in dh.

Nakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'na'.

Māna [M 0.0321] pūjāyaṃ pemane vīmaṃsāyaṃ. Māneti, mānayati. Mātā. Vimāneti, vimānayati, paṭimāneti, paṭimānayati. Mānanā, sammānanā, vimānanā, vimānaṃ, vimānanaṃ, mānito.

In honoring, in affection, in investigation. He honors, he esteems. Mother. He dishonors, he slights; he disdains, he treats contemptuously. Honoring, veneration, dishonoring, disdain, contempt, honored.

Amānanā yattha santo, santānaṃ vā vimānanā;

Hīnasammānanā vāpi, na tattha vasatiṃ vase.

Where the good are not honored, or the good are dishonored, or even the lowly are honored, there one should not reside.

Vīmaṃsati, vīmaṃsā, vīmaṃsiyatīti vīmaṃsiyamāno. Vīmaṃsanto.

He investigates, investigation, is investigated—thus being investigated. Investigating.

Tattha mānetīti pūjeti, aṭṭhakathāsu pana “mānentī”ti etasmiṃ ṭhāne ayamattho dassito “mānentīti manena piyāyanti. Pūjentīti paccayehi pūjentī”ti. So vevacanatthappakāsanavasena vuttoti gahetabbo. Mānanapūjanasaddā hi pariyāyasaddattā vevacanasaddā eva. Vimānetīti avamaññati. Vimānanti sobhāvisesayogato visiṭṭhamāniyatāya vimānaṃ, visesato mānetabbanti hi vimānaṃ, devānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ byamhaṃ.

Therein, 'māneti' means 'honors' or 'reveres'. However, in the commentaries, in this place, the meaning of 'mānentī' is shown thus: 'Mānentī means they hold dear with the mind. Pūjentī means they honor with requisites.' This should be understood as stated by way of revealing synonymous meanings. For the words 'mānana' and 'pūjana', being words with the same meaning, are indeed synonyms. 'Vimāneti' means to disrespect. 'Vimāna' means a mansion distinguished by its special abundance of beauty, thus worthy of special esteem; for 'vimāna' means that which is to be especially honored; it is the heavenly mansion that is the dwelling place of the gods.

Mana thambhe. Thambho cittassa thaddhatā. Māneti, mānayati. Māno.

The root 'mana' is in the sense of 'stiffness'. Stiffness is rigidity of mind. He esteems, he values. Conceit.

Thana devasadde. Devasaddo meghasaddo, thaneti, thanayati.

The root 'thana' is in the sense of 'the sound of gods'. The sound of gods is the sound of a cloud; it roars, it thunders.

Yathāpi megho thanayaṃ, vijjumālī satakkaku.

Just as a thundering cloud, flashing with lightning, hundred-peaked,

Thalaṃ ninnañca pūreti, abhivassaṃ vasundharaṃ.

fills the highlands and the lowlands, raining upon the earth.

Yathā pāvusako megho, thanayanto savijjuko.

As a rain cloud in the rainy season, thundering and with lightning,

Ūna parihāniyaṃ. Ūneti, ūnayati. Ūno loko.

The root 'ūna' is in the sense of 'decline'. It declines, it causes to decline. The world is deficient.

Dhana sadde. Dhaneti, dhanayati, dhaniyyati. Dhani, dhanaṃ.

The root 'dhana' is in the sense of 'sound'. It sounds, it causes to sound, it is sounded. Wealthy, wealth.

Tattha [M 0.0322] dhanīti saddo. Dhananti santakaṃ, tañhi mama idanti dhanāyitabbaṃ saddāyitabbanti dhananti. Ayaṃ pana dhātu icchāyampi vattati. “Mātā hi tava irandhati, vidhūrassa hadayaṃ dhaniyyatī”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha dhaniyyatīti pattheti icchati.

Therein, 'dhanī' means 'sound'. 'Dhana' means possessions, for it is to be treated as wealth and proclaimed with the thought, 'this is mine'; therefore it is called 'dhana'. However, this root also functions in the sense of desire. The Pāli passage illustrates: "Your mother is afflicted, the heart of Vidhūra yearns." Therein, 'dhaniyyati' means to crave, to desire.

Thena coriye. Corassa bhāvo coriyaṃ. Yathā sūriyaṃ, yathā ca dakkhiyaṃ. Theneti, thenayati. Theno, thenetvā.

The root 'thena' is in the sense of 'thievery'. The state of a thief is thievery. Like 'sūriyaṃ', and like 'dakkhiyaṃ'. He steals, he causes to steal. Thief, having stolen.

Tanu saddopatāpesu. Tāneti, tānayati. Idhāyaṃ savuddhikā. Tanādigaṇe vitthāratthavasena “tanoti, tanute”ti avuddhikā.

The root 'tanu' is in the sense of 'sound' and 'affliction'. It stretches, it extends. Here, this has 'vuddhi'. In the 'tanādi' group, with the meaning of expansion, 'tanoti, tanute' are without 'vuddhi'.

Tavaggantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in the 'ta' group.

Pakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'pa'.

Ñapa tosananisānesu. Ñāpeti, ñāpayati, paññāpeti, paññāpayati, paññatti.

The root 'ñapa' is in the sense of 'appeasement' and 'sharpening'. He makes known, he causes to know; he declares, he causes to declare; designation.

Ettha ca niddese “paññāpetī”ti padaṃ nidassanaṃ. Tattha paññāpetīti katanibbacanehi vākyāvayavehi vitthāravasena niravasesato desitehi veneyyānaṃ cittaparitosanaṃ buddhinisānañca karotīti attho. Papubbo nikkhipane. Āsanaṃ paññāpeti, paññāpayati. “Āsanaṃ paññapetī”ti rassattampi dissati. Amatassa dvāraṃ paññapeti, paññā. Kārite “puriso purisena āsanaṃ paññapāpetī”ti ekameva padaṃ. Tāni “paññāpeti, paññāpayatī”ti rūpāni yadā “ñā avabodhane”ti imissā rūpāni siyuṃ, tadā [M 0.0323] hetukatturūpāni bhavanti. Ettha pana suddhakatturūpāni tabbācakattā.

And here in this explanation, the word 'paññāpeti' is an illustration. In this context, 'paññāpeti' means that by means of word-elements with explanations made, taught in detail and without omission, it brings about the satisfaction of mind in the trainable ones and a sharpening of wisdom. With 'pa' as a prefix, it is in the sense of 'laying down'. One prepares a seat, arranges it. The short form 'āsanaṃ paññapetī' is also seen. One sets up the door to the deathless; wisdom. In the causative, 'puriso purisena āsanaṃ paññapāpetī' is a single word-form. Those forms 'paññāpeti, paññāpayati,' when they are forms from 'ñā in understanding,' then they are causative forms. Here, however, they are non-causative forms because they are expressive of that meaning.

Lapa viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ. Lapeti, lapayati. Lāpo, lapanaṃ, ālāpo, sallāpo, kathāsallāpo, lapitaṃ.

The root 'lapa' is in the sense of 'clear expression in speech'. He speaks, he causes to speak. Speaking, talk, conversation, discussion, conversation, what is spoken.

Byapa dāhe. Jhāpeti, jhāpayati. Jhatto, jhānaṃ.

The root 'byapa' is in the sense of 'burning'. It burns, it causes to burn. Burnt, burning.

Tattha jhattoti khuddāpareto pācanagginā jhāpitoti jhatto, “jhattā assu kilantā”ti ca pāḷi. Jhānanti nīvaraṇadhamme jhāpetīti jhānaṃ, savuddhikaṃ. Kārite pana – jhāpāpeti, jhāpāpayati.

Therein, 'jhatto' means 'burned by the digestive fire, hence consumed' when one is afflicted by hunger; and there is also the Pāli passage, 'jhattā assu kilantā' (they were exhausted and worn out). 'Jhāna' means that which burns up the hindrances; thus it is called 'jhāna', with vowel strengthening. In the causative, however, it is 'jhāpāpeti', 'jhāpāpayati'.

Rūpa rūpakriyāyaṃ. Rūpakriyā nāma pakāsanakriyā. Rūpeti, rūpayati. Rūpaṃ.

The root 'rūpa' is in the sense of 'activity of forming'. The activity of forming is called the activity of making apparent. It forms, it makes apparent. Form.

Tattha rūpanti rūpayatīti rūpaṃ. Vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti attho. Divādigaṇe panāyaṃ “rūpaṃ ruppane”ti bhijjanādiatthaṃ gahetvā ṭhitā.

Therein, 'rūpa' is so called because it forms or makes apparent. The meaning is that it manifests an alteration of appearance and a state that captivates the heart. In the 'divādi' group, however, this root 'rūpa' is established with the meaning of 'breaking', etc., as in 'ruppane' (in breaking).

Kappa vidhimhi. Vidhi kriyā. Sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti. Kappayati. Moro vāsamakappayi. Sīhaseyyaṃ pakappentaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāmi gotamaṃ.

The root 'kappa' is in the sense of 'arrangement' or 'method'. Method is action. He arranges the lion's posture. He arranges. The peacock arranged its dwelling. I pay homage to the Buddha Gotama, who arranges the lion's posture.

Kappa vitakke vidhimhi chedane ca. Kappeti, kappayati, moro vāsamakappayi. Kappitamassu. Pakappeti, pakappayati. Saṅkappeti, saṅkappayati. Kappo, saṅkappo, vikappo. Kappasamaṇo iccādīni.

The root 'kappa' is in the sense of 'thought', 'method', and 'cutting'. He arranges, he makes; the peacock fashioned a dwelling. Trimmed beard. He plans, he imagines. He intends, he resolves. An aeon, intention, alternative. An ascetic for an aeon, and so forth.

Tattha kappoti paricchedavasena kappiyatīti kappo. Saṅkappoti saṅkappanaṃ. Vikappoti vividhā kappanaṃ, atthassa anekantikabhāvo. Idha kappasaddassa atthuddhāro bhavati.

Therein, 'kappa' is so called because it is determined by way of limitation. 'Saṅkappa' is intending. 'Vikappa' is various kinds of determination, the state of the meaning being indefinite. Here is an elucidation of the meaning of the word 'kappa'.

Kappasaddo [M 0.0324] abhisaddahanavohārakālapaññattichedanavikappalesasamantabhāvādianekattho. Tathā hissa “okappanīyametaṃ bhoto gotamassa, yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti evamādīsu abhisaddahanamattho. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti evamādīsu vohāro. “Yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”ti evamādīsu kālo. “Iccāyasmā kappo”ti evamādīsu paññatti. “Alaṅkato kappitakesamassū”ti evamādīsu chedanaṃ. “Kappati dvaṅgulakappo”ti evamādīsu vikappo. “Atthi kappo nipajjitu”nti evamādīsu leso. “Kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā”ti evamādīsu samantabhāvo.

The term 'kappa' has many meanings, such as acceptance, usage, time, designation, cutting, alternative, possibility, and totality. For example, in phrases like, 'This is acceptable to the Venerable Gotama, as is fitting for one who is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One,' it conveys the meaning of acceptance. In statements like, 'I allow, monks, the use of fruit under five ascetic practices,' it refers to usage. In expressions such as, 'Where I dwell perpetually,' it denotes time. In phrases like, 'Thus, Venerable Kappa,' it signifies designation. In statements like, 'Adorned with trimmed hair and beard,' it implies cutting. In phrases such as, 'A two-finger alternative is permissible,' it indicates alternative. In expressions like, 'There is a possibility to lie down,' it suggests possibility. And in statements like, 'Having illuminated the entire Bamboo Grove,' it conveys totality.

Atha vā kappasaddo saupasaggo anupasaggo ca vitakkavidhānapaṭibhāgapaññattikālaparamāyuvohārasamantabhāvābhisaddahana chedana viniyoga vinaya kriyā lesantara kappataṇhādiṭṭhiasaṅkhyeyyakappamahākappādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa “nekkhammasaṅkappo abyāpādasaṅkappo”tiādīsu vitakke āgato. “Cīvare vikappaṃ āpajjeyyā”tiādīsu vidhāne, adhikavidhānaṃ āpajjeyyāti hi attho. “Satthukappena vata bho sāvakena saddhiṃ mantayamānā na jānimhā”tiādīsu paṭibhāge, satthusadisenāti ayañhi tattha attho. “Iccāyasmā kappo”tiādīsu paññattiyaṃ. “Yena [M 0.0325] sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”tiādīsu kāle. “Ākaṅkhamāno ānanda tathāgato kappaṃ vātiṭṭheyya kappāvasesaṃ vā”tiādīsu paramāyumhi. Āyukappo hi idha “kappo”ti adhippeto. “Anujānāmi bhikkhave pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjitu”ntiādīsu samaṇavohāre. “Kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā”tiādīsu samantabhāve. “Saddhāsaddahanā okappanā abhippasādo”tiādīsu abhisaddahane, saddhāyanti attho. “Alaṅkato kappitakesamassū”tiādīsu chedane. “Evameva ito dinnaṃ, petānaṃ upakappatī”tiādīsu viniyoge. “Kappakatena akappakataṃ saṃsibbitaṃ hotī”tiādīsu vinayakriyāyaṃ. “Atthi kappo nipajjituṃ, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī”tiādīsu lese. “Āpāyiko nerayiko, kappaṭṭho saṅghabhedako, kappaṃ nirayamhi paccatī”ti ca ādīsu antarakappe.

Alternatively, the word 'kappa,' whether with or without prefixes, is seen in contexts such as thought, arrangement, resemblance, designation, time, lifespan, usage, completeness, confirmation, cutting, application, disciplinary action, pretext, interval-eon, craving, views, incalculable eons, great eons, and so on. For instance, in phrases like, 'The thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will,' it pertains to thought. In statements like, 'One may make a modification regarding robes,' it refers to arrangement—meaning an additional arrangement. In expressions such as, 'Indeed, we did not recognize the Teacher’s likeness when conversing with the disciple,' it denotes resemblance—meaning like the Teacher. In phrases like, 'Thus, Venerable Kappa,' it signifies designation. In statements such as, 'Where we dwell constantly,' it refers to time. In expressions like, 'If he wishes, Ānanda, the Tathāgata may remain for an eon or the remainder of an eon,' it pertains to lifespan—here, 'kappa' is intended as lifespan. In phrases like, 'I allow, monks, the eating of fruit under five ascetic usages,' it denotes ascetic usage. In statements such as, 'Illuminating the entire Bamboo Grove,' it conveys completeness. In expressions like, 'Faith, trust, conviction, confidence,' it refers to confirmation—meaning faith. In phrases like, 'Adorned with trimmed hair and beard,' it implies cutting. In statements such as, 'Likewise, what is given here benefits the departed,' it signifies application. In expressions like, 'What is made according to rule is stitched together with what is not made according to rule,' it pertains to disciplinary action. In phrases like, 'There is a pretext to lie down; let me lie down,' it suggests a pretext. In statements such as, 'One destined for the downfall, hell-bound, abiding for an eon, a schismatic in the Saṅgha, suffers for an eon in hell,' it refers to an interval-eon.

“Na kappayanti na purakkharonti,

Dhammāpi tesaṃ na paṭicchitāse;

Na brāhmaṇo sīlavatena neyyo,

Pāraṅgato na ca pacceti tādī”ti

They do not form concepts or prefer anything; no doctrines are accepted by them. A brahmin is not to be led by morality and vows; one who has gone to the far shore, being such, does not return.

Ādīsu taṇhādiṭṭhīsu. Tathā hi vuttaṃ niddese “kappoti uddānato dve kappā taṇhākappo diṭṭhikappo”ti. “Anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe”tiādīsu asaṅkhyeyyakappe[M 0.0326]. “Cattārimāni bhikkhave kappassa asaṅkhyeyyānī”tiādīsu mahākappe. Iccevaṃ –

And so forth, in craving and views. As it is said in the Niddesa: 'Kappa' from the summary means two kappas: the craving-kappa and the view-kappa. 'In many world-cycles of contraction, in many world-cycles of expansion,' etc., refers to the incalculable eon. 'Monks, these four are the incalculable [periods] of an eon,' etc., refers to the great eon. Thus—

Vitakke ca vidhāne ca, paṭibhāge tatheva ca;

Paññattiyaṃ tathā kāle, paramāyumhi ca chedane.

In thought and in arrangement, and likewise in resemblance; in designation, and likewise in time, and in lifespan and in cutting.

Samantabhāve vohāre, abhisaddahanepi ca;

Viniyoge ca vinaya-kriyāyaṃ lesakepi ca.

In totality, in usage, and also in firm conviction; in application and in disciplinary action, and also in a pretext.

Vikappantarakappesu, taṇhādiṭṭhisvasaṅkhaye;

Kappe ca evamādīsu, kappasaddo pavattati.

In arrangements and in interval-eons, in craving and views, in incalculable eons; and in eons and so forth, the word 'kappa' occurs.

Kapi gatiyaṃ. Kampeti, kampayati, gacchatīti attho. Imāni calanatthe pavattahetukatturūpasadisāni bhavanti. Calanatthe hi “kampa kampane”ti dhātuyā “kampatī”ti akammakasuddhakatturūpaṃ. “Kampetī”tiādīni sakammakāni hetukatturūpāni “idampi dutiyaṃ sallaṃ, kampeti hadayaṃ mamā”ti akammakāya dhātuyā sakammakarūpadassanato.

The root kapi is in the sense of movement. It shakes, it causes to shake; the meaning is 'it goes.' These forms, which operate in the sense of movement, are similar to the causal agent form. For in the sense of movement, from the root kampa 'to shake,' kampati is the simple intransitive agent form. Forms such as kampeti are transitive causal agent forms, because a transitive form of the causal root is seen in the line: 'This second dart, too, shakes my heart.'

Khapi khantiyaṃ. Khampeti, khampayati.

The root khapi is in the sense of patience. It endures, it causes to endure.

Thūpa samussaye. Samussayo āroho ubbedho. Thūpeti, thūpayati. Thūpo, thūpikā.

The root thūpa is in the sense of heaping up. Heaping up is ascent, height. It heaps up, it causes to heap up. A stūpa, a small stūpa.

Tapa khaye. Tapeti, tapayati.

The root tapa is in the sense of wasting away. It wastes away, it causes to waste away.

Upa pajjane. Upeti, upayati.

The root upa is in the sense of approaching. It approaches, it causes to approach.

Capa kakkane. Capeti, capayati.

The root capa is in the sense of agitation. It agitates, it causes to agitate.

Suppa māne. Suppeti, suppayati.

The root suppa is in the sense of measuring. It measures, it causes to measure.

Ḍapa ḍipa saṅghāte. Ḍāpeti. Ḍāpayati. Ḍepeti, ḍepayati.

The roots ḍapa and ḍipa are in the sense of striking together. From ḍapa: it strikes together, it causes to strike together. From ḍipa: it strikes together, it causes to strike together.

Kapa [M 0.0327] avakampane. Kapeti, kapayati. Kapaṇo. Kapaṇoti karuṇāyitabbo. Aññattha pana “kappatī”ti rūpaṃ vadanti.

The root kapa is in the sense of trembling. It trembles, it causes to tremble. A wretched person. A wretched person is one to be pitied. Elsewhere, however, they state the form is kappati.

Gupa kupa dhūpa bhāsāyaṃ. Gopeti, gopayati. Kopeti, kopayati. Dhūpeti, dhūpayati.

The roots gupa, kupa, and dhūpa are in the sense of speaking. From gupa: it speaks, it causes to speak. From kupa: it speaks, it causes to speak. From dhūpa: it speaks, it causes to speak.

Kipa dubballe. Kipeti, kipayati.

The root kipa is in the sense of weakness. It weakens, it causes to weaken.

Khepa peraṇe. Peraṇaṃ cuṇṇikaraṇaṃ, khepeti, khepayati.

The root khepa is in the sense of crushing. Crushing is making into powder. It crushes, it causes to crush.

Tapa pīṇane. Tapeti, tapayati.

The root tapa is in the sense of tormenting. It torments, it causes to torment.

Āpu lambane. Āpeti, āpayati. Āpo.

The root āpu is in the sense of attaining. It attains, it causes to attain. Water.

Tapa dāhe. Tapeti, tapayati. Tapo, tāpo. Ātāpo, santāpo. Kārite – tāpeti, tāpayati. Tattha tapoti akusalānaṃ tāpanaṭṭhena tapo, sīlaṃ.

The root tapa is in the sense of burning. It burns, it causes to burn. Austerity, heat. Ardor, torment. In the causative: tāpeti, tāpayati (it causes to burn). Therein, tapo (austerity) is so called because it burns up unwholesome states; it is virtue.

Opathapa thapane. Opeti, opayati. Na tesaṃ koṭṭhe openti. Thapeti, thapayati. Thapito. Thapayitvā paṭicchadaṃ vavaṭṭhapeti. Voṭṭhabbanaṃ.

The roots opa and thapa are in the sense of placing. From opa: it places down, it causes to place down. 'They do not place them in their granary.' From thapa: it places, it causes to place. Placed. 'Having placed the cover, he arranges it.' Arrangement.

Ettha ca “vi ava thapeti, vi ava thapana”nti chedo. Ettha purime saralopo thassa ṭhattaṃ visadisabhāvena dvittañca. Pacchime pana saralopo, avassa okārattaṃ, thassa ṭhattaṃ, passa vattaṃ, vassa dvittaṃ, vakāradvayassa ca bakāradvayaṃ bhavati. Voṭṭhabbananti ca byavatthāpakacittassa nāmaṃ. Nakāralope “voṭṭhabba”nti aparampi rūpaṃ bhavati.

And here the analysis is 'vi ava thapeti' and 'vi ava thapana.' Here, in the first case, there is elision of a vowel, 'th' becomes 'ṭh', and there is doubling. In the second case, however, there is elision of a vowel, 'ava' becomes 'o', 'th' becomes 'ṭh', 'p' becomes 'v', 'v' is doubled, and the two 'v's become two 'b's. And voṭṭhabbana is the name for the determining consciousness. With the elision of 'na', another form, voṭṭhabba, also occurs.

Māpa māpane. Paṇṇasālaṃ māpeti, māpayati. Yo pāṇamatimāpeti, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā.

The root māpa is in the sense of measuring. He has a leaf-hut built; he causes it to be built. 'Whoever destroys a living being.' 'A well-built leaf-hut.'

Yapa yāpane. Yāpanaṃ pavattanaṃ. Tena so tattha yāpeti. Yāpayati. Yāpanā.

The root yapa is in the sense of sustaining. Sustaining is maintaining. 'With that, he sustains himself there.' It causes to sustain. Sustenance.

Tattha [M 0.0328] yāpetīti idaṃ yādhātussa payogatte sati kāritapadaṃ bhavati. Tathā hi “uyyāpenti nāmā”ti pāḷi dissati.

Therein, this word yāpeti, when it is a usage of the root yā, is a causative form. For indeed, the Pāli text 'they indeed send out' is seen.

Pakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in -pa.

Phakārantādhāturūpāni appasiddhāni.

Forms of roots ending in -pha are not established.

Bakārantadhātu

Roots ending in -ba.

Samba sambandhe. Sambandho daḷhabandhanaṃ. Sambeti, sambayati. Sambalaṃ.

The root samba is in the sense of connection. Connection is a firm bond. It connects, it causes to connect. Provisions.

Sabi maṇḍale. Maṇḍalaṃ parimaṇḍalatā. Rūpaṃ tādisameva.

The root sabi is in the sense of a circle. A circle is roundness. The form is just the same.

Kubi acchādane. Kumbeti, kumbayati.

The root kubi is in the sense of covering. It covers, it causes to cover.

Lubi dubi addane. Addanaṃ hiṃsā. Lumbeti, lumbayati. Dumbeti, dumbayati.

The roots lubi and dubi are in the sense of oppressing. Oppressing is harming. From lubi: it oppresses, it causes to oppress. From dubi: it oppresses, it causes to oppress.

Pubba niketane. Niketanaṃ nivāso. Pubbeti, pubbayati.

The root pubba is in the sense of a dwelling. A dwelling is a residence. It dwells, it causes to dwell.

Gabba māne. Māno ahaṃkāro. Gabbeti, gabbayati. Gabbanaṃ, gabbito. Tattha gabbatīti na saṅkucati.

The root gabba is in the sense of pride. Pride is egotism. It is proud, it causes to be proud. Pride, proud. Therein, 'is proud' means 'does not shrink'.

Bakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in -ba.

Bhakārantadhātu

Roots ending in -bha.

Bhū pattiyaṃ. Patti pāpanaṃ. Sakammikā dhātu. Bhāveti, bhāvayati. Pabhāveti, pabhāvayati. Itthambhūto. Cakkhubhūto, ñāṇabhūto, dhammabhūto, brahmabhūto.

The root bhū is in the sense of attainment. Attainment is reaching. It is a transitive root. It attains, it causes to attain. It fully attains, it causes to fully attain. Become thus. Become the eye, become knowledge, become Dhamma, become Brahma.

Tattha [M 0.0329] bhāvetīti puriso gacchantaṃ purisamanugacchanto pāpuṇātīti attho. Esa nayo sesakriyāpadesupi. Ettha ca “bhāvetī”tiādīni yattha sace “bhū sattāya”nti dhātuyā rūpāni honti, tattha hetukatturūpāni nāma honti. “Bhāveti kusalaṃ dhamma”ntiādīnettha nidassanapadāni. Bhāvetīti hi vaḍḍhetīti attho. Idha pana suddhakatturūpattā pāpuṇātīti attho. Itthambhūtoti imaṃ pakāraṃ bhūto patto. “Cakkhubhūto”tiādīni pana “bhū sattāyaṃ, bhū pattiya”nti dvigaṇikānaṃ dvinnaṃ dhātūnaṃ vasena aṭṭhakathāṭīkānayanissitaṃ atthaṃ pakāsayissāma āgamikānaṃ kosallatthāya. Tattha cakkhubhūtoti yathā cakkhu sattānaṃ dassanatthaṃ pariṇeti, evaṃ lokassa yāthāvadassanasādhanato dassanakiccapariṇāyakaṭṭhena cakkhubhūto. Atha vā cakkhu viya bhūtotipi cakkhubhūto. Paññācakkhumayattā vā sayambhūñāṇena paññācakkhuṃ bhūto pattoti cakkhubhūto. Viditakaraṇaṭṭhena ñāṇabhūto, asādhāraṇaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ bhūto pattoti ñāṇabhūto, aviparītasabhāvaṭṭhena, pariyattidhammappavattanato vā hadayena cintetvā vācāya nicchāritadhammamayoti dhammabhūto. Bodhipakkhiyadhammehi vā uppannattā lokassa ca taduppādanato anaññasādhāraṇaṃ vā dhammaṃ bhūto pattoti dhammabhūto. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūto. Atha vā brahmaṃ vuccati maggo tena uppannattā lokassa ca taduppādanattā, tañca sayambhūñāṇena bhūto pattoti brahmabhūto. Evaṃ dvinnaṃ dhātūnaṃ vasena vutto attho veditabbo.

Therein, bhāveti means: a person following another who is going reaches him. This same method applies to the remaining verbs. And here, forms such as bhāveti, when they are forms of the root bhū in the sense of 'being,' are called causal agent forms. 'He develops a wholesome state' and so on are examples here. For bhāveti means 'he develops.' But here, because it is a causal agent form, it means 'he attains.' 'Become thus' means having become, having attained, this state. As for 'become the eye' and so on, for the skill of those versed in the scriptures, we will explain the meaning based on the two roots, bhū 'in the sense of being' and bhū 'in the sense of attainment,' relying on the method of the commentaries and subcommentaries. Therein, 'become the eye' means: just as the eye leads to seeing for beings, so he is 'become the eye' because he is the leader for the task of seeing, by being the means for the world to see things as they really are. Or, he is 'become the eye' because he has become like an eye. Or, because he consists of the wisdom-eye, or because he has become, has attained, the wisdom-eye with self-originated knowledge, he is 'become the eye.' He is 'become knowledge' because he is the instrument of knowing, or because he has become, has attained, unique knowledge. He is 'become Dhamma' because of his undeluded nature, or because he consists of the Dhamma uttered by voice after having reflected in his heart, due to his propagating the Dhamma of the scriptures. Or because he has arisen from the qualities of enlightenment and because he produces them for the world, or because he has become, has attained, the unique Dhamma, he is 'become Dhamma.' He is 'become Brahma' in the sense of being supreme. Or, the path is called 'brahma'; because he has arisen from it and produces it for the world, and because he has become, has attained, it with self-originated knowledge, he is 'become Brahma.' Thus the stated meaning should be understood according to the two roots.

Aparāni cettha nidassanapadāni veditabbāni. “Tātā mayaṃ mahallakā suddhodanamahārājaputtaṃ buddhabhūtaṃ sambhāveyyāma vā no vā, tumhe tassa sāsane pabbajeyyāthā”ti ca “atha [M 0.0330] kho therā bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ revataṃ sahajātiyaṃ sambhāviṃsū”ti cāti. Aññānipi panettha “manussabhūto, devabhūto”tiādīni yojetabbāni. Tathā hi saṃsāramocakapetavatthu aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “manussabhūtātimanussesu jātā, manussabhāvaṃ vā pattā”ti attho saṃvaṇṇito.

And other examples here should be understood. 'Dears, we are old. Whether we get to meet the son of King Suddhodana who has become a Buddha or not, you should go forth in his teaching.' And: 'Then the elder bhikkhus met with the venerable Revata, who was born at the same time.' Other examples such as 'become a human, become a deva' should be connected here. For in the commentary on the Saṃsāramocakapetavatthu, the meaning is explained thus: 'manussabhūtā means born among superhumans, or having attained the human state.'

Bhū avakampane. Ayampi sakammako. Bhāveti, bhāvayati. Manobhāvanīyā bhikkhū.

The root bhū is in the sense of trembling. This too is transitive. It moves, it causes to move. 'Bhikkhus who are to be cherished by the mind.'

Ettha ca bhāvetīti anukampati puttaṃ vā bhātaraṃ vā yaṃkiñci. Manobhāvanīyāti “dīghāyukā hontu bhadantā arogā abyāpajjā”ti evamādinā bhāvetabbā anukampitabbāti manobhāvanīyā. Aññattha pana manobhāvanīyāti manovaḍḍhanakāti attho. Yesu hi diṭṭhesu mano vaḍḍhati, “te manobhāvanīyā”ti vuccanti.

And here bhāveti means one has compassion for a son, a brother, or anyone at all. 'To be cherished by the mind' means those who should be cherished, for whom one should have compassion with such thoughts as: 'May the venerable ones be long-lived, healthy, and free from affliction.' Elsewhere, however, manobhāvanīyā means 'those who develop the mind.' For those on seeing whom the mind develops are called 'those who are to be cherished by the mind'.

Labha ābhaṇḍane. Labheti, labhayati.

The root labha is in the sense of addressing. It addresses, it causes to address.

Jabhi nāsane. Jambheti, jambhayati.

The root jabhi is in the sense of destroying. It destroys, it causes to destroy.

Lābha pesane. Lābheti, lābhayati. “Labha lābheti dhātussa rūpāni ce, kāritarūpāni bhavanti.

The root lābha is in the sense of sending. It sends, it causes to send. If these are forms of the root labha in the sense of 'getting,' they are causative forms.

Dabhī bhaye. Īkārantāyaṃ dhātu, tena saniggahītāgamāni rūpāni na bhavanti. Dabheti, dabhayati.

The root dabhī is in the sense of fear. This root ends in -ī; therefore, forms with a nasal augment do not occur. It fears, it causes to fear.

Dūbha santhambhe. Dūbheti, dūbhayati.

The root dūbh is in the sense of stiffening. It stiffens, it causes to stiffen.

Vambha viddhaṃsane. Vambheti, vambhayati. Vambhanā. Chabbaggiyā bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ vambhenti.

The root vambh is in the sense of disparagement. It disparages, it causes to disparage. Disparagement. 'The group-of-six bhikkhus disparage a bhikkhu.'

Bhakārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of roots ending in the letter bha.

Makārantadhātu

Roots ending in the letter ma.

Ātena [M 0.0331] camu dhovane. Āpubbo camudhātu dhovane vattati. Ācameti, ācamayati. Ācamanakumbhī.

The root camu, when preceded by the prefix Ā, is used in the sense of washing. It rinses, it causes to rinse. A water-pot for rinsing.

Ettha pana “tato hi so ācamayitvā licchavī, therassa datvā yugāni aṭṭhā”ti appasakkārapetavatthupāḷippadeso nidassanaṃ. Tattha ācamayitvāti hatthapādadhovanapubbakaṃ mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā. Ayaṃ pana dhātu bhūvādigaṇikatte “camatī”ti bhakkhanatthaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati.

Here, a passage from the Pāli of the Appasakkārapetavatthu serves as an example: 'tato hi so ācamayitvā licchavī, therassa datvā yugāni aṭṭhā.' There, ācamayitvā means having rinsed the mouth after washing the hands and feet. This root, however, belonging to the bhūvādi group, is also taken in the sense of eating, as in camati.

Kamu icchākantīsu. Kāmeti, kāmayati. Kāmo, kanti, nikanti, kāmanā, kāmayamāno,kāmento, abhikkantaṃ. Abhikkantavaṇṇā.

The root kamu is in the senses of desire and loveliness. It desires, it causes to desire. Desire, loveliness, contentment, longing, desiring, desiring, surpassing. Of surpassing beauty.

Ettha ca kāmoti rūpādivisayaṃ kāmetīti kāmo. Kāmiyatīti vā kāmo, kilesakāmavatthukāmavasenetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kileso hi tebhūmakavaṭṭasaṅkhātañca vatthu “kāmo”ti vuccati. Māropi vā devaputto “kāmo”ti vuccati. So hi accantakaṇhadhammasamaṅgitāya papañcasamatikkantepi buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvake attano vase ṭhapetuṃ kāmetīti “kāmo”ti vuccati.

Here, kāma is so called because one desires objects such as forms. Or, kāma is that which is desired. This should be understood in terms of sensual desire as defilement and sensual desire as object. For both defilement—that is, the round of existence in the three planes—and the objects of desire are called kāma. Even Māra the devaputta is called 'Kāma.' For he, being endowed with exceedingly dark qualities, desires to keep under his control even the Buddha, paccekabuddhas, and the Buddha's disciples—who have transcended conceptual proliferation—and therefore he is called 'Kāma.'

Vuttañcetaṃ porāṇakaviracanāyaṃ –

And this was stated in an ancient poetic composition:

“Vande vandehamassatthaṃ, yattha santajjito jito;

Kāmo kāmoghatiṇṇena, buddhena vasatā satā”ti;

“I bow, I bow to the Assattha tree, where the threatener, Kāma, was conquered by the mindful, abiding Buddha, who has crossed the flood of sensual desire.”

Imāni panassa nāmāni –

These, moreover, are his names:

Kāmo namuci kaṇho ca, vasavattī pajāpati;

Pamattabandhu madano, pāpimā dammakopi ca;

Kandappo ca ratipati, māro ca kusumāyudho;

Kāma, Namuci, and Kaṇha; Vasavattī, Pajāpati; Pamattabandhu, Madana, and Pāpimā; Dammakopī and Kandappa, Ratipati, Māra, and Kusumāyudha.

Aññe [M 0.0332] aññānipi vadanti. Tāni sāsanānulomāni na hontīti idha na dassitāni. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana “māro, namuci, kaṇho, pamattabandhū”ti cattāriyeva nāmāni āgatāni.

Others mention other names as well. Since they are not in conformity with the Dispensation, they are not shown here. In the commentaries, however, only four names are found: Māra, Namuci, Kaṇha, and Pamattabandhu.

Idāni abhikkantasaddassa bhūvādigaṇe “kamu padavikkhepe”ti vohārasīsena vuttassa kamudhātussa vasena idha ca “kamu icchākantīsū”ti vuttassa kamudhātussa vasena atthuddhāraṃ kathayāma. Abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanesu dissati. “Abhikkantā bhante ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho”tiādīsu khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”tiādīsu sundare.

Now we shall explain the meaning of the word abhikkanta based on the root kam from the bhūvādi group, mentioned under the heading 'kam in the sense of stepping forward,' and also based on the root kam mentioned here in the sense of 'desire and loveliness.' The word abhikkanta is seen in the senses of passing, beauty, excellence, and approval. In the sense of passing, as in: 'Venerable sir, the night has passed, the first watch is over, the Saṅgha has been sitting for a long time.' In the sense of beauty, as in: 'This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons.'

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti

“Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with spiritual power and glory, with surpassing beauty, illuminating all the quarters?”

Ādīsu abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ bhante”tiādīsu abbhanumodane. Iccevaṃ –

In such passages, in the sense of excellence. In such passages as, ‘Excellent, venerable sir!’, in the sense of approval. Thus:

Khayasmiṃ sundare ceva, atho abbhanumodane;

Abhirūpe abhikkanta-saddo dissati sāsane.

In passing away and in beauty, and also in approval and in excellence, the word abhikkanta is seen in the Dispensation.

Thoma silāghāyaṃ. Silāghā pasaṃsā. Thometi, thomayati. Thomito, thomanā.

The root thom is in the sense of praise. Praise means commendation. The forms are thometi and thomayati. Derived forms are thomito and thomanā.

Yama aparivesane. Yameti, yamayati. Yamo.

The root yam is in the sense of restraining. The forms are yameti and yamayati. The noun is Yamo.

Sama [M 0.0333] vitakke. Sāmeti, sāmayati. Samā. Nisāmeti, nisāmayati. Nisāmanaṃ. Paṭisāmeti, paṭisāmayati. Paṭisāmanaṃ.

The root sam is in the sense of thinking. The forms are sāmeti and sāmayati. A derived noun is samā. With the prefix ni-, the forms are nisāmeti and nisāmayati, and the noun is nisāmanaṃ. With the prefix paṭi-, the forms are paṭisāmeti and paṭisāmayati, and the noun is paṭisāmanaṃ.

Tattha samāti saṃvaccharo, so “samā”ti itthiliṅgavasena vuccati. “Yo yajetha sataṃ sama”nti ettha hi samāsaddo itthiliṅgo, upayogavasena pana “sama”nti vutto.

Therein, samā means a year; it is expressed as samā in the feminine gender. For in the quote, ‘Yo yajetha sataṃ sama,’ the word sama is feminine, but it is cited as sama based on usage.

Imāni saṃvaccharassa nāmāni “saṃvaccharo, vaccharo, samā, hāyano, sarado, vasso”tiādīni bhavanti. Nisāmetīti vitakketi upadhāreti. Ettha hi “iṅgha maddi nisāmehi, nigghoso yādiso vane”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha nisāmehīti vitakkehi upadhārehīti attho. Paṭisāmetīti bhaṇḍaṃ guttaṭṭhāne nikkhipati.

These are the names for a year: saṃvaccharo, vaccharo, samā, hāyano, sarado, vasso, and so on. Nisāmeti means one thinks, one considers. Here the Pāli example is: ‘Come, Maddi, consider what kind of noise this is in the forest.’ There, nisāmehi means ‘think,’ ‘consider.’ Paṭisāmeti means one puts away goods in a protected place.

Sama ālocane. Ālocanaṃ pekkhanaṃ. Sāmeti, sāmayati. Nisāmanaṃ.

The root sam is in the sense of looking at. Looking at means seeing. The forms are sāmeti and sāmayati. A derived noun is nisāmanaṃ.

Ettha pana nisāmetīti pekkhati oloketi. Tathā hi “iṅgha maddi nisāmehi, cittaṃ rūpaṃva dissatī”ti pāḷi dissati. Tattha hi nisāmehīti olokehīti attho. Dhātūnamatthātisayena yogoti vacanato pana upasaggayogato vā savanepi ayaṃ vattati. Tathā hi “tato kaṇhājināyāpi, nisāmehi rathesabhā”tiādikā pāḷiyo dissanti. Tattha nisāmehīti suṇohīti attho.

Here, however, nisāmeti means one sees, one looks at. Thus the Pāli is seen: ‘Come, Maddi, look, a variegated form like a painting appears.’ There, nisāmehi means ‘look.’ However, in accordance with the principle that roots have a variety of meanings, or because of its connection with a prefix, this root also functions in the sense of hearing. Thus Pāli passages such as the following are seen: ‘Then, O bull among charioteers, listen even to the black antelope skin.’ There, nisāmehi means ‘listen.’

Ama roge. Ameti, amayati. Andho. Bilaṅkapādo andhanakho.

The root am is in the sense of sickness. The forms are ameti and amayati. A derived word is andho. For example: ‘lame of foot, with diseased nails.’

Tattha andhoti naṭṭhanayano vuccati. Andhanakhoti pūtinakho. Ubhayathāpi sarogattaṃ sūcitaṃ.

Therein, andho means one whose eyes are destroyed. Andhanakho means one with rotten nails. In both cases, a state of sickness is indicated.

Bhāma [M 0.0334] kodhe. Bhāmeti, bhāmayati.

The root bhām is in the sense of anger. The forms are bhāmeti and bhāmayati.

Goma upalepane. Gometi, gomayati.

The root gom is in the sense of smearing. The forms are gometi and gomayati.

Sāma svāntane āmantane. Svāntanaṃ sāmappayogo. Āmantanaṃ avhāyanaṃ pakkosanaṃ. Sāmeti, sāmayati.

The root sām is in the senses of consoling and addressing. Consoling is the use of conciliation. Addressing is calling or summoning. The forms are sāmeti and sāmayati.

Saṅgāma yuddhe. Saṅgāmeti, saṅgāmayati. Dve rājāno saṅgāmesuṃ. Saṅgāmo. Āto gamu īsamadhivāsane. Āgameti, āgamayati, kāmāvacaradhamme nissāya rūpārūpadhammo samudāgameti, samudāgamayati. Upāsako dhammasavanantarāyaṃ anicchanto “āgametha āgamethā”ti āha. Samudāgamanaṃ, āgamanaṃ. Āgamento, āgamayamāno.

The root saṅgām is in the sense of battle. The forms are saṅgāmeti and saṅgāmayati. For example: ‘Two kings battled.’ The noun is saṅgāmo. The root gam with the prefix ā is in the sense of waiting for a little while. The forms are āgameti and āgamayati. For example: ‘Relying on sense-sphere phenomena, form and formless phenomena arise and are caused to arise.’ And: ‘A lay follower, not wishing for an obstacle to hearing the Dhamma, said: “Please wait, please wait!”’ Derived nouns are samudāgamanaṃ and āgamanaṃ. Derived participles are āgamento and āgamayamāno.

Tatra āgametīti īsakaṃ adhivāseti. Samudāgametīti sampavattati. Bhūvādigaṇe “gamayatī”ti hetukattuvasena vuttaṃ, idha pana upasagganipātapubbakāni katvā “āgametī”tiādīni suddhakattuvasena vuttānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Therein, āgameti means one waits for a little while. Samudāgameti means one occurs or proceeds. It should be understood that while in the bhūvādi group gamayati is said to be in the causative sense, here forms such as āgameti, being preceded by prefixes and particles, are said to be in the simple active sense.

Makārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of roots ending in the letter m.

Iti cu rādigaṇe pavaggantadhāturūpāni

Thus in the curādi group are the forms of roots ending in the labial class.

Samattāni.

Completed.

Yakārantadhātu

Roots ending in the letter y.

Yu jigucchāyaṃ. Yāveti, yāvayati. Yavo.

The root yu is in the sense of loathing. The forms are yāveti and yāvayati. A derived noun is yavo.

Byaya khaye. Byayeti, byayayati. Abyayībhāvo.

The root byaya is in the sense of destruction. The forms are byayeti and byayayati. A derived noun is abbyayībhāvo.

Byaya cittasamussagge. Tādisaṃyeva rūpaṃ.

The root byaya is in the sense of abandoning thought. The forms are just the same.

Yakārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of roots ending in the letter y.

Rakārantadhātu

Roots ending in the letter r.

Para gatiyaṃ. Pareti, parayati. Ettha ca “iti kho ānanda kusalāni sīlāni anupubbena aggāya parentī”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Tattha aggāya parentīti arahattatthāya gacchanti.

The root para is in the sense of going. The forms are pareti and parayati. Here, the Pāli passage is an example: “Thus indeed, Ānanda, wholesome virtues gradually lead to the highest.” There, “lead to the highest” means they go to the state of arahantship.

Gara uggame. Gareti, garayati. Garu.

The root gara is in the sense of rising. The forms are gareti and garayati. A derived noun is garu.

Cara asaṃsaye. Careti, carayati.

The root cara is in the sense of faring without doubt. The forms are careti and carayati.

Pūri appāyane. Pūreti, pūrayati.

The root pūri is in the sense of filling. The forms are pūreti and pūrayati.

Vara icchāyaṃ. Vareti, varayati. Varo, varaṃ, varanto. Ete varānaṃ caturo varemi. Etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare.

Vara: in the sense of wishing. Vareti, varayati. Varo, varaṃ, varanto. “These four boons I choose. This boon, O Sakka, I choose.”

Tattha varoti variyate varitabboti varo. Varanti varetīti varaṃ, icchanto patthentoti attho.

Therein, 'varo' is that which is chosen or ought to be chosen. 'Varaṃ' is so called because they choose or he chooses; the meaning is desiring, aspiring.

“Mahāmahārahaṃ sakya-muni nīvaraṇā raṇā;

Muttaṃ muttaṃ sudassanaṃ, vande bodhivaraṃ vara”nti

“The great and greatly precious Sakyamuni, free from hindrances and defilements; Released, released, beautiful to behold, I venerate the excellent Bodhi, the best.”

Purāṇakaviracanāyaṃ “vara”nti padassa viya. Evaṃ varetīti varanto. Vareti varemi icchāmi yācāmi. Kārite “pavāretī”ti rūpaṃ, icchāpetīti attho. Nisedhanatthe panidaṃ kāritaṃ na hoti.

Like the word “vara” in the compositions of ancient poets. Thus, one who chooses is 'varanto'. The verb is `vareti`; `varemi` means 'I choose', 'I desire', 'I ask'. In the causative, the form is 'pavāreti', meaning 'he causes to wish'. However, this causative is not used in a prohibitive sense.

Sara akkhepe. Sareti, sarayati. Saro. Saroti saddo.

Sara: in the sense of casting. Sareti, sarayati. Saro. Saro means a sound.

Sāra dubbalye. Sāreti, sārayati. Dubbalo bhavatīti attho.

Sāra: in the sense of weakening. Sāreti, sārayati. The meaning is that one becomes weak.

Kumāra kīḷāyaṃ. Kumāreti, kumārayati. Kumāro, kumārako. Kumārī, kumārikā.

Kumāra: in the sense of playing. Kumāreti, kumārayati. Kumāro (a boy), kumārako (a young boy). Kumārī (a girl), kumārikā (a young girl).

Ettha [M 0.0336] kumārayati tattha tattha kīḷatīti kumāro. So eva atidaharattā kumārako. Esa nayo itaratrāpi.

Here, ‘kumāro’ is so called because he plays here and there. He is a ‘kumārako’ because he is very young. This method applies elsewhere as well.

Sūra vīra vikkantiyaṃ. Vikkanti vikkamanaṃ. Sūreti, sūrayati. Vīreti, vīrayati. Sūro, vīro. Sāsanikehi pana saddhammavidūhi evaṃ dhātusabhāvānampi sūravīrasaddānaṃ nibbacanaṃ na dassitaṃ, kevalaṃ pana tattha tattha “sūroti visiṭṭhauro”ti ca “mahāvīroti mahāvikkanto”ti ca “vīroti vīriyavā”ti ca atthavivaraṇamattameva dassitaṃ.

Sūra, Vīra: in the sense of valor. Valor means striding forth. Sūreti, sūrayati. Vīreti, vīrayati. Sūro (a hero), vīro (a warrior). However, by those learned in the true doctrine, such a derivation of the words “sūra” and “vīra” from the inherent nature of the roots has not been shown; rather, only mere explanations of meaning have been shown in various contexts, such as “‘sūro’ means ‘one with a distinguished chest,’” “‘mahāvīro’ means ‘one of great prowess,’” and “‘vīro’ means ‘one who is energetic.’”

Pāra tīra kammasampattiyaṃ. Kammasampatti nāma kammassa parisamāpanaṃ niṭṭhāpanaṃ. Pāreti, pārayati. Tīreti, tīrayati. Pāraṃ. Tīraṃ. Vikkamāmi na pāremi, bhūmiṃ sumbhāmi vegasā. Taṃ kiccaṃ tīretvā gato. Santīraṇaṃ, tīraṇapariññāti ca ādīni ettha dassetabbāni.

Pāra, Tīra: in the sense of accomplishing action. Accomplishment of action means the completion and finishing of action. Pāreti, pārayati. Tīreti, tīrayati. Pāraṃ (the far shore). Tīraṃ (the near shore). “I strive, I do not reach the far shore, I shake the earth with speed.” Having finished that task, he went. Santīraṇaṃ (investigation), tīraṇapariññā (full understanding through investigation), and so on should be shown here.

Tattha na pāremīti chindituṃ na sakkomīti attho.

Therein, ‘na pāremi’ means ‘I am unable to cut off’.

Īra khepane. Īreti, īrayati.

Īra: in the sense of shaking. Īreti, īrayati.

Jara vayohānimhi. Jareti, jarayati. Jarā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “jīratī”ti pāṭho.

Jara: in the sense of decline of age. Jareti, jarayati. Jarā (old age). In the Pāli, however, the reading is “jīratī” (he decays).

Vara āvaraṇe. Vāreti, vārayati. Nivāreti, nivārayati. Nivāretā. Parivāreti, parivārayati. Parivāro. Pavāreti, pavārayati. Pavāraṇaṃ. Pavāraṇanti nisedhanaṃ vā kāmyadānaṃ vā.

Vara: in the sense of obstructing. Vāreti, vārayati. Nivāreti, nivārayati. Nivāretā (one who prevents). Parivāreti, parivārayati. Parivāro (retinue). Pavāreti, pavārayati. Pavāraṇaṃ (invitation). “Pavāraṇa” means either prohibition or voluntary offering.

Dhara dhāraṇe. Dhāreti, dhārayati. Ādhāro, ādhārako, dhammo iccādīni.

Dhara: in the sense of holding. Dhāreti, dhārayati. Ādhāro (support), ādhārako (supporter), dhammo (Dhamma), and so on.

Tattha dhammoti anekavidhesu dhammesu lokuttaro uppādito sacchikato ca catūsu apāyesu saṃsāre vā [M 0.0337] satte apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo. Atha vā sotāpannādīhi ariyehi dhāriyati, nu puthujjanehītipi dhammo. Catubhūmiko pana sakalakkhaṇaṃ dhāretīti dhammo. Kakkhaḷattādinā phusanādinā santiādinā sakasakabhāvena paṇḍitehi dhāriyati sallakkhiyatītipi dhammo. Tepiṭako pana pāḷidhammo sakatthaparatthādibhee atthe dhāretīti dhammo. Keci tu vidū “pāpake akusale dhamme dhunāti kampeti viddhaṃsetīti dhammo”ti dhūdhātuvasenapi nibbacanaṃ vadanti, taṃ maggadhamme atīva yujjati, phalanibbānapariyattidhammesu pana pariyāyena yujjati.

Therein, “Dhamma” is so called because the transcendent Dhamma, produced and realized among various dhammas, upholds beings, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery or into the cycle of existence. Or, it is called “Dhamma” because it is upheld by the noble ones, from stream-enterers onward, and not by ordinary people. The fourfold Dhamma is called “Dhamma” because it upholds its own characteristics. It is also called “Dhamma” because the wise uphold and discern it through hardness, contact, peacefulness, and so on, each in its own nature. The Tipiṭaka, the Pāli Dhamma, is called “Dhamma” because it upholds meanings beneficial to oneself and others. Some scholars, however, say that the derivation is from the root “dhū” (to shake), meaning “it shakes, agitates, and destroys evil, unwholesome states,” which is very fitting for the path Dhamma, but only figuratively applies to the fruition, Nibbāna, and the Dhamma of learning (pariyatti).

Dhammasaddo pariyattihetuguṇanissattanijjīvatādīsu dissati. Ayañhi “dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāti suttaṃ geyya”ntiādīsu pariyattiyaṃ dissati. “Hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu hetumhi.

The word “Dhamma” is seen in contexts such as learning, cause, quality, non-sentience, lifelessness, and so on. For indeed, in “he learns the Dhamma, the suttas, the geyyas,” and so on, it is seen in the sense of learning. In “knowledge of cause is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma,” and so on, it is seen in the sense of cause.

“Na hi dhammo adhammo ca, ubho samavipākino;

Adhammo nirayaṃ neti, dhammo pāpeti suggati”nti

“Indeed, Dhamma and what is not Dhamma do not have the same result; what is not Dhamma leads to hell, Dhamma brings one to a good destination.”

Ādīsu guṇe. “Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā honti. Dhammesu dhammānupassī viharatī”tiādīsu nissattanijjīvatāyaṃ.

And so on, in the sense of quality. In “At that time, there are phenomena. One dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena,” and so on, it is seen in the sense of non-sentience and lifelessness.

Atha vā dhammasaddo sabhāvapaññāpuññapaññattiāpattipariyattinissattanijjīvatāvikāraguṇapacca- yapaccayuppannādīsu dissati. Ayañhi “kusalā dhammā akusalā dhammā abyākatā dhammā”tiādīsu sabhāve dissati.

Alternatively, the word “Dhamma” is seen in various contexts such as nature, wisdom, merit, designation, transgression, learning, non-sentience and lifelessness, modification, quality, cause, and what has arisen from a cause. For indeed, in phrases like “wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, indeterminate phenomena,” and so on, it is seen in the sense of nature.

Yassete [M 0.0338] caturo dhammā, saddhassa gharamesino;

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, sa ve pecca na socatī”ti

“Whoever possesses these four qualities—a faithful householder: truth, Dhamma (wisdom), steadfastness, and generosity—that one does not grieve after passing away.”

Ādīsu paññāyaṃ.

And so on, in the sense of wisdom.

“Na hi dhammo adhammo ca, ubho samavipākino;

Adhammo nirayaṃ neti, dhammo pāpeti suggati”ntiādīsu

“For truly, Dhamma and what is not Dhamma do not have the same result; what is not Dhamma leads to hell, Dhamma brings one to a happy destination,” and so on.

Puññe. “Paññattidhammā, niruttidhammā, adhivacanādhammā”tiādīsu paññattiyaṃ. “Pārājikā dhammā, saṅghādisesā dhammā”tiādīsu āpattiyaṃ. “Idha bhikkhu dhammaṃ jānāti suttaṃ geyyaṃ veyyākaraṇa”ntiādīsu pariyattiyaṃ. “Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā honti. Dhammesu dhammānupassī viharatī”tiādīsu nissattanijjīvatāyaṃ. “Jātidhammā jarādhammā maraṇadhammā”tiādīsu vikāre. “Channaṃ buddhadhammāna”ntiādīsu guṇe. “Hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu paccaye. “Ṭhitāvasā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā”tiādīsu paccayuppanne.

In the sense of merit. In “designations, linguistic expressions, appellations,” and so on, in the sense of designation. In “Pārājika offenses, Saṅghādisesa offenses,” and so on, in the sense of transgression. In “Here, a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma—suttas, geyyas, and vyākaraṇas,” and so on, in the sense of learning. In “At that time, there are phenomena. One dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena,” and so on, in the sense of non-sentience and lifelessness. In “subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to death,” and so on, in the sense of modification. In “of the six Buddha-qualities,” and so on, in the sense of quality. In “knowledge of cause is the analytical knowledge of Dhamma,” and so on, in the sense of cause. In “the established element, the stability of Dhamma, the orderliness of Dhamma,” and so on, in the sense of what has arisen from conditions.

Atha vā dhammasaddo pariyattisaccasamādhipaññāpakatipuññāpattiñeyyādīsu bahūsu atthesu diṭṭhappayogo. Tathā hi “idha bhikkhu dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇātī”tiādīsu pariyattiyaṃ dissati. “Diṭṭhadhammo pattadhammo”tiādīsu sacce. “Evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto ahesu”ntiādīsu samādhimhi. “Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo”ti evamādīsu paññāyaṃ. “Jātidhammānaṃ bhikkhave sattāna”nti evamādīsu pakatiyaṃ. “Dhammo have rakkhati dhammacāri”nti evamādīsu puññe. “Cattāro pārājikā dhammā”tiādīsu [M 0.0339] āpattiyaṃ. “Kusalā dhammā”tiādīsu ñeyye. Evaṃ dhammasaddappavattivisayā vividhā aṭṭhakathācariyehi dassitā, tattha tattha pana ādisaddena yuttivisayādayo ca atthā gahetabbā. Tathā hi dhammasaddo –

Alternatively, the word “Dhamma” is seen applied in many meanings such as learning, truth, concentration, wisdom, nature, merit, transgression, the knowable, and so on. For instance, in phrases like “Here, a bhikkhu learns the Dhamma,” and so on, it is seen in the sense of learning. In “One who has seen Dhamma, attained Dhamma,” and so on, it refers to truth. In “Such were the qualities of those Blessed Ones,” and so on, it refers to concentration. In “Truth, Dhamma (wisdom), steadfastness, generosity,” and similar phrases, it refers to wisdom. In “Bhikkhus, beings are subject to birth,” and so on, it refers to nature. In “Dhamma, indeed, protects one who practices Dhamma,” and so on, it refers to merit. In “The four Pārājika offenses,” and so on, it refers to transgression. In “Wholesome phenomena,” and so on, it refers to the knowable. Thus, the various domains in which the word “Dhamma” is applied have been shown by the commentators. In each case, meanings such as appropriateness and others should be understood accordingly. Indeed, the word “Dhamma”—

“Nesa dhammo mahārāja, yaṃ tvaṃ gaccheyya ekako;

Ahampi tena gacchāmi, yena gacchasi khattiyā”ti

“Great king, it is not proper that you should go alone; I also go by that path by which you go, O warrior.”

Ādīsu yuttiyaṃ vattati. “Manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇa”ntiādīsu visaye. “Satañca dhammo na jaraṃ upetī”ti ettha nibbāne vattati. Tatra yā nissattatā, sā eva nijjīvatā. Yo ca hetu, so eva paccayo.

And so on, it functions in the sense of appropriateness. In “Depending on mind and phenomena, mind-consciousness arises,” and so on, it is seen in the sense of object. In “And the Dhamma of the good does not age,” here it refers to Nibbāna. There, whatever is non-sentience, that itself is lifelessness. And whatever is the cause, that itself is the condition.

Iccevaṃ –

Thus indeed—

Pariyattipaccayesu, guṇe nissattatāya ca;

Sabhāve ceva paññāyaṃ, puññe paññattiyampi ca.

In learning and conditions, in quality and non-sentience; And in nature and wisdom, in merit and designation as well.

Āpattiyaṃ vikāre ca, paccayuppannakepi ca;

Saccasamādhipakati-ñeyyesu yuttiyampi ca;

Visaye ceva nibbāne, dhammasaddo pavattati.

In transgression and modification, and also in what has arisen from conditions; In truth, concentration, nature, and the knowable, and in appropriateness; In object and Nibbāna, the word “Dhamma” is applied.

Keci pana dhammasaddassa pavattivisayānaṃ dasadhāva paricchedaṃ vadanti.

Some, however, state a tenfold division of the spheres of application of the term 'dhamma'.

Ñeyyamagge ca nibbāne, sabhāve atha jātiyaṃ;

Mane visayapuññesu, bhāve pāvacanepi ca;

Imesu dasasvatthesu, dhammasaddo pavattati.

In the knowable, the path, and Nibbāna; in inherent nature and in birth; in the mind, in sense objects, and in merits; in existence and also in the teaching; in these ten meanings the term 'dhamma' is used.

Tatra atthuddhāroti samānasaddavacanīyānaṃ atthānaṃ uddharaṇaṃ atthuddhāro.

Therein, 'extraction of meaning' is the extraction of meanings from homonymous terms; this is the extraction of meaning.

Rakārantadhāturūpāni.

Root forms ending in 'ra'.

Lakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'la'.

Pāla [M 0.0340] rakkhaṇe. “Rakkhaṇaṃ, tāṇaṃ, gopanaṃ, avanaṃ, pālanaṃ, rakkhā, rakkhaṇā, gutti” iccete pariyāyā. Pāleti, pālayati. Pālako, buddhapālo. Ambapālī gaṇikā. Samo bhavatu pālinā. Pālito, pālanaṃ, pāḷi.

Pāl, in the sense of protection. 'Protection, shelter, guarding, defense, preservation, protection, the act of protecting, security'—these are synonyms. He protects. A protector, Buddhapāla. Ambapālī the courtesan. May he be equal to the protector. Protected, protection, Pāḷi.

Ettha pāḷīti atthaṃ pāletīti pāḷi, lassa ḷattaṃ. Atha vā antodakaṃ rakkhaṇaṭṭhena mahato taḷākassa thirā mahatīti pāḷi viyāti pāḷi, pariyattidhammo. Aparo nayo pakaṭṭhānaṃ ukkaṭṭhānaṃ sīlādiatthānaṃ bodhanato sabhāvaniruttibhāvato buddhādīhi bhāsitattā ca pakaṭṭhānaṃ vacanappabandhānaṃ āḷīti pāḷi.

Herein, 'Pāḷi' is so called because it protects the meaning; hence pāḷi, with the l becoming ḷ.
