Or, just as a great and firm embankment (pāḷi) of a large lake protects the water within, so too is the Pāḷi, the scriptural teaching (pariyattidhammo). Another method: because it makes known the meaning of excellent and sublime things such as virtue, because of its nature as the definitive language, and because it was spoken by the Buddha and others, it is a 'row' (āḷi) of excellent verbal compositions, hence 'Pāḷi'.

Pāḷisaddo pāḷidhamme, taḷākapāḷiyampi ca;

Dissate pantiyañceva, iti ñeyyaṃ vijānatā.

The word 'Pāḷi' is seen in the sense of the Pāḷi Dhamma, and also of a lake's embankment; it is also seen in the sense of a row; thus it should be understood by the discerning.

Ayañhi “pāḷiyā atthamupaparikkhantī”tiādīsu pariyattidhammasaṅkhāte pāḷidhamme dissati. “Mahato taḷākassa pāḷī”tiādīsu taḷākapāḷiyaṃ. “Pāḷiyā nisīdiṃsū”tiādīsu pantiyaṃ, paṭipāṭiyā nisīdiṃsūti attho. Imasmiṃ panatthe dhātuyā kiccaṃ natthi. Pāṭipadiko hi pantivācako pāḷisaddo.

For this word is seen in the Pāḷi Dhamma, which is reckoned as the scriptural teaching, in such phrases as 'examining the meaning of the Pāḷi.' In such phrases as 'the embankment of a great lake,' it is seen in the sense of a lake's embankment. In such phrases as 'they sat in a row,' it is seen in the sense of a row; the meaning is 'they sat in sequence.' In this last meaning, however, the root has no function, for the word 'Pāḷi' denoting a row is a nominal stem.

Tila sinehane. Teleti, telayati. Telaṃ, tilo, tilaṃ.

Til, in the sense of oiling. He oils; he lubricates. Oil, the sesame plant, a sesame seed.

Tattha tiloti tilagaccho. Tilanti tapphalaṃ. Tato pana nikkhanto sineho telaṃ. So hi “tilānaṃ idanti tela”nti vuccati. Yadi evaṃ “sāsapatela”ntiādivacanaṃ na yujjeyyāti? No na yujjati, “tilasinehane”ti evaṃ vuttāya tiladhātuyā sāmaññato yassa [M 0.0341] kassaci sinehassa vacanato. Tena “sāsapatelaṃ, madhukatela”ntiādayo sāsane payogā dissanti. Mayaṃ pana tiladhātuvasena nipphannānaṃ tilagacchatapphalavācakānaṃ “tilo, tila”nti saddarūpānaṃ pakāsanamukhena “tilānaṃ idanti tela”nti vadāma, na pana tena vacanena sāsapādīnaṃ sinehassa atelattaṃ vadāma. Atha kiñcarahīti ce? Taddhitavidhāne viññunaṃ kosallatthaṃ tilasaddaṃ paṭicca “tilānaṃ idanti tela”nti vadāma. Sinehasaṅkhātassa sāsapādīnaṃ telassa vacanaṃ na jahāma, tasmā udāharaṇappakāsane “tilo, tilaṃ, tela”nti avatvā “telaṃ, tilo, tila”nti amhehi vuttaṃ. Idañhi vacanaṃ telassa sāmaññato sinehe pavattiṃ dīpeti. Teneva ca sāsane “tilatelaṃ, sāsapatela”ntiādinā visesavacanampi dissatīti niṭṭhametthāvagantabbaṃ. Apica telasaddo yebhuyyena tilatele vattati, yathā migasaddo hariṇamigetipi daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Therein, tilo refers to the sesame plant; tilaṃ means its fruit. The unctuous substance extracted from it is telaṃ (oil). For it is said: 'This of the sesame seeds is oil.' If so, would expressions such as 'mustard oil' not be correct? No, it is not incorrect, because of the general application to any unctuous substance of the root til, which is stated in the sense of 'oiling.' Thus, usages such as 'mustard oil' and 'madhuka oil' are seen in the teaching. We, however, explain 'oil' as 'this of the sesame seeds' by way of demonstrating the word-forms tilo and tilaṃ, which are derived from the root til and denote the sesame plant and its fruit; but by this statement we do not deny that the unctuous substance of mustard and so on is oil. If you ask what the reason is, we say 'this of the sesame seeds is oil' based on the word tila for the sake of the skill of the wise in forming secondary derivatives. We do not abandon the word 'oil' for the unctuous substance of mustard and so on. Therefore, in presenting the examples, we have said 'oil, sesame plant, sesame seed' (telaṃ, tilo, tilaṃ) instead of 'sesame plant, sesame seed, oil' (tilo, tilaṃ, telaṃ). This statement shows the general application of 'oil' to any unctuous substance. For this very reason, specific expressions such as 'sesame oil' and 'mustard oil' are also seen in the teaching. This should be understood as the conclusion here. Furthermore, the word 'oil' is mostly used for sesame oil, just as the word miga (beast) should be understood as also used for a deer.

Jala apavāraṇe. Jāleti, jālayati. Jālaṃ, jālā. Jālanti macchajālaṃ. Jālāti aggijālā.

Jal, in the sense of kindling. He kindles. A net, a flame. Jālaṃ means a fish-net. Jālā means a flame of fire.

Khala soceyye. Soceyyaṃ sucibhāvo. Khāleti, khālayati. Pakkhāleti, pakkhālayati.

Khal, in the sense of purity. Purity is the state of being clean. He washes. He washes off; he rinses.

Tala patiṭṭhāyaṃ. Tāleti, tālayati. Tālo, talaṃ.

Tal, in the sense of establishing. He establishes; he fixes. Palmyra tree, a surface.

Ettha tāloti tiṇarājarukkho. Talanti pāṇitalabhūmitalādi. Tañhi tālayati patiṭṭhāti ettha vatthujātanti talaṃ.

Herein, tālo means the palmyra tree. Talaṃ refers to the palm of the hand, the surface of the ground, and so on. It is called talaṃ because a collection of things is established or stands firm on it.

Tula ummāne. Toleti, tolayati.

Tul, in the sense of weighing. He weighs.

Dula [M 0.0342] ukkhepe. Ukkhepo uddhaṃ khipanaṃ. Doleti, dolayati. Dolā.

Dul, in the sense of tossing up. Tossing up is throwing upwards. He swings. A swing.

Ettha ca doliyati ukkhipiyati yattha nipanno dārako, yathānipannako vāti dolā.

And here, that in which a child who is lying down, or anyone lying down, is swung or tossed up, is a dolā.

Vula nimmajjane. Voleti, voyalati.

Vul, in the sense of immersing. He immerses.

Mīla nimīlane. Mīleti, mīlayati. Mīlanaṃ, ummīlanaṃ, nimīlanaṃ.

Mīl, in the sense of closing the eyes. He closes the eyes. Closing, opening, shutting.

Mūla rohane. Mūleti, mūlayati. Mūlaṃ. Esā hi yadā patiṭṭhāyaṃ vattati, tadā bhūvādigaṇikā, “mūlatī”ti cassā rūpaṃ.

Mūl, in the sense of rooting. He causes to take root; he establishes. A root. When this root is used in the sense of establishing, it belongs to the bhū-group, and its form is mūlati.

Tattha mūlanti mūlayati rūhati rukkhādi etenāti mūlaṃ. Atha vā mūlayati chinnopi koci etena acchinnena punadeva rūhatīti mūlaṃ. Vuttañhi –

Herein, a mūla is so called because by means of it a tree or the like is caused to take root and grows. Or, it is a mūla because by means of it, when it is uncut, something that has been cut grows again. For it has been said:

“Yathāpi mūle anupaddave daḷhe,

Chinnopi rukkho punadeva rūhati;

Evampi taṇhānusaye anūhate,

Nibbattati dukkhamidaṃ punappuna”nti;

Just as a tree with roots unharmed and firm, though cut down, grows up again, so too, as long as the underlying tendency to craving is not uprooted, this suffering is generated again and again.

Mūlasaddassa atthuddhāro heṭṭhā bhūvādigaṇe vutto.

The extraction of the meaning of the word mūla has been stated below under the bhū-group.

Kala pila khepe. Kāleti, kālayati. Kālo. Pileti, pilayati.

Kal and pil, in the sense of casting. He casts. Time. He casts.

Ettha kāloti samayopi maccupi. Tatra samayo tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ āyuṃ kālayati khepeti divase divase appaṃ appaṃ karotīti kāloti vuccati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Herein, kālo means both time and death. Therein, time is called kālo because it casts away, that is, it diminishes, the lifespan of beings day by day, making it ever less; thus it is called kālo. And this has been said:

“Kālo ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā;

Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto, sabhūtapacaniṃpacī”ti.

Time devours all beings, including itself; but he who devours time has cooked the cooker of all beings.

Maccu [M 0.0343] pana kālayati tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ khepeti samucchedavasena nāsetīti kāloti vuccati. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā “kāloti maccu. Kālayati sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ nāsetīti kālo. Kālena maccunā kato nāsitoti kālakato”ti. “Maraṇaṃ hindaṃ maccu maṭṭu cuti kālo antako nikkhepo”ti maraṇassābhidhānāni.

Death, however, is called kālo because it casts away, that is, consumes, the life of beings, destroying it by way of complete annihilation. Therefore the commentators have said: 'Kālo means death. It is kālo because it casts away, that is, destroys, the life of beings. One whose end is made (kato) by time (kālena), that is, by death, is kālakato (deceased).' 'Death (maraṇaṃ), dying (maccu, maṭṭu), passing away (cuti), time (kālo), the end-maker (antako), the laying down (nikkhepo)'—these are designations for death.

Sulla sajjane. Sulleti, sullayati.

Sull, in the sense of preparing. He impales.

Ila peraṇe. Ileti, ilayati.

Il, in the sense of moving. He moves.

Vala bharaṇe. Vāleti, vālayati. Vālo.

Vala, in the sense of bearing. He bears; he carries. Horse-hair.

Lala icchāyaṃ. Laleti, lalayati.

Lala, in the sense of desire. He desires; he sports.

Dala vidāraṇe. Dāleti, dālayati, padāleti, padālayati. Kudālo.

Dala, in the sense of splitting. He splits; he splits apart. A spade.

Kala gatisaṅkhyānesu. Kāleti, kālayati. Kālo, kalā. Kalāti avayavo. Sā hi kālayitabbā saṅkhāyitabbāti kalā.

Kala, in the senses of motion and enumeration. He drives; he enumerates. Time, a portion. A kalā is a part. It is called kalā because it is to be impelled or to be enumerated.

Sīla upadhāraṇe. Upadhāraṇaṃ bhuso dhāraṇaṃ, patiṭṭhāvasena ādhārabhāvo. Sīleti, sīlayati. Sīlaṃ, sīlanaṃ.

Sīla, in the sense of upholding. Upholding is firm retention, the state of being a support in the sense of a foundation. He practises. Virtue, concentration.

Ettha sīlanti sīleti upadhāreti taṃsamaṅgīpuggalaṃ apāyesu uppattinivāraṇavasena bhuso dhāretīti sīlaṃ. Atha vāsīliyati upacāriyati sappurisehi hadayamaṃsantaraṃ upanetvā dhāriyatīti sīlaṃ. Sīlananti bhūvādigaṇe avippakiṇṇatāsaṅkhātaṃ samādhānaṃ vuccati. Tattha “sīlatī”ti rūpaṃ, idha pana ādhārabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ upadhāraṇaṃ vuccati. Ettha ca “sīleti, sīlayatī”ti rūpāni. Aṭṭhakathāsu hi “kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ [M 0.0344] patiṭṭhāvasena ādhārabhāvo upadhāraṇa”nti vutto.

Herein, sīla is so called because it upholds: it firmly holds the person endowed with it by preventing his rebirth in the planes of misery. Or, it is sīla because it is practised, that is, frequented, by good people, being held by them as dear to their hearts. Sīlana in the bhū-group refers to concentration, defined as non-distraction. There the form is sīlati. Here, however, upholding, defined as the state of being a support, is meant. And here the forms are sīleti and sīlayati. For in the commentaries it is said: 'Upholding is the state of being a support, in the sense of a foundation, for wholesome qualities.'

Vela kālopadese. Veleti, velayati. Velā. Keci “vela iti dhātusaddo na hotī”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ, porāṇehi saddasatthavidūhi “velayatī”ti rūpassa dassitattā.

Vela, in the sense of indicating time. He indicates time. Time. Some say, 'The root-word vela does not exist,' but this should not be accepted, since the form velayati has been shown by the ancient grammarians.

Pala mūla lavanapavanesu. Lavanaṃ chedanaṃ, pavanaṃ sodhanaṃ. Pāleti, pālayati. Palaṃ. Palaṃ nāma mānaviseso. Lokassa vimatiṃ pāleti lunāti sodheti cāti palaṃ. Mūleti, mūlayati. Saddasatthavidū pana “mūlayati kedāraṃ, mūlayati dhañña”nti payogaṃ vadanti.

Pala and Mūla, in the senses of cutting and cleansing. Cutting is severing; cleansing is purifying. From Pala: Pāleti, pālayati: he protects. Palaṃ: a pala. A pala is a specific measure. It is called a pala because it protects from, cuts off, and cleanses the world's doubt. From Mūla: Mūleti, mūlayati: he prices. Grammarians, however, state the usage: 'He prepares the field, he buys the grain.'

Thūla paribrūhane. Paribrūhanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ. Thūleti, thūlayati. Thūlo puriso. Thūlā javena hāyanti.

Thūla, in the sense of making stout. Making stout is increasing. Thūleti, thūlayati: he makes stout. A stout man. The stout decline with speed.

Pala gatiyaṃ. Paleti, palayati. Atthaṃ paleti na upeti saṅkhaṃ. Paleti rasamādāya. Yathā suttaguḷaṃ yattakehi suttehi veṭhitaṃ, tattakehi eva palayati.

Pala, in the sense of going. He goes away. 'He goes to ruin, he does not come to be reckoned.' 'He goes away, taking the essence.' Just as a ball of thread that has been wound with a number of threads unwinds by just that much.

Ciṅgula paribbhamane. Ciṅguleti, ciṅgulayati. Ciṅgulayitvā. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “yāvatikā abhisaṅkhārassa gati, tāvatikaṃ gantvā ciṅgulayitvā bhūmiyaṃ papatī”ti. Tattha ciṅgulayitvāti paribbhamitvā.

Ciṅgula, in the sense of whirling. Ciṅguleti, ciṅgulayati: it whirls. Ciṅgulayitvā: having whirled. Here the Pāli text is: 'As far as the motion of the volitional formation extends, having gone that far, it whirls and falls to the ground.' Therein, 'ciṅgulayitvā' means 'having whirled'.

Lakārantadhāturūpāni.

The forms of roots ending in 'l'.

Vakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'v'.

Divu parikūjane. Parikūjanaṃ gajjanaṃ. Deveti, devayati. Devo ca paridevitvā. Devoti megho.

Divu, in the sense of lamenting. Lamenting is thundering. Deveti, devayati: he laments. 'And the god, having lamented.' Devo means the cloud.

Divu [M 0.0345] addane. Addanaṃ gandhapisananti vadanti. Deveti, devayati.

Divu, in the sense of rubbing. Addana is said to mean rubbing with perfume. Deveti, devayati: he rubs.

Civa bhāsāyaṃ. Civeti, civayati.

Civa, in the sense of speaking. Civeti, civayati: he speaks.

Vakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'v'.

Sakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 's'.

Pusa posane. Poseti, posayati. Imāni rūpāni kiñcāpi bhūvādigaṇikaṃ “posetī”ti rūpaṃ paṭicca hetukatturūpāni viya dissanti, tathāpi “aññepi devo posetī”tiādikassa curādigaṇikarūpassa dassanato suddhakattuvasena vuttānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ pana kāritaṭṭhāne “posāpeti, posāpayatī”ti hetukatturūpāni icchitabbāni.

Pusa, in the sense of nourishing. Poseti, posayati: he nourishes. Although these forms appear like causative forms, such as `poseti` which can be derived from the Bhū-group root, they should be understood as simple active forms of the Curādi-group, as seen in instances like 'another god also nourishes.' However, in causative constructions, the forms `posāpeti` and `posāpayati` should be used.

Pesa paṭiharaṇe. Peseti, pesayati.

Pesa, in the sense of sending or dispatching. Peseti, pesayati: he sends; he dispatches.

Pisa balapāṇanesu. Piseti, pisayati.

Pisa, in the sense of crushing or striking. Piseti, pisayati: he crushes.

Pasi nāsane. Paṃseti, paṃsayati.

Pasi, in the sense of destroying. Paṃseti, paṃsayati: he destroys.

Jasi rakkhaṇe. Jaṃseti, jaṃsayati.

Jasi, in the sense of protecting. Jaṃseti, jaṃsayati: he protects.

Silesa silesane. Sileseti, silesayati. Sileso.

Silesa, in the sense of joining. Sileseti, silesayati: he joins. Sileso: joining.

Lūsa hiṃsāyaṃ. Lūseti, lūsayati.

Lūsa, in the sense of harming. Lūseti, lūsayati: he harms.

Punsa abhimaddane. Nakāro niggahītatthaṃ. Puṃseti, puṃsayati. Napuṃsako. Dhātunakārassa lope “poso” iccapi rūpaṃ.

Punsa, in the sense of subduing. The 'na' is for the purpose of nasalization. Puṃseti, puṃsayati: he subdues. Napuṃsako: neuter. With the elision of the 'na' of the root, the form 'poso' also occurs.

Tattha na puṃsakoti itthibhāvapumbhāvarahito puggalo. So hi puriso viya sātisayaṃ paccāmitte na puṃseti abhimaddanaṃ [M 0.0346] kātuṃ na sakkotīti napuṃsakoti vuccati. Keci pana “na pumā, na itthī”ti napuṃsakoti vacanatthaṃ vadanti. Tathā hi saddasatthavidū taṃ puggalaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgavasena napuṃsakanti vadanti.

Herein, 'napuṃsaka' means a person devoid of the state of being a woman or a man. For he, unlike a man, cannot excessively subdue enemies, cannot crush them, hence he is called 'napuṃsaka.' Some, however, state the meaning of 'napuṃsaka' as 'not male, not female.' Thus, indeed, grammarians speak of that person as 'napuṃsaka' in the sense of the neuter gender.

Dhūsa kantikaraṇe. Dhūseti, dhūsayati.

Dhūsa, in the sense of cutting. Dhūseti, dhūsayati: he cuts.

Rusa rosane. Rosanaṃ kopakaraṇaṃ. Roseti, rosayati. Roso. Rosoti kodho.

Rusa, in the sense of angering. Rosana means causing anger. Roseti, rosayati: he angers. Roso: anger. Roso means anger.

Byusa ussagge. Byoseti, byosayati.

Byusa, in the sense of abandoning. Byoseti, byosayati: he abandons.

Jasa hiṃsāyaṃ. Jāseti, jāsayati.

'Jasa'—in the sense of harming. 'Jāseti,' 'jāsayati'—he harms.

Daṃsa daṃsane. Daṃseti, daṃsayati. Daṃsano. Daṃsanoti danto. Daṃsanti khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā etenāti daṃsano.

'Daṃsa'—in the sense of biting. 'Daṃseti,' 'daṃsayati'—he bites. 'Daṃsano'—biter. 'Daṃsano' means tooth. They bite chewable or edible things with this, hence it is 'daṃsano'.

Dasi dassane ca. Cakāro daṃsanaṃ apekkhati. Daṃseti, daṃsayati. Vidaṃseti, vidaṃsayati sūriyo ālokaṃ.

'Dasi'—in the sense of seeing, and also biting. The particle 'ca' refers to 'daṃsana' (biting). 'Daṃseti,' 'daṃsayati'—he shows. The sun illuminates the light.

Tassa santajjane. Tasseti, tassayati puriso core.

'Tassa'—in the sense of threatening. 'Tasseti,' 'tassayati'—the man threatens the thieves.

Vassu sattibandhane. Sattibandhanaṃ samatthatākaraṇaṃ. Vasseti, vassayati.

'Vassu'—in the sense of making capable. 'Sattibandhana' means making capable. 'Vasseti,' 'vassayati'—he makes capable.

Jasa tāḷane. Tāḷanaṃ paharaṇaṃ. Jāseti, jāsayati.

'Jasa'—in the sense of striking. 'Tāḷana' means striking. 'Jāseti,' 'jāsayati'—he strikes.

Pasa bandhane. Pāseti, pāsayati. Pāso. Pāsanti bandhanti satte etenāti pāso, sakuṇapāsādi.

'Pasa'—in the sense of binding. 'Pāseti,' 'pāsayati'—he ensnares. 'Pāso'—snare. They bind beings with this, hence it is a 'pāso', like a bird snare and so on.

Ghusi visaddane. Visaddanaṃ ugghosanaṃ. Ghoseti, ghosayati. Ghoso.

'Ghusi'—in the sense of proclaiming. 'Visaddana' means proclaiming aloud. 'Ghoseti,' 'ghosayati'—he proclaims. 'Ghoso'—proclamation.

Lasa silyayoge. Silyayogo lāsiyaṃ nāṭakanāṭanaṃ recakadānaṃ. Lāseti, lāsayati. Lāsento, lāsentī[M 0.0347]. Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “vādentiyāpi lāsenti, naccantiyāpi lāsenti, lāsentiyāpi naccantī”ti. Tattha lāsentīti yā uplavamānā viya uṭṭhahitvā lāsiyanāṭakaṃ nāṭenti, recakaṃ denti.

'Lasa'—in the sense of graceful dancing. 'Silyayoga' means graceful dancing, performing dramas, and giving gestures. 'Lāseti,' 'lāsayati'—he dances gracefully. 'Lāsento,' 'lāsentī'—dancing gracefully (masc.), dancing gracefully (fem.). Here is the Pāli text: "Even while playing music, they dance gracefully; even while dancing, they dance gracefully; even while dancing gracefully, they dance." In this context, 'lāsentī' refers to those who, having risen as if leaping up, perform the lāsiyā dance and give gestures.

Bhūsa alaṅkāre. Bhūseti, bhūsayati. Vibhūseti, vibhūsayati. Bhūsanaṃ, vibhūsanaṃ.

'Bhūsa'—in the sense of adorning. 'Bhūseti,' 'bhūsayati'—he adorns. 'Vibhūseti,' 'vibhūsayati'—he embellishes. 'Bhūsanaṃ,' 'vibhūsanaṃ'—adornment, embellishment.

Vasa sinehanachedāvaharaṇesu. Avaharaṇaṃ corikāya gahaṇaṃ. Vāseti, vāsayati. Vasā.

'Vasa'—in the sense of affection, cutting, and removing. 'Avaharaṇa' means taking by theft. 'Vāseti,' 'vāsayati'—he removes. 'Vasā'—fat.

Tāsa vāraṇe. Vāraṇaṃ nivāraṇaṃ. Tāseti, tāsayati.

'Tāsa'—in the sense of preventing. 'Vāraṇa' means preventing. 'Tāseti,' 'tāsayati'—he prevents.

Dhasa uñche. Dhāseti, dhāsayati.

'Dhasa'—in the sense of gleaning. 'Dhāseti,' 'dhāsayati'—he gleans.

Bhasa gahaṇe. Bhāseti, bhāsayati.

'Bhasa'—in the sense of taking. 'Bhāseti,' 'bhāsayati'—he takes.

Pusa dhāraṇe. Poseti, posayati, ābharaṇaṃ dhāretīti attho.

'Pusa'—in the sense of holding. 'Poseti,' 'posayati'—he holds; the meaning is 'he wears ornaments'.

Tusi pisi kusi dasi bhāsāyaṃ. Tuṃseti, tuṃsayati. Piṃseti, piṃsayati. Kuṃseti, kuṃsayati. Daṃseti, daṃsayati.

'Tusi,' 'Pisi,' 'Kusi,' 'Dasi'—in the sense of speaking. 'Tuṃseti,' 'tuṃsayati'—he speaks. 'Piṃseti,' 'piṃsayati'—he speaks. 'Kuṃseti,' 'kuṃsayati'—he speaks. 'Daṃseti,' 'daṃsayati'—he speaks.

Khusi akkosane. Khuṃseti, khuṃsayati. Khuṃsanā.

'Khusi'—in the sense of scolding. 'Khuṃseti,' 'khuṃsayati'—he scolds. 'Khuṃsanā'—scolding.

Gavesa maggane. Gaveseti, gavesayati. Gavesako, gavesito, gavesanā, gaveṭṭhi.

'Gavesa'—in the sense of searching. 'Gaveseti,' 'gavesayati'—he searches. 'Gavesako'—seeker, 'gavesito'—searched, 'gavesanā'—searching, 'gaveṭṭhi'—investigation.

Vāsa upasevāyaṃ. Vāseti, vāsayati. Vāso, āvāso.

'Vāsa'—in the sense of dwelling. 'Vāseti,' 'vāsayati'—he dwells, he causes to dwell. 'Vāso,' 'āvāso'—dwelling, habitation.

Hisi hiṃsāyaṃ. Hiṃseti, hiṃsayati.

'Hisi'—in the sense of harming. 'Hiṃseti,' 'hiṃsayati'—he harms.

Nivāsa acchādane. Vatthaṃ nivāseti, nivāsayati. Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā.

'Nivāsa'—in the sense of covering. 'Vatthaṃ nivāseti, nivāsayati'—he puts on a garment, he causes a garment to be put on. 'Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā'—having dressed in the forenoon.

Aṃsa [M 0.0348] saṅghāte. Aṃseti, aṃsayati. Aṃso, aṃsā.

'Aṃsa'—in the sense of joining. 'Aṃseti,' 'aṃsayati'—he joins, he causes to join. 'Aṃso,' 'aṃsā'—a shoulder, shoulders.

Ettha ca aṃsoti koṭṭhāsopi khandhopi vuccati. Aṃsāti arisarogo.

And here, 'aṃso' is said to mean both a portion and an aggregate. 'Aṃsā' means a disease of the shoulder.

Misa sajjane. Meseti, mesayati.

'Misa'—in the sense of preparing. 'Meseti,' 'mesayati'—he prepares, he causes to prepare.

Rasa assādane. Raseti, rasayati. Raso. Rasiyate assādiyate janehīti raso.

'Rasa'—in the sense of tasting. 'Raseti,' 'rasayati'—he tastes, he causes to taste. 'Raso'—taste. It is called 'raso' because it is tasted and savored by people.

Rasa sinehane. Raseti, rasayati. Raso.

'Rasa'—in the sense of affection. 'Raseti,' 'rasayati'—he shows affection, he causes to show affection. 'Raso'—affection.

Tattha rasetīti sinehati. Rasoti sineho, sinehasambandho sāmaggirasoti vuccati, yaṃ sandhāya brāhmaṇā bhagavantaṃ “arasarūpo samaṇo gotamo”ti avocuṃ.

Therein, 'raseti' means to show affection. 'Raso' means affection; the connection of affection is called 'the essence of harmony,' referring to which the brahmins said of the Blessed One, 'The ascetic Gotama is without essence.'

Siya asabbappayoge. Seseti, sesayati. Seso. Vipubbo atisaye, vipubbo atisaye, vipubbo sisadhātu atisaye vattati, viseseti, visesayati. Viseso, visiṭṭho, visesanaṃ.

'Siya'—in the sense of non-universal application. 'Seseti,' 'sesayati'—he leaves a remainder, he causes a remainder to be left. 'Seso'—remainder. When prefixed with 'vi', it is in the sense of excellence; when prefixed with 'vi', it is in the sense of excellence; the root 'sis' prefixed with 'vi' functions in the sense of excellence. 'Viseseti,' 'visesayati'—he distinguishes, he causes to distinguish. 'Viseso,' 'visiṭṭho,' 'visesanaṃ'—distinction, distinguished, distinguishing.

Missa sammisse. Misseti, missayati. Sammisseti, sammissayati. Misso, misso, missito, sammissito, sammisso iccādīni. Alambusājātake missāti itthīnaṃ vattabbanāmaṃ, purisehi saddhiṃ sammissanatāya.

'Missa'—in the sense of mixing. 'Misseti,' 'missayati'—he mixes, he causes to mix. 'Sammisseti,' 'sammissayati'—he mixes thoroughly, he causes to mix thoroughly. 'Misso,' 'misso,' 'missito,' 'sammissito,' 'sammisso,' and so on. In the Alambusā Jātaka, 'missā' is a term used for women, because of their mingling with men.

Jusa paritakkane. Joseti, josayati.

'Jusa'—in the sense of deliberation. 'Joseti,' 'josayati'—he deliberates, he causes to deliberate.

Masa pahāsane. Maseti, masayati.

Masa: in the sense of mocking. He mocks, he causes to mock.

Marisa titikkhāyaṃ. Mariseti. Marisayati.

Marisa: in the sense of patience. He endures, he causes to endure.

Pisa pesane. Peseti, pesayati. Pesako, pesito.

Pisa: in the sense of sending. He sends, he causes to send. A sender, sent.

Ghusa [M 0.0349] sadde. Ghoseti, ghosayati. Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā. Ghoso.

Ghusa: in the sense of sound. He proclaims, he causes to proclaim. They joyfully proclaimed at the Bodhi-platform. A sound, a proclamation.

Disī uccāraṇe. Deseti, desayati. Desako, desetā, desito, desanā.

Disī: in the sense of uttering or expounding. He teaches or expounds, he causes to teach or expound. A teacher or expounder, a teacher or expounder, taught or expounded, a teaching or exposition.

Vasa acchādane. Vāseti, vāsayati. Nivāseti, nivāsayati. Vatthaṃ.

Vasa: in the sense of covering. He clothes, he causes to clothe. He puts on, he causes to put on. A garment, a cloth.

Sakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'sa'.

Hakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ha'.

Araha pūjāyaṃ. Araheti, arahayati. Arahā, arahaṃ. “Arahā, khīṇāsavo, asekkho”ti arahato nāmāni.

Araha: in the sense of worship or worthiness. He is worthy, he causes to be worthy. An Arahant, a worthy one. 'Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, one beyond training' are names of an Arahant.

Sineha sinehane. Sineheti, sinehayati.

Sineha: in the sense of anointing or affection. He shows affection, he causes to show affection.

Varaha hiṃsāyaṃ. Varaheti, varahayati. Varāho.

Varaha: in the sense of harming. He harms, he causes to harm. A boar.

Varāhoti sūkaropi hatthīpi vuccati. “Eṇeyyā ca varāhā cā”ti ettha hi sūkaro “varāho”ti vutto, “mahāvarāhassa…pe… nadīsu jaggato”ti ettha pana hatthī “varāho”ti.

'Varāho' is said to refer to both a pig and an elephant. In the phrase 'Eṇeyyā ca varāhā cā,' 'varāho' is used for a pig, whereas in 'mahāvarāhassa…pe… nadīsu jaggato,' 'varāho' is used for an elephant.

Raha cāge. Raheti, rahayati.

Raha: in the sense of abandoning. He abandons, he causes to abandon.

Caha parikatthane. Caheti, cahayati.

Caha: in the sense of boasting. He boasts, he causes to boast.

Maha pūjāyaṃ. Maheti, mahayati. Mahito rājā mahārājā. Vihāramaho, cetiyamaho.

Maha: in the sense of worship or honor. He honors, he causes to honor. The honored king, the great king. A monastery festival, a shrine festival.

Piha icchāyaṃ. Piheti, pihayati. Pihā, pihālu, apiho, pihanīyā vibhūtiyo.

Piha: in the sense of desire. He desires, he causes to desire. Desire, desirous, not desiring, desirable possessions.

Kuha [M 0.0350] vimhāpane. Kuheti, kuhayati. Kuhako. Kuhayati lokavimhāpanaṃ karotīti kuhako. Kuhanā.

Kuha: in the sense of bewildering or deceiving. He deceives, he causes to deceive. A deceiver. He is called a 'kuhako' because he causes bewilderment to the world. Deception.

Saha parisahane. Parisahanaṃ khanti. Saheti, sahayati. Sahanaṃ. Bhūvādigaṇikassa panassa “sahatī”ti rūpaṃ.

Saha: in the sense of enduring. Endurance is patience. He endures, he causes to endure. Endurance. However, for this root belonging to the Bhūvādi group, the form is 'sahati'.

Garaha vinindane. Garaheti, garahayati. Garahā. Bhūvādigaṇikassa panassa “garahatī”ti rūpaṃ.

Garaha: in the sense of blaming or censuring. He blames, he causes to blame. Blame, censure. However, for this root belonging to the Bhūvādi group, the form is 'garahati'.

Hakārantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in 'ha'.

Ḷakārantadhātu

Roots ending in 'ḷ'.

Taḷa tāḷane. Tāḷeti, tāḷayati. Patāḷeti, patāḷayati. Tāḷaṃ. Tāḷanti kaṃsatāḷādi.

Taḷa: in the sense of striking. He strikes, he causes to strike. He strikes down, he causes to strike down. A strike, a beating. They strike bronze cymbals, etc.

Taḷa āghāte. Pubbe viya rūpāni.

Taḷa: in the sense of striking. The forms are as before.

Khaḷa bhede. Khaḷeti, khaḷayati.

Khaḷa: in the sense of breaking. He breaks, he causes to break.

Iḷa thavane. Iḷeti, iḷayati.

Iḷa: in the sense of praising. He praises, he causes to praise.

Juḷa peraṇe. Joḷeti, joḷayati.

Juḷa: in the sense of urging. He urges, he causes to urge.

Pīḷa avagāhane. Pīḷeti, pīḷayati. Nippīḷeti, nippīḷayati. Pīḷanako, pīḷito, pīḷā, pīḷanaṃ, nippīḷanako.

Pīḷa: in the sense of pressing or oppressing. He presses or oppresses, he causes to press or oppress. He thoroughly presses or oppresses, he causes to thoroughly press or oppress. An oppressor, oppressed, oppression, the act of oppressing, one who thoroughly oppresses.

Laḷa upasevāyaṃ. Lāḷeti, lāḷayati. Upalāḷeti, upalāḷayati. Bhūvādigaṇaṭṭhāya pana vilāsanatthe vattamānāya etissā “laḷatī”ti rūpaṃ.

Laḷa: in the sense of serving or fondling. He fondles, he causes to fondle. He fondles, he causes to fondle. However, for this root, when it belongs to the Bhūvādi group and occurs in the sense of sporting or playing, its form is 'laḷati'.

Siḷa seḷane. Seḷeti, seḷayati. Seḷento. Ettha seḷetīti seḷitasaddaṃ karoti.

Siḷa: in the sense of moving or shaking. He moves or shakes, he causes to move or shake. Moving, shaking. Here, 'seḷeti' means it makes a rustling sound.

Avaggantadhāturūpāni.

Forms of roots ending in unclassified consonants.

Curādī [M 0.0351] ettakā diṭṭhā, dhātavo me yathābalaṃ;

Suttesvaññepi pekkhitvā, gaṇhavho atthayuttito.

These roots, beginning with the Curādi group, have been seen by me according to my ability; having examined them in the suttas and elsewhere, you should grasp them in accordance with their meaning.

Curapamukhagaṇo me sāsanatthaṃ pavutto,

Supacurahitakāmo tampi sikkheyya dhīro;

Supacuranayapāṭhe satthuno tañhi sikkhaṃ,

Piyusamiva manuññaṃ atthasāraṃ labhetha.

The group headed by Cura has been expounded by me for the sake of the teaching. The wise one, desiring abundant benefit, should also train in that. For, by training in that well-abundant method and text of the Teacher, one would obtain the essence of meaning, which is delightful like nectar.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise, in the ninefold division of the Teaching with its commentary, and in the three Piṭakas, regarding the modes of expression—

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

—in the grammatical treatise called Saddanīti, composed for the sake of proficiency.

Curādigaṇaparidīpano aṭṭhārasamo paricchedo.

The Eighteenth Chapter: The Elucidation of the Curādi Group.

19. Sabbagaṇavinicchaya

19. The Determination of All Groups

Ito paraṃ pavakkhāmi, sabbagaṇavinicchayaṃ;

Sotūnaṃ paṭubhāvatthaṃ, parame piṭakattaye.

Henceforth I shall expound the determination of all groups, for the sake of the listeners' proficiency in the supreme three Piṭakas.

Paccayādivibhāgehi, nayehi vividhehi taṃ;

Sukhaggāhāya sotūnaṃ, suṇātha mama bhāsato.

For the easy comprehension of the listeners, listen to me as I explain that by means of the divisions of affixes and so on, and by various methods.

Tattha paṭhamo bhūvādigaṇo, dutiyo rudhādigaṇo, tatiyo divādigaṇo, catuttho svādiguṇo, pañcamo kiyādigaṇo, chaṭṭho gahādigaṇo, sattamo tanādigaṇo, aṭṭhamo curādigaṇo, imasmiṃ bhagavato pāvacane aṭṭhavidhā dhātugaṇā bhavanti. Etesu vikaraṇapaccayavasena –

Herein, the first is the bhūvādi group, the second is the rudhādi group, the third is the divādi group, the fourth is the svādi group, the fifth is the kiyādi group, the sixth is the gahādi group, the seventh is the tanādi group, and the eighth is the curādi group. In this teaching of the Blessed One, there are eight kinds of root-groups. Among these, by means of the modifying affixes—

Bhūvādito akāro ca, sānusāro rudhādito;

Akāro cevivaṇṇo ca, ekārokārameva ca.

From the bhūvādi group, the 'a' affix; from the rudhādi group, that with anusāra; also the 'a' affix and the 'i' vowel, and the vowels 'e' and 'o' as well.

Yapaccayo divādimhā, ṇu ṇā uṇā suvādito;

Kyādito pana nāyeva, ppaṇhā pana gahādito.

The affix 'ya' from the divādi group; 'ṇu', 'ṇā', and 'uṇā' from the svādi group; 'ṇā' indeed from the kiyādi group; and 'ppaṇhā' from the gahādi group.

Oyirā [M 0.0352] tu tanādimhā, ṇe ṇayā ca curādito;

Aggahitaggahaṇena, paccayā dasa pañca ca.

'O' and 'yira' from the tanādi group; 'ṇe' and 'ṇaya' from the curādi group. By including those not previously mentioned, the affixes are fifteen in all.

Hiyyattanī sattamī ca, vattamānā ca pañcamī;

Catassetā pavuccanti, sabbadhātukanāmikā.

The hiyyattanī (imperfect past), the sattamī (optative), the vattamānā (present), and the pañcamī (imperative)—these four are said to be named sabbadhātuka.

Etesu visayesveva, akāro suddhakattari;

Aññatra kha cha sādīhi, sahāpi cupalabbhati.

In these contexts alone, the 'a' affix is found as a prefix; elsewhere, it is also found together with 'kha', 'cha', 'sa', and so forth.

“Bhavati hoti sambhoti, jeti jayati kīyati;

Ḍeti yāti iti eti, avati koti saṅkati.

“Bhavati, hoti, sambhoti (he becomes, he is, he originates); jeti, jayati (he conquers, he wins); kīyati (it is bought); ḍeti (he flies); yāti, eti (he goes, he comes); avati (he protects); koti (he cuts); saṅkati (he doubts).”

Bhikkhati pivati pāti, vadeti vadati” iti;

Bhūvādidhāturūpāni, bhavantīti pakāsaye.

“Bhikkhati (he begs), pivati (he drinks), pāti (he protects), vadeti, vadati (he speaks, he says)”—thus one should declare that these are forms of the bhūvādi root group.

Rūpaṃ “rundhati rundhīti, rundheti puna rundhiti;

Sumbhoti”ccādīrūpāni, rudhādīnti dīpaye.

One should explain that forms such as: “rundhati, rundhīti (he obstructs), rundheti (he causes to obstruct), puna rundhiti (he obstructs again), sumbhoti (he crushes)” are of the rudhādi group.

“Dibbati sibbati ceva, yujjati vijjati tathā;

Ghāyati hāyati”ccādi, rūpamāhu divādinaṃ.

They say that forms such as: “dibbati (he plays, he shines), sibbati (he sews), yujjati (it is joined), vijjati (it is found), ghāyati (he smells), hāyati (he diminishes)” are of the divādi group.

“Suṇoti ca suṇāti ca, vuṇoti ca vuṇāti ca;

Pāpuṇāti hinotī”ti, ādirūpaṃ suvādinaṃ.

The initial forms of the svādi group are: “suṇoti and suṇāti (he hears), vuṇoti and vuṇāti (he chooses), pāpuṇāti (he attains), hinoti (he sends forth/abandons).”

“Kināti ca jināti ca, dhunāti ca munāti ca;

Asnāti”ccādirūpañca, kyādīnanti vibhāvaye.

One should discern that forms such as: “kināti (he buys), jināti (he conquers), dhunāti (he shakes off), munāti (he knows), asnāti (he eats)” belong to the kiyādi group.

“Gheppati paṭiggaṇhāti, saṇhañca saṇhakoti ca;

Kaṇhaṃ taṇhā ca tiṇhuṇha”-miccādi ca gahādinaṃ.

Forms such as: “gheppati (it is taken), paṭiggaṇhāti (he receives)”; and “saṇhaṃ” (subtle) and “saṇhakoti”; and “kaṇhaṃ” (black), “taṇhā” (craving), “tiṇha” (sharp), and “uṇha” (hot)—these and others are of the gahādi group.

“Tanoti ca karoti ca, kayirati sanoti ca;

Sakkota’ppoti pappoti”-ccādirūpaṃ tanādinaṃ.

Forms such as: “tanoti (he stretches), karoti (he makes), kayirati (it is made), sanoti (he gains), sakkoti (he is able), appoti (he obtains), pappoti (he reaches)” are of the tanādi group.

“Coreti corayante ca, cinteti cintayanti ca;

Manteti”ccādikañcāpi, rūpamāhu curādinaṃ.

They say that forms such as: “coreti (he steals), corayanti (they steal/cause to steal), cinteti (he thinks), cintayanti (they think/cause to think), manteti (he consults)” are also of the curādi group.

Vikaraṇavasenevaṃ, rūpabhedo pakāsito;

Dhātūnaṃ dhātubhedādi-kusalassa matānugo.

Thus, the diversity of forms of the roots has been explained by means of the modifying affixes, following the opinion of one skilled in the distinctions of roots and so on.

Kiriyāya [M 0.0353] dhāraṇato, dhātavo ekadhā matā;

Dvidhāpi ca pavuccanti, sakammākammato pana.

By virtue of conveying action, roots are considered to be of one kind; but they are also spoken of as twofold, according to being transitive (sakammaka) or intransitive (akammaka).

Tattha sakammakā nāma, gamibhakkhādayā siyuṃ;

Ṭhāsādayo akammā ca, upasaggaṃ vinā vade;

Therein, the transitive, namely, would be `gami`, `bhakkha`, and so on; and the intransitive are `ṭhā`, `sī`, and so on, when spoken of without a prefix.

Sakammakakammabhūto, divu iccādayo puna;

Gahetvāna tidhā honti, evañcāpi vibhāvaye.

Again, there are those that are both transitive and intransitive, such as `divu` and so on; including these, the classification becomes threefold. Thus should one also discern.

Sakammake dvidhā bhitvā, ekakammadvikammato;

Akammakehi saddhiṃ te, tividhāpi bhavanti hi.

Indeed, by dividing the transitive into two—according to having one object or two objects—they, together with the intransitive, also become threefold.

Akammakā rutāyeva, ekakammā gamādayo;

Honti dvikammakā nāma, duhikaravahādayo.

The intransitive are known as such; the single-object transitive are `gam` and so on; and those called double-object transitive are `duh`, `kar`, `vah`, and so on.

Sakammākammakattamhi, dhātūnamupasaggato;

Niyamo natthi so tasmā, na mayā ettha vuccati.

Regarding the transitivity or intransitivity of roots arising from prefixes, there is no fixed rule; therefore, that is not discussed by me here.

Ekaṭṭhānā gamiccādī, dviṭṭhānā bhūpacādayo;

Tiṭṭhānā svādayo evaṃ, ṭhānatopi tidhā matā.

Roots such as gami (to go) are of one place; roots such as bhū (to be) and paca (to cook) are of two places; roots such as su (to hear) are of three places. Thus, from the perspective of place also, they are considered threefold.

Gupādayo niyogena, ākhyātatte savuddhikā;

Vaca turādayo na hi, vuddhikā kāritaṃ vinā;

Roots like gupa (to protect) and so forth necessarily undergo vowel gradation when used as verbs; but roots like vaca (to speak) and tura (to hasten) and so forth do not undergo vowel gradation without the causative affix.

Khi ji iccādayo dhātū, savuddhāvuddhikā matā;

Iti vuddhivasenāpi, tividho dhātusaṅgaho.

Roots such as khi (to destroy) and ji (to conquer) and so forth are considered to optionally undergo vowel gradation; thus, by way of vowel gradation also, the collection of roots is threefold.

Aluttavikaraṇā ca, luttavikaraṇā tathā;

Luttāluttavikaraṇā, evampi tividhā siyuṃ.

And there are those with unelided conjugational signs, and likewise those with elided conjugational signs, and those with both elided and unelided conjugational signs—thus, they may also be threefold.

Tatrāluttavikaraṇā, gami rudhi divādayo;

Pā bhādayo jiniccādī, kamato itare siyuṃ.

Among them, those with unelided conjugational signs are, for example, gami (to go), rudhi (to obstruct), diva (to play) and so forth; those with elided conjugational signs are, for example, pā (to drink) and bhā (to shine) and so forth; and the others, in order, are those with both elided and unelided conjugational signs, such as ji (to conquer) and so forth.

Suddhassarā ekassarā, tathānekassarāti ca;

Tidhā bhavanti yuyātā-pābhālādī karādayo.

And pure-vowel roots, single-syllable roots, and multi-syllable roots—thus they are threefold, such as yu (to join), yā (to go), tā (to cross), pā (to drink), bhā (to shine), lā (to take), and so forth, and kara (to do) and so forth.

Catudhādinayo cāpi, labbhamānavasena ca;

Gahetabbo nayaññūhi, yathāvuttānusārato.

The fourfold method and others too, according to what is obtainable, should be grasped by those skilled in methods, in accordance with what has been stated.

Puna [M 0.0354] suddhassarā dhātū, ekassarā ca sattadhā;

Āivaṇṇauvaṇṇanta-eontavasā matā.

Again, pure-vowel roots and single-syllable roots are considered sevenfold, according to whether they end in ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, or o.

Avaṇṇivaṇṇuvaṇṇante-kārantānaṃ vasena ve;

Anekassaradhātū ca, sattadhāva pakittitā.

And multi-syllable roots are also declared to be sevenfold, according to whether they end in a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, or e.

Evaṃ pannarasadhāpi, dhātūnamidha saṅgaho;

Tappabhedaṃ pakāseyyuṃ, iuiccādinā vidū.

Thus, the collection of roots here is fifteenfold; the wise should explain their divisions by means of 'i', 'u', and so forth.

Tatra “igatiyaṃ, i ajjhayane, u sadde” iccete suddhassarā dhātavo. Yā rā lā iccādayo ekassarā ākārantā. Khijiniiccādayo ekassarā ikārantā. Pīiccādayo ekassarā īkārantā. Khu du ku iccādayo ekassarā ukārantā, bhū hū iccādayo ekassarā ūkārantā. Khe je se iccādayo ekassarā ekārantā. So iccādayo ekassarā okārantā.

Therein, the roots 'i' in the sense of 'going,' 'i' in the sense of 'study,' and 'u' in the sense of 'sound'—these are the pure vowel roots. Those such as 'yā,' 'rā,' and 'lā' are single-syllable roots ending in 'ā'. Those such as 'khi,' 'ji,' and 'ni' are single-syllable roots ending in 'i'. Those such as 'pī' are single-syllable roots ending in 'ī'. Those such as 'khu,' 'du,' and 'ku' are single-syllable roots ending in 'u'; those such as 'bhū' and 'hū' are single-syllable roots ending in 'ū'. Those such as 'khe,' 'je,' and 'se' are single-syllable roots ending in 'e'. Those such as 'so' are single-syllable roots ending in 'o'.

Kara paca saṅgāma iccādayo anekassarā akārantā, omāiccādayo anekassarā ākārantā, saki iccādayo anekassarā ikārantā. Cakkhī iccādayo anekassarā īkārantā. Andhuiccādayo anekassarā ukārantā. Kakkhū iccādayo anekassarā ūkārantā. Gile mile iccādayo anekassarā ekārantāti evaṃ pannarasavidhena dhātusaṅgaho.

Roots such as 'kara,' 'paca,' and 'saṅgāma' are multi-syllable and end in 'a'. Those such as 'omā' are multi-syllable and end in 'ā'. Those such as 'saki' are multi-syllable and end in 'i'. Those such as 'cakkhī' are multi-syllable and end in 'ī'. Those such as 'andhu' are multi-syllable and end in 'u'. Those such as 'kakkhū' are multi-syllable and end in 'ū'. Those such as 'gile' and 'mile' are multi-syllable and end in 'e'. Thus the collection of roots is of fifteen kinds.

Atha tettiṃsavidhenapi dhātusaṅgaho bhavati. Kathaṃ?

Further, the collection of roots is also of thirty-three kinds. How so?

Dhātū suddhassarā ceva, puna cekassarāpi ca;

Kakārantā khakārantā, gantā ghantā ca dhātavo.

The roots are: pure-vowel, and also single-syllable; and roots ending in 'ka,' ending in 'kha,' ending in 'ga,' and ending in 'gha'.

Cakārantā chakārantā, jantā jhantā ca ñantakā;

Ṭakārantā ṭhakārantā, ḍantā ḍhantā ca ṇantakā.

Roots ending in 'ca,' ending in 'cha,' ending in 'ja,' ending in 'jha,' and ending in 'ña'; roots ending in 'ṭa,' ending in 'ṭha,' ending in 'ḍa,' ending in 'ḍha,' and ending in 'ṇa'.

Tantā ceva tathā thantā, dantā dhantā ca nantakā;

Pantā phantā bakārantā, bhantā mantā ca yantakā.

And roots ending in 'ta,' likewise ending in 'tha,' ending in 'da,' ending in 'dha,' and ending in 'na'; roots ending in 'pa,' ending in 'pha,' ending in 'ba,' ending in 'bha,' ending in 'ma,' and ending in 'ya'.

Rantā [M 0.0355] lantā vakārantā, santā hantā ca ḷantakā;

Iti tettiṃsadhā ñeyyo, dhātūnamidha saṅgaho.

Roots ending in 'ra,' ending in 'la,' ending in 'va,' ending in 'sa,' ending in 'ha,' and ending in 'ḷa'. Thus the collection of roots here is to be known as thirty-threefold.

Mate satthussa ḍhaṇaḷā, padādimhi na dissare;

Tenekassaradhātūsu, ḍhaṇaḷā na kathīyare.

In the Teacher's opinion, the letters 'ḍha,' 'ṇa,' and 'ḷa' are not found at the beginning of a word. Therefore, among the single-syllable roots, those beginning with 'ḍha,' 'ṇa,' and 'ḷa' are not mentioned.

Ikārantatikāranta-vasena tu yathārahaṃ;

Nāmaṃ sambhoti dhātūnaṃ, itippaccayayogato.

The name of a root is formed with an '-i' ending, as is appropriate; and a noun is formed from the application of a suffix such as '-ti'.

Pacibhikkhichidikhādi, karoti bhavati gami;

Gatigacchatihotīti, ādivohāramuddhare.

One should set forth the primary conventional expressions, such as: paci, bhikkhi, chidi, khādi; karoti, bhavati, gami; gati, gacchati, and hoti.

Evaṃ tettiṃsabhedehi gahitesu nikhilesu dhātūsu –

Thus, when all the roots have been grasped according to these thirty-three divisions—

Sahahiṃsaīhavasā, sīhasaddagatiṃ vade;

Sahanato hananato, sīhoti hi garū vaduṃ.

One should explain the derivation of the word 'lion' from the roots sah (to endure), hiṃs (to harm), and īh (to strive). For the teachers have said that it is a 'lion' (sīha) because of its enduring (sahana) and its striking (hanana).

Tathā hi sīho vātātapādiparissayampi sahati, “kiṃ me bahūhi ghāṭitehī”ti attano gocaratthāya khuddake pāṇe agaṇhanto, “māhaṃ khuddake pāṇe visamagate saṅghātaṃ āpādesī”ti anuddayavasena sahitabbe khuddakasattepi sahati. Hiṃsitabbe pana kāyūpapanne sūkaramahiṃsādayo satte hiṃsati, tasmāpi “sīho”ti vuccati. Yathā pana kantanaṭṭhena ādiantavipallāsato takkaṃ vuccati, evaṃ hiṃsanaṭṭhenapi sīhoti veditabbo. Atha vā sabbiriyāpathesu daḷhavīriyattā suṭṭhu īhatīti sīho. Vuttañhi –

For a lion endures the dangers of wind, heat, and so on. Not taking small creatures for its prey, it thinks, 'What is the use to me of killing many?' and, 'May I not bring destruction upon small beings that have gone astray.' Thus, out of compassion, it endures even small creatures that ought to be spared. But it harms those creatures that ought to be harmed, such as boars and buffaloes, which possess large bodies. Therefore it is also called a 'lion' (sīha). Just as the word 'takka' (logic) is derived from 'kantana' (cutting) by a reversal of the beginning and the end, so too 'sīha' is to be understood from the meaning of 'harming' (hiṃsana). Alternatively, because it strives well (suṭṭhu īhati) with firm energy in all postures, it is a 'lion' (sīho). For it is said:

“Yathā sīho migarājā, nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame;

Alīnavīriyo hoti, paggahitamano sadā”ti.

'Just as the lion, the king of beasts, whether sitting, standing, or walking, is ever of unflagging energy, with mind uplifted.'

Aparo nayo –

Another method:

Sahanā ca hiṃsanā ca, tathā sīghajavattato;

Sīho iccapi bhāseyya, sakyasīhassa sāsane.

From enduring (sahana) and harming (hiṃsanā), and likewise from swift speed (sīghajavattā), one might explain the word 'lion' in the teaching of the Sakyan Lion.

Vuttañhi [M 0.0356] suttanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saharā ca hananā ca sīghajavattā ca sīho”ti.

For it is said in the Commentary to the Suttanipāta: 'A lion (sīha) is so called because of its roar (sara), its striking (hanana), and its swiftness (sīghajavattā).'

Idāni tadatthuddhāro vuccate, sīhasaddo “sīho bhikkhave migarājā”tiādīsu migarāje āgato. “Atha kho sīho senāpati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī”tiādīsu paññattiyaṃ. “Sīhoti kho bhikkhave tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”tiādīsu tathāgate. Tattha tathāgate sadisakappanāya āgato.

Now the extraction of its meaning is stated. The word 'lion' occurs in the sense of the king of beasts in such passages as: 'Bhikkhus, the lion is the king of beasts.' It occurs as a proper name in such passages as: 'Then the general Sīha approached the Blessed One.' It occurs in the sense of the Tathāgata in such passages as: 'Bhikkhus, "lion" is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.' There, in reference to the Tathāgata, it is used by way of comparison.

Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Herein it is said:

Sīhe paññattiyañcāpi, buddhe appaṭipuggale;

Imesu tīsu atthesu, sīhasaddo pavattati.

'In the sense of the animal, the lion; also as a proper name; and for the Buddha, the matchless person—in these three meanings the word 'lion' is used.'

Rūpiruppatidhātūhi, rūpasaddagatiṃ vade;

“Rūpayati ruppatī”ti, vatvā nibbacanadvayaṃ.

One should explain the derivation of the word 'form' (rūpa) from the roots 'rūp' and 'rupp'. Having stated, 'it forms' (rūpayati) and 'it is afflicted' (ruppati), one explains the twofold derivation.

Vuttañhetaṃ garūhi “rūpayatīti rūpaṃ, vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti attho”ti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “rūpanti kenaṭṭhena rūpaṃ? Ruppanaṭṭhenā”ti. Bhagavatā panetaṃ vuttaṃ “kiñca bhikkhave rūpaṃ vadetha, ruppatīti kho bhikkhave tasmā rūpanti vuccati. Kena ruppati, sītenapi ruppatī”ti vitthāro. Atthuddhāro panassa heṭṭhā vuttova.

This has been stated by the teachers: 'It is form (rūpa) because it forms (rūpayati); the meaning is that by undergoing a change of appearance, it manifests a state that goes to the heart.' And this too is said: 'Form (rūpa)? In what sense is it form? In the sense of being afflicted (ruppana).' This has been stated by the Blessed One: 'And what, bhikkhus, do you call form? It is afflicted (ruppati), bhikkhus, therefore it is called form (rūpa). By what is it afflicted? It is afflicted by cold,' and so on in detail. But the extraction of its meaning has been stated below.

Pasavatemanatthena, dhātunā udinā pana;

Samuddasaddanipphattiṃ, vadeyya matimā naro.

A wise person should state the derivation of the word 'ocean' (samudda) from the meaning of 'flowing forth' and 'going,' and from the root 'ud'.

Ettha [M 0.0357] hi samuddoti aṭṭhahi acchariyabbhutadhammehi samannāgatattā samuddati attasannissitānaṃ macchamakarādīnaṃ pītisomanassaṃ pasavati janetīti samuddo. Ayamasmākaṃ khanti. Aṭṭhakathācariyā pana “samuddanaṭṭhena samuddo, kiledanaṭṭhena tenamanaṭṭhenāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti vadanti. Milindapañhe pana āyasmā nāgaseno “bhante nāgasena samuddo samuddoti vuccati, kena kāraṇena āpaṃ udakaṃ samuddoti vuccatī”ti milindena raññā puṭṭho āha “yattakaṃ mahārāja udakaṃ, tattakaṃ loṇaṃ, yattakaṃ loṇaṃ, tattakaṃ udakaṃ, udakasamattā samuddoti vuccatī”ti. Tadā raññā milindena “kallosi bhante nāgasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha hi samaṃ udakena loṇaṃ etthāti samuddoti nibbacanaṃ veditabbaṃ “nīloda”ntiādīsu viya. Tattha bhadantanāgasenamatañca amhākaṃ matañca pakatisamuddaṃ sandhāya vuttattā na virujjhati, aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ matampi “taṇhāsamuddo”ti ca “samuddopeso”ti ca āgatāni samuddasarikkhakāni ca taṇhācakkhusotādīni sandhāya vuttattā na virujjhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, it is a 'samudda' because, being endowed with eight amazing and wonderful qualities, it gladdens (samuddati) and generates (pasavati) joy and gladness for the fish, sea-monsters, and others that depend on it. This is our view. The commentators, however, say: 'It is called samudda in the sense of surging up (samuddana), in the sense of moistening (kiledana), and in the sense of wetting (temana).' In the Questions of Milinda, when asked by King Milinda, 'Venerable Nāgasena, the ocean is called samudda. For what reason is the great water called samudda?' the Venerable Nāgasena said: 'As much water as there is, great king, so much salt there is; as much salt as there is, so much water there is. Because of the equal measure with the water (udakasamattā), it is called samudda.' Then King Milinda said, 'You are clever, venerable Nāgasena!' Here, the etymology of samudda should be understood as 'that wherein salt is equal (sama) with water (uda)', similar to 'nīloda' and so on. In this matter, the view of the venerable Nāgasena and our own view do not conflict, since they are stated with reference to the natural ocean. It should be seen that the view of the commentators also does not conflict, since it is stated with reference to things comparable to an ocean that are mentioned as 'the ocean of craving' and 'this too is an ocean,' such as craving, the eye, the ear, and so on.

Khādadhātuvasā cāpi, khanudhātuvasena vā;

Khanito vāpi dhātumhā, dhāto khaṃpubbatopi vā;

Khandhasaddassa nipphattiṃ, saddakkhandhavidū vade.

Those who know the collection of words should state the derivation of the word 'aggregate' (khandha) as being from the root 'khād' (to eat), or from the root 'khan' (to dig), or from the root 'khan' in its passive sense ('dug'), or from the root 'dhā' (to place) preceded by 'khaṃ' (emptiness).

Tattha “saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhāpi dukkhā”ti vacanato sayampi dukkhadhammoyeva samāno jātijarābyādhimaraṇadukkhādīhi anekehi dukkhehi khajjati khādiyatīti khandho, teheva dukkhehi khaññati avadāriyatītipi khandho, khaniyati parikhaññatītipi khandho, attena vā attaniyena vā tucchattā khaṃ suññākāraṃ dhāretītipi khandho, rūpakkhandhādi. Atthuddhārato pana –

Therein, according to the saying, 'In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering,' it is an 'aggregate' (khandha) because, being itself simply a phenomenon of suffering, it is eaten up and devoured (khajjati, khādīyati) by many kinds of suffering, such as that of birth, aging, illness, and death. It is also an 'aggregate' because it is dug up and torn apart (khaññati, avadārīyati) by those same kinds of suffering. It is also an 'aggregate' because it is dug up (khaniyati) and excavated (parikhaññati). Furthermore, it is an 'aggregate' because, being void of self or what belongs to a self, it bears (dhāreti) the mark of emptiness (khaṃ), the character of voidness. This applies to the form aggregate and so on. But as to the extraction of its meanings:

Khandhasaddo [M 0.0358] rāsiguṇa-paṇṇattīsu ca rūḷhiyaṃ;

Koṭṭhāse ceva aṃse ca, vattatīti vibhāvaye.

One should understand that the word 'khandha' is used in the sense of a heap, a quality, a designation, and by convention; and also in the sense of a portion and a part.

Vuttañhetaṃ sammohavinodaniyaṃ vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ – khandhasaddo sambahulesu ṭhānesu nipatati rāsimhi guṇe paṇṇattiyaṃ rūḷhiyanti. “Seyyathāpi bhikkhave mahāsamudde na sukaraṃ udakassa pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ “ettakāni udakāḷhakānī’ti vā ‘ettakāni udakāḷhakasatānī’ti vā ‘ettakāni udakāḷhakasahassānī’ti vā ‘ettakāni udakāḷhakasatasahassānī’ti vā, atha kho asaṅkhyeyyo appameyyo mahāudakakkhandhotveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”tiādīsu hi rāsito khandho nāma. Na hi parittakaṃ udakaṃ udakakkhandhoti vuccati, bahukameva vuccati, tathā na parittakaṃ rajo rajakkhandho, na appamattakā gāvo gavakkhandho, na appamattakaṃ balaṃ balakkhandho, na appamattakaṃ puññaṃ puññakkhandhoti vuccati. Bahukameva hi rajo rajakkhandho, bahukā ca gavādayo gavakkhandho, balakkhandho, puññakkhandhoti vuccanti. “Sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho”tiādīsu pana guṇato khandho nāma. “Addasā khā bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamāna”nti ettha paṇṇattito khandho nāma. “Yaṃ cittaṃ mano mānasaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandho”tiādīsu rūḷhīto khandho nāma. Svāyamidha rāsito adhippeto. Ayañhi khandhaṭṭho nāma piṇḍaṭṭho pūgaṭṭho ghaṭaṭṭho rāsaṭṭho, tasmā rāsilakkhaṇā khandhāti veditabbā. Koṭṭhāsaṭṭhātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Lokasmiñhi iṇaṃ gahetvā codiyamānā “dvīhi khandhehi dassāma, tīhi khandhehi dassāmā”ti [M 0.0359] vadanti. Iti koṭṭhāsalakkhaṇā khandhātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Evamettha “rūpakkhandhoti rūparāsi rūpakoṭṭhāso, vedanākkhandhoti vedanārāsi vedanākoṭṭhāso”ti iminā nayena attho veditabbo. “Khandhe bhāraṃ. Khandhato otāreti, mahāhanusabhakkhandho”tiādīsu pana aṃso “khandho”ti vuccati.

This is stated in the Sammohavinodanī, the commentary to the Vibhaṅga: The term 'khandha' occurs in many places: in the sense of a heap, a quality, a designation, and by convention. In such passages as: 'Just as, bhikkhus, in the great ocean it is not easy to get a measure of the water by saying, "There are so many measures of water," or "so many hundreds of measures of water," or "so many thousands of measures of water," or "so many hundreds of thousands of measures of water," but it is reckoned as a great mass of water, innumerable, immeasurable,' 'khandha' means a heap. For a small amount of water is not called a 'mass of water'; only a large amount is. Similarly, a small amount of dust is not called a 'mass of dust'; a few cows are not called a 'herd of cows'; a little strength is not called a 'mass of strength'; a little merit is not called a 'mass of merit.' For only a large amount of dust is called a 'mass of dust,' and many cows and so on are called a 'herd of cows,' a 'mass of strength,' and a 'mass of merit.' But in such passages as 'the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration,' 'khandha' means a quality. In the statement, 'The Blessed One saw a large log of wood being carried along by the current of the river Ganges,' here 'khandha' is used by way of designation. In such passages as 'Whatever is mind, mentality, consciousness... the aggregate of consciousness,' 'khandha' is used by convention. Here, in this context, it is intended in the sense of a heap. For this meaning of 'khandha' is the meaning of a lump, a mass, a collection, a heap. Therefore, the aggregates should be understood as having the characteristic of a heap. It can also be said that they have the characteristic of a portion. For in the world, when pressed for repayment of a debt, people say, 'We will pay in two portions,' or 'We will pay in three portions.' Thus, it can also be said that the aggregates have the characteristic of portions. In this way, the meaning here should be understood according to this method: 'The aggregate of form is a heap of form, a portion of form; the aggregate of feeling is a heap of feeling, a portion of feeling.' But in such phrases as 'a burden on the shoulder,' 'he takes it down from his shoulder,' and 'one with great bull-like shoulders,' 'khandha' means 'shoulder' (aṃsa).

Āpubbayatato cāpi, āyūpapadato puna;

Tanuto tanito vāpi, āyatanaravo gato.

The term 'āyatana' is derived from striving, and again from the arising of what comes; also from the body or from stretching.

Vuttampi cetaṃ – āyatanato, āyānaṃ vā tananato, āyatassa ca nayanato āyatananti veditabbaṃ. Cakkhu rūpādīsu hi taṃtaṃdvārārammaṇā cittacetasikā dhammā sena sena anubhavanādikiccena āyatanti uṭṭhahanti ghaṭanti vāyamantīti vā vuttaṃ hoti. Te ca pana āyabhūte dhamme etāni tananti vitthārentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Idañca anamatagge saṃsāre pavattaṃ atīva āyataṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ yāva na nivattati, tāva nayanti, pavattayantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Iti sabbepime dhammā āyatanato, āyānaṃ vā tananato, āyatassa ca nayanato āyatananti vuccanti.

And this was said: 'It should be understood as an āyatana because it is a source of striving (āyatanato), or because it stretches out what comes (āyānaṃ tananato), or because it leads on what is long (āyatassa nayanato).' For in regard to the eye, forms, and so on, the mind and mental factors, having their respective doors and objects, strive, arise, exert themselves, or make an effort with their own function of experiencing, and so on; this is what is meant by 'striving.' And these bases stretch out, they extend, those states that constitute what comes; this is what is meant by 'stretching out what comes.' And as long as this exceedingly long suffering of saṃsāra, which has been proceeding in the beginningless round of rebirths, does not cease, they lead it on, they keep it going; this is what is meant by 'leading on what is long.' Thus all these phenomena are called āyatanas because they are a source of striving, or because they stretch out what comes, or because they lead on what is long.

Apica nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ākaraṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena sañjātidesaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhena āyatanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi “loke issarāyatanaṃ vāsudevāyatana”ntiādīsu nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ āyatananti vuccati. “Suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ rajatāyatana”ntiādīsu ākaro, sāsane pana “manorame āyatane, sevanti naṃ vihaṅgamā”tiādīsu samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ[M 0.0360]. “Dakkhiṇāpatho gunnaṃ āyatana”ntiādīsu sañjātideso. “Tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”tiādīsu kāraṇaṃ.

Furthermore, āyatana should be understood in the sense of a dwelling place, a mine, a meeting place, a place of origin, and a cause. For in such phrases as 'the lord's domain (issarāyatana) in the world, the domain of Vāsudeva (vāsudevāyatana),' āyatana means a dwelling place. In such phrases as 'a gold mine (suvaṇṇāyatana), a silver mine (rajatāyatana),' it means a mine (ākaro). In the Dispensation, however, in such phrases as 'in a delightful resort (manorame āyatane), birds frequent it,' it means a meeting place. In such phrases as 'the Southern region is the birthplace of oxen (gunnaṃ āyatana),' it means a place of origin. And in such phrases as 'one attains the state of a witness right there whenever there is a cause for mindfulness (sati satiāyatane),' it means a cause.

Cakkhuādīsu cāpi cittacetasikā dhammā nivasanti tadāyattavuttitāyāti cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ. Cakkhādīsu te ākiṇṇā tannissitattā tadārammaṇattā cāti cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ ākaro. Cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ tattha tattha dvārārammaṇavasena samosaraṇato. Cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ sañjātideso tannissayārammaṇabhāvena tattheva uppattito, cakkhādayo ca nesaṃ kāraṇaṃ tesaṃ abhāve abhāvato. Iti nivāsaṭṭhānaṭṭhena ākaraṭṭhena samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṭṭhena sañjātidesaṭṭhena kāraṇaṭṭhenāti imehi kāraṇehi ete dhammā āyatananti vuccanti, tasmā yathāvuttenatthena cakkhu ca taṃ āyatanañcāti cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… dhammā ca te āyatanañcāti dhammāyatananti evaṃ tāvettha atthato viññātabbo vinicchayoti. Iccevaṃ –

And in the eye, etc., mind and mental factors dwell, since their occurrence is dependent on them; thus the eye, etc., are their dwelling place. They teem in the eye, etc., because they are dependent on them and have them as their object; thus the eye, etc., are their mine. The eye, etc., are also their meeting place, because they meet there by way of the respective doors and objects. The eye, etc., are also their place of origin, because they arise right there, having them as their support and object. The eye, etc., are also their cause, because in their absence, they too are absent. Thus, for these reasons—in the sense of a dwelling place, a mine, a meeting place, a place of origin, and a cause—these phenomena are called 'āyatanas.' Therefore, according to the meaning stated, 'the eye which is an āyatana' is the eye-base... 'the dhammas which are an āyatana' is the dhamma-base. Thus the detailed analysis should be understood here in this way according to the meaning. Thus—

Nivāso ākaro ceva, jātideso ca kāraṇaṃ;

Samosaraṇaṭṭhānañca, vuccatā’yatanaṃ iti;

A dwelling, a mine, a place of birth, a cause, and a meeting place: this is called 'āyatana'.

Vidividehi dhātūhi, akārapubbakehi vā;

Antavirahitasaddū-papadena junāpi vā.

Avijjāsaddanipphatti, dīpetabbā sudhīmatā.

The derivation of the word 'ignorance' should be shown by the wise: from the root 'vid' (to know), preceded by the negative 'a'; or from the root 'ju' (to impel), connected with the word for 'endless'.

Ettha pūretuṃ ayuttaṭṭhena kāyaduccaritādi avindiyaṃ nāma, aladdhabbanti attho, taṃ avindiyaṃ vindatīti avijjā, tabbiparītato kāyasucaritādi vindiyaṃ nāma, taṃ vindiyaṃ na vindatīti avijjā. Khandhānaṃ rāsaṭṭhaṃ, āyatanānaṃ āyatanaṭṭhaṃ, dhātūnaṃ suññaṭṭhaṃ, saccānaṃ tathaṭṭhaṃ, indriyānaṃ adhipatiyaṭṭhaṃ aviditaṃ karotīti [M 0.0361] avijjā. Dukkhādīnaṃ pīḷanādivasena vuttaṃ catubbidhaṃ atthaṃ aviditaṃ karotīti avijjā, antavirahite saṃsāre sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu satte javāpetīti avijjā, paramatthato avijjamānesu itthipurisādīsu javati, vijjamānesupi khandhādīsu na javatīti avijjā.

Here, because they are unsuitable to be undertaken, bodily misconduct and so on are called 'what should not be found' (avindiyaṃ), that is, what should not be acquired. It finds what should not be found; thus it is 'ignorance' (avijjā). Conversely, bodily good conduct and so on are called 'what should be found' (vindiyaṃ). It does not find what should be found; thus it is 'ignorance' (avijjā). It makes unknown the meaning of the aggregates as a heap, the meaning of the bases as sources, the meaning of the elements as voidness, the meaning of the truths as reality, and the meaning of the faculties as sovereignty; thus it is 'ignorance.' It makes unknown the fourfold meaning of suffering, etc., spoken of in terms of oppression, etc.; thus it is 'ignorance.' It impels beings in the endless round of rebirths, through all kinds of becoming, wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings; thus it is 'ignorance.' It impels towards what does not exist in an ultimate sense, such as a woman or a man, and it does not impel towards what does exist, such as the aggregates; thus it is 'ignorance.'

Yaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “apica cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ vatthārammaṇapaṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannā naṃ dhammānaṃ chādanatopi avijjā”ti vuttaṃ, etaṃ na saddatthato vuttaṃ, atha kho avijjāya chādanakiccattā vuttaṃ. Tathā hi abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ –

As to what is said in the Commentary: 'Moreover, ignorance is so called because it also covers the base and object of eye-consciousness and so on, and the phenomena of dependent origination and the dependently arisen,' this is not stated according to the word's etymology, but because covering is the function of ignorance. For this is stated in the Subcommentary to the Abhidhamma:

“Byañjanatthaṃ dassetvā sabhāvatthaṃ dassetuṃ ‘apicā’tiādimāha, cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ vatthārammaṇāni ‘idaṃ vattu, idamārammaṇa’nti avijjāya ñātuṃ na sakkāti avijjā tappaṭicchādikā vuttā, vatthārammaṇasabhāvacchādanato eva avijjādīnaṃ paṭiccasamuppādabhāvassa, jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paṭiccasamuppannabhāvassa ca chādanato paṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannachādanaṃ veditabbanti. Tattha duggatigāmikammassa visesappaccayattā avijjā ‘avindiyaṃ vindatī’ti vuttā, tathā visesapaccayo vindanīyassa na hotīti ‘vindiyaṃ na vindatī’ti ca, attanissitānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ pavattāpanaṃ uppādanaṃ āyatanaṃ, sammohabhāveneva anabhisamayabhūtattā ‘aviditaṃ aññātaṃ karoti, antavirahite javāpetī’ti vaṇṇāgamavipariyāyavikāravināsadhātuatthavisesayogehi pañcavidhassa niruttilakkhaṇassa vasena tīsupi padesu akāravikārajakāre gahetvā aññesaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ lopaṃ katvā jakārassa ca dutiyassa āgamaṃ katvā avijjāti vuttā”ti.

'Having shown the literal meaning, he states 'Moreover...' etc., to show the meaning of its intrinsic nature. Because by means of ignorance it is not possible to know of the bases and objects of eye-consciousness, etc., 'This is the base, this is the object,' ignorance is said to be their concealer. It should be understood that it conceals dependent origination and the dependently arisen because, by concealing the intrinsic nature of the base and object, it conceals the fact that ignorance, etc., are dependent origination and that aging-and-death, etc., are dependently arisen. Therein, because it is a specific condition for kamma that leads to a bad destination, ignorance is said to 'find what should not be found.' Likewise, because it is not a specific condition for what should be found, it is said that 'it does not find what should be found.' The setting in motion and production of eye-consciousness and so on, which are dependent on oneself, is 'āyatana.' Because it is essentially delusion and thus uncomprehended, it 'makes the unknown unknown' and 'impels in the endless.' It is called 'avijjā' through the fivefold method of etymological analysis—by way of letter insertion, transposition, modification, elision, and the connection of a root with a special meaning—by taking the modification of the letter 'a' and the letter 'j' in three places, eliding other letters, and inserting a second letter 'j'.'

Arahadhātuto [M 0.0362] ñeyyā, arahaṃsaddasaṇṭhiti;

Arārūpapadahana-dhātuto vāthavā pana.

The formation of the word 'arahant' should be known from the root 'arah' (to be worthy); or else from the root 'han' (to destroy) with the prefix 'ara' (enemy).

Rahato rahito cāpi, akārapubbato idha;

Vuccate assa nipphatti, ārakādiravassitā.

Here its derivation is also stated from 'raha' (secrecy) and 'rahita' (devoid), preceded by 'a'; and it is based on the sound 'āraka' (far).

Tathā hi arahanti aggadakkhiṇeyyattā cīvarādipaccaye arahati pūjāvisesañcāti arahaṃ. Vuttañca –

For, because he is worthy of the highest offerings, he is worthy of the requisites such as robes and of special veneration; therefore he is an Arahant. And it is said:

“Pūjāvisesaṃ saha paccayehi,

Yasmā ayaṃ arahati lokanātho;

Atthānurūpaṃ arahanti loke,

Tasmā jino arahati nāmameta”nti.

Because this Lord of the World is worthy of special veneration along with the requisites, and the name 'Arahant' is appropriate to the meaning in the world, therefore the Victor is worthy of this name.

Tathā so kilesārayo maggena hanīti arahaṃ. Vuttañca –

Likewise, he has slain the enemies, the defilements, with the path; therefore he is an Arahant. And it is said:

“Yasmā rāgādisaṅkhātā, sabbepi arayo hatā;

Paññāsatthena nāthena, tasmāpi arahaṃ mato”ti.

Because all the enemies, designated as lust and so on, have been slain by the Protector with the sword of wisdom, for that reason too he is deemed an Arahant.

Yañcetaṃ avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhiṃ puññādiabhisaṅkhārāraṃ jarāmaraṇanemiṃ āsavasamudayamayena akkhena vijjhitvā vibhavarathe samāyojitaṃ anādikālappavattaṃ saṃsāracakkaṃ, tassa so bodhimaṇḍe vīriyapādehi sīlapathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya saddhāhatthena kammakkhayakaraṃ ñāṇaparasuṃ gahetvā sabbe are hanītipi arahaṃ. Vuttañca –

And because he has destroyed all the spokes of this wheel of saṃsāra—a wheel that has been rolling on from time without beginning, with a navel of ignorance, existence, and craving, spokes of formations such as merit, a rim of old age and death, and yoked to the chariot of non-becoming—having pierced it with the axle of the arising of the taints, and standing firmly on the ground of virtue with the feet of effort at the enlightenment seat, and wielding with the hand of faith the axe of knowledge that destroys kamma, he is also an Arahant. And it is said:

“Arā saṃsāracakkassa, hatā ñāṇāsinā yato;

Lokanāthena tenesa, arahanti pavuccatī”ti.

Because the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed by the Lord of the World with the sword of wisdom, therefore he is called 'Arahant'.

Tathā attahitaṃ parahitañca paripūretuṃ sammā paṭipajjantehi sādhūhi dūrato rahitabbā pariccajitabbā parihātabbāti rahā, rāgādayo pāpadhammā, na santi etassa rahāti [M 0.0363] arahaṃ. “Araho”ti vattabbe okārassa sānusāraṃ akārādesaṃ katvā “arahaṃ”nti vuttaṃ. Āha ca –

Furthermore, because the evil states such as lust, which are called 'rahā' (things to be abandoned), should be kept far away, abandoned, and avoided by the virtuous who are rightly practicing to perfectly fulfill their own benefit and the benefit of others, and because he has no such 'rahā,' he is an Arahant. When it should be said 'Araho', by making the substitution of 'a' for 'o' with the anusāra, it is said 'Arahant'. And it is said:

“Pāpadhammā rahā nāma, sādhūhi rahitabbato;

Tesaṃ suṭṭhu pahīnattā, bhagavā arahaṃ mato”ti.

Evil states are called 'rahā' because they should be abandoned by the virtuous. Because they are well abandoned by him, the Blessed One is considered an Arahant.

Atha vā khīṇāsavehi sekkhehi kalyāṇaputhujjanehi ca na rahitabbo na pariccajitabbo, te ca bhagavāti arahaṃ. Āha ca –

Or, because he should not be avoided or abandoned by those whose taints are destroyed, by trainees, and by virtuous worldlings, he is the Blessed One, the Arahant. And it is said:

“Ye ca sacchikatadhammā,

Ariyā suddhagocarā;

Na tehi rahito hoti,

Nātho tenā’rahaṃ mato”ti.

And those who have directly experienced the Dhamma, noble ones with pure pasture, he is not abandoned by them; therefore the Protector is considered an Arahant.

Rahoti ca gamanaṃ vuccati, natthi etassa raho gamanaṃ gatīsu paccājātīti arahaṃ. Āha ca –

And 'raho' is said to mean 'going'. Because he has no secret going, no rebirth in the destinations, he is an Arahant. And it is said:

“Raho vā gamanaṃ yassa, saṃsāre natthi sabbaso;

Pahīnajātimaraṇo, arahaṃ sugato mato”ti.

He for whom there is no secret going in saṃsāra whatsoever, having abandoned birth and death, the Arahant is considered the Sugata (Well-Gone One).

Pāsaṃsattā vā bhagavā arahaṃ. Akkharacintakā hi pasaṃsāyaṃ arahasadaṃ vaṇṇenti. Pāsaṃsabhāvo ca bhagavato anaññasādhāraṇo yathābhuccaguṇādhigato sadevake loke suppatiṭṭhito. Iti pāsaṃsattāpi bhagavā arahaṃ. Āha ca –

Or, due to being worthy of praise, the Blessed One is an Arahant. For etymologists explain the word 'araha' in the sense of praise. And the Blessed One's praiseworthiness is unique, attained through true qualities, and well-established in the world with its deities. Thus, due to being worthy of praise, the Blessed One is an Arahant. And it is said:

“Guṇehi sadiso natthi, yasmā loke sadevake;

Tasmā pāsaṃsiyattāpi, arahaṃ dvipaduttamo”ti.

Because there is none equal to him in virtues in the world with its deities, therefore, due to his praiseworthiness, the Arahant is the Supreme Among Two-footed Beings.

Imāni [M 0.0364] nibbacanāni “araha pūjāyaṃ, hana hiṃsāyaṃ, raha cāge, rahi gatiya”nti imesaṃ dhātūnaṃ vasena idha vuttāni kilesehi ārakattā “araha”nti ca pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvā “araha”nti ca asappurisānaṃ ārakā dūreti “araha”nti ca sappurisānaṃ ārakā āsanneti “araha”nti ca. Nibbacanāni pana dhātusaddanissitāni na hontīti idha na gahitāni. Pasaṃsā pana atthato pūjā evāti “araha pūjāya”nti dhātussa attho bhavituṃ yuttoti idha amhehi gahitā, aṭṭhakathācariyehi tu arahasaddassa labbhamānavasena sabbepi atthā gahitā dhātunissitā ca adhātunissitā ca. Kathaṃ? –

These etymologies are stated here by way of these roots: ‘araha’ in the sense of worship, ‘hana’ in the sense of harming, ‘raha’ in the sense of abandoning, and ‘rahi’ in the sense of going. And because of being far from defilements, he is ‘araha’; and because of the absence of secret evil-doing, he is ‘araha’; and because he is far from ignoble persons, he is ‘araha’; and because he is near to noble persons, he is ‘araha’. However, etymologies that are not based on verbal roots are not included here. But praise, in terms of meaning, is indeed worship, so the meaning of the root ‘araha’ in the sense of worship is suitable to be taken here, and thus it is accepted by us. The commentary teachers, however, have accepted all available meanings for the word ‘araha’, both those dependent on roots and those not dependent on roots. How so?

Ārakattā hatattā ca, kilesārīna so muni;

Hatasaṃsāracakkāro, paccayādīna cāraho;

Na raho karoti pāpāni, arahaṃ tena vuccatīti.

Because he is far from and has destroyed the enemies which are the defilements, that sage, whose spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra are destroyed, and who is worthy of requisites and so forth, does not do evil secretly; therefore he is called an Arahant.

Ṭīkācariyehipi tatheva gahitā. Kathaṃ? –

The subcommentary teachers also accepted it in the same way. How so?

Ārakā mandabuddhīnaṃ, ārakā ca vijānataṃ;

Rahānaṃ suppahīnattā, vidūnamaraheyyato;

Bhavesu ca rahābhāvā, pāsaṃsā arahaṃ jinoti.

He is far beyond the dull-witted, and far beyond even the wise; because secrets are well abandoned, and because he is not to be forsaken by the discerning; and because of the absence of secret conduct in existences, the Arahant, the Conqueror, wins praise.

Yathā pana arahaṃsaddassa, evaṃ arahāsaddassāpi nibbacanāni veditabbāni.

Just as with the word ‘arahant,’ so too should the etymologies of the word ‘arahā’ be understood.

Supubbagamito ceva, supubbagaditopi ca;

Dhīro sugatasaddassa, nipphattiṃ samudīraye.

From being well-gone before, and also from being well-spoken before, the wise one should declare the derivation of the word ‘Sugata’.

Ettha hi sugatoti sobhanaṃ gataṃ etassāti sugato, sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatoti sugato, sammā gatoti sugato, sammā ca gadatīti sugatoti dhātunissitaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā saddanipphatti kātabbā. Vuttañhi aṭṭhakathāsu –

Here, ‘Sugata’ means one whose going is good, thus he is Sugata; one who has gone to a beautiful place is Sugata; one who has gone rightly is Sugata; and one who speaks rightly is Sugata—thus, taking the meaning based on the root, the derivation of the word should be made. For it is said in the commentaries:

“Sobhanagamanattā[M 0.0365], sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā, sammā gatattā, sammā ca gadattā sugato. Gamanampi hi gatanti vuccati, tañca bhagavato sobhanaṃ parisuddhamanavajjaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Ariyamaggo, tenesa gamanena khemaṃ disaṃ asajjamāno gatoti sobhanagamanattā sugato”tiādi.

“Because of his beautiful going, because of having gone to a beautiful place, because of having gone rightly, and because of speaking rightly, he is the Sugata. For going itself is called ‘gata’ (gone), and that of the Blessed One is beautiful, utterly pure, and blameless. What, then, is that going? The Noble Path. By that going, he has gone to the safe destination without obstruction—thus, because of his beautiful going, he is the Sugata,” and so on.

Bhagasaddūpapadato, vanuto vamutopi ca;

Bhagavāsaddanipphattiṃ, pavade aññathāpi vā.

From the word ‘bhaga’ as a prefix, and from ‘vanu’ and also from ‘vamu’, one should declare the derivation of the word ‘Bhagavā’, or also in other ways.

Atrimāni nibbacanāni – bhagasaṅkhātā lokiyalokuttarasampattiyo vani bhaji sevīti bhagavā. Somanassakumārattabhāvādīsu carimattabhāve ca bhagasaṅkhātaṃ siriṃ issariyaṃ yasañca vami uggiri kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya anapekkho chaḍḍayīti bhagavā. Atha vā nakkhattehi samaṃ pavattattā bhagasaṅkhāte sineruyugandharauttarakuruhimavantādibhājanaloke vami, tannivāsitattāvāsasamatikkamanato tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena pajahīti bhagavāti.

Here are these etymologies: Because he partook of, served, and frequented the worldly and supramundane attainments designated as ‘bhaga’ (fortune), he is Bhagavā. Or, because in his existences as Prince Somanassa and others, and in his final existence, he vomited forth (vami), disgorged, and discarded without concern, like a lump of spittle, the fortune (bhaga) consisting of splendor, sovereignty, and fame, he is Bhagavā. Or alternatively, he vomited forth (vami) the container world—Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, Himavanta, and so on—which is designated as ‘bhaga’ because it proceeds together with the constellations; that is, he abandoned it by transcending the state of dwelling therein and by abandoning the sensual desire attached to it; therefore he is Bhagavā.

Paradhātuvasā vāpi, parūpapadatopi vā;

Muto tathā majato ca, mayato munato mito.

Or also by way of other roots, or from the prefix ‘para’; likewise from ‘mu’, and from ‘maj’, from ‘may’, from ‘mun’, from ‘mi’.

Puna mitoti etehi, dhātūhi khalu sattahi;

Vade paramasaddassa, nipphattiṃ jinasāsane.

And again from ‘mi’; indeed, from these seven roots, one should declare the derivation of the word ‘parama’ in the Conqueror’s Dispensation.

Uttamavācīparama-saddena saha aṭṭhahi;

Padehi pāramīsaddaṃ, vade taddhitapaccayiṃ.

With the word ‘parama,’ which expresses the highest, along with eight words, one should declare the word ‘pāramī’ as having a taddhita suffix.

Pārasaddūpapadato, majatopi mutotha vā;

Mayato vā munato vā, mito vā punapi mito.

From the word ‘pāra’ as a prefix; from ‘maj’, or from ‘mu’; or from ‘may’, or from ‘mun’, or from ‘mi’, or again from ‘mi’.

Etehi chahi dhātūhi, mahāpurisavācakaṃ;

Pāramīsaddamīrenti, tato pāramitāravaṃ.

From these six roots, they derive the word ‘pāramī,’ which denotes a great person; from that comes the sound of ‘pāramitā’.

Ettha [M 0.0366] tāva uttamatthavācakaparamasaddavasena pāramīnibbacanaṃ kathessāma. Tato paradhātuvasena, tato parasaddūpapadamudhātādivasena tato pārasaddūpapadamajadhātādivasena.

Here, first, we will explain the etymology of ‘pāramī’ by way of the word ‘parama,’ which expresses the highest meaning. Then, by way of other roots. Then, by way of the prefix ‘para’ and the root ‘mu’ and so forth. Then, by way of the prefix ‘pāra’ and the root ‘maj’ and so forth.

Dānasīlādiguṇavisesayogena sattuttamatāya paramā. Mahābodhisattā bodhisattā, tesaṃ bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramī, dānādikriyā. Atha vā parati pāleti pūreti cāti paramo, dānādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ pālako pūrako ca bodhisatto, paramassa ayaṃ, paramassa vā bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramī, dānādikriyā. Atha vā paraṃ sattaṃ attani mavati bandhati guṇavisesayogenāti paramo, paraṃ vā adhikataraṃ majjati sujjhati kilesamalatoti paramo, paraṃ vā seṭṭhaṃ nibbānaṃ mayati gacchatīti paramo, paraṃ vā lokaṃ pamāṇabhūtena ñāṇavisesena idhalokaṃ viya munāti paricchindatīti paramo, paraṃ vā ativiya sīlādiguṇagaṇaṃ attano santāne minoti pakkhipatīti paramo, paraṃ vā attabhūtato dhammakāyato aññaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ vā tadanatthakaraṃ kilesacoragaṇaṃ mināti hiṃsatīti paramo, mahāsatto, paramassa ayaṃ, paramassa vā bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramī, dānādikriyā.

By virtue of their excellence in qualities such as generosity and virtue, they are supreme (paramā) among beings. The great bodhisattvas are bodhisattvas; their state or action is pāramī, the practice of giving and so forth. Alternatively, because he protects (pāleti) and fulfills (pūreti), he is ‘parama’; the Bodhisattva is the protector and fulfiller of qualities such as generosity. This is of the supreme one, or the state or action of the supreme one is pāramī, the practice of giving and so forth. Or, because he binds (mavati) other beings to himself through the excellence of his qualities, he is ‘parama’. Or, because he purifies (majjati) others more exceedingly from the stains of defilements, he is ‘parama’. Or, because he goes (mayati) to the other shore, the excellent Nibbāna, he is ‘parama’.
