Or, because he knows (munāti) and discerns the other world, like this world, with a special knowledge that serves as a measure, he is ‘parama’. Or, because he places (minoti) an exceedingly great mass of qualities such as morality in his own continuity, he is ‘parama’. Or, because he harms (mināti) and destroys the opposing force, the band of defilement-thieves, which is other than his own being, the Dhamma-body, and which is detrimental to it, he is ‘parama’. He is the great being; this is of the supreme one, or the state or action of the supreme one is pāramī, the practice of giving and so forth.

Aparo nayo – pāre nibbāne majjati sujjhati, satte ca majjeti sodhetīti pāramī, mahāpuriso, tassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramitā. Pāre nibbāne satte mavati bandhati yojeīti pāramī, pāraṃ vā nibbānaṃ mayati gacchati, satte ca māyeti gametīti pāramī, munāti vā pāraṃ nibbānaṃ yāthāvato, tattha vā satte minoti pakkhipatīti pāramī, kilesāriṃ vā sattānaṃ pāre nibbāne mināti hiṃsatīti pāramī, mahāpuriso, tassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā pāramitā, dānādikriyāva. Iminā nayena pāramīnaṃ saddattho veditabbo.

Another method: Because he purifies and cleanses himself on the other shore, Nibbāna, and causes beings to be purified and cleansed, he is ‘pāramī’, the great person; his state or action is pāramitā. Because he binds and joins beings to the other shore, Nibbāna, he is ‘pāramī’. Or, because he goes to the other shore, Nibbāna, and causes beings to go there, he is ‘pāramī’. Or, because he knows the other shore, Nibbāna, as it actually is, or because he places beings there, he is ‘pāramī’. Or, because he harms and destroys the enemies, the defilements, of beings on the other shore, Nibbāna, he is ‘pāramī’. He is the great person; his state or action is pāramitā, which is the practice of giving and so forth. In this way, the meaning of the word ‘pāramī’ should be understood.

Karadhātuvasā [M 0.0367] vāpi, kiradhātuvasena vā;

Kaṃsaddūpapadarudhi-dhātuto vāpi dīpaye;

Karuṇāsaddanipphattiṃ, mahākaruṇasāsane.

Or by way of the root ‘kar’ (to make), or by way of the root ‘kir’ (to scatter); or from the root ‘rudh’ with the prefix ‘kaṃ’, one should reveal the derivation of the word ‘karuṇā’ in the Dispensation of the Greatly Compassionate One.

Tattha karuṇāti paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ hadayakampanaṃ karotīti karuṇā. Kirati paradukkaṃ vikkhipatīti karuṇā. Kaṃ vuccati sukhaṃ, taṃ rundhati vibādhati kāruṇikaṃ na sukhāpetītipi karuṇā.

Herein, because it causes the hearts of the good to tremble when there is suffering in others, it is ‘karuṇā’. Because it scatters and dispels the suffering of others, it is ‘karuṇā’. ‘Kaṃ’ is said to mean happiness; because it obstructs and hinders that, not allowing the compassionate one to be happy, it is also ‘karuṇā’.

Vidividhavidadhātu-vasena paridīpaye;

Vijjāsaddassa nipphattiṃ, saddanipphattikovido.

By way of the roots ‘vid’, ‘vidh’, and ‘vid’, one skilled in the derivation of words should elucidate the derivation of the word ‘vijjā’.

Tattha vijjāti vindiyaṃ kāyasucaritādiṃ vindati yāthāvato upalabhatīti vijjā. Tamokhandhādipadālanaṭṭhena vā attano paṭipakkhaṃ vijjhatīti vijjā. Tato eva attano visayaṃ viditaṃ karotītipi vijjā.

Herein, because it finds and truly comprehends what is to be found, such as good bodily conduct, it is ‘vijjā’. Or, because it pierces its own opponent, such as the mass of darkness, by way of shattering it, it is ‘vijjā’. And for that very reason, because it makes its own domain known, it is also ‘vijjā’.

Medhadhātuvasā ceva, medhādhātūhi ca dvidhā;

Medhāsaddassa nipphattiṃ, medhāvī samudīraye.

Both from the root ‘medh’, and in two ways from the roots ‘me’ and ‘dhā’, the wise one should declare the derivation of the word ‘medhā’.

Tattha medhāti sammohaṃ medhati hiṃsatīti medhā. Pāpake vā akusale dhamme medhati hiṃsatītipi medhā. Atha vā –

Herein, medhā is so called because it crushes, that is, destroys, delusion. Or it is also so called because it crushes evil, unwholesome states. Or else—

“Paññā hi seṭṭhā kusalā vadanti,

Nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ;

Sīlaṃ siriñcāpi satañca dhammo,

Anvāyikā paññavato bhavantī”ti

“The skillful declare wisdom to be best, just as the moon is the king of the stars. Virtue, fortune, and the Dhamma of the good are attendant on one who possesses wisdom.”

Vacanato pana medhati sīlena siriyā satañca dhammehi saha gacchati, na ekikā hutvā tiṭṭhatītipi medhā. Aparo nayo – sukhumampi atthaṃ dhammañca khippameva meti ca dhāreti cāti medhā, ettha metīti gaṇhātīti attho. Tathā hi [M 0.0368] aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ vuttaṃ “asani viya siluccaye kilese medhati hiṃsatīti medhā, khippaṃ gahaṇadhāraṇaṭṭhena vā medhā”ti.

In accordance with that saying, medhā (intelligence) is so called because it goes together with virtue, fortune, and the states of the good, not standing alone. Another method: it is medhā because it quickly comprehends (meti) and retains (dhāreti) even subtle meaning and text; here, meti means 'it grasps.' For so it is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī: 'Like a thunderbolt on a rocky mountain, it crushes—that is, destroys—the defilements; thus it is medhā. Or it is medhā in the sense of quick grasping and retaining.'

Ranjadhātuvasā ceva, rāpubbatiratopi ca;

Rattisaddassa nipphattiṃ, saddatthaññū vibhāvaye.

The knower of word-meanings should explain the derivation of the word ratti (night) from the root rañj (to delight), and also from 'crossing over' preceded by 'rā'.

Ranjanti sattā etthāti ratti, rā saddo tiyyati chijjati etthāti ratti, sattānaṃ saddassa vūpasamakāloti attho.

Beings delight (ranjanti) herein, thus it is ratti (night). The sound 'rā' is crossed over or cut off herein, thus it is ratti. The meaning is that it is the time for the calming of the sound of beings.

Mā māne iti soanta, kammanīti cubhohi tu;

Dhātūhi māsasaddassa, nipphattiṃ samudīraye.

From the two roots, mā in the sense of 'to measure' and so in the sense of 'to make an end,' one should declare the derivation of the word māsa (month).

Tathā hi sattānaṃ āyuṃ mānanto viya siyati antaṃ karotīti māso, cittamāsādayo dvādasa māsā. Seyyathidaṃ? Citto visākho jeṭṭho āsāḷho sāvaṇo bhaddo assayujo kattiko māgasiro phusso māgho phagguṇoti. Tatra citto māso “rammako”ti vuccati. “Yathāpi rammake māse, bahū pupphanti vārijā”ti pāḷi dissati. Bhaddo pana “poṭṭhapādo”ti vuccati.

For it is called māso (month) because, as if measuring the lifespan of beings, it destroys, making an end. The twelve months are Citta, Visākha, Jeṭṭha, Āsāḷha, Sāvaṇa, Bhadda, Assayuja, Kattika, Māgasira, Phussa, Māgha, and Phagguṇa. Of these, the month Citta is called 'Rammaka,' as a canonical passage is seen: 'Just as in the delightful month, many water-born flowers bloom.' The month of Bhadda, however, is called 'Poṭṭhapāda.'

Atha vā māsoti aparaṇṇavisesassapi suvaṇṇamāsassapi nāmaṃ. Tattha aparaṇṇaviseso yathāparimite kāle asiyati bhakkhiyatīti māso, itaro pana “mama ida”nti masiyati āmasiyati gaṇhiyatīti māsoti vuccati.

Or else, māsa is also the name for a type of pulse or a gold māsaka coin. In the case of the pulse, it is called māsa because it is eaten or consumed at a specified time. But the other is called māsa because it is touched or grasped with the thought, 'This is mine.'

Saṃpubbavadacarehi, saṃvacchararavassa tu;

Nipphattiṃ samudīreyya, sakyasīhassa sāsane.

In the teaching of the Lion of the Sakyans, one should declare the derivation of the word saṃvacchara (year) from the roots vad (to speak) and car (to fare) with the prefix saṃ.

Tathā hi taṃ taṃ sattaṃ dhammappavattiñca saṅgamma vadanto viya carati pavattatīti saṃvaccharo.

For it is called saṃvacchara (year) because it proceeds as if speaking (vadanto) in conjunction with (saṅgamma) the occurrence of this and that being and phenomenon.

Bhidibhikkhidhātuvasā[M 0.0369], atha vā bhayavācakaṃ;

Bhīsaddaṃ purimaṃ katvā, ikkhadhātuvasena ca;

Bhikkhusaddassa nipphattiṃ, kathayeyya vicakkhaṇo.

A discerning person should state the derivation of the word bhikkhu (monk) from the roots bhid (to break) and bhikkh (to beg); or else, by taking first the sound bhi, which expresses fear, and then from the root ikkh (to see).

Tathā hi kilese bhindatīti bhikkhu. Chinnabhinnapaṭadharotipi bhikkhu. Bhikkhanasīlotipi bhikkhu. Saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhati, ikkhanasīloti vā bhikkhu.

For he is a bhikkhu because he breaks the defilements. He is also a bhikkhu because he wears robes that are cut and broken. He is also a bhikkhu because he has the habit of begging. Or he is a bhikkhu because he sees fear in saṃsāra, or has the habit of seeing it.

Sadabhidīhi dhātūhi, sabbhisaddagatiṃ vade;

Sappurise ca nibbāne, esa saddo pavattati.

From the roots sad and bhid, one should state the meaning of the word sabbhi. This word applies to a good person and to Nibbāna.

Atrimāni nibbacanāni – sīdanasabhāve kilese bhindatīti sabbhi, sappuriso, yo “ariyo”tipi “paṇḍito”tipi vuccati. Apica sīdanasabhāvā kilesā bhijjanti etthāti sabbhi, nibbānaṃ, yaṃ “rāgakkhayo”tiādināmaṃ labhati. Tathā hi saṃyuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ “yasmā nibbānaṃ āgamma sīdanasabhāvā kilesā bhijjanti, tasmā taṃ sabbhīti vuccatī”ti.

Herein are these derivations: He breaks the defilements, which have a sinking nature; thus he is a sabbhi, a good person, who is also called 'noble' and 'wise.' Furthermore, it is sabbhi because herein the defilements, which have a sinking nature, are broken; this refers to Nibbāna, which obtains such names as 'destruction of lust.' For so it is said in the Saṃyutta Commentary: 'Because on account of Nibbāna the defilements, which have a sinking nature, are broken, therefore it is called sabbhi.'

Etthetaṃ vadāma –

Herein, we say this:

“Yasmā nibbānamāgama, saṃsīdanasabhāvino;

Klesā bhijjanti taṃ tasmā, sabbhīti amataṃ’bravu”nti.

"Because, having come to Nibbāna, the defilements, which by nature sink down, are broken, therefore the deathless ones have called it sabbhi."

Brūdhātusadadhātūhi, bhisisaddassa sambhavaṃ;

Guṇehi brūhitā dhīrā, porāṇācariyā’bravuṃ.

The wise ancient teachers, augmented by virtues, spoke of the origin of the word bhisi (mat) from the roots brū (to speak) and sad (to sink).

Tathā hi bravantā ettha sīdantīti bhisīti bhisisaddassa sambhavaṃ porāṇā kathayiṃsu.

For the ancients explained the origin of the word bhisi (mat) thus: Because speaking (bravantā), they sink down (sīdanti) on it, it is a bhisi.

Sukhadhātuvasā cāpi, supubbakhādatopi vā;

Supubbakhanuto vāpi, sukhasaddagatiṃ vade.

One should state the meaning of the word sukha (happiness) as from the root sukha; or from the root khād (to eat) with the prefix su; or also from the root khan (to dig) with the prefix su.

Sukhanti [M 0.0370] hi sukhayatīti sukhaṃ. Yassuppajjati, taṃ sukhitaṃ karotīti attho. Suṭṭhu dukkhaṃ khādatītipi sukhaṃ. Suṭṭu dukkhaṃ khanatītipi sukhaṃ.

For sukha (happiness) is so called because it makes one happy. The meaning is that for whomever it arises, it makes that one happy. It is also sukha because it thoroughly eats up suffering or because it thoroughly digs out suffering.

Dukkhadhātuvasā cāpi, dupubbakhādatopi vā;

Dupubbakhanuto vāpi, dukkhasaddagatiṃ vade.

One should state the meaning of the word dukkha (suffering) as from the root dukkha; or from the root khād (to eat) with the prefix du; or also from the root khan (to dig) with the prefix du.

Dukkhanti hi dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ. Yassuppajjati, taṃ dukkhitaṃ karotīti attho. Duṭṭhu sukhaṃ khādatītipi dukkhaṃ. Duṭṭhu sukhaṃ khanatītipi dukkhaṃ. Atha vā dvidhā sukhaṃ khanatītipi dukkhaṃ.

For dukkha (suffering) is so called because it makes one suffer. The meaning is that for whomever it arises, it makes that one suffer. It is also dukkha because it badly eats up happiness or because it badly digs out happiness. Or else, it is dukkha because it digs out happiness in two ways.

Gandhadhātuvasā cāpi, gamudhātuvasena vā;

Gamudhādhātuto vāpi, gandhasaddagatiṃ vade.

One should state the meaning of the word gandha (smell) as from the root gandh; or from the root gam; or also from the roots gam and dhā.

Tathā hi gandhayatīti gandho, attano vatthuṃ sūcayati “idaṃ sugandhaṃ, idaṃ duggandha”nti pakāseti, paṭicchannaṃ, vā pupphaphalādiṃ “idamettha atthī”ti pesuññaṃ karonto viya ahosīti attho. Atha vā gandhayati chindati manāpagandho sugandhabhāvena duggandhaṃ, amanāpagandho ca duggandhabhāvena sugandhanti gandho. Ettha pana gandhasaddassa chedanavācakatte –

For it is gandho (smell) because it indicates (gandhayati); it points out its own source, revealing, 'This is fragrant, this is foul-smelling.' The meaning is that it is as if it were engaging in slander, revealing a hidden flower or fruit by saying, 'This is here.' Alternatively, it is gandho because it 'indicates,' that is, it 'cuts off' (chindati): a pleasant smell cuts off a foul smell by its fragrant nature, and an unpleasant smell cuts off a pleasant smell by its foul-smelling nature. Here, regarding the word gandha as denoting 'cutting'—

“Atijātaṃ anujātaṃ, puttamicchanti paṇḍitā;

Avajātaṃ na icchanti, yo hoti kulagandhano”ti

"The wise desire a son who is superior-born or conformably-born; they do not desire one who is inferior-born, who is a destroyer of the family."

Ayaṃ pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Vāyunā vā nīyamāno gacchatīti gandho. Kaccāyanasmiñhi “khādāmagamānaṃ khandhandhagandhā”ti khādaamagamiiccetesaṃ dhātūnaṃ yathākkamaṃ khandha andhagandhādesā vuttā. Atha vā gacchanto dhariyate soti gandho. Vuttañhetaṃ bhadantena buddhadattācariyena veyyākaraṇena niruttinayadassinā “dhariyatīti gacchanto, gandho sūcanatopi vā”ti.

This Pāḷi is an illustration. Or, it is gandho because, being carried by the wind, it goes. For in Kaccāyana's grammar, khandha, andha, and gandha are stated to be substitutes for the roots khād, am, and gam respectively, as in the rule 'khādāmagamānaṃ khandhandhagandhā.' Alternatively, it is gandho because it is held while going. This has been stated by the venerable teacher Buddhadatta, the grammarian skilled in discerning the method of etymology: 'It is held while going; or gandha is from indicating.'

Rasadhātuvasā ceva, ramāsadhātutopi ca;

Rasasaddassa nipphattiṃ, āhu dhammarasaññuno.

Those who know the taste of the Dhamma speak of the derivation of the word rasa (taste) as from the root ras (to taste) and from the roots ram (to delight) and as (to eat).

Rasoti [M 0.0371] hi rasanti taṃ assādentīti raso, ramantā taṃ asantītipi raso. Vuttampi cetaṃ “ramamānā na’santīti rasoti paridīpito”ti. Tatrāyamattho – devamanussādayo sattā yasmā ramamānā naṃ dhammajātaṃ asanti bhakkhanti, tasmā taṃ dhammajātaṃ raso nāmāti niruttaññūhi paridīpitoti. Padacchedo pana evaṃ veditabbo –

Rasa (taste) is so called because they savor it; thus it is rasa. Or, because delighting (ramantā), they eat (asanti) it; thus it is rasa. And this has been said: 'Because delighting, they eat it, thus rasa is explained.' Here the meaning is this: because beings such as devas and humans delighting eat that Dhamma-nature, therefore that Dhamma-nature is called rasa—so it has been explained by those skilled in etymology. The division of the words, however, should be understood thus:

Naṃ asanti na santīti, padacchedo siyā tahiṃ;

Kammakārakabhāvena, attho hi tattha icchito.

The word-division there should be naṃ asanti, not na santi. For the meaning intended there is in the sense of the accusative case.

Iti vuttānusārena, avuttesu padesupi;

Yathārahaṃ nayaññūhi, nayo neyyo susobhano.

Thus, in accordance with what has been said, even in cases not stated, a suitable and elegant method should be inferred by those who know the method.

Dhātucintāya ye muttā, anipphannāti te matā;

Te cāpi bahavo santi, pītalohitakādayo;

Those words that are devoid of analysis by roots are considered underived. And there are many such, like pīta, lohita, and so on.

Nipphanne api dhātūhi, sadde dhagāitiādayo;

Anipphannaṃva pekkhanti, gavādividhibhedato.

Even with words derived from roots, such as dhaga and so on, they regard them as if underived because of the different rules for words like gava.

Tathā hi “gacchatīti go”, iti vuttapadaṃ puna;

Anipphannaṃ karitvāna, “gāvo” iccādikaṃbravuṃ.

For, having taken the word ‘go,’ which is explained as 'it goes,' they treat it again as an underived stem and form ‘gāvo’ and so on.

Ekantena anipphannā, saddā viḍūḍabhādayo;

Dhāturūpakasaddā ca, “pabbatāyati”ādayo.

Words such as Viḍūḍabha are entirely underived, as are denominative verbs such as pabbatāyati (it acts like a mountain).

Seyyathidaṃ? “Viḍūḍabho, tisso, yevāpano, pītaṃ, lohitaṃ” iccevamādīni nāmikapadāni anipphannāni bhavanti. “Nīlaṃ, pītaṃ, yevāpanako” iccādīni pana nīlavaṇṇe pītavaṇṇe. Ke re ge saddeti dhātuvasena āgatattā nīlatīti nīlaṃ, pītatīti pītaṃ, ye vā pana itivacanena bhagavatā kiyate kathiyateti yevāpanakoti nibbacanamarahantīti nipphannānīti vattabbāni. Keci panettha vadeyyuṃ “nanu nīlati pītatītiādīni kriyāpadāni tepiṭake buddhavacane na dissantī”ti? Kiñcāpi [M 0.0372] na dissanti, tathāpi etarahi avijjamānā purāṇabhāsā esāti gahetabbāni. Yathā hi “nāthatīti nātho”ti ettha kiñcāpi “nāthatī”ti kriyāpadaṃ buddhavacane na dissati, tathāpi nātha yācanopatāpissariyāsīsanesūti dhātuno diṭṭhattā aṭṭhakathācariyā gaṇhiṃsuyeva, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi kriyāpadaparihīno dhātu vucceyya.

For example? Nominal words such as 'Viḍūḍabha,' 'Tissa,' 'Yevāpana,' 'Pīta,' and 'Lohita' are underived. But words such as 'Nīlaṃ,' 'Pītaṃ,' and 'Yevāpanako,' referring to blue color, yellow color, and a fixed term respectively, are derivable. Since they come from roots, they are to be called derived: 'it is blue' (nīlati), thus nīlaṃ; 'it is yellow' (pītati), thus pītaṃ; and because it is stated or said by the Blessed One with the words 'ye vā pana,' it is yevāpanako. Some might say here: 'But surely verbal forms like nīlati and pītati are not seen in the Buddha's word in the Tipiṭaka?' Although they are not seen, they should be taken as an ancient usage that is now non-existent. For example, regarding 'he protects (nāthati), thus he is a protector (nātho),' although the verbal form nāthati is not seen in the Buddha's word, the commentary teachers accepted it because the root nāth is seen with the meanings of asking, oppressing, ruling, and blessing. This should be seen in the same way. For a root would not be spoken of if it were devoid of a verbal form.

Kiñca bhiyyo – yathā “yāva byāti nimīsati, tatrāpi rasatibbayo”ti jātakapāḷiyaṃ imasmiṃ buddhuppāde devamanussānaṃ vohārapathe asañcarantaṃ purāṇabhāsābhūtaṃ “byātī”ti kriyāpadampi dissati, tathā “nīlati, pītatī”tiādīhipi purāṇabhāsābhūtehi kriyāpadehi bhavitabbaṃ. Tattha yāva byātīti yāva ummīsati. Ayañhi tasmiṃ kāle vohāro, yasmiṃ kāle bodhisatto cūḷabodhi nāma paribbājako ahosi. Yathā pana viḍūḍabhasaddādayo dhātuvasena anipphannā nāma vuccanti, tathā “pabbatāyati, samuddāyati, cicciṭāyati, dhūmāyati, duddubhāyati, mettāyati, karuṇāyati, mamāyati” iccevamādayo ca “chattīyati, vatthīyati, parikkhārīyati, dhanīyati, paṭīyati” iccevamādayo ca “atihatthayati, upavīṇayati, daḷhayati, pamāṇayati, kusalayati, visuddhayati” iccevamādayo ca dhātuvasena anipphannāyeva nāma vuccanti.

What is more? Just as in the Jātaka text, the verb “byātī” is seen in the phrase “yāva byāti nimīsati, tatrāpi rasatibbayo,” which is an archaic expression not current in the speech of gods and humans at the time of this Buddha’s appearance. Similarly, it must be so with archaic verbs like “nīlati” (becomes blue), “pītatī” (becomes yellow), etc. Here, “yāva byātī” means “until it opens.” For this was the usage at the time when the Bodhisatta was the wandering ascetic named Cūḷabodhi. Just as words such as “viḍūḍabha” are called underived from a root, so too are verbs like “pabbatāyati” (behaves like a mountain), “samuddāyati” (behaves like an ocean), “cicciṭāyati” (crackles), “dhūmāyati” (smokes), “duddubhāyati” (rumbles), “mettāyati” (is friendly), “karuṇāyati” (is compassionate), “mamāyati” (is possessive), and others like “chattīyati” (desires an umbrella), “vatthīyati” (desires clothes), “parikkhārīyati” (desires requisites), “dhanīyati” (desires wealth), “paṭīyati” (desires a bowl), and verbs like “atihatthayati” (overextends the hand), “upavīṇayati” (plays the lute), “daḷhayati” (strengthens), “pamāṇayati” (measures), “kusalayati” (makes skillful), “visuddhayati” (purifies)—all these are called underived from a root.

Tattha “pabbatāyatī”tiādīsu saṅgho pabbatamiva attānamācarati pabbatāyati, evaṃ samuddāyati. Saddo cicciṭamiva attānamācarati cicciṭāyati. Vatthu dhūmamiva attānamācarati dhūmāyati. Saddo duddubhaiti ācarati duddubhāyati, bhikkhu mettāyati, tathā karuṇāyati. “Mama ida”nti gaṇhati mamāyati. Achattaṃ chattamiva ācarati chattīyati. Aputtaṃ [M 0.0373] puttamiva ācarati puttīyati, sissaṃ ācariyo, attano pattamicchati pattīyati. Evaṃ vatthīyati, parikkhārīyati, cīvarīyati, dhanīyati, paṭīyati. Hatthinā atikkamati atihatthayati. Vīṇāya upagāyati upavīṇayati. Daḷhaṃ karoti vīriyaṃ daḷhayati. Pamāṇaṃ karoti pamāṇayati. Kusalaṃ pucchati kusalayati. Visuddhā hoti ratti visuddhāyati.

Here, in phrases like “pabbatāyati,” the Sangha acts like a mountain, thus “pabbatāyati,” and similarly “samuddāyati.” A sound acts like a crackle, thus “cicciṭāyati.” An object acts like smoke, thus “dhūmāyati.” A sound acts like a drum, thus “duddubhāyati.” A monk is friendly, thus “mettāyati,” and similarly is compassionate, thus “karuṇāyati.” Grasping “this is mine,” one is possessive, thus “mamāyati.” One treats that which is not an umbrella as an umbrella, thus “chattīyati.” One treats one who is not a son as a son, thus “puttīyati,” as a teacher treats a student. One desires one’s own bowl, thus “pattīyati.” Similarly for “vatthīyati,” “parikkhārīyati,” “cīvarīyati,” “dhanīyati,” and “paṭīyati.” One surpasses with an elephant, thus “atihatthayati.” One sings along with a lute, thus “upavīṇayati.” One makes effort firm, thus “daḷhayati.” One makes a measure, thus “pamāṇayati.” One asks about what is skillful, thus “kusalayati.” The night becomes pure, thus “visuddhāyati.”

Tatrāyaṃ padamālā – “pabbatāyati, pabbatāyanti. Pabbatāyasi, pabbatāyatha. Pabbatāyāmi, pabbatāyāmā”ti iminā nayena aṭṭhannaṃ vibhattīnaṃ vasena sesaṃ sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ, evaṃ “samuddāyati, chattīyatī”tiādīsu. Tatra kāritavasenapi “pabbatāyantaṃ payojayati pabbatāyati, puttiyantaṃ payojayati puttīyati” iccādi padasiddhi bhavati. Ayaṃ pana padamālā – pabbatāyati, pabbatāyanti. Pabbatāyasi. Sesaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Iccevaṃ dhātuvasena nipphannānipphannapadāni vibhāvitāni.

Here is the paradigm: “pabbatāyati, pabbatāyanti. Pabbatāyasi, pabbatāyatha. Pabbatāyāmi, pabbatāyāmā”—in this manner, the rest should all be connected in terms of the eight verbal endings, likewise with “samuddāyati, chattīyatī,” etc. There, also by causative usage, the word formations become like “pabbatāyantaṃ payojayati pabbatāyati” (he causes one who acts mountain-like), “puttiyantaṃ payojayati puttīyati” (he causes one who acts son-like), etc. This is the paradigm: “pabbatāyati, pabbatāyanti. Pabbatāyasi.” The rest should be connected. Thus, words derived and underived from roots have been explained.

Idāni dhātugaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, adhātulakkhaṇaṃ, kāritapaccayayogaṃ, sakāritekakammadvikammatikammapadaṃ, ūhanīyarūpagaṇaṃ, dhātūnaṃ ekagaṇikadvigaṇikategaṇikapadaṃ, suddhakattuhetukattupadarūpaṃ, kammabhāvapadarūpaṃ, ekakāritadvikāritapadaṃ, akāritadvikammakapadañca sabbametaṃ yathārahaṃ kathayāma.

Now, we shall discuss the characteristics of root groups, the characteristics of non-roots, the application of causative suffixes, single-object, double-object, and triple-object words in the causative, the group of inferable forms, single-group, double-group, and triple-group words of roots, pure agent and causal agent word forms, passive and impersonal word forms, single-causative and double-causative words, and non-causative double-object words—all these appropriately.

Tatra sabbadhātukanissite suddhakattuppayoge suddhassaradhātuto vā ekassarato vā anekassarato vā apaccayassa parabhāvo bhūvādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇavasena, visesalakkhaṇavasena pana ākhyātatte ikārantānekassaradhātuto saha apaccayena niccaṃ niggahītāgamanañca nāmikatte niggahītāgamanamattañca bhūvādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Ākyātatte kattari dhātūhi apaccayena saddhiṃniyatavasena niggahītāgamanaṃ rudhādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇavasena, visesalakkhaṇavasena [M 0.0374] pana ākhyātatte kattari dhātūhi ivaṇṇekārokārapaccayehi saddhiṃ niyatavasena niggahītāgamanañca nāmakatte aniyatavasena niggahītāgamanamattañca rudhādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Kattari dhātūhi ādesalābhālābhino yapaccayassa parabhāvo divādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Kattari dhātūhi yathārahaṃ ṇu ṇā uṇāpaccayānaṃ parabhāvo svādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Kattari dhātūhi nāpaccayassa parabhāvo kiyādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Kattari dhātūhi ākhyātatte appakatarappayogavasena nāmikatte pacurappayogavasena ppaṇhāpaccayānaṃ parabhāvo gahādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Kattari dhātūhi yathāsambhavaṃ oyirappaccayānaṃ parabhāvo tanādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Ākhyātatte kattari dhātūhi sabbathā ṇeṇayappaccayānaṃ parabhāvo curādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇavasena, visesalakkhaṇavasena pana ākhyātatte ikārantadhātuto saha ṇe ṇayapaccayehi niccaṃ niggahītāgamanañca nāmikatte niggahītāgamanamattañca curādigaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Gaṇasūcakānaṃ paccayānamaparattaṃ adhātulakkhaṇaṃ. Iti dhātugaṇalakkhaṇamadhātulakkhaṇaṃ vibhāvitaṃ.

Among these, in the application of primary suffixes before sabbadhātuka endings, the occurrence of the ‘a’ suffix after a verbal root with a pure vowel, or a single vowel, or multiple vowels, is the characteristic of the Bhū group in terms of general characteristics. However, in terms of specific characteristics, in the finite verb form, the constant insertion of the niggahīta together with the ‘a’ suffix after a verbal root with multiple vowels ending in ‘i’, and in the nominal form, merely the insertion of the niggahīta, is the characteristic of the Bhū group. In the finite verb form, in the active voice, the constant insertion of the niggahīta together with the ‘a’ suffix after verbal roots is the characteristic of the Rudhādigaṇa in terms of general characteristics. However, in terms of specific characteristics, in the finite verb form, in the active voice, the constant insertion of the niggahīta together with the ‘i’, ‘e’, and ‘o’ suffixes after verbal roots, and in the nominal form, merely the inconstant insertion of the niggahīta, is the characteristic of the Rudhā group. In the active voice, the occurrence of the ‘ya’ suffix after verbal roots, whether a substitute is obtained or not, is the characteristic of the Divā group. In the active voice, as appropriate, the occurrence of the ‘ṇu’, ‘ṇā’, and ‘uṇā’ suffixes after verbal roots is the characteristic of the Svā group. In the active voice, the occurrence of the ‘nā’ suffix after verbal roots is the characteristic of the Kiyā group. In the active voice, the occurrence of the ‘ppa’ and ‘ṇhā’ suffixes after verbal roots, with infrequent application in the finite verb form and frequent application in the nominal form, is the characteristic of the Gahā group. In the active voice, as possible, the occurrence of the ‘o’ and ‘yira’ suffixes after verbal roots is the characteristic of the Tanā group. In the finite verb form, in the active voice, the occurrence of the ‘ṇe’ and ‘ṇaya’ suffixes after verbal roots in all cases is the characteristic of the Curā group in terms of general characteristics. However, in terms of specific characteristics, in the finite verb form, the constant insertion of the niggahīta together with the ‘ṇe’ and ‘ṇaya’ suffixes after a verbal root ending in ‘i’, and in the nominal form, merely the insertion of the niggahīta, is the characteristic of the Curā group. The non-occurrence of suffixes that indicate the groups is the characteristic of non-roots. Thus, the characteristics of the root groups and non-roots have been explained.

Kāritapaccayassa yoge “ṇe ṇayo ṇāpe ṇāpayo cā”ti ime cattāro kāritapaccayā.

In the application of causative suffixes, these four, namely “ṇe”, “ṇaya”, “ṇāpe”, and “ṇāpaya”, are the causative suffixes.

Ṇe ṇayāsuṃ uvaṇṇantā,

Ādantā pacchimā duve;

Sesato caturodve vā,

Ṇayoyeva adhātuto.

The ‘ṇe’ and ‘ṇaya’ suffixes apply to roots ending in ‘u’;

The last two, ‘ṇāpe’ and ‘ṇāpaya,’ apply to roots ending in ‘ā’;

From the rest of the roots, apply the four or two suffixes;

Only ‘ṇaya’ applies to non-roots.

Tatra sāveti, sāvayati. Bhāveti, bhāvayati, obhāseti, obhāsayati. Imāni kārite uvaṇṇantadhāturūpāni.

There, sāveti, sāvayati (causes to hear). Bhāveti, bhāvayati (causes to be; develops). Obhāseti, obhāsayati (causes to shine; illuminates). These are causative forms of roots ending in ‘u’.

Dāpeti[M 0.0375], dāpayati. Hāpeti, hāpayati. Nhāpeti, nhāpayati. Nahāpeti, nahāpayati. Ākārantadhāturūpāni.

Dāpeti, dāpayati (causes to give). Hāpeti, hāpayati (causes to diminish). Nhāpeti, nhāpayati (causes to bathe). Nahāpeti, nahāpayati (causes to bathe). These are forms of roots ending in ‘ā’.

Soseti, sosayati. Sosāpeti, sosāpayati. Ghosāpeti, ghosāpayati. Akārantadhāturupāni.

Soseti, sosayati (causes to dry). Sosāpeti, sosāpayati (causes to dry). Ghosāpeti, ghosāpayati (causes to proclaim). These are forms of roots ending in ‘a’.

Maggo saṃsārato lokaṃ ñāpeti, ñāpayati. Idhāturūpāni niggacchāpetīti etesamattho. Imāni hi nipubbāya idhātuyā vasena sambhūtāni hetukatturūpāni. Tathā hi suddhakattubhāvena maggo sayaṃ ñāyati, saṃsārato niggacchatīti ñāyoti vuccati.

The path makes known to the world the way out from saṃsāra; it makes it known. The meaning of these forms from the ‘i’ root is ‘causes to go out’. For these are causative forms that have arisen by means of the ‘i’ root with the prefix ‘ni’. Thus, by its causative nature, the path itself is known, and it is called ‘the way’ because it leads out of saṃsāra.

Pāveti, pāvayati, udhāturūpāni. Vadāpetīti etesamattho. Imāni hi papubbāya udhātuyā vasena sambhūtāni hetukatturūpāni. Tathā hi “yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāvā”ti suddhakattupadaṃ āhaccabhāsitaṃ dissati.

Pāveti, pāvayati, are forms of the ‘u’ root. Their meaning is ‘causes to speak’. For these are causative forms that have arisen by means of the ‘u’ root with the prefix ‘pa’. Thus, the pure active form “yo ātumānaṃ sayaṃ eva pāvā” (who himself speaks of himself) is seen spoken as an instance of āhaccabhāsita.

Khepeti, khepayati. Kaṅkheti, kaṅkhayati, kaṅkhāpeti, kaṅkhāpayati. Ācikkhāpeti, ācikkhāpayati. Ivaṇṇantadhāturūpāni.

Khepeti, khepayati (causes to destroy). Kaṅkheti, kaṅkhayati (doubts), kaṅkhāpeti, kaṅkhāpayati (causes to doubt). Ācikkhāpeti, ācikkhāpayati (causes to announce). These are forms of roots ending in ‘i’.

Khiyeti, khiyayati. Milāyeti, milāyayati. Ekārantadhāturūpāni.

Khiyeti, khiyayati (causes to waste away). Milāyeti, milāyayati (causes to fade). These are forms of roots ending in ‘e’.

Siyeti, siyayati. Okārantadhāturūpāni.

Siyeti, siyayati (causes to cool). These are forms of roots ending in ‘o’.

Pabbatāyāyati, puttiyāyati. Adhātunissitāni rūpāni. Iminā nayena sesāni avuttānipi rūpāni sakkā viññātuṃ viññunā pāḷinayaññunāti vitthāro na dassito. Iti kāritapaccayayogo saṅkhepena vibhāvito.

Pabbatāyāyati (behaves like a mountain), puttiyāyati (desires a son/behaves like a son). These are forms dependent on non-roots. In this manner, the remaining forms, even those not stated, can be understood by the wise, skilled in the method of the Pāli texts; therefore, a detailed explanation is not given. Thus, the application of causative suffixes has been briefly explained.

Idāni [M 0.0376] sakāritekakammādīni brūma –

Now we shall speak of single-object verbs in the causative, and so on.

Akammakā ekakammā, dvikammā vāpi honti hi;

Kāritapaccaye laddhe, sakammā ca dvikammakā.

Intransitive verbs become single-object verbs, or even double-object verbs;

When the causative suffix is obtained, transitive verbs become double-object verbs.

Sayaṃ sodheti so bhūmiṃ, sodhāpeti paremahiṃ;

Naraṃ kammaṃ kārayati, viññeyyaṃ kamato idaṃ.

He himself cleans the ground; he causes others to clean the ground. He causes a man to do work. This should be understood in order.

Dvikammikā sambhavanti, tikammā ettha dīpaye;

“Issaro sevakaṃ gāmaṃ, ajaṃ nāyeti” iccapi.

Double-object verbs arise, and triple-object verbs are illustrated here; for example, “Issaro sevakaṃ gāmaṃ, ajaṃ nāyeti” (The lord causes the servant to lead the goat to the village).

“Naro narena vā gāmaṃ, ajaṃ nāyeti”iccapi;

Kammatthadīpakaṃyeva, karaṇaṃ ettha icchitaṃ.

Also, “Naro narena vā gāmaṃ, ajaṃ nāyeti” (A man causes the goat to be led to the village by a man); here, the instrument is desired as merely indicating the object.

Iti sakāritekakammādīni vibhāvitāni.

Thus, single-object verbs in the causative, and so on, have been explained.

Idāni ūhanīyarūpagaṇaṃ brūma – hoti, bhoti, sambhoti, idaṃ bhūvādirūpaṃ. Sumbhoti, parisumbhoti, idaṃ rudhādigūpaṃ. Nindati, vinindati, bandhati, idaṃ bhūvādirūpaṃ. Chindati, bhindati, rundhati, idaṃ rudhādirūpaṃ. Deti, neti, vadeti, anveti, idaṃ bhūvādirūpaṃ. Rundheti, paṭirundheti, idaṃ rudhādirūpaṃ. Buddheti, palibuddheti, idaṃ curādirūpaṃ. Jayati, sayati, palāyati, milāyati, gāyati, idaṃ bhūvādirūpaṃ. Hāyati, sāyati, nhāyati, idaṃ divādirūpaṃ. Kathayati, cintayati, bhājayati, idaṃ curādirūpaṃ. Gabbati, pagabbati, idaṃ bhūvādirūpaṃ. Kubbati, krubbati, idaṃ tanādirūpaṃ. Hinoti, cinoti, idaṃ svādirūpaṃ. Tanoti, sanoti, karoti, idaṃ tanādirūpaṃ. Cinteti, cintayati, idaṃ katturūpañceva hetukatturūpañca. Kanteti, kantayati, idaṃ hetukatturūpameva. Bhakkheti, bhakkhayati, vādeti, vādayati, idaṃ suddhakatturūpañceva hetukatturūpañca. Miyyatīti kattupadañceva kammapadañca. Bhāvethāti bahuvacanañceva ekavacanañca. Saṃyamissanti anāgatavacanañceva atītavacanañca. Anusāsatīti ākhyātañceva nāmikañca. Gacchaṃ vidhamaṃ nikkhaṇanti nāmikañceva [M 0.0377] ākhyātañca. Ettha ākhyātatte gacchanti anāgatavacanaṃ, vidhamanti atītavacanaṃ, nikhaṇanti parikappavacanaṃ, sabbaṃ vā etaṃ padaṃ anāgatādhivacanantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭateva. Iminā nayena aññānipi ūhanīyapadāni nānappakārato yojetabbāni. Imāni padāni dubbiññeyyavisesāni mandabuddhīnaṃ sammohakarāni ācariyapācariye payirupāsitvā vedanīyānīti ūhanīyarūpagaṇo vibhāvito.

Now we shall explain the group of forms requiring inference—hoti, bhoti, sambhoti: these are a form of the Bhū-group. Sumbhoti, parisumbhoti: these are a form of the Rudh-group. Nindati, vinindati, bandhati: these are a form of the Bhū-group. Chindati, bhindati, rundhati: these are a form of the Rudh-group. Deti, neti, vadeti, anveti: these are a form of the Bhū-group. Rundheti, paṭirundheti: these are a form of the Rudh-group. Buddheti, palibuddheti: these are a form of the Cur-group. Jayati, sayati, palāyati, milāyati, gāyati: these are a form of the Bhū-group. Hāyati, sāyati, nhāyati: these are a form of the Div-group. Kathayati, cintayati, bhājayati: these are a form of the Cur-group. Gabbati, pagabbati: these are a form of the Bhū-group. Kubbati, krubbati: these are a form of the Tan-group. Hinoti, cinoti: these are a form of the Su-group. Tanoti, sanoti, karoti: these are a form of the Tan-group. Cinteti, cintayati: these are both agent forms and causative forms. Kanteti, kantayati: these are purely causative forms. Bhakkheti, bhakkhayati, vādeti, vādayati: these are both agent forms and causative forms. Miyyatīti: this is both an agent form and a passive form. Bhāvethāti: this is both a plural and singular form. Saṃyamissanti: this is both a future tense and past tense form. Anusāsatīti: this is both a verbal form and a nominal form. Gacchaṃ vidhamaṃ nikkhaṇanti: this is both a nominal form and a verbal form. Here, regarding verbal aspects, gacchanti is future tense, vidhamanti is past tense, nikhaṇanti is the optative mood, and all these forms can also be spoken of as future expressions. In this way, other inferential forms should be applied in various manners. These words, being difficult to understand due to their subtle distinctions, are confusing to those of weak intellect and should be learned by attending upon teachers and preceptors. Thus, the group of inferential forms has been elucidated.

Idāni ekagaṇikādīni vadāma – dhā dhāraṇe, bhūvādigaṇikavasenāyaṃ ekagaṇikā sakammikā dhātu. Bhagavā sakalalokassa hitaṃ dadhāti vidadhāti, puriso atthaṃ saṃvidheti, nidhiṃ nidheti, imāni suddhakattari bhavanti. “Saṃvidhāpeti, vidhāpetī”ti imāni hetukattari bhavanti. Kamme pana bhāve ca “anuvidhīyatī”tiādīni bhavanti. Tathā hi kamme “nidhi nāma nidhīyatī”ti ca “dhīyati dhapiyatīti dheyya”nti ca rūpāni dissanti. Tattha kamme “kammaṃ sattehi anuvidhiyyati, kammāni sattehi anuvidhiyyanti. Bho kamma tvaṃ sattehi anuvidhiyyasi, ahaṃ kammaṃ sattehi anuvidhiyyāmī”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ. Bhāve pana “satto dukkhaṃ anuvidhiyyati, sattā dukkhaṃ anuvidhiyyanti, to satta tvaṃ dukkhaṃ anuvidhiyyasī”ti yojetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo ativiya sukhumo pāḷinayānukūlo.

Now we speak of single-group roots and so forth – 'dhā' means 'to hold'. According to the Bhū-group method, this single-group root is transitive. The Blessed One bestows and provides welfare to the entire world, a person accomplishes a purpose, one stores a treasure—these are examples of active voice forms. "Causes to arrange, causes to provide"—these are examples of causative forms. In the passive and the impersonal, forms like "is arranged accordingly" arise. For example, in the passive: "A treasure is called 'nidhi' because it is stored (nidhīyati)," and "It is called 'dheyya' because it is held (dhīyati) or deposited (dhapiyati)." Here, in the passive: "Action is conformed to by beings (kammaṃ sattehi anuvidhiyyati), actions are conformed to by beings (kammāni sattehi anuvidhiyyanti). O action, you are conformed to by beings (bho kamma tvaṃ sattehi anuvidhiyyasi), I, action, am conformed to by beings (ahaṃ kammaṃ sattehi anuvidhiyyāmi)." In the impersonal: "A being undergoes suffering accordingly (satto dukkhaṃ anuvidhiyyati), beings undergo suffering accordingly (sattā dukkhaṃ anuvidhiyyanti). O being, you undergo suffering accordingly (bho satta tvaṃ dukkhaṃ anuvidhiyyasi)." This method is extremely subtle and in accordance with the Pāli tradition.

Nāmikapadatte “dhātū”tiādīni bhavanti. Tattha dhātūti salakkhaṇaṃ dadhāti dhāretīti dhātu. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana “salakkhaṇadhāraṇato dukkhavidhānato dukkhadhānato ca dhātū”ti vuttaṃ. Dhātūti pathavīdhātādidhātuyo. Tattha salakkhaṇadhāraṇatoti yathā titthiyaparikappito pakati attāti evamādiko sabhāvato natthi, na evametā, etā pana salakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhātuyo[M 0.0378]. Dukkhavidhānatoti dukkhassa vidahanato. Etā hi dhātuyo kāraṇabhāvena vavatthitā hutvā yathā ayalohādidhātuyo ayalohādianekappakāraṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ vidahanti. Dukkhadhānatoti anappakassa dukkhassa vidhānamattato avasavattanato, taṃ vā dukkhaṃ etāhi kāraṇabhūtāhi sattehi anuvidhīyati, tathāvihitañca taṃ etesveva dhīyati ṭhapiyati, evaṃ dukkhadhānato dhātuyo. Apica nijjīvaṭṭho dhātavoti gahetabbaṃ. Tathā hi bhagavā “cha dhātuyosaṃ bhikkhu puriso”tiādīsu jīvasaññāsamūhanatthaṃ dhātudesanaṃ akāsīti. Yo pana tattha amhehi bhāvaṭṭhāne “satto dukkhaṃ anuvidhiyyatī”ti tipurisamaṇḍito ekavacanabahuvacaniko paṭhamāvibhattippayogo vutto. So –

In the sense of a nominal term, 'dhātu' and similar ones arise. There, 'dhātu' means that which holds or sustains its own characteristic. In the commentaries, however, it is said: 'It is called "dhātu" because of bearing its own characteristic, because of the production of suffering, and because of the foundation of suffering.' 'Dhātu' refers to the earth element and other elements. Among these, 'bearing its own characteristic' means that, unlike the imagined self posited by heretics, such as the primordial nature or the self, which has no inherent nature, these elements do possess their own inherent nature and sustain it—thus they are called 'dhātus.' 'Production of suffering' means because of the production of suffering. For these elements, being established as causes, produce the manifold suffering of saṃsāra, just as mineral elements such as iron ore produce various things such as iron. 'Foundation of suffering' means that, due to the mere production of immense suffering, beings are not under their own control. Alternatively, that suffering is inflicted upon beings through these very elements as causes, and being so conditioned, it is deposited and established within them. Thus, because they are the foundation of suffering, they are called 'dhātus.' Furthermore, the meaning of being soulless should be taken from the elements. For the Blessed One taught the discourse on the elements, such as 'A person, monks, consists of six elements,' in order to eradicate the perception of a living being. However, in that context, the use of the nominative case in singular and plural forms, adorned with the three persons—such as 'a being undergoes suffering accordingly' (satto dukkhaṃ anuvidhiyyati)—was stated by us in the impersonal sense. That—

“Dūsito giridattena, hayo sāmassa paṇḍavo;

Porāṇaṃ pakatiṃ hitvā, tassevānuvidhiyyatī”ti ca

"Corrupted by Giridatta, the horse Pandava, belonging to Sama, abandoning its former nature, conforms to him alone."

“Mātā hi tava irandhati, vidhurassa hadayaṃ dhaniyyatī”ti ca “te saṃkilesikā dhammā pahīyissantī”ti ca imāsaṃ pāḷīnaṃ vasena sārato paccetabbo. Tattha paṇḍavo nāma asso giridattanāmakassa assagopakassa pakatiṃ anuvidhiyyati anukarotīti attho. Ettha ca yadi kattupadaṃ icchitaṃ siyā, “anuvidadhātī”ti pāḷi vattabbā siyā. Yadi kammapadaṃ icchitaṃ siyā, “paṇḍavenā”ti tatiyantaṃ kattupadaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, evaṃ avacanena “anuvidhiyyatī”ti idaṃ bhāvapadanti siddhaṃ. Na kenaci ettha vattuṃ sakkā “divādigaṇe kattari vihitayapaccayassa vasena vuttaṃ idaṃ rūpa”nti, dhādhātuyā divādigaṇe appavattanato, ekantabhūvādigaṇikattā ca. Dutiyappayoge pana yadi kattupadaṃ icchitaṃ siyā, “dhanute”ti pāḷi vattabbā siyā. Yadi kammapadaṃ icchitaṃ siyā, “dhātuyā”ti vattabbaṃ siyā[M 0.0379]. Evaṃ avacanena “dhaniyyatī”ti idampi bhāvapadanti siddhaṃ. Ettha “dhaniyyatīti pattheti, icchatīti attho”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Dhanu yācane”ti dhātu esā ekantena tanādigaṇeyeva vattati. Tatiyappayoge “pahīyissantī”ti yadi bhūvādigaṇe “hā cāge”ti dhātuyā rūpaṃ siyā, kattari “pajahissantī”ti rūpaṃ siyā, “kasmā no pajahissatī”ti ettha viya. Kammapadaṃ pana “pajahiyissantī”ti siyā. Yasmā “pahīyissantī”ti idaṃ divādigaṇe “hā parihāniya”nti dhātuyā rūpattā “pahāyissantī”ti kattupadarūpaṃ siyā “ājañño kurute vegaṃ, hāyanti tattha vaḷavā”ti akammakassa kattupadarūpassa dassanato, tasmā “pahāyissantī”ti avatvā “pahīyissantī”ti vacanena yapaccayo bhāve vattatīti ñāyati.

"Your mother indeed grieves; the heart of the bereaved is distressed," and "those defiling states will be abandoned"—these Pāli passages should be understood according to their essence. Here, the term 'paṇḍavo' refers to a horse of the horse-keeper named Giridatta, meaning that it follows or imitates his nature. If an active form were intended here, the Pāli should be 'anuvidadhāti.' If a passive form were intended, the agent 'paṇḍavena' (in the instrumental case) should be stated. Thus, by not stating that, 'anuvidhiyyati' is established as an impersonal form. No one can claim here that this form is stated by means of the ya-suffix prescribed for the active voice in the Divādi group, because the root dhā does not occur in the Divādi group and belongs exclusively to the Bhūvādi group. In the second usage, if an active form were intended, the Pāli should be 'dhanute.' If a passive form were intended, 'dhātuyā' should be used. Thus, by not stating that, 'dhaniyyati' is also established as an impersonal form. Here, the commentary states: "'dhaniyyati' means 'desires,' the meaning is 'wishes.'" The root dhanu 'to beg' belongs exclusively to the Tanādi group. In the third usage, 'pahīyissanti,' if this form were from the root hā 'to abandon' in the Bhūvādi group, the active form would be 'pajahissanti,' as in 'why would he not abandon (kasmā no pajahissati)?' The passive form, however, would be 'pajahiyissanti.' Since 'pahīyissanti' is derived from the root hā 'to decline' in the Divādi group, the active form would be 'pahāyissanti,' as shown by the example 'the thoroughbred exerts speed, the mares decline there (ājañño kurute vegaṃ, hāyanti tattha vaḷavā),' where the active form is shown. Therefore, instead of saying 'pahāyissanti,' the use of 'pahīyissanti' indicates that the ya-suffix is functioning in the impersonal sense.

Keci panettha vadeyyuṃ “so pahīyissati. Te saṃkilesikā dhammā pahīyissanti. Rūpaṃ vibhaviyyati. Aggijāhi pubbeva bhūyate’tiādīsu yapaccayo kammeyeva vihito, na bhāve. Kammakattuvasena hi ime payogā daṭṭhabbā, sayameva pīyate pānīyaṃ, sayameva kaṭo kariyateti payogā viyā”ti. Taṃ na, evañhi sati “pajahiyissantī”tiādīni sakammakadhāturūpāni vattabbāni “pīyate kariyate”ti rūpāni viya. Ettha pana bhāvaṭṭhāne kattuno ṭhitabhāvo heṭṭhā nānappakārena dassitoti na vutto. Ye saddasatthe mataṃ gahetvā sāsanikā garū bhāve adabbavuttino bhāvassekattā ekavacanameva, tañca paṭhamapurisasseva “bhūyate devadattena devadattena sampattiṃ anubhavananti attho”ti payogañca tadatthayojanañca [M 0.0380] vadanti. Tesaṃ taṃ vacanaṃ pāḷiyā, aṭṭhakathādīhi ca na sameti, tasmā yathāvuttoyevattho āyasmantehi dhāretabbo.

Some here might say: "'It will be abandoned; those defiling states will be abandoned; form will be destroyed; it is brought about by fire beforehand'—in such cases, the ya-suffix is prescribed for the passive voice, not for the impersonal. For these usages should be seen as reflexive passive forms, like 'water is drunk by itself,' 'a mat is made by itself.'" That is not so, for if it were, expressions like 'pajahiyissantī' would have to be passive forms of transitive verbs, like 'pīyate' (is drunk) and 'kariyate' (is made). Here, however, in the impersonal sense, the state of the agent's abiding is shown below in various ways, but it is not stated. Those teachers in the Dispensation who, adopting the opinion of grammarians, say that in the impersonal voice—which refers to a non-substance—only the singular of the third person is used, citing the usage 'bhūyate devadattena' with the explanation 'it means Devadatta experiences prosperity,' their statement does not accord with the Pāli texts or the commentaries. Therefore, the meaning should be understood by the venerable ones just as explained above.

Jara roge. Jarati, jariyyati. Jaravayohāniyaṃ. Jīrati, jiyyati. Imā dvepi bhūvādi gaṇikavasena ekagaṇikā. Tāsaṃ ayaṃ sādhāraṇarūpavibhāvanā. “Yena ca santappati, yena ca jariyyatī”tiādi. Tattha yena ca jariyyatīti yena tejogatena kupitena ayaṃ kāyo ekāhikādijararogena jariyyati jarati. Atha vā yena ca jariyati yena ayaṃ kāyo jīrati indriyavekalyataṃ balakkhayaṃ palitavalitādiñca pāpuṇāti.

The root jar (is used in the sense of) disease. Its forms are jarati and jariyyati. (The root) jar (is also used in the sense of) decline in age. Its forms are jīrati and jiyyati. These two, by virtue of belonging to the Bhūvādi group, are of a single group. This is a general exposition of their forms. For example: "by which one is afflicted, and by which one decays." Here, "by which one decays" means that by an agitated fiery element, this body decays, that is, it grows old, through a disease of decay lasting a day or more. Alternatively, "by which one decays" means that this body grows old, reaching a state of weakened faculties, decline of strength, gray hair, wrinkles, and so on.

Mara pāṇacāge. Bhūvādigaṇikoyaṃ akammako ca. Satto marati, miyyati. Kiñcāpi ayaṃ dhātu “mara pāṇacāge”ti vacanato sakammako viya dissati, tathāpi “putto marati. Kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno jāyati ca jiyyati ca miyyati cā”ti evamādīnaṃ kammarahitappayogānaṃ dassanato akammakoyevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atthayojanānayena pana maratīti pāṇaṃ cajatīti kammaṃ ānetvā kathetuṃ labbhati. “Marati, miyatī”ti imāni suddhakattupadāni, “satto sattaṃ māreti, mārayati, mārāpeti, mārāpayatī”ti imāni kāritapadasaṅkhātāni hetukattupadāni. Ettha ca yo amataṃ sattaṃ maraṇaṃ pāpeti, so vadhako māreti mārayati mārāpeti mārāpayatīti ca vuccati. Satto sattehi māriyati mārāpiyatīti imāni kammapadāni. Bhāvapadamappasiddhaṃ. Evamaññatrāpi pasiddhatā ca appasiddhatā ca upaparikkhitabbā.

The root mar (is used in the sense of) abandoning life. It belongs to the Bhūvādi group and is intransitive. A being dies (marati, miyyati). Although this root appears transitive from the definition 'mara, in abandoning life,' it should be seen as intransitive due to usages without an object, such as 'a son dies' and 'Alas, this world has fallen into distress—it is born, grows old, and dies.' However, by way of exegesis, an object can be supplied: 'marati' means 'it abandons life.' 'Marati' and 'miyati' are simple active verbs. 'Satto sattaṃ māreti, mārayati, mārāpeti, mārāpayati' (a being kills another being, causes to kill, has someone kill, causes someone to have kill) are causative active verbs, also known as agentive-causative verbs. Here, one who brings a living being to death is called a killer (vadhako) and is said to kill (māreti, mārayati) or cause to kill (mārāpeti, mārāpayati). 'Satto sattehi māriyati, mārāpiyati' (a being is killed by others, is caused to be killed) are passive verbs. The impersonal verb is not common. Similarly, elsewhere too, what is common and uncommon should be examined.

Khāda bhakkhaṇe. Ayaṃ pana bhūvādigaṇikavasena ekagaṇiko sakammako dhātu. Khādati, saṅkhādati, imāni suddhakattupadāni[M 0.0381]. Puriso purisena purisaṃ vā pūvaṃ khādeti khādayati khādāpeti khādāpayati, imāni hetukattupadāni. Ettha ca yo akhādantaṃ khādantaṃ vā khādāhīti payojeti, so khādāpako khādeti khādayati khādāpeti khādāpayatīti ca vuccati. Khajjati, saṃkhajjati, saṅkhādiyati. Imāni kammapadāni. Atrapanāyaṃ pāḷi “atītaṃ pāhaṃ addhānaṃ rūpena khajjiṃ, seyyathāpāhaṃ etarahi paccuppannena rūpena khajjāmi. Ahañceva kho pana anāgataṃ rūpaṃ abhinandeyyaṃ, anāgatenapāhaṃ rūpena khajjeyyaṃ, seyyathāpetarahi khajjāmī”ti. Bhāvapadaṃ na labbhati sakammakattā imassa dhātussa. Bhūvādigaṇo. Ayaṃ nāmadhātu ekantarudhādigaṇikoti appasiddho.

The root khād (is used in the sense of) eating. This root belongs to a single group, the Bhūvādi group, and is a transitive root. Khādati and saṅkhādati are simple active verbs. Puriso purisena purisaṃ vā pūvaṃ khādeti, khādayati, khādāpeti, khādāpayati (a man causes another man to eat a person or a cake)—these are agentive-causative verbs. And here, one who urges another, whether they are eating or not, saying 'Eat!', is called an instigator (khādāpako) and is said to cause to eat (khādeti, khādayati, khādāpeti, khādāpayati). Khajjati, saṅkhajjati, and saṅkhādiyati are passive verbs. In this context, there is this Pāli passage: 'In the past, I was consumed by form, just as now I am consumed by present form. If I were to delight in future form, I would be consumed by future form, just as now I am consumed.' The impersonal verb is not found for this root because it is transitive. It belongs to the Bhūvādi group. This root is not commonly considered to belong also to the Rudhādi group.

Divādigaṇe tā pālane. Lokaṃ tāyati santāyati. Imāni sakammakāni suddhakattupadāni. Hetukattupadaṃ pana kammapadañca bhāvapadañca appasiddhāni.

In the Divādi group, the root tā (is used in the sense of) protecting. It protects the world (lokaṃ tāyati), it thoroughly protects it (santāyati). These are transitive, simple active verbs. However, the agentive-causative verb, the passive verb, and the impersonal verb are not common.

Sudha saṃsuddhiyaṃ. Cittaṃ sujjhati visujjhati. Imāni akammakāni suddhakattupadāni. Sodheti, sodhayati, sodhāpeti, sodhāpayati, imāni hetukatturūpāni. Ettha ca yo asuddhaṃ ṭhānaṃ suddhaṃ karoti, so sodhako sodheti, sodhayatīti vuccati, esa nayo aññatrāpi īdisesu ṭhānesu. Yo pana asuddhaṭṭhānaṃ sayaṃ asodhetvā “tvaṃ sodhehī”ti aññaṃ payojeti, so sodhāpako sodhāpeti sodhāpayatīti vuccati. Esa nayo aññatrāpi īdisesu ṭhānesu. Tathā hi “kāreti, kārayati, kārāpeti, kārāpayatī”tiādīsu ayaṃ nayo na labbhati, evaṃ labbhamānanayo ca alabbhamānanayo ca sabbattha upaparikkhitabbo. Imā panettha pāḷiyo –

The root sudh (is used in the sense of) becoming pure. The mind becomes pure (cittaṃ sujjhati), becomes thoroughly pure (visujjhati). These are intransitive, simple active verbs. Sodheti, sodhayati, sodhāpeti, sodhāpayati—these are agentive-causative forms. And here, one who makes an impure place pure is called a purifier (sodhako), and it is said sodheti, sodhayati. This is the principle in other such cases as well. But one who, without purifying an impure place himself, directs another, saying, 'You purify it,' is called one who causes to purify (sodhāpako), and it is said sodhāpeti, sodhāpayati. This is the principle in other such cases as well. For this principle is not found in such cases as kāreti, kārayati, kārāpeti, kārāpayati. Thus, the principle that is applicable and the principle that is not applicable should be examined in every case. Here are the Pāli passages on this:

“Paccantadesavisaye, nimantetvā tathāgataṃ;

Tassa āgamanaṃ maggaṃ, sodhenti tuṭṭhamānasā”ti ca

“In the borderland territory, having invited the Tathāgata, they cleanse the path for his coming with delighted minds,” and

“Maggaṃ [M 0.0382] sodhemahaṃ tadā”ti ca. Imā hi pāḷiyo sahatthā sodhanaṃ sandhāya vuttā. “Āyasmā pilindavaccho rājagahe pabbhāraṃ sodhāpeti leṇaṃ kattukāmo”ti pana pāḷi, “kiṃ bhante thero kārāpetī”ti, “pabbhāraṃ mahārāja sodhāpemi leṇaṃ kattakāmo”ti ca pāḷi. Imā parehi sodhāpanaṃ sandhāya vuttā. “Kassa sodhiyati maggo”ti idaṃ kammapadaṃ, bhāvapadaṃ pana appasiddhaṃ. Iminā nayena yāva curādigaṇā yojetabbaṃ.

“At that time, I cleansed the path.” These Pāli passages are spoken in reference to cleansing with one's own hand. But this Pāli passage: “The Venerable Pilindavaccha was having the slope at Rājagaha cleansed, desiring to make a cave dwelling,” and this Pāli passage: “Bhante, what is the elder having done?” and “Great king, I am having the slope cleansed, desiring to make a cave dwelling.” These are spoken in reference to having others do the cleansing. “For whom is the path being cleansed?”—this is a passive verb. The impersonal verb, however, is not common. By this principle, the analysis should be applied up to the Curādi group.

Dvigaṇikatte subha sobhe. Sobhati vatāyaṃ puriso. Subha pahāre. Yo no gāvova sumbhati sumbhoti iccapi dissati. “Sumbhotī”ti ca kaccāyanamate rūpaṃ, imāni kattupadāni. Nagaraṃ sobheti, sobhayati. Puriso purise coraṃ sumbheti, sumbhayati, sumbhāpeti, sumbhāpayati. Imāni hetukattupadāni. Kammabhāvapadāni labbhamānālabbhamānavasena yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbāni. Bhūvādirudhādigaṇikarūpāni.

Regarding roots belonging to two groups: subha (is used in the sense of) shining. “Indeed, this person shines.” Subha (is also used in the sense of) striking. In the usage “who strikes us like a bull,” the form is sumbhati; the form sumbhoti is not seen. The form ‘sumbhoti’, however, is a form according to the opinion of Kaccāyana. These are active verbs. “He makes the city shine, causes it to shine.” “A man causes another man to strike a thief”—sumbheti, sumbhayati, sumbhāpeti, sumbhāpayati. These are causative active verbs. The passive and impersonal verbs should be formed as may be possible, according to whether they are found or not. These are forms belonging to the Bhūvādi and Rudhādi groups.

Paca pāke. Puriso bhattaṃ pacati. Nerayiko niraye paccati. Kammaṃ paccati. Bhattaṃ paccati. Pāramiyo paripaccanti. Phalāni paripaccanti, pakkāni hontīti attho. Garavo pana –

Paca (is used in the sense of) cooking or ripening. A man cooks rice. A being in hell is cooked in hell. Kamma ripens. Rice is cooked. The perfections mature. The fruits ripen fully; the meaning is, ‘they become ripe.’ The teachers, however, say:

Ñāṇayuttavaraṃ tattha, datvā sandhiṃ tihetukaṃ;

Pacchā paccati pākānaṃ, pavatte aṭṭhake duveti ca –

“There, having established a three-rooted connection with the best (consciousness) associated with knowledge, two of the eight resultants later ripen in the course of existence,” and—

“Asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāra-vipākāni na paccatī”ti ca evaṃ pacatipadassa dvigaṇikarūpassa sakammakattaṃ icchanti. Evaṃ pana sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane kuto labbhā. Tepiṭake hi buddhavacane “kappaṃ nirayamhi paccati. Yāva pāpaṃ na paccati. Nirayamhi [M 0.0383] apacci so”ti evaṃ akammakattaṃyeva dissati. Ettha vadeyyuṃ “nanu paca pāke’ti ayaṃ dhātu sakammako, tena ‘paccatī’ti padassa divādigaṇikarūpassapi sato sakammakattaṃ yujjati, tasmāyeva ‘paccati pākānaṃ pavatte aṭṭhake duve’tiādīsu vutta”nti. Ettha vuccate – yathā “chidi dvidhākaraṇe, bhidi vidāraṇe”ti dhātūnaṃ rudhādigaṇe pavattānaṃ “rukkhaṃ chindati, bhittiṃ bhindatī”ti rūpapadānaṃ sakammakattepi sati divādigaṇaṃ pattānaṃ tesaṃ dhātūnaṃ “udakaṃ chijjati, ghaṭo bhijjatī”ti rūpapadāni akammakāniyeva bhavanti, yathā bhūvādigaṇe pavattassa pacadhātussa “bhattaṃ pacatī”ti rūpapadassa sakammakattepi sati divādigaṇaṃ pattassa “niraye paccati, kammāni vipaccantī”ti rūpapadāni akammakāniyeva bhavanti.

“It does not ripen the unprompted and prompted resultants.” Thus they desire a transitive meaning for the verb ‘paccati’ as a form belonging to two groups. But where can such a usage be found in the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries? For in the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka, only an intransitive meaning is seen, as in: “He is cooked in hell for an eon”; “As long as the evil has not ripened”; “He was cooked in hell.” Here they might say: “Surely the root paca in the sense of cooking is transitive. Therefore, it is proper for the verb ‘paccati,’ even when it is a form of the Divādi group, to be transitive. That is why it is said in such passages as ‘two of the eight resultants ripen…’ etc.” To this it is replied: Just as for the roots chidi (to cut in two) and bhidi (to split), which belong to the Rudhādi group, the verbal forms ‘he cuts the tree’ and ‘he breaks the wall’ are transitive, yet when these same roots belong to the Divādi group, their verbal forms ‘the water is cut’ and ‘the pot is broken’ are only intransitive; so too for the root paca, which belongs to the Bhūvādi group, while the verbal form ‘he cooks rice’ is transitive, yet when it belongs to the Divādi group, its verbal forms ‘he is cooked in hell’ and ‘karmic actions ripen’ are only intransitive.

Athāpi vadeyyuṃ “nanu ca bho yathā ‘āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsū’ti ettha “āsavato cittāni vimucciṃsū’ti ca ‘āsavehi kattubhūtehi cittāni vimucciṃsū’ti ca evaṃ divādigaṇikassa dhātussa ‘vimucciṃsū’ti rūpapadassa akammakattañca sakammakattañca bhavati, tathā ‘niraye paccati, kammāni vipaccantī’ti ca akammakattenapi bhavitabbaṃ. ‘Paccati pākānaṃ pavatte aṭṭhake duve, asaṅkhāraṃ sasaṅkhāravipākāni na paccatī’ti sakammakattenapi bhavitabba”nti. Akammakatteneva bhavitabbaṃ, na sakammakattena, “paccati pākāna”ntiādinā vuttappayogānaṃ “āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsū”ti payogena asamānattā. Tathā hettha “vimucciṃsū”ti padaṃ kammarahitakattuvācakayapaccayantampi bhavati kattusahitakammavācakayapaccayantampi. “Vimucciṃsū”ti imassa hi padassa kammarahitayapaccayavantattā “āsavehī”ti karaṇavacanaṃ apādānakārakavācakaṃ bhavati. ‘Cittānī”ti paccattavacanaṃ pana kattukārakavācakaṃ bhavati. Tathā “vimucciṃsū”ti padassa kattusahitakammavācakattā “āsavehī”ti [M 0.0384] karaṇavacanaṃ kattukārakavācakaṃ bhavati. “Cittānī”ti paccattavacanaṃ pana kammakārakavācakaṃ bhavati. Ayaṃ nayo “paccati pākāna”ntiādinā vuttappayogesu na labbhati. Tathā hi tattha paccattavacanaṃ kattāraṃ vadati, upayogavacanaṃ kammaṃ vadatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kārite “puriso purisena purisaṃ vā bhattaṃ pāceti pācayati pācāpeti pācāpayatī”ti ca, “anante bodhisambhāre, paripācesi nāyako”ti dassanato pana “paripāceti, paripācayatī”ti ca rūpāni bhavanti. Imāni hetukattupadāni. Kamme – yaññadattena odano paccate, bhāvapadaṃ appasiddhaṃ. Imāni bhūvādidivādigaṇikarūpāni. Iminā nayena aññānipi dvigaṇikarūpāni yojetabbāni.

Then they might say: “But sir, just as in the case of ‘the minds were liberated from the taints,’ the verb ‘vimucciṃsu,’ belonging to the Divādi group, can be both intransitive and passive—as in ‘the minds were liberated from the taints’ and ‘the minds were liberated by the taints as agents’—so too in ‘he is cooked in hell’ and ‘karmic actions ripen,’ it should be intransitive, and in ‘it ripens two of the eight resultants…’ and ‘it does not ripen the unprompted and prompted resultants,’ it should be transitive.” We reply: It must be only intransitive, not transitive, because the usage in ‘it ripens the resultants,’ etc., is not the same as the usage in ‘the minds were liberated from the taints.’ For here the word ‘vimucciṃsu’ can end in the -ya- suffix that indicates an agent without an object (intransitive), or it can end in the -ya- suffix that indicates an object with an agent (passive). Because the word ‘vimucciṃsu’ can end in the -ya- suffix indicating an agent without an object, the instrumental ‘āsavehi’ has the sense of the ablative (‘from the taints’), and the nominative ‘cittāni’ has the sense of the agent (‘the minds’). And because it can indicate an object with an agent, the instrumental ‘āsavehi’ has the sense of the agent (‘by the taints’), and the nominative ‘cittāni’ has the sense of the object (‘the minds’). This principle is not found in the usages cited beginning with ‘it ripens the resultants.’ For in that case, it should be understood that the nominative case expresses the agent, and the genitive case expresses the object. In the causative: ‘A man has another man cook rice,’ etc., and from ‘the Leader brought to maturity the immeasurable requisites for enlightenment,’ the forms are ‘paripāceti’ and ‘paripācayati.’ These are causative active verbs. In the passive: ‘Rice is cooked by Yaññadatta.’ The impersonal verb is not common. These are forms of the Bhūvādi and Divādi groups. By this principle, other forms belonging to two groups should also be analyzed.

Tegaṇikatte su pasave. Hetuphalaṃ savati, pasavati. Su savane. Saddho dhammaṃ suṇoti, suṇāti. Su hiṃsāyaṃ. Yodho paccāmittaṃ sunāti. Imāni yathākkamaṃ bhūvādisvādikiyādigaṇikāni kattupadāni. Tathā hetunā phalaṃ saviyyati, unnādasaddo pathavīundriyasaddo viya suyyati. Yodhena paccamitto suniyyati. Imāni kammapadāni. Bhāvapadaṃ na labbhati sakammakattā imesaṃ dhātūnaṃ. Iminā nayena aññānipi tegaṇikarūpāni upaparikkhitvā yojetabbāni. Atra panāyaṃ nayavibhāvanā –

Concerning roots belonging to three conjugational groups: The root su in the sense of ‘producing.’ A cause produces a fruit: savati, pasavati. The root su in the sense of ‘hearing.’ A faithful person hears the Dhamma: suṇoti, suṇāti. The root su in the sense of ‘harming.’ A warrior crushes an enemy: sunāti. These, in respective order, are active voice forms belonging to the Bhūvādi, Svādi, and Kiyādi groups. Likewise: ‘by a cause a fruit is produced’ (saviyyati); ‘a loud sound is heard like the sound of the earth’ (suyyati); ‘by a warrior an enemy is crushed’ (suniyyati). These are passive voice forms. The impersonal form is not found because these roots are transitive. By this method, other forms belonging to three groups should also be examined and constructed. Here, now, is the exposition of the method:

Bhvādirudhādikā dhātū, svādidivādikā tathā;

Rudhādikadivādiṭṭhā, bhūvādikacurādikā.

Roots belonging to the Bhūvādi and Rudhādi groups, and likewise to the Svādi and Divādi groups; those belonging to the Rudhādi and Divādi groups, and to the Bhūvādi and Curādi groups.

Bhūvādikagahādiṭṭhā, bhvādisvādikiyādikā;

Evamādippabhedehi, vitthārentu vicakkhaṇā.

Those belonging to the Bhūvādi and Gahādi groups, and to the Bhūvādi, Svādi, and Kiyādi groups—with these and other such distinctions, let the wise elaborate in detail.

Iccevaṃ saṅkhepato yathārahaṃ ekagaṇikadvigaṇikategaṇikavasena suddhakattuhetukattukammabhāvapadāni ca sakāritekakammāni [M 0.0385] ca sakāritadvikammāni ca sakāritatikammāni ca dassitāni.

Thus, in brief and as appropriate, by way of roots belonging to one, two, and three conjugational groups, the forms for the simple active, causative active, passive, and impersonal voices have been shown, as well as causative forms with one object, with two objects, and with three objects.

Idāni ekakāritadvikāritapadānaṃ vacanokāso anuppatto, tasmā taṃ vadāma. So antakammani. Arahattamaggo mānaṃ siyati, kammaṃ pariyosiyati. Imāni tāva suddhakattupadāni. Ettha mānaṃ siyatīti mānaṃ samucchindati. Kammaṃ pariyosiyatīti kammaṃ nipphajjati. Pari ava iccupasaggavasena hi idaṃ padaṃ akammakaṃ bhavati, attho pana “pariyosānaṃ gacchatī”ti sakammakavasena gahetabbo. Attanā vippakataṃ attanā pariyosāpeti. Idamekaṃ kāritaṃ hetukattupadaṃ. Ettha pana pariava iccupasaggavasena akammakabhūtassa sodhātussa laddhakāritapaccayattā ekakammameva sakāritapadaṃ bhavati. Attanā vippakataṃ parehi pariyosāvāpeti. Idaṃ dvikāritaṃ hetukattupadaṃ. Ettha ca pana pari ava iccupasaggavasena akammakabhūtassa sodhātussa laddhakāritapaccayadvayattā dvikammakaṃ sakāritapadaṃ bhavati. “Pariyosāvāpetī”ti idampi pari ava pubbasmā sodhātumhā ṇāpe ṇāpe iti paccayadvayaṃ katvā avasaddassokārañca katvā tato yakārāgamañca anubandhaṇakāralopañca paṭhamapaccaye pakārassa vakārañca dvīsu ca ṭhānesu pubbasaralopaṃ katvā nipphajjatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Now the occasion has arisen to speak of forms with one causative suffix and with two causative suffixes; therefore we shall speak of them. The root so is used in the sense of 'ending.' 'The path to Arahantship destroys conceit' (Arahattamaggo mānaṃ siyati); 'the work comes to an end' (kammaṃ pariyosiyati). These are simple active voice forms. Here, 'destroys conceit' means it eradicates conceit. 'The work comes to an end' means the work is accomplished. Because of the prefixes pari- and ava-, this form becomes intransitive, but the meaning should be understood in an active sense as 'it reaches conclusion.' 'One brings to completion by oneself what was undertaken by oneself' (Attanā vippakataṃ attanā pariyosāpeti). This is a causative active form with one causative suffix. Here, since the root so, which has become intransitive due to the prefixes pari- and ava-, has received a causative suffix, the causative form has only one object. 'One causes others to bring to completion what was undertaken by oneself' (Attanā vippakataṃ parehi pariyosāvāpeti). This is a causative active form with two causative suffixes. And here, since the root so, which has become intransitive due to the prefixes pari- and ava-, has received two causative suffixes, the causative form has two objects. The form pariyosāvāpeti should be understood as being formed from the root so preceded by pari- and ava- by adding the two suffixes ṇāpe and ṇāpe, changing the o of the root to ā, inserting the augment y, eliding the indicatory ṇ, changing the p of the first suffix to v, and eliding the preceding vowel in two places.

Idāni tā pāḷiyo atthantaraviññāpanatthaṃ āhaccadesitākārena ekato kathayāma – “attanā vippakataṃ attanā pariyosāpeti, āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Attanā vippakataṃ parehi pariyosāvāpeti, āpatti saṅghādisesassā”ti ettha “bhikkhū”ti hetukattupadaṃ ānetabbaṃ. Attanā vippakatanti ettha ca attanāti vippakaraṇakriyāya kattukārakavācakaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Vippakatanti kammakārakavācakaṃ [M 0.0386] upayogavacanaṃ. Attanā pariyosāpetīti ettha pana attanāti abyayapadabhūtena sayaṃsaddena samānatthaṃ vibhatyantapatirūpakaṃ abyayapadaṃ, sayaṃsaddasadisaṃ vā tatiyāvibhatyantaṃ abyayapadaṃ. Tathā hi “attanā pariyosāpetī”ti vuttavacanassa “sayaṃ pariyosāpetī”ti attho bhavati “attanā ca pāṇātipātī”tiādīsu viya. Parehi pariyosāvāpetīti ettha pana parehīti kammakārakavācakaṃ karaṇavacananti gahetabbaṃ, “sunakhehipi khādāpentī”ti ettha “sunakhehī”ti padaṃ viya. Ettha hi yathā “rājāno coraṃ sunakhe khādāpentī”ti upayogavasena attho bhavati, tathā “bhikkhu attanā vippakataṃ pare jane pariyosāvāpetī”ti upayogavasena attho bhavati. Evaṃ imasmiṃ acchariyabbhutanayavicitte bhagavato pāvacane dvikāritapaccayavantampi padamatthīti sārato paccetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo sukhumo sāsane ādaraṃ katvā āyasmantehi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo. Yassa hi atthāya idaṃ pakaraṇaṃ karimha, na ayaṃ attano mati, atha kho pubbācariyānaṃ santikā laddhattā tesaññeva matīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Now, to clarify the meaning of other canonical passages, we shall discuss them together in a connected discourse: 'Having undertaken something by oneself, one brings it to completion by oneself: this is an offense entailing suspension. Having undertaken something by oneself, one causes it to be brought to completion by others: this is an offense entailing suspension.' Here, the causative agent 'a bhikkhu' should be supplied. In 'undertaken by oneself' (attanā vippakataṃ), attanā is an instrumental form expressing the agent of the action of undertaking. Vippakataṃ ('what was undertaken') is an accusative form expressing the object. But in 'brings it to completion by oneself' (attanā pariyosāpeti), attanā is an indeclinable word in the guise of a case-inflected form, with the same meaning as the word sayaṃ ('oneself'), or it is an indeclinable in the third case similar to the word sayaṃ. For the statement attanā pariyosāpeti means 'one completes it oneself,' just as in such phrases as 'by oneself a killer of living beings.' In 'causes it to be brought to completion by others' (parehi pariyosāvāpeti), parehi should be taken as an instrumental form expressing the object, like the word sunakhehi ('by dogs') in 'they have it eaten by dogs.' For just as the meaning is expressed by the accusative in 'kings have dogs (sunakhe) eat a thief,' so too the meaning is expressed by the accusative in 'a bhikkhu causes other people (pare jane) to bring to completion what was undertaken by himself.' Thus, it should be confidently accepted from its essence that in this astonishing and marvelous teaching of the Blessed One there exists even a word with two causative suffixes. This method is subtle; it should be carefully kept in mind by the venerable sirs who have respect for the Teaching. For the purpose for which we have composed this treatise, this is not our own opinion; rather, since it was received from the ancient teachers, it should be seen as their opinion.

Idāni akāritadvikammikapadānaṃ vacanokāso anuppatto, tasmā tāni kathayāma, tāni ca kho dhātuvasena evaṃ veditabbāni savinicchayāni. Seyyathidaṃ?

Now the occasion has arisen to speak of non-causative forms with two objects. Therefore, we shall discuss them, and they are to be understood with discrimination according to the root. What are they?

Duhikaravahipucchi, yāci bhikkhi ca nibrūti;

Bhaṇivadivacibhāsi, sāsidahināthadhātu.

The roots duh (to milk), kar (to do), vah (to carry), pucch (to ask), yāc (to beg), bhikkh (to beg), ni+brū (to tell), bhaṇ (to speak), vad (to speak), vac (to speak), bhās (to speak), sās (to teach), dah (to burn), and nāth (to ask for help).

Rudhi ji cipabhutīti, ye te dvikammakā dhīrā;

Pavadumapi viyuttā, kāritappaccayehi ca.

The roots rudh (to obstruct), ji (to conquer), ci (to collect), and so on—these the wise have declared to be ditransitive, even when they are without causative suffixes.

Apādānādike pubba-vidhimhā sahime’bravuṃ;

Upayogavacanassa, nimittanti sanantanā.

The ancients have stated that, in contrast to the previous rule concerning the ablative and other cases, for these roots the secondary object is a mark of the accusative case.

Ete [M 0.0387] duhādayo dhātū, tikammāpi bhavanti tu;

Kāritappaccaye laddhe, iti ācariyā’bravuṃ.

But these roots, duh and so on, can also have three objects when they receive a causative suffix; so the teachers have said.

Tatrimāni udāharaṇāni – gavaṃ payo duhati gopālako. Gāviṃ khīraṃ duhati gopāladārako. Tattha payoti upayogavacanaṃ, “yaso laddhā na majjeyyā”ti ettha “yaso”ti padamiva. Manogaṇikassa hi īdisampi upayogavacanaṃ hoti aññādisampi. Issaro gopālaṃ gavaṃ payo duhāpeti. Gopālena gāvo khīraṃ duhitā. Gohi payo duhatīti ettha apādānavisayattā dvikammakabhāvo natthi. “Visāṇato gavaṃ duhaṃ, yattha khīraṃ na vindatī”ti ettha pana apādānavisayattepi gavāvayavabhūtassa visāṇassa visuṃ gahitattā “gavaṃ khīraṃ duhanto”ti dvikammikabhāvo labbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Duhino payogoyaṃ.

Here are the examples: 'A cowherd milks milk (payo) from a cow (gavaṃ)' (gavaṃ payo duhati gopālako). 'A cowherd's boy milks milk (khīraṃ) from a cow (gāviṃ)' (gāviṃ khīraṃ duhati gopāladārako). There, payo is in the accusative case, like the word yaso in 'Having gained fame (yaso), one should not become intoxicated.' For a word belonging to the manogaṇa group, the accusative can be of this kind or another. 'A master has a cowherd (gopālaṃ) milk milk (payo) from a cow (gavaṃ)' (issaro gopālaṃ gavaṃ payo duhāpeti). 'By a cowherd, cows were milked of their milk' (gopālena gāvo khīraṃ duhitā). In the phrase 'one milks milk from cows' (gohi payo duhati), since the source is expressed by the instrumental, there is no ditransitive construction. But in 'milking a cow from the horn (visāṇato gavaṃ duhaṃ), where one finds no milk,' although the source is expressed by the ablative, because the horn, which is a part of the cow, is taken separately, the ditransitive construction 'milking milk from the cow' is obtained. This is the usage of the root duh.

Karotissa payoge kaṭṭhamaṅgāraṃ karoti, suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ karoti, sace je saccaṃ bhaṇasi, adāsiṃ taṃ karomi. Ettha ca aṅgāraṃ karotīti pariccattakāraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Kaṭṭhañhi aṅgārabhāvassa kāraṇaṃ, aṅgāre kate kāraṇabhūtassa kaṭṭhassa kaṭṭhabhāvo vigacchati. Kaṭakaṃ karotīti idaṃ apariccattakāraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Suvaṇṇañhi kaṭakabhāvassa kāraṇaṃ, kaṭake katepi kārakabhūtassa suvaṇṇassa suvaṇṇabhāvo na vigacchati, atha kho visesantaruppattibhāvena sampajjati. Adāsiṃ taṃ karomīti idaṃ pana ṭhānantaradānavasena vuttaṃ “uparājaṃ mahārājaṃ karomī”ti ettha viya. Tattha “issaro purisena purisaṃ vā kaṭṭhamaṅgāraṃ kāreti. Tathā suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ kāretī”ti tikammikappayogopi daṭṭhabbo. Tathā “brahmadatto rajjaṃ kāretī”ti, “brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente”ti dvikammakappayogo.

In the usage of karoti: 'one makes charcoal from wood' (kaṭṭhaṃ aṅgāraṃ karoti); 'one makes a bracelet from gold' (suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ karoti); 'if you speak the truth to me, I will make you a non-slave-girl' (adāsiṃ taṃ karomi). Here, 'making charcoal' is said in the sense of the material cause being abandoned. For wood is the cause of charcoal, and when charcoal is made, the wood that is the cause ceases to be wood. 'Making a bracelet' is said in the sense of the material cause not being abandoned. For gold is the cause of the bracelet, and even when the bracelet is made, the gold that is the cause does not cease to be gold, but rather it attains a different special quality. 'I will make you a non-slave-girl' is said in the sense of bestowing a different status, as in 'I will make the viceroy king.' Here, a tritransitive usage should also be seen: 'A master has a man make charcoal from wood' (issaro purisena purisaṃ vā kaṭṭhaṃ aṅgāraṃ kāreti); 'similarly, one has a bracelet made from gold' (suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ kāreti). Likewise, 'Brahmadatta has the kingdom ruled' (brahmadatto rajjaṃ kāreti) and 'while Brahmadatta is having the kingdom ruled' (brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente) are examples of ditransitive usage.

Ettheke [M 0.0388] vadeyyuṃ “nanu ca bho ettha ekameva kammaṃ dissati, kenāyaṃ payogo dvikammikappayogo hotī”ti. Kiñcāpi ekameva dissati, tathāpi atthato dveyeva kammāni dissantīti gahetabbaṃ. Tathā hi brahmadatto rajjaṃ kāretīti ettha brahmadatto attano rājabhāvaṃ mahājanena kārayatīti attho. Evaṃ pana atthe gahite “rajjaṃ kārehi bhaddante, kiṃ araññe karissasī”tiādīsupi tvaṃ attano rājabhāvaṃ amhehi kārāpehi, attānaṃ rajje abhisiñcāpehi, mayaṃ taṃ rajje abhisiñcitukāmāti attho samatthito bhavati.

Here some might say: 'Sirs, surely only one object is seen here. How, then, is this usage a ditransitive one?' Although only one object is seen, it should be understood that in meaning two objects are perceived. For in 'Brahmadatta has the kingdom ruled,' the meaning is 'Brahmadatta causes his own kingship to be brought about by the populace.' When the meaning is grasped in this way, then in such passages as 'Venerable sir, have the kingdom ruled! What will you do in the forest?', the meaning is established as: 'You should have us establish your kingship; have yourself anointed in the kingdom; we wish to anoint you in the kingdom.'

Brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārenteti etthāpi brahmadatte attano rājabhāvaṃ mahājanena kārayanteti attho bhavati. Sāsanasmiñhi kāritavisaye karaṇavacanaṃ upayogatthaññeva dīpeti, tasmā atthato dveyeva kammani dissantīti vadāma. Ayamattho abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ cakkhundriyādinibbacanatthavibhāvanāya dīpetabbo. Tathā hi abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ “cakkhudvāre indattaṃ kāretīti cakkhudvārabhāve taṃdvārikehi attano indabhāvaṃ paramissarabhāvaṃ kārayatīti attho. Tañhi te rūpaggahaṇe attānaṃ anuvatteti, te ca taṃ anuvattantī”ti. Yadi pana karadhātu dvikammako, evaṃ sante “brahmadatto rajjaṃ kāretī”tiādīsu laddhakāritapaccayattā “kāretī”tiādīhi padehi tikammakehiyeva bhavitabbanti? Na, niyamābhāvato, tādisassa ca payogassa vohārapathe anāgatattā.

In the case of 'Brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente' (When Brahmadatta is causing the kingdom to be ruled), the meaning is that Brahmadatta causes his own state of kingship to be brought about by the great populace. For in the Dispensation, in the sphere of the causative, the instrumental case only indicates the meaning of connection. Therefore, we say that in terms of meaning, only two objects are seen. This meaning should be elucidated in the Abhidhamma Subcommentary in the explanation of the meaning of the definition of the eye-faculty and so forth. For in the Abhidhamma Subcommentary it is said: 'It causes the state of being a faculty in the eye-door' means that, in the state of being the eye-door, it causes its own state as a faculty, its supreme lordship, to be brought about by those things connected with that door. For it makes them follow itself in the grasping of forms, and they follow it. But if the root 'kara' is ditransitive, then in that case, in expressions like 'Brahmadatto rajjaṃ kāreti' (Brahmadatta causes the kingdom to be ruled), because the causative suffix has been obtained, should the words like 'kāreti' necessarily have three objects? No, because there is no fixed rule, and because such a usage has not come into the path of conventional speech.

Kaṭṭhaṃ purisena aṅgāraṃ kataṃ. Suvaṇṇaṃ kammārena kaṭakaṃ kataṃ, dāsī sāmikena adāsiṃ katā, evampettha dvikammakappayogā veditabbā. Suvaṇṇena kaṭakaṃ karotīti ettha [M 0.0389] hi visesanatthe pavattakaraṇavisayattā dvikammikabhāvo na labbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo aññatrāpi upaparikkhitvā yathāsambhavaṃ netabbo. Karotissa payogoyaṃ.

Wood was made into charcoal by a man. Gold was made into a bracelet by a goldsmith. A female slave was made a non-slave by her master. Thus, in these cases, usages with two objects should be understood. When saying 'he makes a bracelet with gold,' here, it should be noted that the state of having two objects is not obtained because it is the sphere of the instrument acting in the sense of a qualifier. This principle should be examined elsewhere and applied as far as possible. This is the usage of 'karoti'.

Vahiādīnaṃ payoge rājapurisā rathaṃ gāmaṃ vahanti. Ayaṃ rājā maṃ nāmaṃ pucchati. Parābhavantaṃ purisaṃ, mayaṃ pucchāma gotamaṃ. Āyasmā upāli āyasmatā mahākassapena vinayaṃ puṭṭho. Devadatto rājānaṃ kambalaṃ yācati. Te maṃ asse ayācisuṃ. Dhanaṃ taṃ tāta yācati. Brāhmaṇo nāgaṃ maṇiṃ yācati. Nāgo maṇiṃ yācito brāhmaṇena brahmunā āyācito dhammadesanaṃ bhagavā. Tāpaso kulaṃ bhojanaṃ bhikkhati. Ajaṃ gāmaṃ neti. Ajo gāmaṃ nīto. Mutto campeyyako nāgo, rājānaṃ etadabravi.

In the usage of verbs like ‘vahati’ (to carry): The king’s men carry the chariot to the village. This king asks me my name. We ask Gotama about the man who is declining.
